Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:09:00 UTC
21:09:00 KST

Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
September 10, 2026
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.
There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.
As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.
"Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.
"Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital.
Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low
Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.
Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.
Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.
That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.
Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.
"The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.
Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar
Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.
Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings.
Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.
Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.
Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed.
Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University.
Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.
With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.
Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston.
Japan willing to restore normal ties?
Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.
Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar.
"I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said.
Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.
Will the West reengage with Myanmar?
As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.
Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.
Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.
"But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said.
Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.
On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.
"I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now."

Primark expands Gulf footprint with first Saudi Arabia store
British-Irish budget fashion retailer Primark is set to expand across the Gulf with the launch of its first store in Saudi Arabia, following successful openings in Dubai and Kuwait.
Operating in partnership with Alshaya Group, the companies announced on Thursday that Primark will open its first-ever Saudi Arabian store at The Avenues in Riyadh in March 2027.
In a statement, Alshaya Group CEO John Hadden said the company was "incredibly proud" to be opening in Saudi Arabia, confirming there would be "more stores to follow in the Kingdom".
Ahead of its Saudi launch, Primark is due to open its first store in Bahrain at City Centre Bahrain on 23 September, followed by its first Qatar store at Doha Festival City on 29 October.
Primark's interim CEO Eoin Tonge said the retailer's reception in Kuwait had been "amazing", adding that it demonstrated "the potential of our brand in the Middle East".
"Today is an exciting moment for us and our growth ambitions, as we move forward with plans to reach 21 countries," Tonge added.
The latest expansion builds on Primark's existing presence in Kuwait and its three-store rollout in the UAE.
Like other major fast-fashion retailers, Primark has faced criticism from labour rights and environmental campaigners over its low-cost, high-volume business model.
Many have raised concerns over wages and working conditions within garment supply chains, pressure on suppliers and the environmental impact of mass-produced inexpensive clothing.
Primark says its low prices are made possible through its scale, efficient buying and low operating costs rather than compromising ethical or quality standards. The company has introduced ethical-trade and sustainability programmes, including commitments on more sustainable materials, product durability and reducing its environmental impact.
The retailer opened its first three UAE stores earlier this year at Dubai Mall, City Centre Mirdif and Mall of the Emirates in Dubai, following its regional debut in Kuwait last October.

Gaza's hospitals and homes struggle to keep generators running as oil shortages bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:07:30 UTC
21:07:30 KST

Gaza's hospitals and homes struggle to keep generators running as oil shortages bite
CAIRO/GAZA, Sept 10 - As power cuts cascade through one of Gaza's largest functioning hospitals and patients wait for treatment in sweltering wards, medics warn that shortages of engine oil and spare parts are causing generators to seize up, putting lives at risk.
The crisis is spreading beyond hospitals, where soaring costs for oil and diesel are making electricity from neighbourhood generators increasingly unaffordable for families that depend on it.
Gaza has been without grid electricity since the start of Israel's military offensive in the territory, launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Israel halted electricity supply and restricted the import of fuel as well as engine oil, describing them as measures to punish Hamas.
Those restrictions have continued despite an October 2025 U.S.-brokered ceasefire that brought an end to full-scale fighting but has failed to halt Israeli attacks, secure Hamas' disarmament or relieve Gaza's humanitarian and energy crises.
Ahmed Al-Nabris, an internal medicine specialist at Nasser Hospital, said shortages of fuel, engine oil and spare parts had forced the hospital into an austerity plan that includes rotating power cuts between buildings.
"Patients are in severe danger, because any power cut puts their lives at serious risk," said Nabris.
One of the hospital's four generators is now out of service, and the largest two of the remaining three are under strain, he said. Normally, engine oil in generators should be changed every 250 operating hours, but shortages have forced technicians to extend that interval to around 1,000 hours.
Al-Nabris said the hospital's electrical system had suffered repeated damage since an Israeli military raid in early 2024. A solar energy system was destroyed and never replaced, while both a main and backup generator were lost. Israel has accused Palestinian militants of using Gaza hospitals as bases.
DWINDLING SUPPLIES
Fatima Abu Taima, a patient at Nasser Hospital who suffers from pulmonary fibrosis, says those needing to be hooked to a ventilator or nebulizer have to wait as electricity is rotated among departments.
"We keep waiting, counting down the seconds and minutes," she said. "You have to wait for the electricity to come back."
The mother of four said her condition had worsened since the outbreak of war in 2023, forcing her to move into the hospital.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement in August that thousands face greater risks of illness and death because restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts are undermining hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps and water trucks.
Dwindling supplies had forced humanitarian groups to turn to the local market, it said, where locals say prices have surged to $1,300 per litre from about $3 before the war.
Israel's COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, said in a statement that a mechanism coordinated with the international community facilitates the entry of engine oil, generator spare parts, ambulances and other hospital equipment into Gaza under monitoring and oversight.
COGAT said that mechanism is "aimed at preventing advanced equipment from falling into the hands of Hamas and ensuring that such equipment reaches the population directly".
COST OF HOME ELECTRICITY HAS SOARED, RESIDENTS SAY
Beyond hospitals, the shortage has hit Gaza's network of private and neighbourhood generators that provide homes with a few hours of electricity a day.
Palestinian and U.N. records showed earlier this year that at least two-thirds of Gaza's population of about 2 million were still living in more than 1,000 displacement sites across the territory, with severe shortages of water and electricity. Residents say only a tiny portion can afford to pay for private generators.
Yasser Ashour, who sells electricity from generators he owns, said that despite the pressing need for steady power supplies — especially for those with medical conditions or serious injuries — staying in business has become increasingly difficult as prices for engine oil, diesel and spare parts have soared.
The shortages have driven up the cost of electricity supplies to homes around 20-fold in the past months, residents said. Still, many have little choice but to pay.
Alaa Al-Hourani, 65, who suffers from liver fibrosis and low oxygen levels, said his struggles to secure costly food and water sometimes left him unable to afford electricity.
"It is suffocating and agonizing, but there is nothing we can do. We have nothing but cardboard to fan ourselves," he said. REUTERS

UMCC plans to draw about $70 mln from NEQSOL Holding over two years if regulatory environment improves
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:05:26 EEST
21:05:26 KST

Operating and capital investment at United Mining and Chemical Company (UMCC, UMCC Titanium) has exceeded UAH 2 billion since its privatization in October 2024, and a two-year investment plan agreed with the supervisory board envisages drawing about $70 million more from owner NEQSOL Holding B.V.
Implementation of this investment plan, which would allow UMCC to reach breakeven by 2028, depends on decisions to lift export controls on rutile and zirconium concentrates, company management told journalists.
Rishad Aliyev, NEQSOL Holding B.V.'s head of investor relations and UMCC's first deputy general director, said the company increased production this year after privatization and operational stabilization last year: output in the first half of 2026 exceeded 84% of the company's entire 2025 output, and it managed to win back customers in the U.S., Mexico and EU countries.
However, the company faces a number of challenges affecting its operations, particularly export restrictions: it currently cannot fully sell its main products, which account for about 50% of gross value, on external markets, referring to restrictions on rutile and zircon exports introduced after privatization.
UMCC lost out on about $35 million in foreign currency revenue since privatization was completed due to its inability to sell its products, according to Aliyev.
"The company could have earned this money and invested it both in modernizing production and increasing output volumes," he said.
Lifting restrictions on the sale of rutile and zircon concentrate would also positively affect NEQSOL Holding's ability to participate in the auction for the sale of the Demurinsky mining and processing plant (Dnipropetrovsk region), scheduled by the State Property Fund for Oct 20, since there is currently no final decision on the matter, Aliyev said.
State Property Fund head Dmytro Nataluha, for his part, said the introduction of new forms of control over the company's products after privatization negatively affects its investment appeal, since the investor purchased it under different conditions.
The fund said it is ready to work together with business and relevant state bodies to find balanced solutions to the issue.
UMCC also faces logistics difficulties exporting products from its Vilnohirsk mining and metallurgical plant (VMMP) to the U.S. Due to shelling and problems with the Odesa route, the company is considering alternative shipping routes by rail to Romania or Poland, with subsequent loading onto vessels. The company spends millions of dollars a year on such shipments, according to UMCC operations director Valeriy Zakharenko.
"So this is a big problem for us. Doubling the cost of transporting one tonne of product, for example, reduces our margin to zero," Zakharenko said.
Other factors affecting the company's operations cited included a shortage of workers, proximity to the front line, and electricity costs.
UMCC CEO Dimitri Kalandadze said the company currently needs to stabilize production and reach planned capacity, carry out modernization, and subsequently move from exporting raw materials to deeper processing and producing higher value-added products in Ukraine.
The company plans to soon begin extracting raw materials at the "Phase II" section of the Yurske deposit in Zhytomyr region, while three quarries are currently operating at "Phase I," according to the operations director. The company is also considering the Bukynske site as another prospective extraction area.
As previously reported, UMCC's net loss grew 2.5-fold year-on-year in January-June this year, to UAH 745.4 million, while revenue for the period rose 34.8% to UAH 1.1171 billion.
UMCC posted a net loss of UAH 2.1182 billion in 2025, compared with a net profit of UAH 17.1 million a year earlier, while its revenue fell 47% to UAH 1.5108 billion.
"The 2025 financial results were negative, a loss, but this was largely due to the company's transition to international financial accounting standards, and to writing off liabilities that were on the company's books," Aliyev explained.
In October 2024, Tsemin Ukraine LLC, part of the NEQSOL Holding group, acquired UMCC at a privatization auction for nearly UAH 4 billion. After completing the necessary regulatory procedures, the company officially passed into the new investor's ownership in June 2025. UMCC has since operated as part of the international NEQSOL Holding group, which has businesses in several countries and industries.
UMCC has two branches — the Vilnohirsk mining and metallurgical plant (VMMP, Dnipropetrovsk region) and the Irshansk mining and processing plant (IMPP, Zhytomyr region). UMCC's core business is open-pit titanium ore mining, along with the production and wholesale trade of titanium ore concentrates (zircon, ilmenite, rutile, kyanite-sillimanite, staurolite and quartz sand).

Gallery: Mythbústers' comics exhibition opens at Estonian Academy of Arts
The Estonian Academy of Arts (EKA) in Tallinn has opened "Mythbústers," a Nordic‑Baltic comics exhibition featuring works by 16 artists reflecting their perspectives on life in the region.
The works on display were originally published in a Latvian comic book magazine at the end of last year. The exhibition has since toured various countries, and at the end of September the works will move on from EKA to Helsinki.
According to participating artist Liisa Kruusmägi, comic books and strips are well suited to the exhibition format, as this gives people who do not normally read comic books a chance to become acquainted with the medium. She is also optimistic about Estonia's comic book scene.
"We have the famous Joonas Sildre, who has published a lot and whose work is also translated, with English‑language editions available in bookshops, but of course there could be more," Kruusmägi said.
She encouraged more people to try their hand at the genre. "I encourage people to make comics, and EKA has had comic book courses and similar things over the years, so I hope it develops somehow," she said.
Kruusmägi added that she does relatively little with comics herself. "I've contributed to that comics magazine a few times and published a little on my own. I would also like to publish a graphic novel myself, but for me it is difficult because it also requires good writing skills," she added.
The exhibition is open in the foyer at EKA at Põhja pst 7 until the end of the month.

Tight Israeli election: Netanyahu is trying to not lose votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:02:48 UTC
21:02:48 KST

Breadcrumb
A tight Israeli election: Netanyahu is desperately trying to not lose votes
General trends in opinion polls published in recent days indicate that the electoral contest in Israel remains tight and that the gap between the two blocs could ultimately be decided by just two or three seats, following the closure of Israel's electoral lists on Tuesday evening, 8 September.
According to recent opinion polls, the current governing coalition is expected to win around 52 seats out of 120, while the opposition bloc is projected to secure between 53 and 55 seats, with Arab parties winning around 13 seats.
The opposition bloc is seeking to raise its tally to around 56-57 seats, bringing it closer to the possibility of forming a government without relying heavily on Arab parties.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu aims to keep the opposition below the 55-seat threshold, based on the assessment that any alternative government would then need, in one way or another, the support of at least one Arab list, even if that support were limited to abstaining from a confidence vote.
The Netanyahu camp is betting that a minority government based on 55 or 56 Knesset members and requiring external Arab support would face sustained political and public pressure and attempts to delegitimise it. This could shorten its lifespan and weaken its ability to govern.
Israeli electoral lists
Under these circumstances, the shape and order of Israeli electoral lists, as well as the inclusion of new figures with public or political weight, have assumed an importance that goes beyond the parties' internal calculations.
They could directly affect each camp's ability to tip the balance in an election that appears extremely close.
This explains the rush by Israeli parties in recent days, ahead of submitting their lists to the Central Elections Committee, to reshuffle their ranks and complete their alliances.
Within the opposition camp, the days before the submission of Israel's electoral lists saw intensive efforts to rearrange the internal contest and settle two central questions: which party would be the largest in the bloc, and who would lead it in the race for the premiership?
The most prominent development was the completion of the alliance between Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid under the "Together" list, whose final composition was announced last Sunday, 6 Sep.
Lapid retained about 40% of the positions on the joint list, while the leading positions included administrative and security figures.
The formation of the Bennett-Lapid alliance was accompanied by high expectations that it could become the central force in the opposition camp and that Bennett could emerge as the leading candidate for prime minister.
However, these expectations were not realised.
The alliance failed to secure leadership of the bloc and remained at around 12-13 seats in most opinion polls.
The alliance created direct competition within the opposition camp, particularly with the "Yashar" party led by Gadi Eisenkot, who moved within a short period from a relatively secondary political position in the 2022 election to the strongest candidate in the bloc for prime minister and to leading the largest party in it, according to recent opinion polls, which give it around 24-25 seats.
This rise is particularly significant because "Yashar" remains a new party, lacking an established party structure, broad grassroots support, branches and organisational cadres comparable to those of established parties.
Its list also does not yet include a large number of well-known political figures.
Eisenkot therefore sought in the days before the lists were submitted to strengthen his list with political, security and administrative figures who have a public profile and relative acceptance within Israeli society, with the aim of consolidating his momentum in the polls and preventing a decline after the final composition of the list was revealed.
In this context, Hili Tropper, who defected from Blue and White, led by former defence minister Benny Gantz, joined him last Sunday after the collapse of the partnership he had formed with Yoaz Hendel.
Tropper was placed sixth on the "Yashar" list.
The move reflects Eisenkot's attempt to broaden the party's image from a list centred mainly on him into a wider political framework capable of competing not only for centrist votes but also for leadership of the opposition camp.
At this stage, Eisenkot is trying to prevent the race for leadership of the opposition camp from becoming an open contest, not only with the "Together" alliance but also with the Yisrael Beiteinu party led by Avigdor Lieberman.
Yisrael Beiteinu is one of the main representatives of the secular nationalist right in the Israeli party map.
Historically, it has relied on a broad electoral base among immigrants from the former Soviet Union while making continued efforts to expand its presence among other sections of Israeli society.
When presenting his electoral list, Lieberman announced that he considered himself a candidate for prime minister.
However, this ambition does not, so far, correspond with the electoral strength given to him by opinion polls, with his party receiving only around eight seats in most polls published in recent days.
Nevertheless, his declaration of candidacy reflects the multiple centres of power within the opposition camp and confirms that the camp has not yet settled on the identity of the candidate who will lead it against Netanyahu.
Thus, the days before the submission of the lists in Israel were decisive for opposition parties, which were occupied with trying to organise the internal contest, consolidate the positions of parties and candidates, and divide shares within the bloc.
So far, these moves have not reduced the opposition's overall strength, which has remained stable at around 54-55 seats in most recent polls.
However, they have also failed to raise its expected representation.
The Democrats party, led by Yair Golan, concluded its internal elections last July.
Most of its prominent lawmakers retained leading positions on the list, alongside the inclusion of figures associated with protest movements against the Netanyahu government.
Unlike the centrist parties, the party is not currently fighting for survival or negotiating a merger. Instead, it appears more stable organisationally and politically.
The party has so far enjoyed a clear degree of internal cohesion, which spared it the need for emergency arrangements in the final hours before the lists were submitted.
Indeed, the party had begun its election campaign some time ago, benefiting from the stability of its position in opinion polls and the clarity of its political identity compared with other parties in the opposition camp.
In the coalition camp, Netanyahu worked on two parallel tracks.
The first was to try to reduce the risk of wasting right-wing votes by pushing for mergers or understandings between smaller parties that might fail to cross the electoral threshold.
The second was to complete the Likud list and add figures from outside the party who could help broaden its support base and improve its electoral share.
The contest over the ordering of the lists has thus become a key part of the struggle for every seat, rather than merely an organisational stage preceding the election.
The Likud list was not closed until hours before the closure of Israel's electoral lists, as Netanyahu retained several positions in which he is entitled to directly appoint candidates, known within the party as "reserved positions".
Netanyahu has already used this authority to secure Defence Minister Israel Katz fourth place and Foreign Minister Gideon Saar fifth place.
In the final hours before the lists were submitted, he continued working to bring in figures with a public profile and broad popularity in an attempt to increase the appeal of the Likud list and broaden its electoral base, which could help the party improve its share in the upcoming election.
However, Netanyahu's most serious problem does not come from within Likud itself but from the parties to its right, particularly far-right parties.
Foremost among them are Religious Zionism, led by Bezalel Smotrich, and Jewish Power, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Ben-Gvir refused to contest the election on a joint technical list with Religious Zionism, preferring to run independently in an attempt to consolidate his position as the leading far-right leader in Israel.
Netanyahu's concern was heightened by the emergence of a new far-right party, "Amkha Yisrael", led by Ofer Winter, a former Israeli army commander and one of the figures associated with the hardline religious Zionist current.
The presence of multiple lists in this camp means that some right-wing votes could be distributed among small parties hovering around the electoral threshold, increasing the risk of wasting votes that could prove decisive in a closely fought contest to form the next government.
Winter is Netanyahu's problem
Smotrich, whose party had remained around the electoral threshold in a large number of polls in recent months, succeeded in reaching an agreement with Moshe Feiglin and the far-right "Zehut" party to contest the election on a joint list.
Recent opinion polls indicate that the merger achieved its main objective, with the alliance now clearing the electoral threshold and winning around five or six seats.
As for Itamar Ben-Gvir, he preferred to contest the election on an independent list as part of his effort to consolidate his position as the leading far-right leader.
In this context, he worked to strengthen the Jewish Power list by bringing in Knesset member Tali Gottlieb, who moved from Likud, and placing her second on the list.
Opinion polls give the party around seven or eight seats, allowing Ben-Gvir, unlike in his previous attempts, to contest the election from a more secure electoral position.
Meanwhile, former general Ofer Winter insisted on contesting the election independently and submitted his electoral list last Monday, despite pressure from Netanyahu to push him to join the alliance between Smotrich and Feiglin.
Winter's party currently receives around four seats in opinion polls, putting it close to the danger zone around the electoral threshold.
Winter's decision to keep his list independent is therefore a source of concern for Netanyahu, because even a limited decline in its popularity could lead to the loss of a bloc of right-wing votes and seats.
Netanyahu's problem is therefore not distributed equally among the components of the far right.
Ben-Gvir is now relatively far from the danger of falling below the electoral threshold, while the Smotrich-Feiglin alliance has improved Religious Zionism's chances of crossing it.
By contrast, Ofer Winter's party remains the most vulnerable link and the greatest source of concern for Netanyahu, because even a limited decline in its popularity could lead to the loss of right-wing votes that his camp urgently needs in a contest that could be decided by one or two seats.

Australian study finds low PFAS levels in rainwater
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:02:38 CST
21:02:38 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- An Australian study has found low levels of PFAS, or "forever chemicals," in rainwater collected in Melbourne, with concentrations of two well-known compounds below current drinking water guideline values.
Researchers from Australia's RMIT University and the Environment Protection Authority Victoria detected eight of 30 PFAS compounds tested in rainwater samples collected on three occasions between 2024 and 2025, according to a statement released by RMIT on Thursday.
"In our samples, concentrations of the two most well-known PFAS -- PFOS and PFOA -- were below current Australian drinking water guideline values, which should provide some reassurance for people who use rainwater as a source of drinking water," said lead researcher Professor Oliver Jones from RMIT's School of Science.
Based on the concentrations measured, researchers estimated rainfall could deliver about 10.6 kg of PFAS to Port Phillip Bay in the state of Victoria each year, equivalent to about 5.5 grams per square kilometer.
PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a large family of human-made chemicals used in products including firefighting foams, food packaging, textiles, cosmetics and non-stick cookware. PFAS can travel long distances in the atmosphere on dust particles or tiny water droplets before returning to the environment through rain, the researchers said.
The estimate suggests rainfall could be an important pathway for PFAS entering waterways, alongside wastewater, urban runoff and landfill. The researchers hope the findings will support broader monitoring of PFAS in Australian rainfall and improve understanding of how these chemicals move through the environment.
The findings, published in Environmental Chemistry and Toxicology, also found that rain linked to air traveling over land had higher PFAS concentrations than rain linked to air traveling over the ocean, suggesting urban and industrial areas may be important sources of airborne PFAS deposited elsewhere through rainfall. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Crimes of Japan's "poison gas island" must not be concealed - A visit to Okunoshima
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:01:56 CST
21:01:56 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Okunoshima, a small island covering only about 0.7 square kilometers in the Seto Inland Sea of Japan, is known today as "rabbit island" for the wild rabbits roaming across it, attracting tourists from Japan and abroad.
But during wartime, the island was a major hub operated by the Imperial Japanese Army to manufacture poison gas, where chemical warfare agents were produced and used to inflict suffering on countless innocent people. It was, in reality, a "poison gas island."
Recently, Xinhua reporters visited Okunoshima together with members of Japanese civic groups dedicated to historical research, Japanese students, and Chinese students studying in Japan.
Japan established a comprehensive system for chemical warfare during the war. The facility on Okunoshima produced poison gas; the Sone Manufacturing Plant in Kyushu was responsible for filling chemical agents into shells; the Narashino Army School in Chiba Prefecture trained personnel for chemical warfare.
Japan's production and use of chemical weapons violated the Geneva Protocol. To conceal its activities, the Japanese military kept the construction and operation of the poison gas facility on Okunoshima secret throughout the war.
According to the Okunoshima Poison Gas Museum, the island was under round-the-clock security. On trains traveling along the coast opposite the island, windows facing the sea had to be covered. At one point, Okunoshima was even removed from maps.
Akio Kusumoto, a member of the Japanese civic group engaged in passing on atomic bomb experiences, said the island produced various types of poison gas, including the vomiting agent "Red No. 1," blister agents "Yellow No. 1" and "Yellow No. 2," and the lethal agent "Brown No. 1."
"It is said that the poison gas produced there enveloped the entire island like air pollution, with toxic substances settling downward. According to testimonies, the gas filled the air, and the ground appeared to be covered in a white fog," said Shizuyo Yamauchi, head of the Japanese civic group Poison Gas Island Historical Research Institute.
Most of the poison gas produced on Okunoshima was transported to China and used on battlefields, causing large numbers of casualties among Chinese military personnel and civilians. Some chemical shells were abandoned in China, where they have continued to pose a threat to local residents.
"Starting a war is itself an act of aggression. In particular, on this island, they manufactured poison gas in violation of international treaties and used it on the battlefield," Yamauchi said.
"The abandoned chemical weapons are still taking Chinese lives, polluting the environment and threatening people's lives today. What a grave crime that is," she added.
Following Japan's surrender in 1945, the poison gas facility destroyed its stockpiles and burned relevant documents in an apparent effort to prevent the crimes from being exposed.
Today, the remaining ruins on the island still bear traces of Japan's efforts to cover up that history. At the site of the former Nagaura Poison Storehouse, vegetation has covered the ground and roof, but its darkened interior walls remain clearly visible.
Kusumoto said that when handling the poison gas after Japan's defeat, the military first pumped the gas out of storage tanks before removing the tanks. As toxic residues were believed to have remained on the walls, flamethrowers were reportedly used to burn them.
Even today, 81 years later, the history of the "poison gas island" remains little known in Japan.
Taichi Koseki, a student from Kansai Gaidai University who joined the visit, said it was his first time learning about the island's history. "I knew about the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, but I had no idea that there had been a poison gas factory on this island in the same prefecture," he said.
In contrast, Okunoshima has been widely promoted as "rabbit island" and a tourist destination.
Japanese photojournalist Kenji Higuchi said that, ultimately, the Japanese government wants to remove the label of "poison gas island" and does not want people to remember what happened there.
Asami Ogura, an associate professor at National Institute of Technology, Kure College, said this history is now hardly taught in Japanese schools.
Japanese people should learn about the fact that Japan once manufactured poison gas and caused extremely serious harm to China, Ogura said, adding that she would share what she had seen and learned on the island with her students.
Kusumoto said that many people remain unaware of this history of perpetration; to ensure this history is not erased and to prevent such a tragedy from repeating itself, these historical facts should be fully conveyed to the public. ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Army buys Scorpion Light mortar systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:00:58 UTC
21:00:58 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Global Military Products a $12.9 million contract on September 3, 2026, to integrate Scorpion Light 81mm mortars onto Infantry Squad Vehicle-Utility platforms.
- Soldiers fired 20 rounds from two Scorpion Light systems in under two minutes during Exercise Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines.
The U.S. Army has awarded Global Military Products a $12.9 million contract to integrate its Scorpion Light 81mm mobile mortar system onto the Army’s Infantry Squad Vehicle-Utility platforms.
The company announced the award on September 3, 2026, under the Department of Defense Ordnance Technology Consortium’s Other Transaction Authority framework.
The deal covers pairing the Tampa-based company’s mortar system with Army digital fire control technology and government-furnished M253 mortar barrels, mounted on the ISV-U, a lighter, faster variant of the Army’s new troop-carrying vehicle. Each ISV-U can carry a Scorpion Light system and 72 mortar rounds, according to earlier Army testing of the platform.
The Army’s 2nd Battalion, 35th Infantry Regiment tested Scorpion Light at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii, in October 2025 as part of the Transformation in Contact 2.0 program, an effort that puts experimental gear in soldiers’ hands ahead of wider fielding decisions. During that trial, Global Military Products said the system could fire eight rounds and relocate in under two minutes, with roughly 30 seconds needed to fire the first round and another 30 seconds to displace after the last.
Soldiers from the same battalion, assigned to the Multi-Purpose Company, 2nd Battalion, 35th Infantry Regiment, 25th Infantry Division, took the ISV-mounted system into Exercise Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines. There, soldiers fired 20 rounds from two Scorpion Light systems in under two minutes during live-fire operations, according to Global Military Products.
“The enhanced capabilities provided by the next-generation Scorpion mobile mortar system directly support the Army’s Transformation Initiative and its transition toward smaller, more agile and highly lethal combat formations prepared to address emerging threats in complex operational environments,” said James Knight, Director of Business Development, Global Military Products. “We worked closely with Army stakeholders and soldiers to continuously evaluate, iterate and refine the Scorpion platform based on operational feedback. This contract award reflects the success of that collaboration and our commitment to delivering a fully integrated mobile mortar capability that increases lethality, improves operator safety, and provides unmatched tactical mobility for the warfighter.”
The system’s fire control setup links to the Army’s Nett Warrior networked communications gear, letting a crew hand off targets between systems and process fire missions digitally rather than working the numbers by hand. Global Military Products has said the mortar can also fire from a special baseplate on nearly any surface and can take guidance from third-party targeting systems.
Global Military Products and the Army developed Scorpion Light over roughly two years through the Soldier Enhancement Program and a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement, using direct feedback from troops in the field. The company has not disclosed how many Scorpion Light systems the new contract will deliver or a timeline for fielding beyond the current round of testing and integration work.

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks heightened US fears of threats from abroad, Americans are now considerably more worried about attacks by domestic extremists than foreign groups, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The poll also found Americans are split on whether the country is safer than before 9/11. Some 36% said the US is about as safe as it was before the attacks, while 32% said it is safer and 29% said it is less safe.
On September 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked by reported Al-Qaeda members, who crashed them into New York City’s World Trade Center and the Pentagon outside Washington, DC, killing 2,977 people.
The attacks sparked decades of violence as part of the US’s so-called “War on Terror”, including US-led invasions of both Afghanistan and Iraq, and related conflicts that killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, as well as many troops.

Psilocybin prevents chemotherapy-induced nerve damage in new preclinical study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

Recent research suggests that giving mice a compound found in magic mushrooms before chemotherapy can prevent the debilitating nerve damage that often accompanies cancer treatment. The findings indicate that psilocybin protects nerve fibers by keeping their cellular powerhouses moving and functioning properly. The study was published in Science.
Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy is a condition where cancer drugs damage the long sensory nerves that extend from the spinal cord to the hands and feet. This damage leads to pain, numbness, and an extreme sensitivity to cold. Because the condition can be severe and long-lasting, doctors often have to reduce a patient’s chemotherapy dose or stop the treatment entirely.
“Almost everyone who gets any of the most common cancer chemotherapies for all the most common cancers will develop peripheral neuropathy that can be experienced as mild numbness, tingling, to pins and needles or to most severe as continuous burning sensations,” said study co-author Patrick M. Dougherty, a professor of pain medicine research at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
“This is in spite of the fact that none of these cancer drugs are given at the maximum dose to kill cancer cells, but at lesser doses to avoid neurotoxicity,” he told PsyPost. “While many patients will improve over time, others suffer this negative impact for years.”
Medical scientists have worked to understand exactly how these drugs harm the nerves. For example, a 2014 review established that chemotherapy agents tend to damage mitochondria, the small structures inside cells that generate energy. These energy factories are especially important for sensory nerves, which require a constant supply of power along their extensive, thread-like extensions, called axons.
Subsequent work, such as a 2024 study, demonstrated that keeping mitochondria moving along these nerve fibers helps shield them from the physical degeneration caused by chemotherapy. In a parallel area of study, a 2018 study provided evidence that psychedelic compounds can stimulate specific growth pathways to rebuild and protect nerve connections.
The authors of the new study connected these pieces of evidence. Psilocybin, the active ingredient in certain mushroom species, activates a specific receptor on the surface of cells known as the serotonin 2A receptor. Because this receptor is involved in both nerve adaptability and mitochondrial regulation, the scientists hypothesized that administering psilocybin before chemotherapy might trigger a protective rescue mechanism, preventing the nerve damage before it begins.
“Interventions for pre-established neuropathy have not worked out, so the goal here was to find a way to protect the nervous system to keep neuropathy from ever developing,” Dougherty explained.
“There is an urgent need for treatments that prevent nerve injury without interfering with lifesaving chemotherapy,” added study co-leader Moran Amit, an assistant professor of head and neck surgery at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. “These findings offer important insights into how psilocybin may protect nerves before damage occurs, rather than treating symptoms after they become persistent.”
The research, co-led by Dougherty and Amit, utilized a combination of mouse behavioral models and human tissue analysis. To test their hypothesis, the scientists gave mice two doses of psilocybin before administering common chemotherapy drugs, such as cisplatin and paclitaxel. They then subjected the mice to up to six cycles of chemotherapy, mimicking a clinical treatment schedule.
To measure nerve damage, the researchers tested the animals’ responses to physical pressure and cold temperatures over the course of eight months. The team also used mice with oral tumors to check if psilocybin interfered with the chemotherapy’s ability to shrink the cancer.
In addition to the animal models, the researchers examined human sensory neurons grown in the lab. They also looked at fresh peripheral nerve tissue taken from 29 human surgical patients. Using advanced live-cell imaging, they watched how mitochondria moved inside these human nerve fibers when exposed to chemotherapy with and without psilocybin.
The scientists found that just two preventive doses of psilocybin kept the mice from developing the physical hypersensitivity and cold sensitivity typically caused by the chemotherapy drugs. The mice maintained normal baseline sensitivity scores, and this protective effect lasted across all six cycles of treatment and throughout the eight-month follow-up period.
Notably, psilocybin did not reduce the cancer-killing effectiveness of the chemotherapy. The tumor-bearing mice that received psilocybin showed the same reduction in tumor size as those that only received chemotherapy. Systemic immune markers also remained unchanged, suggesting the treatment targets the nerves without altering the body’s general response to cancer.
The team discovered that psilocybin operates through two distinct pathways to achieve this protection. In the brain, it helped normalize electrical activity that is typically disrupted by chronic pain. In the peripheral body, it directly protected the structure and function of the sensory nerve endings in the skin.
When looking closely at the nerve cells, the researchers noticed that chemotherapy ordinarily causes mitochondria to stall, halting their journey down the long nerve axons. This starvation of energy at the distant nerve endings leads to their structural decay. Psilocybin prevented this traffic jam.
By activating the serotonin 2A receptor, psilocybin engaged a specific signaling chain that controls the molecular motors responsible for transporting mitochondria. By keeping the mitochondria moving, psilocybin ensured the nerve endings received the energy they needed to survive the toxic stress of the chemotherapy.
“Psilocybin does more than reduce pain signals by protecting the nerves themselves through energy delivery,” Dougherty noted. “This neuroprotective effect could help patients withstand the stress of chemotherapy, maintaining sensation, mobility and quality of life during treatment and long into survivorship.”
The researchers also found that the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin were not strictly necessary for this nerve protection. When they treated mice with a nonhallucinogenic compound that targets the exact same serotonin 2A receptors, the animals received an equivalent level of protection against the nerve damage.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that a single dose of psilocybin reduced neuropathic pain sensitivity in mice. It is worth noting that the older study evaluated treating established pain via central brain remodeling, whereas the new study evaluated preventing the pain prophylactically by preserving peripheral nerve function. Another study covered by PsyPost later in 2026 similarly demonstrated psilocybin’s ability to calm pain networks in rodents, again focusing on existing central pain rather than preventing peripheral damage.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relies heavily on mouse models and isolated human tissues. Laboratory tests on human nerve cells provided promising outcomes, but clinical trials involving human patients are needed to see if the preventive treatment works safely and effectively in a real-world medical setting.
“The study offers an interesting mechanistic and preclinical rationale for investigating psilocybin in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, particularly through its potential effects on mitochondrial trafficking and neuronal resilience,” said Andres Ort, a physician and member of the Neurophenomenology of Consciousness Lab at the University of Zurich who was not involved in the research.
“However, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence that psilocybin prevents or treats chemotherapy-induced neuropathy in patients,” Ort told PsyPost. “The translational gap between experimental models and clinical oncology remains substantial, and questions around dosing, timing, safety, drug interactions, psychiatric screening, blinding, and meaningful patient-centered outcomes will need careful evaluation.”
“The prospect of self-medication would be best avoided,” Dougherty cautioned. “If the work is validated, access to psilocybin would come to be available through your oncologist.”
It is also important to note that the timing of the treatment appears strict. The study indicates that psilocybin only works as a preventive measure in this context. When the researchers tried administering chemotherapy first and waiting for the nerve damage to set in, the psilocybin did not reverse the injury. Patients would likely need to receive the compound before every cycle of chemotherapy to maintain the protective effect.
Despite these constraints, the researchers are optimistic about the drug’s clinical potential. “The results of this study are very promising and have opened a new angle for potential therapeutic intervention in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy,” Dougherty said.
The team is already moving forward with an upcoming Phase 2 clinical trial, called NeuroGuard, to evaluate psilocybin during chemotherapy in patients with multiple cancer types. “A clinical trial will be opening soon for patients receiving cisplatin, but other chemotherapies will now also need to be tested to determine whether psilocybin may protect from their neurotoxicities,” Dougherty added.
“The most important next step is a well-designed, adequately powered clinical trial assessing not only neuropathy symptoms, but also function, quality of life, cancer-treatment adherence, and safety in the relevant oncology population,” Ort noted.
“If this work holds up, it may be a therapy integrated to all cancers,” Dougherty explained. “This would impact the approximately 2,000,000 new cancer cases expected in 2026, based on 2025 numbers in just the US.”
This work is part of UT MD Anderson’s Cancer Neuroscience Program, which examines the interactions between cancer and the nervous system. “At UT MD Anderson, we are actively exploring the multiple facets of psychedelics to pursue interventions that improve the lives of our patients,” Amit concluded.
The study, “Psilocybin prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy through mitochondrial trafficking preservation,” was authored by Mario Heles, Lilach Pasvolsky, Hinduja Sathishkumar, Shorook Naara, Yen Vu, Caitlyn L. Stewart, Tongxin Xie, Frederico O. Gleber-Netto, William McCarthy, Dan Yaniv, Shashank S. Kamal, Hajira Elahi, Pengyu Zhu, Megan L. Uhelski, Jordan Chatwin, Andrew Lara, Danielle L. Stolley, Michael R. Migden, Z-Hye Lee, Shiyanth Thevasagayampillai, Preethi H. Gunaratne, Kaoutar Ait-Ahmad, M. J. Kuykendall, Sebnem Ece Eksi, Lorenzo Cohen, Jeremy C. Borniger, Eyal Gottlieb, Gregory H. Jones, Patrick M. Dougherty, and Moran Amit.

How to choose the perfect wine for aperitivo hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:00:36 UTC
21:00:36 KST

Beginnings are important. As a writer, I’m all too aware of this: from the right introduction, the rest tends to flow. The same logic applies to drinks: a good beginning eases proceedings. For this reason, I am unbendingly particular about how I take my morning coffee and, if I’m drinking, what form an evening’s aperitif should take. Life’s too short for bad beverages, after all.
An aperitif is arguably less a specific drink than an appetite-whetting moment with a glass of something. But what? Typically, when it comes to wine, an aperitif will be light and crisp, with any fruit character at the more green or citrussy end of the spectrum. Brioche-y sparkling wine, be that champagne, crémant or something English, and dry sherry such as fino and manzanilla, with their savoury notes, are traditional choices to ready your palate for food.
One of my favourite wine discoveries of the past year or so has been Bodegas Alvear in the Montilla-Moriles region of Andalusia, which produces wines made exclusively with pedro ximénez (PX), a grape famous for producing the darkest, stickiest sherries out there. Its Tres Miradas cuvée in today’s pick is a unique dry white wine made with old vine PX grown in chalky soils; it has a light sherry note thanks to being aged under a layer of natural yeast (flor), but it is both fresh and structured, making for the sort of high-impact aperitif I’m after.
Wines from maritime climates, particularly cooler ones, tend to be a safe bet, too, bringing the salinity and minerality I’m looking for to stimulate appetite. A txakoli from Spain’s Basque region, say, with punchy, citrus-apple notes and a touch of spritz to surprise the palate. Muscadet, made from the melon de bourgogne grape in the westernmost Loire, is another great, unsung white: crisp, affordable and a fine aperitif. Take a road trip along the northern French coast, and you’ll be spoiled for pre-dinner deals on a plate of oysters and a glass of this stuff. It’s often bottled sur lie – that is, with dead yeast cells that give the wine a rounder, almost bready flavour that works particularly well as an aperitif. Ocado has several available, with some for less than a tenner.
There is also a breed of aperitif wine that both readies you for a meal and sees you all the way through it. Muscadet and its southern French cousin picpoul de pinet do this, as do albariño and zesty bourgogne aligoté, which usually has that Burgundian butteriness that can be hard to leave behind. Pale rosé is also a classic aperitif choice, as happy on its own as with a plate of crudites or a bowl of peanuts. The Pink Flamingo rosé in my pick, made in Europe’s largest organic vineyard in the Camargue wetlands west of Marseille, has a coastal freshness that I’d happily enjoy before, during and after a meal. After all, endings are as important as beginnings.
Six wines that work brilliantly as aperitifs
Oliver Dubois Muscadet 2023/4 £10.50 (with “mix six”) Majestic, 12%. A straightforwardly crowd-pleasing muscadet: lean, green and a great price.
Pink Flamingo Organic Camargue Rosé £12.50 Waitrose, 12%. You’ll never want aperitif hour to end, nor does it have to. This peachy-pink, daisy-fresh number is food friendly, too.
Rezabal Txakoli 2025 £13.50 The Wine Society, 11%. Make your aperitif a Basque one with this energetic and petillant txakoli.
Alvear Tres Miradas 2022 £17.50 The Whisky Exchange, ?13%. Green orchard fruit meets almonds and sourdough.
Fortnum’s Muscadet Sur Lie Domaine de la Morinière £12.95, 11.5%. A lovely example of a muscadet aged on the lees. Lemony, saline and richly textured.
Crémant de Loire, Domaine Catherine et Pierre Breton NV £23.40 Sip Wines, 13%. Possibly the perfect crémant, combining 40% red grapes with chenin blanc for a fizz that’s as generous as it’s refreshing.

US-Israel strikes against Iran have systematically undermined human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

US-Israel strikes against Iran have systematically undermined human rights
In February 2026, the US and Israel launched large-scale joint military strikes against Iran. This blatant military operation, conducted without authorization from the UN Security Council, drew strong condemnation from the international community.
The fighting has ebbed and flowed, and negotiations have been fraught with setbacks. After more than half a year of conflict, reportedly over 3,750 Iranian civilians have been killed and more than 33,000 wounded; regional countries have also suffered collateral damage, and strategic corridors have been repeatedly blocked. UN Secretary-General António Guterres lamented that the war is inflicting immense human suffering.
One may well ask: How can the US - which has long styled itself as a "beacon of human rights" and frequently used human rights as a pretext to criticize other nations - so flagrantly trample on the human rights of the Iranian people? Here are some shocking facts.
Attacking civilians, killing women and children - violations of the right to life. Women and children are the most vulnerable in war, and they pay the heaviest price. UN data show that among Iranian civilian casualties, approximately 500 are women and over 2,500 are children. Just recently, a heavy bomb dropped by US forces on July 30 over a civilian residential area in southern Iran hit a family of five, instantly killing a couple and their two-year-old child. On the very day the US-Israel forces started their airstrikes, a missile struck a girls' elementary school, killing all 168 students - a tragedy that shocked the world.
Carrying out assassinations and attempting regime change - violations of the right to self-determination. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government. A nation's future and destiny can only be decided by that nation itself; bombs and threats can never replace the choice of the people. The US and Israel have carried out successive "decapitation" strikes against Iran's supreme leader and other senior political and military officials. This is a classic case of extrajudicial execution. Even UN human rights experts, who have long been critical of Iran's human rights record, have clearly stated that international law does not accept extrajudicial "justice," and have urged the US to respect the Iranian people's right to self-determination.
Destroying homes and turning people into refugees - violations of economic, social and cultural rights, and the right to development. According to reports, the US-Israel military operations have so far destroyed over 125,000 civilian facilities in Iran, including 339 hospitals, 857 schools and 32 universities. Since the latest escalation of the Middle East crisis, over 4.1 million people in countries such as Iran and Lebanon have become displaced, and about 117,000 have fled to other countries seeking asylum. War is tearing families apart and creating an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. Homes may be rebuilt, but lost lives, shattered childhoods, and missed educational opportunities cannot be recovered.
Poisoning the air and cutting off water supplies - violations of environmental and health rights. As multiple oil depots in Iran were hit and set ablaze, toxic pollutants were released into the air, even causing toxic rain in some places. This has led to breathing difficulties and illness or disability among local residents. In a separate incident, US forces struck a desalination plant on Qeshm Island, affecting the water supply to 30 villages. The World Health Organization has issued warnings that "black rain" and acid rain pose a real danger to the Iranian people. The environmental damage caused by just a few months of war may take decades to repair.
Damaging cultural heritage and desecrating religious sites - violations of freedom of belief and cultural rights. Persian civilization is a shared treasure of humanity.
However, US and Israeli bombing has already damaged at least 149 historical landmarks and museums across 20 Iranian provinces, including five UNESCO World Heritage sites. UNESCO has expressed deep concern and called for all necessary measures to protect both people and cultural heritage sites. As Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi pointed out, "Iran's cultural heritage is not merely the national asset of Iranians; it is part of the shared memory of humanity." Destroying cultural heritage means destroying the collective memory of humankind - it is cultural genocide.
The use of force by the US and Israel against Iran shows the world that the international rule of law is taking the heaviest blow, that human rights and humanitarian principles are being most deeply trampled on, and that the moral decay of US "neo-imperialism" is being most starkly exposed. The military operations have not only ruthlessly stripped the Iranian people of their basic human rights, but also pushed the entire Middle East toward a humanitarian abyss, shaking the very foundation of world peace. Every bomb dropped on schools, hospitals, residential neighborhoods, and millennia‑old monuments is a heavy blow to human rights values and the bottom line of humanity.
Without peace, human rights are just empty words. Only by upholding peaceful dialogue and abandoning the obsession with the use of force, by adhering to multilateralism and rejecting unilateralism and hegemonism, can we save lives from the terror of war and prevent civilization from being swallowed by the flames of conflict. This is the enduring pursuit of the international human rights cause and the deepest aspiration of humanity as we work to build a community with a shared future.
The author is a commentator on international affairs.

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger' - Biblical or a missed opportunity?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:56:00 UTC
20:56:00 KST

As a good-vibes-only record of the Live '25 Tour, 'Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger' does an admirable job. But the oddly coy documentary fails to meaningfully address the Gallagher brothers' reconciliation, or why the 2025 reunion was such a phenomenon.
I confess that I wasn’t exactly madferit when heading into Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger.
Ever since Oasis’ headline-dominating reunion, followed by their 41 stadium shows in 14 countries last year, I’ve reached my Gallagher limit. Beyond the fan worship which makes me think that people have lost all sense of perspective when it comes to Oasis, the release of a documentary chronicling the whole shebang reeked of a prolonged promotional campaign - the next step in a continuing cash-in coup about two gobby and freshly reunited siblings who haven’t released any new material in 18 years.
Still, you gotta roll with it, and I took the time to attend a special IMAX screening of Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern’s documentary, and emerged nearly won over.
As a rousing concert film and a love letter to Oasis fans, Don’t Look Back In Anger gets a lot right, capturing the euphoria the band has generated with their unlikely comeback. This is chiefly thanks to the sound design by The Zone of Interest's Tarn Willers and James Mather, Haris Zambarloukos' stellar cinematography, and some nifty editing by George Cragg and Martina Zamolo. Their talents brilliantly conspire to make the reunion feel impactful - even exhilarating at times.
As a meaningful chronicle of how the comeback came to be and what it represents, it’s not quite biblical.
Don’t Look Back In Anger is frustrating in the way it glosses over all the juicy stuff and skirts the irresistible narrative of how two bickering brothers went from repeatedly calling each other twats to publicly reconciliating.
It begins with an extended montage of the 90s glory days leading to the sudden and ugly falling out in 2009 during Paris’ Rock en Seine festival.
“Le groupe n’existe plus,” an announcer informs the crowd.
Cut to the band’s first rehearsal together in May 2025. No explanation as to what made this possible, no insight into who reached out to who, or how the animosity was dealt with... Before you know it, it's opening night in Cardiff.
While most films would have built up to this moment and chosen to end the film on the crescendo, the directors - and Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, here on scripting duties - decide to focus on the music as their film settles into a predictable rhythm and hagiographic tone. Concert clips follow, interspersed with portraits of fans and snippets of interviews with Liam and Noel, who come off as bafflingly well-behaved. As charming as some of these segments are, the brothers' uncharacteristically tame demeanour only contributes to the niggling feeling that the reason behind all of this is a big PR-mandated payday.
This cash grab sensation could have been dismissed had the filmmakers been able to delve more meaningfully into why the band continues to generate overwhelming devotion in fans in Britain and around the world, and why the 2025 reunion was such a cultural and social phenomenon. Sure, emotional fans are seen and heard gushing; and granted, this is about looking forward, not backwards. However, had some of the platitudes been excised in favour of something more resonant about the need for mental time travel leading to the possible mythologising of the "good old days" so that a sense of communion is achieved in trying times, then this could have been a fascinating documentary about overcoming divisions.
There is a clumsy montage teasing this, showing quick-cut footage of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, the rise of AI, but all that's left is Liam declaring: “When Oasis split up, everything went to shit.”
Bold statement, r'kid, as I think you'll find that everything went tits up in 2016 when David Bowie's death tore the fabric of the universe... And speaking of "shit", think again if we're getting any acknowledgement regarding the infuriating dynamic ticket pricing scandal. "There are no cheap seats..." according to the frontman.
For a band that has built a reputation as one "of the people", I audibly scoffed.
For all my bellyaching, Don't Look Back In Anger could have been worse and come off as a cynical puff piece. As a good-vibes-only record of the Live '25 Tour, it does an admirable job. As a sincere snapshot of crowds united by a common appreciation, it's undeniably uplifting. My quibbles persist only because I wanted to be won over, finally, and instead got something which feels like a missed opportunity. Don’t Look Back In Anger could have been a far more cathartic and compelling story of reconciliation and healing had it focused on the difficulties of the past to better look towards a more peaceful future. Instead, audiences will get Noel admitting that his brother Liam is “delightful”.
Still, diehard fans will be too busy singing along to care, while more casual audience members will make do with some admittedly terrific concert footage.
For me, I take some satisfaction in knowing that Don't Look Back In Anger will soon head to Disney+, making it the sweariest film to ever stream on the platform. Unless they decide to re-release an R-rated cut of Ratatouille with Little Chef muttering "fuck" and "cunt" when the yellow summer squash isn't mandolined properly. Now that's definitely maybe something worth considering...
"Hello, Disney? What are your thoughts on sweary revivals?"
Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger is out in select theatres on Friday 11 September before streaming on Disney+ later this year.

U.S. Marines’ new drone killer gets confirmation from V2X
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:55:39 UTC
20:55:39 KST

- V2X confirmed a $19 million U.S. Marine Corps contract for Tempest counter-drone vehicles on September 8, 2026, covering delivery, training and support.
- A related Pentagon notice from August 11 put the deal at roughly $19.06 million for 10 vehicles built by V2X subsidiary Vertex Modernization and Sustainment.
V2X confirmed on September 8, 2026, that it has been awarded a $19 million contract by the U.S. Marine Corps to deliver Tempest counter-drone vehicles, along with the maintenance, software and training needed to keep them running.
The announcement puts a public face on a deal the Pentagon had already disclosed. A contract notice dated August 11 identified the recipient as Vertex Modernization and Sustainment, an Indianapolis-based company operating as part of V2X, and put the value at roughly $19.06 million for 10 Tempest vehicles. Work under that award runs through August 10, 2027. V2X’s own release did not repeat the vehicle count, describing the deal only as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, a structure that sets up a framework for future orders rather than locking in a fixed total.
Tempest is a lightweight, four-wheel-drive vehicle built on a modified Can-Am Maverick X3, a commercial off-road buggy fitted with dual missile launchers and a sensor package for spotting and tracking drones. It fires AGM-114L Longbow Hellfire missiles, the radar-guided version of a weapon originally built for Apache attack helicopters, against what the military classifies as Class 2 and Class 3 unmanned aircraft, a category that spans small reconnaissance drones up to systems approaching the size of a light aircraft.
The vehicle already has a combat record. At least two Tempest units have operated in Ukraine, where Ukrainian forces have credited the system with shooting down 21 Shahed drones, the Iranian-designed loitering munitions Russia has fired into Ukrainian cities by the hundreds.
“Unmanned aerial systems are fundamentally changing the modern battlefield, creating an urgent need for counter-UAS solutions that are mobile, effective, and ready to operate in demanding environments,” said Jeremy C. Wensinger, President and Chief Executive Officer of V2X. “Tempest demonstrates what V2X does exceptionally well: respond to an urgent customer need and rapidly take a capability from concept and integration through fielding and sustainment. By bringing together our engineering, technology integration, logistics, and mission expertise, we can move with speed to deliver mission-ready solutions that directly address emerging threats.”
V2X first showed Tempest publicly at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference in October 2025, pitching it as a low-cost, easily repaired answer to small attack drones. The company says the vehicle’s commercially derived design keeps sustainment simple, since many parts can be sourced from civilian suppliers rather than specialized defense manufacturers.
V2X has not said whether the Marine Corps order announced this week covers the same 10 vehicles disclosed in August or represents an expansion under the IDIQ framework. The company also has not disclosed additional financial terms beyond the roughly $19 million figure or said how many Tempest vehicles the Marine Corps might eventually field.

Xinhua shared a photo of the scene showing a large ship called the Ocean Melody docked at a yard, with several fire trucks stationed in front of it.
Ocean Melody is a 190-metre long bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to vessel tracking website MarineTraffic, which located the ship as moored in Qingdao.
'Profound lesson'
Qingdao is a major international maritime hub, connected to more than 700 ports in over 180 countries and regions, according to state media.
The Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding yard operates as a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation.
Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".
There have been several major industrial accidents in China over the last year, where safety regulations are often lax.
In August, an explosion and ensuing fire at a shipyard in Fujian province killed one fire and rescue worker and injured 12 others, according to state media.
China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings last November, after a huge blaze engulfed several tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.
In May, a blast at a fireworks factory in central China killed 37 people, marking one of the nation's deadliest industrial accidents in years.

System for controlling drones without satellite navigation unveiled in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:52:24 UTC
20:52:24 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Geoscan has unveiled an optical navigation system for drones in conditions where satellite navigation is unavailable, the company reported.
The solution was recognized as the best in the "Autonomous Navigation" category at the Dronosapiens Games engineering and technical competition organized by the Aeronext Association, it noted.
"Geoscan Group presented an optical navigation system without GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at the Dronosapiens Games engineering and technical competition organized by the Aeronext association. The system is designed to control UAVs during aerial photography and territorial monitoring in areas without satellite navigation. Geoscan’s solution was named the best in the "Autonomous Navigation" category based on the results of three days of testing," the statement said.
The algorithm uses data from an onboard camera: the system compares the captured images with a satellite map of the area. To navigate the intended flight zone, a feature map is generated in advance. Thus, the satellite base map is automatically downloaded from available sources.
"In our projects, we encounter satellite navigation interference, radio signal jamming, and spoofing even during flights that have been approved by all relevant authorities. The need to operate under such conditions compelled us to develop an autonomous optical navigation system. We began pilot operations of our solution earlier this year. This is now one of the key technologies for the UAV industry, without which further market development is hardly possible," Geoscan CEO Alexey Yuretsky emphasized.
During the competition, the Geoscan 201 drone autonomously took off from the launch pad and successfully completed the designated route. The operator did not manually correct the flight--the drone independently determined its position and altitude. The proposed system can be used for flights covering distances of up to hundreds of kilometers. Experts are currently developing a version of the algorithm that will be able to operate at night using a thermal imaging camera.

BJP leaders were among the first to jump onto the trend. Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal shared an AI-generated photograph of himself dressed in a grey suit and aviators, writing simply: "Vibing to the 80s trend."

The BJP's official X handle also shared some original pictures of Prime Minister Narendra Modi believed to be from the 1980s era.

I thought I’d join the trend the old-fashioned way," he wrote, sharing photographs that were actually taken during the decade.
The pictures included Tharoor with his sons Ishaan and Kanishk.
What is the trend?
The trend itself is simple. Users upload a present-day selfie to AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini and ask them to recreate the image as if it had been taken in the 1980s.Unlike a regular vintage filter, the AI rebuilds the photograph around the person’s face, adding everything from big hairstyles and retro clothes to film grain and old-school studio lighting.The result is a polished throwback image that looks straight out of an old photo album or Bollywood publicity still. The trend has spread rapidly across Instagram and X, with influencers, celebrities and now politicians joining in.

Algeria decided to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates after what it described as the "exhaustion of all means to preserve bilateral ties", Algerian state media said on Thursday. State media later said the decision was a result of what it described as the UAE's "provocative and hostile actions".
The UAE Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Algerian media outlets have in the past sharply criticised the UAE, accusing it of seeking to sow regional discord.
