He described ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as "brotherly", while accusing the unnamed country of meddling in Algeria's internal affairs and seeking to destabilise it.
Tensions escalated further in February, when Algeria began the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE that was signed in Abu Dhabi in May 2013.
Tebboune has often referred to the UAE in speeches as a "micro-state" or "statelet" seeking to destabilise several countries in the region.
"Wherever they set foot, blood flows," he said in a televised interview in July, adding that the UAE has had a "very negative impact".
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," he added.
At the time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break "would have happened long ago" had Algeria not sought to avoid "deepening divisions" in the Arab world.

Australia declares its new air defense missile system combat ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:48:52 UTC
20:48:52 KST

- Australia's Army declared Final Operational Capability for NASAMS on September 9, 2026, with 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery as the first operational unit.
- The system, built under the SRGBAD project with Raytheon Australia and Norway's Kongsberg, uses Australian CEA Technologies radar and Hawkei-mounted launchers.
Australia’s Army has declared Final Operational Capability for its National Advanced Surface to Air Missile System, confirming the ground-based air defense system is ready to support Australian Defence Force operations. Defence announced the milestone on September 9, 2026.
NASAMS is built to detect, track and destroy cruise missiles, aircraft, helicopters and drones. The system was delivered under the Short Range Ground Based Air Defense project, known as SRGBAD, part of a broader air and missile defense setup that also draws on ships and fighter aircraft to protect ADF personnel and infrastructure.
Soldiers from Adelaide’s 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, are the first operational unit to field the system. The regiment, based at Woodside in South Australia, ran live-fire trials and qualification training as part of the phased rollout that led to this week’s declaration.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability for NASAMS marks a significant milestone in strengthening Australia’s integrated air and missile defence capability,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles. “NASAMS provides Army with a modern, highly capable air defence system that enhances our ability to protect Australian Defence Force personnel, critical assets and infrastructure from a range of airborne threats.”
Raytheon Australia is the prime contractor on SRGBAD, running under the Army’s long-standing LAND 19 Phase 7B program. NASAMS itself was co-developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, and Kongsberg Defence Australia built the system’s Fire Distribution Centres locally before handing final units to Raytheon Australia last year. The SRGBAD program is valued at roughly A$2.5 billion.
The Australian version pairs the Norwegian NASAMS design with locally built CEA Technologies radar, the CEATAC and CEAOPS active electronically scanned array systems, mounted alongside launchers on Hawkei protected mobility vehicles. Raytheon’s AN/AAS-52 Multispectral Targeting System adds day and night optical tracking. The setup replaces the Army’s older RBS-70 man-portable air defense missiles.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability delivers a world-leading capability for Defence and provides a major boost to Australia’s integrated air and missile defence,” said Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy. “Australian-designed radar technology is a key part of this capability, highlighting the important contribution local industry makes to Australia’s national security.”
NASAMS is in service with, or on order for, more than a dozen countries. Ukraine has used the system in combat against Russian cruise missiles and drones since 2022, giving the design an operational record beyond Australia’s own trials. Defence has not disclosed how many NASAMS batteries or launchers 16th Regiment will ultimately operate; the regiment is expected to field two batteries once full capability is reached.
Each NASAMS troop is built around a Fire Distribution Centre, a CEATAC radar, an optronic sensor vehicle and several launchers, with the Hawkei launchers and canisters carried on MAN/Rheinmetall HX77 trucks. The missile load is a mix of AIM-120 AMRAAM and Sidewinder missiles, the same interceptors used on Australian and allied fighter jets.
Sustainment of the system will run primarily through Australian-based support contracts already in place with CEA Technologies and Raytheon Australia.

Like Robinson, she lauds the fact that some of the ViZionaries are members of other faiths. “Some of our strongest advocates are people who have chosen to stand with Israel because they believe in values. They're willing to speak up even when there's nothing personally compelling them to do so. It's just because they believe in what Israel stands for. Those voices reach audiences that sometimes the Jewish community cannot reach, and it brings Israel into different communities and cultures and faiths into conversations that demonstrate that supporting Israel is not just about being Jewish.”
Hankin shares that JNFutures enables young people to grow in Jewish leadership within the JNF-USA community. “JNFutures allows young people to have opportunities to serve on boards, to lead missions like JLIM (JNFuture Leadership Institute Mission to Israel), build campaigns, engage donors, participate in the conversations that we're talking about amongst themselves, and develop relationships with the JNF-USA community, both in the United States and in Israel. JLIM (JNFuture Leadership Institute Mission to Israel) is really the first step to helping young people with passion for Israel to truly have a voice in what happens in the future going on there.”
With this year’s cadre of young Zionist ViZionaries and JNFutures, Robinson is optimistic about the Jewish future. “I met all of our young people. They're smarter, greater, more philanthropic, more involved, and more engaged in debate than any other generation I've ever seen.
“We are one, and we believe in life, and they're turning on the lights and taking those people out of the darkness. And I say, let us make sure we are not only celebrating them, but also working with them and honoring them. That’s what we're doing with the Jerusalem Post and the Jewish National Fund-USA’s ViZionaries.”

Algeria cuts ties with UAE over 'hostile' actions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:46:13 UTC
20:46:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria cuts ties with UAE over 'hostile' actions
Algeria has cut diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates following years of mounting tensions, accusing Abu Dhabi of increasingly "provocative or hostile" actions despite repeated warnings from Algiers.
The Algerian foreign ministry announced the decision on Thursday, saying the government had "exhausted all means" of preserving bilateral relations with the Gulf state.
The UAE ambassador was summoned to the foreign ministry in Algiers and formally informed of the decision, according to the statement. He was given 48 hours to comply with the measure.
"Faced with the increasing provocative or hostile actions emanating from the United Arab Emirates, Algeria has exercised a great deal of restraint and a high sense of responsibility," the ministry said.
It said Algiers had repeatedly drawn the Emirati side's attention to its concerns and warned it of the "serious consequences" that could result from what it described as "regrettable and unjustified behaviour".
"Despite these numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates continued to persist in these actions, which have reached limits where they can no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, nor remain without a response," the statement added.
The ministry did not specify which actions had directly triggered Thursday's decision, but relations between Algeria and the UAE have deteriorated considerably in recent years amid disagreements over regional affairs and repeated Algerian accusations of Emirati interference.
Years of mounting tensions
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has repeatedly criticised the UAE without always naming it directly, accusing the Gulf state of attempting to interfere in Algeria's internal affairs and destabilise countries across the region.
In a televised interview in July, Tebboune referred to the UAE as a "micro-state" and accused it of having a "very negative impact" wherever it became involved.
"Wherever they set foot, blood flows," Tebboune said at the time. "We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," he added.
The Algerian president also suggested at the time that relations had come close to being severed previously.
"A diplomatic break would have happened long ago," he said, explaining that Algeria had refrained from taking the step because it did not want to contribute to further divisions within the Arab world.
Tebboune has previously contrasted Algeria's relationship with the UAE with its ties to other Gulf countries, describing relations with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and Oman as brotherly while accusing an unnamed Gulf state, widely understood to be the UAE, of interference.
Regional disputes
The tensions extend beyond bilateral relations, with Algeria and the UAE frequently taking different positions on regional conflicts and political disputes.
Algeria has long emphasised the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of other states and has maintained particularly strained relations with neighbouring Morocco, with which it severed diplomatic ties in 2021.
The Western Sahara dispute remains at the heart of the Algeria-Morocco rivalry. Algiers supports the Polisario Front and the Sahrawi right to self-determination, while Rabat claims sovereignty over the disputed territory.
The UAE's close relationship with Morocco has consequently been a source of friction with Algeria. Abu Dhabi became the first Arab country to open a consulate in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara in 2020, in a move welcomed by Rabat.
Algerian media close to the authorities have also accused the UAE of links to the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia, known by its French acronym MAK, which Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021.
The allegations are particularly sensitive in Algeria, where authorities regard separatist movements as a threat to the country's territorial integrity. The UAE has denied broader accusations that it seeks to destabilise Algeria.
The two countries have also found themselves at odds over developments elsewhere in North Africa and the Sahel, where competing alliances and approaches to regional conflicts have contributed to growing distrust.
Algeria has sought to position itself as an opponent of foreign intervention and has repeatedly called for political solutions to regional crises, while Algerian officials and media have accused Abu Dhabi of pursuing an interventionist foreign policy.
There was no immediate public response from the UAE to Algeria's announcement.

Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:44:19 UTC
20:44:19 KST

Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch food and product safety authority NVWA is taking enforcement action against four Irish livestock transporters over the treatment of very young calves shipped to the Netherlands, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.
The calves are given almost nothing to drink during a journey of at least 50 hours, which breaches EU animal welfare rules, the NVWA said. The transporters have been given a year to change their working methods or face financial penalties.
The animals, mostly bull calves under two months old, are loaded onto trucks in Ireland and put on a ferry to France. After a 19-hour crossing they are unloaded to rest and drink, then driven on to the Netherlands.
EU rules say animals must be fed during transport where “necessary”, which the European Commission and the NVWA interpret as at least every 12 hours. The Irish authorities disagree and have not intervened.
According to the NVWA, the trucks have no drinking systems suitable for milk, and calves of this age have to be helped to drink. The Irish government has itself said that is “practically impossible” on the ferry.
“That means the animals can no longer go directly from Ireland via France to the Netherlands in one go,” NVWA inspector Annebeth van Aartsen told NOS. “The transport would have to be organised differently.”
The Dutch veal sector said earlier it wanted to stop the Irish imports in 2026 because of the suffering involved, but a NOS investigation this year found the transports were still going on.
The NVWA had previously said it could not act because most of the violations take place at sea, outside Dutch jurisdiction. The action follows an enforcement request by animal welfare groups Eyes on Animals and Dier&Recht.

Germany tests nationwide alert systems as disaster and conflict scenarios grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:43:51 UTC
20:43:51 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Germany held a nationwide warning day on Thursday, testing sirens, smartphone alerts and other channels used to warn the public in a crisis or disaster.
Alerts were sent via television, radio, smartphones, Cell Broadcast, warning apps and digital city information boards. Sirens and other local channels such as loudspeaker vans were also used in places that took part.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the exercise showed the systems work. “Today’s nationwide warning day shows our warning systems function reliably, reach our population in the most varied ways and are an important part of our high-performing civil protection,” he said.
Grit Tuengler, president of the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK), called the sixth warning day a success and said the federal warning system and linked channels can alert millions of people in a real emergency. She thanked the municipalities and partners from mobile operators to technical service providers.
The first nationwide warning day in September 2020 was marred by failures, and the drill was paused for a year. It has been held annually since 2022. Officials say the systems are needed for scenarios ranging from natural disasters to a military attack on Germany. The BBK is asking residents to report their experiences on its website. The results will be evaluated scientifically and used to improve the systems.

Sánchez’s release of declassified Ceuta files turns into ‘own goal’
Official notes show Spanish intelligence services warned of a mass incursion, contradicting the government’s claim that the surge could not have been predicted.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addresses the congress of deputies on the government's handling of the situation in Spain's North African enclave Ceuta after a mass influx of migrants, at the lower house of parliament in Madrid on September 3, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might have hoped declassifying official files on this summer’s mass migrant surge into Ceuta would vindicate his government’s handling of the crisis.
Instead, the documents are threatening to make a political mess even messier, in what one of Sánchez’s parliamentary allies described as an “own goal.”
According to papers published by the prime minister’s office on Wednesday, Spanish intelligence agencies and security forces issued numerous warnings that a mass incursion could happen — days before 72,000 migrants surged into one of Spain’s North African territories on July 30.
Advertisement
One day before the influx, Spain’s National Intelligence Service warned the Civil Guard and the Government Delegation in Ceuta — the office representing the Sánchez government in the city — that it had detected messages calling for a mass crossing the following day.
“There is a call on social media for an assault by fence and sea tomorrow,” an intelligence agent wrote in a WhatsApp message to the delegation’s chief of staff, adding that the groups discussing the surge had 180,000 followers.
Hours later, the intelligence service sent an urgent message to its Moroccan counterparts warning of the planned incursion and thanking Rabat for its “invaluable and continued collaboration in this matter.”
The documents also include 18 reports noting an increase in unauthorized entries into Ceuta earlier in the summer, and a July 8 letter from the Civil Guard proposing border security be reinforced.
The Spanish government insists the documents show there was no way of preventing the migrant surge. The reports did not predict “the scale, nature, or probability” of what happened afterward, Sánchez said in a post on X.
Government Delegate in Ceuta Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano on Thursday downplayed the warnings received by his office, arguing that they could not be considered to be formal alerts because they were relayed by WhatsApp instead of official channels.
Advertisement
But political groups from across the spectrum haven’t bought the government’s interpretation of the documents.
Ester Muñoz, parliamentary spokesperson for the center-right People’s Party, said the files proved the government had failed to prevent “the invasion and the deaths” and called for snap elections so Spaniards can “decide if we want to have a prime minister who lies to us.”
Francesc-Marc Álvaro, a lawmaker from the Republican Left of Catalonia and one of Sánchez’s parliamentary allies, said he was baffled by the decision to publish documents that appeared to contradict the government’s narrative.
“This is an own goal,” he said, adding that “in any other advanced democracy, someone would step down for this.”
“The polycrisis in Ceuta is on a higher level than all the messes we have gone through up to this legislature,” adding that the situation was undermining the government’s standing at home and abroad.

The SBU counterintelligence service detained an FSB killer from the Russian Federation who, according to the investigation, was supposed to carry out the contract killing of a well-known public activist in the Kyiv region. The Prosecutor General’s Office reported this, UNN reports.
Details
According to the investigation, the suspect was acting on orders from a representative of the FSB of the Russian Federation and was supposed to kill a well-known public activist—the co-founder of one of the volunteer battalions. UNN’s sources in law enforcement agencies learned that the intended victim was to be the well-known Ukrainian activist and co-founder of the Mykola Pirogov First Volunteer Mobile Hospital, Hennadiy Druzenko.

He had been monitoring the potential victim’s hourly daily routine and movements for a long time, and had also received the coordinates of a weapons cache from the FSB, from which he took a pistol with ammunition and a silencer. According to the instructions of the Russian special service, the perpetrator was supposed to spend the night in the forest, near the public figure’s home, and kill him with several shots from an ambush
The detainee turned out to be a 19-year-old resident of Mykolaiv recruited by the enemy. He came to the attention of enemy intelligence through his activity on social media. In particular, the suspect published posts supporting fascist and Nazi ideology.
During searches, three pistols with silencers and ammunition were found and seized from him, as well as smartphones containing evidence of work for the Russian special services.
The detainee was notified of suspicion under the following articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
-  Part 2 of Article 111 (high treason committed under martial law); 
-  Part 1 of Article 14, paragraph 11 of Part 2 of Article 115 (preparation for the intentional contract killing); 
-  Part 1 of Article 263 (illegal handling of weapons, ammunition or explosives). 
The suspect is currently in custody and faces life imprisonment.

Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:39:56 UTC
20:39:56 KST

Yemen’s Houthi rebels are making a concerted drive to take full control of the country’s Red Sea coast, claiming control of the key port of Mocha, in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years.
Seizure of the coast would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two chokepoints for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.
The Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), a London-based defence and security thinktank, said the situation in Yemen was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope it could put more pressure on the rebels than they could withstand.
The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.
By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.
The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.
The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested rebel forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.
The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged the rebels’ ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.
The clashes have ranged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis found themselves being forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.
The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.
“A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”
He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”
The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The escalantion to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior Houthi delegation from the group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.
The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni rebels described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.
Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli attacks.

Russia’s glide bomb strikes hit a new monthly record in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:39:49 UTC
20:39:49 KST

- Ukraine's General Staff data, compiled by OSINT group Oko Gora, records 8,766 Russian glide bomb uses in August 2026, an average of 283 a day and a new monthly high.
- The figure builds on a documented rise through 2026, with open-source monitors separately logging 8,385 uses in July and 8,266 in June.
Russian aircraft dropped 8,766 glide bombs on Ukrainian front-line positions in August 2026, the highest monthly total recorded since the invasion began, according to Ukrainian General Staff figures compiled by the OSINT monitoring group Oko Gora.
The total works out to an average of 283 bombs a day over the 31-day month. Oko Gora put the increase over July at roughly 5 percent. The figure extends a climb that has run almost without interruption since early 2025, when monthly totals sat closer to 3,500.
Independent open-source trackers have logged the same upward trend using their own counts. Figures compiled from open-source strike monitoring and reported by bne IntelliNews put Russia’s Aerospace Forces at 8,385 glide bombs launched at Ukraine in July, up 1.4% from 8,266 in June, an average of 270 a day.
French outlet Conflits, citing the same Ukrainian General Staff data relayed through Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, described the July total as a monthly record dating back to February 2022, with growth of about 45% over the first half of 2026. The August figure from Oko Gora would mark a new high above that July record.
The weapon behind the totals is not new. It is a Soviet-era FAB gravity bomb, first produced in the 1950s, fitted with a UMPK kit: a set of pop-out wings and a satellite-guidance unit. The added hardware turns a dumb bomb into a stand-off weapon that a jet can release from tens of kilometers away rather than flying over the target. Versions fitted with small jet engines extend that range further, allowing launch aircraft such as the Su-34 to stay further back from Ukrainian air defenses.
Bomb sizes in regular use range from the FAB-500 up to the FAB-1500 and the larger FAB-3000, a roughly 1,387 kg high-explosive weapon that Russia has used against hardened or larger targets. Janes has documented footage of a UMPK-fitted FAB-3000 released from an Su-34 over Ukraine. The glide kits give Russian forces a way to deliver a large explosive payload at long range without the cost of a cruise missile, though accuracy remains poor compared with guided munitions, and Russian claims about precision have drawn skepticism from open-source analysts.
The weapons have continued to hit populated areas away from the front. On August 3, Russian planes dropped eight glide bombs in about 90 minutes on residential districts of Zaporizhzhia, killing one person and wounding dozens, according to regional chief Ivan Fedorov.
Ukraine’s General Staff has not published a separate account of how many of the August strikes used jet-powered UMPK variants versus older unpowered kits, or how many bombs were aimed at front-line positions as opposed to rear-area infrastructure.

Palestinian tunnel found near Jerusalem security wall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:38:56 UTC
20:38:56 KST

A tunnel discovered last month near the West Bank security barrier outside Jerusalem was sealed Wednesday night by Border Police and IDF forces, authorities said.
The tunnel was found near the communities of Givon and Givat Ze’ev, northwest of Jerusalem. Its entrance had been concealed inside an ancient, dried-up water cistern near the Palestinian village of al-Jib. An examination found that the tunnel was at an advanced stage of excavation.
Following intelligence and operational activity after the tunnel was discovered Aug. 28, Border Police officers conducting surveillance in the area arrested a suspect carrying digging tools.
Chief Superintendent Eliyahu Tubul, commander of the northern battalion of the Jerusalem-area Border Police, told ynet that authorities treat attempts to cross the barrier illegally as potential security threats rather than merely attempts by Palestinians to enter Israel for work.
“From my perspective, this isn’t an illegal worker who wants to work in Israel. Anyone like this is an infiltrator who could be the next terrorist to carry out an attack inside Israel,” Tubul said.
He said the latest discovery was not an isolated case and described several other attempts to dig beneath or through the barrier around Jerusalem.
“Ten months ago, we received precise intelligence and uncovered a sewage pit through which they were digging a tunnel into Israeli territory beyond the wall,” he said. “Not long ago, we identified digging along the Qalandiya route, and suspects were arrested while digging. Two weeks ago, officers identified crumbling in the wall in Kafr Aqab and heard digging. We entered through the hole that had been carved out and arrested two suspects during the activity.”
In the latest case, Tubul said, the suspects took advantage of the dried-up water cistern near al-Jib to conceal their excavation.
“We marked the location and left it. We conducted surveillance and intelligence work and kept watch on it,” he said. “Two days ago, we spotted a young man arriving and digging, and we caught him in the act on the village side. We examined the tunnel and discovered they had dug deep and reached within 5 meters,” or about 16 feet, “of the barrier from their side.”
‘Looking for every possible way’
Tubul said authorities were concerned not only about Palestinians attempting to enter Israel illegally for employment but also about the possibility that tunnels could be used by terrorists or to smuggle weapons.
“Alongside infiltration for work in Israel, we have previously seen terrorists enter this way,” he said. “These are also potential routes for transferring weapons into Israel. Our operating assumption in the Border Police is that anyone attempting to infiltrate could be the next terrorist, particularly ahead of the Jewish High Holiday season.”
Tubul said a lucrative smuggling industry had developed around Palestinians seeking to enter Israel without permits from the West Bank.
“This is driven by greed among those running the infiltration industry from the West Bank, an industry that generates large sums of money,” he said. “A West Bank resident who infiltrates Israel pays an operator 800 to 1,200 shekels,” about $265 to $400, “sometimes just to put up a ladder so he can climb over the wall.”
Tubul said such attempts to scale the barrier have become far less common over the past year because of the danger involved. He said Border Police officers may open fire at people attempting to cross in certain circumstances.
Since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack that triggered the Gaza war, Israel has sharply restricted the entry of Palestinian workers from the West Bank, leaving many who previously worked inside Israel unable to cross through regular channels.
“The smugglers who bring in infiltrators are looking for every possible way to get West Bank residents into Israel,” Tubul said. “They disguise themselves as women or ultra-Orthodox Jews at crossings and we uncover them. They hide in garbage trucks or behind false compartments in trucks. The smugglers know we are applying heavy pressure at the crossings, so they are looking to tunnels.”
Tubul said authorities now regard sewage pits, water cisterns and areas of easily excavated soil along the barrier as potential locations for tunnels leading from the West Bank to the Israeli side.
“Any sewage pit or ground that is easy to dig through has the potential to be used for a tunnel from the West Bank that emerges beyond the wall,” he said.
Border Police conduct foot patrols along the route and use surveillance cameras and drones in an effort to identify signs of tunneling, Tubul said.
Until about a year ago, he said, Palestinians seeking to enter Israel without permits frequently climbed over the barrier near Highway 60, with the number at times reaching into the hundreds.
“Border Police managed to shut down the phenomenon after about a year,” Tubul said. “That is forcing them to look for alternatives.”

NHS reports busiest ever summer as heatwaves drive up hospital admissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:37:12 UTC
20:37:12 KST

The NHS faced the “busiest summer in its history” as the UK experienced a series of heatwaves, health officials have said, while the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England has risen to its highest level for nine months.
The health secretary said “extreme demand” on the service was “no longer confined to winter” and NHS leaders warned that the service had “never gone into winter on the back of such a heavy summer”.
Figures show A&E attendances in June, July and August reached nearly 7.3m, the highest ever over a summer period, according to NHS England. This is almost 1m higher than the equivalent period in 2022 when 6.4m attendances were recorded over the summer months.
Ambulances also dealt with a record number of callouts – about 2.4m – between June and August, NHS England said.
An estimated 7.33m treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of July, relating to 6.21 million patients, according to NHS figures – up from 7.27m treatments and 6.15 million patients at the end of June.
The numbers are the highest since October 2025, when the list stood at 7.40m treatments and 6.24 million patients.
Long waits for NHS hospital treatment in England have also increased. An estimated 111,379 people had been waiting more than a year to start routine treatment at the end of July, up from 105,711 at the end of June.
An estimated 65.4% of patients in July began hospital treatment within 18 weeks of referral, down from 65.8% in June but above the target of 65% that the government and NHS England set for March of this year.
Labour previously pledged that by July 2029, 92% of patients would be seen within 18 weeks for routine hospital treatment such as hip and knee replacements. But leading surgeons have said it is unlikely the target will be met.
Prof Frank Smith, the senior vice-president of the Royal College of Surgeons of England, said: “Our analysis shows that, if the pace of improvement seen over the last two years continues, no region in England will restore the 18-week standard by 2029.”
The NHS England figures show that an average of 2,973 patients in England received corridor care each day in August, with 2,296 in A&E departments and 677 in other hospital areas.
Commenting on the summer pressures facing the health service, Sarah Woolnough, the chief executive of the King’s Fund thinktank, said: “The NHS is now facing a twin crisis with summer joining winter as a major pressure on services and leaving little room for staff and the system to recover between peak periods. Extreme heat is now an NHS pressure point, not just a weather story.
“If ministers want to protect patients, staff and performance, they need to treat climate resilience and delivering a radical shift to prevention as core health policy.’
Dr Vicky Price, the president of the Society for Acute Medicine, said: “Behind the national figures are teams describing relentless pressure, a lack of meaningful solutions and morale at a low ebb. Staff continue to work tirelessly, but goodwill cannot compensate indefinitely for structural problems that remain unresolved.”
The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “This has been the most demanding summer on record for our A&E and ambulance staff, with heavy pressure on our NHS and winter still to come. I want to pay tribute to the incredible dedication of NHS staff.
“Despite unprecedented demand, they managed to see a record number of patients within four hours in A&E over the summer. With the support of this government, the NHS has worked hard to strengthen its ability to respond to these challenges, but the reality is that extreme demand is no longer confined to winter.
“That’s why we’re backing the NHS with record investment and rolling out plans to support services through both summer and winter pressure.”

States, municipalities to drive next phase of India deregulation: Niti Aayog member Gauba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:36:11 UTC
20:36:11 KST

MUMBAI: States and municipalities will have to drive the next phase of India’s deregulation, with reforms in areas such as land use, building permits, pollution consents and business licences critical to making it easier to do business, NITI Aayog member Rajiv Gauba said.Speaking at the Global Fintech Fest, Gauba said the next generation of reforms should focus on making the everyday task of doing business simpler, rather than only pursuing large, headline-grabbing measures. He said India needed to move beyond the persistence of the “Inspector Raj” by scrutinising the maze of laws, regulations, permissions, registrations and renewal requirements imposed by governments at the Centre, state and city levels.“The next generation reform has to be to liberate the industry and citizens at large from this stifling chokehold of rules, regulations, permissions,” Gauba said.The approach, he said, should be based on trust, with regulations tested against the principle of “Jan Vishwas”. Licences should be required only for activities involving national security or serious risks to human health or the environment. In other cases, registration should be automatic rather than subject to a government “yes or no”.
Where licences are necessary, they should have perpetual or long-term, 10-year validity, while inspections should be risk-based rather than random.Gauba pointed out that several areas that directly affect investment and economic activity, including land-use changes, building permits, pollution consents and various business licences, fall within the jurisdiction of state and municipal governments.The Centre, he said, should promote model regulations, share templates and best practices and create incentives for states to implement them. Central transfers and fiscal support can be linked to reforms, with the Special Assistance Scheme for Capital Investment and the Urban Challenge Fund providing examples of funding being tied to reforms and projects.One major opportunity lies in easing building regulations. Gauba said changes to requirements relating to setbacks, ground coverage and parking could unlock five to six times more built-up area. This could allow hospitals to add floors and hotels to build more rooms, while increasing land supply could help reduce hotel tariffs by 35% and make affordable housing more accessible.
Tourism and hospitality also need deregulation, he said. Tour operators currently require various state-level permits despite holding an All India Tourist Permit, while hotels face multiple health, trade and liquor licences across venues and locations. The committee has recommended sweeping reforms in these areas, and the deregulation task force is now working with states to implement them.

China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25
September 10, 2026
At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday.
State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)."
The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported.
Cause remains unclear
Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added.
Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".
It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire.
The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders.+

UK deepens reliance on Musk's SpaceX, spending nearly $40 million on satellite services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:32:29 UTC
20:32:29 KST

UK deepens reliance on Musk's SpaceX, spending nearly $40 million on satellite services
LONDON, Sept 10 - Britain has spent nearly $40 million on SpaceX satellite services, deepening its reliance on Elon Musk's company for military communications despite growing European concerns about dependence on U.S. security infrastructure.
The spending was disclosed to Reuters in response to a freedom of information request and makes Britain the first country outside the U.S. to publicly acknowledge adopting Starshield, SpaceX's service for military and intelligence missions. Starlink is marketed to consumer and commercial users.
Britain's defence ministry said it has about 1,000 Starshield terminals and 500 Starlink terminals. It has spent about £13 million ($17.6 million) on Starshield, including terminals and airtime, and £16.5 million on Starlink.
The disclosure comes at a time when European governments are seeking to bolster their own defence capabilities amid concerns over Washington's long-term commitment to the continent's security.
Musk repeatedly publicly criticised Britain's government during the premiership of Keir Starmer, who was recently replaced by fellow Labour party politician Andy Burnham.
Britain's defence ministry began using Starlink in mid-2022 and more recently has been shifting operational military communications traffic to Starshield, Reuters reported in June, citing people familiar with the matter.
Militaries have been adopting Starlink since Ukraine began using the network extensively following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, including for battlefield communications and drone operations.
SpaceX has increasingly drawn a distinction between Starlink and Starshield. Musk has said Starlink is intended for civilian use, while Starshield is marketed to government and national security customers. SpaceX did not respond to questions, including which countries have access to Starshield.
Britain's defence ministry said it adopted Starshield after SpaceX mandated that Starlink only be used for morale, welfare, recreation and training purposes. The ministry said Starshield offers "enhanced encryption, military-specific terms of service, the highest level of network prioritisation, flexible licensing arrangements, and expanded coverage."
For the UK, Starshield uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink but operates through dedicated terminals and separate ground-based network gateways, the ministry said.
According to the ministry's response to Reuters, Britain began using Starshield airtime with existing Starlink terminals in 2024. It purchased its first dedicated Starshield terminals last year.
Britain also has its own military satellite communications network, Skynet, and is a shareholder in France-based Eutelsat, which runs the only major operational low-Earth orbit (LEO) broadband satellite constellation besides Starlink.
MUSK WANTS MILITARIES TO USE STARSHIELD
Starshield can cost substantially more than Starlink, according to pricing information disclosed by the ministry.
It said two Starshield plans are available in Britain: £5,500 a month for five terabytes of data and an unlimited plan costing £25,000 a month. By comparison, UK Starlink business customers can pay £1,830 a month for two terabytes of global data, alongside a range of cheaper plans with lower data allowances or more localised coverage.
Starshield terminals cost between £4,000 and £7,000 each, according to a person familiar with the matter. That is at least double the advertised price of business-grade Starlink terminals.
Reuters reported earlier this year that SpaceX increased fivefold the price charged to the Pentagon for Starlink services used to guide kamikaze drones during operations against Iran, angering some U.S. officials. Musk said the increase reflected the use of Starlink rather than Starshield, which he said should have been used instead.
At least some other U.S. partners are also evaluating the service. New Zealand is trialling Starshield "to investigate its usefulness" in supporting military operations, a spokesperson for the New Zealand Defence Force told Reuters.
Starshield is based on Starlink technology. In some cases, SpaceX develops dedicated satellite constellations for U.S. government customers. In its most recent quarterly results, the company said the U.S. government had awarded more than $6 billion in multi-year Starshield contracts, primarily through two major U.S. Space Force programmes for LEO constellations.
Since launching Starlink in 2020, SpaceX has built the world's largest low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation. The business has become the company's biggest source of revenue and helped underpin its recent stock market debut, the largest initial public offering on record. REUTERS

In an interview with the Vedomosti newspaper, Medvedev said nuclear weapons can be used in specific cases based on Russia’s nuclear doctrine and dismissed the definition of his country’s rhetoric on their use as “hints.”
“This is not a scare tactic; it is reality. Russia’s nuclear doctrine -- under which the country reserves the right to use such weapons if its security is threatened -- can hardly be described as a mere hint,” he said.
Medvedev, a former president and prime minister, said important clarifications have been made to the document, specifying the conditions under which Russia would employ nuclear weapons, while the list of military threats designated for their implementation has also been expanded.
He reminded that “aggression” against Russia or Belarus, which are formally part of a union state since 1999, by any non-nuclear state, with the participation or support of a nuclear power, will be considered as an attack on both countries.
“We have every right to respond to a critical threat to our sovereignty. The final decision will be made by the head of state,” Medvedev expressed.
He accused the West of trying to bring the world to the “brink of nuclear apocalypse,” naming strikes on Russian cities, among others, as “aggressive actions that could one day trigger World War III.”
Medvedev said Russia’s military capability would allow it to strike the Ukrainian capital and key NATO targets, leaving “not one stone left standing.”

“However, our patience is not limitless. This ultimate option remains a last resort, to be used only when all other measures have failed. Today, we are but a few steps away from it -- mere seconds on the Doomsday Clock,” he added.

Empty shelves, shattered warehouses: Ukraine's Jews prepare for fifth Rosh Hashanah at war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:30:26 UTC
20:30:26 KST

To supply sweet holiday kits to tens of thousands of Jews in the embattled country, Chabad Ukraine said it is "working under complex hardships” to give hope that “the sweet tradition of Rosh Hashanah won't stop."
Amid intensifying shelling in Ukraine's cities, Ukraine's Jewish communities remain on high alert ahead of the High Holy Days.
Kyiv's Jewish communities have weathered repeated attacks on the capital. On August 29, Reuters reported that at least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone attack on a Kyiv-area ammunition depot sparked a detonation. Moscow's air attacks on Kyiv and surrounding regions dragged into a third straight day, killing residents, damaging homes, and derailing daily life.
This follows an unfortunate pattern, as a Russian strike on July 2 launched 74 missiles and 496 drones overnight, killing at least 20 people and wounding more than 90, according to Ukrainian authorities, sending Jewish families back into shelters just a day after they'd returned from a respite camp run by the Jewish Relief Network Ukraine (JRNU) in the Carpathian Mountains.
However, as fighting in the country becomes routine, with the sounds of explosions having become part of daily life, community rabbis are working around the clock to produce mass amounts of kosher honey, essential to the unique culture of Rosh Hashanah.
Essential food products to be unloaded at foot of Jewish centers in various cities
The main phase of the operation has officially commenced: a fleet of massive aid trucks set out from supply centers toward dozens of Jewish communities scattered throughout the country.
Huge pallets of essential food products were unloaded at the foot of Jewish centers in various cities, then transported directly to community members' homes through an internal, organized, and dignified distribution system.
The diverse list of food items included poultry, fresh meat, locally produced jars of honey, dairy products, canned goods, various spreads, honey cakes specially airlifted in from Israel, and festive honey pastries imported from Zaporizhzhia.
To add extra value to the package, informational pamphlets were included. Beautifully designed and adapted into the local language, they explain the meaning of the High Holy Days and include a unique, rich calendar combining Jewish content with images from community life.
'Situation has become extreme'
Jewish communities in Ukraine are reportedly expecting record participation this year in synagogues and various holiday activities. As such, Jewish resilience continues to thrive. "We are preparing for an unprecedented number of worshippers who will come to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur prayers," says Rabbi Simcha Levenharts, a Chabad emissary in Kyiv who is coordinating the distribution effort.
"The situation has become extreme in recent days," Levenharts said. "Warehouses in the area have been destroyed, and the shelves in stores are simply empty. People can barely go shopping because the chains are closed for many hours because of the alarms."
JRNU said some Rosh Hashanah supplies were brought by air from Israel, including honey cakes and other holiday goods. Communities are also distributing chicken, meat, and jars of honey.
Despite the worsening security situation, Jewish leaders say they are preparing for unusually high synagogue attendance over Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
"We are preparing for an unprecedented number of people to come to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur prayers," Levenharts said.
"After such a long and exhausting period of war and uncertainty, people are looking more than ever for togetherness and tradition, so they don't break and can remain strong."
Chabad organizing massive logistical efforts to ensure holidays marked with greatest possible dignity
The JRNU, which is behind the distribution of aid packages to the country's Jews, made a strategic decision: to produce most of the basic food and holiday products on Ukrainian soil itself, at special local factories prepared in advance for this purpose.
The Kyiv area is surrounded by logistics hubs and giant warehouses that have absorbed serious hits and daily bombardments in recent weeks, but by some miracle, the factory chosen for producing the pure honey has remained standing.
While these logistics hubs are absorbing heavy bombardment and shelling, Chabad is organizing massive logistical efforts to ensure the holidays are marked with the greatest possible dignity and to strengthen communal solidarity despite the dangers on the ground.
As the noise of the machines mixes with air-raid sirens, the production workers continue working there under constant alertness. In addition to the honey factory, which was certified kosher by Rabbi Yehoshua Vishetzki of the "Ukrkosher" kashrut system, special meat and poultry slaughter operations have also been certified kosher under strict standards, amid the chaos of war.
JRNU has spent the war years building local production and distribution infrastructure – including factories, kosher slaughter operations, and a delivery network – to sustain religious life for Ukraine's Jewish population without relying on imports that wartime logistics make unreliable.
The honey factory near Kyiv is ostensibly one facet in that system, illustrating both the scale of the effort and the risks involved in running it inside an active war zone.
In the Jewish community of Kyiv, connecting to tradition by “manufacturing kosher food in Ukraine not only instills local pride but aids the country’s struggling economy as well”, says Chabad.org.
Drones fall near Kremenchuk rabbi's home
The security threat has reached Jewish community leaders directly.
Rabbi Shlomo Salamon, chief rabbi of Kremenchuk, said two drones fell close to his home this week.
"Just today, a few hours ago, two UAVs fell right near our home and immediately brought us back to the difficult atmosphere of the war," Salamon said.
"In days like these, when food warehouses are being bombed, and you can feel the shortages and uncertainty in the stores, the joy of receiving these substantial and festive food packages is enormous," he said.
In Poltava, Chief Rabbi Yosef Segal said residents were also encountering shortages.
"Many stores are dealing with empty shelves, and there is a shortage of basic food products," Segal said, adding that holiday food packages were providing both practical help and emotional support.
In Cherkasy, Rabbi Dov Axelrod said preparations for Rosh Hashanah were continuing despite the deteriorating security situation.
"The preparations for the holiday fill the synagogue and the community with a feeling of togetherness, family, and hope for a better and sweeter year," he said.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report that the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang's nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site's second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building's construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
Expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea's nuclear program violated UN Security Council resolutions.
"The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi's statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency's authority. North Korea's mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had "no legal right… to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT," referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

eDNA-based monitoring helping identify invasive crawfish species in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

eDNA-based monitoring helping identify invasive crawfish species in Estonia
Traditional monitoring methods are insufficient to manage invasive species that threaten Estonia's native crayfish. However, eDNA, or environmental DNA, can help detect these species quickly and effectively, according to a doctoral thesis defended at the Estonian University of Life Sciences.
Invasive non-native crayfish species are spreading to new areas in Estonia's fresh waters, threatening the European or noble crayfish, the country's only native crayfish species. A doctoral thesis defended at the Estonian University of Life Sciences shows that traditional monitoring methods alone are not enough to control the spread of non-native species. However, the use of environmental DNA, or eDNA, makes it possible to detect non-native crayfish more effectively and at an earlier stage of their spread.
Michael Oliewo Aluma, a junior researcher at the Estonian University of Life Sciences' Chair of Aquaculture, examined the spread of invasive non-native crayfish species in Estonia in his doctoral thesis, "Distribution patterns of invasive non-native crayfish species and eDNA-based monitoring in Estonian inland waters for the conservation of noble crayfish (Astacus astacus L.)." He assessed the suitability of eDNA for monitoring noble crayfish, non-native crayfish and the pathogen that causes crayfish plague. The study combines long-term distribution monitoring with molecular methods to support the conservation of noble crayfish and freshwater biodiversity.
Signal crayfish spreading to new territories
The study found that since 2008, signal crayfish have become established in at least five new locations in Estonia and are spreading beyond previously known areas. At the same time, noble crayfish populations have disappeared from several locations, including Riksu Stream and the mouth of the Pärnu River. The findings indicate that the spread of invasive non-native crayfish species may have contributed to the decline or disappearance of native noble crayfish populations.
In his doctoral thesis, Michael Oliewo Aluma also assessed the effectiveness of the catch-based monitoring methods currently in use. The study found that while test trapping is an important monitoring tool, it has a limited effect on reducing invasive non-native crayfish populations. Trapping methods may also fail to detect populations that are small or have only recently begun to spread.
DNA in the water betrays species presence
In a significant innovation, Michael Oliewo Aluma and his colleagues used eDNA to monitor crayfish and crayfish plague in Estonia. They analyzed genetic material found in water, which makes it possible to identify species without catching them.
Using eDNA, the research team successfully detected the presence of noble crayfish, signal crayfish and spiny-cheek crayfish, as well as the crayfish plague pathogen (Aphanomyces astaci). Detection accuracy reached 100 percent for noble crayfish and 87.5 percent for signal crayfish.
The Estonian University of Life Sciences research team also participated in a large-scale interlaboratory proficiency test comparing the performance of eDNA analyses at different European laboratories. The results confirmed that the methodology used in Estonia is reliable and comparable to that of other European laboratories, supporting the wider adoption of eDNA-based monitoring.
Aluma said environmental DNA does not completely replace traditional monitoring methods but can significantly complement them. "It helps detect invasive species and pathogens earlier, thereby providing better opportunities to protect noble crayfish," the doctoral thesis author said.
The doctoral thesis concludes that preserving biodiversity in Estonia's fresh waters requires an integrated approach combining traditional monitoring with new molecular methods. eDNA-based monitoring provides a strong foundation for the early detection of invasive non-native crayfish species and crayfish plague. It could also be incorporated into national monitoring programs in the future.
The full doctoral thesis is available in the Estonian University of Life Sciences digital repository, EMU DSpace.
--
Editor: Airika Harrik, Marcus Turovski

Asylum applications fall to lowest level in EU since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:28:52 UTC
20:28:52 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The number of asylum applications lodged in EU+ countries fell to its lowest first-half level since 2021, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) said Thursday.
EU+ countries received around 332,000 applications for international protection in the first six months of 2026, a 17% decline from the same period last year.
The EU+ comprises the 27 EU member states as well as Norway and Switzerland.
The agency said the decline, which has continued since late 2024, reflected a change in the nationalities seeking asylum amid Syria’s “fragile but ongoing political transition,” as well as EU cooperation with countries of origin and transit.
It added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East had not resulted in an increase in asylum applications in the EU+.
Afghans submitted the highest number of applications at 39,000, down 7% year-on-year. Applications from Venezuelans fell by nearly one-third to 33,000, with 93% lodged in Spain.
Applications from Bangladeshis, meanwhile, rose 13% to 20,000.
France received the largest number of applications at 69,000, accounting for about one-fifth of the EU+ total. It was followed by Italy with 66,000 and Spain and Germany with 55,000 each.
Together, the four countries received around three-quarters of all applications.
Greece recorded the highest number relative to its population, receiving 23,000 applications, roughly one for every 400 residents.
The EU+ recognition rate stood at 31%, meaning fewer than one-third of first-instance decisions resulted in applicants being granted international protection.
Around 56% of applications came from nationalities that may be subject to border or accelerated procedures under the EU’s new asylum rules because of low recognition rates or designation as safe countries of origin.

He said the plant was attacked with Russian Lancet-type loitering munitions and emphasized that the occupying forces do not care about "Americans, their property or the concerns of senators." Filatov called for "involving the Foreign Ministry and shouting about this to the whole world."
Earlier Thursday, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha said Russian occupying forces had attacked the enterprise in Dnipro again, killing two people and injuring two others. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said the strike damaged a food industry enterprise, next to which a fire broke out and was extinguished by rescuers.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said repeated Russian attempts to strike the sunflower oil production facility of U.S. company Bunge in Dnipro were part of Russia's systematic attacks on U.S. businesses in Ukraine. According to him, the attack was not a mistake but was deliberate, as Russian forces had repeatedly attempted to strike the facility.
Bunge is one of the world's largest agribusiness companies and is part of the so-called "ABCD quartet" of global grain traders, together with Cargill, ADM and Louis Dreyfus.
Bunge has operated in Ukraine since 2002 and is one of the country's leading grain exporters and sunflower oil producers. The company's main assets in the country are its subsidiary Suntrade, a network of grain elevators, a terminal at the Mykolaiv seaport, and the Dnipropetrovsk oil extraction plant, which produces the popular Oleina brand of cooking oil. In addition, in 2025 the company received approval to acquire the Vinnytsia oil extraction plant (ViOi), further expanding its production capabilities in the Ukrainian market.

From Gaza to Lebanon: The Same Media Playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:27:41 UTC
20:27:41 KST

Breadcrumb
How Gaza's media playbook reached Lebanon
What we're seeing in the Western media coverage of Lebanon very much mirrors what we saw and what we continue to see in terms of the coverage of the Gaza genocide.
But what we saw in Gaza was not new. It reflected a longer pattern of dehumanisation directed at Palestinians and, more broadly, the Arab world. That framework has translated easily into coverage of Lebanon.
The same patterns reappear: omissions that obscure Israeli responsibility, the misuse of language such as "ceasefire", chronic underreporting, and the assumption that almost any Israeli action can be justified in the name of destroying Hezbollah, just as similar arguments were used to justify actions against Hamas in Gaza.
In Lebanon, this often takes the form of headlines that describe destruction without clearly identifying who is carrying it out. The deliberate nature of the destruction is frequently absent from reporting, even when Israeli officials have been open about plans that involve the displacement of Shia communities and the clearing of Shia villages. Instead, media coverage often relies on sanitised language such as "evacuation", masking the coercive reality on the ground.
The result is systematic underreporting.
When organisations such as Amnesty International conclude that Israel is committing the war crime of unlawful transfer, those findings often receive little attention in mainstream Western media. More broadly, statements and reports from NGOs documenting abuses frequently struggle to gain significant coverage.
Yet the underlying logic remains the same. The idea that an entire village can be destroyed in the pursuit of Hezbollah echoes the rationale used in Gaza, where vast destruction was justified through the stated objective of eliminating Hamas.
If those tactics were normalised in Gaza, it is hardly surprising to see them reproduced in Lebanon.
What much of the media adopted was essentially the language of the Gaza playbook, and that same framework was then applied to Lebanon.
But that is precisely the problem. Gaza is not a playbook. It is a genocide, involving some of the gravest crimes of our time.
And yet, through that framing, what emerges is a whitewashing of the genocide itself, alongside the normalisation of similar tactics in Lebanon and, increasingly, in territories occupied by Israel in Syria.
At the heart of all this is a failure to contextualise Israel as an expansionist state. Without that broader context, these actions are presented as isolated security measures rather than as part of a larger political and territorial project.

EU must assume political leadership in space policy: French president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:26:33 UTC
20:26:33 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron called on the EU Thursday to assume stronger political leadership over its space policy, warning that Europe remains “fragile” in a sector increasingly linked to sovereignty, security and economic competitiveness.
“The European Union must fully assume political leadership over an ambitious, clear and demanding space policy,” Macron told the first International Space Summit at the Grand Palais in Paris.
Macron said the bloc should pursue “genuine technological independence” and retain the ability to choose its partners for critical capabilities.
“Europe must rank among the world’s leading players, particularly in communications and artificial intelligence,” he said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen echoed Macron's call for greater cooperation, warning that Europe's current strengths do not guarantee its future position.
“To remain at the forefront, Europe must act together, invest at scale, and turn our market into a competitive advantage,” she said.
The global space economy is expected to nearly triple from around $630 billion today to $1.8 trillion by 2035, von der Leyen added.
She said the Commission had proposed €131 billion ($152 billion) for defense, security and space under the EU's next long-term budget, five times the funding currently available.
Macron stressed the need for large-scale, affordable access to space, saying Europe should be capable of launching several hundred metric tons into orbit annually at competitive costs.
“Europe cannot invest billions in these rockets and then purchase launches only sporadically,” he said.
Von der Leyen said the Commission and the European Space Agency were committed to developing a new European vision for access to space by pooling demand and acting as an anchor customer for European launches.
“This is how we keep a competitive space transport industry in Europe, and keep our independent access to space,” she said.
Macron announced that France would invest €20 billion through 2030 in the space sector, along with an additional €40 million through the French space agency CNES for an observation program.
Von der Leyen also highlighted the growing security dimension of space, citing threats including signal jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks on satellite networks.
“Our security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space,” she said, adding that the EU is developing a European Space Shield to strengthen defenses and address critical capability gaps.
Macron also warned that “space is no longer a sanctuary,” calling for stronger international governance.

Fact check: Why is Russia claiming Western 'interference' in Duma elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:26:03 UTC
20:26:03 KST

Fact check: Why is Russia claiming Western 'interference' in Duma elections?
As the Russian legislative elections near, the Moscow propaganda is accusing the West of plotting to disrupt the vote — the same charge Western governments have repeatedly leveled against the Kremlin.
Russia's upcoming elections for the State Duma, the lower house of the parliament, between Sept. 18 and 20 are seen by democracy watchdogs as little more than a rubber stamp for the regime's grip on power.
Yet in recent months, Russian officials and media have stepped up claims that Europe plans to tamper with the process.
Russia's foreign intelligence alleged on Aug. 31 that the EU plans "provocations" at polling stations in Russia and abroad and, together with Ukraine, plots cyberattacks against Russia's election infrastructure.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in comments reported on Sept. 8, claimed the EU is training "secret" monitors to watch the Duma vote.
And Vasily Piskaryov, head of the State Duma commission "investigating foreign interference," alleged that "extremist" groups plan to conduct "fake exit polls" at Russian embassies.
Piskaryov also accused "European NGOs," designated as "undesirable organizations," of recruiting Russian-speaking citizens to pose as fake electoral experts and spread disinformation amid the election campaign.
Russian officials have not provided evidence of their claims — which were widely reported by Russian state and pro-state media — and the EU has dismissed the accusations in comments to the Kyiv Independent.
"It is not the first time that Russian authorities accuse Western states of interfering in Russian elections without any compelling evidence," Julia Smirnova, a disinformation researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), a Germany-based monitoring agency, told the Kyiv Independent.
Smirnova listed three main goals of the narrative: discrediting any criticism by the exiled Russian opposition, casting Russia as a country besieged by foreign powers, and distracting from its own interference abroad.
Siege mentality
Democracy watchdogs regard Russian elections as neither free nor fair, citing vote-buying, coercion, and a crackdown on the opposition, according to the U.S.-based NGO Freedom House.
While the ruling United Russia party is all but certain to win, certain Kremlin-aligned parties are allowed to run as "systemic opposition" to create the appearance of democratic competition.
Parties diverting from the Kremlin line — like the "pro-peace" Yabloko party — are not allowed to run. "Non-systemic" opposition politicians have been imprisoned, branded extremists, forced into exile, or killed.
Russian authorities have also been systematically dismantling any independent monitoring infrastructure.
Golos, Russia's only independent election watchdog, was designated a "foreign agent" in 2013 and later dissolved.
Only state-sanctioned actors are permitted to monitor Russian elections, with independent NGOs and international organizations, such as the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, being shut out.
In violation of international law, Russia is also planning to hold parliamentary elections in the occupied Ukrainian territories, which it regards as its "new" regions.
Expecting widespread criticism of the elections' legitimacy, the Kremlin is preemptively dismissing such criticism as outside meddling.
"The recent accusations are aimed, firstly, at discrediting any criticism of the Russian regime by exile media or politicians as foreign interference," Smirnova told the Kyiv Independent.
They are also meant to reinforce the image "of Russia being under attack by foreign powers."
As the expert notes, the Kremlin has similarly denounced Western support for Russian civil society during the Russian elections in 2011 and 2012, or their coverage by Western media, as "interference."
And the Kremlin propaganda launched a similar campaign ahead of the previous State Duma elections in 2021, accusing the West at the time of trying to discredit the process, and Western media of "spreading fakes" about the election.
Distraction and 'whatabaoutsim'
Yet another goal of Russia's unfounded accusations, Smirnova says, is the Kremlin's attempt to distract from its own election interference.
When Lavrov accused Europe of plotting to send "secret monitors" to the Duma elections, he also lashed out at the EU over alleged tampering in the Romanian presidential election.
Romania's constitutional court in December 2024 annulled the results of a presidential vote and ordered a rerun after Romanian intelligence identified a Russian-backed social media campaign to prop up the fringe far-right presidential candidate Calin Georgescu.
German authorities reported a Russian-linked disinformation campaign before the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt — won by the far-right, Kremlin-friendly AfD party — and France is investigating possible Russian interference ahead of its own 2027 presidential vote.
"By accusing the EU of what Russia is currently doing itself in European countries, Russian intelligence agencies are using the tactics of 'whataboutism' and hollowing out the notion of election interference," Smirnova commented.

Former Western Special Forces Allegedly Trained Russians in Europe After Full-Scale Invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:25:49 UTC
20:25:49 KST

- Category
