Former Western Special Forces Allegedly Trained Russians in Europe After Full-Scale Invasion
Former members of Western special forces, including personnel reportedly linked to Britain’s elite Special Air Service, may have trained Russian citizens and even active-duty military personnel at private combat centers in Europe after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to an intelligence assessment obtained by The Telegraph on September 9.
The assessment reportedly reaches that conclusion with a “high degree of confidence” and is now being examined by Australia’s intelligence service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The memo was prepared for the Australian Secret Intelligence Service based on interviews with two former Australian special forces members and a serving reservist.
Those interviewed said they had been approached about instructor positions at private training facilities in Bulgaria and Serbia where Russian clients were allegedly receiving military instruction.
One of the facilities named in the assessment is Alfa-Metal, a private training center in Bulgaria offering special forces-style courses and advanced sniper instruction.
Courses cost roughly €4,000 per participant and are marketed toward clients including private military contractors, bodyguards, and corporate security personnel.
According to the intelligence memo, European private training centers continued accepting Russian citizens even after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, including for advanced close-quarters combat courses.
The people interviewed for the assessment said employees at the center indicated Russian nationals were still receiving training there as recently as 2025.
The allegations raise particularly serious questions because Alfa-Metal publicly presented itself as having access to instructors with extensive Western military experience.
The company’s website displayed an image of the SAS emblem, while Alfa-Metal also advertised for a British instructor with a special forces background. In addition, it included instructors with the Australian Commando Regiment, US police forces, and the US Navy SEALs background.
An instructor profile on the company’s website additionally featured a man who claimed 12 years of service within US Army Special Operations Command, listing experience in counterterrorism, Ranger training, airborne operations, jungle warfare and long-range surveillance.
According to The Telegraph, Alfa-Metal has strongly denied the central allegations. The company said it had not trained Russian citizens since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion and denied ever employing former SAS personnel.
The training center initially also rejected allegations of links to Alfa Region, a Russian private security company.
After The Telegraph questioned Alfa-Metal about material on its own website, however, the company acknowledged that the two businesses had maintained “historical professional contacts.”
The relationship is significant because Alfa Region has promoted the Bulgarian training center and advertised courses involving instructors said to have experience in special forces and police units from several countries.
The intelligence findings have not been independently verified by The Telegraph.
Sources connected to the SAS have also questioned whether former members of the unit were actually involved in training Russians, arguing that such activity would run directly against the culture and values associated with Britain’s special forces community.
The Australian Secret Intelligence Service is now examining the allegations contained in the memo. Findings from that investigation could ultimately be shared with Britain, the United States and other members of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, The Telegraph noted.
The UK Defense Ministry declined to comment on matters involving British special operations forces or intelligence.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia has bypassed Western sanctions to acquire advanced 3D-printing equipment comparable to technology used in Rolls-Royce manufacturing, helping Moscow cut the cost of its jet-powered drones roughly in half as it rapidly expands production.

Breakthrough in talks with MHA on legislative powers: Ladakh grps
NEW DELHI: Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra said on Thursday that the Union Territory is moving towards seeking constitutional safeguards for its local population under Article 371, along with the creation of a UT-level elected body with legislative and financial powers.Kundra said a meeting of the sub-committee was held at the ministry of home affairs on Wednesday with the leadership of the Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance from Ladakh. Discussions focused on incorporating a special provision under Article 371 to protect the interests of the local population.He said the next meeting is scheduled for October, with the administration hoping to have an advanced draft of the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill ready by then.
What Ladakh is seeking
The proposed framework would include a Union Territory-level body elected directly through constituencies and vested with legislative and financial powers.The move comes amid demands for greater constitutional protection for Ladakh following its transition into a Union Territory.
Articles 371 contain special provisions for specific states. These provisions differ from one state to another but broadly seek to protect local political, cultural, social and economic interests.
Article 371-A, for instance, provides special safeguards for Nagaland. Articles 371-B and 371-C provide for special committees in the Legislative Assemblies of Assam and Manipur and similiarly other provisions are there for other states.If a new Article 371 provision is introduced specifically for Ladakh, it would be significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory rather than a state.The proposal would therefore require a constitutional arrangement tailored to a Union Territory, potentially making it different from the existing Article 371 provisions that primarily apply to states.

Houthis seize Red Sea port city in push to seize Bab el-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:24:28 UTC
20:24:28 KST

The Houthis' latest offensive is meant to replicate Iran's Hormuz blockade in the Bab el-Mandeb, with Red Sea coastal towns and islands in the crucial waterway among their next military objectives.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday and were advancing towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a Yemeni military source said.
Witnesses said they saw Houthi forces entering the city while chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
The city which has been held by Yemen’s internationally recognised government has been under sustained attack since early August, when more than 25 missiles struck it in a matter of days and forced port operations to halt.
The Yemeni government is yet to publicly confirm Mokha has fallen.
The Houthis, who control about one-third of Yemen's territory — albeit the most densely populated parts — are vying to seize and potentially disrupt the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
Together with Hormuz, cargo traffic through Bab el-Mandeb accounts for one quarter of daily petroleum and crude shipments, and nearly one-third of the world's maritime trade.
The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.
Yemen's government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".
Major-General Sadeq Duwaid, spokesman for the Yemeni government-affiliated National Resistance Forces controlling areas adjacent to the strait, earlier warned that the Houthi siege of Mokha was a key manoeuvre to build operational footing along the Red Sea coast.
"Through their continued attacks on Mokha and its port, the Houthi militia seeks to establish a presence along the shores of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and transform the area into a situation resembling that of the Strait of Hormuz," Major-General Duwaid said in mid-August.
The coastal town of Dhubab and Perim Island — a rocky volcanic island that sits in the middle of the strait and divides it into two shipping channels — are now considered to be the Houthis' central military objective.
Fighting continues to escalate
Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis launched a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
They also launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held territory.
The Houthis reported on Thursday that about 40 airstrikes were launched by Saudi forces in a fresh salvo.
"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.
On Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of "potential danger" in two areas, Khamis Mushait and Abha.
Inching towards Bab el-Mandeb
The Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.
A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 had largely halted years of active warfare, yet it never resulted in a lasting political settlement.
The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they held territory less than 100 kilometres away.
The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the internationally recognised government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".
Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.
The group previously severely disrupted cargo traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb with their campaign against what they said was Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was a show of support for Palestinians.

Such evacuations can appear counterintuitive to people outside Ukraine. However, Russian drones are now deliberately pursuing trains. A direct hit can ignite a locomotive or passenger carriage within minutes, leaving those inside little time to escape.
The purpose of abandoning train carriages is to put as much distance as possible between individuals and the train, which may be the intended target.

Ukraine’s railway system continues operating despite repeated attacks and prolonged air raid alerts. Services are frequently delayed, rerouted, or temporarily halted, while damaged locomotives, tracks, and power systems are repaired.
For passengers, journeys increasingly depend not only on schedules but also on drone-monitoring reports and rapid evacuation orders.

AI firms ‘begging to be regulated,’ feel ‘compelled to race’ toward deadly technology: Ex-Anthropic researcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:22:09 UTC
20:22:09 KST

A former Anthropic researcher who warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could threaten humanity said Wednesday that AI companies are genuinely seeking regulation but feel compelled to keep competing for fear of falling behind their rivals.
“These people are also completely genuine when they are begging to be regulated,” Jacob Coxon, 27, told CNN's Anderson Cooper.
“They find themselves in this scenario where they're compelled to race towards building a deadly technology, and they would love for some sort of international body to allow them to approach it at a reasonable pace,” he said.
Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday after previously working at OpenAI, drew widespread attention with a post on US social media platform X saying the two companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
The post had garnered 143 million views by Thursday. His remarks have also received support from other AI safety researchers.
Evan Hubinger, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, responded to Coxon's post on X by saying he personally estimated the risk of AI killing all humans at more than 10% within the next decade, while acknowledging that current models pose a low extinction risk.
In the CNN interview, Coxon sought to clarify that he does not believe existing AI systems are capable of causing human extinction.
“Right now, there's no risk of extinction,” he said. “The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages in infrastructure, but they're not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction.”
His concern, he said, is the speed at which those capabilities are advancing and what could happen if AI systems become capable of improving themselves.
“I think what's just crazy is to look at the rate of progress, and there is a very real possibility that in the immediate future ... next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen,” Coxon said.
Asked how such a scenario could unfold, Coxon pointed to what he described as a real-world precedent.
"The precise scenario sounds a little bit like science fiction. It sounds like something that's not real, but I think it is frighteningly real, and it's easiest to understand it if you think about real things that happened two months ago," he said.
"Two months ago, OpenAI agents, AIs hacked into third-party infrastructure entirely of their own accord, and this was like a concentrated hacking spree that they carried out of their own volition. I think that if you extrapolate into the future the level of capabilities of these AIs, with the same independent volition, they could cause extreme havoc."
He described the most concerning possibility as AI being used to conduct AI research itself, allowing systems to progressively increase their own capabilities.
“The AI just gets smarter and smarter with no human involvement necessary,” Coxon said.
“A couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they're close to replacing them,” he said, adding that humans were still needed but that “quite plausibly within a year, we'll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas.”   
Coxon raised concerns before resignation
According to an NBC News report on Wednesday, Coxon had expressed similar concerns privately before his resignation in messages to Anthropic colleagues on the workplace platform Slack.
“I've recently become more concerned about the degree and imminence of this risk,” he wrote, according to the report, warning that without international coordination, superintelligent AI could pose a risk of human extinction.
He also said he planned to publicly criticize the industry while making clear that he did not blame individual Anthropic employees for the situation.
Coxon said he had initially intended simply to leave Anthropic rather than make a public intervention.
“I thought I can't be part of this anymore,” he told CNN. “I did not expect it to go this viral.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders has cited Coxon's post and renewed calls for Congress to act on AI regulation.
A recent NBC poll also found that 70% of American adults are more worried about AI than excited by it.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia has sought similar wet-lease agreements with several countries since international sanctions were imposed after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, disabling Russian airlines from legally accessing foreign aircraft and spare parts, Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported, citing The Moscow Times.
Moscow has approached countries in Central Asia, as well as Qatar, Kuwait, and Ethiopia, over such arrangements.
Ethiopia reportedly rejected Russia’s proposal in summer 2025, saying the government did not have the authority to order the state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to lease out aircraft.
There were also concerns that such an arrangement could expose the airline to US secondary sanctions.
So far, there have been no known agreements under which an airline from another country has leased aircraft to a Russian carrier under a wet-lease arrangement.
Russia’s aircraft shortage
Russian airlines have been cut off from not only purchasing new Boeing and Airbus aircraft, but also from legally obtaining parts and servicing many of the planes already in their fleets.
Ukraine Hits Russian Oil, Port Infrastructure in Strikes Stretching From Arctic to Caspian
Foreign-made aircraft account for roughly two-thirds of Russia’s civilian aircraft fleet and carry around 90% of the country’s air passengers.
Nearly 20% of the aircraft operated by Russia’s largest airlines have been grounded because of difficulties obtaining spare parts, according to calculations made by Russian newspaper Kommersant.
Of the 673 aircraft operated by Russia’s 11 largest airlines, which account for more than 90% of the country’s passenger traffic, 130 were not in service during the summer, Kommersant reported.
Under normal circumstances, airlines typically have no more than around 10% of their fleets out of service at the same time for scheduled maintenance.
Excluding Aeroflot, Russia’s largest airline group, eight carriers had nearly one-third of their fleets grounded, with 93 of 322 aircraft out of service.
In April 2025, Russian President Vladimir Putin allowed Russian airlines to lease aircraft from foreign companies under wet-lease arrangements, when previously, such leasing was permitted only between Russian airlines and only for domestic flights.

Space-based surveillance: Dhruva to get key systems worth €5m from Safran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:18:20 UTC
20:18:20 KST

French aerospace major Safran Space signed key contracts worth over €5 million with Indian space-tech startup Dhruva Space.
BENGALURU: French firm Safran Space, under contracts worth more than €5 million, will supply critical systems, including optical payloads, for satellites being built as part of India’s Space-Based Surveillance-3 (SBS-3) programme by Dhruva Space, a release from the French President’s Office has confirmed.The contracts, signed during the International Space Summit in Paris, cover communication systems, inertial navigation units, optical payloads and ground stations for the constellation, which is planned to be deployed between 2027 and 2030.SBS-3, a strategic project approved by the Cabinet Committee on Security, will comprise 52 satellites in low Earth and geostationary orbits and is aimed at providing the armed forces with persistent surveillance, secure communications and greater situational awareness across India’s land and maritime areas of interest.The programme marks an expansion of the private sector’s role in India’s strategic space capabilities. Of the 52 satellites, 31 are to be built by private industry, with the remaining 21 being built by Isro. The private-sector allocation has been divided among three companies: Antaris will build 15 satellites, while Pixxel and Dhruva Space will build eight each.Dhruva’s eight satellites therefore form part of the private-sector component of the larger SBS-3 constellation, rather than a separate constellation.
The programme is expected to improve the frequency with which strategic areas can be observed and strengthen India’s ability to monitor developments along its borders and across the Indian Ocean Region.The Safran contracts will give Dhruva access to a range of French technologies for the satellites and associated ground infrastructure. Safran said the cooperation illustrates the rise of Indian New Space and the ability of French industry to support the development of India’s sovereign space capabilities. The company also said the partnership could open the way to further cooperation under future phases of the SBS programme.The Paris summit also produced two other India-related announcements. French launch-services provider RIDE! signed an agreement to launch two satellites for TakeMeToSpace, an Indian company developing orbital data centres. The deal builds on RIDE!’s collaboration with Indian space companies, including the launch of a European atmospheric re-entry capsule aboard Isro’s PSLV.
Separately, French Earth-observation company U-Space and Indian company Axiscades signed a commercial cooperation agreement to explore the Indian microsatellite market, addressing both commercial and institutional demand.Together, the three announcements point to a widening India-France space relationship spanning strategic surveillance, satellite launches and commercial satellite manufacturing, with Indian private companies increasingly at the centre of the cooperation.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

From Al-Hudaydah to Mocha: Rapid developments reshape Yemen’s military map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:18:04 UTC
20:18:04 KST

- Yemeni media reports Houthi control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah, potentially giving group control over entire Al-Hudaydah province
- Houthi forces reportedly reach strategic Mocha port near Bab al-Mandab Strait after government forces withdraw south toward Lahej
Yemen has seen rapid military developments along its western coast, changing control of key areas as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.
Yemeni media reported Thursday that Houthi forces had reached the strategic Mocha port in southwestern Taiz province, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, after taking control of the Hays and Al-Khawkhah districts in southern Al-Hudaydah province.
The developments, if confirmed, would give the Houthis control over the entire Al-Hudaydah province on the Red Sea, strengthening their position along Yemen’s western coast and bringing them closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Before the reported advance, Hays and Al-Khawkhah were controlled by government forces, particularly the National Resistance Forces led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh.
The developments are part of a rapidly escalating military confrontation between the Houthis and government forces, reviving concerns that the conflict could widen after years of relative calm.   
Hays and Al-Khawkhah  
The Houthis took control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah following the withdrawal of government forces from the two districts amid intense fighting, according to local sources.  
The independent Al-Masdar Online website reported that Houthis had taken control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah in southern Al-Hudaydah, as well as large areas of districts in western Taiz.  
It added that the group had reached Mocha port after government forces withdrew south toward Lahej province.  
The strategic importance of Hays and Al-Khawkhah lies in their location along Yemen’s western coast. Control of the two districts could allow the Houthis to advance more rapidly toward areas of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz while opening new routes toward coastal areas near Bab al-Mandab.   
Toward Mocha  
Following the reported withdrawal of government forces from Hays and Al-Khawkhah, Houthi forces advanced toward the strategic city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, near Bab al-Mandab.  
Al-Masdar Online reported that the Houthis had reached Mocha port, while other Yemeni media outlets reported that the group had taken control of the city, coinciding with the withdrawal of government forces toward Lahej.  
There was no official comment from the government or the Houthis on the developments in Mocha.  
Mocha holds major military significance as it is one of Yemen’s closest cities to Bab al-Mandab, one of the world’s most important maritime passages linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and carrying ships traveling to and from the Suez Canal.   
Forces regroup  
Earlier Thursday, the 2 December news agency, which reports on the government-aligned National Resistance Forces, quoted Saleh as ordering armed forces along the western coast to “reorganize their ranks.”  
Saleh said the western coastal forces, including the National Resistance, Giants Brigades, Nation’s Shield forces and units from the Taiz military axis, had suffered significant casualties in recent days while confronting a Houthi offensive that he said was “planned by Iran.”  
He ordered the formation of an alternative command center in a secure location to regroup the forces in consultation with the Arab coalition leadership and Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council.  
According to the agency, joint forces had already established a command center south of Mocha in Taiz following Houthi “breakthroughs” across several combat fronts under heavy fire involving various types of weapons.  
The media office of the government authority in Al-Hudaydah, meanwhile, said military units operating on the Hays front in southern Al-Hudaydah and western Taiz were being reorganized.  
It said the move was part of a plan to organize deployments, redistribute forces, conduct a coordinated field operation and reorganize defense.   
Al-Jawf front  
The Houthi advance along parts of the western coast came a day after government forces announced that they had captured large areas in Al-Jawf province in northeastern Yemen, near the Saudi border.  
On Wednesday, the Yemeni army said in a statement that its forces had captured the Al-Mutahaffat area, Al-Masariya Hill and adjacent hills north of Al-Faraid Hill in the northern Al-Labanat Al-Olya area of Al-Jawf.  
It said government forces had also taken control of earthworks and trenches stretching about 20 kilometers from Al-Duhaida positions through Al-Saara to Bir Al-Maraziq, east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.  
The army said its forces were continuing military operations amid heavy human and material losses among Houthi fighters, claiming that several fighters had been captured or neutralized and others wounded.  
It added that government warplanes had carried out targeted airstrikes against Houthi gatherings and positions, destroying several military vehicles and pieces of combat equipment.  
Al-Jawf is strategically important because it shares a land border with Saudi Arabia and lies near the Houthi-controlled provinces of Saada, Amran and Sanaa. It also borders the oil-rich provinces of Hadhramaut and Marib, which are under government influence.  
The developments come amid Yemen’s broadest escalation since 2022, when a UN-sponsored truce was initiated before the peace process stalled and military confrontations resumed in July.    
Map of control  
The Houthis control most of northern and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Dhamar, Al-Bayda, Ibb and Al-Mahwit, as well as Al-Hudaydah and most of Hajjah and Saada provinces. They also control areas of Taiz, Lahej and Al-Dhalea.  
Government forces and their allies, meanwhile, control the interim capital Aden in the south, as well as Al-Mahrah in the far east, Hadhramaut, Shabwa and Abyan, in addition to most of Lahej, Taiz and Al-Dhalea provinces.  
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Türkiye targets quantum, space tech in new research and development push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:18:03 UTC
20:18:03 KST

Ankara prepares to overhaul its research and development (R&D) incentives to foster the development of critical technologies, especially targeting space and quantum areas, to reduce the country’s foreign reliance, according to its three-year economic roadmap.
The Medium-Term Programme (MTP) covering 2027-2029 aims to strengthen the Turkish technology ecosystem through targeted investments and entrepreneurship to meet the sector’s rapidly evolving requirements through state funding for existing R&D centres, tech development zones and business incubators.
The roadmap outlines the need to fund early-stage tech startups with massive potential to become unicorns, or companies with a valuation of $1 billion.
Plans are under way to maintain a specialisation model to help large-scale private R&D centres and technoparks focus on developing innovative solutions in emerging fields, with state research funding directed towards deep technologies including cybersecurity, autonomous systems, quantum computing, hypersonic systems and next-generation materials.
Ankara will also support the fields of nanotechnology, biotechnology, sensors, chips, batteries, nuclear and renewable energy technologies, as well as blockchain and robotics.
The MTP plans to establish strategic collaborations among research institutions, universities and private-sector companies working in these fields.
Türkiye’s National Space Programme will involve research initiatives on developing and commercialising high-value satellite and space technology to expand domestic production capacity in this area.
Ankara also plans to establish the research infrastructure necessary to build next-generation railway technologies and eco-friendly propulsion systems to contribute to meeting net-zero emissions targets in transportation.
The MTP outlines new financial mechanisms to be introduced to evaluate, fund and commercialise local patents, trademarks and industrial designs.
The Turkish government will use a university-industry collaboration model to fund specialised research facilities, product-focused platforms and state-of-the-art testing labs.
Türkiye aims to seek global research collaborations in strategic technologies to cement the global footprint of its domestic ecosystem and expand its overall development capacity.

In Kryvyi Rih, five people were injured, as apartment buildings and private homes were damaged.

The Houthis are testing the limits of Saudi restraint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:17:23 UTC
20:17:23 KST

The Houthis are testing the limits of Saudi restraint
Riyadh needs to restore deterrence without being pulled back into a prolonged Yemen war.
The renewed escalation in Yemen is no longer simply a Yemeni battlefield development. For Saudi Arabia, it is becoming a direct test of national security, economic resilience and the kingdom’s ability to prevent the wider regional war from spilling further across its borders.
The latest Houthi attacks have demonstrated this clearly. Missiles and drones have hit civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring dozens of civilians and causing fires and temporary disruption at energy facilities. The attacks came as fighting intensified in Yemen and around the western coast, while the Houthis continued to threaten maritime traffic in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia therefore faces two interconnected threats: Attacks on its territory and attempts to disrupt the maritime routes on which regional and international trade depends.
This creates a difficult strategic equation for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has spent the past several years trying to move away from direct military involvement in Yemen and towards diplomacy, de-escalation and support for a political settlement. A return to an open-ended war would contradict that strategy and impose unnecessary political and economic costs.
But restraint cannot mean accepting repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
A different security environment
The security challenge today differs considerably from the first years of the Yemen war.
Saudi Arabia has strengthened its air and missile defences, improved coordination between its military and security institutions and accumulated considerable experience in countering drones and ballistic missiles. It is therefore much better prepared to defend its territory than it was a decade ago.
Yet the Houthi threat has also evolved.
The group possesses a combination of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and increasingly sophisticated drones. Even when most incoming weapons are intercepted, relatively inexpensive systems can impose disproportionate defensive costs and create uncertainty around airports, industrial facilities, border communities and energy infrastructure.
This means Saudi security cannot depend on interception alone. No air defence system can guarantee a perfect shield indefinitely.
The strategic objective must therefore be deterrence: Convincing the Houthis that attacks on Saudi territory will impose costs greater than any political or military benefit they expect to obtain.
This does not necessarily require returning to the large-scale military campaign of previous years. Riyadh has more options today. These include intelligence operations, strengthening Yemeni government forces, improving border security, disrupting missile and drone supply networks and, where necessary, conducting proportionate operations against facilities directly involved in attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The distinction is important. Saudi Arabia does not need to choose between doing nothing and returning to a full-scale war.
The economic front
The economic consequences are equally important.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s largest energy exporters, which makes attacks on its oil infrastructure internationally significant even when physical damage is limited. The latest attacks affected energy facilities and contributed to renewed concern in already nervous global oil markets.
There is an apparent paradox here: Regional instability can push oil prices higher and temporarily increase Saudi oil revenues. But higher prices caused by war should not be confused with economic benefit.
Saudi Arabia’s economic strategy under Vision 2030 depends increasingly on stability, investment, tourism, logistics, technology and the development of major projects outside the oil sector. Persistent missile and drone attacks can raise insurance and transport costs and affect perceptions of regional risk even if the kingdom’s underlying economy remains strong.
The greater strategic concern is maritime security.
Saudi Arabia occupies a strategic position between two of the world’s most important energy corridors: The Strait of Hormuz to the east and Bab al-Mandeb to the west. Disruption of both routes represents a serious challenge not only for Saudi Arabia but for the global economy.
This is why the Red Sea dimension of the Yemen conflict is particularly important. Bab al-Mandeb connects the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. A sustained Houthi ability to threaten shipping there would increase freight and insurance costs and potentially divert vessels around Africa.
Saudi Arabia, however, possesses an important strategic advantage: Its energy infrastructure is not completely dependent on the Gulf. The kingdom can transport significant quantities of oil through its East-West pipeline to terminals on the Red Sea. This provides an alternative to Hormuz and gives Riyadh greater strategic flexibility.
That advantage does not, however, eliminate Saudi Arabia’s exposure to insecurity elsewhere in the Red Sea, including around Bab al-Mandeb.
Protecting Bab al-Mandeb should therefore be understood not simply as a Saudi or Yemeni interest but as an international economic and security requirement.
Avoiding the Houthi trap
The greatest danger for Riyadh may be political rather than purely military.
The Houthis could benefit from drawing Saudi Arabia back into an extensive war. It would allow them to portray the conflict once again as a confrontation between Yemen and an external power rather than a struggle among Yemenis over the future of their state.
Saudi Arabia should avoid this trap.
Confronting the Houthis must remain fundamentally a Yemeni responsibility. The internationally recognised Yemeni government and its forces should carry the principal burden of confronting Houthi expansion on the ground, while Saudi Arabia provides political, economic, intelligence and defensive support.
This is particularly important on the western coast. If the Houthis consolidate their military position around strategic areas overlooking the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, the consequences will extend far beyond Yemen.
The objective should not be to retake Sanaa through another large-scale air campaign or restart an indefinite regional war. It should be to prevent the Houthis from using military force to change the regional balance, threaten neighbouring states or threaten international maritime arteries.
Diplomacy backed by deterrence
Saudi policy is therefore likely to operate on several tracks simultaneously.
First, Riyadh will continue strengthening its air and missile defences and protecting critical infrastructure. Second, it can increase support for Yemeni government forces while avoiding unnecessary direct involvement in ground combat. Third, it will seek broader regional and international cooperation to secure the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
At the same time, diplomatic channels should remain open.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly demonstrated its preference for a negotiated settlement in Yemen. But negotiations are sustainable only when both sides believe that escalation carries unacceptable costs.
Diplomacy, therefore, must be backed by credible military power.
Saudi Arabia has strong incentives to prevent Yemen from becoming another permanent front in the wider regional confrontation. The kingdom’s economic transformation requires stability, while its geopolitical interests require secure borders, uninterrupted energy exports and freedom of navigation.
But the same logic that encourages restraint also places limits on it.
If attacks on Saudi cities, civilians and energy infrastructure continue, Riyadh will increasingly regard the issue not as intervention in the Yemeni civil war but as the defence of Saudi territory.
That distinction will shape what comes next.
Saudi Arabia does not need another prolonged Yemen war. Nor does Yemen. But avoiding one requires restoring deterrence while preserving the possibility of a political settlement.
The most effective Saudi strategy, therefore, is neither unlimited escalation nor passive restraint. It is calibrated pressure: Defend the kingdom, strengthen legitimate Yemeni institutions, protect the Red Sea, keep diplomatic channels open and make clear that attacks on Saudi territory will carry consequences.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

UK ministers explore raising price of water for some users amid shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:14:04 UTC
20:14:04 KST

Ministers are exploring making water more expensive for some users, in the face of severe supply shortages.
Despite the UK being a famously wet country, the precarious nature of the water supply has been made particularly acute this summer, with almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales in drought and 27 million people facing restrictions on their water use.
As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency has estimated that, without action, England’s water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055.
Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency, said that to plug this severe and growing gap, the value of water needed to increase.
“If someone wants an abstraction licence from the Environment Agency, what they pay for is the cost of producing the licence. They don’t pay anything towards the value of that water,” she said.
While millions of households in England are paying record levels for their water bills, Wakeham said that, for big industrial customers, the more water they used, the less they paid.
There was a “lively conversation” going on about whether we could “completely reframe the way we value and pay for water”.
“It’s the beginning of a conversation, but ministers have asked us to look at the value of water and how our abstraction licensing system works,” she said.
The Guardian recently revealed that less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people. Some of these businesses, which include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, face no requirements to cut their consumption.
With the government committed to make England an AI superpower, there are also questions about where water-hungry datacentres will get their resources from. Water UK, the body representing the UK water industry, warned the UK would not have enough water for future datacentres.
“The reason datacentres are water-hungry is because water is so cheap,” said Wakeham.
Dr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist and policy adviser, said: “Every day, people are doing their bit to save water, but they are being hit with higher bills and hosepipe bans while big business gets cheap water access. At a time when the country is facing water stress due to climate change, it is absurd that major companies have access to water that is cheaper for them, per litre, the more they use. This has to change. The whole abstraction policy and licensing needs to be rewritten from a blank sheet of paper to make it fit for a country facing summer droughts and a biodiversity crisis.”
Environment Agency permitting means datacentres are required to use drinking water only. Water UK has estimated that datacentres in England use 6.6m litres of drinking water every day. With the government’s ambition to triple datacentre capacity by 2030, this could increase to 19.8m litres a day. Jon Chappell, the trade body’s deputy director, said this was “unforgivable” and a “genuine failing of government”.
Wakeham agreed there was an issue with drinking water being used for cooling and industrial supply, and said the agency was “working with the government to look at different ways of pricing and valuing water to make sure that the right water goes to the right places”. She said this could result in water becoming more expensive for industrial users.
“The overarching message is that water is so cheap that often it’s not managed, because it’s cheaper just to use more water,” Wakeham said.

====================================================================================================

IDF Intel. Chief Shlomi Binder's crusade to block Iran from getting nukes - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:13:19 UTC
20:13:19 KST

From the mid-1990s until August 2024, a running line of top Mossad and IDF officials made it their mission to block Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
When Shlomi Binder was sworn in as the Military Intelligence chief in August 2024, he took up the baton and has pursued the crusade with a tenacity possibly unmatched in history.
There have been some great Mossad and IDF officials in office who have accomplished extraordinary missions to keep the Islamic Republic’s nuclear charge at bay.
But Binder is the man who ordered and managed the bombing of Natanz, Isfahan, and dozens of other sites, and provided the critical intelligence used by the US to bomb Fordow in June 2025.
He is also the major-general who directed the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the dissection of Iran’s ballistic missile and wider military apparatus.
To be sure, the air force dropped the bombs, and the Mossad delivered on key special missions. But if Israel struck Iran around a staggering 4,000 times in June 2025 and around an unthinkable 18,000 times in 2026, the intelligence for well over 90% of those strikes came from Binder and his juggernaut IDF intelligence teams.
Where has Binder’s crusade left Iran’s nuclear weapons program, five months after the 2026 war and 15 months after the 2025 war?
The Jerusalem Post has learned that the positives are that Iran currently has no centrifuges enriching uranium, all or most of its more enriched uranium is not yet easily accessible, and that most of the regime’s nuclear facilities were destroyed or forced out of operation by the 2025-2026 strikes.
There has been no period of time in decades where enrichment was brought down to zero.
For decades, its facilities expanded and never really contracted, and while operations attributed to the Mossad managed to take one or more facilities offline for temporary periods, at no point was the whole active program broken or shuttered.
Even during “pause” periods from 2003 to 2007 and from 2015 to 2018, large aspects of Iran’s nuclear program were frozen, not broken, and new aspects were almost always being built, even if under the radar.
However, the Post has learned that despite these achievements, future concerns are greater than hoped for right after the 2025-2026 operations.
While the vast majority of Iran’s 20,000 centrifuge fleet was destroyed or rendered unusable, a not insignificant number of centrifuges survived deep underground.
Moreover, multiple sources have expressed concern to the Post that even if only a few hundred advanced IR-6 centrifuges (for enriching uranium) can be salvaged and hooked up again at some medium-term point, that could be enough, at some later undefined point, to secretly weaponize enough uranium for a bomb.
Also, multiple sources are worried that the Iranians could pull off some kind of clandestine digging mission to extract their more enriched uranium from under rubble and underground in a way that sidesteps US and other surveillance.
Regular satellite reports by the Institute for Science and International Security and others show that Iran has added structures on an ongoing basis to block certain areas from continuous satellite coverage.
These same open-source reports have noted the Iranians digging in a variety of areas, sometimes not all that close to the main parts of a nuclear facility that was struck.
Digging underground from a distance could take months or years to smuggle out the 60% enriched uranium, or in some areas 20% enriched uranium. But only maybe around one tenth would need to be clandestinely transferred to have a basis for a nuclear weapon.
Binder’s view is not that Iran is likely to outwit American and Israeli intelligence, but neither does he want to underestimate or discount Iranians’ often surprising and powerful resourcefulness.
That means that the key to the whole picture to some extent is again shifting from uranium enrichment to weapons group issues.
One of the highest priorities – but less reported aspects – of the Israeli attacks on Iran’s nuclear program sites was hitting not only the enrichment facilities, but also the facilities for converting enriched uranium into uranium metal and into hemispheres for use on a nuclear warhead.
Without these and other items, even large quantities of weaponized uranium will do Iran no good, because it will not be able to deliver the uranium 1,000 or more kilometers away in Israeli territory.
The Post understands that thwarting Tehran from rebuilding such weapons group facilities is one of Binder’s top focuses, and so far the regime has not made any serious progress on the issue.
All of this leaves a highly complex picture where the nuclear program is far more damaged than some critics have said, but where there are more gaps in that damage than top Israeli officials, political or defense, admitted right after each round of fighting.
Iran’s nuclear program was set back by some years, and its ability to reconstitute it was also set back. Yet in some ways, Iranian ingenuity has kept the threat alive and able to return, even if less broadly and with great difficulty.
Pickaxe Mountain
Major news was made in a July 13 interview on the Hugh Hewitt Show, when US President Donald Trump said, “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready,” while in another breath said, “We see no activity there.”
Pickaxe Mountain, once operational, will be the deepest underground nuclear facility the Iranians have ever built, significantly deeper than even the Fordow underground nuclear facility. It is hotly debated whether even the extremely unique and expensive 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetrator mega bunker buster bomb could penetrate it.
The second part of Trump’s statement about Iran’s nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain – that there is no activity there; or as the hawkish Institute for Science and International Security has put it, that the facility is still not operational – is the major reason that neither the US president nor Israel has ordered a strike to date, despite his first statement promising to attack.
Across the board, top US and Israeli defense sources told the Post in classified briefings earlier in the summer that there was no current threat from the site, and that the best reason to target it would, at most, be to eliminate a potential future threat.
All of these views contradicted the stunning July 14 reports by The Wall Street Journal and CNN that Israeli intelligence had told the US that Iran had moved thousands of centrifuges and also enriched uranium to Pickaxe Mountain.
In an article on the issue on July 21, none of the several sources that had told the Post that there was no current threat at Pickaxe Mountain clarified the matter, despite several attempts by the Post to get to the bottom of the dispute.
Since then, the Post has more recently clarified the issue.
Both the Mossad and IDF intelligence view Pickaxe Mountain as a strategic threat that must be removed at some point, because it is so difficult to attack.
In addition, both agencies highly prefer to do so before it becomes operational and before the Iranians manage to move sufficient assets there to operate centrifuges and enrich uranium.
The Post understands that what occurred in July was that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hoped to get Trump to strike Iran, with Pickaxe Mountain being one of the top-of-the-line potential targets.
Senior Israeli defense officials leaned into the issue also because they thought it might be a unique chance to finally rid themselves of the hovering potential threat.
It remains somewhat unclear whether Israeli political officials exaggerated how operational Pickaxe Mountain was, whether one or more Israeli defense officials assisted with this, or whether American officials afterward exaggerated what they had been told.
But as of early September, the Post understands that Pickaxe Mountain remains high on Binder’s list of concerns, but that the facility is still not operational.
One recent change is that some Israeli officials have voiced to the Post greater confidence than in the past about the ability of allied air forces to disable the facility, even if destroying it might not be possible.
All of this highlights that Binder’s view is that the Iranian threat has not passed, that any agreement that gives Tehran the right to enrich to 3.67%, like the 2015 deal, would keep the threat alive, and that Israel must be ready for the real possibility of needing to attack the Islamic Republic at some point in the not-so-distant future.
What about recent talk of Russia providing Iran with supersonic missiles which will be harder for Israel to shoot down?
No one is getting too detailed on this issue yet, and some of the challenges are just starting to evolve, but it does not yet seem to be at the top of the IDF’s list of concerns about Iran.
Regime change
While Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz, and Mossad Director Roman Gofman still mention regime change publicly and privately, that term has mostly disappeared from the IDF lexicon.
IDF officials are no less enthusiastic about the idea in theory. Regime change has the best chance of promising a long-term end to Iran threatening the Jewish state.
But IDF high command officials, including Binder, were highly skeptical that the regime would easily and quickly fall when they went to war with the Islamic Republic in early 2026, and they believe the chances of this occurring are even more dubious now.
Neither Binder nor other top IDF officials favored the plan to try to use the Kurds to foment an internal rebellion.
While Netanyahu and top officials in the Mossad believed that, along with other moves which Trump vetoed, supporting a Kurdish internal insurgency could potentially radically alter the playing field, Binder and others viewed this move as possibly propping up the regime.
The majority of Iran – regime supporters and opposition – is Shi’ite.
Just as the Kurds often see the Iranian Shi’ites as outsider oppressors, many of the Shi’ites, even those who hate the regime, hate or distrust the Iranian Kurds even more.
In other words, Binder and others in the IDF high command worried that bringing the Kurds in as an officially Israel-US sponsored kingmaker could lead to the largest group of opposition Shi’ites changing sides back into the hands of the regime.
They also noted other major issues, such as that dropping lots of bombs makes protesting harder.
While some said that careful coordination could lead to enabling protests to grow by only bombing regime oppression forces, this never really occurred in a significant way, and most protesters were just too scared and stayed home.
Of those who did not stay home, Binder and the IDF high command would note that many of the bravest protesters were killed during the largest fight between the protesters and the regime over January 8-9 or were killed or tortured after the main war ended on April 7.
None of this means that Binder and the IDF have given up on regime change.
But they believe that it will take longer than some in the Mossad believe, and compared to Netanyahu’s promises, and that in the immediate short term it may even be difficult to make progress, with progress waiting for the medium term when protesters regain their daring.
Despite these truths, Binder and the IDF high command were highly optimistic about the jump in pressure on Iran in late August-early September, with the pace of economic deterioration jumping significantly.
They hope this elevated economic pressure will give the US the upper hand in the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz and the nuclear issue.
All of the talk about the US has also crystallized a realization from Israeli intelligence: instead of leaving the Middle East, Trump has put the American military on the front lines of managing most of Israel’s conflicts with its neighbors.
With one brief 24-hour exception, Israel and Iran have not fought since April 7, whereas Washington and Tehran have been going at it at low-grade military levels sometimes for weeks on end.
The US is managing aspects of Israel’s conflicts with Hezbollah and Hamas, and trying to encourage deconfliction and cooperation between Jerusalem and Damascus.
Lebanon
The UN has said that 360,000 Lebanese remain uprooted from their homes due to the war and the IDF security zone in southern Lebanon.
At the height of the invasion, over 1.1 million Lebanese had been uprooted.
The Post has learned that IDF intelligence estimates that around 500,000 Lebanese have still not returned to their homes, some because they cannot, and some out of fear of IDF forces nearby, or because of low-grade fighting between Hezbollah and the IDF.
This factor is the single largest pressure on Hezbollah to reduce its threat to Israel.
Despite Iranian attempts to protect Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Post learned, a little before it became public last week, that the IDF succeeded in a slow and grueling siege to defeat a sizable Hezbollah force that had been trapped in a standoff with the IDF at Ali Taher Ridge for months.
IDF intelligence correctly analyzed that while an overt and dramatic attack on Ali Taher Ridge might have given Iran an opening to attack Israel in support of Hezbollah, a quiet and gradual wearing down of those Hezbollah forces fell under the Iranians’ radar, or provided them with a face-saving outcome where they could look the other way.
Hezbollah’s FPV fiber cable drone threat is far from gone. But whenever Hezbollah has launched drones, the IDF has responded harshly, either striking a dozen Hezbollah targets or forcing another Shi’ite village to evacuate the area near where the drone launched from.
Binder and the IDF high command are skeptical that the Lebanese army will succeed in evacuating Hezbollah from southern Lebanon areas where it is still operating.
This could leave a standoff regarding how long the IDF remains in parts of southern Lebanon and regarding what conditions will be required of Lebanon-Hezbollah for ongoing partial withdrawals.
There is a similar standoff with Hamas in Gaza. However, even if no one expects Hamas to disappear, Binder and the IDF high command believe they have stronger cards to play versus Hamas given its weaker position.
Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey alliance
While much of the world has viewed the Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey alliance as another move by Riyadh to try to deter Iran from striking it in the future, as it has in 2026, Binder and the IDF high command have specific Israeli concerns.
For example, what if Iran joins the alliance? Although it was built to deter the Islamic Republic, in the messy world of Middle East politics, both sides could decide that integrating Tehran could have advantages.
These advantages for the Saudis and Iran would likely be clear negatives for Israel and could even complicate aspects of relations with the US, if Washington gives critical nuclear and F-35 weapons technologies to Riyadh.
More generally, such an alliance could reduce Israeli influence in the region.
Though highly unlikely, there is even a slim chance that Egypt could join the alliance, which could undermine decades of close Jerusalem-Cairo military cooperation, as set down in the Camp David Accords.
Artificial intelligence revolution
Binder has mostly been known to the public for transforming IDF intelligence from its pre-October 7 state of “bubble thought” and complete reliance on technology to rebuilding human intelligence collection and elevating branches that question conventional wisdom.
However, he is also engineering a new AI revolution in IDF intelligence.
The key is not only using AI to perform data mining against targets, but also to shape human-AI agent relationships so that most or all IDF intelligence officials’ strategic and tactical visions broaden to see and predict big-picture trends before they happen.
In many ways, Binder has brought IDF intelligence back from the brink after October 7 to new highs, now and moving into the future.

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:12:29 UTC
20:12:29 KST

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE
Sept 10 - Algeria said on Thursday it had decided to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates after what it described as a series of "provocative or hostile" actions by Abu Dhabi despite "repeated warnings".
The foreign ministry said the UAE's actions had reached a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable and that it had "exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations."
The UAE ambassador was summoned to the ministry, informed of the decision and given 48 hours to comply, the foreign ministry said.
The UAE Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
Relations between the two countries have come under growing strain in recent years, with Algerian media outlets sharply criticising the UAE and accusing it of seeking to sow regional discord.
Algiers and Abu Dhabi have also taken differing positions on several regional issues. Algeria opposes normalisation with Israel, while the UAE and Algeria's regional rival Morocco established diplomatic ties with Israel under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
The two countries are also on opposing sides of the decades-old Western Sahara dispute. The UAE supports Morocco's claim to sovereignty over the territory where it has a consulate, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks an independent Western Sahara.
The two countries' interests have increasingly intersected in the Sahel, where the UAE has expanded ties with several governments in recent years, while Algeria's relations with some of its southern neighbours have become strained following a series of military coups.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid said last year his country's relations with all Gulf states were warm except for one — a thinly veiled reference to the UAE.
He described ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as "brotherly", while accusing the unnamed country of meddling in Algeria's internal affairs and seeking to destabilise it.
In February, Algeria began the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE that was signed in Abu Dhabi in May 2013. REUTERS

Market for Russian helicopters in India could reach 5,000 aircraft

11:10:23 UTC
20:10:23 KST

NEW DELHI, September 10. /TASS/. India's potential demand for Russian helicopters could amount to around 5,000 aircraft, Tatarstan Industry and Trade Minister Oleg Korobchenko told TASS.
He previously said that Tatarstan was exploring the possibility of localizing production of Russian helicopters in India. These include the Mi-38, Mi-8, Mi-34, and Ansat helicopters.
"We have more than 1,000 helicopters in Russia and a population of 150 mln, while they have a population of 1.5 bln. So if we were to compare the figures even at 30%, and they had the same proportion as we do in Russia, they would accordingly need at least 5,000 helicopters to transport people. Five thousand helicopters would be a huge market for us," he said on the sidelines of the Innoprom India international industrial exhibition.
According to the minister, Tatarstan intends to work with the Indian side on options for localizing Russian helicopter production, maintenance services and technology transfers. The potential volume of investment has yet to be determined. "Our task now is to explore as many possibilities as possible so that India's civil aviation market is receptive to resolving this issue with our Russian helicopters. If that happens, we can then reach agreements on both the market and investment," Korobchenko said.
He added that developing local production and service infrastructure would help expand the presence of Russian helicopters in the Indian market and strengthen cooperation between the two countries.
The Innoprom India international exhibition is being held in New Delhi from September 9 to 11. TASS is the event's general information agency.

Fighting has intensified across western and northern Yemen in recent days, in one of the sharpest escalations since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities.

====================================================================================================

World Insights: From fragile calm to widening war, can Yemen's escalation be contained?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:09:58 CST
20:09:58 KST

by Murad Abdo
ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- After more than four years of fragile calm along Yemen's major front lines, fierce fighting between government forces and the Houthis has spread across the country's western and northern regions, while the Houthis have resumed large-scale attacks inside Saudi Arabia.
Analysts say the latest escalation is putting mounting strain on the informal Saudi-Houthi understandings forged in the wake of the UN-brokered truce in 2022, and should the latest exchange of attacks and retaliatory strikes evolve into a sustained cycle, the risk of a broader escalation would increase substantially.
CURRENT SITUATION
The latest escalation first gathered momentum in western Yemen, where intense fighting erupted in southwestern Taiz province and neighboring Red Sea province of Hodeidah. Houthi forces sought to cut key roads linking Taiz with the government-held Red Sea port of Mocha and advance toward territory near Bab al-Mandab.
"The battle for Bab al-Mandab is not simply about gaining territory inside Yemen," Aden-based political analyst Muqbil Naji told Xinhua. "Whoever can threaten this waterway acquires leverage that extends well beyond Yemen's borders."
The fighting did not remain confined to western Yemen. Government forces subsequently launched a major offensive in Al-Jawf, a northern province bordering Saudi Arabia and located east of the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Fighting has also intensified on other fronts.
The widening battlefield has changed the military dynamics. The Houthis initially pressed their offensive in western Yemen toward areas near Bab al-Mandab, but additional fronts subsequently opened elsewhere, forcing them to redistribute forces.
"Opening multiple fronts by Yemen's government will weaken the Houthis," said Abdul-Salam Mohamad, chairman of the Abaad Studies and Research Center.
As military pressure expanded inside Yemen, the Houthis widened the confrontation beyond the country's borders. The group said Tuesday it fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military and energy facilities across southern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities said attacks on civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran wounded 73 people and caused fires at several energy facilities.
"The attacks on Saudi Arabia should not be viewed separately from what is happening on the ground in Yemen," Naji said, adding that by increasing the costs for Riyadh, the Houthis could be seeking to create a new equation in which Saudi Arabia has greater incentive to restrain military pressure from Yemeni government forces.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg on Monday described the renewed escalation as "extremely alarming," warning that increasingly intense clashes threatened to expand the conflict and further complicate prospects for a political settlement.
BEHIND THE ESCALATION
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government.
The UN-mediated truce that began in April 2022 formally expired six months later, but relative calm largely persisted for years afterward. The period of direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation gradually gave way to an undeclared arrangement under which cross-border attacks and Saudi air operations sharply declined even though no comprehensive peace agreement was reached.
That informal arrangement now lies at the center of the current crisis. Salah Ali Salah, a researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described what remains of that relationship as a "gray area."
Salah said years of conflict management without resolving the war's fundamental political, security and economic disputes helped produce today's vulnerability. Temporary de-escalation can give the parties time to "catch their breath and reposition their military and political strategies," he said.
According to Salah, recent attacks do not necessarily mean the undeclared understandings have collapsed, but they are becoming more fragile and less capable of containing escalation. "Both Riyadh and the Houthis understood the enormous costs of returning to sustained direct warfare," he said, adding that the greater danger lies in "repeated exchanges becoming a sustained cycle of retaliation."
If that happens, Salah said, both sides could begin reassessing the informal "rules of engagement" that have helped contain direct confrontation in recent years, increasing the risk that "a calibrated escalation becomes harder to control."
For now, however, Naji believes Saudi Arabia has not yet decided to return to the open-ended military intervention seen during earlier stages of Yemen's war. "Saudi Arabia still appears to be calibrating its response," he said. "The objective at this stage seems to be deterrence and gradual pressure rather than immediately entering a decisive war."
WHERE DOES ESCALATION LEAD?
The Yemeni analysts agree that a return to the calm of recent years is becoming more difficult, but they differ on what may come next.
Mohamad outlined three possible scenarios. His most likely scenario is continued fighting followed by another temporary truce after significant changes on the battlefield. "The war might halt, or a temporary truce might be reached," he said.
In his assessment, however, such as pause would come after changes in the military balance rather than through an immediate restoration of the pre-escalation status quo.
A second possibility is a much wider war. Continued Houthi attacks inside Saudi Arabia could alter Riyadh's calculations, Mohamad said, potentially leading to stronger Saudi backing for a broad government offensive.
His third scenario -- an early Houthi move toward de-escalation and a restoration of the previous status quo -- is less likely because the military and economic conditions underlying the current confrontation have already changed. "The situation is poised to explode," Mohamad said.
Salah described "a full-scale Saudi-Houthi confrontation as the most dangerous potential outcome, though not the most likely for now." That calculation could change, he said, "if cross-border attacks persist, ground operations widen or a high-impact strike inflicts enough casualties to force either side to fundamentally reassess its response."
The risk, Salah said, is that a confrontation could develop beyond the calculations that initially produced it. A confrontation can begin with controlled attacks designed to signal resolve, he said, but retaliation and counter-retaliation could create a chain reaction that becomes increasingly difficult to stop.
According to Salah, the more likely scenario is "a prolonged period of limited, intermittent escalation." Under this scenario, the parties would continue using military pressure to gain territory and strengthen their bargaining position while keeping some channels of communication open and seeking to avoid an all-out war. ■

China

Zhao Yulong (R) speaks with an online platform editor via video link on the performance of his online video lessons at Chongshan campus of Liaoning University in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Sept. 9, 2026. Zhao Yulong, born in 1984, is a professor and doctoral supervisor of Liaoning University, whose academic focus lies in fiction and traditional Chinese operas in Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911). His recent work has centered on the research on the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West," and how its stories shifted and spread across different ethnic groups, regions and media forms.
Alongside research and teaching, Zhao has also actively engaged in the promotion of this centuries-old classic to the public. He has given talks and public lectures on the tale, and posted educational audio and video lessons on Chinese social platforms, encouraging young people to read the original book and explore the old classic in a new light. Alongside research and teaching, Zhao has also actively engaged in the promotion of this centuries-old classic to the public. He has given talks and public lectures on the tale, and posted educational audio and video lessons on Chinese social platforms, encouraging young people to read the original book and explore the old classic in a new light. He often shares with his students that an open and relaxed attitude is the best way to enter the world of the book. (Photo by Zhang Qingyu/Xinhua)

IAEA board refers Iran to UN Security Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:09:09 UTC
20:09:09 KST

Breadcrumb
IAEA board refers Iran to UN Security Council
The IAEA board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance" in a diplomatic move to pile pressure on the Islamic Republic.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged to be given access.
The resolution, seen by AFP, was adopted by 23 votes in favour, three votes against and eight abstentions, two diplomats told AFP. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
It "requests the (IAEA) director general to report" Iran to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move is seen as largely symbolic as Iran allies China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against Tehran.
'Counterproductive'
Iran condemned the resolution, saying it would "not bring any results".
"This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis," Iran's representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Reza Najafi, told state television.
He also told AFP that the resolution was "completely counterproductive".
The text notes "with grave concern... Iran's continued non-compliance with its obligations" and "reiterates its call upon Iran to urgently remedy its non-compliance".
It also calls on Tehran "to engage seriously and without preconditions in talks aimed at building international confidence in the exclusively peaceful nature of Iran's nuclear programme".
The IAEA has repeatedly said that its lack of information and access poses a "proliferation concern" and has called on Iran to address this with "utmost urgency".
IAEA head Rafael Grossi on Monday said giving the Vienna-based UN nuclear agency access to key nuclear facilities in Iran would have "positive repercussions" for the Islamic Republic.
'Exercise in futility'
Before the June 2025 strikes, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%, which is close to the 90% needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67% limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
Israel and the United States have long accused Iran of wanting to build a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied having any military nuclear ambitions, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group, told AFP that "some see it (the resolution) as an opportunity to add legal pressure to economic strangulation and naval blockade to turn the screws on Iran".
"Ultimately, though, it is an exercise in futility," he added, with Russia and China "likely to ensure that Western pressure hits a wall at the Security Council".

Finland's biggest reactor taking 50-day break for scheduled maintenance
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:08:20 EEST
20:08:20 KST

Scheduled annual maintenance at Finland's largest nuclear reactor, Olkiluoto 3, began on Thursday.
The reactor will be offline for a period of around 50 days and should be wrapped up at the end of October, according to operator Teollisuuden Voima (TVO).
The company noted that scheduled maintenance of the Olkiluoto reactors often tends to raise end-user electricity prices.
According to TVO, the autumn timing of the maintenance was a result of extending its operating cycle to 18 months. OL3 was last serviced in spring 2025, with the next maintenance scheduled for March 2028.
The maintenance includes uranium fuel replacement, necessary repairs and possible modification work. Annual maintenance of Olkiluoto 1 and 2 was already carried out earlier this year.
TVO reported on Thursday that a few hours before the unit's planned disconnection, Olkiluoto 3 was automatically disconnected from electricity production due to a technical fault. The unit was already operating at low power level ahead of the planned shutdown, and the incident posed no danger.
