====================================================================================================

Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:07:29 UTC
20:07:29 KST

Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
MOSCOW – Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church’s latest show of support for President Vladimir Putin’s war.
The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.
Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince’s well-preserved remains in August, hailing them as “an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery” that reinforced the foundations of Russian history.
The Russian Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy’s right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Putin said he had incorporated into Russia in 2022, a move Kyiv rejected as an illegal land grab.
Referring to Donskoy as “the holy commander”, the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russian Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russian troops.
“A fragment of the Grand Prince’s right hand – the very same right hand with which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field – has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers’ spirits,” it said in a statement.
The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russian combat units along the more than 1,000km front line, it said.
Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War II, was declared a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988.
Patriotic push
The carefully choreographed effort to use his remains in a public relations exercise to boost patriotism and morale comes ahead of a parliamentary election later in September.
Russian military and church officials have presented the discovery as a fortuitous find that could help Russian forces prevail in Ukraine, now in the fifth year of a grinding war.
The tour also comes as Russian forces seek full control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and as diplomatic efforts to end the war have yet to yield a breakthrough.
Donskoy’s relics were carried through the streets of Moscow at the weekend in a huge Orthodox procession.
At a ceremony at a World War II memorial in Donetsk on Sept 8, Sergei Kiriyenko, Putin’s first deputy Kremlin chief of staff, joined military commanders and the Russian-installed regional head in kissing the relic and making the sign of the cross as a priest read a prayer.
“Both our military personnel and the people who live in Donbas need strengthening from above, need God’s help and the blessing of our saints,” Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol, a senior Moscow-appointed cleric, said. Donbas is a broader area incorporating Donetsk and neighbouring Luhansk which Russia controls almost in its entirety.
Elsewhere, commanders have presented Donskoy’s remains as evidence that God is on Russia’s side.
The Defence Ministry on Sept 9 released footage of troops in the Sverdlovsk region attending a church service carrying icons and Orthodox flags, alongside an interview with a commander who said the relics would support Russia’s victory.
Critics, however, have accused the Church of breaking with religious protocol to please the Kremlin. They have also questioned why Donskoy’s remains, whose location was broadly known for decades, were recovered and venerated only now, 38 years after he was declared a saint.
“By the fifth year of war, the Church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’,” Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, wrote in a note for the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, whose director Russia has designated a “foreign agent”.
“It had already sent priests to the front lines, instituted mandatory prayers for Russian victory in every church, and flown icons over cities. A state embroiled in war will try to compel all institutions, including religious ones, to participate in it.” REUTERS

Germany says NATO must ramp up defense output for ‘credible deterrence’ against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:07:10 UTC
20:07:10 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
NATO allies must accelerate defense manufacturing if the West is to keep a “credible deterrence’ against Russia, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Thursday.
Speaking to reporters alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, Wadephul said an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month had shown how serious the threat from Moscow has become. German investigators have pointed to Russian intelligence services, and Berlin has announced extensive sanctions in response.
“It is part of a pattern of increasing Russian aggression against Europe and NATO, be it drone incidents or airspace violations affecting a number of allies on the Eastern Flank,” Wadephul said. “We are also seeing an increasing number of hybrid attacks, cyberattacks, hostile activities, sabotage, disinformation campaigns, and attacks on critical infrastructure.”
He said some of those campaigns were meant to spread fear and shape public opinion ahead of recent regional elections in Germany. Wadephul thanked Rutte and other allies for standing with Berlin after Germany made its findings on the Leipzig incident public.
Allies, he said, must stay politically united and do more to build up military strength. “That means investing more, producing faster, and procuring more quickly. Ultimately, it is about credible deterrence—and that only works if we actually possess the necessary capabilities.”
Wadephul repeated that Germany, together with other European allies, will keep raising defense spending, strengthen its armed forces and take on a larger share of responsibility for security inside the alliance.
He said Berlin will continue to give Ukraine strong military support, above all air defense. That includes extra interceptor missiles before winter to protect cities and energy infrastructure, he added.

Around 40 international students unable to enroll at Ghent Uni due to visa issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:03:28 UTC
20:03:28 KST

The Faculty of Bioengineering Sciences at Ghent University is calling on the government to resolve the visa issues affecting international students as a matter of urgency. “The academic year is about to start, and we are still waiting for around 40 students from abroad,” says UGent’s Wim Hoste. “We risk missing out on top academic talent; they bring enormous added value.”
Around 40 international students unable to enroll at Ghent Uni due to visa issues
“In recent years, we have seen an increasing number of problems with visa applications from international students and researchers,” says Wim Hoste. “People from Bangladesh, India, Morocco and other African countries simply cannot get here. Yet they have passed Ghent University’s rigorous selection process and meet the strict requirements set by the authorities. Things go wrong when they apply for a visa.”
Hoste describes this as a wider problem and calls for a decisive solution. The news of the fresh problems comes after difficulties with the visa application of 13 students from Gaza, which sparked debate in the federal government. ‘This really isn’t just about Gaza. Embassies and consulates systematically forward students’ applications to the Immigration Office (DVZ). The DVZ is unable to process the files in time, which means the students cannot leave for Belgium – even though their paperwork is completely in order.’
Administrative processing can drag on
The DVZ confirms that applications are numerous and that deadlines are not always met. “Embassies and consulates grant approval when there is a very strong case. The other cases are sent to the DVZ in Brussels for assessment, often all at the same time,” says spokesperson Paulien Blondeel.
Hoste says the delays are outrageous. “Students and researchers spend months getting everything in order. They have to have 12,000 euros in a blocked account and also pay for the increasingly expensive applications. And then things go wrong in the administration. We’re missing out on top talent as a result.”
“In the meantime, the conditions on being able to stay here during their academic careers have also become stricter. Governments don’t seem to grasp that these top talents represent enormous added value. They aren’t just anyone, but people who truly excel in their disciplines.” Hoste estimates that there are nearly 10,000 foreign students and researchers working across Flanders.
‘Our knowledge-based economy needs highly skilled professionals’
Industry federations Agoria and VOKA have not commented on specific issues but support the general call for action. “Our technology companies, knowledge institutions and research centres need these high-calibre professionals to remain innovative and competitive. We cannot afford to lose them. Especially now that the recent PISA results show that the number of high-calibre professionals in our own country is declining,” says Jan Gatz of Agoria.
“In Ghent, there is a thriving (bio)tech scene where international talent is in huge demand. There is clearly competition to attract people, including from other countries. So, the red tape must be kept to a minimum,” adds Arne Oosthuyse of VOKA.
“These people are developing new techniques, procedures and materials here. We benefit from these innovations, and they also pay off. Without these students, we will quickly fall behind internationally. Our governments are making things difficult for these people, whilst other countries – such as Canada – are specifically targeting these top-tier profiles. There, they are actually allocating more money for this in the budget,” says Hoste.
Hoste disagrees with the assessment recently made by Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt (Flemish nationalist N-VA). In a report on the 13 students from Gaza who wanted to come here, she stated that she feared a domino effect.
“There is absolutely no evidence to support this. The minister is making an unfounded statement about people who are ambitious and want to contribute to our society.”
Last year, the faculty was expecting three people from Gaza. They never arrived.

Yemen forms command centre after Houthis breach western front lines

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

20:02:43 KST

Yemeni government forces announced on Thursday the formation of a command centre south of the western city of Mocha near the Bab al Mandeb Strait, following breaches by the Houthi group on several fronts in the country’s west.
Mocha holds major military importance as it hosts a strategic port and is one of Yemen’s closest cities to Bab al Mandeb, one of the world’s key maritime passages linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden and carrying ships travelling to and from the Suez Canal.
The government-aligned 2 December news agency quoted Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh as saying he had ordered armed forces on Yemen’s western coast to “reorganise their ranks.”
Saleh, who commands the forces, said the National Resistance, Giants Brigades, Nation’s Shield and units of the Taiz Axis had suffered significant casualties in recent days while confronting a Houthi offensive that he said was “planned by Iran.”
Meanwhile, the media office of the government authorities in Al-Hudaydah said in a statement that military units participating in operations around Hays in southern Hudaida province and western areas of Taiz were being reorganised.
It said the measure was part of a plan to “organise the deployment and redistribute forces” in preparation for a coordinated field operation and to reorganize defensive lines.
On the other hand, activists on social media circulated images they said showed Houthi fighters after taking control of the Hays and Al-Khawkhah districts in southern Hudaida.
Government forces and Houthis continued to exchange fire on Wednesday in the provinces of Marib, Al-Bayda, Hudaida, Taiz and Al-Dhalea, resulting in deaths, including among civilians, while government forces sent military reinforcements to Mocha.
The escalation comes amid the broadest wave of fighting in Yemen since 2022, when a UN-brokered truce was reached. The peace process later stalled, with military confrontations resuming in July.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.

The human rights organization says Moscow has used “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices” to recruit citizens from low-income countries such as Sri Lanka, Sierra Leone or Somalia. The tactics include “hollow promises of civilian or non-combat roles,” Amnesty’s Secretary-General Agnès Callamard said.
Amnesty’s report draws from testimonies and interviews of foreign citizens detained in Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps. Some of them told the NGO that Russian authorities coerced them into joining the force when their residence permit in Russia was about to expire.
Advertisement
A Sri Lankan national named as Dinesh said he was approached about joining the army after his Russian work visa had expired. After the two weeks of training, Dinesh was sent to the front line, where he was captured by the Ukrainian army two months later, the report reads.
Others say they were lured into joining the army from abroad under the pretext of doing a different kind of job. A Brazilian man referred to as Pedro in the report told Amnesty he thought he was signing a contract for a well-paid IT job in Russia, and was in fact taken to a military training center and later sent to the front line.
The Kremlin’s tactics to recruit foreign nationals have been the subject of multiple reports and have triggered diplomatic disputes. Countries such as Kenya and Ghana have demanded that Russia stop recruiting their citizens to fight in the war.
Ukrainian authorities estimated in March that at least 27,000 foreign nationals from 135 countries had been recruited by Russia since 2022. The main groups come from Tajikistan, Belarus and Kazakhstan — countries from which there has traditionally been a large flow of migrants to Russia.
A Kremlin spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Family environments shape authoritarian traits differently than dominance preferences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:39 UTC
20:00:39 KST

Genetic predispositions and family environments both shape extreme political views, but they do so in entirely different ways depending on the specific type of attitude. A new study reveals that a desire for social conformity is heavily influenced by household upbringing, while a preference for group dominance stems more from outside personal experiences. The research was published in Behavior Genetics.
Political scientists and psychologists often examine two distinct personality traits to understand polarized socio-political attitudes. The first is Right-Wing Authoritarianism. This concept describes a person’s preference for strict adherence to social conventions, collective security, and obedience to authority.
The second concept is Social Dominance Orientation. This captures a person’s desire for group-based hierarchies and the belief that their own social group is inherently superior to others. Both traits reliably predict prejudice, support for extreme political movements, and a tolerance for discrimination.
Researchers want to know why people develop these distinct views in the first place. Past research has shown that both biological genetics and life experiences play a role in shaping them. It has remained largely unknown whether the specific environmental and genetic sources differ between the two traits.
Psychologists Christian Kandler and Jana Instinske of Bielefeld University in Germany, along with sociologist Edward Bell of the University of Western Ontario, wanted to map exactly how these influences combine. They also aimed to see if the roots of these political attitudes shift as people grow from adolescence into young adulthood.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study of 1,440 German families. This group included identical and fraternal twins, their parents, and their non-twin siblings, encompassing more than 5,000 individuals. The twins belonged to three distinct age cohorts averaging 15, 21, and 27 years old.
Participants answered survey questions designed to measure their levels of both authoritarianism and social dominance. By comparing the attitude similarities between identical twins, who share all their genes, and fraternal twins, who share about half, the team could estimate the mathematical contribution of genetics.
Adding parents and non-twin siblings to the analysis allowed the researchers to account for the specific environments families create. It also let them measure assortative mating. This is the well-documented tendency of people to marry partners who share similar political and social views.
The results showed that genetics shape about the same total amount of variance for both personality traits. The genetic components themselves differed slightly in their structure. Authoritarianism was influenced by both additive genetics, which are straightforward traits passed directly from parents, and nonadditive genetics, which involve complex interactions between different genes.
Social dominance was driven entirely by additive genetic factors. Beyond that basic genetic contribution, the two political orientations diverged completely in their environmental origins. Authoritarianism showed a strong connection to family inheritance and upbringing.
The data indicated that parents who favor social conformity tend to choose partners who feel the same way. These parents then pass down both genetic predispositions and a home environment that reinforces those exact traditionalist views. Researchers refer to this combined biological and environmental inheritance as a passive genotype-environment correlation.
In this scenario, children receive genes that might make them lean toward conformity, and they are simultaneously raised in a household that actively promotes obedience and tradition. Social dominance showed almost no link to this kind of passive family inheritance.
The tendency for parents to match with partners based on dominance preferences was lower, and the home environment played a negligible role in shaping the trait in their children. Instead, a person’s preference for group hierarchy was heavily shaped by their own unique, individual experiences outside the family home.
The researchers suggest this divergence makes sense based on what the traits represent. Authoritarianism involves moral regulation and conformity, which are central to keeping a family unit cohesive. Because these values dictate household rules and religious traditions, they heavily influence mate selection and parenting.
By contrast, a preference for social dominance usually applies to intergroup competition in the broader outside world. A belief in societal hierarchy is less relevant to daily household dynamics, making it less likely to be directly programmed by the family environment.
The team also looked at how these influences changed as the twins aged. They initially suspected that the impact of the family environment would fade as adolescents grew into adults and selected their own surroundings. They hypothesized that genetics would play a larger role as adults sought out social circles and news sources that matched their natural predispositions.
Instead, the data pointed in the opposite direction. For both traits, the total genetic influence remained relatively stable across the age groups. The influence of environments shared specifically by the twins actually increased from adolescence to adulthood.
This twin-specific shared environment was essentially nonexistent for 15-year-olds but became highly relevant for 21-year-olds and 27-year-olds. The researchers suspect that as young adults become eligible to vote, they might engage in more political discussions with their peers and twin siblings. This co-development process could amplify shared social influences during the exact years when political identities solidify.
A few limitations shape how these findings should be interpreted. The study compared different age groups at a single point in time, rather than tracking the same individuals across their entire lives. This makes it difficult to separate genuine developmental changes from generational effects related to the specific time period in which a given cohort was born.
The statistical tests did not yield statistically significant differences between the age cohorts for many of the mathematical model parameters. The researchers note that an even larger sample might be needed to confirm other age-related trends. The study also relied on relatively short survey measures, which can sometimes limit the precision of personality evaluations.
Additionally, the mathematical models required the researchers to assume that genetic and environmental variances remain identical across different generations, which may not perfectly reflect reality given shifting cultural norms. Understanding these origins provides a foundation for making sense of political polarization.
The study, “Sources of Differences in Right-Wing Authoritarianism and Social Dominance Orientation from Adolescence to Adulthood: A Multi-Cohort Twin Family Study,” was authored by Christian Kandler, Jana Instinske, and Edward Bell.

We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down | Garrison Lovely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

On Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, warning that “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”
As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.
Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.
The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quickly find serious holes in even the most secured systems on the planet, including the NSA’s software.
OpenAI quickly followed with an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, which broke out of their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.
And a separate rogue agent swarm gained administrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.
Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systems surpass us at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.
There are growing calls to change that, by creating mandatory incident reporting and third party auditing, liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?
Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casar announced a bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.
This is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.
This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in its charter as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?
Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.
At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. OpenAI executive Dean Ball explains:
“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”
Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”
We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.
After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agents broke their way out of their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader, successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.
Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.
This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reuters reported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”
The site’s logs indicate OpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers that uncovered this swarm said that there have been more discoveries since.
And last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest ever leaps in benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantly harder to monitor because it can do more reasoning without verbalizing it.
The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institute found would also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is also better at figuring out when it is being tested, which researchers have long warned breaks the main way safety is evaluated.
Sam Altman soberly warns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.
Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing to render us obsolete.
That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientists synthesized the first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institute found that AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.
On Tuesday, amid a dispute over credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAI announced “an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russia reportedly used a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.
What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?
The bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts will tell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.
And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.
The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored using verification techniques that don’t assume any good will.
One quick and dirty idea would be to embed auditors within frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications, and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.
This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director John Ratcliffe said of advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.
And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.
- 
  Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, Sept 29)

Teachers at schools can now arrange a deferment in "Reserve+"
Kyiv • UNN
Teachers can arrange a deferment in "Reserve+" without certificates or visiting an Administrative Services Center. The system automatically verifies employment and workload data.
Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions can now apply for a deferment in the Reserve+ app. The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
There is no need to collect certificates or contact a CNAP. The system automatically verifies the data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine
The following conditions must be met to apply for a deferment:
-   the educational institution is the primary place of employment; 
-   teaching workload – at least 0.75 of a full-time position; 
-   the position belongs to the teaching staff of a general secondary education institution; 
-   the employer data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine match. 
It is noted that to apply for a deferment, users need to open the "Services" section in the "Reserve+" app, select "Deferment request," and then — "Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions."
After the automatic data verification, the result will appear directly in the app. If it was not possible to apply for a deferment, the Ministry of Defence advises checking whether the information about the place of employment, position, and teaching workload in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine is up to date.

9/11 and the Substitute Mother
Unknown

11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

In 2001, I lost the world I knew. Twenty-five years later, I’m accidentally rebuilding it.
“I think people think you’re my mother,” my six-year-old niece whispered to me as we walked through the parking lot toward CVS.
“I think you’re right,” I said, smiling back at her impish grin that suggested we were pulling one over on the world. I had picked her up from school and was indulging her request to buy fake nails for our sleepover. She gripped my hand tightly, as a daughter would. We proudly walked through the automatic sliding doors, as one.
I don’t have children of my own, which means my niece is the beneficiary of my pent-up maternal love and obsession. She was born in 2020, and four months later, I left my job as the executive producer of a morning news show in New York and moved to Los Angeles. It was the first time I’d disrupted my ambitious climb up the media ladder, and when my feet landed in the California sand, my role as an aunt became the foundation of my daily life.
Birthdays, ballet recitals, and school performances anchored my calendar. Playing hide-and-seek before dinner, getting ice cream on a Tuesday, and letting her empty my closet for dress-up replaced late-night calls, breaking news, and media dinners. Recently, when my sister traveled abroad for work, my niece wanted assurance that her “substitute mother” would be around. The phrase made me laugh, but also squeezed my heart like a vise. Because I know what it’s like to have a substitute mother.
Daphne Pouletsos worked for the insurance company AON, her office was located in the south tower of the World Trade Center, and she was among the 2,977 victims killed in the 9/11 attacks.
Saza, as we called her, was my mother’s younger sister. Her nickname was a name given by my oldest cousin, Dayna, whose toddler tongue couldn’t say “Aunt Daphne.”
Although Saza lived in New Jersey and I grew up in Virginia, she was a constant light in my life. We drove up north for summers and holidays, and Saza would visit us throughout the year. Once, she hid in the back of our Chrysler minivan when my mom picked my siblings and me up from school, and she revealed herself by suddenly piping into the conversation. We squealed with excitement.
Saza knew how to make a mundane moment sparkle. Her sense of humor was the first thing to enter the room, and sleepovers at her house meant staying up late to watch Saturday Night Live. In my young mind, “The Church Lady” and “Coffee Talk” were extensions of my aunt (it helped that she also had a New Jersey accent). Shimmying our shoulders like “Sprockets” was like a special inside joke. Her laugh could sweeten the sourest mood.
But the best moments with her were always Christmas morning. Saza would come to my grandparents’ house first thing in the morning, the jingle bell on the back door announcing her arrival. She’d sit in the big, blue upholstered wingback chair, her feet tucked under her like a teenager, eyes shining behind her ‘90s rimless glasses. I can’t separate the thrill I got from opening a new baby doll from the joy I got from showing it to her. She would coo with enthusiasm, amplifying my delight. One time, she gave all of her nieces and nephews thick black plastic glasses with rubber banana noses attached. It was the silliest gift I’ve ever received, and one of the best. We took a picture, all piled on top of each other: laughing, goofy, family. Her presence carried a promise that everything was okay. As a kid, I assumed it always would be.
I was studying abroad in the fall of 2001. Classes at University College London hadn’t started yet, so I was traipsing around Europe with a sorority sister. We were at a restaurant in Barcelona when a waiter expressed dismay about “what happened at the World Trade Center.”
“My aunt works there,” I told my friend. But I was sure she was fine. How could she not be?
Still, I found a payphone and called home. My father tried to convey a stoic message: “We don’t know anything yet, we’re calling all the hospitals.”
Then I saw the footage on the TV in our hostel. I couldn’t believe that she could be one of the victims. Not Saza.
As a journalist, I know the questions that are typical in the wake of a tragedy. How old were they? Did she or he have kids? It’s natural. We’re inclined to measure loss by what, or rather, who, is left behind. But the true impact of a person’s life is not reflected in titles or preconceived roles. Every one of the 2,977 victims on 9/11 had a world that was wide and meaningful. You may not know the details of that world, but someone does. And they mourn not just the loss of that person, but the moments they made possible. For me, saying “I lost my aunt on September 11th” doesn’t begin to tell the story. My loss isn’t constricted by norms. Her legacy doesn’t fit neatly into a headline.
How old was she? Forty-seven. No, she didn’t have kids, but she had us. Twenty-five years later, I am 45, and I have my niece. Saza was the person who gave me the gift of knowing what an aunt can be.
While I could never fill her slippers, I feel Saza with me every day. She’s there when my niece and I are feeding the stray cat in my backyard. She’s there when we’re laughing at the Sunday comics. She’s there as we get dolled up in fancy dresses to go to the neighborhood pizza place. I am alive in these moments because she lived.
I wonder what else her life would have included if she had kept living it. What it would be like to have her visit me in Los Angeles. How she, my sister, and I would stay up late watching SNL together. How much love she would pour into life’s middle moments.
And most of all, what joy she would take in getting to know my niece, her namesake: Daphne.

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
September 10, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China.
"Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris.
European-crewed spaceflight
"We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts."
Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station."
He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board."
Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport.
The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance.
'Passengers or pilots?'
Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space.
After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?"
The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration.
"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said.
Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion).
"Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically."

Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.
Best Bluetooth Speaker Overall
Specs
Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.
Best Smart Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
If your house is already full of Sonos speakers, the Sonos Play is an easy addition to justify, with ample smarts and connectivity built-in. It sounds significantly better than the smaller Sonos Roam 2, with an audio performance closer to the brand’s excellent Sonos Era 100, despite being battery powered.
Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.
At 2.9 pounds, it’s just about portable enough for travel, although I was very aware I was carrying it in my backpack. You can also charge your phone from it or add an analog source using Sonos’ optional line-in adapter. If you’re already invested in Sonos’ ecosystem, and don’t mind a regularly-changing Sonos app, it’s hard to think of a more smart speaker.
Best Budget Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Great looks, cute size, and instantly stolen by my tweenage daughter, the Go 5 is my ideal tiny speaker. It weighs next to nothing and fits in the palm of my hand, but the 4.8 watt output sounds considerably less weedy than it has any right to.
The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. Its tough little enclosure is drop-proof and IP68 dust and waterproof. Connectivity is also impressive with Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, 7-band app EQ, and clever pairing (where you bump two Go 5s together to create a stereo pair).
It’s speakers like this that remind me just how we’ve come since the days of sticking my phone in a mug to amplify the tiny built-in speaker. If only I knew where my daughter had put it.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Battery Life
Specs
I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.
Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.
In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. It’s loud enough for small- to medium-sized rooms, and cut through when used outdoors, with weighty bass, decent balance, and no obvious distortion when pushed. The 360-degree presentation spreads music evenly too, so it feels less directional than many rivals.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Sound Quality
Specs
Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.
The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.
Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

AMD unveils ‘personal super computer’ for new era of computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:59:40 UTC
19:59:40 KST

The American chipmaker launched what they have described as a ‘personal supercomputer’ in Berlin on Friday, designed and made for a “completely new era of computing” driven by AI.
The supercomputer, called the Threadripper Halo Station, was unveiled at the German tech event Internationale Funkausstellung by AMD Senior Vice President Jack Huynh.
The Threadripper Halo is an ultra-high-performance workstation equipped with up to two terabytes of system memory, up to 576 gigabytes of high bandwidth memory (HBM3E), along with 96 cores of Threadripper Pro, two MI350P data centre accelerators, all supported by liquid cooling.
Huynh said the new supercomputer is the “most powerful workstation in the world”, capable of running AI models with more than a trillion parameters.
The AMD executive gave a brief demonstration of its potential at the event by generating an entire 3D world and flight simulator from a single prompt.
The company’s pitch is to bring data-centre level AI performance and capacity to a desktop format, as demand for AI rapidly grows around the world.
The supercomputer is slated for release early next year, however AMD are yet to reveal how much it will cost. It is expected that it could exceed €100,000, geared towards corporate and institutional budgets rather than as personal computers as originally pitched.
Yet it will give its consumers a platform to deploy large-language models and agentic AI systems themselves rather than rely on increasingly expensive cloud computing.
The Threadripper Halo Station’s direct competitor is the NvidiaDGX Station, with both able to run large AI models in a desktop form, however they differ in how they approach this challenge.
AMD’s supercomputer dominates on memory capacity and bandwidth, offering more than three times as much memory than Nvidia’s, allowing it to run on trillion parameter AI models locally.
However, Nvidia’s offering more seamless integration when moving code from a local workstation to the cloud and, crucially, it is already available, retailing at around €100,000.
Industry analysts see AMD's announcement as a potential catalyst for reshaping the competitive landscape of the local AI computing market.
With cloud AI subscription costs adding up for many institutions and businesses, demand for computers such as the Threadripper Halo Station to run large models on their own infrastructure will continue.
Therefore, AMD's approach of delivering data-centre-class performance using standardised components to lower the barrier to entry could be a major turning point in the expansion of the AI and personal computing sectors.

IAEA accuses Iran of ‘non-compliance’: Why, and what now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:59:39 UTC
19:59:39 KST

IAEA accuses Iran of ‘noncompliance’
Nuclear watchdog has gone more than a year without inspecting key sites; however Iran says US attacks have made access unsafe.
The Board of Governors of the United Nations nuclear watchdog has passed a resolution accusing Iran of failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation commitments and referring the matter to the UN Security Council (UNSC).
The diplomatic move – backed by the United States and its key European allies – comes more than six months into the US-Israeli war against Iran, and as tensions flare in the Strait of Hormuz, where the US and Iran have traded attacks on vessels in recent days.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brent crude surpasses $100 a barrel as Iran, US escalate attacks
- list 2 of 3Did Iran capture a US submarine? What we know about the underwater drone
- list 3 of 3Why US-Iran war over Hormuz is threatening the Gulf’s waters
Here’s what’s to know about the resolution by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and its implications during the ongoing conflict:
What has the IAEA accused Iran of?
The IAEA resolution expressed “grave concern” over Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), to which it is a signatory.
Under the NPT, Iran is forbidden from producing nuclear weapons and is required to meet IAEA safeguards to verify that any nuclear material it has is for peaceful purposes.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against Iran in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
In its latest resolution, the IAEA board said its “lack of information about previously declared nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it” is a “proliferation concern” that needs to be urgently addressed.
It called on Tehran “to engage seriously and without preconditions in talks aimed at building international confidence in the exclusively peaceful nature of Iran’s nuclear programme”.
It is the first time in 20 years that the IAEA board has passed such a resolution.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has condemned the resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
“This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis,” said Iran’s representative to the UN in Vienna, Reza Najafi.
Najafi said Iran has been unable to provide inspectors safe access to its nuclear sites due to the ongoing conflict. However, he said Iran has “neither stopped nor suspended its safeguards obligations,” adding that “performance is currently impossible under continuing military operations and persistent threats”.
Tehran “will cooperate only to the extent that circumstances and safety permit”, he added.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi appeared to accuse the US, which sponsored the IAEA board resolution along with the United Kingdom, France and Germany, of political posturing.
“They attack Iran’s safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the IAEA Board of Governors,” said Gharibabadi in a post on X.
Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons but insisted it has the right to pursue civilian nuclear technology.
US President Donald Trump has demanded that Tehran completely dismantle its nuclear enrichment programme. The US launched the current war, saying Iran was on the verge of making a nuclear bomb – an assertion not backed by the IAEA as well as the US’s own intelligence agency.
Iran has a legal right to run a civilian nuclear programme under the NPT.
What is the UNSC expected to do?
It is unlikely to take any further action, as Iran’s allies Russia and China are veto-holding members.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group, told the AFP news agency that the IAEA resolution is ultimately “an exercise in futility,” with Russia and China “likely to ensure that Western pressure hits a wall at the Security Council”.
What impact could this have on the US war against Iran?
The US, which has made Iran’s nuclear programme a central point in the ongoing conflict, could cite the IAEA referral as evidence of a potential Iranian nuclear threat.
On the same day as the IAEA report, US President Donald Trump renewed threats to target Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, which has two underground complexes near Iran’s damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
Trump said the US had observed “a little activity” there and would “advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard”.
The US president also reiterated his claim that Iran is seeking a nuclear weapon, adding that the world would be “in deep trouble” if they secured one.
Trump’s repeated warnings about an Iranian nuclear risk and his threats to strike Iran’s nuclear sites come despite his claim last summer that US strikes had “totally obliterated” Iran’s key enrichment facilities.
What is the IAEA’s history with Iran?
The IAEA was highly critical of Iran in the early 2000s, accusing it of failing to declare nuclear material and activities. In 2006, the UNSC imposed sanctions on Iran after it failed to comply with a resolution demanding it end its uranium enrichment programme.
But after Iran agreed to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) with six major global powers, including the US, it agreed to curtail its nuclear programme and open up nuclear sites to extensive, unprecedented IAEA inspection.
Iran remained in compliance for years, but the agreement went south after Trump withdrew the US from the deal in 2018 and reimposed US sanctions on Iran. Tehran retaliated by intensifying its nuclear programme, abandoning the restrictions imposed by the deal.
In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was not complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks against it just days later.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, however, did not back the US claims that Iran was capable of making an atomic bomb. “We did not have any proof of a systematic effort to move into a nuclear weapon,” he told CNN.
The IAEA suspects that Iran has about 400kg (882lbs) of highly enriched uranium, with which 10 nuclear weapons could potentially be manufactured if enriched further.

US urges NATO allies to leave ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:57:16 UTC
19:57:16 KST

The US, further complicating already tense international relations, is pushing for a “systematic dismantling” of the International Criminal Court, urging NATO members to abandon the Rome Statute, writes Politico.
According to three anonymous NATO diplomats, at a closed meeting of ambassadors from 32 NATO member states in Brussels in July, US envoy Matthew Whitaker asked for the alliance’s help in dismantling the ICC and called for abandoning the Rome Statute. Whitaker reportedly concluded his speech by saying that Americans would be careful who supported them.
The pressure to leave the ICC is part of a broader campaign by US President Donald Trump’s administration against international institutions and rules that it sees as restricting US freedom of action. The campaign is driven by US concerns that its officials could be tried for war crimes. The White House is also moving to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, and has pressured companies to withdraw from the Space Summit in Paris. The White House has also launched a series of trade spats.
In addition to Whitaker’s comments, the US mission to NATO issued a statement saying the US would systematically dismantle the ICC’s capabilities and called for steps to withdraw from the Rome Statute. It also called on allies to assess the risks posed by the ICC to their countries, publicly condemn the court’s abuse of power and end support for the ICC. The document says the ICC’s charade must be ended immediately and permanently. Although NATO is not a signatory to the Rome Statute, all alliance members except Turkey and the US have ratified it.
Opposition to the ICC was launched this summer by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio,
who accused the court of undermining US sovereignty. He said on the 13th of July that the ICC and its friends were waging war on the US, not with bullets or missiles, but with the force of statutes and so-called international law. Rubio added that if the court believes it can take away US sovereignty, Americans will show the extent of their resolve.
The ICC was established in 2002 to try individuals accused of the most serious international crimes, including genocide and war crimes. The last investigation against US officials was launched in 2020, when the ICC opened a case into alleged war crimes committed by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The case lost priority a year later. The ICC is now facing calls to investigate US attacks on boats in the Caribbean, which the Americans say are part of a fight against drug trafficking.
The US campaign marks a sensitive moment for NATO. The alliance has been strained by the refusal of many European countries to join Trump’s war on Iran, drawing Trump’s ire. Washington also rattled the alliance when Trump threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland. The alliance managed to bridge the gap at an annual summit in Ankara, but just days later, the US demand to dissolve the ICC renewed tensions. One NATO diplomat said Whitaker’s comments were “quite shocking,” while another added that they were “disappointing.”
Diplomats said that in response to Whitaker’s remarks,
France and the Netherlands defended the ICC and made it clear that they opposed the court’s dissolution.
The US delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment. The French delegation declined to comment on the situation, but stressed its support for the ICC. The Dutch delegation referred to the country’s Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen as saying that the Netherlands fully supports the ICC.
American envoys also spoke of the dual position of European countries. The US State Department said it was determined to closely monitor countries that refuse to “reject the ICC’s false authority” while relying on US assistance. In August, Washington imposed sanctions on top officials of the ICC.
An ICC spokesman said the court remains focused on the independent and unbiased exercise of its mandate, as set out in the Rome Statute, to protect victims and ensure justice.
The campaign against the ICC comes against the backdrop of other US efforts. Washington is trying to get Canada and Europe to take greater responsibility for their own defense. A survey sent to NATO countries in August, asking for their opinions on US foreign policy, including in the Middle East, is being seen as an effort to force them to align with US views in exchange for defense assistance.

Among the many interesting takes on OpenAI's claimed solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, I've been most interested in Sabine Hossenfelder's discussion on YouTube., partly because of the content but mainly because of Google AI's weird transcription. Its first sentence has two odd errors:
Open eye claims to have solved the Navia Stokes Millennium problem.
Elsewhere in the transcript we get 'OpenMai', 'openi', and 'Omei' as references to OpenAI, which you'd think Gemini would "know" about. And Gemini somehow "knows" to capitalize "Navia Stokes Millennium", but not to spell Navier correctly.
There are plenty of other errors, some odder than others, e.g. 'Sam Outman' for "Sam Altman", as you can see for yourself in the transcript and subtitling.
And yes, I know that Sabine's English is accented, but that's exactly the kind of thing that a Language Model is meant to deal with. And here's a native-English-speaker's YouTube commentary on the Navier-Stokes solution (and the allegations that OpenAI stole aspects of the solution from researchers at NYU and Anthropic), in which OpenAI appears several times as 'Open AAI', and "Navier Stokes" is variously rendered as 'Navia Stokes', 'Nabi Stokes', and 'Nabier Stokes'.
Here's what Gemini says about the current automated transcription process:
Q: How does Google now create Youtube transcripts ?
- 
  - Audio Extraction: YouTube pulls the audio track from newly uploaded or existing videos.
- 
  - Speech Recognition: Google uses specialized speech-to-text AI models (evolving from older models like Chirp to advanced tools like Gemini 3.5 Transcribe) to listen to the spoken words.
- 
  - Timestamp Generation: The system matches the recognized words with specific points in the video's timeline to create clickable timestamps.
- 
  - Automatic Publishing: YouTube makes the auto-generated transcript available in a side panel for viewers to read, search, or copy. Creators can also edit or upload custom transcript files.
I could say more about why such embarrassing goofs are now common (basically the text tokenization side of end-to-end models, and their limited context window), but that's for another time.

Disengagement 710: Extremist Israeli minister Ben-Gvir's new ethnic cleansing scheme for Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:54:23 UTC
19:54:23 KST

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir presented a plan last week to ethnically cleanse almost the entire population of Gaza from Palestine over the next seven years, an initiative he has named ‘Disengagement 710’ and made a central plank of his election campaign.
The forcible displacement of civilians from occupied territory is classified as a war crime under the Geneva Conventions, and rights groups, UN experts and governments have already described the plan in those terms.
The scale of the proposal leaves little ambiguity about what it would mean in practice.
It targets 250,000 Palestinians for forced removal from Gaza in its first year, rising to 1.11 million within three years and roughly 1.86 million within seven, a figure that covers nearly the entire population of the Palestinian enclave.
The proposal is built around the premise that Palestinians in Gaza can simply be relocated elsewhere. Each person leaving would reportedly be assigned a destination country, along with funding, legal status, housing and a support package.
But Palestinians in Gaza have made clear that they do not want to leave their homes or be removed from their homeland. For them, the question is why they should be expected to surrender their homes and land in the first place.
This is certainly not voluntary migration, according to Dr Munir Nuseibah, human rights lawyer and professor of law at Al-Quds University.
"Ben-Gvir is using this term (disengagement) because he knows that forced displacement is illegal under international law. It is a war crime according to the Fourth Geneva Convention and a crime against humanity,” Nuseibah tells TRT World.
"This is something Israel has been doing since the Nakba of 1948, displacing Palestinians from their homes to create Jewish-majority areas in regions it has been colonising ever since.”
“Now the Zionist ambition is to colonise Gaza, and the objective is to displace Palestinians, evict them from Gaza, ethnically cleanse them, and then make Gaza ready for Israeli colonisation," Nuseibah adds.
Ben Gvir has also put a price tag on the project. The plan calls for an initial Israeli outlay of 10 billion shekels (approximately US$ 3.3 billion), with a financing framework of up to 50 billion shekels contingent on countries abroad agreeing to take people in.
Yet no amount of funding answers the basic question at the heart of the proposal; why should Palestinians be expected to leave their homes and land in the first place?
When ‘voluntary’ stops being voluntary
Ben Gvir's answer is that they would be choosing to leave. But that choice would happen under conditions that make genuine consent impossible.
Much of Gaza's housing has been destroyed, reconstruction materials remain restricted, and movement in and out of the enclave is heavily constrained.
A person who has lost a home and cannot rebuild it, cannot safely return to it and has limited ability to leave or move freely is making a decision under circumstances fundamentally different from ordinary migration.
Nuseibah describes conditions in Gaza that leave people with little real choice but to leave.
"The Palestinian population in Gaza, which before the genocidal campaign was living in one of the densest areas in the world, is now living on only a third of the territory, in tents, seeking the very essentials of life on a daily basis.”
“They wake up every morning seeking water, food and mere survival. There is no development, no jobs, no education. Everything has been destroyed,” Nuseibah explains.
“Their lives have been set back to the Stone Age, and Israel is blocking every attempt to allow Gaza to be rebuilt,” he adds.
UN human rights experts have warned that removing Palestinians from Gaza under current conditions would amount to forced transfer, regardless of whether the policy is presented as voluntary.
Eight Arab and Muslim states, including Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Qatar, have likewise rejected any displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, calling it a flagrant breach of international law and warning against any attempt to impose a new demographic reality on the occupied Palestinian territory.
The objection is therefore also to creating the conditions and incentives under which leaving becomes the practical alternative to remaining.
That distinction is central to the legal argument.
What Israel is doing is building a coercive environment, using difficult living conditions to push people out of a territory, which is a crime against humanity of forcible deportation and transfer, according to Nuseibah.
"Under such circumstances, we cannot talk about a choice for people to leave.”
“Any Palestinian currently leaving Gaza is not leaving by choice, they are leaving because they are looking for survival, because they are looking for a way to educate their children and simply to live,” he adds.
Gaza as an election issue
Ben-Gvir is not leaving ‘Disengagement 710’ as a campaign slogan. His Otzma Yehudit party wants a dedicated Emigration Ministry, with its own minister and budget, and has made its creation a condition for joining Israel's next coalition.
That would give the plan a direct place in coalition negotiations after October's elections, while allowing Ben-Gvir to position himself further to Netanyahu's right as Israel's far-right competes over what Gaza should look like after the genocide.
Controversial former general Ofer Winter has also included a similar idea in his platform.
Netanyahu has so far kept some distance from the proposal, reportedly voicing reservations in Cabinet even as he has previously used the idea of Palestinian emigration to keep Ben-Gvir inside the government.
Defence Minister Israel Katz has said Israel is waiting for US approval to move forward.
The idea, however, did not begin with Ben Gvir's election campaign. The US proposed in February 2025 that Palestinians leave Gaza, before the White House backed off and said in its subsequent 20-point Gaza plan that the population would remain in the besieged enclave.
For Nuseibah, that history is important because reducing the proposal to an election tactic risks missing the broader policy behind it.
"Ben-Gvir is likely trying to use this ethnic cleansing plan as an element of his upcoming election campaign. But we cannot look at it only as election propaganda.”
“Israel has been trying to displace millions of Palestinians out of Gaza for quite some time. It has tried to pressure Egypt and Jordan, through the US and Germany, to take in Gaza's Palestinian population."
"It has been looking for places to send Palestinians to, and it has facilitated flights to different countries around the world to absorb more of them."
But Nuseibah also sees a clear electoral calculation in the proposal, particularly among the constituency Ben-Gvir is trying to mobilise.
"But of course Ben-Gvir wants to use it in the elections too, because his political base is a group who wants to ethnically cleanse the land and colonise it, driven by a messianic religious framework of thought and ideology," he adds.

Members of the 395-seat House of Representatives are elected by direct universal suffrage using party lists.
