The Trump dividend: What $5,000 would cost and what it could cover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:53:04 UTC
19:53:04 KST

What would Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend buy — and could the US afford its estimated $1.2 trillion cost?
The US president has promised to give every adult citizen a $5,000 (€4,290) payment if Republicans retain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
The proposal could cost almost $1.2 trillion (€1.03 trillion), exceeding the Pentagon’s full 2026 budget request.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend,” Trump told the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, as the party struggles in the polls against the Democrats.
He compared the payments with the dividends distributed by companies to their shareholders, citing “our tremendous strength and success economically”.
Within an hour, Vice President JD Vance appeared to scale back Trump’s proposal, at least in part, by suggesting that wealthy Americans would not receive the payments.
The US had around 240 million adult citizens at the time of the 2024 presidential election, including 174 million registered voters, according to the latest comprehensive US Census Bureau figures. Only about 70% of the voting-age population was registered to vote.
Giving every adult citizen $5,000 would therefore cost almost $1.2 trillion. That is around $220 billion (€189bn) more than the Pentagon’s entire $961 billion (€825bn) budget request for 2026, according to figures by the Congressional Budget Office. Limiting the payment to registered voters would cost around $870 billion.
A $5,000 cheque would give each adult more than they received through the two rounds of direct federal payments approved during Trump’s first term.
What could it cover?
Average US household spending was $78,535 (€67,400) in 2024, or $6,545 (€5,620) a month, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
If two adults sharing a home each received $5,000 (€4,290), their combined payment of $10,000 (€8,580) would cover around 11 months of an average household’s total food spending, or about 18 months of grocery spending. These calculations use 2024 expenditure figures adjusted for the 6.45% increase in consumer prices by July 2026.
Housing was the largest expense, accounting for 33.4% of the average household budget. Households spent $26,266 (€22,540) on housing in 2024, equivalent to around $27,960 (€24,000) in July 2026 prices. Two $5,000 payments would therefore cover just over four months of average housing costs.
The combined payment could also cover around eight-and-a-half months of average transport costs or 18 months of healthcare spending. At almost six times the average household’s annual education spending, it could theoretically cover nearly six years of those costs.
However, the education figure is an average across all households, including those with little or no education spending.
What would it cost?
Trump’s proposal comes shortly after the country’s national debt passed $40 trillion (€34.3 trillion) for the first time. The US is also running an annual budget deficit of nearly $1.8 trillion (€1.54 trillion), while inflation remains a concern.
“The idea that we’ve had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable,” said Marc Goldwein, senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a Washington-based think tank. “We don’t have surpluses to give away.”
Concerns about the country’s debt are being compounded by high government borrowing costs.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note rose above 4.85% on Wednesday, its highest level in nearly three years, before easing slightly, while the 30-year yield climbed to 5.29%, close to the 18-year high of 5.33% reached in August.
Treasury yields help determine borrowing costs across the US economy, so sustained increases can make mortgages and business loans more expensive, slow economic growth and weigh on share prices.
With the government already running a large deficit, it remains unclear how the proposed payments would be financed.
Vance suggested that they could be funded using US tariff revenue.
The government expects to collect about $406 billion (€348 billion) in customs duties during the 2026 fiscal year, according to the US Treasury Department. This includes all customs duties, not only tariffs introduced by Trump.
That would cover only around a third of the estimated $1.18 trillion (€1.01 trillion) cost of paying every adult citizen $5,000 (€4,290). Even limiting the payments to the country’s 174 million registered voters would cost around $870 billion (€747 billion) — more than twice the projected annual customs revenue.
When Trump discussed a similar payment earlier this year, he proposed a $2,000 (€1,720) dividend and said he did not believe he needed congressional approval.
Last year, Trump gave members of the military a $1,776 (€1,520) cheque that he called a “warrior dividend”.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote on X late Wednesday. “Because Republicans (and America) will win!”
However, Congress would need to approve the proposed payments.
Trump’s proposal would be legal because the payment would be available regardless of how someone voted — or whether they voted at all — according to New Mexico-based lawyer John Day.
“This is a campaign promise,” Day said. “It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way.”
Republicans are on the defensive as they seek to protect their narrow House majority against strong political headwinds. Trump is unpopular and polls indicate that most Americans oppose the war in Iran. Even the Senate, which Republicans once appeared well placed to retain, is now considered competitive.

Erik Gamzejev: Both locals and outsiders deliver big at Station Narva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Erik Gamzejev: Both locals and outsiders deliver big at Station Narva
The atmosphere at this year's Station Narva festival was a stark contrast to the repulsive power struggles and throne games over positions that have gone on for years in the same municipality, notes Erik Gamzejev.
The Station Narva festival held last week has, both during and after the event, received abundant praise for its atmosphere, artists, and diverse program, which includes not only music but also art, discussions, excursions, and culinary experiences. Equally important is that this festival has, over nine years, matured in increasingly close cooperation with the capital and local people.
The organizing team led by Helen Sildna, in which the share of Ida‑Viru County residents themselves is steadily growing, has succeeded in making people believe that this festival is done precisely for Narva and Ida‑Virumaa, and not at their expense. That it is not a traveling circus that sets up its tent on site, collects money from locals for the tricks shown, and moves on to the next city. Rather, it is entirely a local thing.
Some distrust between those who live and operate daily in Ida‑Virumaa and those who come from the capital has existed throughout the ages. It intensifies and sharpens when something bigger is undertaken and the parties look only to their own interests.
Hendrik Agur, who moved to Ida‑Virumaa seven years ago and first led Kohtla‑Järve High School and then the Ida‑Viru Vocational Education Center Cosmos, wrote this spring in Põhjarannik newspaper that the development of Ida‑Virumaa is hindered by fragmentation, behind which are specific human patterns: ego, the need for recognition, and the habit of being the only "right voice," and intolerance of another's success.
To those who come from elsewhere, it may seem that some locals are indeed in a defensive circle and do not particularly want to let anyone beside them, because there is a risk that their job, money, and position will be taken away. What has happened in the leadership of some Ida‑Viru towns in recent years also gives reason to feel this. But it is not only an Ida‑Virumaa syndrome, where extreme provincial patriotism and the arrogant attitude of the capital intersect and ruin even initially good intentions. A reasonable and fruitful middle ground often remains unfound.
In Ida‑Viru Russian‑language social media groups, the attitude is constantly reinforced that people have come here from elsewhere in Estonia who are incompetent in their field, but whose only trump card or magic wand is their knowledge of Estonian. One group that has to operate amid such accusations includes, among others, the hundreds of teachers who have come in recent years to help Ida‑Virumaa schools by teaching in Estonian. Let us acknowledge their patience and steady nerves.
Some newcomers, however, create distrust toward themselves when they take the attitude that before them nothing was done here. Or if it was, then completely wrong.
The pot of money in Ida‑Virumaa in recent years called the Just Transition Fund has attracted people who sincerely want to accomplish something transformative for Ida‑Virumaa by investing their time and money.
But certainly there are also those who have little warmth or coldness toward Ida‑Viru, yet still see an earning opportunity through certain projects or programs whose usefulness or positive impact on the region is, to put it mildly, questionable. When support measures open, the winners are primarily the acrobats of project linguistics, of whom there are inevitably more in capital‑city agencies than on site. Thus part of the money intended to improve life in Ida‑Viru tends to accumulate in companies or institutions in the capital.
The best success story is born when local people and capital‑city experts who truly care about Ida‑Virumaa's well‑being manage to create a balanced team. A good result comes from combining the know‑how of experienced actors with the experience and initiative of local people, where both sides feel dignified and equal.
The Station Narva organizers have succeeded in this remarkably well, and that is the key to the festival's success. And this is also what Hendrik Agur strives for at Cosmos, although in that large educational institution it is a much more complicated task.
The atmosphere at this year's Station Narva was a stark contrast to the repulsive power struggles and throne games over positions that have gone on for years in the same municipality.
Among the festival visitors, about half were people from Ida‑Virumaa and the rest were guests from farther away. This is a mutually beneficial ratio. For many open‑minded local people, this is the most anticipated event of the year, by which they set their calendar. Guests, in turn, get a direct personal experience of Ida‑Virumaa and become friends of this region. It is important that a festival visitor brings Ida‑Virumaa emotionally closer to the rest of Estonia. In terms of kilometers, it is close anyway, just a two‑hour drive.
In addition, only at this festival can one experience unique surreal feelings. You stand between the walls of a 700‑year‑old castle. On one side, a couple hundred meters away, is Narva City Hall; on the other side, across the river, equally close, is hostile Russia. Between them are people with gloomy faces waiting at the border point to be let into that country. The castle courtyard is full of joyful and exuberant people. On stage is Propeller, and Peeter Volkonski, gripping the microphone tightly with both hands, sings passionately: "Eila veel muretu ja meeldiv maailm näis…". ("Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away…" – an Estonian-language punk song inspired by The Beatles – ed.)

Switzerland experienced hottest summer ever in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:52:00 UTC
19:52:00 KST

Switzerland experienced hottest summer ever in 2026
The summer of 2026 was the hottest in Switzerland since records began. The average temperature for the period from June to August was 17.2°C, 0.4 degrees higher than that of summer of 2003, MétéoSuisse announced on Thursday.
The national average temperature was also 3.4°C higher than that of the 1991–2020 reference period. The heatwave hit the north-west of the country particularly hard, with a difference of 4.0 degrees compared with the reference period.
The temperature also rose to 39.7°C on July 30 at the Basel-Binningen station, equalling the record high temperature recorded north of the Alps (in Geneva/Cointrin on July 7, 2015), as noted by the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology in its Summer 2026 Climatological Bulletin.
More
Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Many locations reached unprecedented levels: in total, 30 MeteoSwiss stations recorded a new heat record during the summer of 2026. And nearly half of them set this record as early as June.
In Graubünden, Scuol also recorded an “impressive” record: on June 27, 2026, a temperature of 35.1 °C was measured there at an altitude of 1,304 metres.
The number of hot days and tropical nights also soared this summer. Several stations recorded nearly two extra weeks of tropical days compared with the previous record, notably in Neuchâtel and Glarus (+18). The number of tropical nights, meanwhile, reached 50 this summer – eight more than in 2003, according to MeteoSwiss.

Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:50:58 UTC
19:50:58 KST

Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals amounts to human trafficking, Amnesty International says
Russia exploits and deceives foreign nationals to enlist them in its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, and in many cases these practices amount to human trafficking, the human rights organization Amnesty International said in a report published Sept. 10.
Russia primarily targets people from low-income countries in the Global South, the report said. Russian recruiters lure people from abroad under false pretenses and exploit the precarious situation of migrants in Russia by weaponizing overstayed work visas or supposed criminal offenses and offering military service as an alternative to detention or deportation, it added.
"Once victims sign the paperwork, often in a language they do not understand, military commanders restrict their movements, deploy them to the front lines with minimal preparation, and threaten those who seek a way out," the report stated.
The Russian army misrepresents the nature of the work and the risks involved to these foreign nationals as a key tactic to recruit them, according to Amnesty International. Russian recruiters also offer lucrative payments and pathways to Russian citizenship as incentives that rarely are fulfilled, the report said.
Many foreign recruits lack any kind of military training and get deployed to active combat zones after just two weeks of training, in what Amnesty International called "an apparent disregard for human life."
Two Sri Lankan nationals interviewed in the report said they were led to believe they would be working as cooks but were sent to fight on the front lines and captured within weeks by Ukrainian forces. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one said.
"I would never go back there."
Once in the military, Russia often takes away the passports of foreign nationals and severely restricts their movement, the report said.
Pedro, a Brazilian IT professional recruited after signing what he thought was a contract for a well-paid tech job in Russia, said he asked his commander to leave but was told, "If you try to escape, you will either go to jail or we will kill you."
Amnesty International called on Russia to "immediately end all abusive practices involving the military recruitment of foreign nationals" in its report.
"The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol," said Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International.
On March 30, Ukraine had identified 27,407 foreign nationals fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine, up from more than 18,000 in November, with Moscow recruiting them from at least 135 countries, according to the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War.
The headquarters said much of the data on foreign nationals serving in the Russian army is compiled when those fighters are taken prisoner, including through Ukraine's "I Want to Live" project, which encourages those fighting on Russia's side to surrender to Ukrainian forces.
"In total, hundreds of foreigners are currently held in Ukrainian captivity, and their number continues to grow. Each week, Ukraine’s Defense Forces take captive one to three citizens of third countries, whom the Kremlin regime is effectively sending to certain death," the headquarters said.

National Ethnographic Museum celebrates its 120-year history

The National Ethnographic Museum, which is part of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, offers a true journey through time to mark the 120th anniversary of its founding in 1906. The celebrations are held under the motto "120 Years – 120 Minutes at the NEM," providing visitors with even more opportunities to explore the traditions, customs and way of life of Bulgarians across different eras and regions. To mark the anniversary, the museum is offering free admission every weekend from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at its premises located at 1 Knyaz Alexander I Street.
PHOTO BGNES
The
museum’s entire 120-year history has been quite eventful. Its
building was among those most severely damaged during the air raids
on Sofia.
The
majority of the collection was destroyed or suffered water damage,
but
part of it
was saved. In 1953, the museum moved into its current premises—the
former Royal Palace.
"We
have been here ever since—that makes 70 years in the Palace,"
says Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva, current Director of the Institute
of Ethnology and Folklore Studies with Ethnographic Museum at the
Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS), in a special interview for Radio
Bulgaria.
Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva
PHOTO BGNES
In addition to offering a chance to explore diverse collections, the National Ethnographic Museum (NEM) invites friends and enthusiasts to a series of special events, exhibitions and initiatives dedicated to Bulgaria’s rich cultural and historical heritage. Program highlights include the temporary exhibition "Moving to the Countryside" and the exhibition "The Starry Sky: Mythology and Science”. A bilingual album accompanying the latter is also available.
PHOTO BGNES
The
exhibition "The Starry Sky – Mythology and Science"
presents research by ethnographers, ethnologists, and folklorists

The

from the city to the countryside showcases not only  daily life but also the shifts in people's perspectives and

the
choices made by those who decide to leave the city for small

habits.
PHOTO BGNES
The idea behind the commemoration of the 120th anniversary of the National Ethnographic Museum is to present the entire cultural heritage to the general public in an accessible, engaging and interactive way. "When we speak about culture and ethnographic museums, we often primarily think of jewellery, ceramics, and architecture, yet ethnography is actually much more than this. It is linked to people, communities and culture. It is precisely culture that embodies the link between our nation's past and present," Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mila Maeva says.
PHOTO BGNES
Since its creation, one of the country's oldest museums has been dedicated to the traditional culture of Bulgarians and the communities living in Bulgaria. "It is interesting to see how the museum has shifted its focus over the years. Thanks to the long-standing efforts of various researchers, artists, and museum staff, we have amassed the richest collection in Bulgaria," Mila Maeva says.
PHOTO National Ethnographic Museum - BAS
"We plan to significantly enrich our anniversary program over the coming months. We aim at attracting a diverse audience, including children, students, young people, as well as people who have never visited our museum before. We want to make it better known and more visible. Our goal is not merely to showcase our rich collection or host various events but we aim to go further by opening our halls as a space for interaction and engagement with our cultural heritage, which is vast," the director of NEM said in conclusion.

Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:48:51 UTC
19:48:51 KST

Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role
Court also acquits Dow Jones on the charge of dismissal over Selina Cheng’s leadership role with the Hong Kong Journalists Association.
A Hong Kong court has convicted Dow Jones for trying to deter a journalist from taking a union role, but also acquitted the publisher on the charge of dismissal over the role, in a case that raised concerns about media freedom in the city.
Selina Cheng, who was fired by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) in July 2024, had accused the newspaper’s publisher Dow Jones of unlawfully terminating her employment over her role chairing the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) and of trying to prevent her from standing for a union position.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Hong Kong appeals court overturns Jimmy Lai’s fraud conviction
- list 2 of 3Jimmy Lai sentenced: What happened to other HK pro-democracy protesters?
- list 3 of 3Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai sentenced to 20 years in prison
The court found the company guilty on Thursday of trying to prevent Cheng’s right to run for the union chairmanship.
However, the judge sided with Dow Jones’ argument that she was made redundant because of corporate restructuring, and not due to her role as HKJA chair.
The right to take part in a trade union is protected by Hong Kong’s labour laws. An employer found guilty on “prevent or deter” charges could be fined up to 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,755).
“If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters,” Cheng told reporters outside the court after the ruling.
The judge said the company’s requirement that Cheng seek prior permission to take a union role was an “unjustified deterrent” of her rights.
Dow Jones said it disagreed with the ruling and was evaluating next steps.
“The Wall Street Journal has a long and proud history as an employer in Hong Kong. Throughout that time, we have remained deeply respectful of its labour laws and supportive of our employees’ rights, while publishing excellent, impartial journalism about the region,” a spokesperson said.
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.
Cheng launched a private prosecution last year for illegal termination, after filing a complaint with the Labour Department that did not result in a prosecution.
Founded in 1968, the HKJA is Hong Kong’s longest-established journalists’ organisation and one of the last remaining groups advocating for media rights in the city.
Although Hong Kong was once known for its independent news outlets, media freedom has come under strain and many outlets have disbanded since Beijing imposed a 2020 national security law following sometimes violent pro-democracy protests, according to international rankings and HKJA surveys.

Zelenskyy In Canada Seeking Support Amid Destructive Russian Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:47:46 UTC
19:47:46 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Canada in an attempt to shore up support from Ukraine's allies amid destructive Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other major cities.
The Ukrainian leader arrived in the western city of Calgary late on September 9 after a visit to Norway for the funeral of King Harald V and talks on air defense support.
Zelenskyy’s plane was delayed on its way to Oslo after an alert in Moldova that a Russian drone had entered the nearby airspace.
“Canada remains one of our closest partners," Zelenskyy wrote on X after his arrival in Canada. "We value the support of the Canadian people and the decisions that help Ukraine to withstand the war and to protect our people.”
Zelenskyy's visit comes as Russia continued launching intense air attacks on Ukraine, with fresh strikes reported on September 10 in Kyiv, Dnipro, Kramatorsk, Kryviy Rih, and Mykolayiv.
In Dnipro, a major city in east-central Ukraine, Russian forces struck a food-industry facility that had already been damaged in an attack earlier in the day, killing two people and injuring five, including a child, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
Further east, in the Donetsk region, the number of people injured in strikes on the frontline city of Kramatorsk rose to 16, according to the head of the city's military administration. Regional authorities said Russian forces struck the city four times, with impacts recorded near educational facilities and a multistory residential building.
Russian air strikes also hit the southern port city of Mykolayiv and civilian and industrial infrastructure in the surrounding region, killing four people and injuring 19, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said on Telegram.
Moscow has stepped up its air war in recent months, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have taken advantage of Ukraine’s dwindling air defenses.
The attacks have also targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the upcoming winter in what appears to be part of a campaign to demoralize civilians after more than four years of war.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued its own long-range strikes inside Russia.
Overnighton September 9-10, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala in Daghestan. One person died and two were injured in another drone attack in the Voronezh region. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.
The intensifying exchange of strikes has put air defense and the protection of Ukraine's energy infrastructure at the center of Zelenskyy's trip.
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are set to attend events in Calgary, Toronto, and North Bay, as well as a meeting with Canadian cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on September 9 that that Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."
"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," the statement said, adding that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."
On his way to Canada, Zelenskyy made a stopover in Iceland, where he met with the country’s foreign minister, Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir. At the center of the conversation was protecting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and strengthening its air defenses.
With fighting remaining intense, Zelenskyy's diplomatic push comes amid renewed efforts to find a path toward ending the war.
After months of stalled talks on ending the conflict, hopes have been raised by a flurry of diplomatic moves.
Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump on September 8, a conversation that the Kremlin described as "constructive and quite frank."
"We had a great conversation. He [Putin] is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters on September 9, adding, "These are two people that are tired of fighting."
Putin has given no sign he is ready for a cease-fire unless Kyiv makes major concessions it has rejected, including ceding territory in the eastern Donbas region that Russian troops have been unable to take by force.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov suggested that Putin told Trump that an immediate cease-fire could be secured if the United States would end all support for Kyiv.
On September 9, the Financial Times reported that CIA director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a bigger role in US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, citing unnamed sources the paper said indicated the roles of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner might be scaled back to make room for Ratcliffe.
In a post on X, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called the FT story "incorrect and ridiculous." CIA spokeswoman Liz Lyons, also on X, wrote: "This reporting is false."
Witkoff and Kushner have led the talks with Moscow and Kyiv for the last year and a half.
According to the FT, officials close to Ratcliffe have told their European peers that in addition to maintaining contact with intelligence agencies in both Russia and Ukraine, the CIA director would now play a more active role in shuttle diplomacy.

AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton says 10% risk of human extinction from AI 'not unreasonable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:42 UTC
19:45:42 KST

Büşra Nur Çakmak
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Nobel laureate and artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton said estimating a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction within the next decade is "not unreasonable," adding to a growing chorus of warnings from researchers working at the forefront of the technology.
Hinton, often described as the "Godfather of AI," told BBC's Newsnight on Wednesday that humanity has never before created entities that could potentially become more intelligent than humans, making the risks difficult to predict.
"We've never created beings that may soon be smarter than us. We don't know what's going to happen," Hinton said.
Asked whether there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans, potentially within a decade, Hinton said it would be "very foolish" to assume the risk was as low as 1%.
"A 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate to me. But nobody really knows how to give a sensible estimate," he said.
Hinton warned that advanced AI would not necessarily need to control physical systems to pose a severe threat.
"The first thing to realize is it doesn't even have to be able to act in the real world to cause devastation," he said, adding that AI could create "complete chaos just by talking to people."
He said highly capable systems could also be used to design dangerous biological or computer viruses and conduct devastating cyberattacks.
Hinton's warning comes amid similar concerns raised by researchers working at leading AI companies.
Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who has previously worked on foundational AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday, accusing both companies of racing toward self-improving superintelligence despite the potential risks.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon said.
He also warned that people developing advanced AI systems privately harbor fears that the technology could pose an existential threat by the end of the decade.
Evan Hubinger, who leads Alignment Science at Anthropic, publicly backed Coxon's concerns, saying Tuesday that he personally believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Hubinger stressed that current AI systems pose little immediate danger, saying his main concern is the potential emergence of superintelligence through recursive self-improvement, where AI systems could autonomously create increasingly powerful successors.
Hinton stressed that researchers need to determine how to build advanced AI systems that do not develop goals harmful to humanity.
"We have to figure out how to design it so that it won't want to," he added.

‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.
It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.
“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.
Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.
The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.
“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.
“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.
Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.
In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.
Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”
Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.
The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.
“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.
Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.
The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.
Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”

The RNLI is increasing security after a backlash from far-right agitators over the lifeboat charity’s involvement in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing them to UK shores.
Volunteers have been told by the charity’s bosses that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they feel this might put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.
There has been a heavy security presence around RNLI bases on the south coast of England over the last few days, with police and private guards monitoring some areas.
At the charity’s headquarters in Poole, barriers have placed around a memorial sculpture to RNLI volunteers who lost their lives and around a rose bed to mark the 200th anniversary of the charity. A viewing platform into the headquarters has been closed off.
The RNLI has said it will continue to rescue asylum seekers in the Channel despite the attacks from far-right activists following its involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth.
But after Sunday’s protest, the RNLI’s chief executive emailed volunteers to say security processes were being reviewed.
Volunteers were asked to challenge people near lifeboat stations if they did not have ID, but advised not to engage with members of the public if they felt uncomfortable.
Staff at the Portsmouth lifeboat station close to where the asylum seekers landed on Sunday have been approached by members of the public and asked to explain the RNLI’s actions.
The RNLI has said workers have been subjected to online and physical abuse and there have been “baseless” rumours circulating that the charity had housed asylum seekers or moved them to secret locations after helping them to shore.
Three police forces have been involved in protecting RNLI volunteers, staff and buildings. Dorset police have been helping keep the headquarters secure while Hampshire officers have patrolled RNLI stations in Portsmouth.
Sussex police were investigating “offensive and threatening commentary towards RNLI volunteers”. Images of some RNLI crew members who were apparently involved in the operation on Sunday were published on social media with the accusation that they were complicit in an “invasion” of the UK.
About 50 protesters, including members of the Poole Patriots and Hampshire Resistance attended a demonstration outside the RNLI’s headquarters in Poole on Wednesday.
Protest leaders handed out rape alarms to women, claiming they were at risk from men brought into the UK by the RNLI, and called for people to stop donating to the charity.

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ comes to auction at Sotheby’s, may fetch up to $377,000
- Princess Diana's iconic 1994 "revenge dress" is up for auction at Sotheby's, expected to fetch up to £220,000 (S$377,050) during Luxury Week in New York on Dec 9.
- The black silk gown, designed by Christina Stambolian, was worn the same night Prince Charles admitted infidelity, symbolising Diana's confident public statement.
- The dress will be exhibited in London, Hong Kong, and Geneva before the auction, marking its first public display in nearly 30 years.
AI generated
The “revenge dress” worn by the late Princess Diana in 1994 is up for auction at Sotheby’s for the first time in nearly three decades.
The black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian is estimated to fetch as much as £220,000 (S$377,050) when it goes on sale on Dec 9 during Sotheby’s Luxury Week in New York, the auction house said on Sept 10.
Diana wore the dress in June 1994 as she arrived at the Serpentine Gallery in London for a fund-raising dinner. It gained notoriety because the then Prince Charles (now King Charles III) – from whom she had been separated for nearly two years but not yet divorced – was widely expected to say in a national television interview broadcast that same evening that he had been unfaithful to her.
According to a later documentary, her decision to wear the dress was a last-minute one after initially setting aside a more traditional Valentino outfit. “She wanted to look a million dollars,” her former stylist Anna Harvey said on the programme, according to Vogue. “And she did.”
Stambolian’s off-the-shoulder dress features an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train. It will make its first public appearance at Sotheby’s in London during Fashion Week from Sept 17 to 21, followed by further exhibitions in Hong Kong and Geneva, before it goes to New York for the auction.
The dress was previously sold at auction in 1997, according to Sotheby’s, without giving details.
In 2023, a black, ballerina-length velvet gown owned by Diana was sold at Julien’s Auctions in Hollywood for US$1,148,080, 11 times its estimated price.
Charles and Diana were divorced in 1996 and she died in a car crash in Paris the following year at age 36. BLOOMBERG

Israel killed a family of four, including two children, when its military targeted their home in northern Gaza's Beit Lahia Thursday, according to Palestinian sources.
An Israeli airstrike killed a man, his wife, and their two daughters, aged 8 and 12, health officials said, as the Israeli military escalated the bombardment of houses over the past two days.
"The bodies of four members of the Ahmad family were recovered in pieces after an Israeli strike hit a house in the Beit Lahia Project area in the northern Gaza Strip," an official at al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said.
The Israeli military didn't immediately comment on the attack.
A Palestinian security source in Gaza said that Israeli warplanes struck after midnight in Beit Lahia and separately in the heart of the Jabalia refugee camp, with Israeli forces also firing on tents of displaced people and ambulances.
"Israel continues its violations in the Gaza Strip," the security source added.
The airstrike is consistent with a recent trend of Israeli bombardment of houses as its military struck at least six homes across the enclave in the past two days, causing damage to nearby houses and tent shelters and forcing many families to flee, residents and medics said.
Some owners of the houses, or their neighbors, got a call from the military ordering them to leave the area shortly before missiles struck the buildings, residents said.
The Israeli military did not comment directly on the strikes on houses, but said Wednesday it had hit three areas across the Gaza Strip and dismantled three alleged weapons storage.
Ismail al-Thawabta, director of the Gaza government media office, denied Israeli allegations saying that Israel's targets were "the civilians and their homes."
Meanwhile, several people injured were taken to al-Shifa Hospital early Thursday after Israeli military vehicles and a drone opened fire on shelters and tents housing the displaced in Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, WAFA news agency reported.
Israeli warplanes also carried out an airstrike near Kamal Adwan Hospital in the camp.
Separately, Israeli naval vessels opened heavy fire in the waters off Khan Younis and in areas east of the central Gaza Strip.
The attacks marked the latest Israeli violations of the U.S.-backed cease-fire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025.
The truce halted large-scale fighting but Israel continuously violates the cease-fire and undermines efforts to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the Gaza conflict and establish permanent peace.
More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire took effect, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have died.
The Israeli army has killed over 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 in a brutal war since October 2023 that has destroyed or damaged much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

BDS co-founder dismisses as 'empty talk' Adidas apology over Israeli soldier campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:42:26 UTC
19:42:26 KST

Aybüke İnal Kamacı
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
- 'The fact that Palestine is home to the highest number of child amputees in the world makes this marketing choice even more obscene,' Omar Barghouti tells Anadolu
- 'Boycotts apply pressure on corporations, for instance, by speaking their language: profit,' he says
-  Critics have called Adidas campaign featuring Israeli amputee soldier tone-deaf
The Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement has dismissed as “empty talk” an apology posted by Adidas over an ad campaign featuring an amputee Israeli soldier.
Speaking to Anadolu, BDS co-founder Omar Barghouti said: "The fact that Palestine is home to the highest number of child amputees in the world makes this marketing choice even more obscene; it celebrates the very instrument of that suffering."
The German sportswear brand has faced growing criticism and calls for a boycott after choosing retired Israeli soldier Shalev Biton as the face of its “single shoe service” campaign.
Critics have called the campaign tone-deaf, saying it ignores the large number of Palestinians who have lost limbs as a result of Israeli attacks on the Gaza Strip.
"It's no wonder that an immediate and organic global boycott took off," said Barghouti, a Palestinian human rights activist and recipient of the 2017 Gandhi Peace Award.
"This isn't Adidas just being tone-deaf or insensitive; it is an absolute affront to the Palestinians whose loved ones have been killed by Israel, and who have lost limbs to Israeli attacks," he said.
Commenting on Adidas' apology, which was posted on a regional account rather than through a broader corporate statement, Barghouti said: "Now Adidas is in damage control mode. Their so-called apology is empty talk.
“Those affected by this image are millions of Palestinians living under Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza, its illegal military occupation of Palestinian territory, and its decades-long settler-colonial apartheid regime."
Barghouti said the company's decision to feature the soldier “normalizes the violence of an occupying army and profits from the normalization of apartheid.”
Barghouti called on Adidas to remove the Israeli soldier from all promotional materials and channels immediately and establish a company-wide ethical policy governing partnerships, spokespersons, ambassadors and testimonials.
"Until then, we reiterate our full support for holding Adidas accountable via global boycotts," he said.  
How BDS works
Barghouti said the BDS movement advocates boycotting companies, services and institutions it considers complicit in Israel's actions against Palestinians, based on clear criteria.
"BDS targets complicity, not identity. It targets institutions, not individuals," he said.
He said boycotts seek to exert financial pressure on corporations.
"Boycotts apply pressure on corporations, for instance, by speaking their language: profit.
“If a corporation faces financial, legal, or reputational risks due to its complicity in Israel's crimes, it is more likely to end its involvement, as our long experience proves."
Barghouti stressed, however, that boycotts are only one part of the movement's strategy.
"BDS also calls for divestment and other forms of nonviolent pressure as well as lawful, targeted sanctions," he said.
He said the three strategies -- boycotts, divestment and sanctions -- are designed to reinforce one another by applying pressure on institutions, corporations and governments.
"With these three tactics we can, and will, achieve our goal of freedom, justice and equality for Palestinians everywhere," he said.

Swiss firms 'in line for $2bn US tariff refunds'

Swiss firms ‘in line for $2bn US tariff refunds’
Swiss companies could receive as much as $2 billion in United States tariff reimbursements, according to economists at UBS bank.
The biggest potential refunds for goods exported between April 2025 and February 2026 relate due on precision and medical instruments as well as watches, UBS said on Thursday. The remainder is primarily for coffee, machinery and electrical equipment.
The reimbursements are due after the tariff regime initially imposed by President Donald Trump was struck down by the Supreme Court. UBS cautioned that exporters may not receive the full benefit because refunds formally accrue to importers.
+ US tax yo-yo blurs situation for Swiss companies
Looking ahead, the bank expects that headline US tariffs on Switzerland will eventually rise to 15% from the current 12.5%, in line with the framework trade deal both countries agreed in November.
Economist Meret Muegeli highlighted that effective levies are well below that level – currently around 6% – because pharmaceuticals, Switzerland’s biggest export, are largely exempt.
UBS analysts also said Switzerland’s outsized 1.5% growth in the second quarter probably overstates the economy’s underlying strength, though it still points to an improvement.
+ ‘We’ll have to live with US tariffs,’ warns SECO head
“That seems somewhat exaggerated and not fully reflecting reality,” said Alessandro Bee. “But we are seeing signs of a recovery.”
For 2027, UBS expects unemployment to decline and inflation to remain below 1%.
He sees the Swiss National Bank deliver its first interest-rate increase around the middle of the year, though there’s a risk that policymakers start raising borrowing costs earlier. Officials meet for their third rate decision of the year later this month.

The court cited 'strong suspicion of abuse of office' against Lalu in IRCTC hotels case
NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Thursday ordered the framing of charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad Yadav and others in the alleged IRCTC hotels money laundering case, observing that there was a strong suspicion of abuse of office during his tenure.The court said railway officials manipulated the tender process under Prasad’s stewardship to facilitate the award of leases for IRCTC-run hotels in Ranchi and Pune. It also said the nature, timing and course of the investigation in the case were not inspired by political vendetta, reported PTI.
The court also ordered framing of charges against former Bihar chief minister Rabri Devi, her son Tejashwi Yadav, Lara Projects, Sujata Hotels and four others. The charges include corruption, criminal conspiracy and cheating against Lalu Prasad, while Rabri Devi and Tejashwi face conspiracy and cheating charges.The case stems from alleged irregularities in the award of contracts to operate two IRCTC hotels. The CBI has alleged that the tender process was manipulated and conditions were tweaked to favour Sujata Hotels during Lalu Prasad's tenure as railway minister. The ED has alleged that the transactions were part of a larger money-laundering conspiracy.The accused have pleaded not guilty and the case will now proceed to trial. The framing of charges and the court's observations at this stage do not amount to a finding of guilt.

Vance appears to walk back Trump’s offer of $5,000 ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms – US politics live
Vice-president suggests payment would not go to all and would be paid for by tariff revenues despite supreme court rulings against much of Trump’s program
Vice-president JD Vance appeared to partially row back on Donald Trump’s outlandish claims that every adult citizen in the US would receive $5,000 if the Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour long speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”.
But Vance, speaking after the president, suggested the so-called dividend payments would not go to the wealthy and that it could be paid for by US tariff revenues – though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.
Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The White House has yet to release details on Trump’s announcement.
Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”
The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.

Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.

In other developments:
In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power.

Zaluzhny: lack of technology, funding prevents Ukraine from seizing initiative from Russia

2026-09-10

Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience, but state funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited, which is why private investment can and must become a mutually beneficial solution for both sides, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny notes.
"Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience. No other country can offer more relevant experience for developing new arms, modernization, and tactics for their application. However, the lack of technology and funding prevents seizing the initiative from Russia and its partners," Zaluzhnyi said during a speech at the Defence & Resilience Tech Scale Up Showcase in London, the text of which was published in his column on the Interfax-Ukraine agency's website on Thursday.
He called on Ukraine's partners to increase financial and technological investments in arms production in Ukraine, not only to reduce Russia's military potential, but also to strengthen their own defense capabilities.
"State funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited. Therefore, private investments can and must become a beneficial solution for both sides. Creating clear mechanisms for cooperation with Great Britain at the institutional level will help attract private capital, technologies, and ultimately create new markets and develop long-term cooperation between the defense industries of Ukraine and its partners," the diplomat said.
Zaluzhnyi stated that Ukraine has gained significant experience in drone production, but the component base, and especially its production, currently remains outside Ukraine, which precludes possibilities for scaling and modernization in the long term, "where marketing gives way to strategy and the outline of victory finally becomes visible." "Even now, these investments are vital in countering urgent threats such as ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
He noted that achieving victory or a dignified peace requires systemic impact on Russia's ability to continue the war, rather than isolated technological solutions.
"Systemic impact means implementing strategies to achieve the main goal: victory over the enemy. Naturally, building such a systemic impact is possible only with appropriate strategies. These strategies must be based on implementing financial and technological policies that enable producing today what is needed tomorrow, or better yet, the day after tomorrow. And what is needed today should be taken from storage facilities as something produced yesterday. Defense production must be part of a war strategy, not the other way around, where war is made to justify someone's promises and profits. Only in this way is it possible to seize the initiative, impose one's will on the enemy, and demand terms from them," Zaluzhny concluded.

OpenAI urges mandatory US safety rules as AI systems grow more autonomous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:39:24 UTC
19:39:24 KST

Dilara Hamit
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
OpenAI urged the US Congress on Wednesday to establish mandatory national safety requirements for the most advanced artificial intelligence systems, warning that voluntary commitments were no longer sufficient as AI capabilities rapidly advance.
"We want to work with Congress on mandatory, capability-based national AI safety regulation," Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane wrote in a company blog post.  
“The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments," he added.  
OpenAI called for capability-based regulation that could evolve with the technology, including common testing standards, independent safety assessments, stronger cybersecurity protections and mandatory reporting of serious incidents.
The requirements should apply to the small number of well-resourced laboratories developing frontier systems rather than to startups, smaller developers or researchers working with less capable models, the company said.
OpenAI also called for mechanisms to monitor progress toward recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems would independently help create increasingly capable generations of artificial intelligence.
The company said fully autonomous recursive self-improvement was not taking place and should not be pursued unless it could be done safely.
AI was already accelerating parts of the research used to develop and align new models, however, with some agents completing tasks that would take skilled researchers several days, it added.
OpenAI said governments should establish shared safety thresholds for determining when AI development should be slowed or stopped, while preserving meaningful human oversight.
The company said it would halt the development or deployment of systems that presented unacceptable risks and could not be sufficiently safeguarded.
It also advocated for compatible international standards for measuring AI capabilities, managing risks and determining when development should be restricted, arguing that failures involving frontier systems could have consequences beyond the countries where they were created. 
OpenAI backs California legislation
OpenAI also announced its support for four AI-related bills in California, saying it would continue backing state-level safeguards until Congress adopted a national framework.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed two of the measures, SB 813 and AB 1405, into law on Wednesday.
SB 813 requires the California Government Operations Agency to establish a process for designating qualified independent organizations capable of assessing AI risks. AB 1405 requires the agency to establish a registry for AI auditors and introduces independence, transparency and accountability standards for their work.
The two other bills endorsed by OpenAI have passed the state legislature and await action by the governor.
SB 1119 would introduce child-safety requirements for companion chatbots, including age assurance, risk assessments, independent audits, parental controls and safeguards against harmful content.
AB 1864 would require gene-synthesis providers and manufacturers of benchtop synthesis equipment to comply with federal screening standards intended to reduce biological risks.
OpenAI acknowledged that it had not previously supported some of the bills but said it reconsidered its position following recent advances in AI capabilities. 
Agents accessed external systems during tests
The policy call follows a series of incidents in which advanced AI agents gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
OpenAI disclosed in July that models being tested with reduced cybersecurity restrictions exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to escape an isolated evaluation environment and obtain access to the open internet.
The agents subsequently accessed production infrastructure belonging to AI platform Hugging Face in an attempt to obtain answers for a cybersecurity benchmark.
OpenAI’s investigation found that agents had established unauthorized communication channels, including a persistent message board, allowing otherwise separate agents to exchange information, coordinate their efforts and divide tasks.
The company said the incident did not affect OpenAI customer data, product functionality or availability.
AI developer Anthropic separately disclosed Wednesday that it had identified a fourth incident involving one of its Claude models gaining unauthorized access to a real third-party system during testing.
Anthropic said all four incidents occurred during cybersecurity evaluations conducted in a third-party environment. The company said a configuration problem had left the systems connected to the internet and that the models were running without the safeguards normally used in publicly available versions.

How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:38:53 UTC
19:38:53 KST

How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach
Long-range Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s key gas plants, raising questions about the conflict’s next phase.
Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border, on Wednesday, signalling that Ukraine has further developed its military capabilities as the Russia-Ukraine war continues through its fifth year.
Unconfirmed videos circulating on social media show large clouds of thick, dark smoke and fire at the Novy Urengoy plant in western Siberia, recorded from a distance. Dmitry Artyukhov, the governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region, wrote on Telegram that the drone attacks had been intercepted and “debris from the drone caused a fire upon impact”. There have been no reports of deaths or injuries.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Zelenskyy’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone on way to Oslo, Norwegian PM says
- list 2 of 3Trump says Putin wants to make a deal to end Ukraine war
- list 3 of 3Russian attacks kill 7 in Ukraine as Kyiv targets gas plants deep in Arctic
Since the start of the war, Ukraine has dramatically increased its capacity for the mass production of low-cost drones and has more recently been specifically targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure and logistical hubs.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the latest long-range attack “completely justified” on social media. It came just days after special United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv with new proposals to end the war, although no specific details were shared on the new proposals.
While attacks on Russia’s and Ukraine’s capitals were halted during the three-day visit earlier this week, they immediately resumed following their departure.
But what does this new, long-range capability on Ukraine’s side mean for the next phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war?
What do we know about the Ukrainian drones used in the strike?
The Ukrainian Armed Forces says it hit two critical Russian gas processing plants, in Novy Urengoy and Purovsky district, with FP-1 drones produced by Fire Point, a Ukrainian company specialising in the production of long-range drones.
The pink FP-1 drone – Fire Point FP-1 UAV – is about 6 metres (20ft) wide and can travel at 140-180km (87-112 miles) per hour. It costs less than $60,000 to produce each drone, an amount that is considered low.
The furthest an FP-1 drone had travelled before the Novy Urengoy attack was in July, when it hit an oil refinery in the city of Omsk in southwestern Siberia, about 2,500km (1,550 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
How significant are these attacks?
The Kremlin’s envoy to the Urals, Artem Zhoga, said Wednesday’s attack by Ukraine was the first to reach the Arctic.
The targets were two Russian gas processing plants in the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky districts of Yamalo-Nenets.
The Yamalo-Nenets region hosts about 80 percent of Russia’s natural gas production and two-thirds of its gas reserves, as well as 13 percent of the country’s oil reserves. Gas reserves in this region stand at 26.5 trillion cubic metres; global gas needs stand at about 4.2 trillion cubic metres per year.
Novy Urengoy is known as the gas capital of Russia due to its vital production for the Russian gas and oil industry.
The ability of Ukraine to reach targets here means it could unleash much more damage on Russia’s economy, which depends heavily on energy exports for income – especially as Russia has been under international economic and trade sanctions since it first invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Videos of Russian citizens queueing for petrol were shared widely on social media earlier this year, despite Russia holding one of the world’s largest reserves of gas and oil.
How will this affect Europe?
The attack on Russian gas infrastructure could have serious consequences for the European Union as member states heavily depend on supplies of Russian gas.
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the EU implemented sanctions on Russian oil and gas and began to invest in efforts to become less reliant on Russian energy.
But the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which previously moved about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, means that Europe is once again struggling for gas imports.
Gas prices in Europe rose above 80 euros ($93) per megawatt-hour this week, the highest price since 2023, according to the Dutch TTF, a wholesale market that sets the price benchmark for European gas.
Current gas reserves in Europe stand at about 65 percent, compared with 80 percent last year, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Dwindling reserves are currently a particular worry for the continent as it heads into winter.
EU member states were urged to start storing gas in March, shortly after the US and Israel started the war on Iran. But the European Court of Auditors released a report on Wednesday stating that member states have not invested enough in other energy sources to be able to phase out Russian gas, and that the bloc’s “crisis‑response objectives often cannot be demonstrated”.

Ukraine’s GrimTech Develops LA-80 Counterpart to Russia’s Molniya Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:38:22 UTC
19:38:22 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine’s GrimTech Develops LA-80 Counterpart to Russia’s Molniya Drone
Ukrainian defense company GrimTech is finalizing the development of the Grim LA-80, a fixed-wing strike drone designed to carry payloads of up to 5 kilograms and operate at ranges of up to 80 kilometers, Militarnyi reported on September 10.
According to the outlet, the company representative presented details of the new system during the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland. The drone is structurally similar to Russia’s Molniya-type UAVs, while its developers are focusing on combining extended range and payload capacity with a relatively low production cost.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Grim LA-80 is primarily intended to strike stationary targets behind Russian lines, including fortifications, dugouts, protective shelters, and military equipment that remains in fixed positions for extended periods.
According to Militarnyi, the drone’s range varies depending on the payload. With a payload of around 2 kilograms, the LA-80 could theoretically fly up to 100 kilometers, although the reliability of the communications link remains the main limiting factor at longer distances.
The company is considering several options for controlling the drone, including a conventional radio link, digital video transmission, and Starlink satellite communications. GrimTech views satellite connectivity as the preferred option for maintaining more stable control over longer distances.
For serial production, the LA-80’s fuselage is expected to be manufactured using vacuum forming, a process intended to reduce weight, increase durability, and facilitate faster production. The wings will be made from foam, while aluminum tubes and plywood will also be incorporated into the airframe.
GrimTech does not manufacture warheads for the LA-80, with munitions instead expected to be installed by Ukrainian military personnel. The drone’s payload compartment is being designed to accommodate different types of munitions, including those with relatively large diameters. The configuration will also allow the position of the payload to be adjusted to maintain the aircraft’s balance.
“We are finalizing and refining the product to ensure its quality, and we are working to produce a test batch that can be sent to the front for testing and field trials,” GrimTech representatives told Militarnyi.
About Molniya
Russia’s Molniya drone first appeared in November 2024 as a low-cost, mass-producible strike UAV designed primarily for frontline operations.
Built like a small aircraft, the Molniya uses inexpensive materials such as plywood, plastic, and cardboard. Its simple construction contributes to a relatively low radar signature, making conventional detection more difficult.
Powered by an electric motor, the drone can carry a payload of around 3–5 kilograms, fly up to 30–40 kilometers, and reach speeds of up to 90 km/h. Twin-motor variants have also been developed.
With an estimated cost of just $300–$400 per unit, Russian forces can deploy Molniya drones in large numbers, relying on their low price to make mass attacks economically viable.
The Grim LA-80 is one of several new Ukrainian defense systems presented at the MSPO exhibition. Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom also unveiled a new surface-to-air missile intended for modernized Strela-10 systems and the newly developed Desna air defense system.
The RK-2PZ missile is based on the Barrier anti-tank guided missile, which was developed from the R-2 missile family.

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Hit 2,379 Russian Targets in One Day, Including Aircraft and Drone Launch Sites

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Hit 2,379 Russian Targets in One Day, Including Aircraft and Drone Launch Sites
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) struck or destroyed 2,379 Russian targets over the past 24 hours, including personnel, drone launch sites, electronic warfare systems, and aircraft, the force reported.
According to the USF, its units struck 437 Russian personnel during the reporting period, with 193 reported killed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes also targeted 51 drone launch sites and 26 radar, electronic intelligence, electronic warfare, and communications systems. Ukrainian drone units also hit 191 vehicles and 13 artillery systems.
A significant share of the targets were Russian unmanned aerial vehicles. The USF reported striking or destroying 379 drones, including copter- and fixed-wing-type UAVs, as well as Shahed and Gerbera drones.
Two Russian aircraft or helicopters were also among the targets hit during the day, according to the statement. The USF did not specify the types of aircraft involved or the extent of the damage.
The latest figures add to a broader campaign by Ukraine’s drone forces targeting Russian personnel and military equipment. Between September 1 and 9, USF units reported striking a total of 18,580 Russian targets, including 3,726 personnel.
The campaign comes amid continued Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian civilians, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning that Moscow must face consequences for its strikes.
Kyiv came under a Russian drone attack on September 9, when a drone struck a residential high-rise, injuring six people, including a pregnant woman.
Fragments of Shahed drones and shattered glass were scattered around the residential buildings following the attack. A response headquarters was subsequently established at the site to assist residents.
“Moscow must not enter the winter believing that its missile and drone terror will simply go unpunished. Aggression must be stopped here and now so that it does not spread further. It is important that sanctions and support for Ukraine work effectively toward precisely this goal,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine has also increasingly used long-range drones to target high-value Russian military assets far from the frontline. In separate operations over a six-week period, Ukrainian forces damaged two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers at the Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region, targeting aircraft that Russia is no longer able to produce.
The Telegraph reported on September 9 that both operations were carried out by a specialized long-range unit of Ukraine’s Security Service. Satellite imagery shows that one Tu-95 lost its tail section in a July 19 strike, while another sustained significant damage to its right wing in a second attack on August 28.

Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
Unknown

2026-09-10

19:38:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
Ukrainian drones struck the Makhachkala International Commercial Seaport on Russia’s Caspian coast overnight on September 10, hitting a strategically important transport hub linked to maritime traffic with Iran roughly 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
The Ukrainian OSINT community Exilenova+ published footage of the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Makhachkala reported explosions around the port during the overnight raid, marking the first known Ukrainian strike on port infrastructure in the city.
The target is particularly significant because Makhachkala serves as one of Russia’s principal maritime gateways on the Caspian Sea and maintains extensive shipping links with Iran.
The port has been used by vessels traveling between Russia and Iranian ports, including routes associated with the movement of military cargo and components for Iranian-designed drones supplied to Moscow.
Cargo arriving through Makhachkala can then move farther into Russia by road, rail and air, making the port part of a broader logistics network connecting Iranian suppliers with Russian military infrastructure.
Makhachkala is also Russia’s only ice-free deepwater commercial port on the Caspian Sea, allowing it to operate year-round.
The facility handles both liquid and dry cargo, with oil and petroleum products playing an increasingly important role in its operations.
Cargo volumes have surged during Russia’s war against Ukraine. During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, an increase of 42.5% compared with the same period last year.
Oil accounted for more than 2.08 million tons of that total, rising nearly 50% year over year.
The acceleration was already evident earlier in 2026. Cargo turnover reached 1.4 million metric tons during the first four months of the year and climbed to 2.11 million tons by the end of June, roughly 50% above the same period in 2025.
Liquid cargo drove most of that expansion. During the first half of the year alone, the port handled nearly 1.57 million metric tons of oil and other liquid cargo.
Previously, Ukraine’s Security Service used long-range drones to strike multiple military and logistical targets across Russia overnight on July 25, including maritime targets in the Caspian Sea.
Ukrainian drones struck several targets in the Caspian Sea, including the Filanovsky offshore oil platform, the sanctioned cargo vessel Port Olya 2, the dry cargo ship Begey, and a Russian Project 12418 Molniya missile boat.
Ukrainian military intelligence further reported that Begey had been used to transport ammunition, artillery shells, body armor, and helmets from Iran across the Caspian Sea. During voyages between Iranian and Russian ports, the vessel’s crew allegedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to Ukrainian authorities.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine carried out a drone attack against a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Mediterranean Sea, striking the vessel 12 times as it allegedly transported Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia.
