Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
Juliette Garside
Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.”
“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.
Macron meets Stubb for talks on Ukraine, European security
Over in France, it looks like Emmanuel Macron is focusing not only on future space endeavours, but also on very down-to-earth issues of European security.
Aside from his space conference (11:01), he met for talks with Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb on “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, European security, and ways to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy.”
“Finland and France are closer than ever before. France is an important partner for Ukraine and the whole of Europe,” Stubb said.
Despite its low-key format, the meeting is worth noting given Stubb’s central role to all diplomatic efforts on Ukraine, as he is one of the few European leaders that have a genuinely good rapport with the US president, Donald Trump, and so is closely involved in all relevant discussions on Ukraine, Russia and European security.
By the way, we will be liveblogging the Swedish election night for you here on Europe Live, straight from Stockholm, so make sure to join us on Sunday night.
Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of key election this weekend
Swedes will vote on Sunday in a tight election that will be another litmus test of whether far-right parties should join the government, as the Sweden Democrats, with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe, poll at around 19% of the vote and could join the ruling centre-right coalition led by Ulf Kristersson.
The Guardian’s Ashifa Kassam visited Sweden recently to take stock of the atmosphere in the country ahead of the vote, and look at how migration and religion are being weaponised for political purposes.
“Not far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know about Islam.
For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – or Fråga en Muslim – campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back.”
Rutte’s visit is not the only show in town in Berlin today, as the leader of the United Arab Emirates is paying a state visit to Germany, and is expected to sign off on multi-billion deals on energy, technology, and transport.
Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is getting the full treatment and was welcomed with military honours by president Frank-Walter Steinmeier this morning, before meeting chancellor Friedrich Merz later today.
AFP noted that the UAE is Germany’s largest trading partner in the Gulf, with bilateral trade topping $15bn last year, and many big German companies have a presence there including BMW, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp and rail operator Deutsche Bahn.
The UAE meanwhile has made major investments in Germany, including in the chemical industry and offshore wind power.
Inexplicably, there is no joint press conference scheduled as part of the visit.
Just as Rutte and Wadephul talk about the role played by the US in today’s Nato, German chancellor Friedrich Merz gets in early with his comments on tomorrow’s 9/11 anniversary in the US.
“That the 25th anniversary of 9/11 is approaching soon touches us deeply. We Germans felt back then just how much connects us with our American friends. We knew: the terrorist attacks were also aimed at our way of life.
Germany is also today determined, together with the USA, to stand up for the values that define and unite us: freedom, democracy, and respect.
But that doesn’t change the underlying tensions between the administrations in Germany and the US – after all, only yesterday Merz cancelled his planned phone call with Trump, with media speculating about a possible link with the US president’s public show of support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (Europe Live, Wednesday).
Wadephul and Rutte get asked if they are sure the US would still defend Europe.
Rutte says “absolutely” and that he has “no doubt.”
He then goes on his usual spiel about “a big irritant” in the US’s relationship with Nato on spending, and how it needs to be resolved and how Europe is “finally addressing it.”
He says there are sometimes some answers or social media posts that “are hard to understand” – a likely swipe at Trump’s recent comments on the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt – but generally “we really have no doubt that the United States are ready to defend us and will be staying with us.”
Germany needs to 'show we have learned our lesson' from Weimar Republic, foreign minister says
Wadephul also makes a very strong point there, as he says:
“We have to defend our democracy. And, Germany knows from the Weimar Republic, what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system? And now I think we have to show that we have learned our lesson.”
Wadephul gets asked about how to convince the electorate to spend more on defence, also in the context of the UK government’s internal discussions on that point.
He says you need to speak with the electorate and explain that Nato and supporting Ukraine “has the purpose of securing our freedom and security in Europe.”
He says "that is what Andy Burnham is also doing in the UK, as far as I ma able to follow it from here.”
When he eventually gets round to the question, Rutte says, erm, it’s not for him to comment on party politics.
“We have an alliance of 32 countries and whoever is elected is then the elected leadership of that country,” he says.
He acknowledges that politics is “rough” and “a contact sport,” but eventually does not address the underlying point anyway.
He gets pressed on that further, with a specific reference to France and Germany, and what would it mean for the alliance if far-right parties won power there.
But once again seeks to evade the question, as he effectivelly says “let’s see what happens.”
“I have every confidence that whoever is elected in whichever election will stay the course when it comes to the key elements of investing in defence, making sure Ukraine will not lose this war.”
Wadephul goes back to the Leipzig drone attack, stressing its hybrid character: both in terms of actual, physical damage, but also in terms of its influence on “hurting … social coherence in Germany” and potentially influencing regional elections in Germany.
He says “we have to be prepared for that, and we have to stand together” in a show of resilience against radical forces within the country.
Rutte doesn’t immediately answer a question on whether he is concerned by the rising support for far-right parties, but instead repeatedly praises Germany for its response to the Leipzig incident.
'We cannot be naive' about the threat posed by Russia, Nato's Rutte says
Wadephul talks about his recent experience of visiting Ukraine, and seeing “raid alerts not only by night, but also the whole day over.”
But he says, despite that, you could see high spirits from the Ukrainians who are ready to defiantly keep defending their country.
Rutte says Russia remains to pose long-term threat to Europe, with its entire economy focused on defence and war preparations.
He says “we cannot be naive” about Russia in what feels like a bit of a swipe at suggestions of peace talks with Moscow as he has no illusions:
“I know you will always have people telling you: oh, if you would only sit down with Putin and this and that… This is long-term. It is a threat. We cannot be naive.”
Nato's Europeans 'increasingly understand taking greater responsibility for our own security is not optional,' Rutte says
Rutte says “there was a belief that we could continue doing more with less, and that the United States would keep doing the heavy lifting for us,” but this has changed in the last few years.
“I see a real mindset shift. Europeans increasingly understand that taking greater responsibility for our own security is not optional. That rebuilding our armed forces is indeed essential … increasing our defence industrial base is not only good for our security, it is good for our economies too. And that security is not something the US should do for us, but with us.”
Russia's actions are 'reckless, dangerous and a threat to life,' Nato's Rutte warns, but says they only strengthen resolve to help Ukraine
In his speech, Rutte repeatedly praises Germany’s role within Nato, and then eventually gets to his stark assessment of the situation in Ukraine – and Europe.
He says:
“Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine are unrelenting. Russia is suffering enormous losses, now estimated at more than 40,000 killed or seriously wounded every month. Think about it for a moment. Over 40,000 every month.
Despite those heavy losses, Putin shows no willingness to bring the war to an end.
Instead, Russia repeatedly strikes Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, often targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and at the same time, the list of Russia’s malign hybrid activities across Europe grows longer and longer: cyber-attacks, sabotage, arson, airspace violations, drone incidents.
…
The latest hostile actions by Russia are reckless, dangerous and a threat to life. But we are not intimidated. We know these are the tactics of a desperate regime that is failing to meet its objectives in Ukraine. Putin thinks he can divide us, destabilise us and weaken our support for Ukraine. But he will fail. These malicious actions are having the opposite effect.”

Taiwan's MicroIP wins NT$630 million smart housing contract

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — MicroIP Inc.’s edge AI business is expanding from technology development into large-scale commercial projects.
The company announced Thursday that it secured a NT$630 million (US$20 million) system integration contract for a smart residential development in northern Taiwan. The first phase of system planning and project management is expected to begin in October.
The project will include AI-based visual recognition and systems for managing energy use. It will also connect smart devices throughout the residential community, allowing data to be processed and shared in real time, according to CTEE.
Edge AI processes data on the devices that collect it instead of sending it to remote servers. This can speed up processing, reduce data sent to the cloud, and keep residents' personal data stored locally.
The size of the contract is notable given MicroIP's existing business scale. The company recorded annual revenue of about NT$49 million in 2025, putting the new project at nearly 13 times that amount.
Based on the project schedule, industry analysts expect a larger share of the contract value to be recognized in 2027 and 2028, when hardware and software integration for the main construction phase takes place. More broadly, the contract could move MicroIP beyond individual chip and AI software design projects toward managing complete edge AI systems.

Taiwan financial sector’s China exposure falls to NT$787.9 billion in June
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:53 UTC
17:07:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Financial exposure to China held by Taiwan’s banking, insurance, and securities sectors totaled NT$787.94 billion (US$25.02 billion) at the end of June, down 2.48% from a year earlier, according to Financial Supervisory Commission data.
Local banks accounted for NT$727.45 billion of the total, down 2.93% year-on-year, per Liberty Times. Their exposure as a share of net worth fell to a record low of 13.8%, 1.4 percentage points lower than a year earlier, mainly because investments in China fell more than 20%.
FSC Banking Bureau Deputy Director-General Chang Chia-kuei (張嘉魁) said banks remain cautious about China-related risks as economic growth slows and property risks increase, per CNA. Local banks have maintained a conservative approach to lending and investment, he said.
The insurance sector had NT$53.2 billion in exposure to China, up 6.61% from a year earlier and equal to 0.13% of its NT$39.6 trillion in total assets, per UDN. The exposure was held entirely by life insurers, with the increase from May mainly reflecting gains in Chinese stocks and a stronger Chinese yuan against the Taiwan dollar.
The securities, futures, and investment trust sectors had a combined China exposure of NT$7.29 billion, down 15% from a year earlier and equal to 0.73% of their net worth. Securities firms accounted for NT$4.5 billion, futures firms NT$95 million, and investment trust and consulting firms NT$2.69 billion.
FSC Securities and Futures Bureau Secretary-General Wang Hsiu-ling (王秀玲) said securities firms’ exposure rose NT$150 million in June as they increased their holdings of Chinese bonds. She said exposure was down NT$1.39 billion from a year earlier, mainly because securities firms reduced financial investments in their proprietary trading positions.

Kuwait condemns Netanyahu’s incursion into Mount Hermon in Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:36 UTC
17:07:36 KST

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Kuwait on Thursday condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s illegal entry into Syria’s Mount Hermon and called on the UN Security Council to take action to halt attacks on the sovereignty of the Arab country.
Netanyahu entered the occupied Syrian area of Mount Hermon on Wednesday accompanied by Defense Minister Israel Katz, in a move that observers viewed as part of his campaign ahead of Knesset elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
In a statement, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry strongly condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” into Syrian territory, describing it as a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a “blatant breach” of international law.
The ministry said continued Israeli incursions and attacks inside Syrian territory represented an “escalation that undermined security and stability in the region.”
It reaffirmed Kuwait’s “full support” for Syria’s independence and sovereignty over all its territory.
The ministry also called on the UN Security Council to fulfill its responsibilities by stopping the attacks and ensuring Israel’s compliance with relevant international resolutions, stressing the need to respect the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement of Forces between Syria and Israel.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday also condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” as a “provocative” move and a violation of the country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law.
Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also called it a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a “blatant breach” of international law.
In a video filmed during his visit, Netanyahu, wearing a bulletproof vest, said he was standing at the summit of Mount Hermon on the eve of the Jewish New Year, pointing to Damascus, Lebanon and the Syrian Golan Heights.
Netanyahu claimed Israel had established unprecedented “absolute control” over the area stretching from Mount Hermon toward the Yarmouk River.
He said Israel would not allow “terrorist forces” to establish a presence near its borders.
Katz, meanwhile, signaled that Israel intended to maintain its occupation of the area. “We are here on Mount Hermon, and we will not move from here,” he said in a separate video.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognized by the international community.

New Taipei repairs sewage pipe without digging up road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:29 UTC
17:07:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — New Taipei's Water Resources Department said Thursday that it repaired a 33-meter-long sewage pipeline in one day without digging up the road, according to a press release.
The department said the pipeline on Wugu District's Xincheng 6th Road was badly corroded and leaking. It said excavating the pipe from 6 meters below ground would slow traffic and risk damaging other utility lines, disrupting residents.
Department Director-General Song De-ren (宋德仁) explained that the section is crowded with utility lines, including water, gas, electricity, and telecommunications. He said digging would require crews and heavy machinery and take at least two to three weeks to complete.
The department said it instead fed thick composite strips down a manhole, then wound them together to reinforce the inside of the pipe. It used camera footage and on-site inspection to carry out the repairs.
The department said the city's sewage pipeline network is 2,693 km long and has more than 79,000 manholes, making it the largest in Taiwan. It said that to keep up with maintenance, it introduced the spiral winding technique more than a decade ago, with more than 80 km of old pipelines repaired as of 2026.

IN BRIEF: Civilian killed as Ukraine launches 448 drones at Russia overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:06 UTC
17:07:06 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Air defenses shot down 448 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea last night, the Defense Ministry reported.
Drone debris fell on a private house in the town of Borisoglebsk in the Voronezh Region, killing a woman and injuring two other people. Twenty-eight civilians were injured in a Ukrainian unmanned boat attack on the seafront in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
TASS has gathered the key information about the consequences of the attacks.
Scale of attacks
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 448 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aircraft (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 9 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 10 (5:00 p.m.-5:00 a.m. GMT), the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the drones were downed over the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Rostov, Tula, Dagestan, Kalmykia and Krasnodar regions, as well as Crimea, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
- About 90 drones were destroyed in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Taganrog, Novoshakhtinsk, Volgodonsk and 16 districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on the Max social media platform.
- Air defenses shot down 19 Ukrainian UAVs over the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed ten Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
Consequences
- Drone debris fell on a private house in Borisoglebsk, Voronezh Region, regional Governor Alexander Gusev said on Max.
- The incident caused a fire that killed a woman born in 1983.
- Another two people were injured and received medical assistance on the spot.
- A fire resulting from a drone strike destroyed a residential building in an urban district in the Voronezh Region; the windows of a technical college were damaged, as were the door of a cultural center, two power lines, an electricity pylon, a bus, and a car.
- The windows of an apartment building and a private house were shattered in another district, along with six cars and a garage.
- Falling drone fragments caused fires at port infrastructure facilities in Makhachkala and the Avar Music and Drama Theater, acting head of Dagestan Fyodor Shchukin said on Max.
- The fires were promptly extinguished; there were no casualties.
- Drone debris damaged two private houses and several cars in the Millerovsky District of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
- Four private houses lost electricity due to power line damage.
- Dry grass caught fire after drone fragments came down in the Tarasovsky District; there were no casualties and the fire has been put out.
Unmanned boat attack on Sochi
- A fire broke out on the seafront in Sochi following an attack involving unmanned boats, the regional crisis center reported.
- Emergency response teams are working at the scene.
- According to the latest reports, 28 people, including two children, were injured.
- Three adults and a child remain hospitalized.
- Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin said that their lives were not in danger.
- The crisis center added that beach infrastructure and a part of the Primorskaya Embankment had been damaged.
- Proshunin ordered his deputies and district heads to promptly take measures to ensure sanitary safety and restore infrastructure facilities.

These are the best airports in the world, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:06:16 UTC
17:06:16 KST

Spain’s Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport and Germany’s Düsseldorf Airport were named the best airports in the world.
Your idea of the best airport in the world might look very different to mine.
Maybe you think the best part about travelling abroad is the duty-free shopping? Maybe you care more about how far away you are from the city centre? Or maybe you judge an airport on the number of destinations it serves directly?
Thankfully for us, Consumer Choice Center has compiled a new edition of the World Consumer Airport Index that takes all of the above, and more, into account, to reveal the very best airports around the globe.
Split into two rankings – one for those with more than 47.2 million passengers per year, and one serving below that number – the index also looks at whether or not a hub has direct access to the metro or national rail services, how easy the connections are between gates and terminals, the choice of airlines available, the average delays, and whether or not there is a hotel in it.
Airports are also awarded bonus points if security waiting times are under three minutes, and if they do not have nighttime curfews.
The result? Drum roll, please…
Both the best large and small airports around the world globally are in Europe, with Spain’s Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport topping the chart for the former, and Germany’s Düsseldorf Airport for the latter.
Both of these airports performed well on security waiting times, with passengers passing through Barcelona waiting just three minutes, while in Düsseldorf, processing is almost instantaneous.
The worst airports – and why
Among the large airports, the worst-ranked include Antalya, Guangzhou Baiyun and Frankfurt.
For smaller airports, those who fared poorly include Seoul Gimpo, Punta Cana, and London Stansted.
These airports all have problems in common, including extreme distances from city centres, no ride-hailing options separate from taxi companies, poor access to railway services, long security wait times and a high percentage of average delays.
The top large airports around the world
- Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport, Spain
- Leonardo da Vinci-Fiumicino Airport, Rome, Italy
- Los Angeles International Airport, USA
- Bangkok Suvarnabhumi International Airport, Thailand
- Charles de Gaulle Airport, Paris, France
- King Abdulaziz International Airport, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
- London Heathrow Airport, UK
- Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport, Spain
- Tokyo International Airport (Haneda), Japan
- Dubai International Airport, United Arab Emirates
The best small airports globally
- Düsseldorf Airport, Germany
- Zurich Airport, Switzerland
- Copenhagen Airport, Denmark
- Helsinki Airport, Finland
- Milan Malpensa Airport, Italy
- Oslo Gardermoen Airport, Norway
- Munich Airport, Germany
- Vancouver International Airport, Canada
- Brussels Airport, Belgium
- Berlin Brandenburg Airport, Germany

Production designer of a Russian TV series arrested on treason charges. He lived in Kyiv and came to Russia to renew his passport.

Production designer of a Russian TV series arrested on treason charges. He lived in Kyiv and came to Russia to renew his passport.
Russian authorities have accused Alexander Kondratov, the 52-year-old production designer of the TV series Likvidatsiya “Liquidation,” of treason, the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona reported.
Investigators opened the case on August 5. Kondratov’s defense attorney, Natalia Tikhonova, told reporters that investigators viewed “at least six publications” he posted online as constituting treason. It was not specified what they contained.
Kondratov, who was born and raised in Moscow, has lived in Kyiv since 2012, where his family remains. He had traveled to Russia to renew his international passport, the human rights group Memorial wrote. He was detained at Vnukovo Airport on May 5. Before he was charged with treason, Kondratov was subjected to so-called “carousel arrests,” and in total spent more than 70 days in a pretrial detention center.
The detective series Likvidatsiya “Liquidation” premiered in 2007, following criminal investigators fighting crime in postwar Odesa in 1946. Its cast included Vladimir Mashkov, Mikhail Porechenkov, Sergei Makovetsky, and Konstantin Lavronenko. Kondratov’s work on the series earned him the Golden Eagle Award and a TEFI Award.

World Suicide Prevention Day: what do the latest EU and Spain figures show?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:04:23 UTC
17:04:23 KST

Suicide deaths in the EU fell slightly in 2023 and are below levels a decade ago. Three in four victims are men. In Spain, figures show a fall, as the WHO calls to end stigma.
48,370 people died by suicide in the European Union in 2023, but the mortality rate continues to fall and is now below the level recorded a decade ago.
This is the picture painted by the latest Eurostat data (source in Spanish), published to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, marked every 10 September to raise awareness of this public-health issue, tackle stigma and promote prevention. Suicide accounted for 1% of all deaths recorded in the EU that year. The standardised rate was 10.4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, compared with 10.6 in 2022 and 12.2 in 2013.
Differences between countries remain large. Lithuania recorded the highest rate in the EU, with 18.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, followed by Slovenia (16.4) and Hungary (16.1). The lowest rates were in Cyprus (3.5), Greece (4.3) and Malta (5.5).
Men accounted for 76.4% of all suicide deaths in the EU. The crude rate was 16.9 per 100,000 men, compared with 5 among women. Mortality also increases with age, reaching 17.3 per 100,000 among people aged 65 and over.
Suicides fall for the third year in a row in Spain
The most recent national figures point in the same direction. In 2025, 3,808 people died by suicide in Spain, 3.7% fewer than in 2024, when 3,953 deaths were recorded, according to provisional data from the National Statistics Institute (INE). (source in Spanish)
This is the third consecutive year of decline since the 4,227 deaths recorded in 2022. In 2025, suicide was the third external cause of death in Spain. Among men, however, it was the leading one, with 2,784 deaths.
Spain has an Action Plan for Suicide Prevention 2025–2027, which tackles the issue from a public-health perspective. Its priorities include improving the information available, addressing stigma and the myths surrounding suicide, strengthening early detection and healthcare provision and improving coordination between the different sectors involved.
The plan (source in Spanish) also focuses on awareness-raising and responsible communication, making it easier to access support services and preventing suicide among people and groups in situations of particular vulnerability.
Breaking the stigma, talking and seeking help
The World Health Organization (WHO) is dedicating its World Suicide Prevention Day campaign (source in Spanish) to the slogan "Changing the Narrative on Suicide" ('cambiar la narrativa sobre el suicidio'). In 2026 its call to action is "Start the Conversation" ('iniciar la conversación'), which aims to challenge myths and stigma and encourage people to talk about what is happening to them and seek help.
For the WHO, changing the narrative also means driving changes in public policy, improving access to quality care and implementing evidence-based prevention strategies. The organisation estimates that more than 720,000 people die by suicide every year worldwide. Seventy-three per cent of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, and suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 globally.
The WHO stresses that asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase the risk and can help them feel understood.

AI making it difficult for central banks to determine growth potential: BIS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:01:53 UTC
17:01:53 KST

AI is making it harder for central banks to determine an economy’s potential growth rate.
Mumbai: AI is making it harder for central banks to determine an economy’s potential growth rate, as technological change increases uncertainty around productivity, potential output and the natural rate of interest, BIS general manager Pablo Hernández de Cos said.
“AI is reshaping demand, supply and financial markets simultaneously, making the economy harder to read and increasing uncertainty around the transmission of monetary policy,” Hernández de Cos said at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai on Thursday.While the objectives of monetary policy remain unchanged, AI-driven structural changes could make some of the key variables that guide policy harder to estimate, he said. Potential output and the natural rate of interest are already subject to significant uncertainty, and rapid changes driven by AI could widen measurement errors and increase discrepancies between actual and estimated output gaps.The longer-term economic impact of AI is also uncertain, Hernández de Cos said, pointing to three scenarios outlined in the BIS Annual Economic Report. In one, AI produces a bounded productivity boost that permanently raises the growth trend.
In another, AI generates self-reinforcing, transformative growth as the technology improves itself. A third scenario, the “demand bottleneck”, sees automation diverting income from labour towards further AI investment, eventually weakening consumer spending and causing productivity and output growth to stall.These scenarios could have very different implications for the natural rate of interest and inflation, he said. Stronger productivity growth could raise r-star, while a demand bottleneck could eventually push it below pre-AI levels and become disinflationary.“The takeaway from this analysis is that there is considerable uncertainty about the long-term effects of AI,” Hernández de Cos said. The eventual outcome would depend on how much AI progress relies on consumer demand, how competition affects profit margins in the AI sector and how quickly AI products and infrastructure depreciate.Hernández de Cos flagged financial-stability risks from the AI investment boom, with concentrated equity valuations, capex outpacing cash flows and rising reliance on debt/private credit. Opaque “circular financing” between chipmakers, hyperscalers and AI firms could amplify losses if AI returns disappoint, turning the investment boom into a bust.AI could also deliver major productivity gains, with studies showing 10-65% task-level gains and 20-50% time savings; median estimates suggest a 0.5 percentage-point annual boost to total factor productivity. But benefits will be uneven: AI may augment skilled work while displacing routine cognitive jobs, with informal workers in developing economies particularly vulnerable. Early displacement is emerging in customer support, programming and administration, making reskilling essential.
Advanced economies are better placed to capture near-term gains, though preparedness varies sharply among emerging markets. India has an opportunity to close the gap by building on its digital public infrastructure. Rather than replicate full AI ecosystems, countries should target comparative advantages across chips, cloud, data, models and applications, including local-language models and domain-specific data.For central banks, AI raises the premium on measurement, judgement, policy agility and international cooperation. Its economic impact will ultimately depend on policy choices, including investment in digital infrastructure and skills, competition, data governance and sound institutions.

BAE Systems to rebuild two Mk 45 guns for U.S. Navy warships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:00:59 UTC
17:00:59 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $38.2 million to a BAE Systems contract to overhaul two Mk 45 Mod 4 naval guns, with work completing by March 2030.
- The Mk 45 Mod 4 is the main deck gun on Navy destroyers and cruisers, upgraded with a reinforced mount and digital fire control for a 50% increase in firing energy.
The U.S. Navy has added $38.2 million to a BAE Systems contract to overhaul two Mk 45 Mod 4 naval guns, the main deck gun mounted on the Navy’s destroyers and cruisers.
Naval Sea Systems Command issued the cost-plus-incentive-fee modification to an existing contract, funded through fiscal 2024 shipbuilding money that will remain available beyond the current fiscal year. Work will be done at BAE Systems’ facility in Louisville, Kentucky, with completion expected by March 2030.
The Mk 45 is a 127 mm (5-inch), 62-caliber gun that BAE Systems describes as the lightest, most compact and most widely deployed 5-inch naval gun in the world, with more than 260 units delivered to the U.S. Navy and 10 allied navies, including Australia, South Korea, Japan and Denmark. It serves as the primary deck gun on the Navy’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, handling missions ranging from shore bombardment to surface and limited air defense.
The Mod 4 configuration BAE Systems is overhauling these guns to includes a structurally reinforced mount that increases firing energy by about 50%, letting rounds travel faster and farther, along with a fully digital control system with a touch-screen interface and a lower-maintenance, reduced-signature gun shield. Paired with the Navy’s 5-inch Cargo projectile and an improved propelling charge, the Mod 4 gun can hit targets more than 20 nautical miles (37 km) away.
BAE Systems has steadily won similar Mk 45 overhaul and upgrade work in recent years. In January 2025, the company received a $70 million contract that added funding to a prior $47 million order, with a BAE Systems executive at the time citing Houthi attacks on U.S. Navy ships in the Red Sea as a reminder of why deck-gun firepower matters for self-defense at sea.

Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:00:19 UTC
17:00:19 KST

The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, a new report warned on Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last year.
With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025 and thousands of aid workers losing their jobs, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report.
In 2025, only those whose lives were in immediate danger became the focus, while support for longer-term issues and the ability to recover from crises was drastically scaled back.
Jennifer Doherty, co-author of the report produced by the humanitarian organisation Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap), said: “The impacts were not felt equally. The combination of reduced funding and restrictive politics meant women, children, elderly people and displaced people were especially hardest hit.”
Doherty, who said up to 23% of humanitarian staffing was estimated to have been lost in 2025, said: “Specialised services closed and targeted support became harder to sustain.”
According to the report, funding fell to an estimated $33.3bn (£24.6bn) in 2025, from a peak of $47.5bn in 2022.
While USAID sustained the most dramatic cuts, with a 55% reduction in 2025, there were also cuts by other leading donors, with 13 of the top 20 reducing their aid donations last year.
The report also highlighted the growing pressure from governments on how aid could be spent, such as the US spending freeze on programmes considered driven by diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
The aid cuts also meant that for the few people who did receive support, the targeted amount for each person dropped from $178 in 2021 to $90 in 2025, despite the actual needs of each person having risen to $255.
An aggravating factor was that governments not only failed in their duties to protect civilians but were also often actually endangering people. States were responsible for 64% of attacks on healthcare workers and largely responsible for violence that affected aid workers through the use of airstrikes.
Yemen was one of the countries badly affected by aid cuts, with nutrition worsening and diphtheria cases rising because vaccination campaigns were suspended.
Mohammed Bahashwan, Action for Humanity’s country director in Yemen, said diminishing levels of aid were exacerbating the crises faced by families.
“Problems are not occurring separately. A family may have lost its income, be unable to afford food, have a malnourished child and still need to travel considerable distances or pay costs they cannot afford to access healthcare,” he said.
The report said there were examples of the humanitarian system mobilising to support those most in need, often led by local aid organisations, and of diaspora networks stepping in. But it also said the international system did not coordinate well with these networks and that it was often local aid organisations and staff who were worst affected by cuts.
Meg Sattler, chief executive of the Vienna-based organisation Ground Truth Solutions, which carries out regular surveys of people who need aid, said there should be more focus on localisation because the international humanitarian system had not adapted fast enough or pushed back against the cuts and stipulations imposed by the US.
“We have definitely spoken to people feeling the pinch of this contraction. It is especially causing distress where aid is now considered ‘life-saving only’ and isn’t letting people do things such as send their kids to school or save to start a business – things that would help them be less reliant on aid in the future,” she said.

Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity | Pieter Omtzigt and Emanuel Delia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:00:19 UTC
17:00:19 KST

Nine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, was assassinated by a car bomb outside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder.
Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association.
We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law.
We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it.
The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure.
But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed.
Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, he gave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma, the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted he passed confidential information about the police investigation to Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma.
But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends.
The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle.
Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law.
The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating.
There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings.
Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta.
Malta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across the European Union. Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union.
This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem.
On Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom.
The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary.
Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further.
Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta.
Europe owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability.
The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else.
Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again.
- 
  Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in Malta

Developing knowledge with social values in mind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:00:07 UTC
17:00:07 KST

Developing knowledge with social values in mind
The Education University of Hong Kong emphasises programmes that can make a positive impact on society
The educational ethos of “cultivating values and nurturing people” is based on a classic Chinese saying that emphasises building good morals and a sense of social responsibility alongside academic and technical knowledge.
At the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK), this ethos drives the institution’s approach to its growth strategy, from the way its undergraduate and postgraduate programmes are designed to its research work and the partnerships it is building around the world to share knowledge and best practices. The university took inspiration from the Chinese saying to coin its own philosophy of “nurturing talent while cultivating virtues”.
“Education and technology, as well as talent development, is really a discussion about the possible future of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area, to stay competitive and innovative,” says Professor John Lee Chi-kin, president of EdUHK.
“We must think of how we nurture people – not just what they know, but how they use AI wisely and effectively, how they resolve problems across disciplines and how they hold on to integrity,” he adds, noting that this year marks a significant milestone for the institution.
“EdUHK is celebrating the 10th anniversary of its retitling,” Lee explains. “The growth in the last decade mirrors the expanding role of education in the modern world.” In 2016, the former Hong Kong Institute of Education became the city’s eighth publicly funded university and officially changed its name to reflect this status.
Lee notes that the university is broadening its role: “It is moving beyond traditional teacher training to lead in education, research culture, innovation and multidisciplinary solutions that create real social impact.”
EdUHK expanded its undergraduate programme to include what the institution categorises as “non-teacher education programmes” in arts and humanities, social sciences, management, sciences and health technologies. The university offers bachelor’s degrees in creative and digital arts, digital Chinese culture and communication, and heritage education and arts management, as well as artificial intelligence and educational technology, speech pathology and rehabilitation, and sports science and coaching.
Through the teacher education programmes, graduates are eligible to apply to become a registered teacher with the Education Bureau of Hong Kong. These programmes are structured as five-year “co-terminal double degree” courses of study, which allow students to combine a bachelor’s degree in education with another degree in arts, science or social science.
Lee explains: “Our society needs to develop people who can cross disciplinary boundaries, so all 13 of our education degrees are now called co-terminal double degrees. A future science teacher is also a graduate in environmental management; a future math teacher is also equipped in artificial intelligence.”
This focus on meeting the practical needs of society also drives EdUHK’s approach to its research work, with teams at the university developing AI-powered projects for the education field. One is a robot called Joey, which teachers can use to customise English language learning for kindergarten and primary school pupils. Another is EmoCare, a mobile app aimed at helping children manage their mental well-being, which combines an AI-powered chatbot with the “Perma” model for positive psychology developed by renowned psychologist Dr Martin Seligman.
“I think education for society means lifelong learning and professional development, as well as turning research into real-world social impact,” Lee says.
In addition, EdUHK is complementing its undergraduate and postgraduate degree offerings and initiatives through new partnerships established with educational institutions in Asia, the Middle East and Europe – such as the memorandum of understanding (MOU) that the university signed with Nazarbayev University in Kazakhstan, the University of Groningen in the Netherlands and Emlyon Business School in France. And across the border, EdUHK has established its Shenzhen Research Institute and Shenzhen Educational Development Centre.
“These venues allow our researchers to work with partners in the Chinese mainland in different areas including knowledge transfer and sharing, research and other training activities,” Lee says.
EdUHK’s efforts to expand its academic and research programmes are reflected in the latest edition of the QS World University Rankings, where the university is ranked No 7 globally and No 2 in Asia in the subject of education and training.
Looking back on what EdUHK has achieved in its first 10 years as a full-fledged university, Lee says: “The 10th anniversary is a comma, not a full stop. Our next decade is about education with impact. We are dedicated to talent development that adapts to a changing world.”

China’s global expansion offers German firms opportunity, but they see window narrowing
German chamber notes how some members see ‘golden window to partner up’ with Chinese companies as competition, trade tensions and possible EU measures raise risks
While German companies operating in China increasingly view the global expansion of local firms as a chance to collaborate, the window of opportunity is narrowing as Chinese firms rapidly develop the expertise needed to expand overseas on their own, according to a new report.
The internalisation of Chinese companies has emerged as the most frequently cited business opportunity for German firms in China, selected by 36 per cent of survey respondents and up from 20 per cent in 2022, according to a report published on Thursday by the German Chamber of Commerce in China.
Engagement takes several forms, with nearly half of surveyed German businesses supplying products or services to Chinese companies operating abroad, while a quarter help those companies meet international standards.
But the report – which drew on findings from the chamber’s 2025-2026 business-confidence survey of 627 member companies, as well as interviews with 11 executives between April and June this year – noted that these opportunities to collaborate would not last indefinitely.
“The broader finding is that Chinese companies are rapidly developing overseas experience themselves,” Oliver Oehms, executive director and board member of the German Chamber of Commerce in northern China, said at a press briefing in Beijing on Thursday.
“They are developing their own local networks or ecosystem, and obviously, they are quick learners, and they are getting familiar with the respective standards in the target market,” Oehms said, adding that German capabilities presenting partnership opportunities were becoming less distinctive over time.
Oehms noted that one executive from an automotive supplier called the next 18 months a “golden window to partner up”. Once that window closes, Chinese companies may have gained enough operational experience to expand globally on their own, the executive warned.

Trump made the promise of a so-called “Trump dividend” at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday night. He said the money would have to be spent in the U.S., although he did not offer details on how that restriction would be enforced. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000, very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.”
Such a plan would require congressional approval. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R, Ohio) endorsed the proposal and said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend after the election.
The proposal could also have significant economic consequences. The U.S. has roughly 240 million adult citizens, according to Census Bureau data, putting the proposal’s cost at approximately $1.2 trillion. Unless offset by new revenue or spending cuts, the payments would likely widen the federal budget deficit—which totaled nearly $1.8 trillion in fiscal 2025—and could add to inflationary pressures.
Vice President J.D. Vance later narrowed the proposal, suggesting that wealthy Americans would not qualify. He added that the payments could be financed by tariff revenue, which amounted to around $154.5 billion in the first 10 months of fiscal 2026 through July.
Trump suggested that the dividend would be financed by “tremendous economic success” from his policies.
“The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs, they don’t take in money, all they know is poverty,” the President said.
In his first term, Trump authorized two rounds of congressionally-approved stimulus checks during the COVID-19 pandemic. On Wednesday, he also compared the promised dividend with the $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” announced for military service members in December, which was funded by a congressionally approved housing supplement.
Some, however, are skeptical about the idea.
Rep. Chip Roy, (R, Texas) told Politico, “I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1 trillion.”
The Democratic National Committee said Trump and Republicans have repeatedly promised rebate checks that never materialized.
The President previously promised to send $2,000 tariff dividends to Americans. He also endorsed returning 20% of DOGE savings to taxpayers and depositing $1,000 or more into eligible Americans’ health savings accounts. None of these payments has gone out: the DOGE and tariff dividends were never enacted, and the HSA legislation—a Republican alternative to extending enhanced ACA premium tax credits, which expired at the end of 2025—failed in the Senate. The Administration is reportedly preparing a $500 rebate for some unsubsidized ACA enrollees.
“Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” DNC Rapid Response Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.”
Trump’s pledge comes at a low point for his popularity in his second term. His approval rating fell from 47% at the beginning of the term to 33% in mid-August, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Americans have expressed growing dissatisfaction with the economy and the war in Iran, now in its seventh month. Concerns about affordability, intensified by wartime supply disruptions, have propelled progressive Democratic candidates to a series of primary victories.
The President cast the congressional elections as a referendum on his presidency, telling voters at the convention to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
“If the Republicans win, you win with us,” Trump said. “Now all we have to do is win.”

Israeli authorities are considering plans to build 1,670 new housing units in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said late on Wednesday.
In a statement, the commission said the development came shortly after 12 Western countries decided to impose trade restrictions on products from illegal settlements and called on Israel to halt settlement expansion.
It said the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has approved 104 new illegal settlements and established 160 agricultural settlement outposts since taking office in late 2022.
The plans, which have reached the final approval stage, include 365 new housing units in the Maale Amos settlement southeast of Bethlehem and 200 in the Talmon settlement northwest of Ramallah.
The commission said the plans also include establishing three new illegal Israeli settlement areas from scratch: Amihai on the Ramallah-Nablus border, Ein Yitav in Jericho and Maoz Tzvi in the Jenin area.
The projects would include 749 housing units across 1,125 dunams (113 hectares), while 95 units would be added to the Peduel settlement and 259 to Alei Zahav in Salfit. Two additional units are planned for the Givat Zeev settlement northwest of occupied East Jerusalem.
The commission said the plans show that Israel is seeking not only to expand existing settlements but also to establish new and permanent settlement centres across Palestine’s occupied West Bank.
Under international law, the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, is considered part of the Occupied Palestinian Territory; and a core part of the territory of the State of Palestine. The transfer of an occupying power’s population into occupied territory is considered illegal under international law.
Despite this, Israel has accelerated the expansion of existing settlements and the construction of new ones in the occupied West Bank in recent years.

Yemeni government says campaign to retake Sana'a from Houthis has begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:58:52 UTC
16:58:52 KST

Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive against the Houthi terror group on several fronts, with senior officials describing the campaign as an effort to retake Sana’a after years of relative military stalemate.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Deputy Defense Minister Maj. Gen. Samir al-Sabri said on official Yemeni television that “the decision to liberate Sana’a has been finalized and taken decisively,” adding that government forces were advancing on several fronts. He said the objective was to restore state institutions and end Houthi control of the capital.
The Iranian-backed Houthis have controlled Sana’a since late 2014. Saudi Arabia launched Operation Decisive Storm with a Saudi-led coalition in March 2015, followed by Operation Restoring Hope the next month, but neither campaign succeeded in removing the group from the capital.
Fighting eased after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, though Yemen remained divided between Houthi-held territory in the north and areas administered by the internationally recognized government and southern forces. Calls for southern secession have further complicated efforts to rebuild a unified state.
Government officials say the current campaign has brought advances in the governorates of Al-Jawf, Al-Bayda, Taiz, and Al-Hudaydah. Those claims have not been independently verified in full, though recent reporting has confirmed intensified fighting in Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda.
Col. Majid al-Nuzaili, the official spokesperson for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said on X that “the Houthi group has attempted over the past years to impose on Yemeni society a project that transcends politics, attempting to alter the very nature of the religious, social, and cultural life that Yemenis have known throughout their history.”
He continued, “We do not want Yemen to become a replica of Iran, nor do we want to import centuries-old sectarian and historical conflicts into our country, nor do we want Yemenis to be forced to endure disputes that have never been their primary concern.”
In recent days, Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have stepped up operations against Houthi positions. The renewed fighting has coincided with Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi authorities said Houthi attacks on Sept. 8 struck sites in Abha, Jazan, Najran, and Khamis Mushait, injuring 73 people and causing fires and operational disruptions at energy facilities. The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for Saudi military operations in Yemen.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthi movement’s spokesperson, said on X that the operations in Yemen constituted “Saudi aggression.” He asserted that “Saudi Arabia is carrying out these operations,” not the Yemeni army, and threatened further attacks if the campaign continued.
Preparations Began Early
Hamed al-Ruba’i, a retired colonel in the Yemeni army, told The Media Line, “The battle to liberate Sana’a effectively began several years ago, through preparations, unifying the ranks of the armed forces, winning over Yemeni tribes, and securing military equipment, supplies, plans, training, and other resources.”
He continued, “The plan was clear: we wouldn’t begin until we were completely ready for this battle to ensure its success. Now is the most opportune moment, as the whole world has become aware of the danger posed by the Houthi militia, after their repeated targeting of several neighboring countries, shipping in the Bab el Mandeb Strait, and maritime traffic in the Red Sea, actions carried out on Iranian orders.”
Al-Ruba’i emphasized that “the most important thing was training, effective plans, and mobilizing the tribes, as Yemeni unity is what will defeat the Houthis.”
Street Battles and Changing Tactics
Yemen’s mountainous northern provinces, including Sana’a and Sa’dah, pose a major obstacle to any attempt to dislodge the Houthis. More than a decade of air campaigns has not removed the group from its northern strongholds, leaving any offensive dependent on ground forces and local alliances.
Ahmed al-Sabahi, a Yemeni military analyst, told The Media Line, “The battle to liberate Yemen from the Houthis will depend on the armed forces’ ability to engage in street battles to eliminate what remains of them.”
He added, “Now there is a tribal army and the Yemeni army, and they all know this terrain, how to hide in it, and from where to retaliate against the Houthis. This is what we are seeing in the current operational approach.”
Mohammed al-Kamel, a military analyst, told The Media Line, “The Yemeni army has changed its war tactics against the Houthis, starting with cutting off their supply lines, launching surprise attacks, and opening multiple fronts.”
He continued, “Drones are also being used in some attacks, and there are also warplanes providing air cover for the ground forces. Therefore, the armed forces’ tactics this time are more serious in liberating Sana’a.”
Al-Kamel added, “The Yemeni armed forces may have obtained the drones from Turkey, and several other arms sources.”
He said the Houthis had “lost a significant portion of its forces due to the operations it has carried out over the past three years, including targeting ships in the Red Sea, shelling Israel, and also the attacks on Saudi Arabia. With Iran’s involvement in the war with America, it has not supplied the Houthis with the necessary weapons and sufficient equipment, and they are perhaps now at their weakest point.”
Political support and regional risks
In a Sept. 8 statement on X, the US Embassy in Yemen said, “The Houthis started this conflict and must bear the consequences of their aggression. The Republic of Yemen is the sole legitimate government and has every right to defend its people and end the Houthis’ ability to inflict terror.”
At a press conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Tuesday, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan said that “the Houthis have opened a Pandora’s box for themselves.”
He added, “The Houthis prioritize their narrow, self-serving interests over the interests of Yemen and resort to violence whenever they are in a difficult position.”
Faisal bin Farhan continued, “The path for diplomacy to deal with the Houthis remains open.”
Saudi Arabia also said in a Foreign Ministry statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency that “the Kingdom reserves the right to respond to these attacks in self-defense.”
Potential Turkish, Pakistani participation
Dr. Awad al-Quraini, a Yemeni political analyst, told The Media Line, “Turkish or Pakistani forces may participate in operations to deter the Houthis, should Saudi Arabia declare that it is under attack and hostile operations, in accordance with the Mecca Agreement recently signed in Saudi Arabia.”
Al-Quraini added, “If Turkey and Pakistan enter the fray, the Houthis will fall within days. They made a mistake by targeting Saudi Arabia under this recently signed security agreement.”
He said that Turkey’s participation could involve equipment, drones, and warplanes, while Pakistan could provide ground forces.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August. The agreement includes collective-defense language, but the governments have not publicly defined the military commitments or procedures that would follow an attack on a signatory.
No Turkish or Pakistani deployment to Yemen has been announced.
Life under Houthi rule
Residents of Sana’a have endured severe economic hardship during more than a decade of Houthi rule, according to interviews with people in the capital. Humanitarian conditions, public services, salaries, and access to basic goods remain central concerns.
Munther Mohammed, a Yemeni citizen living in Sana’a, told The Media Line, “We are living in dire circumstances. Salaries aren’t even enough to buy bread for the entire month. There are no hospitals, no services, and none of the basic necessities for a human life. We can’t leave the governorate easily.”
He continued, “We want to get rid of the Houthis by any means necessary.”
Mohammed al-Dhubyani, a former Yemeni trader, agreed with Munther, telling The Media Line, “We pay taxes to the Houthis, and they often confiscate our goods. There are no regular salaries, and living has become difficult for everyone.”
The Houthis Say They Are Ready
Samir al-Numairi, a Yemeni journalist aligned with the Houthis, told The Media Line, “The Houthis will be able to deter this aggression. They have enough weapons, and they launched one of the largest attacks on Saudi Arabia, and they have more.”
He continued, “The Ansar Allah [Houthi] group will not submit to any compromises, and they will not sit at the negotiating table. They have significant military capabilities that they have built to deter any aggression, and they are ready for it.”

The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Indonesia orders Netflix to pay US$4.3m in music royalties or face shutdown
Netflix has agreed to pay music royalties it owed in South Korea and faces a tax demand on its income in Australia, media reports say
The National Collective Management Organisation (LMKN), a government-supported agency overseeing the country’s royalty system, said the streaming platform had not paid music royalties since entering the Indonesian market 10 years ago, the Jakarta Globe reported.
“The amount is estimated at around 75 billion rupiah, which Netflix must settle for the period since it opened access to its commercial digital service in Indonesia in 2016,” LMKN secretary general Bigi Ramadha Putra said in a statement on Wednesday.
Netflix is required to pay royalties under Indonesia’s 2014 copyright law, a 2021 government regulation on the management of song and music copyright royalties, and a 2025 regulation by the Law Ministry, according to Bigi.
“Netflix, as a digital platform conducting commercial activities in Indonesia, is required to respect copyright regulations and fulfil its obligations to rights holders,” he said.
Should the platform continue to drag its feet, LMKN plans to take the matter to the Law Ministry and the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry.
“If an obligation has been established but remains unfilled, then we must pursue the legal mechanisms available to us,” Bigi said. “If the regulations are not complied with, we will propose that access to Netflix in Indonesia be shut down.”
