Germany 'rebuilding pillars' of national security
Published September 10, 2026last updated September 10, 2026
What you need to know
- German Interior Minister Dobrindt says Germany needs stronger powers to counter drones and hybrid threats
- Energy CEO Markus Krebb said rules designed for 'peacetime' are no longer enough against sabotage
- German inflation rose to 2.9% in August, its highest level since late 2023
- The increase was driven mainly by higher energy prices, especially fuel and heating oil
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday September 10, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
NATO chief praises Germany as driver of European defense
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has praised Germany as a driving force behind efforts to strengthen Europe's defense capabilities, while warning that the threat from Russia remains high.
Speaking at the closing of the German Foreign Ministry's annual ambassadors' conference in Berlin, Rutte welcomed the government's decision to raise defense spending to 3.5% of gross domestic product by 2029.
Germany now spends more on defense than any other European country and has become a major driver of arms production, Rutte said.
"You have shifted into sixth gear on defense," he said.
Turning to Russia's war against Ukraine, Rutte said Moscow was continuing its attacks unabated and suffering more than 40,000 soldiers killed or seriously wounded each month.
He also warned that Russian hybrid attacks in Europe were increasing, including cyberattacks, sabotage and operations involving drones.
Following the drone incident in Leipzig in early August, Rutte assured Germany of NATO's full solidarity. The German government has blamed Russia for the attempted attack.
Rutte said NATO would continue supporting Ukraine while accelerating efforts to strengthen its own defense capabilities.
Europe was increasingly taking responsibility for its own security, he said, with the goal of building "a stronger European pillar in a strong NATO."
German Finance Ministry rejects Ifo defense debt criticism
Germany's Finance Ministry has rejected criticism from the Ifo Institute over the government's use of additional borrowing for defense spending.
The ministry said Ifo had applied the wrong benchmark when calculating how much of the extra debt had actually resulted in higher defense expenditure.
"The Ifo study does not apply the legal criteria that the Bundestag and Bundesrat enshrined in the Basic Law [Germany's constitution] with the exemption of defense spending from the debt brake," the ministry said.
"The study is therefore legally and methodologically wrong. It is comparing apples with oranges."
Ifo: Germany diverted 'debt brake' defense borrowing to other spending
The Munich-based Ifo economic research institute has accused the German government of using additional borrowing intended to create more room for defense spending for other purposes.
The Ifo said on Thursday that 38.5% of the additional debt taken on in 2025 under an exemption from Germany's constitutional debt brake did not translate into additional defense and security spending.
"A large part of the additional debt did not lead to additional defense spending," Ifo researcher Emilie Höslinger said. "Instead, the extra spending capacity freed up in the core budget was used for other purposes."
Germany changed its constitutional debt rules in March 2025, exempting defense and certain security spending above 1% of gross domestic product from the country's debt brake.
The measure was approved by the outgoing parliament with the support of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union, the center-left Social Democratic Party and the Greens.
Ifo found that relevant defense-related spending increased by €17.6 billion ($20.6 billion), while €28.6 billion ($33.5 billion) in debt was taken on under the exemption.
That left €11 billion ($12.9 billion) in additional borrowing that did not correspond to additional defense and security expenditure, Ifo said — equivalent to 38.5% of the total.
Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended plans to give security authorities greater investigative powers, accusing critics of putting people's safety at risk amid what he described as a heightened threat to Germany.
Speaking during a parliamentary debate on his ministry's 2027 budget, Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union, said the proposed powers were necessary to "protect our freedom."
"The threat level is high and is coming from different places," Dobrindt said.
He pointed to an explosives-laden drone discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport as evidence of the security challenges facing Germany, adding that Russia was clearly behind the incident and that it was "not an isolated event."
Dobrindt has pushed for stronger measures against drones and hybrid threats. He said under his leadership, the federal and state governments have established a new joint drone defense center, while a Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats (GAZ Hybrid) opened in June.
"We are rebuilding the pillars of security architecture," Dobrindt said on Thursday.
The Interior Ministry's budget is set to increase by more than €950 million ($1.1 billion) to €16.7 billion ($19.5 billion).
The Federal Criminal Police Office and Federal Police are among the agencies set to receive additional personnel.
Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, which is responsible for cybersecurity, is also due to receive more funding.
Sonja Eichwede, deputy parliamentary leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, highlighted additional spending planned for the Federal Agency for Technical Relief, saying it was important for civil protection and disaster response.
Germany sees sharp fall in asylum applications, says interior minister
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended the government's tougher migration policy, pointing to a sharp fall in asylum applications and continued controls at the country's borders.
"We have turned the migration wave into a migration turnaround," Dobrindt, of the Bavarian conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), told parliament during a budget debate on Thursday.
He said first-time asylum applications were down by around 75% compared with 2024.
"That is the result of control, direction and a clear stance," Dobrindt said.
Dobrindt said Germany was no longer Europe's number one destination for irregular migration.
According to European Union asylum data released on Thursday, Germany recorded approximately 55,000 applications in the first half of 2026, making it the country with the fourth-highest number of applications.
According to Dobrindt, 60,000 attempted irregular entries had been prevented at Germany's borders since the current parliamentary term began, while 1,700 suspected people smugglers had been arrested.
He said border controls would remain in place beyond September 15.
Dobrindt said the government was pursuing the same approach at European level.
He pointed to reforms of the EU's Common European Asylum System and said Germany wanted to step up returns of people whose asylum applications had been rejected.
According to Dobrindt, 42,000 people without grounds to remain had been returned from Germany to their countries of origin.
He said the next goal was to reach agreements with third countries on so-called return hubs — centers outside the EU where rejected asylum seekers could be sent.
What prompted the warning on infrastructure?
Police this week arrested a 48-year-old man suspected of trying to sabotage power lines near coal-fired power stations in North Rhine-Westphalia, Brandenburg and Saxony.
Investigators believe he used homemade rockets to fire conductive material across high-voltage lines, causing short circuits in some cases. Several units at a power station near Bergheim, west of Cologne, were reportedly taken out of operation for several days, while two short circuits were caused at a substation near the Jänschwalde power station in Brandenburg.
Authorities have linked letters claiming responsibility for the attacks to the suspect. The letters reportedly justified the sabotage as part of a campaign against electricity generation from fossil fuels.
The case has intensified concerns about the vulnerability of Germany's critical infrastructure. This includes sectors such as energy, information technology and transport whose disruption could lead to supply shortages, public-safety problems or other serious consequences.
German inflation rises to 2.9% on energy costs
Inflation in Germany rose to 2.9% in August, driven largely by sharply higher energy prices, the Federal Statistical Office confirmed on Thursday.
The annual rate was the highest since late 2023, up from 2.8% in July and 2.3% in June.
Energy prices rose 10.5% compared with August last year, accelerating from an 8.3% increase in July.
Motor fuels cost 27.7% more than a year earlier, while heating oil prices jumped 49.6%.
"Particularly noticeable was the rise in energy prices, especially for fuels, which was mainly caused by the Iran war," said Federal Statistical Office President Ruth Brand.
Other household energy costs fell, however. Electricity prices were down 5.5%, natural gas including operating costs fell 2.9% and district heating was 1.0% cheaper.
Food prices were only 0.1% higher overall than a year earlier, after a 0.4% rise in July.
Some products became significantly more expensive, including eggs, up 15.2%, fresh vegetables, up 5.2%, and fish and seafood, up 4.4%.
Butter was 29.9% cheaper, while fresh fruit fell 5.6% and dairy products 5.5%.
Inflation across the eurozone also remains above the European Central Bank's 2% target.
The ECB could raise its key interest rate on Thursday for the second time this year, from 2.25% to 2.50%. It increased rates in June for the first time in almost three years before leaving them unchanged in July.

German military evaluating 30 AI tools for introduction from 2027
BERLIN, Sept 10 - The German military is evaluating 30 artificial intelligence tools to speed up battlefield decision-making, aiming to deploy such a system from 2027, a senior military official told business daily Handelsblatt.
"The exploration is ongoing, and I'm optimistic that we will have a prototype in the second quarter of 2027," the chief of the military's cyber command, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum, told the paper, with full implementation expected in 2028.
The war in Ukraine has highlighted how drones and satellites generate vast streams of data, making the battlefield transparent as never before while creating a need for AI to process information at a speed impossible for humans to match.
Most of the AI tools under review are made by German companies, with French firm ChapsVision among the few foreign businesses in the race, the paper said.
In April, Daum for now ruled out purchasing the Maven Smart System, the best-known AI tool of its kind, made by U.S. data analytics and defence software company Palantir.
The U.S., NATO commands and several allies are deploying Palantir's Maven to analyse battlefield data, including images and video, to improve situational awareness and speed up decision-making.
Concerns over dependence on the U.S. and data sovereignty have fuelled resistance against Palantir in parts of Europe at a time when the U.S. is seen as a potentially unreliable ally after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to quit NATO. REUTERS

Türkiye has become Europe’s largest credit card market, surpassing Spain in the number of credit cards in circulation, according to a Mastercard report citing European Central Bank data.
Based on European Central Bank data cited by Mastercard,
The report said Türkiye had 142 million credit cards and 319 million bank cards, including prepaid cards, while card payments reached 24.1 trillion Turkish Liras in 2025.
According to the report, increasing digital payment penetration in Türkiye from the current 69 percent to levels approaching 95 percent in more mature markets could further boost the economy.
Digital payments supported household consumption through faster and alternative payment options, generating an estimated economic impact of nearly 1.5 trillion liras in 2025, the report said.
Travel spending contributed the most, at 546 billion liras, followed by the restaurant sector at 427 billion liras. Furniture and electronics, apparel, and accommodation were also among the sectors benefiting from digital payments.
The share of card payments in household spending reached 54 percent for personal cards and 69 percent when commercial cards were included in 2025.
The report noted that Türkiye’s expanding card payment infrastructure has made spending easier for foreign visitors and increased the country’s attractiveness as a tourism destination.
Tourism revenues rose from $7.6 billion in 2000 to nearly $65 billion in 2025, while the share of card payments in tourism revenues increased from 15 percent to around 38 percent, according to the report.
As a result, digital payments contributed 388 billion liras, or approximately $9.8 billion, to Türkiye’s tourism revenues in 2025.

Lockheed’s cruise missile contract crossed $10 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:39:52 UTC
16:39:52 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $826 million to its Lockheed Martin missile contract, pushing its total value past $10 billion for the first time.
- The contract covers continued JASSM and LRASM production through July 2030, with deliveries also going to Poland, the Netherlands, Japan and Finland.
The U.S. Air Force has added $826 million to its bulk missile contract with Lockheed Martin, pushing the total value of the deal past $10 billion for the first time.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, issued the contract modification for continued production of the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, known as JASSM, and the Long Range Anti-Ship Missile, known as LRASM. The award brings the contract’s total cumulative value to $10.48 billion, up from $9.65 billion. Work will be done at Lockheed Martin’s Orlando, Florida, facility, with completion expected by July 31, 2030.
The same contract crossed $9.485 billion in August 2025, when the Air Force added roughly $4.3 billion covering JASSM lots 22 through 26 and LRASM lots 9 through 12, with deliveries running to Poland, the Netherlands, Japan and Finland under Foreign Military Sales agreements. This latest $826 million addition keeps that same production line running rather than opening a new one. The funding is split across fiscal 2024, 2025 and 2026 missile procurement accounts, Navy weapons procurement funds, research and development money, operations and maintenance funds, and Foreign Military Sales money, reflecting how deeply intertwined U.S. and allied orders have become on this program.
JASSM is a stealthy, long-range cruise missile built to strike heavily defended, fixed or moving targets on land from outside the range of most enemy air defenses. The baseline version has a range of about 370 km (230 miles), while the extended-range JASSM-ER variant, now the more common configuration in Air Force inventories, reaches roughly 1,000 km (620 miles). JASSM has been in Air Force service since 2009 and is cleared to fly on the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, B-1B and B-52, giving multiple aircraft types a common long-range strike weapon rather than each platform needing its own missile. LRASM is a derivative of the JASSM-ER airframe adapted to hunt and destroy ships at sea, carrying a roughly 450 kg (1,000-pound) warhead. It flies on U.S. Navy F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and U.S. Air Force B-1B bombers today, with F-35 and F-16 integration work also underway to expand which aircraft can carry it.
Allied demand for both missiles has kept growing beyond the four countries already named on this contract. The U.S. State Department cleared a potential $842 million sale of JASSM-ER missiles to Denmark for its F-35s in June 2026, and approved a separate sale of JASSM-ER to Italy in December 2025. Australia and Finland have flown JASSM on their F/A-18 fleets for years, while Poland remains the only customer outside the U.S. to field the longer-range JASSM-ER, integrated on its F-16C/D fleet since deliveries began following a 2016 order. Israel has also been in discussions with Washington over a potential JASSM purchase.
The contract falls under the Pentagon’s Large Lot Procurement approach, which buys missiles in large multi-year batches rather than through smaller annual orders. The Air Force and Lockheed say the structure lowers the cost per missile, stabilizes Lockheed’s supply chain, and lets production ramp up faster than year-by-year contracting would allow. Lockheed opened a dedicated JASSM and LRASM factory in Troy, Alabama, in 2021 and added a 225,000-square-foot automated production facility in 2022 to support the higher volumes, incorporating robotic paint lines and automated forecasting tools.
Lockheed opened a dedicated JASSM and LRASM factory in Troy, Alabama, in 2021 and added a 225,000-square-foot automated production facility in 2022 to support the higher volumes, incorporating robotic paint lines and automated forecasting tools. The company has said ramping up production of both missiles is central to keeping pace with demand from the U.S. military and its growing list of allied customers.

Türkiye to stay course on disinflation program: Finance minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

16:37:04 KST

Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek (AA Photo)
Türkiye will maintain its economic program and deliver disinflation despite difficult global and geopolitical conditions, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek has said.
Şimşek joined Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz and Presidency of Strategy and Budget head İbrahim Şenel at the Presidential Complex on Sept. 9 for an international media meeting on Türkiye’s 2027-2029 Medium-Term Program (OVP).
“The only criticism we would accept is that we have been ambitious in our targets. We have, and there is, of course, a cost associated with that. But the commitment is there,” he said. “We will stay the course and deliver. What is important is the direction of travel.”
Şimşek said returning to a free-floating exchange rate is desirable because it acts as a shock absorber, but lower inflation, better-anchored inflation expectations and two-way foreign-exchange flows are needed first.
“This is not about being afraid of returning to a free float. It is about getting the conditions right,” he said, calling speculation over an imminent change “baseless.”
Şimşek rejected claims that the 2027 inflation target was revised upward to permit looser monetary policy.
“The idea that the inflation target for 2027 was revised upward in order to loosen monetary policy never came onto our agenda,” he said.
Şimşek said Türkiye’s disinflation program began in earnest in mid-2024, noting that international experience showed inflation typically takes 3.4 years to return to pre-shock levels.
“If you take that as a reference — 2025, 2026, and then essentially the end of 2027 — I think we’ll be back to pre-shock levels,” he said.

Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:36:30 UTC
16:36:30 KST

Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.
Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.
Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.
As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.
Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.
The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.
Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.
In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

Former Australian of the Year Grace Tame has clarified comments she made during an ABC interview about reports of sexual violence by terrorist group Hamas.
Ms Tame faced criticism after a March ABC Radio Sydney interview in which she likened reports of mass sexual assault during the attacks on October 7, 2023, to "propaganda".
After several months, Ms Tame posted to Instagram on Thursday, saying those comments were "misinterpreted".
"There is something I have wanted to clarify for a while, which I regret not clarifying sooner," she said.
"I stand with survivors of sexual violence everywhere, no matter who they are."
She continued in her Instagram video to allege her views were based on Human Rights Watch reports, where they were "unable to find evidence to support the claim that Israeli women were raped en mass on October 7, 2023".
United Nations officials in 2024 found there were reasonable grounds to believe conflict-related sexual violence, including rape and gang rape, occurred at several locations during Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel.
"However, I do not deny the legitimate accusations of rape made by individual Israeli women, including accounts of gang rape," Ms Tame said.
"I believe Israeli survivors, I believe Jewish survivors, as I believe all survivors. While the intention of my remarks was not to imply otherwise, I acknowledge and sincerely apologise for any harm their mischaracterisation has caused."
Grace Tame interviewed over previous comments
Ms Tame had appeared on ABC Radio Sydney to discuss her interpretation of the phrase "globalise the intifada".
She also responded to claims she had been selective in her outrage and accusations she had never spoken on behalf of the Israeli women believed to have been sexually assaulted on October 7.
"I'm not going to sink to the level of entertaining any kind of propaganda," she said at the time.
"Those things have been debunked.
"Awful things are being perpetrated by both sides. This is not selective outrage. I'm outraged by all of the violence."
Her interview was met with criticism from the Israeli embassy in Australia , which accused Ms Tame of losing her "moral compass".
The ABC Ombudsman later found the interview did not breach editorial standards, and met "the standards for ensuring accuracy in live radio interviews".
The embassy in Canberra had also raised concerns over previous comments by Ms Tame about her use of the phrase "globalise the intifada".
She was criticised by federal MPs and the NSW premier for leading a chant using the phrase at a rally against Israeli President Isaac Herzog during his visit to Australia.
"Globalise the intifada" is a contentious phrase that the state government has been considering outlawing under revised hate speech laws.
The word "intifada" means "shaking off" in Arabic and has been used to refer to two periods of violent Palestinian protest against Israel.
Members of the Jewish community have described it as a hateful call for violence.
In the interview with ABC Radio Sydney, Ms Tame said she understood the phrase "to be a call for widespread resistance" against the actions of Israel.

US backs Lebanon’s authority over war, peace decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:36:19 UTC
16:36:19 KST

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The US Embassy in Beirut said on Thursday that decisions on war and peace should rest exclusively with the Lebanese state, voicing support for the government’s efforts to assert sovereignty through the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF).
“Every day, the Lebanese people make it clear they prefer Lebanese state institutions over Hizballah’s weapons,” the embassy said in a statement on US media company X.
The embassy said southern Lebanon “does not belong to regional actors or militias” and expressed support for the Lebanese government’s stated goal of asserting sovereignty in the area.
It said the Lebanese army should enforce that sovereignty and ensure that “decisions of war and peace lie exclusively with the Lebanese state.”
The mission added that Washington “applauds” communities in southern Lebanon for favoring Lebanese state institutions over Hezbollah’s weapons.
The statement comes amid ongoing US-sponsored negotiations between Lebanon and Israel over Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon and the disarmament of non-state armed groups.
This week, Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji said at the 166th session of the Arab League Council in Cairo that US-sponsored negotiations were the “most effective way” to halt Israeli attacks and compel Israel to withdraw behind internationally recognized borders.
Lebanon and Israel have held seven rounds of direct negotiations under US sponsorship. The first five rounds were held in Washington, culminating in a 14-point framework agreement signed on June 26, while the sixth and seventh took place in Rome.
The latest round concluded on Aug. 6 after three days of talks covering military, political, legal and border issues, as well as prisoners.
The framework provides for a phased Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of non-state armed groups.
Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon, which it started in early March after Hezbollah's retaliation to the Iran war, despite the framework agreement. According to figures released by the Lebanese Health Ministry in late August, the attacks have killed more than 4,000 people and injured over 12,000.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:34:39 UTC
16:34:39 KST

The European Commissioner for Agriculture, Christophe Hansen, tells Euronews this has been “a very challenging summer” for farmers, with many “losing their harvests” due to extreme climate conditions.
Europe is recovering after a summer of heatwaves and droughts that have devastated crops and left many farmers facing huge financial losses. To help farmers cope, the European Commission is urging member states to make use of "flexibilities" in the EU's farm subsidy programme.
But Hansen admits no new money will be available for farmers. Instead, he asks for the “solidarity” of consumers and advises against expecting “a certain quality” of produce this year.

Fire on a ferry near the Philippines claims at least five lives
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10

Fire on a ferry near the Philippines claims at least five lives
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out aboard the MV June Aster near Palawan: five people were killed and dozens are missing. 43 passengers were rescued.
A fire broke out on a passenger ferry in the Philippines, claiming the lives of five people, while dozens are considered missing; however, 43 passengers were rescued. This reports the Associated Press, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the MV June Aster ferry was near its destination, Coron, in Palawan province, when a fire broke out on board at around 6:45 p.m. on Wednesday. After the fire was extinguished, the vessel remained afloat but listed, while smoke continued to rise from the charred hull for a long time. Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said that rescue operations are still ongoing.
We continue to conduct search-and-rescue operations
A Coast Guard ship, speedboats, a military vessel, other government boats, as well as private volunteers and fishermen joined the search
Bad weather and high waves posed a challenge for rescuers. The ferry was approximately 4 nautical miles (7.4 kilometers) from the village of Turda, where Coron is located, when it sent a distress signal, but strong sea currents carried it 7.68 nautical miles (14.2 kilometers) away from Turda
The Coast Guard also contacted a ship that was nearby to monitor the ferry's passengers and coordinated with coastal villages in case the rescued people reached the shore.
We remind you
A PKP Intercity train collided with a concrete mixer truck and derailed. One person was killed, about 20 passengers were injured, and four are in serious condition.

‘Not right’ to discuss Merz's future a day after AfD's win in Saxony-Anhalt, CDU politician says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:33:25 UTC
16:33:25 KST

CDU politician and German MP Günter Krings calls the Saxony-Anhalt election results “devastating”, saying the situation is “even worse than expected” after the far-right AfD won 43.8% of the vote.
It would not be “responsible” for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to talk about "changing the Chancellor" just one day after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) swept to electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt, CDU politician and German MP Günter Krings has told Euronews.
He says his party should focus its energy on addressing its “low” credibility, and also points the finger at the European Union, saying that “a significant part of the anger of the voters comes from the EU’s decisions”.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern German state on Sunday, more than double its showing five years ago.
That was well ahead of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2%, losing about half of its support. It's putting mounting pressure on the Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity has fallen to record low levels in opinion polls.

Béla Anda, chief spokesman for the federal government under Gerhard Schröder, says it will be “very hard” for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to regain control after the AfD’s landslide victory in regional elections.

Russian marketplace sellers started storing goods in own warehouses after drone strikes
Almost all sellers who work with Wildberries have started storing their goods in their own warehouses following Ukrainian drone strikes on the marketplace’s logistics facilities.
Citing data from the bank Tochka, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported that the share of sellers using the FBS (Fulfillment by Seller) model — in which goods are stored and shipped from the seller’s own warehouse — had nearly doubled to 97.4% by the end of August. A similar trend appeared at Ozon, where the share of sellers using their own warehouses rose by 7.8 percentage points, to 73.1%.
The share of sellers using the FBO (Fulfillment by Operator) model — where goods ship from the marketplace’s own warehouse — fell at both companies.
Wildberries told Kommersant it has indeed seen growing seller interest in FBS but stopped short of calling it a mass shift, with marketplace representatives saying sellers are trying to combine both models. Ozon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Experts polled by Kommersant said marketplaces charge higher commissions to sellers who use their own warehouses, but noted that for goods with steady demand, relying on a marketplace’s warehouse still offers advantages, including faster delivery.
Ukrainian troops have used drones to attack all of Wildberries’ major warehouses since mid-July. Ozon’s logistics facilities were also struck.
As of early August, the damage to Wildberries and its sellers from the drone strikes was estimated at hundreds of billions of rubles.
On September 9, Deputy Industry and Trade Minister Roman Chekushov said that not all of the logistics facilities damaged in Ukrainian drone strikes should necessarily be rebuilt. According to him, it’s first necessary to understand “how logistics will be restructured.”

IED master of arts graduates deploy design against the loss of common goods

IED MASTERS of arts EVOLVE PRACTICE THROUGH DESIGN X COMMONS
Marking an evolution in how design intervenes within contemporary society, the Master of Arts programs at Istituto Europeo di Design (IED)treat the discipline as a mediator between communities and common goods. Grounded in the understanding of commons as the material and immaterial resources that multiple communities engage with as the collective heritage of humanity, the overarching theme of Design X Commons elevates these graduate thesis projects past formal styling exercises and traditional product development. Combining research alongside speculative design strategies, the emerging designers confront climate vulnerability, urban privatization, labor exploitation, and spatial inequality to reshape collective urban futures.
IED Master of Arts Exhibition | all images courtesy of Istituto Europeo di Design (IED)
POSITIONING DESIGNERS AS AGENTS OF SOCIAL EQUALITY
IED structures its two-year Master of Arts programs to foster independent critical thinking in response to systemic global issues. Central to this educational model is the concept of common goods, encompassing both natural resources such as water, land, and air, as well as immaterial assets like cultural knowledge, open data, and public spaces. The institute positions the management of these resources, known as commoning, as a fundamental design practice. Through research, material testing, and participatory methods, graduates learn to challenge traditional industrial habits and build regenerative models that support both human and environmental ecosystems.
IED’s Master of Arts graduates present their thesis projects under the umbrella ‘Design X Commons’
GRADUATE PROJECTS SPOTLIGHT ECOLOGICAL REGENERATION AND SOCIAL equality
This design approach materializes in graduate work that targets specific local vulnerabilities while developing frameworks adaptable to global conditions. At IED Milano, Michele Martelloni addresses coastal erosion along the Apuan shoreline with ‘Systemic Reef’. The project transforms the industrial tetrapod into a porous, modular structure designed to dissipate wave energy and encourage marine life colonisation. The designer integrates waste marble powder from local quarries into a structural mixture, establishing a five step protocol for systemic coastal management.
‘Systemic Reef’ operates at the intersection of territorial knowledge, material research, and ecological urgency
In the Visual Communication program, Ana Sofia Camacho created ‘En la Olla. Narratives of Joyful Subversion’, a project that explores cultural identity. She focuses on everyday Latin American expressions, showing how creative play acts as a form of resistance against long standing social challenges. Camacho organizes these visual symbols into a series of objects that function as a collection and a manifesto, elevating local traditions and street culture into recognized, valuable contributions to modern creative practice.
the project reinterprets structural violence while challenging the dehumanizing legacy of colonization
At the intersection of spatial politics and climate adaptation, Olga Matsiuk developed ‘Where did water go? Urban bathing as a Common Practice Responding to an Ecosocial Emergency in Milan’ to address urban water accessibility. Framing water access as a basic human right, the project centers on a temporary public bathing festival around an underused fountain in Piazza Kaisserlian. The installation brings community members together to enjoy shared space while advocating for the reopening of nearby closed public swimming facilities.
framing public water access, the thesis acts as a political gesture of resistance against urban privatization
At IED Roma, Elena Bicocchi targets neighborhood revitalisation through ‘Strada domestica’, a project created for the Tuscolano district in collaboration with local authorities. The design reclaims Via Valesio from automobile traffic, expanding the comfortable qualities of domestic space into the street. Opening connected residential courtyards to community activities and adding flexible public structures called habitats, Bicocchi turns a vacant roadway into a resident-managed civic center.
through community-focused design, the ‘Strada domestica’ revitalizes a marginalized urban area
In the Textile Design program at IED Firenze, Ruby Berryman developed ‘Invisible Hands’ to examine human rights within Tuscany’s luxury fashion supply chain. The research highlights labor conditions affecting immigrant workers behind the Made in Italy label. To address these issues directly, Berryman created Mani Visibili, an online platform offering legal guidance, union resources, and a secure space for worker organizing.
the project ‘Invisible Hands’ reveals the complex social dynamics shaping contemporary fashion manufacturing
Focusing on geographic migration, Anna Leccese created ‘Punto di Ritorno’ within the IED Torino Interaction Design program to explore youth movement between southern and northern Italy. The project examines young people from Puglia who moved away for study or work and are considering moving back. The platform addresses the complex process shaped by personal desires, uncertainties, and career expectations, guiding individuals through well informed transitions back to their home region.
‘Punto di Ritorno’ examines the spatial and social conditions that enable displaced youth to return to their hometown
Virginia Urro responds to the urban housing crisis with ‘COHO MUNITY’, an interior design project based at IED Torino. The proposal converts the disused Manifattura di Moncalieri industrial site into an accessible, flexible cohousing ecosystem. Retrofitting existing building stock instead of constructing new facilities, Urro integrates shared domestic spaces and modular living units designed to reduce urban isolation and lower environmental impact.
transforming a disused industrial building into a housing scheme, ‘COHO MUNITY’ prioritizes shared spaces

Digital Worlds and the Limits of Frictionless Space: Rethinking Scale and Materiality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Historically, the way we design has been closely linked to the way we build. Architecture moved through physical testing, trial and error, projection drawings, mock-ups, and physical models: each introducing a new layer of abstraction, but still remaining tied to material, scale, and construction. The introduction of CAD significantly changed this dynamic. At first, it was largely understood as the computerization of precise geometry for construction. Over time, however, digital tools moved earlier into the design process, replacing sketching, physical trial and error, model-making, and other forms of thinking that had once kept scale and material close at hand.
The lineage of architectural design can therefore be understood, in part, as an evolution of abstractions. Some have been extraordinarily productive. Plans and sections, for example, isolate particular dimensions of architecture while still allowing the mind to reconstruct the whole. They flatten, cut, and reduce, but they do not abandon the building. Through the combination of drawings, one can understand rooms, circulation, structure, openings, and spatial relationships without becoming lost in the complexity of the project. Their abstraction is disciplined because it remains tied to an architectural reality that must eventually be measured, built, and inhabited.
Other abstractions move closer to escapism. Digital modeling, especially through the seemingly infinite zoom of the screen, allows architecture to escape the limits of paper size, drawing scale, and even bodily comprehension. It is an extremely powerful and constructive tool, capable of objectifying almost anything: a screw, a wall assembly, a tower, a city, or an entire mountainous landscape. The only apparent limitation becomes computing power, rather than the scale of the drawing, the reach of the hand, or the ability of the body to understand what is being represented. This freedom has driven much of the design process over the last 10 to 20 years, if not dominated it, precisely because it is convenient, manageable, and apparently without obvious drawbacks.
Related Article
The Continued Relevance of Models in Architecture's Digital Era
Yet this freedom presents an implicit bias. It erases many of the limitations that once reminded architects that buildings are not weightless. Architecture has gravity, thickness, tactility, resistance, maintenance, and scale. Digital tools can make these conditions visible, but they often default to making them disappear. Rather than keeping the designer in contact with physical reality, they can distance the design process from the very conditions through which architecture derives much of its meaning.
The Loss of Measure
Scale is one of architecture's most basic forms of knowledge: something that can be trained and developed, yet remains extremely difficult to master or make intuitive. It is not simply a number assigned to a drawing, but an internalized bodily relationship to dimension. A room feels narrow because shoulders, furniture, doors, and movement make it so. A ceiling feels low because the body senses the pressure of what is above it. Even a monumental space depends on the relative smallness of the body to make its vastness legible.
In digital environments, this form of relational measure begins to weaken. The camera can glide through space without effort, while zooming in and out almost indefinitely, limited less by bodily movement than by the capacities of the computer itself. The eye can occupy positions the body never could. Other dimensions are similarly liberated from physical limits: a room can expand endlessly, a wall can become infinitely thin, and a column can disappear if it disturbs the image. This liberation is productive, enabling forms of imagination that may otherwise have been impossible. Yet it also introduces a paradox: what results may be visually powerful without necessarily being spatially convincing. Scale becomes an effect, or an afterthought, rather than a relationship.
Materiality undergoes a similar transformation. In physical drawings and models, materials resist complete abstraction. Even in a simple paper model, the thickness, edge, stiffness, and grain of the paper begin to inform how the model is made and how it is read, unlike the seemingly weightless planes of a digital environment. On a construction site, these conditions become more explicit: timber has grain direction, concrete records its formwork and joints, and metal reveals the processes of cutting, bending, fastening, and weathering. Materials are never only appearances; they are records of extraction, fabrication, assembly, labor, use, weathering, and touch.
In digital space, materiality often becomes texture. Wood becomes a map, concrete a surface effect, glass a degree of transparency, and metal a reflection. These simulations can be sophisticated and beautiful, but they can also detach material from consequence. A digital surface may appear rough without being abrasive or aged without having weathered. It can carry the image of materiality without the obligations of matter.
This matters because architecture is never only seen. It is entered, cleaned, touched, heard, repaired, and crossed over time. When design methods privilege the frictionless image, architecture risks losing contact with these slower forms of material knowledge. The problem is not that digital worlds lack real material. It is that they can train architects to accept materiality as appearance without resistance, while also creating a false sense of control for clients who may come to believe that any material can be specified primarily for visual preference, without fully understanding its physical benefits, limitations, performance, and character.
Implied Physicality
If digital environments are to remain architecturally meaningful, they do not need to imitate physical buildings literally. Virtual architecture does not need to pretend that every wall is brick, every floor is concrete, or every structure is buildable. Part of its value lies precisely in its ability to test spatial conditions that physical architecture cannot easily produce. But even the most speculative digital world can still retain some form of implied physicality.
Implied physicality is the sense that a space understands weight even when it has none. A digital wall may not need to hold anything up, but it can still suggest mass, thickness, and resistance that might be tested against physical reality. A floor may not need to carry load, but it can still imply material depth by being tested and reconfirmed through physical modeling, rather than existing only as an accumulation of infinitely thin planes.
This is where architecture has something important to contribute to digital culture. As AI-generated imagery, virtual environments, gaming worlds, and speculative renders become increasingly easy to produce, visual novelty alone is no longer enough. Architecture can offer a different standard of judgment: not simply whether a space looks impressive, but whether it resists escaping architectural reality altogether—whether it communicates scale, sequence, material implication, and inhabitation, and whether those qualities can be meaningfully conveyed to the stakeholders who encounter it.
The most compelling digital worlds are therefore not necessarily those that escape all constraints, but those that choose their constraints carefully. They may suspend gravity while still communicating weight. They may invent impossible materials while still giving those materials behavior, thickness, or consequence. In other words, they do not reject physicality; they reconstruct it through implication, while allowing digital speculation to develop in parallel with an understanding of the real, physical world.
Returning to the Ground
The question is not whether architecture should be liberated from constraint. Every act of design requires some liberation from existing conditions. Without abstraction, architecture would only reproduce what already exists. But liberation becomes shallow when it removes and escapes from the very forces that allow architecture to be understood: gravity, material resistance, bodily scale, and the slow intelligence of making.
Digital tools have expanded architecture's imaginative field, and that expansion should not be dismissed. They allow designers to move fluidly through size, test complex geometries, simulate environments, and invent worlds beyond the limits of physical constraints. But they also require a more conscious discipline. The more easily architecture can become an image, the more carefully it must remember what distinguishes space from scenery.
Digital worlds are not weightless simply because they are virtual. They become weightless when they forget how architecture touches the ground. To design for virtual space, then, is not to abandon architectural knowledge, but to reassert it under new conditions. The future of digital architecture may depend not on escaping scale and materiality altogether, but on finding new ways to keep them active as forms of spatial knowledge—embedded, tested, and consciously intertwined throughout the design process.

Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:29:00 UTC
16:29:00 KST

Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Alongside military defense, it is equally necessary to significantly and visibly strengthen the protection of the country's internal security, because threats do not begin only in a crisis or wartime, nor are they carried out solely by military means, writes Kristjan Pärt.
The three saboteurs who set out to torch defense industry company Milrem Robotics on the night of August 15 were already sitting in Latvian police detention cells as suspects just a couple of days later. How was it possible to catch them so quickly? Perhaps cadets at the Estonian Academy of Security Sciences will hear the answer in a surveillance course — but even then, only 10 or more years from now.
The investigation is ongoing. We will determine whether the sabotage against Estonia was carried out in the interests of a state or organization and, if so, which one. But at this point, one's thoughts inevitably turn to Hando Runnel's poem "Jälle" ("Again"):
"Again the winds are howling, again the tempests roar.
Again from the east come herds of elk and bears."
Estonia's strength lies in its open society, democratic system of government and rule of law. Those strengths, however, can also present a window of opportunity to those who see our way of life as a thorn in their side.
Because of Estonia's geopolitical location, our internal security — and the country's overall security situation — is most strongly affected by external factors and developments, whether political, socioeconomic or technological, as well as by external threats, hostile foreign states and non-state organizations operating across borders.
Among hostile foreign states, Russia is the principal threat to European security, along with, indirectly, the regimes that support it. Other threats include violent extremist and terrorist groups, as well as international criminal organizations and networks. Each uses covert, nonmilitary methods to achieve its objectives, seeking to exploit the vulnerabilities of open societies and democratic ways of life — or the limited capabilities of security and law enforcement agencies.
The security of the state and society is threatened both by direct hostile activity and by harmful effects or external dependencies that materialize as a result of our own vulnerabilities.
If a hostile foreign state can gather intelligence on our territory without risk, influence our society or specific target groups and prepare positions that can be used to provoke a crisis or support a military operation, the conditions have been created for further escalation.
When strategic vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the damaging effects on security can also emerge gradually and insidiously.
Depending on the specific risks and the area affected, the consequences may include damage to the state's internal sovereignty or to Estonia's status as a nation-state, the fragmentation of society, the spread of radicalization and violent extremism, growing anti-state attitudes among certain groups in society or deepening economic or energy dependence on high-risk countries. These are all threats that military defense capabilities can neither mitigate nor repel.
Russia carries out its nonmilitary hostile activities even before a crisis becomes perceptible or aggression becomes visible — in other words, during what we understand as peacetime. Damaging and weakening other countries and societies through nonmilitary and hybrid methods is part of Russia's foreign policy doctrine, with its aggressive intelligence and security services playing an integral role.
Russia's primary objective is not to seize territory, but to create a situation in which another country's ability to make decisions and resist has already been weakened before a crisis begins or in which that country has surrendered a significant part of its self-determination. A strong defense force alone is not enough to counter such a strategy. The state must also be capable of mitigating risks and detecting and preventing threatening activities at an early stage.
In short, ensuring national security requires both strategic risk mitigation and sufficient operational capabilities. The first of these involves reducing vulnerabilities in society and its institutions. This requires consistent policy measures with a broad, society-wide and nationwide impact that must also mitigate so-called creeping threats to our security and sovereignty.
A strategy for reducing vulnerabilities means assessing risks, developing policy and engaging society in ways that increase resilience to attacks of any kind, harmful influences on society and external dependencies.
Resilient societies are characterized by shared fundamental values, trust within the country, citizens' voluntary contributions and the ability to cope with and recover from different crises.
Examples of decisions aimed at reducing Estonia's vulnerabilities include the transition to Estonian-language education, visa restrictions and restrictions on real estate purchases by citizens of aggressor states, as well as the introduction of up-to-date continuity and security requirements for the country's vital services and digital service providers.
In the long term, many measures aimed at reducing the country's vulnerabilities directly support internal security and the principle of domestic peace enshrined in our Constitution.
The second prerequisite for maintaining security is the ability to detect and prevent hostile activity at any time, in both military and nonmilitary domains. This is where the strategic role of internal security begins: protecting the continued existence and functioning of the state.
The task of internal security agencies is to ensure that hostile states, their intelligence and security services or extremist groups cannot operate in Estonia in ways that threaten our constitutional order or the security of society as a whole. The primary responsibility for this rests with the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).
Interior Ministry Secretary General Tarmo Miilits recently wrote about freedom, which resonates with those who can hear it. He rightly emphasized that the internal security services, which work around the clock to counter threats that have already reached Estonia, are the country's final line of defense for safety and security before the Defense Forces have to leave their training grounds and actually go into battle.
Counterintelligence, border security and migration monitoring and the prevention and disruption of hostile influence operations, terrorism and sabotage are proactive measures for ensuring national security. Their purpose is to respond effectively to offenses that have already been committed but, even more importantly, to detect and counter activities threatening Estonia's security before they develop into a broader crisis. Maintaining these capabilities, however, requires up-to-date legal powers, technological capabilities and sufficient resources.
These two main lines of action — reducing vulnerabilities and maintaining readiness to prevent or counter various attacks — complement one another and create an environment in which acting against Estonia becomes difficult, costly and ineffective for those who threaten us.
The Milrem Robotics sabotage case is a good illustration of why maintaining internal security requires a physical presence and the ability to respond at the scene, but also, of course, the capacity to collect, process and lawfully use information necessary for security purposes.
In today's digital societies, detecting and proving many such crimes increasingly depends on technological capabilities and the use of digital footprints. In its first internal security advisory submitted to the interior minister, the ISS described this as striking a balance between preventing threats and ensuring access to data.
"Security and law enforcement agencies must have effective tools to protect security in today's digital society and to detect and prove crimes that have been committed using digital evidence," the ISS wrote in its advisory. Of course, that means access to data, but it also means ensuring that the use of data and oversight are proportionate.
A legal framework that reflects the threats we face and enables action is a critical part of the capacity to ensure internal security. If the state can identify threats in time and respond to them, it can preserve public safety while also safeguarding people's freedoms and the functioning of the democratic system. A democratic state becomes stronger when it is able to prevent threats lawfully and proportionately.
Believe it or not, keeping the capabilities of Estonia's internal security agencies up to date is not a narrow institutional interest of the interior ministry, the ISS or the PPA, just as developing national defense is not a narrow institutional interest of the Ministry of Defense or the Defense Forces. All of this is a strategic investment in the continued existence of the Estonian state and in our sovereignty.
Like military national defense, the development of internal security capabilities requires stable and predictable funding. This makes it possible to pursue developments that meet contemporary requirements and reflect the current threat landscape, recruit highly capable people, provide continuous staff training, invest in forward-looking technologies and much more.
Military national defense and internal security are not competitors, but partners that complement one another. One prepares the country for a military crisis; the other helps do everything possible to prevent hostile activity within the country from escalating into a crisis. A strong defense force without robust internal security leaves an adversary free to act against us in areas where weapons are not used. Likewise, strengthening internal security alone is not enough without credible military deterrence and defense capabilities. Estonia needs both.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

"Members have clearly noticed government efforts to improve the regulatory environment, and this year those gains are reinforced by steadier U.S.-China relations," said Jeffrey Lehman, chair of AmCham Shanghai. "We urge both countries to build on the momentum of recent engagement and lock in a stable, transparent framework that is conducive to cross-border trade and investment."
Eric Zheng, president of AmCham Shanghai, emphasized the great importance of the Chinese market, mainly from two dimensions.
China remains one of the most efficient manufacturing bases in the world and continues to be a highly strategic market for members' products and services, Zheng said. "That underpins the positive sentiment," he added.
Chinese operations also contributed to the global and domestic business performance of U.S. companies, the survey showed.
Among members with U.S. operations, three-quarters confirmed that their China presence benefits their U.S. operations in some way, with one-third emphasizing that their China presence enhances the global competitiveness of their U.S. operations.
A notable strategic shift is also emerging, with more surveyed companies adopting a global-oriented strategy. The "in China for the world" strategy has become the top business priority for 29 percent of surveyed companies in 2026, surpassing the "in China for China" model chosen by 24 percent.
More respondents are also betting on China-based innovation, the report said. Half of surveyed members with China-based research and development (R&D) facilities plan to increase R&D spending this year, up sharply from one-third in 2025.
The report is based on AmCham Shanghai's 2026 China Business Survey of 262 member companies.
In a vote of confidence in the Chinese market, General Motors (GM) in August announced a 20-year extension of its joint venture partnership with Chinese automaker SAIC Motor, with it now running to 2047.
"We will continue to strengthen our performance here in China by developing products and technologies in China, for China, and bringing them to market faster," said John Roth, GM senior vice president & president of GM China. The joint venture plans to launch at least 30 new energy vehicle models by 2030.
"We see meaningful opportunities to grow beyond China. SAIC-GM has strong local capabilities across engineering, manufacturing and quality, and we can apply those strengths in select international markets, including the Middle East, Africa, South America, Mexico and Asia-Pacific," Roth said.
"Foreign companies continue to value the Chinese market for its scale and dynamism and, increasingly, as a base for serving the world," noted Jeff Yuan, head of tax at PwC China, adding that China remains a critical part of their global strategy for innovation, production and sourcing. ■

Study finds earliest evidence of habitual drug use
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:28:34 CST
16:28:34 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered what may be the earliest evidence of habitual drug use, dating "betel nut" use among early human foragers to as early as 25,000 years ago, tens of thousands of years before agriculture.
A team led by Australia's Griffith University archaeologists found evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier in time than previously supposed, according to a university statement released Thursday.
The team, working with Indonesian archaeologists, combined biochemical and archaeological evidence to trace the prehistoric roots of betel nut, one of the world's most popular addictive stimulants and an ancient drug used throughout much of the Asia-Pacific region.
The study, published in Science Advances, reports the discovery of extremely rare skeletal remains of two early human foragers from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, one dating to 25,000-16,000 years ago, the other to 7,600-6,300 years ago.
Both hunter-gatherers display highly unusual deep, rounded tooth grooves, a marker the researchers established was caused by a previously unknown drug-use behavior: habitual sucking of whole betel nuts, researchers said.
Biochemical analyses also detected arecoline in the foragers' dental tissues, providing strong evidence for betel nut ingestion, they said, adding that experiments showed that sucking intact betel nuts can release enough arecoline to have a physiological effect and alter brain function.
Betel nut use was previously thought to have emerged around the Neolithic or Bronze Age, about 3,500 years ago.
The findings suggest habitual psychoactive substance use existed among hunter-gatherers tens of thousands of years before farming, and betel nut-sucking may represent the earliest evidence of drug use yet recorded. ■

New B-21 hangar heads to Missouri’s Whiteman Air Force Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:26:50 UTC
16:26:50 KST

- The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a B-21 radio frequency hangar at Whiteman Air Force Base.
- Whiteman, which currently hosts the Air Force's entire B-2 fleet, is set to become the B-21 program's second main operating base after Ellsworth.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a new radio frequency and measurements hangar for the B-21 Raider stealth bomber at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri.
The facility will include space for one B-21 aircraft, along with supporting workshops, material storage, and administrative offices. Three companies bid on the project, which the Corps solicited online. Work is expected to be finished by September 25, 2029. The Army Corps’ Kansas City district is managing the contract, funded through fiscal 2026 military construction dollars.
The B-21 is the aircraft the Air Force is counting on to anchor its bomber fleet for decades to come. Built by Northrop Grumman as a nuclear-capable stealth bomber, it first flew in November 2023 and remains in low-rate initial production, with the Air Force and Northrop Grumman announcing an agreement in February 2026 to expand production capacity and speed up deliveries. The Air Force has said the B-21 is designed to penetrate the kind of heavily defended airspace that older bombers can no longer survive in, and the service confirmed in July 2026 that the aircraft will fly with a two-person crew. The program has continued hitting test milestones through 2026, including an aerial refueling demonstration with a KC-135 tanker in April.
Whiteman is set to become the B-21’s second main operating base, after the Air Force picked the installation over Dyess Air Force Base in Texas. Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota became the program’s first main operating base in 2021 and currently serves as the B-21’s formal training site; Air Force leadership visited Ellsworth in July 2026 to mark what the service called a historic milestone in that base’s B-21 facilities work. Whiteman already hosts the Air Force’s entire fleet of B-2 Spirit stealth bombers, 19 aircraft in total, two of which have been lost in crashes over the years.
The B-21 is being built to gradually replace both the B-2 and the older B-1 Lancer, which the Air Force expects to begin retiring around 2031 and 2032 as it moves toward a two-bomber fleet alongside the B-52.
A radio frequency and measurements hangar is used to test an aircraft’s radar signature and electronic systems in a controlled environment, work that matters for a stealth bomber designed to evade enemy radar. Conti Federal has built several other B-21 support facilities at Ellsworth, including a $31.7 million fuel cell maintenance hangar awarded in October 2024, part of what the company has described as a broader, multi-year construction effort tied to the bomber’s rollout.

====================================================================================================

U.S. Air Force signs $149M deal to keep its bunker busters in production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:22:22 UTC
16:22:22 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded four manufacturers a combined $149 million in contracts to build large penetrator warhead cases for bunker-busting bombs.
- The Eglin Air Force Base-run competition drew four offers, with work expected to run through September 2033 if a contract option is exercised.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded four manufacturers a combined $149 million to build metal cases for large bunker-busting bombs, splitting the work across small forging and machining shops rather than a single prime contractor.
Superior Forge and Steel of Lima, Ohio; Ellwood National Forge of Irvine, Pennsylvania; Faxon Machining LLC of Cincinnati, Ohio; and Grand Valley Manufacturing of Titusville, Pennsylvania each received a firm-fixed-price, cost-type indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract for what the Air Force calls large penetrator warhead case assembly production. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Attack Weapons Branch at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, ran the competition and received four offers before making the awards.
The contracts cover manufacturing of the warhead cases and their components, including both full-scale and subscale versions used for testing. Work at all four companies is expected to wrap up by September 7, 2033, if the Air Force exercises an option to extend the deal. The Air Force obligated just $10,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development funding at the time of the award, a placeholder amount typical for IDIQ contracts where the government orders and pays for specific quantities of work over time rather than committing the full ceiling value upfront.
A large penetrator warhead case is the hardened metal shell built to survive the impact of slamming into a hardened target, like a bunker or tunnel complex, before the explosive charge inside detonates.
The Air Force’s existing weapon in this category is the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a 13,600 kg (30,000-pound) bomb built by Boeing that carries a roughly 2,700 kg (6,000-pound) warhead and is dropped from B-2 and B-52 bombers. The Pentagon used GBU-57 bombs against Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility in June 2025.
The Air Force is also developing a successor weapon, the Next Generation Penetrator, after awarding Applied Research Associates a two-year design and prototyping contract in September 2025. Boeing is partnered with ARA on that program, building the new weapon’s tail kit. The Air Force notice announcing this week’s case-assembly awards did not specify which penetrator program, or programs, the contracts will supply.

====================================================================================================

Trump's Iran campaign echoes the post-9/11 'forever wars' - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:22:04 UTC
16:22:04 KST

When Donald Trump campaigned for a second term in the White House, he promised to be a “president of peace” who would stop foreign wars, not start them.
Now, a quarter-century after the September 11, 2001, attacks that triggered America’s global “war on terror,” he is entangled in an unpopular conflict of his own making that analysts say risks becoming his version of a “forever war."
With the 9/11 anniversary at hand, Trump’s war against Iran is drawing comparisons in foreign policy circles to the long, divisive conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq that preceded it. It is also prompting questions about whether the US has again failed to learn the lessons of past conflicts or prepare a clear exit strategy.
“Trump has broken an important post-Iraq and Afghanistan constraint in Washington against launching another major, open-ended war in the Middle East,” said Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy, a Washington think tank. “That could leave his successor inheriting ... an entrenched US-Iran confrontation.”
Administration officials have said the war against Iran is nothing like the protracted post-9/11 engagements.
During the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, the US removed hostile governments, committed thousands of ground troops who took and held territory, suffered and inflicted much higher casualties, and struggled to instill Western-style governance.
US mired in war of attrition
This time, the US is relying mainly on air and naval power, operations that have damaged Iran militarily and economically but have not defeated it or spurred Iranians to overthrow their rulers as Trump initially urged.
But after six months of war, the United States is mired in a battle of attrition punctuated by bursts of hostilities - exemplified by this week's exchange of attacks on oil tankers - while Trump tries to tighten the economic noose around Tehran.
Analysts warn it is likely to drag on well past the US midterm elections in November, when voters' opposition to the war could threaten Trump's Republican Party's chances of keeping control of Congress.
And, much like those earlier conflicts, there is no obvious exit even as the economic costs weigh on US consumers.
Tehran’s disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed US gasoline prices higher. The war has weakened Trump’s approval ratings and undermined Washington’s international standing, which was also one of the repercussions from the Iraq and Afghan wars.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Trump alone had “possessed the courage” to confront Iran over its nuclear program, that he had achieved all of his objectives, and that Iran's economy was being crippled by stepped-up sanctions and a US maritime blockade.
She did not respond directly to Reuters' questions on how the Iran conflict fits into America’s legacy of post-9/11 wars.
Lessons ignored?
Analysts say Trump has failed to heed the central lessons of the post-9/11 era, which began after al-Qaeda militants crashed planes into New York’s World Trade Center and the Pentagon outside Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.
Those include the steep political downsides of long wars and the dangers posed by an entrenched foe fighting for its survival.
The attacks led to decades of conflict, starting with the invasion of Afghanistan, where al-Qaeda leaders were sheltering, and followed by the 2003 invasion of Iraq, based on what turned out to be faulty intelligence that it was developing weapons of mass destruction.
The twin wars undertaken by President George W. Bush overstretched the US military and destabilized the Middle East.
The resulting US public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, and he won a second term in 2024, vowing to avoid military adventurism and focus on Americans’ economic concerns.
But similar to how the Bush administration underestimated the insurgencies the US would face in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump and his aides have miscalculated Iran’s resiliency and ability to throttle a fifth of the world’s energy shipments, analysts say.
Notably, Trump’s "Operation Epic Fury" launched alongside Israel on February 28 was not precipitated by a 9/11-type national trauma but was deemed by critics to be a war of choice. Experts have disputed Trump’s claims that Tehran’s nuclear program posed an imminent threat to the US
Iran may be taking a page from Afghanistan’s Taliban, who returned to power five years ago after a chaotic US withdrawal, that a determined foe can outlast Washington’s superior firepower while domestic pressure erodes its resolve.
The Iran conflict has also illustrated the cost of going to war with few allies on board.
Bush secured significant international support before launching his Iraq and Afghan campaigns, though that backing waned over time.
By contrast, Trump attacked Iran with little prior consultation or explanation and has found European and Asian leaders mostly resistant to his demands for assistance.
Relations with Trump had already been strained by his threat to seize Greenland, his questioning of NATO’s utility, his reduction of weapons supplies to Ukraine and his sweeping tariffs on trade partners.
High cost for allies
The conflict has also mirrored the Iraq invasion in terms of a regional spillover that seemed to catch Washington off-guard, in this case Tehran’s retaliation against US Gulf allies.
With Iran’s neighbors quietly seeking to de-escalate a conflict they never wanted, a Gulf official lamented that the administration might be making some of the same errors of the post-9/11 wars.
“What was the (US) strategy here?” asked the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Saudi analyst Aziz Alghashian described "a sense of limitation and helplessness in the Gulf about the wars that are taking place due to the whims of the United States."
While the Iraq and Afghan wars ended as unpopular conflicts, both started with solid support at home.
Trump’s war enjoyed no such honeymoon in public opinion.
Most Americans were against it from the outset, and he has even drawn criticism from prominent figures associated with his “America First” movement.
Trump had initially expected to replicate his quick win from a January 3 raid that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.
But the Iran campaign instead has hardened into an uneasy stalemate that has not achieved most of Trump’s shifting objectives, including shutting down its nuclear program, and has depleted the Pentagon's missile stockpiles.
Still, Trump is not without defenders.
Mark Dubowitz, head of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an anti-Iran think tank in Washington, denied Trump had plunged the US into an endless war and insisted he had scored successes that would eventually bring victory.
“It’s been a 47-year war waged by the Islamic Republic against America,” Dubowitz said. “And now we’ve struck back.”
