As Trump prepared to deliver a keynote address on Wednesday in Dallas, prices for Brent Crude, the global benchmark, rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since July, a reminder of the conflict’s continued fallout for global markets.
Nevertheless, supporters who spoke to Al Jazeera still saw the president as the man to rally Americans to vote Republican in November, as the party fights to hold onto control of the House of Representatives and Senate.
But some voiced concern – or confusion – over the impact of the war.
“This really is a Trump-a-palooza, as people have been saying,” said Carter Eisinger, a 27-year-old electrician who travelled from Fargo, North Dakota.
“I think some people say that in a derogatory way, but I think it’s very much a complimentary phrase,” he added. “The reality of it is we are in a Trump Republican Party.”
Still, Eisinger struggled to see how the war fit into Trump’s “America First” vision.
“In my opinion, I don’t really see the connection of how a war in Iran helps us here in the country,” he said. “If the Iran war is justified, I’m willing to pay the gas prices, but I haven’t seen that justification.”
He felt a similar confusion about the close relationship between the US and Israel.
“At the end of the day, I’m going to come right back to whatever is best for families, young people, anyone in America,” he said. “If it’s helping Israel in a way that helps us, then great… but it needs to help us first.”
Others were more charitable towards Trump’s approach to the Middle East, even if they saw the war on Iran as a misstep.
Bijay Dixit, a 59-year-old photographer from Houston, Texas, gave Trump high marks on his approach to immigration. He also believed Republicans were the party to steward the economy in the years ahead.
But on Iran, he said there had been a “miscalculation”, even if he agreed with the Trump administration’s position that the war was ultimately a necessary response to the totality of Iran’s actions in the 47 years since the Islamic revolution in 1979.
“Iran needed to be stopped at some point,” he said. “When I say miscalculation, what I mean is underestimation of the capacity of the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps].”
Helen Vennett, a 65-year-old small business owner from Maryland and the chairman of her county’s Republican Party, likened the convention to a high-school pep rally.
“All of us need to have cheerleaders in our life… It just gets you fired up again. You kind of need to know that you’re not alone, that there are believers,” she added.
But while she said she broadly supported the Trump administration’s justification for the war, she acknowledged the potential political fallout.
“It’s a tough one,” she said.
Polls have regularly suggested widespread disapproval among US citizens of the war on Iran, with independents in particular expressing disapproval. Many, in turn, rank affordability as their top issue heading into the midterm vote.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested that only a quarter of Americans think the war is worthwhile.
For its part, the Trump administration has downplayed the prospect of ending the war, focusing instead on efforts to open shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz, over which Iran continues to assert its influence.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday as he departed for the convention, Trump sought to temper expectations that the war would end before November’s pivotal vote.
“I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm,” he said, accusing Iran of intentionally holding out until November.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapons,” he said.
He predicted the war would end swiftly after the final votes have been cast.
“They can’t hold out any longer,” he said.
John Russell, 55, from Rockford, Illinois, who regularly travels to Trump rallies as part of the “Front Row Joe’s” group, said he believed voters would still view the first two years of Trump’s second term as a net positive.
“It’s been a small bump with the gas going up,” he told Al Jazeera from the convention.
“But it had to be done. We can’t allow [Iran] to have a nuclear bomb,” he said, referring to one of the administration’s main justifications for the war.
Tehran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, with military analysts generally agreeing that destroying its nuclear programme would require a major military escalation, involving boots on the ground.
Russell predicted that the Republican Party’s bet would pay off at the polls.
“It’s going to fire up the base,” he said of the convention. “It’s going to switch some independents to vote for the Trump-backed candidates, and they will win.”

Creating a multi-layered security grid in Delhi, one Brics at a time
NEW DELHI: When the 'Flying Kremlin' and other ultra-secure aircraft touch down in Delhi this weekend, they won't just bring Russian President Vladimir Putin and other high-profile world leaders to the Brics Summit, they will land with a fully autonomous fortress-on-wheels featuring personal food-testing labs, decoy dignitaries and armoured limousines built to survive landmines and chemical attacks.As Delhi transforms into an impenetrable, multi-layered defensive grid, security personnel are bracing for a high-stakes security operation where AI-aimed snipers scan rooftops, gesture-recognition cameras spot human posture shifts, commandos slither down ropes from hovering helicopters and anti-graffiti strike teams patrol the streets 24/7, guarding against everything from high-tech threats to stealth protest tactics.
The capital, sources said, hasn't seen security this tight since the 2023 G20 summit, and preparations this time are even more extensive. Unmanned aerial vehicles have been categorised as one of the most potent threats, and systems that can jam drone signals or shoot them down have been installed at several locations.Every dignitary or their hotel or carcade has been assigned a code name or call sign to ensure they are guided smoothly between locations without any overlap or security glitches.
Intelligence inputs have hinted at the possibility of flash protests and spray-painting of inflammatory slogans near the venues, targeting some foreign leaders. Cops have formed anti-graffiti teams for round-the-clock patrolling to thwart any such attempts.President Putin's security grid comprises a sophisticated protective shield managed jointly by Russia's Federal Protective Service (FSO) and Indian counter-terrorism forces. Ground mobility will be centred around his custom-made, heavily armoured Aurus Senat limousine, often referred to as a "rolling bunker". Transported directly from Moscow, the state car is built to withstand chemical attacks, landmines and sniper fire, complete with run-flat tyres and an independent emergency oxygen supply.Up in the air, the Russian leader travels in a specially modified Ilyushin IL-96-300PU aircraft, known as the "Flying Kremlin", which operates alongside decoy jets, advanced missile-defence countermeasures and secure command systems. On the ground, the innermost protective layer comprises elite officers from Russian Presidential Security Service (SBP), supported by advanced FSO teams that sanitise every scheduled and potential itinerary venue. The Russian delegation manages its own strict logistics, travelling with personal chefs, portable testing laboratories for food and drink, and measures to collect biological waste, alongside deploying dummy dignitaries in select hotels to boost operational security.Securing the designated summit hotels in central Delhi, Aerocity and Gurgaon presented one of the most formidable logistical challenges for intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Every hotel is being managed as an independent secure zone under its assigned DCP venue commander, supervised by special commissioner-rank officers overseeing broader zones.
Within each hotel, two rooms have been repurposed into operational command posts: a primary security control room linked directly to Delhi Police's central C4i command node and a secondary contingency room dedicated to emergency management.To prevent unauthorised access, advanced AI cameras equipped with posture-detection and intrusion-alert software monitor perimeter walls and hallways, capable of flagging unusual physical movements like crawling or wall-scaling. Hotel staff have undergone rigorous multi-round background checks conducted by special branch and special cell, with movement restricted strictly to assigned floors using specially programmed digital keycards.

A 119-year-old man from Costa Rica could become the oldest person in the world
Kyiv • UNN
José Flores's age is confirmed by Costa Rican documents, but international verification is still underway. He cites family as one of the secrets to longevity.
119-year-old Costa Rican resident José Flores is seeking official recognition as the oldest person in the world. His age is confirmed by local documents, but the final verification still needs to be carried out by international organizations, Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to his identity card, Flores was born on July 11, 1907. His family and longevity researchers also have his birth certificate, baptismal record, and documents from later periods of his life.
Experts are currently studying historical records. The organizations expected to confirm the Costa Rican man's age include Guinness World Records.
What is the secret to his longevity
Flores worked in rural areas all his life and now lives in Sardinal on the Nicoya Peninsula. The region is considered one of the so-called "blue zones," known for their large number of centenarians.
His granddaughter, Helen Flores, said that the man spends his days at home, resting, joking, and even competing with her in arm wrestling. Flores himself names his family as one of the secrets to his longevity.
Researchers also link the longevity of Nicoya residents to physical activity, a diet of corn and beans, strong family ties, and a calm lifestyle.
If Flores's age receives international confirmation, he may qualify for official recognition as the oldest person in the world.

US says China ‘on track’ to fulfil farm purchases ahead of Xi’s Washington visit
Trump administration trade official says ‘China is ramping up their purchases’ and business is progressing well between two countries
3-MIN READ3-MIN
4
 Listen
Nayan Sethin Washington
The Trump administration on Wednesday said that China is on track to meet its agricultural purchase commitments, with the sector expected to feature prominently in the deliverables for US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s talks in Washington later this month.
“China is ramping up their purchases,” said Luke Lindberg, the US Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs at the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). “We’re seeing that progress happen.”
Speaking at a Council on Foreign Relations event, Lindberg added that China is on track to buy US$17 billion worth of US agricultural products this year, in addition to soybeans, which he said would bring annual sales to US$30 billion.
He noted that China had already met its commitment to buy 12 million metric tonnes of US soybeans in the 2025 season and is “on track right now” to meet the agreed-upon target of 25 million metric tonnes this year.
In the run-up to Xi’s visit, USDA flash reports show a rise in soybean exports to China, crossing 700,000 metric tonnes in the first nine days of September.
The soybean deal was a key outcome of the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea, last year and was expanded after another leaders’ meeting in May in Beijing to include China’s promise to buy at least US$17 billion worth of US agricultural products annually for the next three years.

The Tate brothers were kept in a US jail due to the risk of flight ahead of possible extradition to Britain
Kyiv • UNN
A US court kept Andrew and Tristan Tate in custody due to the risk of flight. Britain is seeking them on charges including rape.
A U.S. court denied influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate bail while they challenge possible extradition to the United Kingdom. The brothers are wanted there on a number of serious charges, including rape, Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
Judge Lauren Louis concluded that the brothers' financial resources and frequent international travel create a significant flight risk.
Although they may not actually possess the extravagant assets they boast about online, the record shows that they have an exceptional ability to flee the jurisdiction
Why Britain wants to prosecute the Tate brothers
Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 following a British request for their extradition. British authorities charged them, among other offenses, with rape, assault, and aiding human trafficking for sexual exploitation. The brothers deny any wrongdoing.
U.S. prosecutors also opposed their release, stating that the brothers could pose a danger to the public. The Tates' attorneys, meanwhile, argued that their extreme public profile makes flight virtually impossible.
Separate criminal proceedings against the brothers are ongoing in Romania. On September 4, Romanian prosecutors charged Andrew Tate, among other offenses, with trafficking minors and money laundering, while Tristan was charged with complicity. They reject these charges as well.
The United Kingdom has until September 16 to submit a full extradition request to the U.S. Department of State. The process of deciding whether to surrender the brothers to British authorities may itself take several months.

Prince William to be joined by sports stars to launch suicide prevention initiative
LONDON - A host of famous British sporting figures will join Prince William to launch a new initiative to help the sports sector do more to help prevent suicide on Sept 10.
The heir to the British throne will be accompanied by British Olympic champions Kelly Holmes, Jason and Laura Kenny, and former England footballer Jill Scott for the event, which coincides with World Suicide Prevention Day. 
The event will be held at English Premier League football club Everton’s ground.
The issue of mental health and suicide prevention is one of William’s key campaigning strands. Last October, he came close to tears as he discussed the impact of suicide with a woman whose husband had taken his own life.
The initiative named On Your Side, which has been produced by the Royal Foundation, William and his wife Kate’s charitable organisation, aims to help people in sporting environments spot warning signs and provide support to individuals before they reach a crisis point.
William’s office Kensington Palace said the toolkit, designed in partnership with the Chasing the Stigma mental health charity, could be used from local clubs to elite organisations.
“It is relevant to everyone involved in sport, including players, coaches, staff, volunteers, families and spectators,” it said.
To mark the launch, the Royal Foundation has produced a short film to highlight suicide prevention which features England football star Harry Kane as well as Formula One driver George Russell.
The Football Association, the Premier League and British Cycling are set to announce commitments to implement the toolkit within their policies and practices, Kensington Palace said.
The National Suicide Prevention Network was launched in 2025 with the help of £1 million (S$1.7 million) of funding from the Royal Foundation. REUTERS

Albares concludes a two-day working visit to Brussels to place Ceuta and Melilla "at the heart of Europe"
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
01:03:20 CEST
08:03:20 KST

Brussels, 9 September 2026.- The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, concluded this Wednesday in Brussels a two-day series of meetings with officials from European institutions aimed at promoting the integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the European Union and placing them "at the heart of Europe". The Minister welcomed the announcement, made public today by the Commissioner for Migration, Magnus Brunner, to provide the €114.7 million requested by Spain. Minister Albares reiterated this request to him during their meeting on Tuesday to reinforce security at the Ceuta border and expedite ongoing procedures to restore normality as soon as possible.
This Wednesday, Albares held a meeting with authorities from the European Committee of the Regions to ensure that Ceuta and Melilla have a permanent presence in the Spanish delegation to this European Union institution.
Subsequently, the Minister held a meeting with the European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, Maroš Šefčovič, in which they assessed the ways to enhance the economic and commercial integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the European Union. They analysed the options for their incorporation into the Customs Union and the formulas that allow for the recognition of the geographical specificity of Ceuta and Melilla within the Union.
The Minister also met with the European Commissioner for the Mediterranean, Dubravka Šuica, with whom he stressed the need to address the challenges of the European southern border and cooperation with the Southern Neighbourhood, promoting stability and cooperation with North Africa, which must play a central role in the next edition of the Regional Forum of the Union for the Mediterranean.
Finally, Albares met with the High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, with whom the Minister stressed that it is imperative that the European Union attaches equal importance to the various threats and challenges of each of its borders so that Europe responds with solidarity and unity in all cases.
With this visit, the Government reaffirms its commitment to continue working together with the European institutions to reinforce the presence of Ceuta and Melilla in the European project and to advance towards a greater participation of both cities in the policies and instruments of the European Union.

MOSCOW – Russian President Vladimir Putin hailed deepening economic relations at talks with Vietnam President and Communist Party General Secretary To Lam on Sept 9.
“We’re very pleased to see you,” Putin told Lam at the Kremlin meeting. Trade between Russia and Vietnam expanded by almost 6 per cent in 2025 and the growth rate has “practically doubled” in the first half of 2026, he said.
The two nations have close defence ties, given Russia’s historic role as Vietnam’s largest military supplier.
The South-east Asian nation has been seeking to upgrade its military capabilities in recent months and diversify its partners as it confronts an increasingly assertive Chinese presence in the disputed waters of the South China Sea.
Energy cooperation is also a major focus of the trip, building on Russia’s longstanding role in Vietnam’s oil and gas sector, as well as the agreement to build the Ninh Thuan 1 nuclear power plant. Prior to that, he visited China and the US, underscoring Vietnam’s efforts to balance relations with its major strategic partners even as it navigates increasing global tensions.
The US and Vietnam continue to wrangle over the terms of a final trade deal after Washington turned up the pressure and launched three simultaneous trade investigations targeting Hanoi’s trade practices. UK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
23:01:08 UTC
08:01:08 KST

John Healey has been urged to fix the £100,000 childcare “cliff edge”, that means some higher-paid employees cut back on work to avoid losing their entitlement.
Since the latest expansion of taxpayer-funded childcare in 2024, families with young children in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care - or none at all, if one of them cross that threshold.
In a new report, researchers from the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation (CenTax) said that, by the end of this parliament in 2030, the average parent crossing this “cliff edge”, will have to earn £124,000, to be no worse off after losing their free childcare.
Arun Advani, director of CenTax, said: “Our analysis shows the childcare cliff edge stands to grow dramatically by the end of this parliament, but there are solutions available to the government.”
The researchers find that “bunching” of incomes just below the threshold suggests that even in 2022 – the latest year for which data is available – about 1,000 families were artificially suppressing their earnings to avoid falling foul of the threshold. That could rise to almost 12,000 by the end of this parliament.
The thinktank, based at Warwick University, also suggested the policy may be incentivising some mothers to drop out of work. Below the £100,000 threshold, 6% of lower-paid partners – usually the mother – are out of work; but above the threshold that rises to 9%.
“The jump in non-working mothers at the point where their partner exceeds £100,000 income suggests the loss of childcare entitlement as a cause, with possible long-term consequences for those mothers’ earnings,” the report said.
CenTax also criticised the fact that the threshold is based on how much parents expect to earn in the year ahead – pointing out that some families appear to be claiming it, despite eventually earning more than £100,000.
It proposes several potential solutions. Restricting free childcare to 15 hours to families above the £100,000 threshold, instead of withdrawing it altogether, would cost £210m by 2030, it said.
Gradually tapering away the entitlement at 28p for each £1 earned above the threshold would be revenue neutral, but less problematic for parents, it adds.
Healey is set to deliver his first budget on 28 October, against a backdrop of renewed fears about higher inflation and febrile global bond markets.
Analysts believe higher than expected interest rates on the Treasury’s debt are likely to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves built up against the government’s fiscal rules.
In his first major speech in Coventry on Monday, Healey promised to put growth at the heart of his approach; but also warned that Labour must “be honest” about the constraints on public spending in the years ahead.
Since taking over as Labour leader in July, Andy Burnham has announced a VAT cut on electricity bills and capped bus fares; but Healey has also suggested the government is keen to do more to give hard-pressed consumers a “breathing space”.

Teachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
23:01:08 UTC
08:01:08 KST

Teachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school attendance that they would take their own children on term time holidays if they could, staff have told a three-year research programme.
Frontline staff do not believe the school system is set up to deal with an ongoing attendance crisis in England and Wales, where nearly one in five children are now missing at least 10% of school, according to a report based on in-depth conversations with teachers.
Despite a hardline approach from schools to tackle the crisis, evidence from focus groups containing teachers from schools in low-income areas suggests many share the same scepticism as parents and pupils about the efficiency of holiday fines, according to the report by youth charity Impetus and policy and polling research firm Public First.
“If I wasn’t a teacher, I would take my daughter out of school and take her on holiday because it would be cheaper,” said one teacher.
Another noted: “If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school in January.”
The report comes as the children’s commissioner warned of tens of thousands of hidden Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), with analysis suggesting that an estimated 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds enrolled in colleges in England are attending less than half the time.
Rachel de Souza warned that the number of Neets is almost twice as large as official figures indicate, according to a new analysis of 262 of England’s 290 college groups, which are not included in Department for Education attendance figures.
“We have a blind spot: hidden Neets slipping through the cracks,” she said. “Young people with all the negative impacts of not being in employment, education or training, but with none of the targeted interventions.”
Researchers compiling the report, A Crisis of Disengagement, spoke to 62 secondary school staff from schools in England where more than 25% of pupils were eligible for free school meals.
They spoke of the work of chasing pupils’ attendance as “relentless” and expressed the view that an occasional holiday or minor absence was less worrying than sustained disengagement.
While some staff saw fines as a necessary tool, many believed they damage trust and undermine the relational work needed to support pupils and families to re-engage with school. “We’ll send a penalty notice out and then we’ve really annoyed that parent,” said one senior leader. “We’ve just broken a relationship between a family that we want to get into school.”
A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25, a sharp rise from pre-Covid levels. Researchers have previously warned of a “seismic shift” in attitudes to attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer believe children needed to be in school full-time. The absence rate for pupils in England in 2025-26 was 6.93%, significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid level of 4.7%
Teachers and senior leaders in schools also argued that gaps in mental health support for struggling students, unmet special educational needs and a paucity of social workers was making their jobs more difficult with schools seen as “the one-stop shop for everything”.
“We’ve got children who should have specialist provision, and they’re in our building every day,” said one senior leader. “We also need external agencies such as CAMHS [Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services] and social workers to have the right capacity and not turn us down.”
Staff also told researchers the most effective interventions were also the hardest – including building relationships, mentoring and home visits.
“I think it takes up a lot of adult hours,” she said. “If you looked proportionally at how time was broken down, attendance is very, very time consuming.”
Susannah Hardyman, the CEO of Impetus, said teachers could not solve the attendance crisis alone. “We now know that not only are pupils, families and teachers unconvinced that every day in school matters, but what we are facing is a wider crisis of disengagement driven by pressures often outside the control of school staff,” she said.

‘Step backwards’: Union leader warns Burnham against political donations cap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

LONDON — Britain’s most powerful union leader has warned Prime Minister Andy Burnham against capping individual donations to political parties in the U.K.
Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, told POLITICO he believes a cap could be a “step backwards” as any new law would likely impact donations from trade unions, not just those from individual tycoons and firms based in Britain.
“We all want to see our politics cleaned up, but I don’t want to see the voices of ordinary working people excluded from politics because we have a badly designed law,” he said in an interview ahead of the TUC’s annual meeting of 47 member unions on Sunday. “Until somebody can give me an assurance that you can design a law that doesn’t silence those voices, then I’m going to be skeptical about it.”
Advertisement
Nowak’s comments give a rare public glimpse of the tensions between Britain’s trade union movement and the ruling Labour Party, to which it donated nearly £5 million in 2025. It presents a test for Burnham, who rode a wave of union support to replace Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, but has staked his reputation on fixing a broken Westminster system.
The prime minister said last week that his government needs to “go further” to reform donation rules after large gifts declared by rival political parties have worried many on the British left. Nigel Farage’s populist right-wing party Reform UK received £9 million from the cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne last year, the largest single political donation from a living person in U.K. history.
Burnham declined MPs’ calls to use the government’s Representation of the People Bill as a vehicle for immediate change, as POLITICO revealed in August, but said the existing Defending Democracy Taskforce in the Cabinet Office will consider future changes.
Nowak said: “I do worry about the impact of individuals making really big individual donations to party politics, but it’s very hard to think about — certainly at this stage — how you would design a system that didn’t cut across trade union donations.
“And in my mind, absolutely unequivocally, trade union donations are the cleanest, most transparent form of political funding in this country. You’re talking about very small contributions made by members who democratically decide how much they pay, what it’s for, whether they affiliate to the Labour Party or not, and I wouldn’t want to see the voices of those workers excluded from politics because we designed the law badly.
“So I wouldn’t rule it out in the future, but anything that potentially captures union political funding, when unions are already incredibly overregulated in this area, I think would be a step backwards.”
Advertisement
The TUC does not donate to Labour itself, and Nowak said he has not raised the issue with Burnham directly.
However, the body represents all 11 of the “affiliated” unions that pay part of their members’ subscriptions into the Labour Party, several of which are concerned about the prospect of a cap. Some unions also make large individual donations to Labour, which was born out of the union movement in the early 1900s.
The TUC wants to ban donations by overseas residents and people who do not pay U.K. tax. However, the issue of individual donations by U.K.-based entities is more politically fraught.
The government declined to back an amendment put forward by Labour MP Stella Creasy to the Representation of the People Bill last week, which would have introduced a cap of £100,000 per year on individual U.K.-based donors — with a carve-out for trade union political funds. Creasy said the latest version of her amendment would have “completely exempt[ed] trade unions” from the cap.
Creasy said that a cross-party group of peers is already working on proposing similar amendments to the bill when it is scrutinized in the House of Lords in the coming months. She added: “Without a cap, it’s clear the amounts of money flooding into our democracy could drown out everyone else’s voices — including the trade unions.”
‘Stakeholders to be managed’
Nowak made his comments as part of a wide-ranging interview ahead of the TUC’s four-day annual meeting in Brighton, where the union body will campaign for a tax rise on banks to fund a permanent “social tariff” lowering energy bills for low and middle earners.
Advertisement
He wrote to ministers this week calling for a “comprehensive plan” to ensure workers have a say on AI practices at their own workplaces. He said: “I think at some stage it will require primary legislation.”
Nowak met Burnham face-to-face on Monday and said they discussed his promises to “reindustrialize” Britain and bring more public sector contracts in-house, as well as the TUC’s push for the government to deliver the Employment Rights Act — Labour’s flagship set of workplace reforms — “in full.”
Some unions will use next week’s Congress, where either Burnham or a senior Cabinet ally is expected to speak, to press the government for a second employment rights bill to go further than the first Act. This would prompt a backlash from many business groups, which argue the new law, passed last December, is already adding burdensome red tape.
Nowak suggested he would back a second bill as part of a future general election manifesto, given many policies from the first Act haven’t been implemented yet. “I think it’s entirely legitimate to say, at the next election, what is Labour’s manifesto going to say about employment rights?” he said. “The idea that the Employment Rights Act is the finished article in terms of U.K. employment law, that nothing else needs to change, I think clearly is not the case.”
Elsewhere, Nowak said the government “could listen more” to unions when drawing up trade deals, as they have “real concerns” about a recent pact with the Gulf Co-Operation Council and ongoing talks about upgrading the U.K.’s free trade agreement with Turkey. “I’ve got concerns about any trade deals that say nothing about labor standards, say nothing about respect for union rights, and say very little about environmental standards — and I’ve made this point directly to [the] government,” he said.
He also said that Burnham’s agenda to move power and resources out of Westminster is not a “panacea,” adding: “I think it’s part of the solution. It’s not the solution in and of itself. Simply devolving powers without devolving responsibilities and real resources I don’t think is going to benefit anybody.”
Advertisement
‘Who knows what will be in the next manifesto’ on Europe
The TUC general secretary — who voiced support for a U.K.-EU customs union in 2025 — appeared to suggest that he believes Labour’s next election manifesto could end the party’s refusal to countenance either a customs union or single market relationship with Brussels.
“We need the closest possible working relationship and closest possible economic relationship,” he said. Citing Donald Trump’s tariffs on the automotive industry, he added: “We’ve got to avoid a situation where we are effectively held hostage by which side of the bed the president of the United States rolls out of in the morning.”
He went on: “Obviously the government has got the red lines it went into the last election with, and the commitments it made in the manifesto. I think the relationship is going to develop over time, and who knows what will be in the next manifesto?
“All I want is when both parties sit down at that U.K.-EU summit, we’re thinking about what is the best possible deal for U.K. jobs, for U.K. workers, and for not just closer economic ties, but also that Britain plays an important role in Europe politically.”
While the TUC does not engage with Farage’s Reform UK, Nowak speaks to the Liberal Democrats and Green Party, whose leader, Zack Polanski, he last met “about four or five months ago.”
Nowak suggested the Downing Street of previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who quit in July under pressure from his own MPs, had not fully appreciated the importance of trade unions to the wider country. “Sometimes it felt there was a sense that unions were stakeholders to be managed,” he said. “We represent millions of people at work … sometimes that was a frustration.”
However, Nowak said he is “heartened” by an initial bounce in poll ratings for Burnham’s Labour. “I’m confident we can get relationships with Andy Burnham and his government on the right footing right from the start,” he added.

Leipzig Sabotage: Why Transport Underpins NATO and Russia’s Defences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Leipzig Sabotage: Why Transport Underpins NATO and Russia’s Defences
Germany’s attribution of the Leipzig drone attack to Russia shows why transport networks now sit at the centre of both NATO’s and Russia’s defence.
The Leipzig airport drone attack, which the German authorities have now formally attributed to Russia, was significant in several ways.
First, while it was technically one in a series of Russian sabotage attacks of NATO infrastructure in Europe – and it essentially failed – the complexity of the approach demonstrated Russia’s increasing investment in undermining NATO, irrespective of the outcome.
Second, it showed that Moscow – and likely NATO itself – remains unclear on the current red lines that would prompt a military response.
And third, it demonstrated why transport infrastructure is so critical in underpinning defence, and the many vulnerabilities that it contains at multiple points along the supply chain. This is just as true for Russia as it is for NATO.
Unpacking Leipzig
In and of itself, the attack is not new. It is not even the first time Leipzig airport, an important NATO hub used for airlifting arms and equipment into Ukraine, has been targeted. Indeed, earlier this year, your author wrote about some of the discernible patterns in Russia’s targeting of NATO infrastructure in this manner, particularly the increased risks to international transport networks and logistics hubs, as Russia continues to test NATO’s red lines.
But as that report suggests, for now Russia’s attacks of NATO infrastructure lack the coordination and coherence to disable transport infrastructure for long periods and cause significant disruption. That said, Russia continues to capitalise on the inconsistencies and poor coordination between European countries transporting aid to Ukraine, particularly vulnerabilities at different stages in supply chains such as loading and unloading at multiple points while vehicles are in transit or idling, providing greater opportunity for sabotage. In this latest incident, available information about the target of attack and the means to attack it fit with previous patterns of Russian intelligence behaviour.
If an ancillary goal of this sabotage is to probe what NATO might do in response, then that line has not yet been clearly delineated
The human factor persists – the suspects have been preliminarily identified as a man of Russian origin but with a Latvian passport, and another with a Belarusian passport, entering Germany on an Italian tourist visa. Russia’s use of third-party proxies – which carries its own risks – has been increasingly common not only due to the strategic distance from the intelligence services that this creates, but also because it is somewhat of a necessary evil, as the GRU has sought to rebuild its deconstructed intelligence operations in Europe after 2022.
Here, the sabotage appears to have been much more carefully coordinated than the various arson attacks that have been attributed to the GRU previously, with multiple nationalities at play, alternative transport routes taken, and an apparent professional degree of understanding of logistics. This is different to the run-of-the-mill Russia-sponsored arson attacks in the UK, which, while damaging, have been mostly a step up from vandalism.
Crucially – this attempt still failed.
But that might matter less to Moscow, as one of the various aims of these sabotage campaigns is amplifying a sense of discord, and the suggestion that Russia is capable of being behind any disruption to transport or cargo services in Europe.
Here, amorphous goals work to Russia’s advantage. If the aim is to intimidate E3 countries like Germany into scaling down support for Ukraine, the opposite has been proven, as Berlin announced soon afterward its intention to increase intelligence sharing and military assistance to Ukraine.
But perhaps for Moscow, no matter. If an ancillary goal of this sabotage is to probe what NATO might do in response, then that line has not yet been clearly delineated. Partly this is because NATO itself does not know what those lines are, and, in the absence of confirmation, Russia is expanding its activities to fill the vacuum left by this uncertainty.
Russia’s Logistical Adjustments
What Leipzig does raise is the importance of defending transport infrastructure, the difficulties in doing so, and some of the longer-term readjustments that may be necessary.
In response to the incident, Germany pledged to boost its air defences using anti-drone shields capable of defusing drone bombs and other IEDs. But the problem is wider than defending a single airport, and requires a shift in how transport networks ought to be considered as a fundament of national security.
It is therefore worth considering how, under pressure from Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s supply chains, Russia is shifting its own infrastructure focus, in a country where transport is considered a vital military organ.
Russia is still regrouping from Ukraine’s comprehensive 40-day campaign against its logistical infrastructure in recent months, and the Kremlin has been forced to confront the long-term security and reliability of its supply chains. Although that campaign did not bring the war to a desired political conclusion, Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign nevertheless poked holes in Moscow’s assumption that its land and maritime supply chains located deep in Russian territory (the tyl, or rear) were immune to attack.
Russia is still battling issues around securing supply chains to the frontline via its southern route, but refocusing its efforts on the High North and the Far East is part of the Kremlin’s intent to both circumvent sanctions and tie up its national security with its infrastructure. Two recent developments demonstrate this well.
First, a new road bridge in the Far East between Russia and North Korea, which was formally announced last year, is now complete – a swift construction turnaround considering the usual issues of corruption or political disagreements that tend to plague infrastructure projects in Russia. The road bridge across the Tyumen River is important – Russia receives ammunitions, troops and missiles from the DPRK via this route, which is geographically difficult for drone systems to target and disable. This bridge will be the main artery for further deliveries of military supplies to Russia in the coming months and is physically challenging to disrupt, ensuring a steady flow of supplies through the winter.
Second, Putin a few days ago launched the Vostok Oil Arctic project – an infrastructure project linking up oilfields in the Krasnoyarsk region with the new Sever Bay port on the Yenisei River, designed to ship oil to consumers in Asia and Europe and take the pressure off some of Russia’s other overloaded ports. This is part of an overarching project connecting sea terminals to rail and Russia’s inland waterways.
These developments are significant because they expand Russia’s network of High North ports that are more difficult to target – Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s Black Sea ports in recent months obstructed shipping via the south, forcing Russia to seek alternative export routes.
This is also a move to connect and secure Russia’s internal waterway systems, which have been long neglected and are a serious vulnerability that Ukraine’s drone attacks laid bare – Russia’s shadow fleet operating along the Don Canal and via the Kerch Strait were essentially sitting ducks. Using alternative waterways in the North comes with its own issues, as many are seasonally operational, underfunded and require expansion to allow an increase in loading capacity. But Russia is clearly shifting and adapting its critical national infrastructure to account for weaknesses in the tyl that the war has pried open.
While this is more challenging for NATO given its geographical expanse and the need for multistate input, Leipzig should remind us that land, sea and air transport networks across the Alliance – and some of the people that operate them – are uniquely vulnerable to exploitation, and require a coordinated effort to harden them against Russia.

38 parties submit candidate lists for Israel’s Knesset election as opposition leads polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:59:40 UTC
07:59:40 KST

Abdelraouf Arnaout and Mohammad Sio
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The last of 38 parties submitted their candidate lists for Israel’s Oct. 27 Knesset election, with opinion polls indicating that 13 could win seats in the 120-member parliament.
The deadline for parties and blocs to submit their lists to the Central Elections Committee expired Tuesday evening. The committee has begun reviewing the lists and examining objections filed against them.
According to the committee’s website, a legally registered party may submit a list containing between one and 120 candidates eligible to stand for election.
A list may also be submitted by two or more parties, and every candidate must provide written consent to have their name included.
Opinion polls suggest that 13 parties could enter the Knesset.
The leading Jewish opposition parties include the Yashar party headed by former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot and the Together party led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
Other prominent opposition parties are the Democrats headed by former deputy army chief Yair Golan and the Yisrael Beiteinu party led by former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc includes his Likud party, the Otzma Yehudit party headed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the religious Shas party led by Aryeh Deri, the United Torah Judaism party and the Religious Zionism party headed by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Among Arab parties, polls indicate that the Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, and the United Arab List headed by Mansour Abbas could win seats.
The People of Israel party led by Ofer Winter and the Reservists parry led by Yoaz Hendel are also competing, with polls offering mixed projections of their chances of crossing the electoral threshold.
By contrast, polls suggest that the Blue and White party headed by former Israeli army chief Benny Gantz will fail to win any seats.
- Objections and disqualifications
According to the Central Elections Committee, objections to candidate lists may be submitted until Sept. 15, while a challenged list or candidate has until Sept. 18 to respond.
If the committee decides to disqualify a candidate, the decision is referred to the Supreme Court for approval. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The committee will publish the final candidate lists in the official gazette no later than Oct. 18, nine days before the election.
Section 7A of the Basic Law: The Knesset provides for the disqualification of a party or candidate if their objectives or actions explicitly or implicitly include denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle by a hostile state or terrorist organization against Israel.
- First announced objection
In the first publicly announced objection, Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth daily reported Wednesday that Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party had filed a petition with the Central Elections Committee seeking to disqualify the United Arab List and Mansour Abbas from the election.
The newspaper quoted Ben-Gvir as claiming that Abbas and his colleagues are “terrorists” and supported the Palestinian group Hamas.
The 39-page petition alleged that the United Arab List “denies Israel’s existence as a Jewish state and supports armed struggle by hostile states and terrorist organizations against it.”
There was no immediate comment from the United Arab List or Abbas regarding the petition.
- First election on schedule since 1988
Knesset elections are held every four years if parliament completes its full term. The Knesset may also be dissolved early through legislation supported by at least 61 lawmakers.
The Central Elections Committee says elections have been brought forward 12 times in Israel’s history.
According to the Israel Democracy Institute, the election for the 26th Knesset will be the first held on schedule since 1988.
The candidate lists now enter a review and objections stage before their final approval, while the election campaign is expected to remain shaped by the political divisions Israel has experienced in recent years.
Forming a government requires the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset.
For weeks, opinion polls have shown the Israeli opposition ahead of Netanyahu’s bloc, complicating the prime minister’s prospects of forming a government after the election.
Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 on charges related to war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians in Gaza.

Rubio to seek $45 million in additional security funding for Ecuador

Rubio to seek $45 million in additional security funding for Ecuador
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Washington would seek $45 million in additional security funding for Ecuador and provide military equipment as the two countries deepen cooperation against drug trafficking. During a visit to Quito, Rubio also announced new sanctions on former Ecuadorian officials involved in bribery and a terrorist designation for an Ecuador-based gang.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Ecuador on Wednesday that he would seek $45 million in additional security funding for the Latin American country, as well as additional equipment, to help tackle drug trafficking.
Rubio met with Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa during a swing through three Latin American countries with leaders closely aligned with US President Donald Trump and his administration's effort to reassert US dominance in the region.
Speaking after their meeting, Rubio said Washington was increasingly working with Noboa's government to crack down on drug trafficking organisations, including with joint strikes on boats believed to be used by drug smugglers.
"These are not ordinary groups. Clearly, they engage in common crime, but they have terrorist capabilities across the region, and that must be confronted. They must be dismantled, they must be defeated, and we are committed to doing that," Rubio said.
Rubio on Wednesday designated the Ecuador-based gang Los Tiguerones as a foreign terrorist organisation, after similar designations were made against two other Ecuador-based gangs last year. The State Department said the group was linked to narcotrafficking and other illicit activity, including the live takeover of an Ecuadorian TV station in 2024.
Read moreRubio kicks off tour in Latin America as US vies for regional influence
Rubio said the US would also be imposing sanctions on seven former Ecuadorian officials involved in bribery.
The Trump administration would ask Congress for $45 million to fund new commitments for Ecuador, as well as a $10 million initiative targeting illegal gold mining, gang recruitment and illicit finance, Rubio said.
He said the US would deliver a 110-foot Coast Guard cutter and five interceptor vessels for the country's navy, in addition to seven already delivered to Ecuador this year for the fight against maritime drug trafficking.
Noboa took office in 2023 vowing a crackdown on violence stemming from Ecuador's increasing role as a drug transit hub, but rights advocates have raised concerns the heavy-handed approach has only created more chaos.
Boat strikes
Rubio, speaking to reporters in Quito, acknowledged that the US campaign to strike suspected drug trafficking boats had shifted to joint strikes with Ecuador, and said decisions on targeting were made on a "strike-by-strike" basis and with the cooperation of Ecuador.
"Our goal is not to go after fishermen. Our goal is to go after drug traffickers," he said in response to questions about criticism over the campaign.
Ecuador's defence minister last week also defended several recent operations where Ecuadorian vessels were intercepted and sunk, saying they were the product of joint investigations to disrupt drug trafficking.
Read moreRubio hails Colombia's new pro-Trump leader De la Espriella on first stop of Latin American tour
The sinkings are the latest in a broader US military campaign known as Operation Southern Spear, which has destroyed some 70 vessels and killed more than 220 people over the past year, drawing criticism from human rights groups and some Latin American leaders who call the strikes extrajudicial killings.
Though the US government has claimed responsibility for dozens of attacks as part of Southern Spear, it has not claimed three others this year which bear the hallmarks of US strikes, involving fishing vessels from Ecuador's Manabi province.
In those incidents crew members, including some interviewed by Reuters, say their vessels were hit with strikes. One boat disappeared, the crews of the other two were repatriated via El Salvador.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Cyber fraud worth 5,044 crore prevented: Govt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:56:53 UTC
07:56:53 KST

NEW DELHI: India is increasingly stopping cyber fraud before money leaves a victim's account. A telecom-led risk system has helped banks and payment platforms prevent suspected fraudulent transactions worth Rs 5,043.7 crore in 15 months, govt said, marking a shift from tracing stolen money to intercepting payments in real time, reports Aabhas Sharma.
The Financial Fraud Risk Indicator (FRI), launched by the department of telecommunications in May 2025, assigns mobile numbers medium, high or very high risk ratings. The alerts are fed directly to banks and UPI platforms, allowing them to warn customers or block risky payments.
Experts said the system's biggest achievement was making fraud operations costlier.
However, fraudsters could turn to SIMs obtained through fraudulent KYC or virtual numbers. An expert said criminals could also evade mobile-number risk scores by obtaining fresh or "aged" SIM cards.

Russia's Sochi port hit in fiery strike by Ukrainian sea drone, officials claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:47:12 UTC
07:47:12 KST

Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
A Ukrainian sea drone struck a port in the Russian Black Sea resort town of Sochi on Sept. 9, local Russian officials claimed.
Known as Russia's "Second Capital," Sochi is home to Russian President Vladimir Putin's official summer residence. Considered a winter playground for Russia’s elite, the city is located approximately 650 to 700 kilometers (400 to 435 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Regional authorities in Russia's Krasnodar Krai reported the Sept. 9 attack, saying that a fire had broken out on a port embankment in Sochi as a result of a Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel (USV) strike, causing infrastructure damage. Eight people were reported injured in the strike.
Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin urged residents to seek shelter and remain calm following the initial strike.
At the time of publication, the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the latest reports nor the extent of the damage caused.
Footage from Sochi residents posted online shows a large, fiery blast next to a beach promenade. Monitoring channel Supernova+ shared videos of Sochi residents seeking shelter amid large explosions — reportedly the work of drone defense systems.
The USV strike also interrupted a concert by Russian singer Tatyana Bulanova being held near the attack site, the Russian opposition news channel Astra reported. Footage shows concert attendees being evacuated, seemingly panicked.
Bulanova has previously expressed support for Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 
According to Astra, the explosion occurred near the Chernomorskaya Zharovnya restaurant, partially destroying it.
The strike comes a week after Ukraine's last major attack against the seaside restort. 
Overnight on Sept. 3, Ukraine's military launched several waves of attacks targeting Sochi. A Ukrainian sea drone reportedly struck and damaged a Russian naval vessel. 
Later in the early hours of Sept. 4, footage posted on several Russian Telegram media channels appeared to show a fire at an oil depot near the city. Days later, flames at the oil depot reignited.
Throughout the war, Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly battered each other's ports.
Targeting a naval base and oil export infrastructure, Ukrainian drones struck the Black Sea town of Novorossiysk on Sept. 9. Ukrainian forces have consistently targeted Russian oil export facilities in the Baltic port of Ust-Luga.
Looking to choke Kyiv's grain exports, Russia has targeted Ukraine's Odesa port and shipping lanes across the Black Sea.

Iran slams IAEA board resolution referring nuclear issue to UN Security Council

TEHRAN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Iran on Wednesday denounced the decision by the UN nuclear watchdog's Board of Governors to refer its nuclear issue to the UN Security Council, labeling the resolution "fundamentally irrelevant" after it was passed earlier in the day over alleged nuclear "non-compliance."
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said in an interview with state-run IRIB TV that Iran has committed no non-compliance, stressing that what they refer to as "non-compliance" stems from the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities.
He also criticized the resolution for demanding Iran fulfill its obligations under the safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) while ignoring that Tehran's move to deny the agency access to its nuclear facilities resulted from "aggressive actions" by the United States and Israel.
Baghaei expressed confidence that the move will fail and only further politicize the IAEA and harm the foundations of the non-proliferation regime.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany, and the United States and reportedly passed by 23 votes in favor, three against, and eight abstentions, "requests the (IAEA) Director General (Rafael Grossi) to report" Iran to the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly.
Iran suspended cooperation with the IAEA in late June 2025 under a parliamentary law, citing the agency's failure to condemn the Israeli and U.S. attacks earlier that month on Iran's nuclear sites and related safety concerns. ■

Apple debuts foldable iPhone Duo

(Xinhua/Wu Xiaoling)
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- U.S. tech giant Apple on Wednesday unveiled its first foldable smartphone, iPhone Duo, along with the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, new Apple Watch models and AirPods at a product launch event held at Apple Park, its headquarters in Cupertino, California.
The iPhone Duo, which starts at 1,999 U.S. dollars in the United States, features a 5.4-inch (13.7-centimeter) outer display that opens to reveal a 7.6-inch (19.3-centimeter) inner display, the largest ever on an iPhone, according to Apple.
When closed, the device is roughly the size of a passport, the company said. When unfolded, it is Apple's thinnest iPhone to date.
The iPhone Duo is made of Grade 5 titanium and features a precision hinge. Its inner and outer Super Retina XDR displays have the same aspect ratio, allowing content to scale proportionally as users switch between the two screens.
The device is powered by Apple's new A20 Pro chip, the same processor used in the iPhone 18 Pro models. Built on a 2-nanometer process, the chip features a six-core CPU, a seven-core GPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine designed to support on-device artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, Apple said.
The foldable phone also features a dual-battery architecture and a custom vapor chamber for thermal management. It offers up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display and 44 hours on the outer display, according to Apple.
Apple has redesigned parts of its iOS 27 operating system to accomodate the foldable form factor. A new Split View feature allows users to run two apps side by side on an iPhone for the first time, while also enabling them to open two windows of the same app.
The iPhone Duo comes with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Apple said Siri AI will begin rolling out as a beta with iOS 27 on Sept. 14 for supported devices set to English, with several additional languages to follow in October.
The iPhone Duo will be available in star white and night sky, with storage options of 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB. Pre-orders will begin on Oct. 16 in more than 70 countries and regions, with availability beginning Oct. 23. The phone will launch in an additional 28 countries and regions on Oct. 30.
Apple also unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, starting at 1,199 dollars and 1,299 dollars, respectively. Both models are powered by the A20 Pro chip and feature a new 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, along with improvements in battery life and sustained performance.
The iPhone 18 Pro models will be available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB of storage. Pre-orders will begin Sept. 12, with availability starting Sept. 18 in more than 65 countries and regions.
Apple also introduced Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, featuring a new Health Sensing System and the S11 chip. The company said the system enables more frequent measurements of heart rate and heart-rate variability, as well as a new readiness score. The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at 399 dollars, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at 799 dollars.
AirPods 5 were also unveiled at the event, bringing Active Noise Cancellation to Apple's entry-level AirPods lineup. The new model starts at 129 dollars, while a version with a wireless charging case and additional controls costs 149 dollars.
The event marked the first major Apple product launch led by John Ternus since he took over as the company's CEO. The introduction of the iPhone Duo marks Apple's entry into the foldable smartphone market. ■

MOSCOW, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Russia's federal budget deficit reached 5.79 trillion rubles (about 68.32 billion U.S. dollars), equivalent to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, in the first eight months of this year, the Russian Ministry of Finance said Wednesday.
According to the ministry, federal budget expenditures totaled 31.72 trillion rubles during the January-August period, up 14.7 percent year on year.
"The faster pace of federal budget spending execution in January-August 2026 stems from the prompt conclusion of contracts and advance financing for certain contracted expenditures," the ministry said in a press release.
Meanwhile, preliminary estimates showed that federal budget revenues totaled 25.93 trillion rubles during the period, up 9.2 percent from the same period in 2025.
Non-oil and gas revenues reached 20.91 trillion rubles, up 18.1 percent year on year, while oil and gas revenues fell 16.7 percent to 5.02 trillion rubles.
According to the release, the decline in Russia's oil and gas revenues during the first eight months of the year was mainly attributable to a weaker U.S. dollar and lower oil prices in the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026. (1 Russian ruble = 0.0118 U.S. dollar) ■

A passenger sleeps on the floor with luggage at Terminal 5 of Heathrow Airport, London, Britain, Sept. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ying)
LONDON, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- More than 2,000 flights were canceled in Britain on Tuesday and Wednesday due to a technical issue, with Heathrow being the worst-hit airport, according to British media.
The affected passengers "are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident," said a statement issued by the UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) on Wednesday.
Cancellations were slowing Wednesday evening and none is scheduled for Thursday, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium.
National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said on Tuesday afternoon that it identified a technical issue with its flight processing system, disrupting departures across the country and causing delays and cancellations.
The 4-hour air traffic outage on Tuesday "left hundreds of thousands of passengers facing cancellations, diversions, and delays," said Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.
"I do not believe this issue was unavoidable," she said, ordering an independent investigation by CAA into the system operated by NATS.
Martin Rolfe, chief executive officer of NATS, said a cyberattack was ruled out as the cause of the disruption. ■

NEW YORK, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks ended lower on Wednesday as global crude oil prices surged past the 100-dollar mark following an escalation in U.S.-Iran hostilities, intensifying inflation fears and reinforcing expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 405.41 points, or 0.77 percent, to 52,380.66. The S&P 500 sank 37.16 points, or 0.48 percent, to 7,636.36. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 168.07 points, or 0.64 percent, to 26,253.34.
Ten of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with industrials and consumer discretionary leading the laggards by dropping 1.51 percent and 1.39 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, energy bucked the trend by rising 1.09 percent.
Brent oil prices breached triple digits for the first time in over a month after the United States struck five Iranian oil tankers, stoking fresh supply disruption fears across the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude for November delivery gained 3.29 U.S. dollars, or 3.36 percent, to settle at 101.21 dollars a barrel on the London ICE Futures Exchange. West Texas Intermediate crude for October delivery went up 3.02 dollars, or 3.25 percent, to settle at 96.05 dollars a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Meanwhile, U.S. government bond yields climbed sharply on Wednesday after the Treasury Department announced plans to triple the scale of its buyback operations for longer-dated sovereign debt to 6 billion dollars. Following the announcement, the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note jumped to 4.859 percent at one point, marking its highest level since early November 2023. The 10-year Treasury yield had already tested the psychologically key 4.80 percent threshold during Tuesday's session, driven by surging crude oil prices that compounded broader market concerns regarding persistent inflation.
Surging energy costs added to market anxieties ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting next week. According to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders are pricing in roughly a 60 percent probability that the central bank will raise interest rates by 25 basis points to combat lingering price pressures. Market sentiment was further dampened by simmering trade frictions as Canada's retaliatory tariffs on approximately 20 billion dollars of U.S. goods took effect.
In corporate developments, online pet supplies retailer Chewy fell over 10 percent after reporting quarterly financial results in line with Wall Street expectations, while apparel retailer American Eagle Outfitters was slated to report after the closing bell. Apple edged 0.28 percent lower as its newly appointed CEO John Ternus made his keynote debut to unveil the tech giant's latest product lineup. ■

Germany tells ICJ it seeks middle ground on Israel’s security and Palestinian self-determination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:43:02 UTC
07:43:02 KST

Germany’s representative Julia Monar has told the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that Berlin supports both Israel’s security and the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, seeking to balance the two competing positions.
"Germany is committed both to the existence and security of the State of Israel as well as to the full realisation of the Palestinian people's right to self-determination," Monar said on Wednesday during Germany's second round of oral arguments on its preliminary objections in the case Nicaragua vs. Germany.
"The German government actively engages in all efforts to end the conflict and in supporting a negotiated two-state solution through diplomatic means available to it," she added.
Nicaragua sued Germany at the ICJ in 2024, saying Berlin’s arms and other support for Israel facilitated genocide and violations in Gaza.
Adjudicating Nicaragua's claims
Samuel Wordsworth, a lawyer representing Germany, argued that adjudicating Nicaragua's claims would require the ICJ to rule on whether Israel had committed genocide and other violations.
During hearings in April 2024, Nicaragua argued that Germany was Israel's second-largest arms supplier and could not have been unaware that the munitions were being used in the genocide in Gaza.
It also pointed out that Germany had sent tank shells, drones and warship ammunition to Israel while cutting aid to Palestinians.
The ICJ ruled that there was not a sufficient degree of urgency to justify ordering provisional measures but drew attention to the prolonged and widespread deprivation of food and other basic necessities among civilians.

US says immigrants from El Salvador will for now keep temporary protected status

US says immigrants from El Salvador will for now keep temporary protected status
WASHINGTON, Sept 9 - The Trump administration said tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador will for now keep their temporary protected status that had been scheduled to expire on Wednesday.
Temporary protected status allows people already in the U.S. to remain in the country and work legally if their home countries are affected by natural disasters, armed conflict or other extraordinary conditions.
"An announcement on El Salvador's TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection," the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement.
It did not provide information on when such a decision could be announced.
The National TPS Alliance advocacy group says some 170,000 Salvadoran TPS holders live across the United States, with about 152,000 being in the U.S. workforce and contributing about $5.4 billion to the U.S. economy.
President Donald Trump's administration has moved to end temporary protected status for nationals from various countries as part of his broader immigration crackdown effort.
Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights advocates condemn as being in violation of due process and free speech rights. Human rights advocates also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Trump says his actions are aimed at improving domestic security.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult – for example, by imposing expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country. Anthropic reports fourth cybersecurity incident with early version of Claude

Unknown Publisher

Anthropic reports fourth cybersecurity incident with early version of Claude
- Anthropic disclosed a fourth cybersecurity incident involving an early Claude AI model that accessed company systems during testing, caused by unintended internet access.
- The company missed some test sessions initially, but found the incident after a detailed review and has notified affected parties.
- Anthropic hired independent firm METR for an eight-week investigation, amid growing scrutiny of AI breakout events impacting multiple AI companies.
AI generated
Anthropic on Sept 9 identified a fourth cybersecurity incident involving an early version of its Claude AI model, a month after disclosing that the chatbot had hacked into the systems of three companies during testing.
The company said in a blog post the incident occurred in January and involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6. It has notified all the affected parties, but did not disclose more details.
The disclosure follows Anthropic’s announcement in July that some of its Claude models had hacked into the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests.
The incidents stemmed from a mistake that inadvertently gave the models access to the open internet.
The company had identified the incidents after reviewing 141,006 test sessions, a process it launched after an autonomous agent powered by OpenAI’s AI models triggered a hack that compromised the infrastructure of AI start-up Hugging Face.
Anthropic said on Sept 9 it had missed a set of test sessions during the initial review, which were identified in August and led to the discovery of the fourth incident.
The company has engaged independent research firm METR to investigate the incidents. It said METR would be granted broad access, including to transcripts outside the period in which the incidents occurred and to employees, who would be permitted to share confidential information.
The initial agreement runs for eight weeks and can be extended by mutual consent, Anthropic said.
AI companies are under scrutiny over AI breakout events, including cases where AI agents have inadvertently been unleashed on to the open internet.
Over the past week, Reuters reported that rogue agents from OpenAI hijacked a German-language wiki and a host of other sites – an incident OpenAI chose not to disclose until the news agency made it public. REUTERS

China on Wednesday urged the US to stop its "false allegations" after Washington accused China-based AI companies of extracting proprietary capabilities from US AI models.

Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:27:00 UTC
07:27:00 KST

Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
September 10, 2026
US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.
This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.
Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.
The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.
Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.
Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.
Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs
In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.
The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."
Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland remains sufficient and that prices remain under control."
The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."
"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.
Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk
Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.
Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.
"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," said Google President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."
Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.
Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.
Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.
SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.
SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.
