A woman takes photos of a Geely E2 electric vehicle on Gran Via in Madrid, Spain, on Sept. 9, 2026. Chinese automaker Geely Auto launched its new electric vehicle, the Geely E2, in Madrid on Wednesday, marking the introduction of its third model in Spain less than six months after it entered the Spanish market. (Photo by Zhang Yuheng/Xinhua)
MADRID, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automaker Geely Auto launched its new electric vehicle, the Geely E2, in Madrid on Wednesday, marking the introduction of its third model in Spain less than six months after it entered the Spanish market.
The new model was unveiled at Madrid's Teatro Capitol, where company representatives, dealers, partners and media gathered for the launch event.
Geely officially entered the Spanish market in March with the Starray EM-i and Geely E5. The arrival of the E2 expands the company's local lineup to three models as it steps up its presence in the country.
Li Lei, managing director of Geely Auto Spain, said the launch represents an important step in the company's strategy in Spain, adding that the company aims to make electric mobility accessible to a broader range of consumers.
The Chinese automaker currently has 50 sales and service points across Spain and plans to expand its network to 80 by the end of 2026.
Geely Auto Group sold more than 3.02 million vehicles globally in 2025, up 39 percent year-on-year. Sales of new energy vehicles reached nearly 1.69 million units, an increase of 90 percent from the previous year, according to the company. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: After years of displacement, Syrian families take their tents home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:55:58 CST
06:55:58 KST

People load household belongings onto trucks as displaced families prepare to return to Ras al-Ain and its countryside from a camp in Syria's northeastern Hasakah province, Sept. 7, 2026. (Str/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali
HASAKAH, Syria, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- For seven years, a tent had been home for Fatima Obeid and her family. On Tuesday, she folded clothes into a suitcase and helped her daughters pack a truck, preparing to take that same tent on another journey -- this time, their real home.
But the home that awaits them may be little more than a pile of rubble.
"We know our homes are destroyed and there is nothing there," Obeid told Xinhua. "So we will take our tents with us and put them up where our homes were. We will live in them temporarily until we can work and rebuild what was destroyed."
Obeid's family is among 689 displaced families leaving camps in northeastern Hasakah province, part of the second organized convoy to return residents to Ras al-Ain and the surrounding areas after nearly seven years in displacement.
Across the camps of al-Tala'ie and al-Twaina, trucks were piled high with mattresses, carpets, water containers, furniture and clothes accumulated over years of displacement. Children moved between the tents and vehicles, some smiling and waving, as adults dismantled the temporary homes they had lived in for years.
For Obeid, the final days in the camp were marked more by anticipation than uncertainty.
"These final moments are filled with joy and happiness for us after all the suffering we have been through," she said, adding that her family had barely slept for two days from the excitement and preparations for the return.
The families fled Ras al-Ain and its countryside during the fighting in northeastern Syria in 2019. Their return, however, is gradual, as security conditions shift and areas are cleared of mines and other war remnants.
Nearby, Munir Ibrahim al-Mohammad, a man in his 70s, sat beside his tent after packing his belongings. Dust on his hands, he watched as his wife and children loaded the family's possessions onto a truck.
"Life here was extremely difficult," he said. "We lived through heat, cold, and rain, amid dirt, dust, and storms. That is camp life, with all its hardship and suffering."
Yet the family will not leave the tent behind.
Al-Mohammad said his house had been completely destroyed, leaving the tent to become their home once again, only this time, on their own land.
"We will take this tent and set it up temporarily where our house once stood, and we will start again," he said. "We hope organizations and the relevant authorities will support us so that we can rebuild our homes and begin a new life."
The return from Hasakah comes amid a broader movement of displaced Syrians back to their communities. Data from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees showed that nearly 2 million internally displaced Syrians had returned to their areas of origin or other locations by July.
But large-scale returns are taking place against a backdrop of damaged housing and infrastructure, strained services and limited livelihood opportunities.
For Abdel Fattah Rdeini, a man in his 60s preparing to leave the camp with his grandchildren, those challenges are deeply personal.
Sitting on a mattress beside his tent, Rdeini laughed with his grandchildren and told them they were finally going home. But his expression changed as he recalled the land, house and possessions he had left behind.
"When I remember the past, I cry. I swear, I cry deeply," he said. "I left behind my land, my house and everything I owned, and now I have nothing left."
"I will start from zero," he continued. "Imagine someone who lived for 50 or 60 years, then lost everything he owned and had to begin again."
Zahra Samou, spokesperson for a committee of displaced Ras al-Ain residents, said the 689 families would face major hardships back in areas scarred by years of destruction.
For many, then, Tuesday's journey could mark the end of displacement, but not the end of hardship.
Around the camp, families were still dismantling tents, tying mattresses and carpets to trucks, and gathering their children and possessions for departure.
For Obeid, what awaited at the other end mattered less than finally being able to return.
"We are going back to our homeland, and we are extremely happy," she said. ■

Contiguous U.S. records warmest summer on record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:55:43 CST
06:55:43 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The contiguous United States experienced its warmest meteorological summer on record in 2026, with the average temperature from June through August reaching about 23.6 degrees Celsius, according to a new report released Wednesday by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The average temperature for the contiguous United States during the summer was about 1.7 degrees Celsius above the 20th-century average and 0.2 degrees Celsius higher than the previous records set in 1936 and 2021, according to the report.
August was also the warmest on record, with the average temperature reaching 24.2 degrees Celsius, about 1.9 degrees Celsius above the 20th-century average. Average daytime maximum temperatures reached 31.4 degrees Celsius, also the highest on record.
Both August and meteorological summer were the warmest on record since 1895 for the contiguous United States, according to the report.
Total precipitation averaged across the contiguous United States in August was about 5.84 cm, about 0.81 cm below the 20th-century average, the report showed. ■

Roundup: Houthis report fresh wave of "Saudi airstrikes" as fighting widens across Yemen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:55:39 CST
06:55:39 KST

SANAA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday that dozens of "Saudi airstrikes" had struck areas under its control over the past 12 hours, as cross-border attacks and expanding ground battles pushed the country's conflict into a new phase of escalation.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement on social media platform X that "Saudi enemy warplanes" had carried out 55 airstrikes over the past 12 hours, hitting Al-Jawf and Saada in northern Yemen, northeastern Marib and Al-Bayda in the center, and the western provinces of Taiz and Hodeidah.
He warned that the strikes "will not go unanswered," but gave no details on the targets, casualties or damage.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on Sarea's latest claims.
The reported strikes came a day after the Houthis launched a wave of missile and drone attacks against targets in southern Saudi Arabia, including energy facilities and a military air base. Saudi authorities said 73 people were injured and fires broke out at several facilities.
The cross-border exchanges have unfolded alongside a sharp escalation inside Yemen, where government forces and the Houthis are fighting on several fronts, most intensely in the country's western areas.
Fierce clashes have centered on areas near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a critical route for international shipping. Government forces have been seeking to halt Houthi advances toward positions overlooking the strategic strait, according to local military sources.
Yemeni government forces said in a statement carried by state-run Saba TV on Wednesday that several Houthi commanders involved in operations near the Bab al-Mandab Strait had been killed or captured. The statement provided no further details, and the Houthis did not immediately comment on the claim.
In the same statement, the forces said their naval units exchanged fire with Houthi boats in the Red Sea, forcing them to retreat toward the Houthi-held port city of Hodeidah.
Farther north, the government forces said on Wednesday they had made additional advances in Al-Jawf and cut Houthi supply routes as part of an expanding offensive in the northern province, which borders Saudi Arabia and lies east of the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
The widening hostilities are taking a growing humanitarian toll, triggering a new wave of displacement across western and southern Yemen.
The government-run Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons Camps said Wednesday that 1,367 families had been displaced from areas in the southwestern province of Taiz, the Red Sea province of Hodeidah and the southern province of Lahj over the previous 24 hours.
That brought the number of families recorded as displaced across the three provinces since the beginning of September to 6,145, according to the unit.
The latest escalation threatens to unravel several years of relative calm on Yemen's major frontlines following a UN-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022. Although the truce formally expired six months later, large-scale fighting remained largely contained until the recent flare-up.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital.
A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. Years of fighting have left the country deeply divided and created a protracted humanitarian crisis. ■

2026-09-10
00:53:40 EEST
06:53:40 KST

For the first time in 20 years, the IAEA has referred the issue of Iran's nuclear program to the UN Security Council
Kyiv • UNN
The IAEA accused Iran of refusing to explain traces of uranium and referred the issue to the UN Security Council. Tehran could face sanctions.
For the first time in 20 years, the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency referred the issue of Iran to the UN Security Council. Tehran was accused of refusing to cooperate with an investigation into the origin of uranium traces at undeclared sites, AP reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The resolution was supported by 23 of the 35 members of the IAEA Board of Governors. China, Russia, and Niger voted against it; another 8 countries abstained, while 1 did not participate in the vote due to arrears.
The document was proposed by the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.
Iran could face new sanctions
Referring the issue to the UN Security Council opens the possibility of imposing sanctions on Iran and freezing its assets. At the same time, AP notes that such measures are unlikely because of Russia and China's veto power.
Western officials suspect that the uranium traces discovered by inspectors may be linked to a secret Iranian nuclear weapons program that may have existed until 2003.
Tehran denies seeking to obtain nuclear weapons and insists that its nuclear program is exclusively peaceful in nature.
Back in June 2025, the IAEA Board of Governors officially found Iran to be in noncompliance with its nonproliferation obligations due to insufficient cooperation with the agency.

US sanctions Chinese-language Xinbi Guarantee marketplace over cyber scams
Unknown

21:48:23 UTC
06:48:23 KST

US sanctions Chinese-language Xinbi Guarantee marketplace over cyber scams
Washington also seizes Telegram channels and US$52 million in cryptocurrency linked to the platform’s alleged illicit operations
The Trump administration sanctioned Chinese-language marketplace Xinbi Guarantee on Wednesday, along with two affiliated organisations, as part of a wider crackdown on transnational cybercrime.
The US Department of Justice also announced it had seized Telegram channels and cryptocurrency wallets tied to the platform, which has over 650,000 users, freezing more than US$52 million in potentially laundered funds in just one day.
“This is not a distant overseas crime story,” said Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, at a press conference. “It is an industrial extraction of American savings run by Chinese transnational criminal enterprises and platforms.”
Wednesday’s operations were conducted by the US Department of Justice’s inter-agency Scam Centre Strike Force, alongside the Department of the Treasury.
Xinbi Guarantee, which runs on the encrypted messaging app Telegram, is accused of enabling scam centres to buy and sell illicit services that target Americans, acting as a central node connecting syndicates with merchants.
Singapore-based SafeW Technology Co and Cambodia-based Anwen Technology Co were also hit by the sanctions over allegations that they provided applications supporting Xinbi’s operations.

Israeli winery CEO, UK kosher wine store vow to weather UK boycott - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:47:24 UTC
06:47:24 KST

British sanctions will impact wine imports and Israeli wineries in the short term, but will have little negative impact in the long term, two wine businesses told The Jerusalem Post.
On Tuesday, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced an import ban on goods from "illegal" settlements in the West Bank. He was joined by 11 other countries that all introduced varying import bans or sanctions.
One of the most affected goods, if the ban goes into effect, will be wine from settlement wineries because they are well-labeled and exported in high numbers.
The Post reached out to Aaron Schapiro of London-based Arele's Kosher Wines, which stocks one of the biggest selections of Israeli and kosher wines in the United Kingdom.
'I'm imagining it will go very hard on us'
"We don't know [the impact] as long as things don't go into effect, but if it does, I'm imagining it will go very hard on us," Schapiro told the Post Tuesday.
He said that many Israeli wines stocked by UK stores are produced in settlement wineries - for example Psagot, Gush Etzion and Shiloh.
"If we can't import them, we will lose more than half of our inventory," he told the Post.
"The thing is, the consumers of these wines specifically want Israeli wines," he explained. "I don't know how far they'll go to find the substitute and to go to the French or go to the Italian. Maybe they will choose to buy just the Israeli wine that is not sanctioned, but that will be a very small amount of wineries.
"So in terms of the effect on our business, then then then then the turnover will be less sales - that's a massive impact."
Schapiro mentioned a friend who stocks Israeli wines in Belgium, which already announced a goods ban in July 2026.
"Some of the wine he is bringing in is from so-called occupied territory, and no one has stopped him. But it's a very risky situation."
Schapiro also raised the question of how Britain and the other boycotting nations will determine what wines to sanction and which are acceptable.
He explained that there are wineries that are situated in internationally recognized Israel, but which grow or obtain their grapes in the settlements, and vice versa. For example, commercial giants like Carmel and Barkan source substantial portions of their grapes or operate industrial park facilities in the West Bank and Golan Heights.
"So, how are you going to know what is coming from where? It's very tricky."
If it does go into effect, Schapiro thinks that importers of kosher settlement wine will be able to exempt it from sanctions by empathizing the religious necessity of having it.
Religious exemptions yield further complications for businesses
Miliband mentioned a religious exemption for imports, and kosher wines and grape juices are required for many Jewish practices and celebrations.
As a result, unfermented kosher grape juice for use at Jewish rituals like Seder or Kiddush is zero-rated for VAT, provided it is prominently marked in English as "for sacramental use only".
Schapiro suggested that kosher wine could be deemed 'for sacramental use' and therefore exempt from the ban. In fact, the same could be said for many, if not all, kosher products exported from Israel.
For these reasons, Schapiro told the Post he is not overly worried about the impact of the sanctions, and thinks it was mainly a political stunt.
"I believe it's something good is gonna come out of this," he told the Post.
The Post also spoke to Psagot Winery CEO Yaakov Berg. Psagot is the largest settlement winery, and exports about 60% of its wines, or around 350,000 to 750,000 bottles a year. Kedem Europe imports Psagot wines into the UK, and major supermarkets such as Tesco also stock them, along with smaller kosher stores like Arele's and Kosher Kingdom.
Berg told the Post on Wednesday that, in the short term, "it will hurt our business" but "in the long term, everything will be okay."
Berg acknowledged that wine is easier to sanction than other products because wineries directly label their products and where they come from, unlike a tomato, which could have been grown anywhere.
But Berg said he has been boycotted many times before, and has survived each time.
"When I started the winery 20 years ago, the first harvest was 3,000 bottles. Last year's harvest, we produced more than 1 million bottles. We really don't care about the boycotts; it's not going to affect us."
"We are proud Jews. We are not afraid of them. We are not going to change anything," Berg added.
Berg nevertheless lamented the sanctions for what they represent for him: pure antisemitism.
He told the Post that he has traveled much of the world, and almost everywhere he has been he has found British history - and "it's not such a nice history."
"Usually the British conquered the place, and then they took everybody as slaves, and it's [relatively speaking] not such a long time ago. The Jewish people, we have a history of 4,000 years here. The land that I'm growing my grapes on, and on which I have my winery, we have been here 4,000 years, and the British people did not even exist yet."
"Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob stood here 4,000 years ago. King David built his kingdom here exactly where I'm standing now, 3,000 years ago."
"And yet this is the only place the British people boycott. It is pure antisemitism. Antisemitism always starts like this. First, they say, we just want to mark the Jews. Then they say, " It's forbidden to buy from the Jews."
"We need to stand up and say: 'You just hate Jews. You just put it in a very nice package."
The longevity of the Jewish people is exactly why Berg is not worried. To those who wish to single out and harm the Jewish people, he has one message: "We are not afraid of you. We are much stronger than you. In 100 years, I'm not sure if England will exist, but I am sure that we will exist here."

Amazon said Kevin Mandia, the founder and former CEO of cybersecurity company Mandiant, is joining its board of directors.

His appointment comes as companies grapple with new cybersecurity threats tied to artificial intelligence. Mandia is also a general partner at Ballistic Ventures, a venture capital firm he co-founded.
"Mandia is a global leader in cybersecurity whose experience building and leading companies that defend the world's most complex organizations — and investing in the next generation of security entrepreneurs through Ballistic Ventures — will help inform the Board's perspective on these opportunities and challenges," Amazon wrote.
Amazon said in a securities filing on Wednesday that Mandia's sister-in-law, Kristin Mandia, is a company employee. She works as a senior online community manager for Amazon Quick, an enterprise AI service, according to LinkedIn.
Mandia was awarded 4,086 shares of common stock as part of his appointment, which will vest in three equal annual installments beginning November 15, 2027, the filing states. Those shares are valued at about $1 million at Wednesday's closing price.

Eastern, western Libyan military commands agree on joint steps toward army’s reunification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:42:48 UTC
06:42:48 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Tarek Chouiref
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Military officials from eastern and western Libya agreed Wednesday on practical steps to deepen coordination between their forces as efforts continue to reunify the country’s divided military.
The agreement was reached in the central city of Sirte at a meeting of the air force, navy and air defense chiefs from both sides, according to separate statements from their general staffs.
Each military branch will prepare an implementation plan covering the measures agreed at the meeting.
The plans include joint exercises and training, coordination on weapons and equipment upgrades, sharing spare parts and military supplies, and cooperation between military academies and training institutions.
The western military command said the talks were also aimed at building trust and removing obstacles to the reunification of Libya’s military.
Further meetings between military departments and branch commands are expected in the coming days.
The meeting follows talks between western Libya’s Chief of General Staff Salah al-Din al-Namroush and his eastern counterpart Khaled Haftar in Luanda on June 30 and in Sirte on July 12.
The July meeting was attended by the UN-backed Joint Military Commission (5+5), the Joint Security and Military Committee (3+3) and the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL).
Libya’s armed forces remain divided between forces affiliated with the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in the west and forces led by Khalifa Haftar in the east.
Military representatives from both sides have held UN-backed talks aimed at reunifying the armed forces under a ceasefire agreement signed in Geneva in October 2020.

Key Event
ASX narrows losses to around $32 billion by the close
After being down by around $50 billion at one stage, the Australian share market narrowed its losses to a $32 billion collective fall in market value by the end of trade.
In the end, both major indices closed down 1%, with the ASX 200 at 8,819 points.

Oil price surge reminds investors of the lingering 'stagflationary tail risk'
As the local market wraps up trade for the day with losses moderating to around 1.2%, an interesting note from Justin Lin, investment strategist at Global X ETFs sent earlier in the day.
"Oil is really smashing the Australian market today," he observes.
"With Brent crude back above $US100 a barrel investors are being forced to confront the prospect that inflation could remain higher for longer and that the RBA may have more work to do.
"For an economy already dealing with sticky inflation, another meaningful increase in energy costs is exactly what the market does not want to see."
Not only would that potentially smash demand in the household sector and push some domestic businesses into severe stress, Lin also worries what the effect on global industrial demand could be.
"Higher metal prices have been enormously supportive for the miners, but if $US100-plus oil reignites global inflation, forces central banks to tighten further and ultimately slows economic growth, demand for industrial commodities could begin to soften materially," he warns.
"That is the stagflationary tail risk that has lingered in the background and is being brought back to the fore today."
Commodities boom revives NSW antimony mine
The worldwide hunt for a little-known critical mineral has seen trucks moving for the first time in more than a decade at the historic Hillgrove mine just outside Armidale.
Larvotto Resources said the price of antimony had more than doubled since it acquired the site in 2023, to $US26,300 ($36,357) per tonne.
"Antimony has just been classified a critical mineral; there is a world shortage [and] the price is much better than what it was five years ago," said managing director Ron Heeks.
Earlier this year, the silvery-grey metalloid was one of the first minerals included in the federal government's $1.2 billion critical minerals strategic reserve as crucial to Australia's economy and national security.
You can read more in ABC New England journalist Brigitte Murphy's story.
The 'Polar Silk Road' doesn't feel like good news…
After a 25-day voyage via the Arctic a Chinese container ship has arrived at Teesport in the UK.
The voyage of the Dubai Tower, operated by Chinese shipping company Sea Legend, shows the potential of Russia's Northern Sea Route (NSR) as a much faster passage between Asia and Europe.
Compared with the traditional route via the Strait of Malacca and the Suez Canal, the NSR cuts the voyage time nearly in half.
But it's not all smooth sailing.
"The route is only navigable for a relatively narrow window in the height of the Northern Hemisphere summer," Edward Rhys Jones, a researcher at Oxford University, told the ABC.
"Even with the Arctic warming three to four times faster than the global average it will be decades before the region is reliably ice-free year-round."
Mr Jones added that the route remained heavily dependent on Russian support, with most vessels requiring Russian icebreaker escorts — a process that requires strict permits and adds significant operational costs.
Obviously, the extreme Arctic warming that is making this route even remotely viable is also major concern.
You can read more in Xiaoning Mo's story below.

Can the US afford an extra $US1.5 trillion outlay?
So DJT has reportedly just floated a USD 5,000 bribe, sorry payment, to all US adults. Let's do the math. 200,000,000 eligible adults say USD 5,000 each USD 1,000,000,000,000 total bill That US 1 Trillion, with a T. #BondMarketThoughts
- Josh
Hi Josh.
I went to the US Census Bureau to do a back-of-the-envelope calculation based on official data.
It seems there are about 300 million adult residents of the United States, which would put the cost of Donald Trump's $5,000 per person promise at up to $US1.5 trillion ($2.07 trillion), or roughly three-quarters of Australia's annual economic output.
(That is assuming absolutely every adult was eligible, which is unlikely when many are non-citizens).
US government debt recently passed $US40 trillion, so I guess you could argue, "What's another 1.5, eh?"
But, as you point out, Josh, bond traders are looking for fiscal constraint, not more profligacy, so more government spending wouldn't be well received.
But it doesn't look like traders are taking the proposal seriously, with US 10-year bond yields basically unchanged after their increase overnight and the Aussie dollar-US dollar exchange rate also fairly unchanged — albeit close to a four-and-a-bit year high.
ABC reporter Brad Ryan was in Dallas for the Republicans' mid-term convention.
Most financial planners now academically qualified
A new report from financial information service Rainmaker finds that 85% of financial advisers now hold qualifications at a bachelor degree level or higher.
"The transition officially concluded at the end of 2025, requiring advisers to meet new education standards either through approved qualifications or the experienced provider pathway, which recognises long-serving advisers with strong compliance records," said Pooja Antil, senior research manager at Rainmaker Information.
The turning point came on January 1, 2019, when the Financial Adviser Standards and Ethics Authority (FASEA) regime came into effect.
As you can see in the above graph, perhaps unsurprisingly, there was a last-minute rush by many planners to meet the minimum qualification requirements before the end of 2025 deadline.
The research found 746 advisers permanently left the financial adviser register in January 2022 alone, following the introduction of the adviser exam requirements — about 10 times the normal monthly exit rate.
Clearly, many people really dislike exams!
"Today's education profile reflects advisers who successfully remained in the profession through the reform period," said Antil.
There have been problems with the smaller pool of advisers, as it has been a factor contributing to the increasing cost of advice.
Then again, it's potentially better to have no financial advice at all than to trust advice from someone inadequately qualified and potentially beset by massive financial conflicts of interest, which was the state of much of the sector before these changes were introduced.
Key Event
Shares fall pretty much everywhere
It's not just the Australian share market that's doing poorly today.
It's pretty much a sea of red everywhere, including:
- Australia's ASX 200 (-1.6%)
- Wall Street's Dow Jones index (-0.8%),
- Hong Kong's Hang Seng (-1.3%),
- Japan's Nikkei (-0.8%), and
- South Korea's KOSPI (-1.1%).
One reason why is because markets are pricing in much higher odds of central banks lifting interest rates across the world.
Who's likely to announce a rate hike?
Over the next three weeks, we'll be hearing from central banks in Australia, the United States, the Eurozone and Japan — and there's a high chance they might all raise interest rates.
Here's how the schedule is looking:
- European Central Bank: The ECB is widely expected to announce a rate hike tonight at 10:15pm (AEST). In fact, markets are pricing in a 100% chance of that happening, according to Bloomberg data. They're also betting there will be two more hikes by April 2027.
- US Federal Reserve: The world's most important central bank will make its decision on September 17. The market is pricing a 63% chance the Fed will hike next Thursday — and that probability rises to 92% in October. All up, markets are expecting three rate hikes in the US by December 2027. If that ends up happening, President Donald Trump will not be happy...
- Bank of Japan: The odds of the BoJ lifting rates on September 18 are sitting at 97%. Beyond that, markets are predicting three rate hikes in Japan by June 2027.
And finally, what about the Reserve Bank of Australia? It's no doubt the one you're most interested to hear about!
The odds of the RBA lifting rates for a fourth time this year are quite high.
When governor Michele Bullock announces the RBA board's decision on Tuesday, September 29, traders collectively think there's a 75% chance it'll be an increase to the cash rate.
And, looking further into the future, the markets are betting there's a 94% chance a fifth hike could happen by March 2027!
You might be thinking: there's a good chance the markets are wrong with their predictions.
That's certainly possible. But these probabilities are factored in by other traders to determine how much shares and currencies should be worth — so that's why we're seeing big falls on global share markets today.

High end homes have led housing downturn, but it is spreading
A nice write up from Zena Chamas and Daniela Pizzirai looking at Cotality data showing how the top end of the property market, especially in Sydney and Melbourne, has been hit first and (so far) hardest by the downturn — see link at the bottom of this post.
However, real estate agency Ray White's chief economist Nerida Conisbee believes that trend is now just starting to turn.
She uses open home attendance as a timely proxy for buyer interest.
"Some of the strongest increases since the [federal] budget have been in premium Sydney and Melbourne markets," Conisbee observes.
"Sydney's Eastern Suburbs has added 0.8 attendees per open, while Melbourne Inner South, North Sydney and Hornsby and Melbourne Inner East are each up around 0.6.
"These are also areas that have experienced some of the largest price corrections over the past year."
On the flip side.
"Many of the largest falls in attendance are occurring in more affordable markets," she notes.
"Adelaide South is down 2.9 attendees per open, Perth North West 2.4, Perth North East 1.7 and Cairns 1.4."
She says it makes sense that areas that have recently been targeted by investors have reacted most to the budget's tax changes.
"The changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax reduce the attractiveness of established housing to investors, and the effect is greatest in markets where investors represent a larger share of demand," Consibee argues.
"Affordable areas initially held up better on price, but they are now losing an important source of buyers as investor activity retreats.
"At the same time, the larger price adjustment at the premium end is beginning to bring owner-occupiers back."
Of course, real estate agencies have a vested interest in the housing market stabilising, but there do seem to be some early signs that some markets are finding a new, lower equilibrium price.
Key Event
Labor releases 'slightly relaxed' gas reservation plan
The Australian government this morning relaxed slightly a proposed rule that would have forced energy exporters to reserve a fixed 20% of natural gas for the east coast market, instead requiring exporters to reserve up to a fifth of production.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen said exporters could provide up to 200 additional petajoules of gas per year, more than enough to avoid the possible shortfalls of up to 140 petajoules forecast by the country's energy market operator.
The proposed policy will ensure "gas is more affordable and the domestic market is always modestly oversupplied," Bowen said in a statement.
As always, you can tell a lot about where a policy has landed from the reaction of vested interests.
Samantha McCulloch, the CEO of Australian Energy Producers — the lobby for the local oil and gas sector — said "the federal government has made a number of sensible changes" to its initial proposal.
These include, "calibrating the reservation requirement more closely to domestic market needs", recognising existing state reservation schemes, and "linking the supply obligation to physically connected domestic gas markets".
"However, the proposed 110% oversupply of the east coast gas market will destroy investment signals and crowd out smaller, domestic-focused producers," argued McCulloch.
"The 'must sell' requirement exacerbates these risks. Producers should not be forced to sell gas below cost or on non-commercial terms."
Major industrial gas user BlueScope Steel put out this response.
"Our initial reading is that the draft legislation maintains many of the important design features that BlueScope and other manufacturers have been seeking. It keeps the gas companies honest," said the company's managing director Tania Archibald.
"We will review the draft legislation in detail including to better understand how calibration of domestic supply obligations against demand will work. We will want to ensure the surplus of gas the government is targeting is delivered."
From that sample, it seems like the government has overall landed more on the side of the gas users than the gas producers.

Key Event
Is 'US fiscal incontinence' and 'mind-boggling' AI investment ushering in 'Bondmageddon'?
At the start of this week, I spoke with financial commentator and former banker Satyajit Das about the two things worrying him most in the global financial system right now: soaring government debt and bond yields, and a potential AI investment bubble of unprecedented proportions.
With substantial moves up in bond yields overnight, are we seeing Das's worries playing out much earlier than even he expected?
News of an expanded US Treasury long-term bond buy-back to $US6 billion failed to dent long-term interest rates, with the yield on 10-year US government debt rising as high as 4.85%, the highest level in almost three years.
Loading...
The US is not alone in facing surging long-term bond yields.
Germany was forced to offer the highest interest rate on 10-year bonds for 17 years overnight at 3.39%.
A few weeks ago, Westpac's chief economist Luci Ellis wrote:
"AI-related investment and US fiscal incontinence add to the existing tendency for the global rates structure to average higher than pre-pandemic."
As Ellis pointed out, a massive wave of big-tech corporate bond issues is competing with government debt to attract investors funds.
Just yesterday, Amazon issued bonds totaling £4.25 billion in the UK, while Uber issued its first euro denominated bond.
Bloomberg reports that, even before yesterday's big bond issues, US corporates had already raised €149 billion in Europe so far this year, on top of their massive $US raisings.
Late last month, Google's parent Alphabet raised $5.5 billion in Australian dollar bonds.
"The scale of the planned global investment in data centres is nothing short of mind-boggling, and it is creating substantial demand for debt finance," noted Ellis last month.
"The "hyperscaler" tech firms (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft) used to be enormous cash generators. Now they are responsible for some of the largest debt issuances in the market."
When I spoke to Das on Monday he quoted Shanaka Anslem Perera.
"Either the gods are being built in the Texas desert, he was referring to the AI data centres, or the greatest financial delusion in human history is unfolding in real time."
As Das says, it may take another year or two to figure out which is true.

El Nino puts India on high health-risk radar, says WHO

El Nino puts India on high health-risk radar, says WHO
NEW DELHI: With dengue cases rising in several parts of the country, a WHO assessment has flagged India among nations facing high or very high health risks as a strengthening El Nino event alters weather patterns across South Asia.El Nino is a periodic warming of surface waters in central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean that can disrupt weather patterns around the world, influencing rainfall and temperatures far beyond the Pacific.WHO's Global Public Health Situation Analysis - El Nino 2026, released on Sept 5, has identified India as being at high or very high risk, with most of South Asia expected to experience drier-than-normal conditions and above-normal heat during Aug-Oct.The warning comes at a time when vector-borne diseases are already rising in parts of the country. In Delhi, 90 dengue cases were reported in Aug, the highest monthly tally this year, taking the total to 311 by Aug 29. Malaria cases also rose from 17 in July to 53 in Aug, taking the year's tally to 119, according to Municipal Corporation of Delhi.
The agency does not link current dengue or malaria cases directly to El Nino, but calls it a risk modifier, with impacts depending on local weather, vulnerability and health-system capacity.
For India, heat is a key concern, with higher temperatures potentially causing heat exhaustion and heatstroke and worsening cardiovascular, respiratory, kidney and metabolic illnesses.Extreme heat may also affect maternal and newborn outcomes. Other concerns include malnutrition, food insecurity and worsening non-communicable diseases. Changes in rainfall and water availability could affect food production, while heavy rain and flooding can increase the risk of leptospirosis, particularly where sanitation and drainage are poor. WHO has also flagged the India-Nepal and India-Bhutan borders, where displacement could increase the risk of cross-border disease transmission.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Hong Kong must plan for the population it wants to have
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Hong Kong must plan for the population it wants to have
As the population ages, becomes more mobile and welcomes more non-locals, data-based planning is needed to inform and improve urban planning
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
Dr Jane Lee, MH, JP, is president of Our Hong Kong Foundation and founding CEO of Hong Kong Policy Research Institute. 
What kind of population is Hong Kong planning for? That is the question the chief executive’s policy address must tackle as the Northern Metropolis begins to take shape.
Much more than just another new town, the Northern Metropolis is Hong Kong’s most consequential project for its next phase of development, expected to house 2.5 million residents and provide 650,000 jobs. The numbers are well known, but they are not the story.
This population of 2.5 million will be like no other. The Northern Metropolis’ deep integration with Shenzhen and the Greater Bay Area means its residents will live, work, study and access services on both sides of the border. As Hong Kong’s population becomes increasingly dynamic and mobile, the Northern Metropolis should serve as the starting point for developing a citywide population strategy that aligns public policies with the realities of a cross-boundary lifestyle.
Hong Kong’s demographic profile is undergoing substantial changes. Fertility remains exceptionally low, at 0.7 to 0.8 births per woman. Residents 65 years and older now account for about 24 per cent of the population. Meanwhile, the number of residents aged 15 to 34 years fell from 1.747 million in 2018 to 1.461 million last year – a decrease of 285,900 people, or 16.4 per cent, in seven years.
At the same time, talent admission schemes since 2022 have brought a more varied population to Hong Kong. According to the latest Immigration Department figures released in March, the government has received about 600,000 applications and approved more than 410,000 as of end-February. Of these, about 300,000 approved cases involved mainland talent and nearly 110,000 involved holders of non-mainland passports. Many have entered finance, innovation and technology, information and communications technology, trade and other professional fields.
These individuals should not be viewed merely as inputs into the labour market. They are new Hongkongers. They are parents considering where their children should study; they are tenants or potential homebuyers; they are users of medical, childcare, transport and community services. Their degree of commitment to Hong Kong will depend not only on the job or investment opportunities, but also on the quality of life the city offers.

Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
Russian forces struck a shopping and entertainment center in the northeastern city of Sumy on Sept. 9, killing at least two and injuring 20, including three children, local authorities said.
A Russian drone hit Sumy's Manufactura mall near the city's center, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Footage released by the agency shows firefighters battling flames engulfing cars, debris strewn through parking lots, and the blood of victims pooling on asphalt outside the mall. All sources of fire have reportedly been extinguished.
Sumy Governor Oleh Hryhorov said on Telegram that the attack killed two people, both 21 years old.
Another 20 people were injured, Hryhorov said, with two men and one woman in serious condition and another woman in extremely critical condition. Three girls, aged 15-16, are among the injured.
Fourteen people have been hospitalized, the governor said.
The deadly strike in Sumy comes as Russia has intensified attacks on Ukraine's supermarkets and shopping centers — even during the day, when stores are crowded with civilians.
In August 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia was deliberately targeting supermarket warehouses, distribution centers, and stores. Later that month, Russia launched a daytime drone strike on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, killing 16 people and injuring 130 others, including 23 children.
The latest attack in Sumy follows a U.S.-brokered peace push in Kyiv and Moscow on Sept. 6-7. While the visit revived a stagnant diplomatic process, it failed to yield a breakthrough or stop Russian missiles from raining on Ukraine in the following days.
"Now, it is crucial for all partners to focus and work on the necessary steps to de-escalate the situation and stop the killings," Zelensky said on Telegram Sept. 9 after the strike on Sumy. "Terrorism is always a threat to many, and we must counter it together."
While the visit by American envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff provided a brief respite from Moscow's attacks, Russia has been using Ukraine's severe shortage of air defense systems to pummel cities across the nation all summer.
July of 2026 saw the most civilians killed or injured in Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in March 2022, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on Aug. 13.

Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:23:45 BST
06:23:45 KST

Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
- Published
Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.
The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.
On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.
Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".
The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."
It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.
The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.
Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.
However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.
Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".
But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.
"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.
Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".
The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.
Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have foreseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".
A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".
Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.
"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

Push to save teacher-librarians as student reading levels decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:23:24 UTC
06:23:24 KST

Petition launched to save teacher-librarians as student performance falters
In short:
A petition to mandate teacher-librarian roles in schools is attracting strong support.
It comes after national studies show an ongoing decline in student reading performance.
What's next?
When completed, the petition will be presented to state and federal education departments.
A petition to mandate teacher-librarian roles in schools has attracted more than 13,000 signatures in less than a week as authors push to stop the critical roles from being phased out by educators.
Children's writer Kate Temple, who penned the Bin Chicken series, launched the petition in response to news last week that teacher-librarians at 58 schools in the Newcastle-Maitland Catholic diocese were being made redundant or getting redeployed.
It comes as international studies found Australian reading performance continued to decline among children, and fewer teenagers were reading for enjoyment.
Temple told 891 ABC Adelaide that the announcement had been a "lightning rod" for an issue that was occurring Australia-wide.
"Teacher-librarians are vital to creating reading cultures in schools," she said.
"They teach really important classes beyond that as well, like digital literacy and media literacies.
"But what I see, as an author that spends quite a lot of time in schools, is how valuable they are at really creating reading for pleasure, which is one of the most vital things when it comes to combating our declining literacy rates."
Temple said teacher-librarians supported a variety of children, from "ambitious readers looking for their next read on their journey", to neurodivergent children who struggled to read.
"Teacher-librarians know a great deal about their student cohort and they're able to really move that whole body of students towards a community that loves reading,"
"Schools that have well-staffed libraries with teacher-librarians have amazing reading cultures, and it doesn't matter what kind of school they are."
Author and illustrator of the children's Macca the Alpaca series, Matt Cosgrove, has also been lending his support to the Students Need School Libraries movement, as have the likes of Andy Griffiths and Terry Denton.
Falling reading performances
The latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) report was released by the OECD this week and found that, among randomly selected samples of 15-year-old student performances, Australia's mean reading performance continued to show a declining trend.
It found that between 2022 and 2025, there was a two-point decrease in the proportion of students who attained the National Proficient Standard (NPS), which followed a two-point increase in the proportion of low performers in reading.
This followed a 37-point decline in Australia's mean reading performance between 2000 and 2025, which dropped seven points between 2022 and 2025 alone to 491 points.
Despite this, the country's reading performance was higher than the OECD average of 461 points, about the same as the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, but lower than the likes of New Zealand, Ireland and Japan, and much lower than the two highest scorers in Singapore (535 points) and Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang in China (527).
- The OECD average for low performers is 31 per cent, and 23 per cent in Australia; high performers is 6 per cent in the OECD and 11 per cent in Australia.
- In Singapore, high performers make up 22 per cent and low performers just 14 per cent.
Australia Reads, the national body for reading, said last year that PISA data, alongside data from the Progress International Reading Literacy Study, and The Decline in Volitional Reading report released in August 2025 by the National Institute of Education in Singapore, found that one in three Australian children could not read proficiently.
It also found that 29 per cent of teenagers were choosing not to read for enjoyment at all, and blamed declines on a lack of reading role models, digital media shortening attention spans, overemphasis on skills rather than enjoyment, and limited access to books and texts.
Teacher-librarians squeezed out
School Library Association of SA president Hajnalka Molloy said that in SA, less than 15 per cent of all schools had a dual-qualified teacher-librarian.
"We are the same price as any other teacher, but we bring those extra skills, extra knowledge of children's literature, connecting with our amazing kid-lit community here in Australia and connecting students to those authors and illustrators, as well as helping children find the book that they're going to love in the format that works for them," she told 891 ABC Adelaide.
She said that prior to 2011, teacher-librarian positions were mandated in SA as a funded position, but changed to a "student-centred funding model" that allowed principals dealing with tight budgets to make "very difficult decisions".
"And often they're not necessarily aware of the impact that a dual-qualified teacher-librarian has on student learning outcomes, particularly in terms of information literacy, reading culture and student wellbeing,"
She said in an era where AI technology was being incorporated into learning environments, it was "more important than ever" to maintain such roles.
Ms Molloy said she had been teaching primary school students to think critically about the value of AI results to their online searches.
"To be aware that even though it answers questions very confidently, it's not necessarily true, accurate or representing all the points of view on a particular issue," she said.
"We know how to help kids find a range of credible sources through print and digital media, help them determine what is credible information, help them look for bias, misinformation, disinformation, and then how to use the various digital tools, AI tools, and use that information ethically as well."
The petition, which has the official support of Australia Reads, the Australian Library and Information Association and the Australian Coalition of School Libraries, was launched on Friday last week and by Wednesday evening had attracted more than 13,000 signatures.
It will be presented to state and federal departments of education.

For the first time in several months, Brent has once again surpassed the psychological threshold of $100 per barrel
Kyiv • UNN
Brent rose to $101.21 following attacks by Iran and the US. The market fears prolonged disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude prices exceeded $100 per barrel and closed at their highest level since late May amid the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. Oil prices rose after new attacks by Iran and the United States heightened concerns about disruptions to energy supplies, Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
Brent crude futures rose by $3.29, or 3.4%, to $101.21 per barrel. During trading, the price reached $101.58. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose by $3.02, or 3.25%, to $96.05 per barrel.
According to Reuters, the market responded to a new wave of escalation between Iran and the United States. Iran said it had attacked 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, while the United States reported destroying five Iranian oil tankers.
Analysts note that the market is increasingly pricing in the risk of prolonged disruptions to energy supplies from the Middle East.
The move toward $100 for Brent and back above it reflects the fact that the market is increasingly being forced to revise its view of how long the crisis in the Middle East will continue to constrain supplies from the region
Risks to the global market are increasing
Particular concern is being caused by the situation around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies passed before the conflict began.
Experts believe that the reciprocal strikes between the United States and Iran significantly reduce the chances of a swift resolution to the conflict and increase risks for the global energy market.
Since the war between Iran and the United States began in late February, Brent prices have already risen to $126.41 per barrel, but later fell below $100. Now, due to the new escalation, oil has returned to triple-digit levels.

President of the European Council António Costa advocated introducing new pan-European taxes that would reduce member states’ direct contributions to the EU budget. He made the statement after talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin, Politico reports, according to UNN.
Details
We cannot demand more from the member states. We need to create new own resources to protect national budgets
The issue has become one of the key points in negotiations on the EU budget for 2028–2034. Germany, which accounts for about a quarter of the bloc’s budget financing, opposes a substantial increase in its expenditures.
Merz demands cuts of hundreds of billions of euros to the EU budget

The European Commission had previously expected to receive about €66 billion annually from new sources of revenue. So far, countries have agreed only to levies under the carbon border adjustment mechanism and on uncollected electronic waste, which together could generate about €20 billion per year.

San Francisco Orders Meta to Stop ‘Allowing’ AI Child Abuse Ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:15:27 UTC
06:15:27 KST

San Francisco’s city attorney has hit Meta with a cease-and-desist letter telling the company to stop “allowing” paid advertisements that include AI-generated child sexual abuse content and asked it to explain how the ads repeatedly ran on its platforms.
On Tuesday, WIRED reported that Meta has run more than 350 ads in recent months that transformed still images of minors—some of them confirmed as real individuals, including a member of a European royal family—into short videoclips that can depict them performing sexual acts. When clicked, these ads would direct people to download AI image- and video-generation apps, some of which could be used to digitally undress people or create other nonconsensual intimate imagery.
The ads, which were discovered by researchers at the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), included some identical ads that had been uploaded multiple times, and in total they reached more than 29,000 accounts in countries in the European Union. The ads that were shown across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads also targeted accounts in the US, Australia, and India. WIRED initially reported on a batch of 53 of the ads at the start of August, but more than 250 of the total number of ads ran on Meta’s platforms after this initial report.
“Meta has failed to address a known issue of AI-generated child sexually explicit ads, while profiting from them," San Francisco city attorney David Chiu says in a statement to WIRED. “These ads are deeply disturbing and cause harm to real children. Meta claims to have zero tolerance for child exploitation, yet the scale and persistence of these issues suggest current efforts are woefully inadequate. This is unacceptable, and Meta must do better.”
“No company—particularly one that claims all advertisements are reviewed and approved prior to distribution and then accepts payment for that distribution—should permit its advertising systems to be used in this manner,” Chiu writes in the four-page letter his office sent to Meta’s lawyers.
The letter raises a host of questions about how Meta’s ad policies and safety systems operate and asks that the company’s legal, child-safety, and advertising staff engage in “prompt discussions” with the city office. “These findings are especially troubling because they do not appear to reflect an isolated failure that Meta corrected when first alerted to the problem,” Chiu writes.
Meta says there is “no indication” that the ads were displayed in San Francisco and this means they are “outside the city attorney's jurisdiction.” While Meta’s ad library, which is a repository of ads, includes some data about ads published in the US, it does not break down where in the US ads may have run.
In response to Meta's jurisdictional claims, City Attorney's Office spokesperson Alex Barrett-Shorter tells WIRED that, because “San Francisco consumers can access the unlawful ads through Meta online spaces,” the matter is the the city of San Francisco's business.
“We find Meta’s response astonishing. Meta appears less concerned about whether they’re guilty of exploiting children than whether San Francisco should say anything about it,” Barrett-Shorter says. “Meta has bigger problems to solve here than determining our jurisdiction.”
Meta previously told WIRED that many of the ads identified by the TTP researchers had already been removed before they were reported—all of them have now been removed for violating its policies—and most had “fewer than 200 impressions” from accounts. “We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” a Meta spokesperson previously said. The company said the “total ad spend” for the 300-plus ads found by the researchers was “under $5,000.”
The letter, which says the City Attorney’s Office has reviewed many of the ads found by the TTP researchers, demands that Meta stop the ads from running on its platforms and explain how the ads managed to avoid its moderation systems and how it escalates and reports ads to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and asks the company to detail how it addresses the advertisers behind the content and repeat offenders.
The letter continues to say the findings suggest “broader systemic problems” with how the company detects potential child sexual abuse in advertising and that it raises “significant legal questions” for the company. “My Office’s objective is not simply to identify past failures but to ensure that Meta puts systems in place that prevent children from being sexually exploited through advertisements Meta is paid to distribute, and that Meta reliably satisfies the legal obligations that arise when it becomes aware of apparent child sexual exploitation,” Chiu writes in the letter.
The findings from the TTP researchers stated that in some cases Meta did not respond to reports the agency made about abusive ads for more than a week, during which the ads were seen by hundreds more people. When some ads were removed, they were initially not marked as containing child sexual abuse content, according to TTP and a WIRED review of Meta’s ad library. “The scale, persistence, and nature of the problems documented here suggest that Meta’s isolated takedown efforts are woefully inadequate,” the letter from Chiu says, requesting Meta provide a response within 28 days.
Meta’s community standards and advertising policies do not allow child sexual exploitation, abuse, or nudity, nor adult exploitation or adult nudity. The company also does not allow the promotion of nudify apps. Meta’s ad standards say that all advertisements are reviewed against its policies using automated, and sometimes manual, reviews. The company has previously removed hundreds of thousands of ads for nudify apps.
Despite Meta taking action against nudify apps, including suing a Hong Kong–based company linked to one set of nudifier platforms and working with other tech companies, researchers continue to find thousands of ads that direct people to the harmful apps and that contain sexual activity and nudity. During WIRED’s reporting on the Tech Transparency Project findings, we identified hundreds of “nudification” ads currently running across Meta’s platforms.
Katie Paul, the director of TTP, says that Meta is “not effectively” addressing the issue, and ads containing child sexual abuse are still appearing on its plaform as of Wednesday. “Meta has claimed it takes a hard stance against child sexual abuse material, but since TTP’s September 8 report published, more brand-new ads have run featuring some of the same children TTP sent to Meta,” Paul says. The organization has reported the ads to Meta and the NCMEC and noted that some had already been removed. Meta did not immediately respond to WIRED’s question about new ads still appearing.
“The findings are clear,” Paul adds. “Meta is not effectively addressing this issue.”
Updated 9/9/2026 at 6 pm ET: Added additional comment from the San Francisco City Attorney's Office.

Trump says Iran war ‘will end immediately’ after US midterm elections

United States President Donald Trump has offered his latest prediction for concluding the war in Iran, indicating that an end date could come after the upcoming US midterm elections.
“This war will end immediately after our election,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday before boarding Air Force One for a trip to Dallas, Texas.

Trump claimed the Iranian government was stalling an end to the war in order to secure a more favourable political environment in the US.
The Democratic Party is angling to take control of one or both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms. Currently, Trump’s Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there,” Trump said of Iran’s strategy for the legislative elections.
He suggested that Iran is counting on Democrats to “leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon”.
“All they want is a nuclear weapon, and if they had a nuclear weapon, the whole world is in deep trouble,” Trump said of Iran.
‘More than a nuclear deal’
When the war against Iran began on February 28, the country’s nuclear programme was a key justification that the US and Israel cited for launching hostilities. Trump and his officials claimed that Iran posed an “imminent” threat to the US and its allies.
Iran, however, has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, instead arguing its uranium enrichment is for civilian power purposes only.
US intelligence reports have also cast doubt on whether Iran was building a nuclear weapon, though concerns have been raised over its levels of enrichment.
Negotiations about Iran’s nuclear energy programme were ongoing at the time of the war’s launch, and the issue has repeatedly cropped up in ceasefire negotiations in the six months since.
Trump had previously withdrawn from a 2015 nuclear deal, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), that would have restricted the amount of uranium Iran was allowed to enrich.
When asked on Wednesday whether the US would restart talks with Iranians on a nuclear agreement, the president suggested his ambitions were larger.
“I’m doing much more than a nuclear deal. There’s a lot more than nuclear,” Trump said.
But he also indicated that negotiations with Iran were not a top priority for the US government.
“We’re not looking for it, to be honest,” Trump said. “Originally, I wanted to make a deal. We’re so far down the line. They have very little country left right now.”
More US strikes to come
Trump’s comments follow remarks from US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who told ABC News on Sunday “there may not” be a nuclear deal.
Wright suggested instead that the US may continue to launch strikes to weaken Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.
The US already carried out targeted strikes on three Iranian nuclear facilities during the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. Trump at the time said those strikes “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear programme.
Negotiations with Iran have floundered in recent months, and the Trump administration has continued to downplay the conflict ahead of the midterm elections.
The war is widely unpopular in the US. A poll last month found that only 31 percent of Americans support the conflict, down from 37 percent in March.
On Wednesday, oil prices rose above $100 a barrel amid renewed US-Iran hostilities, threatening to further increase costs for consumers around the world.
The US military said it struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday in response to attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship.
On Wednesday, Trump said more US strikes would follow: “You’re going to see a lot more.”

Putin once again failed to reach an agreement with Xi Jinping on a new gas pipeline to China because of the price
Kyiv • UNN
Russia-China negotiations on the gas pipeline have stalled due to differences over the price. Moscow wants $250–260, while Beijing wants around $50 per 1,000 cubic meters.
Negotiations between Russia and China on the construction of the Power of Siberia-2 gas pipeline, which Moscow views as a way to partially replace the lost European market, have once again reached an impasse. The sides failed to agree on the price of gas even after the meeting between Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on August 31, The Moscow Times reports, citing the South China Morning Post, writes UNN.
Details
According to SCMP sources, negotiations on the gas pipeline, with a capacity of 50 billion cubic meters per year, which Putin proposed renaming the "Power of Baikal," have currently been suspended.
There is no progress on the price
According to SCMP, China wants to buy Russian gas for approximately $50 per 1,000 cubic meters—the price for households in the Russian Federation. As an alternative, Beijing is considering Russia's domestic price for industrial consumers—approximately $120–130.
Russia wants at least twice as much
Moscow, in turn, is proposing to base the price on the cost of gas under the existing "Power of Siberia-1"—approximately $250–260 per 1,000 cubic meters. Even this price, according to the publication, is approximately 40% lower than Gazprom's contractual gas price for other customers in countries outside the former Soviet Union.
Despite statements by Russian officials that the project is nearing construction, the official statement following the latest meeting between Xi and Putin did not mention the gas pipeline at all. Since 2022, the Russian authorities have stated at least 10 times that agreements on the project are at the final stage.
The agreement is of particular importance to Gazprom after the loss of most of the European market. The company's exports currently amount to approximately 70–80 billion cubic meters per year—the lowest level for Russia since the mid-1980s.

Lithuania Moves Toward Lifting Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Deployments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:07:17 UTC
06:07:17 KST

- Category
- World
Lithuania Moves Toward Lifting Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Deployments
Lithuania’s parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs has voted 7–2 to approve a proposal removing constitutional restrictions against hosting foreign military bases and weapons of mass destruction, according to tv3.lv on September 9.
The decision moves the Baltic nation closer to allowing NATO nuclear forces on its territory, following a broader political consensus reached by parliamentary parties earlier this summer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
If passed by the full Seimas and signed by the president, the measure will strike Article 137 from the Lithuanian Constitution. The clause currently prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases, regardless of NATO collective defense arrangements or security threats from Russia.
Lawmakers supporting the constitutional amendment emphasized that lifting the restriction is essential for regional security and deterrence. Lithuanian Parliamentary Speaker Juozas Olekas highlighted the country's unique position among allies: “When agreeing on common collective defense plans, and especially deterrence, Lithuania looks like a black sheep in the Alliance, as it is the only one with such a restriction.”
Olekas added during the committee hearing: “Nuclear weapons today are the most powerful deterrent capable of stopping an aggressor crossing our borders.”
The Ministry of Justice has voiced strong backing for the change, with Deputy Minister Martynas Dobrovolskis confirming full support during the meeting.
However, some opposition remains within parliament. Raimondas Šukys, a committee member from the Reminisce of Nemunas party, urged lawmakers to hold a consultative referendum before finalizing the constitutional update.
The initiative follows similar action taken by Finland in June, when the Finnish parliament passed legislation permitting the import, transit, and storage of nuclear weapons for national defense purposes. The bill was later signed into law by Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen previously noted that ending the ban strengthens national defense capabilities and ensures full access to NATO's nuclear deterrence framework. The Finnish government stated that its decision came in response to deteriorating European security conditions.

Opals survive in last second after surrendering 20-point lead at World Cup

Opals reach FIBA Women's World Cup quarterfinal after Italy misses last-second shot
In short:
The Opals are through to the World Cup quarterfinals after beating Italy 82-80 despite leading by 20 points at three-quarter-time.
A lay-up by Italian Francesca Pana rolled off the rim after the final siren sounded.
What's next?
Australia will play Spain in the quarters, but will likely have to do so without captain Ezi Magbegor, who suffered a game-ending knee injury in the first quarter against Italy.
A short-handed Australian team is still alive and into the last eight at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup despite surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead before ultimately beating Italy 82-80.
The Opals had a 69-49 lead heading into the final quarter of their qualification final against the Azzurre, but watched the Italians slowly chip away at it over the next eight minutes and 51 seconds before Costanza Verona's three tied the game at 77 with 1:09 left.
Zitina Aokuso made a lay-up off Izzy Borlase's drive to end a three-minute scoring drought for Australia and Ally Wilson's clutch free throws gave them a four-point advantage when Italy was forced to intentionally foul with eight seconds left.
The great escape appeared to be complete until a long-range bomb by Vittoria Blasigh off the inbounds pass left Italy trailing by just one point with five seconds remaining.
Borlase was then sent to the line but made only one of two free throws to give Italy a chance for one last play while down by two, and Francesca Pasa appeared to catch the defence napping by going for the tie rather than the win.
The speedy guard burst past Borlase and got her left-handed lay-up onto the backboard as the siren sounded, but the ball just rolled off the right of the rim and the Opals survived.
"We still have an opportunity to keep fighting and that's what we're going to do," coach Sandy Brondello said.
They moved into a quarterfinal against Spain, but will have to do it without some of their biggest stars.
Having already lost veteran Sami Whitcomb to a knee issue before the tournament and losing WNBA champion Alanna Smith to injury in their opening game against Puerto Rico, the Opals copped another huge blow against Italy.
Captain and star forward Ezi Magbegor played just four minutes of the clash before she went down during a drive to the basket.
Magbegor powered into a seam in the defence but was fouled from the side by Lorela Cubaj, causing her right knee to bend awkwardly inward.
The Seattle Storm star immediately shouted in pain and hit the deck, appearing to be in tears on the floor before being helped off the court by training staff.
"It made my heart sink to see her go down," Brondello said.
"She's so impactful for us and we just pray that she's OK. We don't know. We'll see what the result is tomorrow. She's walking and that's a good sign."
Meanwhile, an ill Jade Melbourne played only three minutes.
Borlase, a rookie guard with the WNBA's Atlanta Dream, picked up the slack and scored a game-high 30 points on 7/13 shooting from the field while knocking down 14 of 16 free throws.
The 21-year-old was named player of the match as she became just the fourth Opal to score 30 points at a World Cup.
"Something we speak about a lot is the Opals legacy," Borlase said.
"We really respect what the girls have done in previous tournaments. They've inspired us to want to play for Australia and I just hope I've inspired someone to tonight to want to play for Australia because there's no greater honour."
The tears were flowing for Italy after its second loss at the tournament by just one bucket, having missed a last-second three-pointer to lose 55-52 to reigning champions USA in the group stage.

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Vietnam and Russia are set to boost their ties in the spheres of defense, security, science and digital transformation, General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam, Vietnamese President To Lam said.

"We have agreed to continue creating favorable conditions for travel between the citizens of our countries, to increase the number of regular and charter flights, and to develop maritime transport routes, as well as road and rail transport corridors," To Lam said.

Canadian finance minister defends tariff countermeasures against US, rules out escalation
