Shifting Poles and Power 35 Years After the End of the Soviet Union
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:04:00 UTC
03:04:00 KST

Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty.
In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities.
The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s.
Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one.
This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. In Eastern Europe, while Belarus became a close ally of Russia, Ukraine hedged and then inched toward the West. In Russian discourse, Ukraine’s desire to join NATO was a threat to Moscow’s security. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world.
What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along? There is a plethora of alliances, blocs, and various other groups in the world today, many which border or reach into the post-Soviet space: From the Western-led NATO, to BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the Collective Security Treaty Organization, each built around the perceived national interests of states, their history and power politics in the region. More recently, one could argue, such groups have formed around religious identity, such as the Mecca Pact involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye. The world is transitioning toward an international system with several centers of power. Whether we call it a multipolar world or something else, the emergence of different poles seems clear.
In the post-Soviet space, over the past three decades, these poles have largely been centered around Russia, China, and the United States. Chinese expansion in the region has reached unprecedented levels in particular. China has replaced Russia as the main trading partner of most of the Central Asian states. While Russia has pursued an alternative Eurasian security order in the post-Soviet space, China’s economic power and the scale of its economic engagement have made it increasingly dominant through its geoeconomic programs, including the Belt and Road Initiative and other credit and assistance schemes.
Until Russia’s war in Ukraine, security and international relations scholars were broadly discussing and researching how interstate war had declined since the Second World War, with more casualties coming from civil wars and domestic unrest.
In my security and international relations classes, we mostly focused on internal conflicts, conflicts involving non-state actors, and terrorism. This thinking changed in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, followed by Israel’s war in Gaza in 2023 and, more recently, the U.S. war in Iran. None of these active wars appears to be ending soon. Multiple conflicts and ongoing Cold War-like rivalries indicate that there are several powers fighting for what they believe is their sphere of influence.
While countries in the Global South have been talking about multipolarity for some time, it was only after U.S. President Donald Trump’s shift towards a more isolationist foreign policy for the U.S., as well as his demands for NATO members to look after their own security, that the topic of multiple poles and spheres of influence has became more serious. This was reinforced by the Canadian prime minister’s reference to the importance of middle powers working together in the new world, presented in a speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The transition toward multiple spheres of influence is accompanied by a shift toward nationalist and isolationist policies.
More recently, Türkiye has emerged as a new pole for the Central Asian states. Four Central Asian states share a common Turkic identity. Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan ,and Türkiye are members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), which brings these countries together around their Turkic identity, while Turkmenistan is an observer. It is perhaps the first organization that unites these states based on their local Turkic languages and culture rather than the prior regional lingua franca, Russian.
It is hard to say if we are now in a fully multipolar world or whether it has always been so for the states in the post-Soviet space. Nationalist tendencies are on the rise in many societies today, for example the rise of Reform U.K. in the United Kingdom, the recent victory of Germany’s far-right AfD, and the growing influence of One Nation in Australia. In this changing global system, we see not only an ideological dimension, reflected in the Western and non-Western divide, but also an identity-driven dimension, as illustrated by the recent Mecca Pact and the OTS. For many states in Central Asia, it remains important to maximize their national interests while coexisting with multiple poles competing for influence in the region – something that has always been the case.

Thirty years of Italian creativity through the vision of architect and designer Marco Poletti. After Almaty and Bishkek, the exhibition—sponsored by the Italian Embassy in Astana, the ICE agency, and the Italian Cultural Institute in Almaty—arrives in the Kazakh capital. A traveling exhibition that explores Italian design as culture, research, and a vision of the future. Italian design takes center stage once again in Central Asia. “The Languages of Time in Design (1995–2026),” the exhibition curated by architect Marco Poletti in collaboration with Gaia Zanotti, opens on September 11 at the “Kulyash Baiseitova” National University of Arts of Kazakhstan, in the heart of Astana. The third stop on an evolving journey—following the successes in Almaty and Bishkek —the project is sponsored by the Italian Embassy in Kazakhstan, the ICE Agency, and the Italian Cultural Institute in Almaty to place Italian creativity at the center of cultural dialogue with Central Asia. The exhibition presents “Made in Italy” in its broadest sense: not merely as an object, but as a synthesis of creativity, research, entrepreneurship, innovation, and memory. Thirty years of design interpreted as a living expression of contemporary Italian culture. By supporting the exhibition’s international tour, the embassy thus strengthens its efforts to foster dialogue between Italy and Central Asia, building bridges between institutions, universities, businesses, designers, and new generations. A universal language that transcends borders and connects Italy’s creative heritage with the emerging sensibilities of the region. As Italian Ambassador Antonello De Riu emphasizes: “The exhibition should not be understood as a mere collection of works, but rather as a cultural device that reflects on the very act of exhibiting, going beyond its original form. It should be conceived as an organism that, at every stage—from Almaty to Bishkek, all the way to Astana—responds to its surroundings, engages with the local context, and is enriched with new meanings. It is concrete proof that Italian creativity does not rest on past successes but constantly challenges itself, year after year.” “The Languages of Time in Design” spans over thirty years of Marco Poletti’s design research, from 1995 to the present. A journey that illustrates design’s ability to interpret society, anticipate its needs, and transform innovation into new ways of living. Step by step, the exhibition has captured and conveyed the various “languages” that design has adopted in its dialogue with technology and contemporary sensibilities.

Earliest known drug use and its consequences discovered in Indonesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:02:35 UTC
03:02:35 KST

Who doesn't love to get stoned out of their gourd? Use of intoxicants isn't even confined to our species – Egyptian fruit bats are known to get drunk on fermenting fruit.
They seem aware of the potential consequences, which include the mucking up of their flying and navigational skills. This explains why some apparently avoid eating overripe fruit and why fruit bat alcoholics aren't a thing.
If only we had bat brains. Some researchers even suspect that agriculture arose around 10,000 years ago as a reliable way to make beer, as opposed to a reliable way to eat.
We already knew that prehistoric peoples used mind-altering substances, but now a report provides the earliest evidence of drug use yet. The skeletal remains of two hunter-gatherers in Sulawesi, Indonesia, indicate that they sucked on mind-altering betel nuts, one as long as 16,000 to 25,000 years ago.
The other one was doing that 6,300 to 7,600 years ago, Adam Brumm of Australia's Griffith University and Marlon Ririmasse of the Pusat Riset Arkeologi Lingkungan research institute in Jakarta reported with an international team in Science Advances on Wednesday.
Why is there such a wide margin of error on the dating for these addled hunter-gatherers? "The site has been challenging, as no charcoal for radiocarbon dating is preserved, so we had to use a combination of methods, including luminescence dating of sediments and uranium-series dating of bones, teeth and stalagmites," Brumm says.
The smoking spliff isn't cave art portraying this horrible habit but the parlous state of the two hunter-gatherers' teeth. Both exhibited hollowed-out rounded grooves in specific molars. The archaeologists believe that this erosion was caused by the compulsive sucking on hard spherical objects – not stones but betel nuts, a thesis supported by the presence of the betel intoxicant arecoline in the hunter-gatherers' dental plaque.
Also, the object clenched between the rear molars of these people was 10 to 20 millimeters (0.8 inches) in diameter, which fits betel nuts on Sulawesi, one of Indonesia's biggest islands.
In any case, the wear pattern on the teeth wasn't typical of routine consumption of anything. The researchers note that betel nuts, also known as areca seeds, have no nutritional value, so they weren't being held in the mouth for that.
Modern folk don't suck betel nuts, we chew them in the form of "betel quids." The quid is made by shelling the nuts and crushing or slicing their seeds, and mixing the mash or slices with calcium hydroxide (slaked lime).
Sometimes the mixture is flavored with spices such as cardamom. The plain or flavored mash is wrapped in a leaf to create a quid, which is inserted into the mouth and chewed. The drug reportedly causes mild stimulation, helping you stay awake, and even mild euphoria.
Regular indulgence leads to tolerance, leading the user to increase the dose, which can cultivate chemical dependence, aka addiction. Side effects of habitual quid chewing include staining your teeth and mouth red, eroding your teeth, and triggering oral or esophageal cancer. Even so, the scientists say that one in 10 people today, from Africa to Asia to Micronesia, chews betel quids.
Well, almost two in 10 people today still smoke cigarettes, knowing full well how bad that is. Withdrawal from betel dependency can involve mood swings and anxiety, not to mention the wicked combo of fatigue and insomnia.
The question is when humankind began to ride the betel beast, and now we learn that in Indonesia it started possibly as long as 25,000 years ago.
Inconveniently for the archaeologists, sucking the nut whole does not stain the teeth red like the modern custom of chewing betel mash in a quid with slaked lime, Brumm explains. The lime triggers a chemical reaction that turns the saliva bright red. But the hunter-gatherers didn't have crimson teeth, just damaged ones.
Did holding a nut in the mouth without accessing the inner seed make these people high? Yes. Remember, today the main neuroactive alkaloid in betel nut, arecoline, is released by chewing the nut processed with slaked lime, but stick that nut in the mouth for a decent while and it releases the desired arecoline, albeit less than one would get by crushing and processing the nut, the team reported based on experimentation.
So plausibly the betel habit began as simply sucking the nuts, and the common assumption that betel addiction began with the onset of agriculture was simply wrong.
In any case, this is the earliest known instance of deliberate inebriation, the team says, helpfully listing known intoxicants of prehistory, as detected by archaeologists. Hitherto the earliest was beer made using barley 11,000 to 13,000 years ago in Israel. Then we have the psychedelics San Pedro cactus and Mescalbean that were used 10,400 years ago in Peru and Texas, while paleo-Indians painted pictures of psychedelic datura 10,000 years ago, and our friend the coca leaf was used 8,000 years ago in Peru. Finally, Psilocybian mushrooms were used 8,000 years ago in the Sahara.
The researchers note that we have no idea when use of any of those began, let alone how the ancients discovered their delights. In short, the list and now the new discovery debunk the vague notion that intoxication began with farming.
The scientists note that early betel use in some form had been suspected in certain ancient teeth, such as 13,000 years ago in Thailand, but the dates were unsure. The earliest proven betel user was also in Thailand but just 3,500 years ago. Now the timeline is much further back.
So we don't know origins or prehistoric rationale, but we know what we like, and one in 10 likes betel quids. What's betel to the other 90 percent?
It is the drupe fruit (which means it has flesh and a pit like a peach) of areca palm trees in tropical regions of South Asia, Southeast Asia and the wider Pacific. We do not chew on its shell; we crush its seed. In time, once we chew the quid and turn our saliva bright red, our teeth will be stained as well.
Sadly, as Brumm and the team suggest, like many an addict today whose habit alleviates the pain of anticipating bad effects in the future, these ancient hunter-gatherers could have found themselves trapped in a loop of sucking on betel nuts to relieve toothache – as this habit worsened their oral health.
Today's betel buffs aren't in a good place either. "Betel quids are chewed in the buccal cheek cavity, with the blood-rich tissue in this part of the mouth allowing the plant compounds to enter the bloodstream more rapidly," the team writes. This practice elevates the risk of oral cancer. The compound's absorption is facilitated by the slaked lime.
When people stopped mouthing the mind-altering nut and began to convert it into chewable quids is a mystery. Maybe in the Neolithic, the scientists suggest.
The researchers note that people sometimes stick stuff in their mouth and just keep it there, not for eating or anything else really – a blade of grass, for instance. But holding a betel in the oral cavity and gnawing or chewing or just sucking on it had deleterious effects, hence the sense that the behavior was compulsive, which suggests that these people were getting high.
And the scientists add that skeletal remains of preagricultural foragers are extremely uncommon in southern Sulawesi. So probably the compulsion and physical dependence goes back far, far before our hunter-gatherers from 16,000 to 25,000 years ago.
Who knows, maybe the inspiration behind the earliest figurative art ever found, the portrait of a warty pig on the very same island of Sulawesi from over 54,000 years ago, wasn't only the swine's charms.

Betel nut traces in 25,000-year-old teeth point to early human drug use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:01:00 UTC
03:01:00 KST

Traces of betel nut in 25,000-year-old teeth earliest-known evidence of human drug use
In short:
Archaeologists have found evidence of a person who used a psychoactive drug up to 25,000 years ago.
Tooth fossils in Indonesia suggest that ancient foragers in the region were sucking on betel nut, possibly as a painkiller.
What's next?
Human drug use is probably older than this sample, but evidence is harder to come by.
Betel nut, one of the most commonly used drugs in the world, appears to have an ancient history.
Fossilised remains of two people, found by archaeologists on the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia, carry traces of the psychoactive substance in their jaws.
One of the fossils is dated between 16,000 and 25,000 years old, making it the oldest known example of human drug use by at least 3,000 years.
The discovery was published today in the journal Science Advances.
Adam Brumm, the study's lead author and an archaeologist at Griffith University, said the two people probably sucked on betel nuts like "gobstoppers".
Professor Brumm, who tried the method himself, said it numbed the mouth.
"I suspect that was the effect that they were after," he said.
Mysterious damaged teeth in Sulawesi caves
A team of Indonesian and Australian archaeologists uncovered the fossils at two separate sites in South Sulawesi.
Both individuals, the younger of which was 6,300 to 7,600 years old, predate the arrival of agriculture on Sulawesi.
Both hunter-gatherers had puzzling, deep marks on their teeth.
"Although they were separated by about 10,000 years of time, they had these really distinctive and very unusual tooth grooves," Professor Brumm said.
"We couldn't explain them."
An analysis of the marks suggested they had been created by repeatedly sucking on a round object, one or two centimetres in size.
"I thought, immediately, betel nut is the most likely possibility," Professor Brumm said.
Betel nut by another method
Betel or areca nut is the seed of a palm native to South-East Asia.
It is one of the most commonly used psychoactive substances in the world, alongside alcohol, caffeine and nicotine.
Today, people typically grind betel nut and mix it with substances such as slaked lime to enhance its psychoactive properties before chewing it.
"We hypothesised that before the development of the betel nut chewing custom, there may have been an earlier stage in the human use of betel nut where they just sucked on the nut itself," Professor Brumm said.
To test this, the team designed an experiment to simulate betel nut sucking.
They soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva, then tested the saliva on frog egg cells genetically engineered to grow human brain receptors.
The results suggested betel nut sucking would affect human brain cells.
"It will alter human brain function, but not to the extent of modern betel nut chewing with slaked lime," Professor Brumm said.
The team then investigated residues on the fossil teeth and found arecoline, the main psychoactive substance in betel nut.
Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University who was not involved in the research, agreed with the conclusion that betel nut sucking caused the tooth marks.
"The early evidence of drug consumption presented here predates any published evidence by thousands of years,"
Previously, the oldest known evidence of drug use was 13,000-year-old beer brewing in Israel.
A painful, addictive treatment
The researchers believe betel nut sucking would have produced a numbing effect on the mouth, and may have been used as a painkiller.
But betel nuts would have damaged teeth in the process, producing deep grooves that would have prompted painful toothaches.
Professor Brumm suggested the damaged teeth were evidence of a "vicious cycle".
"The more they sucked the nut for pain relief, the worse it damaged their teeth and the more they became addicted to sucking the nut to treat that."
Modern-day betel nut use also affects the mouth and teeth, and has been linked to an increased risk of oral cancer.
"You can see the pretty serious negative health consequences and how humans have grappled with those for at least 25,000 years on this island," Professor Brumm said.
Dr Samper Carro said the research could help identify even older uses of betel nut or other drugs.
"I'm convinced that even earlier hominids, such as Neanderthals, would have used natural remedies [like plants, natural compounds and maybe even insects or fungi] to fight pain and infection," she said.
Professor Brumm agreed the practice probably stretched further back into history than their 25,000-year-old sample.
"There's no human society today that doesn't use drugs of some kind,"
"But we just know so little about the deep antiquity of these practices."

A six-decade study links teenage school anxiety to late-life memory complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:49 UTC
03:00:49 KST

Feeling anxious or struggling to keep pace in school during early adolescence is linked to how people view their own memory abilities more than fifty years later. The findings suggest that early-life psychological health can have a lasting association with how individuals perceive their cognitive decline in older age. The research was published in Journal of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences.
Subjective memory refers to a person’s own perception of their everyday memory functioning. This includes noticing how often they forget where they placed an item, lose track of a conversation, or fail to recall something they were just told. As people age, it is incredibly common to experience and report these types of memory difficulties. Some older adults report no changes, whereas others feel their memory is steadily declining.
Scientists are interested in these self-reported memory complaints because they can sometimes serve as an early warning sign for dementia. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that greater declines in self-reported memory over time were associated with higher levels of Alzheimer’s-related proteins in the brain. At the same time, a 2014 meta-analysis found that people’s self-rated memory issues only weakly match their actual memory test scores. Because subjective memory and objective memory often differ, researchers have begun exploring how emotional and psychological traits influence self-reported cognitive decline.
Historically, much of the research on cognitive aging has focused on risk factors present in middle or late adulthood. However, scientists are increasingly looking to the very beginning of life to understand how early experiences shape the aging process. For example, a 2004 study demonstrated that cognitive abilities measured in childhood continue to predict mental performance and health many decades later in old age. Conditions such as a family’s socioeconomic status can dictate a child’s early opportunities, setting them on a path that affects their long-term brain health.
The research, led by Gideon Neidenmark, a doctoral student at Örebro University in Sweden, aimed to understand how an array of childhood factors might forecast memory complaints in old age. The authors noted that existing research rarely tracks individuals from early childhood all the way into their late sixties. By bridging this gap, they hoped to see whether childhood intelligence, social well-being, or school anxiety could predict how people evaluate their own memories nearly six decades later.
“I am fortunate enough to be involved in a longitudinal study called the IDA-project with data spanning six decades,” Neidenmark told PsyPost. “This has enabled questions regarding how our childhood and adolescence are related to our abilities when we get older.”
“I became especially interested in subjective memory because previous research has demonstrated that our own experience of our memory abilities usually does not overlap substantially with our actual memory performance and wanted to understand why that is,” he added.
To investigate this, the researchers used data from the IDA-project, a massive Swedish longitudinal study that began in 1965. They tracked a cohort of participants who were around 10 years old at the start of the study, assessing them again in 1968 at age 13. During these childhood visits, participants completed standardized tests measuring their verbal, spatial, and reasoning abilities. The researchers also gathered official school grades, collected information on the families’ socioeconomic status, and asked the children to fill out questionnaires about their social well-being and any anxiety they experienced in the school context.
In 2022, the researchers sent follow-up questionnaires to the surviving participants, who were now about 67 years old. A total of 625 people completed this phase of the study. The participants filled out a standardized survey detailing their current subjective memory, answering questions about how often they forget things in their daily lives. They also completed a widely used assessment to measure their current levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms.
When analyzing the data, the researchers found that participants who reported higher levels of school anxiety at age 13 tended to report worse subjective memory at age 67. This association was specific to psychological health during early adolescence. Interestingly, the researchers did not find evidence that school anxiety at age 10 predicted memory complaints later in life.
This link between early adolescent anxiety and late-life memory complaints remained steady even after the researchers accounted for the participants’ current anxiety and depressive symptoms.
“I think the most important take-home message is that our childhood and adolescence are related to our abilities in later life, particularly that our psychological health in our youth is related to how we perceive and rate our own memory abilities,” Neidenmark said. “This also persists even when we account for current psychological health.”
In contrast, several other childhood factors did not predict subjective memory in older age. The researchers found no evidence that cognitive ability, school grades, social well-being, or family socioeconomic status at ages 10 or 13 had any bearing on how participants viewed their memory at age 67.
“I think what surprised me the most was that social well-being, socioeconomic status, cognitive ability and school performance during childhood and adolescence were not related to subjective memory in later life,” Neidenmark explained. “It really emphasized what previous literature has found, i.e., that subjective memory may better reflect psychological factors than actual memory performance.”
The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that depression during adolescence was associated with lower cognitive performance over the next six years. The new study extends this timeline considerably, tracking participants over nearly six decades. It is worth noting, however, that the new study focused exclusively on self-reported memory complaints in older age rather than objective cognitive test performance.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The childhood questionnaires used to measure school anxiety and social well-being relied on only a few items, which resulted in relatively low statistical reliability for those specific measures. This lack of precision might explain why factors like early social well-being did not show a relationship with late-life memory complaints. Better measurement tools might yield different results in future studies.
“Like with any articles, we should be cautious about considering these findings as fact or infer causality,” Neidenmark pointed out. “As mentioned, we should be cautious about considering lower psychological health as causing lower subjective memory. Rather, they are related to each other even over such a large time span.”
Additionally, the recent follow-up phase of the study did not include objective memory tests or medical screenings for dementia. Because of this, the researchers could not determine if the participants’ memory complaints reflected actual cognitive decline or merely a pessimistic view of their abilities. The study also experienced attrition over its 57-year span, and the individuals who remained in the project at age 67 generally had better childhood grades and better psychological health than those who dropped out.
Future research could explore whether there is a direct chain of events linking early-life psychological health to late-life memory. Scientists might also look at mid-life factors that could bridge the gap between teenage anxiety and aging. Understanding these pathways could help health professionals design interventions that support both emotional well-being and lifelong cognitive health.
“However, this study and findings could indicate the importance of considering early-life for prevention,” Neidenmark noted. “This study in particular may point to psychological health (in particular school anxiety) as an important factor to consider in this work.”
“My next step is to investigate how these factors in childhood and adolescence are related to actual memory performance and brain structure in later life,” he said. “I hope to understand how this differs to my results from this study, and how they are related.”
The study, “Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades,” was authored by Gideon Neidenmark, Catherine Tuvblad, and Jonas Persson.

Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:02 UTC
03:00:02 KST

What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.
Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.
Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.
“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.
The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.
Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.
Betel nuts are actually the seeds of the Areca catechu palm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.
Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.
The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.
To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.
“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.
“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”
While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.
Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.
“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.

Beit Yisrael could give Ethiopian Israelis a new path to political influence - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

For decades, Ethiopian Israelis have been told to integrate patiently, vote loyally, serve courageously, and accept whatever political position established parties decide to offer them. But democracy is not an immigration office where citizens wait quietly for someone to call their number, and on Tuesday, Gadi Yevarkan offered a different answer: If the existing table has too little room for Ethiopian-Israeli leadership, build a new table and invite all of Israel to sit around it.
Yevarkan, a former member of the Knesset and former deputy minister of public security, launched his new Beit Yisrael party before a large audience in Petah Tikva. His official Knesset record confirms that he has already served inside Israel’s national institutions. Now he is attempting something more difficult: constructing an independent political movement.
I do not know whether Beit Yisrael will cross Israel’s electoral threshold. I do not know how many seats it might receive or whether it will become a significant force in the next Knesset. But something larger than Yevarkan’s personal future occurred in Petah Tikva. An Ethiopian-born Israeli leader stopped asking established parties where they might place him and began asking Israelis whether they would follow him.
That is a democratic breakthrough.
For years, Ethiopian Israelis have entered existing parties only to discover that inclusion and power are different things. Parties celebrate Sigd, praise the courage of Ethiopian soldiers, and display photographs from Operations Moses and Solomon. Yet Ethiopian-Israeli candidates are frequently placed where they have little chance of entering the Knesset or advancing into senior national leadership.
The usual expectation is clear: Join someone else’s movement, deliver your community’s votes, and be grateful for the position you receive.
Beit Yisrael challenges that expectation. Its message is not simply, “Give Ethiopian Israelis representation.” It is: “Ethiopian Israelis can organize a national political force, compete for votes, negotiate in coalition politics, and help determine how public resources are distributed.” That is not separatism. It is democracy.
Political independence for Ethiopian Israelis
Israel’s political system already contains parties built around religious communities, ideological movements, immigrant populations, and distinct social interests. Ethiopian Israelis have the same democratic right to organize. Political independence should not be considered dangerous only when black citizens attempt it.
The more important question is whether Beit Yisrael can become more than an Ethiopian-Israeli protest party. Yevarkan says that it is open to everyone. That ambition must become visible in its leadership, candidates, and policies.
The Ethiopian-Israeli community alone may not provide enough votes to carry a new party into the Knesset. Beit Yisrael must therefore build a wider coalition among Israelis who feel economically ignored, geographically marginalized, or politically taken for granted.
It should speak seriously about national security, equal military or civilian service, the cost of living, education, public safety, social mobility, and the neglect of Israel’s geographic periphery. It should address discrimination without reducing Ethiopian Israelis to permanent victims.
Its message should be one of responsibility: We served this country; we helped build it, and we are prepared to help govern it. The party will also need leaders whose records demonstrate competence beyond electoral politics. One outstanding example is Dr. Nigist Mengesha.
Born near Gondar, Mengesha worked as a social worker in Ethiopia before making aliyah in 1984. She earned a bachelor’s degree in social work from Bar-Ilan University, a master’s degree from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and a doctorate from the University of Sussex. Her research examined educational mediation for Ethiopian students in Israeli schools.
She co-founded the FIDEL Association, which created educational and social programs for Ethiopian Israelis, and served as director-general of the Ethiopian National Project. She worked with the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry, graduated from the Mandel School for Educational Leadership, and led a municipal education department. She also represented Israel at the 2001 UN conference against racism in Durban, and has received significant recognition for her educational leadership.
Beit Yisrael, or another serious national party, should offer her a realistic position on its electoral slate. She should not be recruited merely because she is an Ethiopian-Israeli woman, but rather because decades of educational, municipal, and community leadership have prepared her for national service. Mengesha’s record could also make her a compelling future candidate for the presidency of Israel. That possibility should not sound revolutionary. It should sound overdue.
Imagine what her leadership would communicate to Israelis and the world: A black African Jewish woman, brought to Israel through aliyah, educated in Israeli and international universities, and entrusted with representing the Jewish state.
Such an image would be powerful, but it would not be manufactured public relations. It would express a historical truth. Israel is not a white European colonial project. The Jewish people are a diverse and ancient people whose communities preserved their connections to Jerusalem across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. Israel must stop pretending that qualified Ethiopian-Israeli leaders do not exist. They do. What has been missing is a political structure that is willing to trust us with power.
Beit Yisrael must now prove that it is such a structure. It should publish a serious platform, establish transparent internal rules, recruit women and young leaders, welcome Israelis from beyond the Ethiopian community, and explain precisely how it would use parliamentary power.
It must also avoid the temptation to become merely a bargaining instrument that disappears after securing appointments for a few individuals. Its success should be measured by whether it advances better schools, safer neighborhoods, economic opportunity, fair policing, completed family reunification, and genuine access to national leadership.
One can agree with Yevarkan or disagree with him. One can support Beit Yisrael or vote for another party. But the importance of this moment should be recognized. Ethiopian Israelis are no longer willing merely to be integrated into someone else’s political vision. They are claiming the democratic right to present a vision of their own, not only for Ethiopian Israelis, but for the entire country.
For years, we asked for a place at the table. Gadi Yevarkan has begun building another one. Now the Israeli public will decide who is prepared to sit with us.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

Curacao head coach Dick Advocaat signed a contract extension that will keep him in charge until July 2027, the country's football federation announced on Wednesday.
The Federashon Futbol Korsou (FFK) said the 78-year-old Dutch coach agreed to extend his deal through July 31 next year, citing continuity and stability around the national team.
Advocaat guided Curacao to their first-ever FIFA World Cup in 2026, making the Caribbean island the smallest country by both population and land area ever to qualify for the tournament.
Curacao finished bottom of Group E in their debut appearance, earning one point from a goalless draw against Ecuador.
Advocaat also became the oldest head coach in World Cup history at age 78.
"This is a fantastic group to work with. We have achieved something special together, and I look forward to continuing to build on what we have accomplished with the players and staff," Advocaat said.
The veteran coach resigned in February to focus on his daughter's health before returning to the role in May following the departure of Fred Rutten.
Advocaat, who has managed several national teams and clubs during a coaching career spanning nearly four decades, took charge of Curacao in 2024.
His major club honors include league titles with PSV Eindhoven, Rangers and Zenit St. Petersburg, as well as the 2008 UEFA Cup with the Russian club.
At the international level, he led the Netherlands to the 1994 World Cup quarterfinals and Euro 2004 semifinals, and also coached South Korea and Russia at major tournaments.
FFK Acting President Fabi Constansia said the extension reflected the federation's desire for "continuity and stability" while it continued investing in the development of football in Curacao.

Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:45 UTC
02:57:45 KST

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first folding smartphone. The company announced the device at its annual September event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California.
The iPhone Duo comes in Star White and Night Sky, and costs $1,999 for 256 GB of storage. While preorders kick off on October 16, the device won’t officially go on sale until October 23.
It arrives alongside the pro versions of Apple’s handsets, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, and when you open the Duo up, it reveals a second, 7.6-inch display—remarkably close to the iPad Mini’s screen size. Apple says it kept the aspect ratio consistent across both the front and inner screen for the highest quality when viewing content.
The Duo has a titanium frame with a mirror finish, Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass on the back, and Ceramic Shield 2 glass on the front. It even sports an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, beating Samsung to the punch. (Right now, Google's folding Pixels are the only phones with an IP68 rating.
Apple says the hinge has a “custom variable torque profile” that precisely opens and closes the phone in an “effortlessly smooth” way. When it’s open, Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. As Samsung does with its “Flex Titanium” technology, Apple uses a carbon fiber metal plate below the display to better control the stress caused by bending the display. That, alongside a nano-texture finish, helps keep the display flat and “minimizes crease visibility.” An Apple-designed scratch-resistance coating sits on top.
The Duo weighs 254 grams, is 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded. Compare that to Samsung’s new Fold8, which is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded. If you’ve held an iPhone 17 Pro Max, that’s 233 grams, so the Duo is quite hefty. Bulky devices typically turn customers off—that's why Samsung spent so much time trying to shave off as much weight as possible on its latest folding devices.
Surprisingly, there is no Face ID sensor, likely to save space inside the phone for the folding components. Instead, like some of Apple’s tablets, the iPhone Duo brings back the fingerprint-sensing Touch ID integrated into the side power button. This is also the first iPhone to support the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year, though there’s no way to naturally store the stylus on the edges of the device like the iPad’s magnetic Pencil dock.
Apple says the Duo has the biggest battery ever in an iPhone. Like most book-style folds, it’s a split system where a battery rests on both sides. That will net you up to 31 hours of video playback with the inner display and 44 hours with the outer display—or 24 hours of mixed overall use per charge. It also sports Apple’s new custom C2 modem (with mmWave 5G support in the US) and the A20 Pro, the same chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.
There are only two cameras on the back—a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide. The lack of a telephoto zoom option is a sacrifice even Samsung made on its latest Galaxy Z Fold8. Like most book-like folds, it has two selfie cameras—a 12-megapixel camera on the outer screen and a second “FaceTime camera" on the inner display, though this one is hidden under the display.
There are familiar folding phone features here with the camera, like distracting a kid with a fun cartoon character on the outer screen to get them to look at the camera. Or your subject can preview the photo before you hit capture. The iPhone Duo can stand upright by itself, so you can set it down and it will automatically capture group photos if everyone stands at the ready.
Hardware is just one part of the story, though. The software needs to adapt and take advantage of the larger screen. Apple has been improving how apps adapt to different screen sizes for some time, making it easy for developers to scale apps from the iPhone to the iPad to the Mac, and even visionOS on the Apple Vision Pro. That means you’ll be able to enjoy iPad-like apps when unfolding the iPhone Duo.
Apple says it has moved essential controls to the side, stacked vertically, to maximize screen space. Even the dock is oriented vertically. The software transitions gracefully as you open the phone; apps will show more information—like your inbox and messages—and you can split-screen apps. You can fold it in half and set it down, and the screen will react accordingly.
Folding Time
Apple is a late entrant to the foldable phone market, which has been around since Samsung debuted the first Galaxy Fold in 2019. Since then, phone makers like Honor, Google, Motorola, and Oppo have all made folding phones. In recent years, devices have rapidly gotten slimmer, lighter, and more durable.
The iPhone Duo has a book-like shape and is similar in size to Samsung’s recent Galaxy Z Fold8, reminiscent of Google’s original Pixel Fold. This “passport-style” fold—which stands shorter and unfolds wider than many of the first wave of foldable designs—is better suited for media consumption since it eliminates the severe letterboxing that places thick black bars around the TV show or movie you’re watching.
Apple is expected to help grow a category that has been declining for five straight quarters by 13 percent year over year—potentially capturing up to 30 percent of the foldable market share by the end of 2026, according to IDC’s Nabila Popal, a senior research director. But the folding phone market is still niche, “around 2 percent by the end of this year of the global smartphone market.”
Popal says a recent IDC survey asked consumers whether they were interested in buying a foldable smartphone when it was time to upgrade, and 60 percent said they are not likely to buy one. However, when asked if Apple released a folding smartphone, almost 33 percent said they “absolutely” would.
“Apple has such a strong market pull,” Popal tells WIRED. “The average consumer didn’t know about [memory price increases] until Apple made an announcement that they’re going to increase prices. “Coming into foldables, it's going to create overall excitement for the category. And it's good for the consumer, too. It's always good to have more competition and more choice.”
One area of concern is the device’s durability and repairability, as folding phones are notoriously more prone to damage and are tough to fix. Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of Sustainability at iFixit, tells WIRED her team has never taken apart a foldable they’d call truly repairable.
“Manufacturers have come a long way since the Galaxy Fold first dropped,” she says. “But the gains in durability haven’t come with gains in repairability.”
New Economics
While Apple announced three premium iPhone models today, it is not releasing the base iPhone 18 this year—marking the first time it’s breaking up the launch cycle of the core iPhone lineup. Instead, the iPhone 18 is expected to launch in the spring of 2027 alongside the iPhone 18e and second-generation iPhone Air.
Despite the eye-watering price and the current economic climate, Popal says the iPhone Duo is “guaranteed to be a blockbuster.”
“Apple defied all odds and broke the $1,000 barrier when they first launched the $1,000 smartphone,” Popal says. “Yes, there’s going to be sticker shock, but Apple caters to a very high-end consumer segment who can afford it.”
Over the summer, Apple introduced a new iPhone leasing program to help ease the price of its phones on consumers' wallets, and it’s likely to prove popular with the uber-expensive iPhone Duo. Chamberlain says that for people who replace their phone regularly, it gives them a path to do it where the device gets back into the reuse stream and boosts the refurbished market, which isn’t a bad thing for electronic waste. However, Apple’s leasing agreements mean the device needs to be returned in the condition it was received.
“iFixit is committed to the idea that you should own your shit,” she says. “You should be able to repair things, modify things, hack your own devices. It’s sad to see the tech world move away from that principle, and Apple encouraging people to lease devices instead of buying them.”
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Back to work, not school: Yemen’s crisis forces children to drop out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:37 UTC
02:57:37 KST

Back to work, not school: Yemen’s crisis forces children to drop out
Struggling families in Yemen are forced to choose between education and survival amid mounting economic challenges.
Taiz, Yemen – It was around the middle of the morning, and children at a nearby school were preparing for their break. But 11-year-old Hasnaa Jaber was walking through empty farmland on the outskirts of Taiz city, collecting discarded plastic bottles.
Hasnaa lives with her impoverished family in an informal settlement for people displaced by the country’s more than decade-long war. Instead of going to school, she works alongside her family to help make ends meet.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
- list 2 of 3Qatar says reopening Strait of Hormuz ‘unconditionally’ is a priority
- list 3 of 3Yemen’s war is back: A new battle for Sanaa and the Red Sea
“My dream is to become a teacher. I studied up to the third grade, but then I dropped out of school along with my two older brothers to help my father,” Hasnaa told Al Jazeera.
The new academic year began in government-controlled areas of Yemen on August 30, but Hasnaa and other children from families in difficult financial situations like hers are not in the classroom.
She is one of 3.2 million children who are out of school in Yemen this year, according to an estimate by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). That is an increase on the 1.8 million children UNICEF says were out of school in 2015, during the first year of the war.
Of Hasnaa’s four siblings, only one currently attends school, as she is too young to collect plastic bottles or wash cars – the kind of work the family does.
“My two brothers and I asked my father if we could resume our studies this year,” she said. “He was happy that we wanted to go back to school, but providing basic food for the family remains a major struggle. He promised us that we will go back next year.”
Hasnaa has friends who still attend school, but she feels closest to those who are also out of school, bound by their shared hardship.
“I don’t enjoy spending time with the children who go to school because they look down on us,” she explained. “But next year, I will return to my studies and fulfil my dream of becoming a teacher.”
Food is priority
Hasnaa is able to earn around 1,500 Yemeni rials (around $1) a day selling the plastic bottles she gathers to scrap traders.
That money is welcomed by her father, 35-year-old Jaber Ali, who is struggling to provide for his family. Fighting forced him to flee his hometown, near Taiz, eight years ago.
He doesn’t like the situation his family is in – he never received an education himself, but had hoped his children would.
“I used to work and keep my children in school, but the situation has worsened over the past two years. What I earn from washing cars is no longer enough to provide them with basic food, let alone cover other necessities,” Jaber told Al Jazeera.
Rising living costs and scarce work have squeezed the family. Jaber said school means paying for books, stationery, and other daily expenses he can’t afford.
“I was left with two choices: either send my children to school and watch them starve, or ask them to help me earn a living,” Jaber said. “I had to choose the latter because food is the top priority right now, not education.”
“We must encourage our children to study, and I do my best to keep their spirits up,” he added. “I don’t tell them they will never return to school – I tell them this is just a temporary phase, and I hope conditions will improve so they can resume their education soon.”
Byproduct of war
According to the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP), published by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), nearly 6.6 million Yemeni children are in need of education assistance in 2026. That figure includes children who are out of school, as well as those still enrolled but facing serious barriers to learning, including conflict, poverty, and the collapse of basic services.
Ammar al-Sharjabi, an education expert who has worked with the Ministries of Education in both Sanaa and Aden, explained that the crisis is one of the most severe consequences of the war – particularly when it comes to forcing children to drop out of school.
“Dropping out of school deprives children of their right to education and weakens their chances of securing stable employment in the future, potentially forcing them into hard labour at an early age,” he explained. “At the societal level, persistent dropout rates lead to increased illiteracy, poverty, and unemployment, adversely impacting development and the community’s overall future.”
A source at the Ministry of Education in Aden, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, said economic pressures driving children into work are difficult to fix in light of Yemen’s war – which has escalated dramatically in recent weeks after years of relative calm.
“The ministry is deeply concerned about students dropping out, but this is the direct result of dire economic conditions – not an educational issue that can be solved within the classroom alone,” the source said.
He added that the ministry coordinates with humanitarian organisations to support vulnerable children, but intervention is difficult when parents feel that they have to make their children work.
“This surge in dropouts is a byproduct of the ongoing war and its economic fallout,” he added. “As soon as parents secure a stable source of income, we will see children return to school immediately. No parent wants to see their child deprived of an education.”
Child breadwinners
A recent Save the Children assessment covering around 2,000 households in southern and southwestern Yemen found that 92 percent of those surveyed do not know where their next meal will come from, and 95 percent rely on precarious daily informal labour for their income.
As a result, 84 percent of families could not afford basic educational expenses, such as uniforms and textbooks.
The assessment also found that nearly one in five school dropout cases identified was linked to child labour.
Thirteen-year-old Ahmed Abdulelah is not displaced, but is one of those dropouts.
He left school after his father died of cancer two years ago. The family exhausted its savings on treatment, and Ahmed, the eldest of four siblings, began working at a grocery store.
“My father provided us with everything we needed,” Ahmed said. “But since he passed away, there has been no one else to help us, and I cannot bear to see my mother suffer.”
Unlike many of his peers, Ahmed does not dwell on the grief of dropping out of school. For him, the sacrifice is worth it as long as his younger siblings can stay in class.
And he has no plans to resume his education, believing his window of opportunity has passed. Instead, he has set his sights on becoming a shopkeeper one day.
“I work here so my siblings can finish their education,” he said. “They will make up for what I lost, and I am proud that our family doesn’t have to beg or rely on anyone else.”

In an explanatory note submitted Wednesday in response to the latest report by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, Iran’s mission to the agency pushed back against expectations for routine implementation of safeguards, arguing that such demands are unreasonable given the continued threats and hostilities targeting the country.
The note pointed out that the IAEA itself has previously suspended verification activities and withdrawn inspectors from Iran due to prevailing conditions, and criticized the Director General’s report for omitting references to the aggression against its nuclear facilities.
Iran further contended that current obstacles to safeguards implementation stem from unlawful actions by the United States and Israel, and that Tehran bears no responsibility for these impediments. The mission also rejected the legal basis for any claims concerning the revival of terminated UN Security Council resolutions.
The Iranian mission called on the Director General and the IAEA Board of Governors to set aside political approaches, return to their legal mandates, and explicitly condemn attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities operating under safeguards.
While reaffirming its commitment to its safeguards obligations, Iran expressed readiness to facilitate verification activities once all threats and hostilities have ceased fully and permanently.
Addressing the meeting, Iranian envoy Reza Najafi to the IAEA strongly denounced the UNSC and IAEA for 'closing their eyes on' US-Israeli terrorist aggression
Najafi said that the West sheds crocodile tears over proliferation while failing to simply denounce US-Zionist aggression.
Accoridng to the Iranian envoy, the IAEA not only fails to condemn aggression on Iran, but also to make explicit reference to aggression in its resolution.

Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:14 UTC
02:57:14 KST

Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.
The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.
But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.
Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.
“What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.
Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.”
While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”
Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.
She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”
Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”
Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”
He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”
There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.
Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.
The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.
Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.
“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”
Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”
They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”
Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.
Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.

Delhi poll body said Raghav Chadha’s voter registration in Rajinder Nagar was approved after the mandatory seven-day notice period, while AAP alleged irregularities
NEW DELHI: The Delhi poll body on Wednesday said BJP Rajya Sabha MP Raghav Chadha’s application to be added to the Delhi voter list was approved after due procedure, days after the AAP questioned his inclusion."As per record available, Raghav Chadha, MP (Rajya Sabha) applied for inclusion of his name in Form 6 in AC-39 (Rajinder Nagar) on August 26," news agency PTI quoted Delhi chief electoral officer as saying."The Form was approved by the Electoral Registration Officer of the AC-39 (Rajinder Nagar) after completion of mandatory notice period of 07 days," it added.
The application, numbered U05039D6N2608261200000, was processed under the Election Commission’s prescribed procedure.The AAP, however, rejected the explanation and alleged that Chadha’s name was added to the electoral roll "through the back door". The party also questioned whether political pressure was involved.AAP national media-in-charge Anurag Dhanda demanded that Chadha’s Form 6 be made public and said citizens should be allowed to raise objections against it as they can for any ordinary voter.
Dhanda claimed that Chadha’s name did not appear in any Form 6 received in Rajinder Nagar between September 1 and 7.
He also questioned how Chadha’s name became the 747th entry when the draft roll had 746 voters and the final roll was yet to be published.The CEO office said eligible persons whose names are not on the electoral roll can seek inclusion by submitting Form 6 with the required documents.It also referred to the Election Commission’s May 14 guidelines on the Special Intensive Revision, which state that additions made during the SIR period would receive serial numbers continuing from the last entry in the draft electoral roll.

Ceuta: EU grants Spain €115 million in emergency aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:53:00 UTC
02:53:00 KST

Ceuta: Documents show Spanish intelligence warned of crisis
September 9, 2026
Spain's national intelligence agency issued a warning about possible "mass entries" by migrants into Ceuta a day before more than 70,000 migrants stormed the border fences of the enclave in North Africa, according to documents declassified on Wednesday.
The Spanish government declassified a trove of more than 40 documents, including internal alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies.
One urgent memo sent by the National Intelligence Center to authorities in Ceuta on the day before the incident warned of "several calls to carry out entries into Ceuta."
"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified memo read, “just to give you an idea of its scale."
CENIF, a border division of the National Police, also published a warning about the social media groups a day before the incident.
"Internal communications have been detected in migrant groups in which they are trying to organize mass entries on the night of 29/07/2026," a document from CENIF read.
Sanchez downplays level of warning
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the documents prove his government had not been warned of the magnitude of the crisis that was about to unfold.
He said the National Intelligence Center only alerted authorities in Ceuta and not the military or Ministry of Defense.
"This is understandable because, with the information available at the time, no one could have foreseen the migration crisis that unfolded on the 30th and 31st," Sanchez said on social media. "No competent body did so. Neither in Spain nor in the EU."
EU to fund Ceuta border enhancements
The European Union (EU) on Wednesday announced that it would grant Spain some €115 million ($130 million) in emergency financial aid to help bolster the bloc's external borders and return thousands of individuals who overwhelmed authorities in the country's North African exclave Ceuta in late July.
Spain initially requested the funding on August 24.
Brussels said the funds would help finance "measures to enhance border surveillance, border protection and security-related infrastructure" such as thermal cameras, floating buoy systems and underwater drones: "It will also serve to set up facilities for the screening of migrants, as well as to support returns of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."
"The situation in Ceuta has put pressure on our external borders," said European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen. "Our message remains clear: We are committed to combating illegal migration and ensuring the swift return of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."
What happened in Ceuta?
On July 30 and 31, images of migrants storming the borders of the exclave sent shockwaves across the EU and beyond as more than 72,000 individuals crossed into Spanish territory from Morocco.
Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.
Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have been returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.
The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.
Although Sanchez has said that there is "no solid proof" that Morocco was to blame for the incident, Madrid's top criminal court on Monday opened an investigation into whether African authorities had facilitated the illegal rush.
Edited by: Sean Sinico
