Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:05:12 BST
00:05:12 KST

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen UK deterrence and drive economic growth.
Lady Mayor, thank you very much for hosting this event today and good afternoon, everyone. It’s a real pleasure to be with you today.
Under this one roof we have many leaders and decision makers needed to spark that next generation of defence innovation that we need to keep our country safe and support our allies. So, thank you for giving up your valuable time to be here.
I’m honoured that I get to speak as warm up act to my friend, the Ukrainian Ambassador. I’ve spent a lot of time in Kyiv over the past two years in particular, and the courage of the Ukrainian people is something that we must honour not just in words but in the actual support that we provide for their frontline, for their nation, for the innovators and we do that by not just sending equipment to Ukraine but by partnering, innovating and developing new technologies together.
I know that there are people in this room whose work is not theoretical in that regard and you are making a big difference to our friends in Ukraine so thank you for what you do.
Now, we meet at a point where global geopolitics is more fragile, more disruptive and more changeable. And that means we need an entirely new system of warfighting and deterrence, which means more innovation and new approaches with new weapon systems that revolutionised the battlefield.
Certainly, the way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago. We’re learning the lessons from Ukraine by supporting them, but that means changing the way that the United Kingdom operates.
Now, our most urgent mission right now is to transform Britain’s defence posture and turbocharge innovation. Many of the most critical advances in defence right now are coming from tech startups and tech scale-ups. Agile businesses which are seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed. And so today our challenge is this: how can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible.
Now it was just over two years ago that this government took office and we inherited a defence programme which to be honest and to be frank was unfit to counter the dangers that we now face. We are moving towards warfighting readiness and in doing so we must discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to in Britain, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us. If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces. That is an opportunity for new technology, new thinking, new weapons to be brought to the fore. And in designing new technology, we need to design for the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow.
Now, our supply chains are critical to that. An industry that works in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was. We are changing that. I think it was especially true for those small businesses and scale-ups with amazing products who struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD.
Now since that time, we’ve produced a new blueprint for a completely different type of military and a different type of procurement. We published our Strategic Defence Review, Defence Industrial Strategy and Defence Investment Plan to build a more resilient and warfighting-ready military, backed by a world-class supply chain and we’re bringing industry into the heart of defence the fundamental enabler of everything that we are trying to achieve. To not only make our country more secure, but also more successful and prosperous, by creating high-quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities in every postcode.
I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews, they used to be encouraging me to do it. With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly. Defence spending is an engine for growth. It is a way of re-industrialising. It is a way of creating opportunity. It also keeps us safe.
Now to make our country more secure and more successful we need to create more high quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities. Now if we are to do that SMEs in particular, scale-ups, are really important. Within the MOD, we’ve reformed our system with a new National Armaments Director, Rupert Pearce, coming from a FTSE 100 company, bringing a new corporate approach and energy to the way that we procure.
We’ve established the Defence Office of Small Business growth to help remove those obstacles to entry, cut red tape, and roll out a 50% increase in spend from the MOD with medium and small-sized firms by Summer 2028. That’s moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure, making it easier for small businesses to enter our supply chain.
We’ve published our SME Action Plan to set out what we will do so we can be held accountable for that change, and that supports start-ups, scale-ups, and other companies to be able to grow. And helping small firms navigate the routes to funding is something crucial if you want to get the best out of them. At a national level our Defence Office for Small Business Growth provides the guidance for those routes, removes duplication when we find it and clarifies the entry points where necessary.
At local levels I’m really pleased that the rollout of regional defence and security clusters have been so successful with more regions developing them, creating new regional routes to tailor support for businesses and bring together localised networks of major suppliers, devolved and local governments and importantly provide a forum for investors to meet them and support them as well.
Now, Ukraine has shown us the way to innovate at lightning speed because of the necessity of the war that they are fighting. And as we learn from Ukraine’s lead, defence must harness the resources that Britain possesses not just across tech and engineering sectors, but across finance, consulting and academia as well - to help create, inspire and deliver the change that we need. And finance is obviously key to our topic today.
Now, the government is already increasing defence spending. As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending. But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence. Now, public investment will remain central to that mission as we increase our defence capabilities. But in a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.
So that’s why the Defence Investment Plan sets out the priority areas that we will invest in both now, and later to provide the certainty for investors to understand what type of technologies, what areas of defence will the government invest in, where we also seek investment from the private sector.
And we need to work hard to make sure that Defence and our colleagues in the investment community speak the same language. Because I think, at the moment, there’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other. And speaking the same language with the same necessary data will increase our ability to deliver.
Now, Britain has long prospered when government, industry and finance have worked together and our task today is not to reinvent the finance sectors, but a way of bringing us together to create that new partnership for today’s era.
Now, the prize is significant, not just stronger national defence and security, but a more innovative defence sector and a growing market that helps re-industrialise, but also an opportunity to export to our friends as well. Because it’s not just the United Kingdom that’s investing in defence. Our allies in NATO and further afield are doing the same.
Now, in the Defence Investment Plan, we announced a Defence Investment Unit because investors need a clearer interface with defence and defence needs financial expertise to turn priorities into market-facing propositions, speaking the same language.
Following the autumn budget this year, we will publish the Defence Finance Investment Strategy to set a clear framework for how government and responsible private capital can work together in support of security, resilience and growth. And in December, we will also hold a defence investment summit to turn strategy into delivery and bring together government, industry and investors to accelerate the flow of capital into priority defence capabilities.
Now, before I finish, I want to set out that this is not a theoretical game. This is happening right now and we need to make it easier for it to happen more frequently. In May, 13 British startups were awarded contracts of up to £4 million as part of the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Kraken Technologies, as one of them, which manufactures maritime uncrewed surface vehicles, has since gone on to raise $175 million in a Series B funding round off the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets is another British firm which has secured significant funding from capital. It was just one of three firms selected by the Ministry of Defence to develop a low-cost drone interceptor. Both Kraken and Green Jets received funding from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and NATO Innovation Fund, while the British Business Bank also financed Kraken. And JET Connectivity, a small business which builds novel 5G and 6G communications tools was the only British firm to be admitted to the procedures NATO Diana mission track programme earlier this year from over three and a half thousand participants.
That was fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best, but I know it’s just the tip of the iceberg. There are so many other British, brilliant British companies that we need to be able to support as well.
Now, it is in these uncertain times that not only do friends stand together, which is why the support that we offer in Ukraine is long lasting, is serious and will not change no matter what threats Putin throws at us. It is also in these uncertain times that we need to make it easier to bring private capital and public investment together to create the new defence technologies that we need to keep our nation safe.
But let me finish with a final thought. Today we will not only get a clearer view of the potential on offer in the growing defence industry in the UK, and advice on how you can access more of that market. We also get a chance to keep Britain secure in a more dangerous world. Defence needs to be a national endeavour. A whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour. It is the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence to lead that, but it is not the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence alone. To keep our nation safe, we need every part of society, every part of government and industry to step up to support that resilience, that innovation, and that drive to keep us all safe. Because as we can see from our friends in Ukraine, where deterrence fails, not only is it more and more expensive in treasure and lives and lost opportunity. It’s something that, as everyone here, we must take steps to avoid. That is why deterrence matters. That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win. And all of you in this group can play a part in doing so.
Thank you for what you’re doing here today, and thank you Lady Mayor for bringing us all together.

Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed 2, injured 3
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned an overnight Russian drone strike on the Starokozache international border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, in a Sept. 9 statement on X.
Russia struck the Starokozache border crossing overnight with drones, killing two civilians and injuring three others, Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper said. Rescuers evacuated another 16 people from a bus, according to Kiper.
Sandu also said that a Russian drone forced Moldova to close its airspace temporarily, warning that the Russian advance in Ukraine is moving further west.
"I urge more air defense support for Ukraine," Sandu said.
Earlier in the day, referring to Russian attacks on the border crossing, among others, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that "there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes."
The Southern Regional Directorate of Ukraine's State Border Guard Service announced in a Facebook post on Sept. 9 that border operations had resumed.
"The operation of this border crossing point will help to avoid congestion and traffic build-up on other routes along the border with Moldova. At the same time, security measures for citizens crossing the border will continue to be implemented in response to any (Russian) attempts to attack border infrastructure," the statement reads.
Russia most likely wants to disrupt logistics with its attacks on border crossings, Andriy Demchenko, the spokesman for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said during the national telethon, Suspilne reported.
The attack was the fourth one on a border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine, Demchenko added.
A Russian Shahed-type drone strike overnight on Aug. 25 damaged the Vynohradivka border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in Odesa Oblast, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the time.
In a post on X, Sybiha called on the international community to "condemn Russia's systematic targeting of civilian transport corridors and critical border infrastructure."
Moldova's Foreign Ministry reported on Aug. 27 that five drones violated Moldovan airspace on the night prior.
"We have repeatedly warned about the unacceptable risks posed by Russia's war against Ukraine," the ministry wrote.
A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on Sept. 8, forcing airspace closures, emergency alerts and the scrambling of NATO fighter jets.
The Moldovan military detected an "unmanned aerial vehicle" at 4:20 p.m. local time on Sept. 8, the Moldovan Defense Ministry said in a statement, identifying it as a "Shahed-type" drone that entered the country's airspace from the "direction of … Ukraine."
Spanish F/A-18 fighter jets, deployed as part of a NATO air-policing mission, were scrambled from Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base in Romania as the drone entered Romanian airspace.

PARIS, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The International Space Summit opened in Paris on Wednesday, bringing together delegations from around the world to discuss cooperation in space exploration, economy and security, amid transatlantic tensions highlighted by the reported absence of several major U.S. space companies.
Co-organized by France and Germany, the two-day event brings together nearly 120 foreign delegations, including political leaders and ministers, as well as representatives from international organizations, space agencies, the military, the private sector, and civil society.

Against this backdrop, the summit aims to promote international dialogue on the technological, economic and governance changes shaping space exploration and utilization.
Its agenda centers on three main themes: an international approach to space science, technology, and exploration; addressing issues of the world space economy; and securing space through dialogue, defense, and partnerships.
The Elysee Palace described this summit as an opportunity to affirm Europe's "vision" and "role" in space for the coming decade. ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday that if any vessel enters the "restricted zone" to be announced by Iran in regional waters without coordination, it will be subject to the country's sanction measures.
"If a vessel enters this zone without coordination (with Iran), it will be subject to our sanction measures; meaning that if it seeks to use the Strait of Hormuz in the future, it will not be able to do so, and we will also refuse to provide it with port, insurance, and other required services," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
He said the zone's exact coordinates will be announced in the future, adding that it will generally begin around Iran's southeastern port city of Chabahar and will include parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea as well as the routes that can lead to the Strait of Hormuz.
He described the Strait of Hormuz as the "strait of Iran's power," adding the country will use that power to respond to the "enemy's aggression" and force it to stop it.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas.
Also on Wednesday, Iran's Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the U.S. Army's "aggressive" attack the night before against a number of Iranian oil tankers.
Expressing the condemnation in a statement, it said, "The U.S. military attack on Iranian commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman are considered to be in continuation of the U.S. government's military aggression, naval blockade and economic war against Iran, and in flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter and international law."
It called on the UN and the Security Council to take immediate actions against the "blatant violations" of international peace and security owing to "the U.S. aggressive actions against Iran."
The U.S. Central Command said in a Wednesday post on social media platform X that its forces had "destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers" on Tuesday night in response to the IRGC's targeting of "a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days."
The IRGC announced in separate statements early Wednesday that its forces had targeted within the preceding hours four U.S. vessels, including two destroyers, and eight oil tankers in regional waters, as well as a U.S. air base in Jordan in retaliatory strikes. ■

SANYA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China and Singapore concluded a five-day joint maritime exercise on Wednesday after completing all scheduled drills, as the two countries seek to deepen practical cooperation and strengthen their ability to safeguard regional peace and stability.
The exercise, the fifth of its kind between the two navies, was held in the waters and airspace around the city of Zhanjiang, south China's Guangdong Province. It consisted of two phases, covering in-port exchanges and at-sea drills.
During the in-port phase, the two sides held high-level meetings and planning discussions, and organized ship visits and other activities.
In the maritime phase, participating forces conducted eight drills, including communications exercises, formation maneuvers and aerial photography, at-sea replenishment, and joint search-and-rescue operations.
The Chinese navy said regular joint exercises had further strengthened mutual trust and promoted practical cooperation between the two countries' navies, while enhancing their ability to jointly contribute to peace and stability in the region.
In an earlier interview, Chinese military expert Zhang Junshe said the joint search-and-rescue drills hold significant practical value, given the heavy maritime traffic and complex weather and sea conditions in the South China Sea.
He also noted that live-fire exercises and replenishment-at-sea help enhance the two navies' combat capabilities.
China and Singapore held their first bilateral maritime exercise in 2015. Such joint exercises have become a regular feature of military exchanges between the two countries in recent years. In May 2025, the Chinese Navy dispatched a guided-missile frigate and a mine countermeasure vessel to Singapore for a joint exercise.
In addition to regular joint maritime exercises with Singapore, China also carries out routine joint drills and training with neighboring countries, including Thailand and Cambodia. ■

I’m Taking A Break From Writing This Week. Here’s a look at what I’ve been reading and listening to, instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:03:08 UTC
00:03:08 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
(1) First Up, Some Media I’ve Done Recently
Be sure to check these out for more of my thoughts on AI consciousness, intelligence, and more!
(2) A Podcast On AGI
I really loved listening to this podcast episode. It’s one where three different thinkers on the effects of AGI are interviewed, all with very different opinions on it. I wanted to link the podcast episode, but it wasn’t working (YouTube below)
If you google ‘The AI Skeptics episode on the Longview podcast’ it should pop up pretty easily. For what its worth, I lean towards Arvind Narayanan’s views, though also appreciate Marcus’ point that if we stop spending so much time on LLMs and invent other kinds of technologies, things in the AI space could change and we need to be honest about that. Ed Zitron’s opinions on Hinton are off base imo. I think Hinton does genuinely believe in AI taking over and I suspect it’s rooted in his beliefs about brains. See here for my thinking on this.
(3) Situational Awareness by Leopold Aschenbrenner
I’ve been reading the AI manifesto situational awareness by Leopold Aschenbrenner. This was written in June 2024 and we know a lot has happened since then. Nevertheless, this text is foundational to AGI discourse, and reads as a fascinating sociological analysis to me, more than anything else.
The Manifesto is a lengthy discussion of Aschenbrenner’s predictions about the coming of AGI in 2027 (or thereabouts). The argument is that algorithmic progress (i.e., less data and less compute solving the same amount of problems), unhobbling (i.e., removing certain practical constraints from AI to allow their full scope of intelligence) and AIs reaching something like human level intelligence, will bring about an explosion in super-intelligence.
It backs up the economic and logistical costs required for such an explosion using historical examples (e.g., that during WW2 countries borrowed more GDP-equivalent than would be necessary for AI investment for the coming of AGI) and addresses a variety of common objections to the arguments made. All in all, it’s a fascinating read into the beliefs of those who believe AGI is coming in the near future.
(4) An Article from The Atlantic on Humans Talking About Themselves like They are LLMs
People talking about themselves like they are LLMs? It was only a matter of time, I suppose. But it is happening surprisingly soon (of course, it’s only happening in silicon valley). Nevertheless, well worth knowing about. Read it as a gift article here!
(5) Tech Elites and the Literature of Philip K Dick?
This is a short and interesting read (this should be a gift link) comparing tech elites to Philip K Dick novels from the 60’s and 70’s. It’s funny how literature so often has ways of helping us understand the realities of the world we live in.
(6) Will a Tech-Free world be an Elite Luxury in the Future?
That’s what Dana Suskind argues and I worry it could be true. Another gift link here.
(7) Some reading on the ‘AI is getting out of control’ narrative
An all round refreshing and measured read on AI and cybersecurity incidents.
Thank you for being here, I’ll be back next week with an article as usual ✨

Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:02:30 UTC
00:02:30 KST

Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89.
Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.
With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.
King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.
The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.
The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”
After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.
Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss classes for the occasion.
Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel.
Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.

Ukrainian Defense Forces Hit Russian Mangust Patrol Boat in Crimea

Units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit a Russian Mangust patrol boat in Crimea.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported the strike.
At the time it was hit, the boat was located in Kozacha Bay in Sevastopol.
The extent of the damage is currently being clarified.
The Mangust (Project 12150) is a Russian high-speed coastal patrol boat. The Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Border Guard Service primarily uses these boats, while other Russian security and government agencies use some modifications.
The boat is about 20 meters long, has a maximum speed of up to 50 knots (more than 90 km/h), and a crew of up to six.
The standard armament for these boats is the MTPU-1 Zhalo 14.5 mm naval machine-gun mount. Various configurations have also been reported to support the installation of:
According to open-source data, Russia has 62 Mangust boats in service.
Before the full-scale invasion, Russia’s Border Guard Service used Mangust boats to conduct dangerous maneuvers near Ukrainian ships and boats in the Sea of Azov.
In particular, in September 2018, Project 12150 PSKA-651 conducted dangerous maneuvers near the Ukrainian Maritime Guard boat BG-59 Oniks.

09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
China and the Philippines have exchanged sharp words about the disputed South China Sea, with their latest spat coming after the Philippine defense chief said he received a note from Beijing during a defense forum in South Korea.
Videos of the Seoul Defense Dialogue on Tuesday showed Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr. receiving a note from China while answering a question.
The note contained remarks concerning the disputed South China Sea, according to Teodoro. He responded to the claims one by one as he read them aloud.
"China's position on the South China Sea arbitration is clear, consistent, and firm," said the note. Teodoro responded that Beijing has "no position."
He read from the note: "The arbitration violates fundamental principles of international law." Teodoro responded: "So what you signed, UNCLOS, violates international law," in reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS.
A 2016 decision by the Hague-based Permanent Court of Arbitration concluded China's maritime claims in the South China Sea were not valid.
"The so-called award is illegal, null, and void," the note said. Teodoro replied. "So say you, and (it) has no binding force because you don't want to be subjected to UNCLOS."
"China neither accepts nor recognizes the award," he read from the note. Teodoro responded. "Of course, because you lost."
Teodoro called the note "actual coercion, bullying, and aggression," adding that he would keep it as a memento of "how desperate China is."
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a news conference Wednesday that she was "not sure what exactly happened at the event, but China’s position has always been clear on the so-called 'South China Sea arbitration.'"
Manila "unilaterally initiated the case, which is a distortion and abuse of the UNCLOS dispute settlement mechanism," she said, accusing the Philippines of violating UNCLOS and undermining "its integrity and authority."
She urged Teodoro to "cut the provocations and theatrics, and stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea."
The incident comes amid persistent tensions between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea, where the two countries have repeatedly confronted each other about competing territorial claims.
The area is one of the world's busiest trade routes, with trillions of dollars in annual trade.

EU's plan to gain independence from Russian energy faltering, auditors warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:00:52 UTC
00:00:52 KST

A damning report from the European Court of Auditors identifies insufficient grid infrastructure and interconnectors across EU countries as major barriers to unlocking a fully integrated energy market.
Four years after the European Union launched a plan to break its dependence on Russian oil and gas and accelerate the clean energy transition, an audit presented by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) on Wednesday said the bloc's plan is falling well short of its ambitions.
Russian oil imports have plunged following EU sanctions and gas imports have declined, the ECA auditors noted, but they urge caution against attributing all of that progress to REPowerEU, the plan launched by the European Commission in 2022 to achieve energy sovereignty and end all dependence on Moscow.
"In our view, other factors also contributed to lower gas consumption – and consequently imports – which are not causally linked to the REPowerEU plan. These include mild winters, as well as reduced consumption by households and businesses in response to high energy prices," reads the ECA report.
The 2022 Nord Stream pipeline sabotage, which disrupted a major route for Russian gas to Europe, further accelerated the EU’s push to diversify away from Russian energy and exposed the vulnerability of Europe’s fossil-fuel infrastructure.
Commenting on the ECA report, a Commission spokesperson argued that the REPowerEU "contributed to a drastic reduction of EU imports of Russian natural gas, falling from 152 billion cubic metres in 2021 to 36 billion cubic metres in 2025, reducing the share of Russian gas imports from 45% to 12%".
While the Commission allowed some exceptions to the Russian ban, a complete phase-out of Russian LNG imports takes effect on 1 January 2027, and for Russian pipeline gas in September 2027.
Clean power and grids
The ECA also flagged insufficient renewable energy capacity, which the report describes as "negligible" compared with the Commission's 103GW goal, and grid infrastructure, particularly cross-border electricity connections, as the plan's most striking weakness.
While the EU added more than 200 GW of solar and wind capacity between 2022 and 2024, the ECA auditors said the renewable capacity directly generated by REPowerEU measures was negligible against the 103GW target.
The report warns that the EU risks replacing one form of energy dependence with another by moving away from Russian fossil fuels without building clean domestic generation and the grids needed to support it.
The Commission and several EU countries, such as Portugal and Spain, have consistently flagged the latter as a major hurdle to establishing a fully integrated energy system across the bloc.
Several critics argue that without progress on that front, the EU won't reach its climate and energy goals, and that pouring money into clean energy could lead to curtailment, shutting down electricity generation and driving negative prices – the EU's true energy conundrum.
The ECA audit comes as a blow to Brussels, which seized Russia's invasion of Ukraine to ditch reliance on cheap imported fossil fuels from Moscow, the EU's top supplier until 2022, and accelerate the bloc's Green Deal, its flagship plan for energy and climate transition, to become climate neutral by 2050.
"Four years after its launch, REPowerEU has stalled, even though several hundred billion euros have been made available”, said Mihails Kozlovs, the ECA auditor leading the report.
“We must learn the right lessons now, as the new geopolitical tensions and their impact on energy markets underscore the need to accelerate diversification and prevent future over-reliance on a single supplier."
No money, no EU energy integration
As is often the case in Brussels, the biggest hurdle to an integrated European energy system is a lack of funding.
The EU auditors found that EU countries have committed just €54.3 billion of the €300 billion in additional funding made available through the EU recovery fund – less than one-fifth of the investment initially deemed necessary to meet the plan's goals.
"Informal replies sometimes say that it is cheaper for member states to borrow and get loans. There's also an administrative burden attached – there are issues between grants and loans since grants do not count toward national debt and member states are reluctant to commit to this," Stefano Sturaro, an EU auditor, told reporters on Wednesday.
However, the Commission spokesperson defended the funding, saying it played a "pivotal role" in accelerating implementation of the REPowerEU priorities.
National energy and climate plans were supposed to translate REPowerEU into concrete action, EU auditors warned, but EU countries included few or no specific measures or targets to advance their clean energy goals.
For the EU auditors, Brussels has excelled at promoting energy independence more than financing and building the infrastructure required to sustain it.
However, with a clear investment gap in sight, the Commission's plan now depends on whether EU countries are willing and able to pay for it.
The next political battleground is underway as EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the Council, gear up to lock negotiations on the future of the bloc's power grids by the end of the year.

Japan’s China-facing military build-up confronts labour, budget and political limits
Amid ambitious transformation driven by risk it could be drawn into a Taiwan conflict, Tokyo tackles tough obstacles at home, analysts say
7-MIN READ7-MIN
22
 Listen
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the third of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines the various challenges confronting Japan in its bid to expand its military.
Driven by the growing risk that a conflict over Taiwan could draw Tokyo into a high-intensity confrontation with Beijing, Japan is pursuing its most ambitious military transformation since World War II.
Tokyo is acquiring long-range missiles, embracing drones and expanding defence partnerships stretching from Canberra to London.
Yet, analysts say some of the toughest obstacles to the transformation may lie at home.
As Tokyo prepares to revise its strategic security documents by year’s end, its historic military build-up must contend with growing constraints.
These include a shrinking pool of military recruits, an ageing population, mounting fiscal pressures, an industrial base struggling to expand and lingering questions over how far the Japanese public would support the use of its ascendant military power.

Ministry of Defence policies to tackle unacceptable behaviour
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:00:04 BST
00:00:04 KST

Ministry of Defence policies to tackle unacceptable behaviour
Policies and measures to tackle unacceptable behaviour across Defence, including ways to respond and report it.
Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.
Defence support: sexual offences - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) is taking decisive steps to tackle unacceptable behaviour and ensure a safe, respectful environment for all who serve the nation.
Unacceptable behaviour has no place in Defence and will not be tolerated. These behaviours do not reflect the high values and standards upheld by the vast majority Defence personnel, whether in the British Army, Royal Navy, Royal Air Force, or Civil Service.
Defence is taking action
Defence’s commitment is underpinned by the Raising our Standards Programme (RoS), which was established to prevent and tackle unacceptable behaviour and cultural issues that undermine the values and standards across Defence.
Since 2021, Defence has introduced a series of measures to provide clear and robust guidance to civilian and military personnel on preventing and addressing incidents.
Prevention
Defence is committed to preventing unacceptable behaviour at the earliest opportunity through training, education, and robust policies. These measures aim to set clear expectations, prevent incidents, and build confidence that unacceptable behaviour will be addressed effectively.
- Addressing Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG): A programme is underway to deliver targeted actions to tackle VAWG in Defence, with lessons being used to inform wider action.
- Zero Tolerance policies to Unacceptable Sexual Behaviour: Three Zero Tolerance policies have been introduced to ensure these behaviours are rooted out: a Victim/Survivor Focused Approach Policy, a policy on Sexual Offences and Sexual Relationships Between Instructors and Trainees, and the Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Policy (JSP 769).
- Training and Education: All Defence personnel are required to complete a variety of training packages on standards of behaviour and how to identify and address unacceptable conduct.
- Domestic Abuse Action Plan: Outlines Defence’s commitment to addressing domestic abuse, supporting affected personnel, and ensuring that appropriate action is taken against perpetrators.
Reporting
Everyone working in Defence is encouraged to call out or report behaviour that falls short of Defence’s high standards and values.
To support personnel reporting, Defence has established independent mechanisms to ensure complaints and serious criminal offences are handled appropriately.
- The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC): Investigates allegations of serious criminal wrongdoing across the Armed Forces, and is outside the single Service chain of Command.
- Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU): The VWCU, part of the DSCC, provides comprehensive care and support to victims and witnesses of serious crimes. It ensures that victims are aware of their options in line with the Code of Practice for Victims of Crime.
- Tri-Service Complaints Team: Investigates the most non-criminal serious complaints, such as bullying, discrimination and harassment, outside the single Service chain of command.
- Service Complaints App and Civilian My Complaints App: Faster, easier and simpler ways for Service Personnel to raise Service Complaints and for civilians to raise unacceptable behaviours complaints or more general grievances.
- 
Confidential reporting channels are available 24/7 for military and civilian personnel:
    
  - The Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination (BHD) helpline provides emotional support, guidance, or practical advice from trained BHD advisers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It operates independently from Defence and outside the chain of command or line management structure, and can be used anonymously and is confidential.
  - The Confidential Hotline is the primary point of contact for raising concerns and a source of authoritative and impartial advice and guidance on all aspects of the Raising a Concern (Whistleblowing) Policy and Procedure in JSP 492. The team will review and identify the most appropriate route to resolve concerns. Everyone who works in Defence can use it.
In addition to the independent mechanisms above, a full list of ways to informally and formally respond and report instances can be found by searching ‘Reporting Unacceptable Behaviour’ in Defence internal communication channels.
Enforcement
The JSPs and Raising a Concern policy demonstrate that supporting victims/survivors is a Defence priority. They also provide personnel with greater confidence to raise complaints and believe action will be taken without fear of it impacting them or their career for doing so.
Every allegation is investigated, with appropriate, consistent, and robust consequences for people whose behaviour falls below the high standards of conduct the MOD demands. This can include administrative, disciplinary, criminal action, or termination of employment and/or discharge from the Armed Forces.
Defence have also introduced mechanisms that ensure we are transparent in our actions, learn from feedback and continually improve.
- Armed Forces Sexual Harassment and Sexualised Behaviours Survey: Conducted to gather experiences and perceptions of sexual harassment and sexualised behaviours among service personnel and will provide vital data to inform preventative programmes.
- The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC): Investigates allegations of serious criminal wrongdoing across the Armed Forces, and is outside the singe Service chain of Command.
- Defence Voices Panel: Providing a platform for Defence personnel to share their experiences and views, helping shape our policies and practices.
- External Challenge Panel: Bringing in external experts to provide independent scrutiny and advice on Defence’s approach to tackling unacceptable behaviour.
- Independent Armed Forces Commissioner: Former Air Commodore Polly Miller-Perkins CBE was appointed the UK’s first ever Armed Forces Commissioner in March 2026. They will act as an independent champion and direct point of contact for personnel and their families and have unprecedented powers to investigate welfare issues and raise concerns that impact service life, including equipment, housing, and unacceptable behaviours.
- Service Police Complaints Commissioner: Providing independent oversight of complaints made against the Service Police, ensuring investigations are fair and impartial.
Support and advice
Defence is committed to supporting those affected by unacceptable behaviour through a range of internal and external channels.
For further information:
- access Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.
- access Defence support: sexual offences - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.
- search ‘Call it out - Reporting Unacceptable Behaviour’ on internal systems
JSPs that help tackle and prevent unacceptable behaviour
Joint Service Publication (JSP) documents are produced by the MOD and some are publicly available. Defence personnel can find a full list of JSPs on internal systems by searching ‘JSPs’.
- JSP 763: The MOD Behaviours and Informal Complaints Resolution Policy - a guide for all MOD service and civilian personnel on behaviours and the informal complaints resolution process.
- JSP 831: Redress of individual grievances: service complaints - a guide for MOD service and civilian personnel on the application of policy for service complaints.
- Armed Forces Service Complaints process - information about how to make a UK Armed Forces Service Complaint.
- Zero Tolerance to Unacceptable Sexual Behaviour: A Victim/Survivor focused approach policy - applies to all armed forces personnel.
- Zero Tolerance to Unacceptable Sexual Offences and Sexual relationships between Instructors and Trainees - applies to all armed forces personnel.
- JSP 769: Zero Tolerance to Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) Policy. - applies all MOD service and civilian personnel.
- Tackling Sexual Offending in Defence Strategy - applies to all armed forces personnel.
- Commanding officers guide (manual of service law: JSP 830 volume 1) - a guide to the legislation and reference material on the Armed Forces Act 2006.
- The Military Court Service - provides a criminal court service for the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force in the Court Martial, Summary Appeal Court and Service Civilian Court.
- MOD Serious Crime Unit - information on Defence’s judge-led review into how allegations of serious criminal wrongdoing are raised and investigated in the armed forces.
MOD’s Raising a Concern Policy
The Ministry of Defence raising a concern policy ensures that individuals’ concerns are addressed and resolved at the right level and as quickly and effectively as possible. It reassures individuals of protection from victimisation when raising concerns.

Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination
Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.
If you have experienced a sexual offence, visit Defence support: sexual offences.
Defence personnel can find additional guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and access support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway.
If you have experienced unacceptable behaviour including bullying, harassment, sexual harassment or discrimination, support is available.
This page explains how you can raise a complaint and get support.
Unacceptable behaviour has no place in Defence and concerns will be taken seriously.
You may wish to:
- seek advice
- resolve the issue informally
- make a formal complaint
Support is available whatever approach you choose.
If illegal or criminal behaviour has occurred, this should be reported to the Service Police, MOD Police or civilian police as soon as possible.
If you are unsure if what you’ve seen or experienced is unacceptable behaviour, you can read the definition of the behaviours in Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763) - GOV.UK.
Raise a complaint
Seek informal resolution
In some circumstances, concerns can be resolved informally. Early action can help stop issues escalating, address misunderstandings and restore working relationships.
Informal resolution does not mean the matter is less important or will not be taken seriously. The main difference is that informal processes are often simpler and can help resolve issues more quickly.
Service or civilian personnel may wish to:
- speak directly to the person, if you feel comfortable doing so
- seek advice or intervention from a manager or Chain of Command, adviser or another trusted person
- use local support, mediation or advisory services available within Defence
You can choose to make a formal complaint at any time.
For more information read Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763).
Defence personnel can also find more detailed information on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway.
Service Complaint
Current and former members of the Armed Forces can make a Service Complaint if they believe they have been wronged on a matter that arises under service law.
This can include complaints of bullying, harassment, discrimination and biased, improper or dishonest behaviour.
You can:
- complete the Service Complaint Form on the My Complaint app, accessible via Defence Gateway, or:
- submit a Service Complaint in writing using the form found at Annex F of JSP 831 Part 2 - GOV.UK
For more information read the guidance on the Armed Forces Service Complaints process - GOV.UK or at Redress of individual grievances: service complaints (JSP 831) - GOV.UK.
Civilian Formal Complaint
Defence civil servants, contractors, consultants and agency workers can raise formal complaints or grievances about bullying, harassment, discrimination or victimisation through the MOD Civilian Formal Complaints Process.
You can use the My Complaints App on Defence Gateway to:
- submit a formal complaint
- submit an anonymous complaint
- record an incident, even if you do not wish to make a complaint at that time
If you cannot access the app, contact the DBS HR Advisory and Casework Service:
- civilian personnel enquiry centre: 0800 345 7772 (UK) or +44 1225 747772 (Overseas), 8am to 4pm Monday to Friday
- submit a form via the Digital Workplace (DWP)
- Email: peopleservices@dbs.mod.uk
Support is available whether or not you choose to make a complaint.
Defence personnel can also find more detailed information on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway.
Get support
Support is available whether or not you choose to make a formal complaint. You may want advice, help understanding your options, or simply someone to talk to before deciding what to do next.
You do not need to make a formal complaint to access support. Different services can provide practical advice, emotional support and information about the options available to you.
Defence personnel can find additional guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and access support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway.
Available to all personnel:
Local support
If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.
You can speak to:
- a friend or colleague
- your manager or Chain of Command
- welfare staff
- a diversity and inclusion adviser
- staff networks
- a padre or chaplain
- a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes.
If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.
Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination Helpline
A confidential helpline is available for military personnel, civil servants and contractors.
Trained advisers can provide emotional support, practical advice and guidance on the support available to you. The helpline is open 24/7, 365 days a year and offers a safe, anonymous space to discuss concerns.
Telephone: 0800 014 2381 (UK) or +44 330 008 5942 (Overseas)
Confidential hotline
If you have concerns about wrongdoing, misconduct, illegal activity, safety risks or behaviour that falls below the standards expected in Defence, you can seek confidential advice and guidance for raising a concern and whistleblowing in Defence.
Email: Confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk
Further information can be found in the MOD Raising a Concern Policy.
Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit
The Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.
It is independent of the chain of command and you can self-refer.
Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.
Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.
Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.
Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk
For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.
Support for Service personnel, veterans and their families:
The Armed Forces Commissioner
The role of the Commissioner is to provide independent and impartial oversight of the Service Complaints system for members of the UK Armed Forces.
It is also to act as a direct point of contact for serving personnel and their families who can raise general service welfare concerns that may impact on their service lives and their ability to serve.
- telephone: 0300 369 0689
- enquiry form
- email: contact@scoaf.org.uk
For more information visit the Armed Forces Commissioner website.
Aurora New Dawn
Aurora New Dawn is a charity that provides free and confidential support for UK Armed Forces personnel and their families, including those deployed overseas. It is independent from Defence and the Chain of Command.
The specialist team can support you if you are experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence or stalking.
Call the helpline or WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527
Helpline hours (GMT): 9am to 3pm, Monday to Friday.
WhatsApp service (GMT): Tuesday 9am to 3pm, Wednesday and Thursday 5pm to 8pm, Sunday 10am to 2pm.
For more information visit the Aurora Dawn Armed Forces website.
SSAFA Safe to Serve
SSAFA, the Armed Forces charity, is a source of support for serving personnel, veterans and their families.
SSAFA Safe To Serve is a dedicated support service for women currently serving in HM Armed Forces who are experiencing bullying, discrimination, harassment, or sexual harassment. It is outside the military Chain of Command.
- Telephone: Speak directly to an advisor by calling + 44 800 260 6722
- Webform: Use the webform to send a message
- WhatsApp: Send a message securely on +44 203 807 4400
If you are not a woman currently serving in HM Armed Forces but you would like to speak to SSAFA, please contact SSAFA Forcesline online or telephone +44 800 260 6780 (9am to 5pm Monday to Thursday and 9am to 4pm on Friday).
Veterans UK
Veterans UK provides support and guidance for veterans, former members of the Armed Forces, and their families.
It can provide information on welfare support, compensation schemes, pensions and other services available to the veteran community.
- call: 0808 1914 218
For more information visit Veterans UK.
Support for civilians and contractors:
Employee Assistance Programme (EAP)
If you are a civilian, the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is a confidential service available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It can help with personal or work-related issues. EAP will not share any information with your employer or managers.
Helpline:
- 0800 731 8629 (UK)
- +44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)
- contact form
For more information, visit the Workplace wellbeing website.
If you are deployed or based overseas:
If you are overseas, you can access the same support options as in the UK.
- Bullying, Harassment, and Discrimination Helpline: +44 330 008 5942
- Confidential Hotline for whistleblowing: confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk
- SSAFA Safe to Serve - WhatsApp: +44 203 807 4400
- Aurora New Dawn - Helpline and WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527.
- Employee Assistance Programme - +44 330 008 5959
Other support organisations
If you prefer to seek support outside of Defence, specialist organisations can provide information, advice and practical support.

Defence support: sexual offences

Defence support: sexual offences
Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.
It explains how to:
- report a sexual offence
- get medical help
- get support
You don’t have to make a report at all to receive support.
Report a sexual offence
If you or someone else is in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.
You can report a sexual offence to either the civilian police or the Service Police.
If you are unsure which organisation to contact, either organisation can explain your options and help you access support. You will be listened to without judgement.
It doesn’t matter whether the offence happened recently or in the past.
Civilian police
If you are in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.
If you have a hearing or speech impairment, use the textphone service 18000, or text if you’ve pre-registered with the emergency SMS service.
If you are in danger and you can’t speak or answer questions:
- call 999
- press 55 when prompted and your call will be transferred to the police
Pressing 55 only works on mobiles and doesn’t allow the police to track your location. If you don’t press 55, your call will be ended.
If it is not an emergency, call 101.
Service Police
The Service Police is responsible for policing armed forces personnel and civilians subject to service discipline.
You can report the incident to the Service Police in the UK or overseas if the incident involves a person who is subject to Service Law or a civilian subject to service discipline.
You can:
- call the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630
- attend or call a local Service Police station (the Service Police Crime Bureau will be able to provide a location and contact details)
Specially trained officers will provide support, explain your options, and make sure your needs and wishes are considered.
The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) is an independent, professional and global Service Police force with jurisdiction to investigate serious crime committed by those subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas.
Give information anonymously
If you have information about a sexual offence, you can give information anonymously to Crimestoppers.
- Call on 0800 555 111
- Fill out an anonymous form
If you have experienced a sexual offence and wish to report a crime, you should contact the police directly to get support and advice.
For more information visit the Crimestoppers website.
Get medical help
Medical centre
Your local medical centre or GP practice is a safe place to ask for help.
Medical staff can provide physical and mental healthcare, refer you to specialist services and support your wellbeing at work.
They will not normally share information unless there is a risk of serious harm to you or someone else.
NHS Sexual Assault Referral Centre
A Sexual Assault Referral Centre (SARC) is a specialist NHS service for anyone who has been raped, sexually assaulted or abused.
You can contact a SARC without reporting to the police. You can go at any time, and do not have to go alone.
SARCs can offer medical, practical and emotional support. They have specially trained doctors, nurses and support workers to care for you.
Services are free and available to everyone regardless of gender, age, the type of incident, or when it happened.
Services include:
- crisis care
- medical and forensic examination
- emergency contraception
- sexual health support
- access to a sexual assault advisor
- referral to mental health support and sexual violence support
For more information visit NHS help after rape and sexual assault.
Get support
You can access support whether or not you choose to make a formal report.
There is no wrong way to seek support.
Different services can provide information, practical help and emotional support, depending on what you need.
Defence personnel can find more guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and get support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway.
Available to all personnel:
Local support
If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.
You can speak to:
- a friend or colleague
- your manager or Chain of Command
- welfare staff
- a diversity and inclusion adviser
- staff networks
- a padre or chaplain
- a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes
If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.
Defence Victim Witness Care Unit
The Defence Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.
It is independent of the Chain of Command and you can self-refer.
Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.
Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.
Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.
Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk
For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.
Independent Legal Advisors scheme
The Independent Legal Advisors (ILA) scheme provides free, independent legal advice and guidance for eligible Service and civilian personnel aged 18 or over, where a reported sexual offence is being investigated within the Service Justice System.
The scheme can help you understand the justice process, your legal rights, what to expect during an investigation, how personal information may be requested or used, and the options available if you are unhappy with how your case has been handled.
The ILA will not tell you what decisions to make or advocate on your behalf. Their role is to give you the information and advice you need to understand your options and make informed choices.
Accessing the scheme is voluntary. Referrals can be made by organisations supporting you, including the Service Police, Defence Serious Crime Command or the Victim Witness Care Unit, and will only be made with your consent.

US-Canada trade war escalates, 9/11 25 years on, and a medical first involving a pig
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

US-Canada trade war escalates, 9/11 25 years on, and a medical first involving a pig
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
Twenty-five years ago I was working as a journalist in London. In the early afternoon on September 11, all the televisions on the walls of the open-plan office suddenly showed the same image: the surreal sight of the Twin Towers burning and then collapsing. We heard that a neighbouring building, One Canada Square (also known as Canary Wharf Tower), where I had worked a year earlier, had been evacuated as there were rumours that a plane that had taken off from Heathrow was unaccounted for and, as the then tallest building in the UK and a symbol of capitalism, One Canada Square was an obvious target. As we know, nothing happened, and we got to work trying to explain the seemingly inexplicable.
Twenty-five years later, the deadliest terrorist attacks in history continue to cast a shadow on global affairs and US politics. As the Neue Zürcher Zeitung wrote this week, 9/11 is the “first and last moment in the 21st century that has united Americans”.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
Friday marks 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States – attacks which, according to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ), “changed Americans’ relationship with their country and with the world” and resulted in “deep mistrust and severe polarisation”.
“On the morning of September 11, 2001, time was torn apart,” wrote the NZZ’s deputy editor-in-chief, who began his undergraduate studies in the US just before 9/11. “The world watched spellbound as the images played out on screens: two planes crashing into the Twin Towers, over and over again in an endless loop.”
One consequence of the attacks, in which almost 3,000 people died, was that “Americans saw themselves as victims of a perfidious attack and rallied behind their resolute president”, he said. “This was by no means a given – just a few months earlier [George W. Bush] had won one of the most controversial elections in American history by the narrowest of margins. Yet after September 11, 90% of the population supported him in the polls. That’s a record figure – completely unthinkable today.”
The Republican government capitalised on this support. The CIA detained suspects in secret camps and tortured them. The USA Patriot Act enabled the authorities to carry out house searches on terror suspects without a court order.
“At first, Americans accepted that the state wanted more control and was taking a more aggressive stance both at home and abroad,” the NZZ wrote. “Soon, however, the categories in Bush’s foreign policy became blurred: suddenly, the US wanted to democratise the Middle East and free women from the yoke of Islamism. Oil, gas and other strategic interests also played a role, however. The Americans invaded Iraq in 2003.”
The government’s approval ratings halved, while the US sank ever deeper into the quagmire of “forever wars”, the NZZ continued. “Bush went from being a strong leader to a president who divided the country more than anyone before him: although the Republicans continued to support him, only a tiny minority of Democrats still backed him. This heightened polarisation remains a lasting legacy of the Bush era. The rift between the parties deepened even further under Obama, Biden and Trump.” As a result, the NZZ said 9/11 is the “first and last moment in the 21st century that has united Americans”.
“Since 9/11, Americans have viewed the world outside differently,” the NZZ concluded. “It seems more dangerous, more confusing. And they are withdrawing. Paranoid doomsday-prepping billionaires and increasingly radical militias are the most extreme expression of a culture of fear that is spreading across the US. Ordinary citizens, too, are increasingly retreating to the suburbs and into their communities of like-minded people.”
The Zurich paper said the rise of social media was further reinforcing these filter bubbles. “Today, Americans move in parallel worlds depending on their political convictions. There are many reasons for this. Yet the planes that crashed into the Twin Towers in New York on September 11, 2001, acted as catalysts.”
On Tuesday the White House escalated its trade dispute with Canada by banning the import of certain Canadian products, notably alcoholic drinks, and by raising customs duties on other goods. The Tribune de Genève says there’s no end in sight to the crisis.
A range of products, from mattresses to motorboats and golf buggies, will be subject to a 50% surcharge from September 15, Le Temps reported on Wednesday. An import ban on all kinds of alcoholic drinks as well as dairy products such as whey will come into force on September 29.
Good news, of sorts, is that certain Canadian products will no longer be subject to the 50% surcharge. This list is significantly shorter, but loo paper is on it.
This retaliatory move comes soon after Canada imposed customs duties on American products – in response to surcharges introduced by Washington on August 22.
“To justify the ban on imports of alcoholic drinks from Canada, US President Donald Trump has cited the boycott – which he describes as ‘discriminatory’ – targeting American spirits in Canada,” Le Temps explained. “Since the start of his tariff offensive last year, Canadians have launched a massive boycott of US products: US wines and spirits have disappeared from the shelves in most provinces, which hold a monopoly on their sale.”
As reported in Swissinfo’s US briefing two weeks ago, two-thirds of Canadians support a tough stance towards the US.
“There appears to be no end in sight to the crisis at present,” the Tribune de Genève wrote on Wednesday. “Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned on Tuesday morning that his government’s strategy to reduce dependence on the United States would have a short-term economic ‘cost’ for the country. The ‘cost of inaction’ would be far greater, he said in a video posted on YouTube a few hours after Canada’s tariff retaliation came into force.”
Swiss newspapers were impressed at the weekend by a medical success story in Boston: a pig kidney had functioned for nine months in the body of a 66-year-old man.
“The man’s prospects were bleak,” wrote the Tages-Anzeiger on Saturday. “His kidneys had been severely damaged by diabetes. For two years he had relied on dialysis, which left him utterly exhausted, while the function of his diseased organ continued to deteriorate.” Doctors estimated the probability of him receiving a kidney within the next five years at 9%, and the risk that he would not survive the waiting period at 40%. “Then the doctors devised a plan that was to result in a medical breakthrough.”
The doctors at Mass General Brigham in Boston transplanted a pig’s kidney into the patient, which worked so well that he managed without dialysis for 271 days, the team reported in the science journal The Lancet. Previously, pig kidneys had functioned in the human body for a maximum of two months. “For the first time, a human has benefited from a xenotransplant over a prolonged period,” the Tages-Anzeiger wrote, referring to a transplant from one species to another.
After around six months, damage to the kidney’s blood vessels became apparent, which ultimately led to organ failure. The kidney had to be removed, and the patient returned to dialysis. In the end, he was lucky: 80 days later a human donor kidney was found.
The Tages-Anzeiger pointed out that questions remain – the doctors can’t say why the pig’s kidney eventually failed – but it said there was now a debate about whether xenotransplantation is an option to bridge the waiting time for a human organ.
“For the team at Mass General Brigham, this success offers a potential solution to the global organ shortage,” Le Matin in Lausanne wrote on Saturday. “However, the researchers remain cautious: this involves a single patient, monitored under highly specialised conditions. Further trials will be needed before this type of transplant can be considered on a larger scale.”

Newfound fossils are spilling Denisovan secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Newfound fossils are spilling Denisovan secrets
Teeth and bone bits from a cave in China represent the richest fossil trove outside Siberia
A long-lost cave in southwestern China has offered archaeologists their first real glimpse of Denisovan culture.
Denisovans were a sister species of modern humans and lived across Asia an estimated 400,000 to 30,000 years ago. Researchers have uncovered only a handful of their fossils so far, compared with the thousands of remains of better-known Neandertals.
Now, Bianfu Cave — a new archaeological site at an abandoned quarry in Yunnan Province — has yielded a rich trove of Denisovan fossils. Protein analysis and high-quality X-ray scans have confirmed that the fragment remains found at the site belonged to at least three Denisovans who lived between 167,000 and 134,000 years ago, according to two new studies published September 9 in Nature. The remains were found alongside butchered animal remains and more than 1,300 tools.
The cave “tells us a little about how Denisovans actually lived on the landscape,” says Shara Bailey, a paleoanthropologist at New York University. “Denisovans are becoming a bit less mysterious.”
Denisovans were first discovered in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tooth and finger bone found in a cave in Siberia revealed an entirely new human species. Since then, researchers have found that many modern people — including groups in the Philippines, Tibet, New Guinea and Australia — carry Denisovan DNA.
Yet despite Denisovans’ widespread genetic legacy, with so few fossils, little is known about how they lived. What’s more, archaeologists don’t know much about where some of these fossils were originally buried, or if any other remains or tools were found alongside them. It’s “a little frustrating,” says Bence Viola, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toronto who has studied Denisovan remains from Siberia’s Denisova Cave.
Researchers did find tools alongside Denisovan remains at Denisova Cave. But whether these were made by Denisovans, Neandertals or modern humans, who also occupied the site, is still unknown.
Then in 2019, an ecological restoration project at a quarry in Yunnan Province uncovered numerous fossils in a buried cave. Later excavations revealed four human teeth, two pieces of a skull and a fragment of an arm bone.
Researchers looked for species-specific proteins in the fossils and compared the shape of the teeth to several human species using micro-CT scans to figure out who they belonged to.
As soon as he saw a picture of the tooth, “I immediately assumed that they were probably Denisovan,” says Clément Zanolli, a paleontologist at the University of Bordeaux, France. Indeed, the teeth shared distinct similarities to other Denisovan teeth from Laos and Tibet.
All the samples also carried a Denisovan-specific collagen variant, clinching the identification, says Qiaomei Fu, a molecular paleogeneticist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.
The tools in the cave date between 190,000 and 70,000 years old. The team didn’t find any evidence that other types of humans were around during that 120,000 years that the cave was occupied. This suggests that the tools were made by Denisovans, argue Fu, Zanolli and colleagues. These tools were largely used for processing animal remains, including to break bones, cut meat and scrape hides.
The cave also contained over 1,600 identifiable animal remains, mainly deer and other ruminants. While few fossils showed signs of carnivore gnawing, some bore telltale marks of cutting and scraping, suggesting that Denisovans used tools to handle animal remains, which were later abandoned in the cave.
Denisovan fossils at other sites have been found alongside marmot remains. The presence of butchered deer bones suggests that the species “adapted to their environment. They hunted different things in different ways,” Viola says. Altogether, it provides “a much more complete picture” about Denisovan life.
