Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:33 CST
22:21:33 KST

XIAMEN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- High-tech and high-value-added industries have increasingly become a key focus for foreign investors in China, with their share of total foreign direct investment (FDI) in actual use continuing to rise, according to a report released Wednesday.
The report, issued on the sidelines of the 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT) in Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province, showed that high-tech sectors accounted for about 32 percent of total FDI in actual use in 2025, while the scientific research and technical services sector alone contributed nearly one-fifth of the total.
Multinational corporations are accelerating the establishment of R&D centers in China, positioning the country as a vital node in their global innovation networks, the report said.
In 2025, the scientific research and technical services sector saw 14,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises, an increase of 27.2 percent year on year. Its share of total FDI in actual use has posted steady growth for seven consecutive years.
Despite a challenging global economic landscape, China's foreign investment inflows have shown strong resilience. In 2025, the country registered 70,392 newly established foreign-invested firms, hitting a record high with a year-on-year growth of 19.1 percent.
In the first half of 2026, the number of new foreign-invested enterprises rose 5.3 percent from a year earlier, with FDI in actual use reaching 402.14 billion yuan (about 59.34 billion U.S. dollars).
The report also noted a notable diversification in investment sources, with Belt and Road partner countries becoming a major driver of foreign capital inflows into China.
Compiled jointly by the CIFIT organizing committee and the Development Research Center of the State Council, the China two-way investment report 2026 marks its fourth consecutive annual release.
The CIFIT, often viewed as a barometer of China's outbound investment and inbound FDI, runs from Sept. 8 to 11 this year, drawing delegations from 129 countries and regions. ■

Eastern Africa braces for heavy rains, floods amid grim El Nino forecast
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:32 CST
22:21:32 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Climate scientists have cautioned that El Nino's impact will be severe and vary across eastern Africa, heavily influenced by localized geography and fluctuating Indian Ocean sea temperatures.
Hussen Seid Endris, head of the climate diagnostic and prediction unit at the Intergovernmental Authority on Development's Climate Prediction and Applications Center, told Xinhua that El Nino brings contrasting weather extremes across the region.
Between October and December, the phenomenon drives above-normal rainfall, elevating flood risks in Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania.
"Increased rainfall can be beneficial for crop production, livestock, pasture and water resources," Seid noted. "However, if rainfall is excessive or occurs in short, intense episodes, it can cause flooding, waterlogging, soil erosion, crop damage and losses of livestock and agricultural infrastructure."
Kenya has stepped up its El Nino preparedness by establishing a National Crisis Communication Center. The government also activated its National Contingency Plan to strengthen response capabilities and streamline emergency coordination across vulnerable regions.
In August, Tanzania Meteorological Authority Director General Ladislaus Chang'a told local media that heavy rainfall is set to begin in September and persist throughout the October-December season, extending well into 2027.
"We are issuing two warnings. The first is related to the presence of a strong El Nino heading toward October, November and December. Periods of heavy rainfall could begin as early as September," Chang'a said.
Meanwhile, Alfred Okot Okidi, permanent secretary in Uganda's Ministry of Water and Environment, advised in a weather update that El Nino conditions are expected to peak across Uganda between late October and early November.
"Communities in low-lying and flood-prone areas should relocate to safe areas. Communities are advised to plant trees to reduce run-off speed of the water and install lightning arrestors in risk areas," he said.
Fidele Bingwa, permanent secretary in the Rwandan Ministry of Environment, recently told Rwanda's New Times newspaper that extreme weather conditions can rapidly escalate into severe humanitarian and economic crises.
"For Rwanda, this means preparing for the potential impacts of heavy rainfall, including floods and landslides, and the effects these may have on communities, agriculture and infrastructure," Bingwa said.
The warnings align with broader assessments from the World Meteorological Organization, which designated the Greater Horn of Africa as one of the regions most vulnerable to El Nino's cascading effects.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that, fueled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, the El Nino event is expected to intensify and peak toward the end of the year, with far-reaching impacts continuing into 2027.
Seid called for the use of technology, in particular artificial intelligence, to complement conventional weather forecasting.
"AI can integrate information from satellites, weather stations, numerical models and other sources to generate more timely and actionable early warnings. This is particularly valuable for Africa, where observation networks and computational resources remain limited," he said. ■

PRETORIA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 0.2 percent in the second quarter (Q2) of 2026, snapping a six-quarter growth streak, according to data released by Statistics South Africa (Stats SA) on Tuesday.
The latest data followed a 0.4-percent expansion in the first quarter of the year, and Statistician-General and Head of Stats SA Risenga Maluleke told Xinhua that the contraction was largely in the areas of manufacturing and trade.
Data shows that the trade, catering and accommodation industry contracted by 1.9 percent in Q2, while manufacturing shrank by 1.8 percent, marking its third consecutive quarterly decline.

Speaking to Xinhua, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), which represents almost 2 million workers, called for government action to support workers and the economy.
COSATU Parliamentary Coordinator Matthew Parks said the contraction in key sectors reflected the impact of higher fuel prices and declining global tourism, which had put pressure on workers, consumers, small businesses and the broader economy.
"It is critical that government put in place an economic and social relief package to help shield the working class and the economy from the steep hikes in international oil and thus domestic fuel prices, inflation and the inevitable global economic slowdown," Parks said. ■

Kremlin spokesman comments on Ukraine settlement roadmaps, budget deficit, gas prices

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented on the absence of road maps for the Ukrainian settlement, gas prices and the situation surrounding the budget deficit.
TASS has compiled key statements from the Kremlin Spokesman.
Putin’s schedule
- Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding talks with his Vietnamese counterpart To Lam.
- They will open a modern laboratory for the study of infections via videoconference, and will conclude the program by giving a statement to the press.
- In addition, the Vietnamese leader will be awarded the Leo Tolstoy International Peace Prize.
-. After the completion of To Lam’s state visit program, Putin will hold a number of meetings on domestic political issues.
Ukraine settlement
- The roadmap for the Ukrainian settlement, which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently mentioned, does not currently exist in any form: "We don’t want to, and we won’t discuss any 'points' in a public format," he noted. "Especially since there are no formal roadmaps as of now."
- Russia expects the launch of trilateral Russian-US-Ukrainian negotiations in the foreseeable future: "There is a common initiative, a common political will that has been confirmed, to move toward the resumption of trilateral negotiations. We hope that in the foreseeable future, these negotiations will be resumed."
- "Work on the exchange of prisoners with Ukraine continues."
Russian economy
- Russian authorities ensure macroeconomic stability despite current budget indicators: "Macroeconomic stability is definitely being maintained."
- That is why the current budget deficit, which is a variable figure anyway, is no cause for concern: "This figure [the budget deficit] is not an indicator that should cause any serious concern."
- The government doesn't plan to increase taxes to help stabilize the budget: "There has been no mention of this [tax increases]."
Prisoner exchanges with US
- Exchanges of detained and convicted individuals remain on the agenda of contacts between Russia and the United States, including at the highest level: "We continue to work on the exchange of detainees, arrested individuals and those serving sentences between Russia and the United States. This matter is regularly raised during Russian-American contacts, including at the highest level. You know well that at the request of [US leader Donald] Trump, an American national who was serving a sentence has been released by order of Russian President [Vladimir Putin]. This work continues."
Gas market situation
- Russian gas could have been a cheaper alternative for European countries if they were guided by common sense: "By any logic and based on common sense, Europeans should, of course, be looking for cheaper sources of energy and cheaper gas. Russian gas could have long been a cheaper option for them, including Russian pipeline gas and Russian liquefied natural gas, although LNG is always sold at the spot price."
- There are problems with filling European underground gas storage facilities: "Europeans are currently in a very difficult situation, as has been said repeatedly. They are facing problems with filling their underground gas storage facilities. And even if they reach maximum injection rates, they will no longer be able to complete the process before the onset of winter."
- European exchange-traded gas prices of $950 per 1,000 cubic meters are not at their peak, with new records still ahead: "Even if they [Europeans] reach maximum injection rates, they will no longer be able to do this before winter arrives. This shows that the current level of exchange-traded gas prices is not a record. New records will be set further down the road. And the Europeans are aware of this."
- Political bias is preventing Europe from using the intact Nord Stream pipeline string: "Common sense would suggest that Nord Stream should have been put to use long ago, as one of its strings remains intact and operational. And it can be brought online virtually overnight, so to speak."
- Moscow sees "Europeans hurting themselves, their economies and their people by buying gas on the spot market at a price significantly higher than that of Russian pipeline gas."
Potential trilateral Russia-US-China summit
- A trilateral summit involving Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen: "Certainly, this possibility [a trilateral summit involving Russia, the US President and China at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit] was mentioned earlier as well, and there is such a chance."
Expulsion of Russian diplomats by Hungary
- Hungary’s decision to expel Russian diplomats will negatively affect the relations between Moscow and Budapest: "[Hungary’s unfriendly steps] will definitely have a negative effect. Undoubtedly, this will have negative consequences for the entirety of our bilateral relations."
- Moscow will give Budapest an appropriate response to Budapest’s actions: "As for this specific decision, of course, an appropriate response will be provided, [it] will not go unanswered.
- Russia is open to developing relations with Hungary and does not want to harm Moscow-Budapest ties: "At the same time, we remain open to further developing our ties. We are interested in this, especially since we do not want to harm the long-term history of Russia-Hungary bilateral relations."

China Focus: Top court takes juvenile crime prevention into classroom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:03 CST
22:21:03 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- When China's top judge walked into a Beijing classroom for a back-to-school legal lesson earlier this week, he did not begin with legal provisions or courtroom procedures.
Instead, Supreme People's Court (SPC) President Zhang Jun asked teenagers to think about something closer to their daily lives: how to seek respect, recognition, friendship and a sense of belonging without crossing legal and social boundaries.
Drawing on real-life cases involving minors, Zhang discussed behavioral tendencies that can emerge during adolescence, including an excessive concern with "saving face," a desire to attract attention, and blind loyalty to friends.
Zhang said such needs were not inherently problematic, but should be understood, expressed and pursued within the framework of law and rules. He urged students to distinguish right from wrong, think independently, make calm judgments and dare to say no, rather than blindly following friends. He also said violence could not solve problems but would only escalate conflicts, urging students to de-escalate disputes and resolve them through reason.
The lesson was Zhang's ninth at Beijing No. 2 Middle School, where he serves as a "rule-of-law vice principal." Over the years, his lessons have evolved from basic legal awareness and minors' rights to self-protection, different forms of protection for minors, family-school cooperation, online safety, juvenile crime prevention and, most recently, behavioral guidance for teenagers.
Zhang's role at the school is part of a broader effort to bring legal professionals into classrooms. Under a system formalized nationwide in 2022, primary and secondary schools are required to appoint at least one "rule-of-law vice principal," typically a legal professional from a court, procuratorate, public security organ or judicial administrative department. By the end of 2024, nearly 40,000 judges nationwide were serving in the role, according to the SPC.
Judges, prosecutors and other legal professionals serving as "rule-of-law vice principals" have specialized legal knowledge and extensive experience handling cases involving minors, allowing them to make legal education more practical and targeted, said Yuan Ningning, deputy director of the research base for juvenile affairs governance and law at China University of Political Science and Law. They can also provide professional advice on school governance and help prevent and resolve risks, conflicts and disputes, Yuan added.
The same focus on behavioral guidance is reflected in efforts to strengthen legal education for minors nationwide. Guidelines issued in May by the SPC, the Ministry of Education, the Communist Youth League of China and the All-China Women's Federation called for more targeted education and behavioral guidance, including strengthening awareness of the law and behavioral boundaries, promoting healthy friendships, correcting excessive concern with "saving face," addressing negative emotions, improving conflict-resolution skills and preventing excessive internet use.
The emphasis on prevention comes against the backdrop of a decline in juvenile crime indicators. Official data show that procuratorial organs accepted 91,573 juvenile suspects for review and prosecution in 2025, down 9.8 percent year on year.
Meanwhile, courts nationwide concluded about 38,000 juvenile criminal cases involving 53,000 minors in 2025, with growth in both figures slowing markedly from the previous year. In the first half of 2026, courts concluded 16,300 juvenile criminal cases, down 6.22 percent year on year, according to the SPC.
China has also expanded specialized judicial mechanisms for minors. By the end of 2024, courts nationwide had more than 2,700 juvenile courts. More than 9,100 judges were handling juvenile cases.
The approach extends beyond the courtroom. China is working to strengthen coordination among families, schools, society, the internet, government and the judiciary in protecting minors, with greater emphasis on identifying and addressing risks at an early stage, rather than relying solely on judicial intervention after problems arise.
The Family Education Promotion Law calls for closer coordination among families, schools and society in educating minors, while recent judicial initiatives have also strengthened family education guidance and coordination among the different forms of protection for minors.
In his lesson, Zhang urged students to control their emotions and maintain boundaries. Teachers, he said, should guide students in recognizing behavioral boundaries and identify and correct problematic tendencies at an early stage.
The people's courts will work with all sectors of society to address problems at an early stage and support the healthy development of minors, he added. ■

Doctor: Pärnu methanol tragedy the first major touchstone for Covid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:21:00 UTC
22:21:00 KST

Doctor: Pärnu methanol tragedy the first major touchstone for Covid
Wednesday marks 25 years since the Pärnu methanol tragedy. In September 2001, 154 people suffered methanol poisoning, 68 of whom died.
Raido Paasma, then head of the intensive care unit at Pärnu Hospital and a clinical toxicologist and anesthesiologist, told ETV's "Ringvaade" that although a quarter of a century has passed since the tragedy, he still remembers many of the details.
At the time, Estonia was still a young country, having regained its independence just 10 years earlier, and incomes were limited. People bought alcohol on the black market where it was cheaper than in stores. To maximize their profits, illicit alcohol sellers mixed cheap methanol into vodka to increase the volume.
"People who knew where they could get their illicit vodka went there to buy it. If we look at the date, September 9 is right around the time pensions were paid. People had received their wages and pensions and it was also potato-harvesting season, so they went and stocked up. That's how it happened," Paasma said.
Paasma believes the people who mixed the drinks did not know how much harm they would cause. "To them, it was alcohol. The fact that it had one less H didn't bother them much."
The scale of the methanol poisoning was significant, but Paasma said the proportion of deaths was not exceptionally high compared with previous mass poisonings. "There have also been cases where 70 to 80 percent of those who consumed it died," he said.
Methanol is converted into a toxic metabolite in the body and ethanol is used as an antidote to treat methanol poisoning. During treatment, the concentration of ethanol in the blood must be kept sufficiently high; otherwise, the body begins to break down the methanol. This process produces toxic formic acid.
Drinking methanol does not cause the typical intoxication associated with ethanol. It also tastes different from regular vodka. "A couple of patients told me at the time, 'It was a damn strange drink. I drank it but didn't get drunk at all and it tasted strange too,'" Paasma recalled.
The mass poisoning was a major test for Pärnu Hospital. The hospital did not have sufficient capacity to treat all the patients, so some had to be transferred to other hospitals.
"We distributed the patients because we realized that our capacity to treat them on site was very limited. We could begin initial treatment, but then we needed somewhere with dialysis and greater intensive care capacity than Pärnu had at the time. Estonia's entire healthcare system responded to it and it responded as one. I think it was the first test ahead of the later Covid pandemic."
Paasma estimated that the most difficult period of the crisis lasted about a week and a half. Twenty-five patients died in the hospital, while 43 people were found dead outside the hospital. "When the poisoning has progressed so far that the heart is still working but the brain has already been damaged and the person develops what is known as brain death, unfortunately there is nothing that can be done."
Methanol poisonings still occur in Estonia today, but they are rare. "A month ago, there was a patient who had drunk methanol," Paasma said. "I don't know whether he is still alive. He did not regain consciousness, but his heart was working and he was able to breathe."
Paasma said methanol poisoning nevertheless remains widespread around the world, particularly in Asian countries. He cited three reasons: people seeking cheaper alcohol, poor availability of alcohol and religious restrictions on alcohol.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Marcus Turovski
Source: "Ringvaade"

====================================================================================================

‘A single wrong step’: Women deminers reach where men cannot to protect children in Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:20:51 UTC
22:20:51 KST

In a dry field in Syria’s Idlib countryside, Lama Haj Kaddour holds a detonator, steady and practised.
She and her all-female team have spent hours locating and safely approaching a buried landmine. A short distance away, the rest of the team waits, still and silent.
When the blast goes off, a column of smoke rises from where the mine had been.
Kaddour wears a protective vest over her clothes. Like her colleagues, she dresses fully in black with only her eyes visible, in line with social norms in Idlib.
Fourteen years of civil war have left Syria littered with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW). The threat has followed families back to the villages they fled, even after the end of a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and devastated the economy.
Kaddour is one of 31 women now working in operational roles in Idlib’s demining effort, according to The HALO Trust, an international NGO involved in Syria’s demining work.
They clear landmines, survey contaminated ground and teach communities how to recognise the dangers left behind by the civil war.
Kaddour, a 33-year-old mother of three, left the Hama countryside for Idlib in 2019. She first worked with relief organisations before joining The HALO Trust.
In a conservative region like Idlib, being a woman can carry a particular advantage in demining work.
“A woman working in this field can enter local households and speak directly with women and children in ways her male colleagues often cannot, giving her direct access to a part of the community that is otherwise hard to reach in a conservative context,” Emma Pomfret, Global Media Manager for The HALO Trust, tells TRT World.
Women remain a minority in demining worldwide.
A 2019 survey of a dozen mine action operators published by the Journal of Conventional Weapons Destruction found that women made up only around 20 percent of mine action staff globally, with clearance roles particularly male-dominated.
According to Pomfret, however, more women are entering the field in Syria.
The fall of the Assad regime in late 2024 removed severe operational restrictions that had constrained HALO’s work, she says, allowing the organisation to expand training and clearance into areas including Daraa and the northwest and recruit from a much larger pool of people.
“When the Assad regime fell in December 2024, HALO opened recruitment and training to women, as we do on all of our programmes globally,” she says.
Supporting landmine survivors
In training hubs such as Daraa, women now make up about 20 percent of new demining trainees — eight out of a recent class of 40, according to Pomfret. As HALO expands beyond 250 staff nationwide, women are increasingly working as manual deminers, team supervisors, paramedics and community educators.
The shift is not only about new opportunities. Some of the women joining HALO were widowed during the war and are now the main breadwinners for their families, Pomfret says.
Kaddour's own path into demining began earlier. She started by supporting landmine survivors before training for fieldwork in 2022 and taking on the work of clearing unexploded ordnance herself.
“I could never live with the idea that a single wrong step by my children could set off a landmine that ends their lives, or takes one of their limbs,” Kaddour tells TRT World.
More than three million displaced people have returned to areas badly damaged by the conflict. Many find their homes still standing, but the roads leading to them contaminated.
Raed al-Hassoun, director of clearance operations at Syria’s National Mine Action Centre, tells TRT World that 49 landmine incidents were recorded across the country between the start of 2026 and the end of August, killing 24 people and injuring 61.
On August 31, an unexploded object detonated in the village of Faydat Ibn Muwaina in the Deir Ezzor countryside as children were handling it. Four children were killed and one was injured, according to SANA.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) says at least 3,799 civilians — including 1,000 children and 377 women — have been killed by landmines and cluster munition remnants across Syria since March 2011, with 329 of those deaths recorded since December 2024.
The highest tolls were recorded in Aleppo, with 814 deaths, followed by Raqqa with 676 and Deir Ezzor with 645. Hama, Daraa and Idlib were also among the worst affected.
According to SNHR, the Assad regime, Russian forces and terror groups have planted landmines across Syrian territory since 2011, often without marking or recording their locations.
Siba Abdul Karim, a 36-year-old mother of two who heads the non-technical survey department at The HALO Trust, says floods and heavy rains can expose or move buried mines and other war remnants.
“The danger isn’t necessarily fixed where the war left it,” she tells TRT World
“Floodwater, like what we saw in late August, can reshape the land and carry buried explosive objects with it, rendering old maps insufficient. Ground that seemed safe yesterday can become a fresh hazard after a flood or landslide.”
Abdul Karim and her colleagues have chosen to confront that danger directly.
The women say years of war have made them less afraid of the risks involved in their work.
“Every morning, I say goodbye to my children before leaving for the field. Every evening, when I walk back through the door, I give thanks that I made it home unharmed,” Abdul Karim tells TRT World.
She recalls once calming a child who had found an explosive device, reassuring him before explaining the danger of what he had found.
Also working in the field is Mariam al Asaad, 26, who is married and has an eight-year-old daughter.
For nearly four years, al Asaad has volunteered with the Syrian Civil Defence, also known as the White Helmets, conducting non-technical surveys and risk education and helping map contaminated areas. In 2022, she received specialised training in survey and munitions classification, becoming one of the first women to join Syria’s ERW teams.
Every morning, al Asaad kisses her daughter goodbye before leaving for the field. When she returns home, she faces the challenge of balancing a dangerous job with motherhood.
“I worry all the time about the balance between my daughter and this job,” she tells TRT World.
For al Asaad, the work is also personal. Her father owned land east of Idlib that was contaminated with landmines the family did not know were there.
In 2017, as fighting around Idlib eased, he returned to tend to the family’s olive grove, taking al Asaad’s younger brother, then nine years old, with him.
“A landmine exploded when my brother threw a stone at the ground. It tore into his left foot,” she says.
With no way of knowing how many more mines lay buried there, the family abandoned the land.
“My father spent his final years watching the trees go wild, and the little fruit that still fell just rotted on the ground,” she says. “We ended up buying olive oil every season, even though we had a grove that used to give us our own.”
Al Asaad believes the grief of losing access to the land took a heavy toll on her father’s health.
Waiting for the land back
In the village of Dadikh in the Idlib countryside, Abu Mohammad al Ali, 62, owns land that was once his family’s sole source of livelihood. The war has turned it into a place he can no longer enter.
He grew olive and fruit trees there, relying on the harvest to support his family, before mines and other war remnants contaminated the land.
“We used to come here at first light, plough, plant, and tend to the trees,” al Ali tells TRT World.
“Today I’m afraid to take a single step onto my own land. The trees we worked so hard to grow have died because we can no longer reach them to water them and care for them.”
According to al Ali, his land was the scene of clashes and aerial bombardment during the war.
Assad regime forces, backed by Russian air support, attempted to advance towards the edges of the village but were unable to take the area from local forces.
His land lay along the front line.
Months of fighting left the land heavily contaminated with mines and other remnants of war, making it inaccessible even after the fighting stopped.
“Fear is part of daily life for my family and everyone in the village,” he says.
He recalls an incident in 2025 when a mine exploded on his land while a child was nearby.
Since then, he has struggled with the thought that land that once fed his family could instead kill a child.
“Farmers in Dadikh live between leaving their land and losing their livelihood, or returning to it with the possibility that the next step could be their last,” he says.
“The hardest part is that when I look at my land, I still see it as it used to be. I see the trees, and I remember the seasons we used to wait for. But today I can't get close to it.”
“We just want the mines removed, and to know the land is safe before we send our children there or go back to farming it ourselves,” he adds.
Alongside clearance efforts, UNICEF and its partners are teaching children and families to recognise mine risks before demining teams can reach contaminated areas.
Fouad Mansour, a project manager at UNICEF, tells TRT World that the agency and its partners reached roughly 850,000 children, parents and caregivers with mine-risk education in 2025 and trained around 400 specialists.
“We use pictures, stories, games and visual material to turn a frightening fact into a behaviour a child can remember: don’t touch the strange object, move away from it, and tell an adult or the relevant authority,” he says.
Mansour says UNICEF works with 38 partners across mine clearance, victim assistance, risk education and advocacy.
It has also supported the development of a national risk-education framework integrated into the curriculum in coordination with Syria’s Ministry of Education.
A national effort to bring order
At the national level, Syria’s National Mine Action Centre is coordinating efforts by international and local organisations.
“We are currently developing the national standards that will govern the work of organisations in this field,” Raed al Hassoun says.
“We are also building a national information management system to collect the data that will underpin a roadmap for addressing landmine and ERW risk according to national priorities.”
Among the centre’s priorities is completing a national non-technical survey to determine the location, type and scale of contamination, amid what al Hassoun describes as limited capacity to address the problem's scale.
“Our own figures are still incomplete,” he says, adding that the national survey under way is intended to close that gap.
Military engineering teams from the Ministry of Defence and dedicated units from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management also take part in clearance operations, he says.
“The reconstruction of Syria’s battered infrastructure depends first and foremost on resolving the mine issue,” al Hassoun says, pointing to the Jobar district of Damascus as an example.
At the request of the Damascus governorate, the centre established an operations room that brought together the HALO Trust, the International Committee of the Red Cross, teams from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management, and Red Crescent non-technical survey teams.
Together, they cleared Jobar’s main and side roads, allowing reconstruction work to begin.

Settlements isolate Palestinian communities from their lands in occupied West Bank: Israeli rights groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:20:04 UTC
22:20:04 KST

Abderaouf Arnaout, Ikram Kouachi
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Three Israeli rights organizations said on Wednesday that settlement expansion and land seizures are extending deeper into the occupied West Bank, isolating Palestinian communities from their lands.
A joint report by Yesh Din, Bimkom - Planners for Planning Rights and HaMoked documented the expansion of land seizure policies, occupier violence and movement restrictions, saying such measures have spread from small Palestinian communities in Area C to towns and wider areas across the West Bank.
Area C, which is under Israeli security and civil control, accounts for more than 60% of the occupied West Bank.
According to the report, what may appear to be separate measures – settlement expansion, pastoral outposts, occupier violence and movement restrictions – form a “continuous process” that pushes Palestinians away from their lands and confines them to increasingly smaller areas.
The report examined four cases, including the Al-Rummana community in Jericho in the eastern West Bank, where it said Palestinians face attacks, harassment and movement restrictions.
It also documented the case of Sinjil in the central West Bank, where settlement outposts, fences and closures have contributed to isolating residents from their agricultural lands.
The organizations said the “seizure of Palestinian land, isolation of communities from their lands and fragmentation of Palestinian geographic contiguity collectively constitute part of a process of de facto annexation taking shape on the ground.”
They said measures implemented for years against small communities in Area C are now extending to entire towns and areas deep inside the West Bank.
“The Israeli government is no longer hiding its goal: annexing as much land as possible with as few Palestinians as possible,” the report said.
The organizations added that settlements, outposts, occupier violence and movement restrictions “work together to achieve the same goal,” describing the developments as a “shift from a political project to a reality imposed on the ground.”
Since taking office in late 2022, the current government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has approved the establishment of 104 new settlements, while 160 agricultural settlement outposts have been established in the West Bank, according to Palestinian data.
In the first half of 2026, Israeli occupiers carried out 3,488 attacks in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian government’s Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The attacks killed 17 Palestinians and fully or partially displaced 26 Bedouin and pastoral communities, while 42 new settlement outposts were established, the commission said.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 illegal outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian figures.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. The international community considers Israeli settlements in the occupied territories illegal under international law, a position Israel rejects.

Exhibition explores Glagolitic as a symbol of memory and communication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:19:36 UTC
22:19:36 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
Exhibition explores Glagolitic as a symbol of memory and communication
Wednesday 9 September 2026 15:30
Wednesday, 9 September 2026, 15:30
PHOTO Ani Pertova
Font size
Bulgarian National Radio is hosting an exhibition devoted to the Glagolitic alphabet. Glagolitic was the first European alphabet whose creator is known by name – Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher. The exhibition’s title, Around the World with Glagolitic, reflects its central message: to bring Bulgarians around the world together and remind them of their roots and their past in Bulgaria, wherever they may live and whatever led them to leave the country.
The exhibition is curated by Mira Svilenova, a Bulgarian who has lived in Canada for almost 20 years. Her professional background is in marketing and communications, so her creative interest in language and writing is perhaps no surprise.
In an interview with Radio Bulgaria, Svilenova explained what prompted her to make Glagolitic the central theme of an exhibition:
“I have been working with Glagolitic as an artist for three years now. During that time, I have begun to notice a certain consistency in the way people respond to it, whether I exhibit in Bulgaria or abroad. This exhibition is part of a research project of mine aimed at creating an interactive Glagolitic primer, which should be ready by the middle of 2027.
PHOTO Ani Petrova
“But I am also exploring Glagolitic as a bridge for building international relations and as a tool for media literacy. Today, media and technology move and develop very quickly. They carry culture and identity, and if that happens through Glagolitic, it could prompt us to think more deeply about how culture and identity are transmitted through modern technology.”
Speaking at the opening, BNR Director General Milen Mitev recalled the words attributed to Leonardo da Vinci that “the spirit and the heart must guide the hand, otherwise there is no art”. Contemporary art, he noted, can often be difficult to understand and provoke mixed reactions. This exhibition, however, is different: it carries a sense of Bulgarian cultural memory and of the enduring bond between Bulgarians at home and around the world.
“I am particularly pleased that Glagolitic is at the heart of this exhibition. It was the first alphabet created specifically for writing and understanding the Slavic languages, back in the 9th century. But it is much more than an alphabet – it represents an aspiration for an independent cultural identity and a philosophy encoded in symbols. It is a link to our Bulgarian roots.
PHOTO Ani Petrova
“Perhaps it is only natural that we are seeing growing interest in Glagolitic today. Various calligraphy courses are appearing, and more and more young people are learning to write their names in Glagolitic. This shows that even today, this first Bulgarian script remains an essential part of our identity as Bulgarians.”
Around the World with Glagolitic will remain on display in the Marble Foyer outside BNR’s Studio One until September 25.
The exhibition has been organised with the support of the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad.

Knocking on the king’s door: Jamaica demands answers on slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:19:30 UTC
22:19:30 KST

Why Jamaica’s petition to King Charles is rattling Western capitals
On September 7, 2026, a high-level Jamaican delegation delivered a historic legal petition to Buckingham Palace addressed to King Charles III. Its objective was to compel the monarch, as Jamaica’s head of state, to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the island’s highest court of appeal, three questions that have haunted the British Empire for centuries. Was the forced transportation of Africans to Jamaica and their subsequent enslavement lawful? Did this system constitute a crime against humanity? Does the United Kingdom bear an obligation to make reparation for slavery and its enduring consequences?
Culture Minister Olivia Grange, who led the delegation, shared a photo on X of herself holding the document aloft, captioned: “The petition has been filed.” King Charles III was not present at the handover. British media reported he was on vacation at the time, though Buckingham Palace said it had worked closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition was properly lodged.
Why the date is no coincidence
The day before, on Sunday, September 6, the delegation had taken part in a church service in south London under the theme of “remembrance, justice and repair,” ahead of the formal filing the following day. This timing is no accident: September 6 commemorates the 1781 departure of the slave ship Zong, aboard which more than 140 enslaved Africans were thrown into the sea so their owners could collect an insurance payout. That crime, unpunished for 245 years, now stands as the symbol of a justice the diaspora refuses to let fade into oblivion.
“In relation to the wrongs that were done, we want answers,” Grange told the Associated Press the day before the filing. “Once we get those answers, then our attorneys will determine what the next move is.”
This petition is part of a strategy, built step by step by Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations chaired by Laleta Davis Mattis, with the support of a legal subcommittee led by attorney Bert Samuels, and a team of UK lawyers. The Caribbean Community (CARICOM) has thrown its full weight behind the effort proof that this question reaches beyond the borders of a single island. The entire post-slavery Caribbean is rising behind Jamaica.
The UN slavery resolution as a first step
But it is precisely here that Jamaica’s fight joins Africa’s own, and this link must now be made visible, since Western media have worked hard to keep it quiet. On March 25, 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted, on Ghana’s initiative, resolution A/RES/80/250 – the very first resolution in UN history devoted exclusively to slavery and the transatlantic slave trade.
One hundred and twenty-three states voted in favor. Only three opposed it: the United States, Israel, and Argentina. Fifty-two countries, mostly European including the United Kingdom itself, chose to hide behind abstention.
The resolution designates the transatlantic trafficking of Africans and racialized chattel enslavement as the “gravest crime against humanity.” Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, speaking on behalf of the African Group of 54 states, the UN’s largest regional bloc, declared that voting for the text meant standing on the right side of history. It calls for the restitution of looted cultural property, formal apologies, and opens the door to the consideration of financial compensation. This is an international normative framework, patiently built by the African Union since February 2024, when it proclaimed 2025 the “Year of Justice for Africans through Reparations for Slavery, Colonialism, and Apartheid.”
Jamaican jurist Bert Samuels was not mistaken when he stated that this UN resolution strengthens Jamaica’s legal position against London. Here is the thread that binds Accra to Kingston, the African motherland to the diaspora torn from it. A single struggle is fought on two complementary fronts – one continental and diplomatic, the other insular and judicial, both aimed at the same goal of making the former empire pay for four centuries of human plunder.
A history of reversed debts
To grasp the full weight of this gesture, one must recall that Haiti, the first free black nation of the modern era, was forced in 1825 to pay France a colossal indemnity to “compensate” former slave owners for the loss of their “human property” – a debt that bled Haiti’s economy for more than a century. History, as written by the colonial powers, long decreed that it was the enslavers who deserved compensation, never the enslaved.
Jamaica’s petition overturns this criminal logic. It is no longer the victims who owe the executioner, it is the executioner who must now answer to its victims. This reversal builds on groundwork laid over more than a decade by the CARICOM itself, which as early as 2013 adopted its own ten-point plan for reparatory justice, demanding formal apologies, debt cancellation, technology transfers, and public health programs to offset the health devastation bequeathed by slavery.
The September 7 filing is therefore the legal culmination of a long matured Caribbean strategy that has now chosen to confront head on, in a court of law, the very institution that sanctioned and protected the slave system: the British Crown.
What it means for the diaspora
For the African diaspora across Africa, the Americas, Europe, and the Caribbean alike, this filing is experienced as a long-deferred reckoning. For generations, our elders awaited a political gesture of this magnitude – a formal legal demand addressed directly to the head of the house that organized, financed, and profited from the trade.
Reparations movements that once fought each in their own corner Caribbean organizations, Afro-descendant collectives in the Americas, African diasporas in Europe, activists on the continent itself are beginning to speak with a single voice, carried by recognized institutions: the African Union on one side, CARICOM on the other, and now the UN as a global sounding board.
In West Africa, Jamaica’s move is being followed with particular attention, seen as the natural extension of the fight President Mahama carried to the UN stage. The Africa that watched its children leave in chains is, four centuries later, reunited with a part of its diaspora now come to knock, together, on the same imperial door. In Southern Africa, where the memory of apartheid remains raw, many Pan-African organizations see in this filing further proof that struggles for historical justice slavery, colonialism, apartheid can no longer be treated separately, but must be understood as a single, unified case against the West.
In Europe, among Afro-descendant communities in France, Belgium, and the United Kingdom itself, Jamaica’s petition serves as both a signal of hope and a painful reminder: That our own states of origin or residence still drag their feet on these questions, while little Jamaica, with its modest means, dared to carry the fight directly to the monarch’s door. In the Americas, Afro-descendant movements from Brazil to Colombia are also watching this case closely, seeing in it a potential legal precedent that could be mobilized for their own claims against the former Iberian colonial powers.
This convergence is visibly rattling Western capitals. The United Kingdom’s vote – an abstention, that is, a refusal to choose – speaks volumes about the quiet panic setting in London. One can sense, in the remarks of certain British political figures, particularly within Euroskeptic and identitarian factions, a desire to ridicule Jamaica’s move, to dismiss it as an expensive whim or a political stunt.
The united voice to reclaim the debt
Critical voices, including within the Pan-African movement itself, warn of the risks inherent in the path Kingston has chosen. Entrusting a body like the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council – an institution shaped by the British colonial order itself – with judging the legality of slavery risks a ruling that the trade was, at the time, perfectly “lawful” under the British law then in force. Such a verdict, should it come to pass, would hand Western governments a legal argument to close the reparations file for good.
Some observers have already noted that the Privy Council may look at this petition with a degree of skepticism not over whether slavery was wrong, but over the unusual nature of the legal procedure being invoked.
This is why the battle must never be reduced to this single procedure. Jamaica’s strength lies precisely in waging the fight on multiple fronts at once: the legal path before the Privy Council, the diplomatic path through CARICOM, and now the backing of international law embodied in Ghana’s UN resolution. Prime Minister Andrew Holness has, moreover, announced plans to sever ties with the British Crown and transform his country into a republic – a signal that a rejection of the petition by London could, paradoxically, accelerate that rupture rather than prevent it.
None of these paths, taken alone, will be enough. It is their combination that builds the leverage.
When the Jamaican delegation crossed the palace threshold to deliver its petition, it was the echo of 123 nations gathered in New York this past March 25. It was the voice of the African Union, of Ghanaian President Mahama, of reparations movements from Accra to Bridgetown, from Lagos to Brooklyn. It was the voice of an entire diaspora that now refuses to let the history of slavery remain a closed chapter that was never paid for.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Exports hit a record NT$2.59 trillion (US$82.4 billion) in August, rising 41% from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance said Wednesday.
The ministry said August marked the 34th consecutive month of growth, per CNA. Imports rose 44.3% to NT$1.89 trillion, the third-highest monthly level on record, driven by demand from the AI supply chain, export-related production, and higher raw material prices.
Electronic components led export growth, rising 58% from a year earlier on strong AI demand and higher memory prices and shipments, UDN. Exports to all five major markets grew by double digits in August, with shipments to China and Japan reaching monthly records, per UDN. Exports to the US, ASEAN, Europe, and Japan rose 20.7%, 42.2%, 34.8%, and 32%, while shipments to Mexico and Australia more than doubled.
The ministry said geopolitical conflicts and changes in US tariff policy remain risks to global growth. However, AI adoption, demand for computing power, and investment in AI infrastructure are expected to support the semiconductor and server supply chains and keep exports growing in the second half of the year.

Taiwan delivery platforms face penalties over courier safety training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:19:06 UTC
22:19:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Delivery couriers will be barred from working until they complete safety training after two major traffic violations on the job within six months.
Platforms face fines of NT$100,000 to NT$500,000 (US$3,170 to US$15,870) for letting affected couriers work or failing to handle training, per UDN. The rules take effect Friday following Wednesday’s announcement by the Ministry of Transportation and Communications.
Couriers must finish the course within one month of official notification to their platform, per Knews. At least four hours of instruction must cover driver ethics, defensive driving, and traffic laws.
Authorities may also order the remedial course for conduct, apart from repeat violations, that they judge to have a major effect on road safety. A single major violation within six months would trigger counseling or other corrective steps.
The rules set a separate baseline for training. Platforms must give new couriers one hour of traffic safety instruction, and returning couriers must complete one hour each year beginning the year after they join. Couriers who have not finished the required training cannot take delivery orders.
Fines of NT$20,000 to NT$100,000 apply if platforms miss an official deadline to remedy failures to provide routine training. Other safety management breaches carry penalties of NT$9,000 to NT$90,000 under the Highway Act, per Knews.
Platforms must send regulators updated courier and vehicle lists each month. When a major violation appears in the data, regulators will ask the platform for the courier’s work records before passing the case back to the company.
Hiring checks must verify that couriers have valid licenses, acceptable driving records, and vehicles in normal condition. Platforms must also avoid dispatch arrangements that would push couriers outside traffic rules, including route plans, pickup locations, or delivery points.

Elite players in Spain’s women’s national team and staff to be given access to fertility treatments to ease up pressure and better plan if or when to become mothers. The decision comes as Europe grapples with falling fertility rates.
The players of the Spanish women's national team, including futsal, as well as referees and assistant referees in the top division and federation employees, will have access to treatments including egg freezing, in vitro fertilisation, egg donation and genetic testing, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) announced this week.
The initiative is intended to give women working within the RFEF greater freedom to decide when and if to become mothers. Spain's national team won the FIFA Women's World Cup in 2023.
"If Spain and its national teams are the best in the world on the field, they must also be the best in matters such as work-life balance,“ said the president of the RFEF, Rafael Louzán.
The agreement, which runs until spring 2029, will provide access to reproductive, physical and mental health resources, according to Reyes Bellver, the RFEF’s director of women’s football, who said the aim was “adding up and elevating” efforts in support of female athletes.
It comes as Europe is facing the lowest fertility rates in more than six decades, with the number of live births per woman dropping from 2.62 in 1964 to 1.34 in 2024.
Having access to treatments including egg freezing, IVF, egg donation and genetic testing will allow athletes to make better-informed choices with “less pressure,” referee Alicia Espinosa said.
The federation has partnered with Tambre, a fertility clinic group which will "provide rigorous medical information and specialized support so that all female athletes can freely and without pressure decide whether to become mothers now, later, or never," said Inge Kormelink, CEO of Tambre.
The initiative builds on other measures introduced by the federation to improve work-life balance, including provisions in senior national team competitions for players with children.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:17:40 BST
22:17:40 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.
Attending a misconduct hearing
Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).
Please note the following conditions of entry:
- any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)
- any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time
- priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)
- any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing
- members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session
- no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing
- any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing
- where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment
- no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time
- no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient
- we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible
- members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted
If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.
Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.
Private hearings
Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.
Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:
- all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private
- a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing
- specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness
- specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome
If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.

Battlegroup South infantry begins assault on Druzhkovka — Russian Defense Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:17:02 UTC
22:17:02 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Units of Russia’s Battlegroup South, supported by unmanned systems crews, have secured positions on the outskirts of Druzhkovka (in the Donetsk People’s Republic), and infantry troops are already carrying out successful operations to storm the city, deputy company commander of the battlegroup’s separate unmanned systems regiment with the call sign Artist, said in a video released by the Russian Defense Ministry.
"Our crews have secured positions on the outskirts of Druzhkovka. The infantry is already attempting to storm the city itself — and quite successfully," Artist said.
He noted that the units are operating according to a standard plan: cutting off the enemy’s logistics to prevent the delivery of ammunition and supplies, and making maximum use of drones. "Drones are currently the most important deterrent and the key factor enabling our valiant infantry to advance," the service member added.
According to the deputy company commander, the enemy is trying to create the "right media image" for its audience by dropping flags and sending troop groups into populated areas, but these groups do not return. "Konstantinovka is ours, and we have already advanced far beyond Konstantinovka," he emphasized.
Ukraine loses up to 35 soldiers in 'pocket' in Kharkov region over past day
Ukrainian units have lost up to 35 military personnel in the "pocket" in the Kharkov Region over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry has reported.
"Over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s losses have amounted to up to 35 military personnel, one armored fighting vehicle, two ATVs and four ground robotic systems," the ministry stated.
Russian Armed Forces strike power substation at Nikolayev port
Russian forces struck the Trikhaty power substation, which supports the operation of the port of Nikolayev, overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Trikhaty power substation, which supports the operation of the Nikolayev port, has been struck," the ministry said in a statement.
Earlier, the Russian Defense Ministry also reported that last night, the Russian Armed Forces continued to carry out group strikes on military-industrial facilities, Ukrainian seaports and ships, as well as logistics centers supporting the Ukrainian armed forces.
Russian forces tightening encirclement of Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
Russian troops are tightening the inner ring of the encirclement around Ukrainian units in the Kharkov Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Kharkov region, units of the Battlegroup North are tightening the inner ring of the encirclement around enemy forces," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces hit facility producing unmanned boats, drones in Kiev
Russian forces used precision-guided weapons to hit a warehouse of an enterprise producing unmanned boats, drones and components for them in Kiev overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of strikes by precision-guided ground-launched and air-launched weapons, as well as attack unmanned aerial vehicles, [Russian forces] hit a warehouse of an enterprise producing unmanned boats and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as components for them, in the city of Kiev," the ministry said.
Russia delivers group strikes on military industry sites, Ukraine’s sea ports
The Russian Armed Forces continued to deliver group strikes on Ukraine’s military industrial sites and sea ports overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces continued to deliver group strikes on Ukraine’s military industrial sites, sea ports and vessels, as well as logistics centers used in the interests of the Ukrainian military," the statement said.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian military depots in Nikolayev Region
The Russian Armed Forces delivered an overnight high-precision weapons strike on Ukrainian military and fuel and lubricant storage depots in the Nikolayev Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of attacks by high-precision ground-based and air-based weapons and strike drones, [Russian servicemen] struck the following targets in the Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region: <…> the Nikolayev-2 logistics centers used to store military cargo and equipment for the Ukrainian military, the Elektrotechnika logistics center used to store and distribute drones and their spare parts, the Dimetra company warehouse terminal used to store Ukrainian military equipment, the Zhovtnevoye warehouse terminal used to store fuel, lubricants, and Ukrainian military equipment. [Russian forces] also destroyed six tanks with fuel and lubricants intended for the supply of the Ukrainian military and five warehouses with military cargo," the statement said.
Russia hits Ukrainian Starokazachye checkpoint used for military purposes
The Russian Armed Forces delivered a high-precision overnight strike on the Starokazachye automobile checkpoint facilities in the Odessa region that was used to transport military cargo for the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of attacks by high-precision ground-based and air-based weapons and strike drones, [Russian servicemen] struck the Starokazachye automobile checkpoint logistics sites, which were used to transport military cargo into Ukraine," the statement said.
Russian forces strike logistics, energy facilities used by Ukrainian army in Nikolayev
Last night, the Russian Armed Forces carried out strikes with precision weapons against warehouses, logistics facilities, and energy infrastructure used by the Ukrainian armed forces in the city of Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Ground-and air-based precision weapon and attack drone strikes hit the following targets: <…> in the city of Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region: the Nika Terra cargo terminal used to store fuel, lubricants, and military equipment of the Ukrainian armed forces (three tanks containing fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian army and three storage facilities with military cargo were destroyed), as well as an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production facility and storage warehouse located on the terminal’s grounds; the Metro logistics center, used to store Ukrainian military cargo and equipment," the ministry said in a statement.
The Defense Ministry added that strikes were also carried out against the ATP YUTK logistics center, used to store military cargo and property intended to support the Ukrainian armed forces, and the Nova Poshta logistics center, used for the delivery, distribution, and storage of military cargo and materiel for the armed forces of Ukraine.

Palestine urges firm international action to halt Israeli crimes, dismantle settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:17:02 UTC
22:17:02 KST

Qais Abu Samra, Ikram Kouachi
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Palestine's permanent representative to the UN on Wednesday called on the Security Council and the international community to take firm and immediate action to halt Israeli crimes and ethnic cleansing against Palestinians, end the occupation and dismantle the settlement project.
Riyad Mansour made the appeal in a letter to the current president of the UN Security Council, Jerome Bonnafont, outlining Israeli statements and policies, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
He said Israeli statements reveal plans aimed at “forcibly displacing” Palestinians from their land, alongside an “escalation of crimes in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.”
Mansour cited remarks by Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Sept. 2 about displacing Palestinians from the Gaza Strip “by sea and air and by every possible means,” as well as his threats to wage an all-out war in the occupied West Bank and evacuate residents from Palestinian cities and villages.
He also referred to remarks by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Israel would not withdraw from Gaza and that it controls 60% of the enclave, as well as statements by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir about a plan to displace around 1.86 million Palestinians from Gaza over seven years.
Mansour cited Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's remarks about establishing a new settlement near Bethlehem in southern West Bank, his call to bring in 1 million occupiers and his threats to bring down the Palestinian Authority.
Regarding the West Bank, Mansour pointed to the demolition of Khirbet al-Taban in the Masafer Yatta area and the displacement of more than 70 Palestinians, saying it was part of a broader pattern that has seen more than 47 Palestinian communities displaced and erased since October 2023.
Mansour welcomed measures announced by the UK, France, Canada and other countries against trade ban with illegal Israeli settlements, but called for them to be turned into binding measures, including a complete ban on settlement products, sanctions, asset freezes and travel bans against those involved, as well as an end to the transfer of weapons that could be used in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 illegal outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian figures.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. The international community considers Israeli settlements in the occupied territories illegal under international law, a position Israel rejects.

South Africans warned of record fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:16:35 UTC
22:16:35 KST

South Africans warned of record fuel prices
South African motorists could face record petrol prices from October as the ongoing war in the Middle East has pushed global oil prices close to $100 per barrel for the first time since July.
The latest data from the Central Energy Fund points to increases of about R2 ($0.12) per liter for petrol. This would push the price of 95 ULP up to R28.05 at the coast and R28.92 in Gauteng, beating June’s all-time highs of R27.19 and R28.05, respectively.
Diesel is also set for a significant increase, with the data pointing to hikes of between R1.50 for 500ppm and R1.80 for 50ppm. This will push the price of 50ppm up to R30.29 at the coast and R31.85 inland, close to its all-time highs of R30.62 and R31.38, seen earlier this year.
This warning does come with a disclaimer, as the predictions are based on early-month data, which is a moving target, as much can still transpire in the markets between now and the end of this month.
However, with no signs of the Middle East war de-escalating any time soon, leaving uncertainty around the critical Strait of Hormuz oil passage, the risk is currently skewed towards higher oil prices for the foreseeable future.
October’s predicted increases come in the wake of steep price hikes in September, when petrol rose by R1.34 per litre and diesel by between R2.94 and R3.15.
Higher fuel prices can push up inflation and squeeze household spending. Transport, food and other goods become more expensive as fuel costs feed through supply chains, while motorists have less disposable income to spend elsewhere. That can weigh on economic growth. The Reserve Bank has warned that higher fuel prices can raise inflation while weakening consumption and growth.

Starting September 10, Kyiv Metro stations will operate for an extra hour due to the reduction of curfew hours. The operation of the stations as shelters will not change.

Details
All subway stations will operate for one hour longer in passenger service mode. For example, the Universitet metro station, which currently remains open for entry until 22:38, will be open for entry until 23:38 starting September 10. The metro authorities urged passengers to pay attention specifically to the time the station closes for entry, rather than to the schedules of individual trains.
The operating schedule has been designed so that passengers who enter a station before it closes can travel to any other metro station. At the same time, the operating hours of underground stations as shelters will not change
Reminder

Belgian heat wave caused highest excess mortality since 2000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:14:03 UTC
22:14:03 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Belgium’s heat wave at the end of June caused higher excess mortality than predicted by health institute Sciensano’s forecasting models, with 2,112 more deaths than usual recorded between June 18 and July 12, according to the Belga news agency on Wednesday.
The figure represented a relative excess mortality of 31%—the highest number of additional deaths and the highest relative excess mortality recorded during major heat episodes since 2000.
Unlike previous heat waves, when heat-related mortality was concentrated primarily among older women, the June heat wave also affected a higher proportion of older men and working-age men.
The effects varied across the country, with Wallonia more severely affected and a notable spike recorded in the Liegedistrict.
Sciensano’s scientific forecasting models had predicted high excess mortality based on meteorological and environmental risk factors, including minimum nighttime temperatures. However, actual mortality exceeded these forecasts, particularly during the peak on June 27 and 28.
Koen Blot, head of Infectious Disease Epidemiology at Sciensano, said factors such as baseline health status and socioeconomic conditions could potentially explain the difference between the forecasts and the observed mortality.
Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Blot emphasized that these explanations remain “hypotheses.”
Public Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke said work is already underway on a new heat plan, noting the existing Heat and Ozone Plan is insufficient as a comprehensive preparedness plan. The current plan mainly serves as a phase-based communication tool, while the government aims to establish an integrated inter-federal “Heat-Health Preparedness & Response Plan” by summer 2027.
