Notes from Central Taiwan: Localize Taiwan’s drone capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:56 UTC
01:37:56 KST

Drones are widely recognized as a critical weapons technology of the future. Because of this, the pro-China Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) appear to be obstructing their development. One approach to handling this obstruction is to circumvent it by building robust drone capabilities across a wide swathe of the population. Taiwan is doing just that, but more is needed.
The Penghu County Government on Monday said it was testing flying drones on routes from Magong City (馬公), the county seat, to Jibei Island (吉貝嶼). Because all of the inhabited islands lie within 40km of Magong, drones can easily reach them. The drone program, which may include uncrewed sea vessels, is aimed at offering Penghu residents daily necessities. Whether intentional or not, the program mimics the use of drones to provision front line troops and residents in occupied areas, a key function of drones.
Similarly, the Taipei Times reported this week that healthcare providers on the east coast are building a delivery network for medical goods using drones. Authorities held a live demonstration of a medical drone flight designed to service remote mountain communities. Drones for both routine delivery of medicines and emergency treatments are being studied. The program was inspired in part by the situation after the April 2024 earthquake in Hualien, which saw many mountain communities cut off from medical services.
Photo: AFP
Torrential rains, typhoons and earthquakes can easily cut off services to remote communities and offshore islands. In wartime islands are likely to be without transportation as ferries and aircraft are mobilized for wartime service, and roads to remote communities blocked. It is easy to see how an existing integrated drone-based medical delivery system could be repurposed for wartime use.
Tainan city and the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCIST) in December last year participated in a demonstration of drones in disaster response. The wartime applications of such a system are obvious.
Taiwan Water Corp is already using drones to monitor water quality. It presently operates 11 drones and plans to acquire 10 more by the year’s end. It also uses an unmanned boat to monitor water quality in an artificial lake in Nantou County. Since water facilities will surely be targeted in a Chinese invasion scenario, these are key technology capabilities.
The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), long at the forefront of technology development, has supported a range of civilian drone applications with obvious wartime uses. For example, it developed a drone-based inspection system for assessing damage to bridges and other structures for the high speed rail. It has also developed an automated drone-surveillance system for police use. Both of these have clear wartime applications.
Though at present these systems are technology demonstrations, the existence of local and government agency drone initiatives suggests how the antics of the pro-China parties in the legislature can be circumvented: encourage local governments to develop local drone initiatives that move beyond technology demonstration to actual implementation across a wide range of activities that will be useful in an invasion scenario. The purpose of such programs is to build drone-based capabilities for use in wartime and create robust expertise in drone use at the local level. For areas controlled by pro-Taiwan politicians from the pan-Green parties, this should be considered mandatory.
Such programs could include search and rescue operations, emergency response and border surveillance. Recall that “borders” in Taiwan are watery and have already been penetrated by operatives of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) using small craft. Drone patrols by local governments would be an ideal response, especially if they are rhetorically positioned as safety patrols. Drone-based monitoring of cables, bridges, roads, dikes, wells and other vital infrastructure should be widely implemented across the country.
Photo courtesy of the Hengshan Police Station
Medical deliveries and provisioning of daily necessities should be extended across all the nation’s remote areas and all of its associated islands. In wartime, the skills used to deliver to remote areas and islands will come in handy delivering to friendly areas surrounded by enemy-occupied areas, which will functionally be “islands” and “remote areas.” Even programs that track and map vegetation, wildlife and agriculture would be useful in wartime. Taiwan is already thinking about or implementing some of these programs, but local governments need to start aggressively funding and expanding them.
Note that many of these programs could be implemented on a volunteer basis using Taiwan’s plentiful pool of senior volunteers. Numerous private organizations already offer drone training, as do higher education institutions, since operating drones weighing 2kg or more requires a license. Even schools are now offering summer programs. Local governments should be pushing harder to fund and expand these organizations.
Taiwan wants to turn out 100,000 drones a month by the end of the decade. Wartime assaults will involve tens of thousands of drones on both sides. Ukraine has 80,000 personnel involved in its drone programs, with an estimated 25-40,000 pilots. By contrast, even the well-known Kuma Academy’s introductory course only has capacity for 75 civilian trainees per month, roughly 900 people a year, according to a recent Guardian article.
Taiwan’s civilian drone programs are thus woefully undersupported and underproductive, the more so when the inevitable losses due to combat and psychological trauma in an invasion are considered. They are also out of sync with Taiwan’s potential drone output, even if a large chunk of that is exported as the government plans. Demand for drone operators is going to massively outstrip supply. Taiwan does not have the luxury of trading space for time to implement drone operator training as Ukraine does. It has to enter the war with a large pool of drone operators already well-trained and experienced.
Another reason to get local governments to operate robust drone programs is decentralization. In a Taiwan invasion scenario central government control is going to be spotty and focused on making sure the military responds, especially early in the invasion. The more local governments can cultivate civil defense capabilities, the better off Taiwan will be, and the more Taipei can focus on the national situation. Moreover, independent drone capabilities integrated with local government agencies and officials will also be useful if local governments are cut off from Taipei.
Finally, massively expanding local government and government agency drone operations will force the pro-China parties in the legislature to face the politically unpalatable choices of either attempting to suppress local drone training programs — affecting local voters and displaying their pro-China positions for all to see — or letting drone programs flourish and angering their friends across the Strait. It will also be good for Taiwan and the pro-Taiwan parties to get more locals engaged with drones and civil defense.
If local drone production ramps up, drone pilot production must follow. Local governments need to vastly expand their investment in local drone training and applications. Time may be running out.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

The US now learns what Taiwan knew before
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Taiwan does not need a CIA deputy director to explain that Beijing treats commerce as a battlefield. It has been living that lesson for decades, watching its chip designers get poached, its retired officers get recruited for cash, and its companies get pressured to choose between the Chinese market and their own government’s security priorities. What changed this month is that Washington finally said the quiet part out loud.
CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis told a Washington audience that China’s threat to the US is now “fundamentally different,” because the competition is economic, not military, and that a Chinese company cannot be treated as genuinely private when the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) can absorb or direct it at will.
This is not a new insight in Taipei. It is the working assumption behind every export control on advanced lithography equipment, every debate in the Legislative Yuan about Chinese investment in the semiconductor supply chain, and every prosecution of a retired general caught building a spy network for a bowl of noodles and a modest stipend. Taiwan has spent 30 years treating Chinese capital as a potential delivery mechanism for state power. Washington is only now updating its assumptions to match the country Taiwan has always had to live next to.
The same week Ellis spoke, federal agents in Detroit charged a Chinese national, Zeng Weiheng, with lying about why he had spent 20 minutes photographing cargo planes at O’Hare International Airport. Zeng was not a trained intelligence officer. He was a college student in Canada, allegedly paid by a contact he believed was tied to the CCP to photograph specific aircraft and tail numbers, a task cheap enough and deniable enough that losing him cost Beijing nothing.
Taiwan’s own counterintelligence record is full of Zengs: low-ranking, financially motivated, recruited through family ties or business contacts and disposable by design. The scale is different, the method is not. What the O’Hare case demonstrates on US soil, Taiwanese security services have been documenting for a generation, usually with far less international attention.
The useful thing about Washington’s shift is not that it discovered anything new. It is that it removed a piece of cover that Beijing-friendly voices in Taiwan have relied on for years: the argument that treating cross-strait economic integration as a security risk is paranoid, protectionist or an overreaction driven by Taipei’s politics.
If the CIA argues publicly that a Chinese semiconductor firm cannot be assumed independent of the CCP, then the same logic applies with more force, not less, to a Chinese-linked investment vehicle courting a Taiwanese supplier or to political factions here who insist that deeper economic ties with China are merely business. That argument was always thin; it just got a lot thinner.
None of this should be read as vindication for its own sake. The point of Washington catching up is not that Taipei gets to say it told you so, although it would be entitled to. The point is that shared threat assessment is the precondition for shared policy, on export controls, on investment screening, on the defense package still stalled in the legislature by parties more interested in denying the threat than countering it.
Taiwan has spent years explaining what it is like to share a border with an authoritarian state that does not recognize the line between its companies and its intelligence services. It is a strange kind of relief to watch Washington arrive, slightly out of breath, at the same conclusion.
Clive Hazell is a Kaohsiung-based writer and educator. A 30-year-resident of Taiwan and Japan, he writes on geopolitics, culture and East Asia.

MOL warns foodpanda over docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Delivery platform Foodpanda could face fines up to NT$100,000 per affected worker for illegally docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries based on unilaterally imposed time limits, the Ministry of Labor (MOL) said yesterday.
At multiple recent meetings with local labor officials, the ministry said that such practices by Foodpanda contravene the Delivery Workers’ Rights Protection and Delivery Platform Management Act (外送員權益保障及外送平臺管理法), the ministry said in a statement.
Local labor bureaus can impose fines ranging from NT$20,000 to NT$100,000 per affected courier once they determine the validity of the complaints filed by workers, said Wang Hou-wei (王厚偉), director-general of the ministry’s Department of Labor Relations.
Photo: Chiu Chiao-jen, Taipei Times
Wang did not disclose how many complaints had been filed with local authorities, citing a lack of complete data, but said that all reported cases involved Foodpanda.
Delivery couriers reported facing pay deductions for exceeding estimated delivery times by as little as one to five minutes, calling the policy “unfair” due to “numerous unforeseen and uncontrollable factors on the road,” Wang said.
When delivery delays occur, platforms should look into the causes and handle them via proper mechanisms instead of making unilateral pay deductions, the ministry said.
“Unlawful practices would absolutely not be tolerated,” it added.
Under the law, which came into force on July 21, platforms must pay riders based on the exact time a delivery takes, using a rate of 1.25 times the minimum wage, and no order can pay less than NT$45.
Earlier yesterday, the National Delivery Industrial Union and two other unions issued a joint statement accusing Foodpanda of “maliciously scapegoating delivery workers for order delays” as a pretext for unlawfully docking their pay.
Separately, the Preparatory Committee for the Taiwan Federation of Delivery Industrial Unions said that couriers frequently encounter delays caused by factors beyond their control.
Such situations include understaffed retail stores, long peak-hour restaurant waits, GPS and system glitches, unreachable customers or incorrect delivery addresses, as well as traffic congestion, road closures and severe weather, it said.
It called on couriers to submit formal complaints to local labor departments if they experience illegal pay deductions.
In response, Emma Kuo (郭昕宜), Foodpanda’s director of public affairs and public relations, told reporters that the platform has never refused to disburse riders’ pay due to delivery delays.
The company only asked delivery couriers to clarify unusually long trips, Kuo said, adding that full pay is disbursed as long as a valid explanation is provided.
Kuo made the remarks yesterday afternoon at a news conference announcing a new commercial partner, reports by local Chinese-language media said.

The National Museum of Taiwan Literature and the UK’s National Centre for Writing have signed a memorandum of understanding to train a new generation of English-language translators of Taiwanese literature.
Under the agreement, a “Literature from Taiwan” track is being added to the center’s Emerging Translator Mentorships, which recruits aspiring translators worldwide , and provides mentoring and professional exchanges.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠), who on Tuesday attended the signing in Norwich, England, expressed hope that the partnership would help build a long-term pipeline of translators capable of bringing more Taiwanese literature to British readers.
Photo: CNA
The new partnership would provide another channel for introducing Taiwanese literature to the UK, and create more opportunities for cooperation between Taiwan and the UK, Li said.
National Centre for Writing chair Alan Waters said the center had begun promoting Taiwanese literature even before author Yang Shuang-zi’s (楊?子) Taiwan Travelogue gained international recognition when it won this year’s International Booker Prize.
The center’s 2026-to-2027 program had received 16 applications for the Taiwan literature track, which was a strong response for a program of this kind, Waters said.
The center plans to expand its collaboration with Taiwan next year through writer and translator residencies, as well as a Taiwan literature festival next spring, Waters added.

Türkiye, 7 other countries welcome UK ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

Seyit Şamil Kurt
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday welcomed the UK government's decision to ban imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory and restrict services linked to such settlements.
In a joint statement, the ministers expressed hope that the decision would help mobilize the international community to take similar action in line with international law and hold accountable settlement organizations and individuals engaged in illegal settlement activities.
They also welcomed a joint statement on the two-state solution issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
The 12 countries confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements that are illegal under international law, or to actively consider these and other measures in accordance with their respective national procedures.
The ministers of the eight countries urged the international community to build on these steps and adopt concrete measures to end activities that support or sustain illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
They said the announced measures were in line with international law and relevant UN resolutions, including UN Security Council Resolution 2334 and the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 19, 2024.
The statement cited the obligation of all states not to recognize as legal the situation arising from Israel's unlawful occupation of the Palestinian territory and not to provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by the occupation.
The ministers reiterated their call for Israel to rescind all measures taken in connection with settlement activities, as well as other measures aimed at altering the geographic and demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.
They also stressed that Gaza is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory and called for the "full and immediate implementation" of US President Donald Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
The ministers said the plan should be implemented to ensure security and stability, address the humanitarian situation, facilitate reconstruction and recovery, and lay the foundations for lasting peace.
They reaffirmed that "the only viable path" to achieving a just, lasting and comprehensive peace is the implementation of the two-state solution through the establishment of an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital. 
12 countries announce measures on illegal Israeli settlements
The foreign ministers of the 12 countries announced in a joint statement on Tuesday that they would impose or consider trade restrictions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Who controls the data controls the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

In March, Iranian drones targeted three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), striking two directly and almost hitting the third. It was the first time a commercial data center had been a military target, yet almost nobody outside specialist circles noticed. They should have. The servers holding a country’s data, and the chips running the artificial intelligence (AI) models on which its economy increasingly leans, are no longer background infrastructure. They are as strategic as ports or power grids — and just as exposed.
For most of the past decade, data was something companies mined, and AI was something companies sold — regulated at the margins through privacy law, if they were regulated at all. This framing no longer works. AI now sits inside finance, defense, healthcare and public administration, and it runs on two things most governments do not actually control: the data that train it and the compute that processes it. Countries that ignore this would find their futures being decided in boardrooms where they have no seat.
Many governments have taken note. Global spending on “sovereign AI” would reportedly surpass US$100 billion this year. Over the past few months, Canada, France, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have rolled out national compute funds and GPU allocations. The EU has gone further, treating sovereign AI infrastructure almost as doctrine, which has meant backing Gaia-X to build out European data infrastructure and financing projects such as Mistral AI’s new data center outside Paris.
Illustration: Mountain People
On paper, this looks like sensible diversification away from a handful of US and Chinese firms. In practice, it risks creating something more brittle: a patchwork of national fortresses, each self-sufficient and none capable of talking to the others. Part of the problem is that “AI sovereignty” encompasses at least three things, and most governments are only working on one.
Data residency — keeping citizens’ data within national borders — is the oldest of the three, the easiest to legislate, and the one most policy actually addresses. Compute sovereignty — who owns the chips and data centers doing the processing — is more difficult: a country can wall off its data, but it loses control if those data are processed on infrastructure someone else owns. Governance sovereignty — the ability to set the rules AI systems have to follow, rather than importing whatever standard the country hosting the dominant developers happens to set — is the one almost nobody talks about.
A fragmented regulatory landscape does not help any of this. Roughly 90 countries have some kind of national AI strategy; at least 33 have passed binding legislation. The approaches often clash. The EU’s AI Act, whose main provisions became applicable last month, carries penalties of up to 35 million euros (US$40.6 million) or 7 percent of the offender’s global annual turnover. The US’ AI Action Plan takes the opposite approach, treating deregulation itself as a competitive edge. China’s Global AI Governance Action Plan offers cooperation on AI governance with developing economies, but on Chinese terms.
The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on AI — the first binding international AI treaty — represents real progress, but its enforcement is modest next to the scale of what it is meant to govern. Coordination beyond that has barely started. The UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI has warned of a “race to the bottom,” with jurisdictions competing to offer the most permissive rules rather than the safest ones. Companies running high-risk AI deployments are already shopping for the softest jurisdiction.
Genuine AI sovereignty requires four things, none of which is complicated in concept. Start by putting AI data infrastructure in the same legal category as power grids, with someone clearly on the hook for physical and digital security.
Next, countries building sovereign compute need shared interoperability standards, not just national champions — Gaia-X’s work on data portability is a useful template. A hospital in Lagos or a ministry in Warsaw ought to be able to verify that a system meets baseline safety requirements, regardless of whose infrastructure it is running on.
Oversight needs teeth: audit rights, mandatory incident reporting, and licensing for the handful of frontier models capable of touching critical infrastructure or financial stability. These models should be treated more like nuclear material than ordinary software.
The world needs a real mechanism to stop AI sovereignty from turning into just another axis of inequality. That US$100 billion investment in sovereign compute is happening almost entirely in rich countries. Pooled regional compute, financed and governed jointly by smaller countries, would deliver better results than each of them trying to go it alone.
None of this requires a grand global treaty. The components of a governance framework — including the EU AI Act, the Council of Europe convention, Gaia-X, and the UN’s scientific panel — already exist. The scaffolding connecting them is missing, and building that takes deliberate work. Every year it is delayed, the infrastructure gets bigger and harder to reconfigure. Nobody pouring billions of dollars into data centers and GPUs is waiting around for governance to catch up.
The strikes on those AWS facilities in the Gulf sent a message (whether or not anyone intended it): The infrastructure underpinning a growing share of consequential decisions — who gets a loan, which patients get flagged for treatment, which factories keep running — sits in buildings most governments do not control and cannot fully protect. Data sovereignty, compute sovereignty and governance sovereignty are not conference-room abstractions. They are the precondition for a future shaped by countries’ own citizens — not whoever happens to own the servers.
Bijan Burnard is CEO of D-AI

New Taipei City Councilor Yang Chun-mei (楊春妹) was released on NT$500,000 bail and barred from leaving Taiwan after prosecutors accused her of distributing laundry detergent to voters as part of a vote-buying scheme, the New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday.
Prosecutors said they are investigating allegations that Yang recently distributed laundry detergent and other household goods to voters at several community activity centers, in what is the first suspected vote-buying case involving a New Taipei City councilor in this year’s local elections.
Prosecutors said they searched Yang’s home, office and other locations on Tuesday, finding large quantities of laundry detergent and other household goods allegedly intended for distribution to voters.
Photo: Screen grab from the New Taipei City Council’s Web site
Twenty-one people, including Yang, two assistants and witnesses were questioned, prosecutors said.
Yang and the two assistants are suspected of offering or giving bribes to eligible voters in exchange for votes, they said.
Yang, a four-term Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) councilor representing New Taipei City’s electoral constituency No. 12 for Plains Indigenous Tribes, recently registered to seek a fifth term in this year’s local elections.
One of Yang’s assistants was released on NT$400,000 bail and barred from leaving Taiwan, while the other was released on NT$40,000 bail.
The remainder of those questioned were released afterward, prosecutors said.
Taiwan does not have a fixed price threshold above which an election gift automatically constitutes vote-buying. The key issue stipulated under the Public Officials Election And Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法) is whether the gift is provided as an improper benefit in exchange for specific voting behavior.

Kenyan start-up makes limbs to sign for deaf kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:50 UTC
01:37:50 KST

In a school for the deaf in Kenya, children signed their excitement as a team demonstrated how a robotic arm could revolutionize their studies.
About 300,000 children in the east African nation have a hearing impairment, according to the Kenya Society for Deaf Children, but just 20,000 were enrolled in schools as of 2024.
Kenyan start-up ZeroBionic, cofounded by 22-year-old Norah Kimathi, hopes to tackle some of the educational difficulties they face.
Photo: AFP
It has built a mechanical hand that can translate a teachers’ voice into sign language in real time, allowing deaf children to learn alongside their hearing counterparts.
For the pupils at the Kasarani Treeside Secondary School for the Deaf in Nairobi, there is another element of the technology that is even more promising.
The robotic arms are trialed by deaf teachers to record and store signs using a bodysuit, which ZeroBionic imported for the task.
In the process, they are building a database of technical terms — drawing on English, American and Kenyan signs — that is helping to expand the language and make it easier for deaf children to learn and communicate.
“The biggest challenge we faced actually was in Africa we don’t have a standardized African sign language dataset,” Kimathi said at the company’s tiny lab in Nairobi.
“No one else had built this on the continent... We had to start from scratch,” she said.
Many deaf children in Kenya learn a patchwork of makeshift signs, and the local dialect lacks many technical terms used to teach subjects like math and biology.
Sharon Mumbe, 19, one of the pupils at the deaf school, said it gives her “hope for the future.”
“I’ll be able to understand different concepts better,” she said.
Numerous prototype limbs litter the surfaces in Kimathi’s lab.
The team works with Africa One, a humanoid robot they built, to refine and expand the signs their mechanical arms are able to produce.
Everything has been designed and built in-house, using recycled materials to reduce costs and environmental impact, produced using 3D printers that thump away constantly in the background. Each hand costs about US$350 and can last for up to two years. They are already in 78 schools across Kenya.
They boast a 92 percent speech-to-sign accuracy rate and Kimathi said the results have made all the long hours in the lab worthwhile.
“We know we’re going to put a smile on someone else’s face,” she said.

Getting the tanker war right: A history of blockades from the US Civil War to Iran - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:27:00 UTC
21:27:00 KST

The US is involved in a kind of tit-for-tat tanker war with the Iranians. What began as strikes on Iran by the US and Israel in February has shifted significantly over the last few months. One of the features of the conflict now is the battle for the Strait of Hormuz. That battle is fought in a complex environment and in a unique way.
The Iranian threat to shipping in the Gulf is complex. The Iranians have various types of drones and missiles. Iran also borders the waterway. It’s hard to defend hundreds of miles of waterway. History shows that the country bordering the waterway will have an advantage, even if it is weaker.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has begun a new novel approach to this conflict. It is retaliating when Iran strikes at ships: The US is sinking Iranian tankers.
CENTCOM said on September 9 that “CENTCOM forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed.”
The Iranians have responded, striking at Jordan and continuing to threaten shipping. Success in the Strait of Hormuz is measured in part by whether ships continued to transit. This depends on several factors, some of which involve international shipping and insurance.
Risk plays a big role. No captain or company wants to risk the crew of ships, even if the chances of them being sunk or struck are low.
The US has been conducting naval blockades for hundreds of years
The US has been clearing mines and finding other methods to aid shipping. It appears the US may be slowly gaining the upper hand on several levels. However, the history of naval blockades tells us that achieving success is a long haul.
Consider the US blockade of the Confederate States envisioned in the Anaconda Plan of 1861.
It envisioned blockading the Confederacy, a process that took years.
Other wars have also used blockades. Napoleon attempted a reverse blockade of Britain in 1806, essentially trying to cut off British trade with Continental Europe.
The Germans used U-boats to do the same. At the same time, the Germans were also blockaded in the First and Second World Wars, and they resorted to using various ships to run the blockade. In each instance, what history tells us is that this can take years.
Other examples abound. There was a decade-long siege of Montevideo, Uruguay, in the 20th century. If a small area of Uruguay couldn’t be reduced by blockade, what chance does Iran have? It’s possible that the decision to go to war with Iran directly could lead to a decade-long conflict.
This would be similar to what happened with Iraq after the 1991 war. The US helped secure no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq. It was a complicated mission. The US also has experience with a tanker war, having had to deal with the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s, when both sides targeted shipping.
Can the region get the tanker war right this time? Iran has kept up its warnings. It recently warned South Korea not to get involved in the Gulf conflict. Arab News also reported that Qatar has said that Gulf countries cannot rely solely on the US for security. Iran also said this week it would announce a new “restricted” zone in the Gulf.
Iran believes it has options
“The new restricted zone will begin from where the US blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday in an interview with state TV. Few details were provided on the plan, but Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone would be added to a sanctions list,” Arab News noted.
The challenge now is going to be to see if Iran continues to strike at ships. Can the US go tit-for-tat with the Iranians and strike enough of their ships to make Tehran choose a new path? Even if the sinkings and strikes on the Iranian tankers do make Iran shift tactics, will the Iranians simply find a new way to cause havoc? Will they strike at energy installations, or attack Jordan more than in the past?
One thing is clear about Iran: it believes it has options.
Iran also has a long front line to exploit. Not only is the Iranian border with Iraq and the Gulf hundreds of miles long. It also has a long coastline on the Indian Ocean. In addition, it has proxies in Yemen and other places. The Houthis expanding their role in the Red Sea, for instance, can be seen as a way for Iran to open or exploit a new front.
Getting the tanker war right will be a challenge for the US because of the factors involved. The White House is already signaling that the conflict and high oil prices will continue through the midterms in November.
There doesn’t appear to be much of an appetite to try another deal with Iran. Tehran is duplicitous and isn’t willing to change yet.
Facing such an enemy will be a long road.

US calls for NATO allies to withdraw from Rome Statute, 'systematically dismantle' ICC - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:26:59 UTC
21:26:59 KST

The United States attempted to recruit its NATO allies for a move aimed at “systematically dismantling” the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Politico reported on Thursday.
According to three NATO diplomats, the US administration called on member states of the alliance to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the court’s founding treaty, and end their support for it.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker made the demand during a closed-door meeting of ambassadors from the alliance’s 32 member states, held in Brussels in mid-July. According to the diplomats, Whitaker asked allies to help dismantle the court and concluded his remarks with a warning: “We will be watching closely who stands with America.”
At the same time, the US delegation to NATO circulated a document among the delegations outlining the administration’s demands. “The United States will systematically dismantle the capabilities of the International Criminal Court,” the document stated. Washington asked allies to “immediately take steps to withdraw” from the Rome Statute.
The countries were also asked to “examine the threat” that the United States claims the court poses to them, publicly condemn what was described as the ICC’s “overreach of authority,” and immediately halt “any material support” for it. “Let’s end once and for all the charade of the International Criminal Court,” the document stated.
NATO itself is not a party to the Rome Statute, but all alliance members except the United States and Turkey are members of the court.
France, Netherlands stand against US attack on ICC
The US move sparked opposition during the meeting. France and the Netherlands defended the institution and made clear they did not intend to comply with the American demand.
One diplomat who attended the meeting described Whitaker’s remarks as “quite shocking,” while another said they were “disappointing.”
The US mission to NATO did not respond to Politico’s request for comment. The French delegation declined to address the details of the closed-door discussion but stressed that France’s support for the court was “unwavering.” The Dutch delegation referred to comments by Foreign Minister Tom Brandsen, who said the Netherlands fully supports the court.
According to the report, US envoys also raised the demand in bilateral discussions with European countries. The US State Department warned that it would increase scrutiny of countries that refuse to distance themselves from what it called the court’s “false authority” while continuing to rely on American assistance.
The campaign against the ICC was launched over the summer by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who accused the court of undermining US sovereignty. “The International Criminal Court and its friends are waging war against our country, not through bullets or missiles, but through laws, treaties, and the power of what is called international law,” Rubio said on July 13. “If they believe they can deprive us of our sovereignty, we will teach them the full meaning of American resolve.”
The US campaign against the court stems in part from concerns that American officials and soldiers could face prosecution for war crimes. In 2020, the ICC opened an investigation into alleged crimes by US soldiers in Afghanistan, though the investigation was given lower priority the following year.
The US administration is also acting against the court over proceedings against Israeli officials and the arrest warrants issued for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant.
US sanctions ICC officials, President Tomoko Akane
Last month, Washington imposed sanctions on ICC officials, including President Tomoko Akane.
In response to the US move, an ICC spokesperson said the institution “remains focused on fulfilling its mandate impartially, independently, and in accordance with the Rome Statute, for the benefit of victims and in the name of justice.” The spokesperson added that despite attempts to obstruct its work, the court “remains steadfast and resilient.”
The confrontation comes at a sensitive time in relations between the United States and its European allies. Tensions have risen after many European countries refused to join the US war against Iran, as well as following US President Donald Trump’s previous threats to annex Greenland, an autonomous territory belonging to Denmark, a NATO member.
According to Politico, the demand regarding the ICC was raised shortly after the NATO leaders’ summit in Ankara had reportedly succeeded in reducing tensions. The diplomats estimated that Washington was not attempting to issue an explicit ultimatum to its allies, since the issue was raised as a side topic during a routine meeting. However, they emphasized that raising such a demand within NATO was particularly sensitive because of the United States’ role as the alliance’s de facto leader.

Mao Zedong, Israel and the road not taken - 50 years after leader’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:26:52 UTC
21:26:52 KST

Wednesday, September 9, marked 50 years since the death of Mao Zedong, the Chinese revolutionary leader whose long shadow is still cast over Asian and world geopolitics.
For almost three decades after proclaiming the establishment of the People’s Republic of China in Beijing in October 1949, Mao stood at the center of a political transformation that altered China entirely and reshaped the balance of the Cold War.
Under his leadership, the world’s most populous country emerged from decades of civil war, foreign occupation and internal collapse as a Communist power determined to chart its own course, eventually challenging both the United States and, after the Sino-Soviet split, the Soviet Union for influence across Asia, Africa and the developing world.
His domestic rule brought immense upheaval and suffering, from the Great Leap Forward to the violence and political convulsions of the Cultural Revolution, which together inflicted enormous loss of life and upheaval on China. But abroad, Mao became something larger than the leader of China alone. To revolutionary movements from Vietnam to Africa and the Middle East, Maoism offered an ideology built around guerrilla warfare, peasant revolution and resistance to imperialism, while Beijing sought to present itself as the natural patron of peoples struggling against colonial or Western-backed powers.
Israel occupied a curious place within that worldview, because Mao’s China had not begun as its enemy.
A relationship with an extraordinary trajectory
In fact, the relationship followed an extraordinary trajectory. Israel was the first country in the Middle East to recognize the new Communist government, and the two countries briefly appeared to be moving toward full diplomatic relations, as Chinese officials spoke warmly of friendship with Israel and the Jewish people. Within little more than a decade, however, Mao was receiving the leaders of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) in Beijing, supplying Palestinian terrorists and describing Israel alongside Taiwan as one of the West’s “bases of imperialism in Asia.”
A little over a month before Mao died in Beijing, then-Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin attempted a relatively uncomplicated gesture of international sympathy.
On July 28, 1976, an enormous earthquake had devastated the Chinese city of Tangshan, killing hundreds of thousands of people in one of the deadliest natural disasters of the 20th century. Rabin sent Chinese premier Hua Guofeng a cable expressing Israel’s sorrow over the loss of life and offering medical and other assistance to the Chinese people. Beijing sent it back.
Attached to the returned message was an explanation that, since the People’s Republic of China did not have diplomatic relations with Israel, the Chinese government could not accept the cable.
For a brief moment in the 1950's, full diplomatic relations appeared within reach
It was a final footnote to the relationship that a quarter of a century earlier had appeared capable of ending very differently. Israel had been the first country in the Middle East to recognize the People’s Republic, Israeli officials traveled through Maoist China as guests of the government, and senior Chinese officials had spoken openly of their friendship with Israel and the Jewish people. For a brief period during the 1950s, full diplomatic relations appeared within reach.
Mao, born in Hunan province in 1893, had risen from the son of a prosperous peasant farmer to become one of the founders of the Chinese Communist Party and, eventually, the dominant figure of the Chinese revolution. After decades of civil war, Japanese occupation, the Long March, and the final defeat of Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalists, Mao stood in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square on October 1, 1949, and proclaimed the establishment of the People’s Republic of China.
On January 9, 1950, less than four months after Mao declared the People’s Republic, Israel formally recognized his government as the legitimate government of China. At the time, there was some Chinese sympathy for Zionism, which could be viewed through the lens of revolution and a national liberation movement that had fought British imperial rule.
The Korean War, which broke out later that year and eventually saw Chinese troops fighting American-led UN forces, complicated Israel’s efforts to develop the relationship. Israel was increasingly conscious of its close relationship with the United States, which continued to recognize Chiang Kai-shek’s government on Taiwan as the legitimate government of China and viewed diplomatic engagement with Communist Beijing with deep suspicion.
Even so, the possibility never entirely disappeared, and several years later an unlikely Israeli diplomat in Burma began trying to reopen the door.
David Hacohen, Israel’s man in Rangoon, had become convinced that the young Jewish state could not afford to neglect Asia. Beginning in late 1953, he held discussions with China’s ambassador to Burma, Yao Zhongming, and later met premier and foreign minister Zhou Enlai as the Chinese leader passed through Rangoon following the 1954 Geneva Conference.
The talks quickly became serious enough for trade to be discussed, and produced one of the stranger episodes in the story. According to Hacohen’s account, the Soviet ambassador in Burma joined the conversations and, confronted by the possibility that Washington might object to direct trade between Israel and Communist China, suggested simply sending the goods on a triangular route through Odesa and Siberia.
Beijing subsequently invited an Israeli commercial delegation to China, and in early 1955 Hacohen led a group that spent several weeks touring the country, visiting cities, factories, industrial plants and villages before holding talks in Beijing.
The reception appears to have been extraordinarily warm. A Chinese undersecretary of trade told the delegation that “the Chinese people and their government are great friends of Israel and the Jewish people,” while Hacohen returned convinced that China wanted commercial ties and would respond positively if Israel moved toward diplomatic relations.
There were discussions behind the scenes about what formal relations might look like, yet Israel hesitated. Hacohen later complained of what he called “friendly American pressure,” while Israeli diplomats in Washington worried that moving too quickly toward Mao could damage the country’s increasingly important relationship with the United States.
By the time of the Bandung Conference in April, 1955, China was moving in another direction.
Bringing together 29 Asian and African states in Indonesia, Bandung became a defining moment in the emergence of what would later be called the Third World. Israel was kept away following opposition from Arab participants, while Zhou used the gathering to cultivate governments emerging from colonial rule and to align China increasingly with their causes.
Another blow to Sino-Israeli relations was Israel's participation alongside Britain and France in the 1956 Suez Crisis against Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, which proved particularly damaging in Beijing, where Mao’s China was attempting to present itself as one of the foremost opponents of Western imperialism. Whatever the Chinese had once made of Israel’s own struggle against British rule, the image was now of Israeli forces fighting beside two former European imperial powers against perhaps the most celebrated Arab nationalist leader of his generation.
During the following decade, that perception only hardened.
PLO greeted warmly by China's leadership
The transformation was unmistakable in March 1965 when Ahmad Shukeiri, then chairman of the recently established PLO, arrived in Beijing at the head of a Palestinian delegation. He was given the sort of welcome usually reserved for the representatives of a state, greeted amid flags, drums and crowds before meetings with China’s most senior leadership, including Mao himself.
During his conversation with Shukeiri, Mao offered perhaps the clearest explanation of where Israel had come to sit in his conception of the world.
“Israel and Formosa (Taiwan) are bases of imperialism in Asia,” Mao said. By then, he had come to see Israel and Taiwan in much the same light: as Western-backed footholds in Asia, Israel positioned against the Arab world and Taiwan against Communist China.
Taiwan was among the defining obsessions of Mao’s foreign policy. Chiang Kai-shek and the remnants of the Nationalist government had fled there following their defeat in 1949, surviving under American protection as Mao remained determined that the island would eventually come under Beijing’s control.
China provided PLO with arms, money, military training
China’s support for the Palestinians soon extended well beyond rhetoric. The Chinese provided money, small arms, expertise and military training to Palestinian organizations, although the scale was considerably smaller than was sometimes claimed at the time. Small groups of Palestinian terrorists traveled to China during the late 1960s, where their instruction included guerrilla warfare alongside immersion in Maoist political doctrine and visits to factories, agricultural communes and revolutionary sites.
Some returned to the Middle East as instructors themselves, carrying with them an ideology then reaching the height of its global influence. Even Mao’s Little Red Book found its way onto the battlefield; following an Israeli operation against Palestinian guerrillas in Lebanon in 1972, Israeli troops were reported to have found an Arabic edition of Mao’s sayings among captured propaganda material.
Even during the years of Maoist hostility, however, Israel maintained the position it had taken in 1950 - that Beijing, rather than Taipei, was the government of China.
In October 1971, despite China’s support for Palestinian terror groups and years of bitter rhetoric against Zionism, Israel voted in favor of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, which transferred China’s seat at the United Nations to the People’s Republic and expelled the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek. Israel was among the 76 countries voting in favor.
Five years later came the Tangshan earthquake and Rabin’s returned message.
Mao died several weeks afterward, on September 9, 1976. In the years that followed, China gradually moved away from the revolutionary foreign policy of the Mao era, as Deng Xiaoping placed more emphasis on economic modernization and pragmatic relations abroad. Quiet contacts with Israel developed behind the scenes, and on January 24, 1992, the two countries finally established full diplomatic relations.

How the war in Gaza is changing pregnancy and parenthood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:25:38 UTC
21:25:38 KST

Breadcrumb
'Is it safe to have a child?': How Israel's war is reshaping fertility, pregnancy and parenthood in Gaza
Before Israel's war, for many women in Gaza, the decision to become pregnant began with a simple desire: another child, another room, another name to add to the family. Today, the question has become far more painful: is this the right time to bring a child into the world?
Through my work and conversations with women from Gaza, I began to notice that the ongoing genocide has affected more than women’s ability to become pregnant or access infertility treatment. It has reached a stage that comes even before pregnancy itself: the decision to have a child.
Some women are postponing pregnancy because they do not know where they will be living a month from now. Others fear pregnancy because of shortages of food and medication, or because they no longer trust that they will find a functioning hospital when labour begins.
Couples who married during the war have decided to delay starting a family after diapers, infant formula, medicine, and even basic food became difficult to secure. Others became pregnant during the war, only to have their experiences of pregnancy and childbirth leave them traumatised and unwilling to consider another pregnancy.
In this sense, war does not affect only the children who are born during it. It reshapes the decisions of women and men who are still asking themselves, "Should we have children? When? And how many children can we bring into this world?"
Postponing the idea of family amid war
Amal, 26, has been married for two years and has not yet had a child. Before October 2023, she was preparing for her first pregnancy.
She and her husband, Mahmoud, had begun undergoing the necessary medical tests, and she saw pregnancy as the natural next step in their married life.
Then the war overturned those plans.
Amal now lives in a displacement tent in the al-Mawasi area of southern Gaza. She says she no longer thinks about pregnancy in the same way she did before the war.
"Mahmoud and I were preparing for our first baby. We had started the tests before October, but when we were displaced to a tent in Khan Younis, everything disappeared. How am I supposed to get pregnant when I can’t even find an aspirin or clean food? Pregnancy during war isn’t just a risk; it’s like putting your life in danger."
She pauses before continuing.
"Every day I see women in the tents bleeding and unable to find a hospital. I told my husband to forget about having children altogether until the war ends — if I’m even alive by then."
For Amal, postponing pregnancy is no longer a decision about comfort or financial planning. It has become an attempt to protect herself and a child who has not yet been born.
She once dreamed of having four children. Today, she says that if the situation stabilises, she may have only one.
This change in her idea of family size may seem deeply personal, but it raises a larger question: what happens when war becomes part of the calculations behind fertility decisions that were once based mainly on desire, financial circumstances, and social expectations?
Amal is not the only woman who has spoken to me about delaying pregnancy.
Ibrahim, 28, and Reem, 22, married in the middle of the war, after their second displacement. Before getting married, they had planned to start a family immediately.
But their marriage itself took place under circumstances that bore little resemblance to a normal beginning to married life.
They now live in a remaining room of a damaged house in Deir al-Balah.
"Our wedding was held under a tarpaulin, with a displacement meal of canned beans. I can’t carry the guilt of bringing a child into a tent, where they might have to drink salty water," Ibrahim tells The New Arab.
"The price of a pack of diapers alone now requires months of budgeting. It’s absolutely not the time to have children. We’re barely surviving one day at a time."
Reem says, "My heart breaks every time I see displaced children. I wanted to become a mother as soon as I got married, but fear is stronger than emotion. Postponing pregnancy hurts us, but right now it is the only form of mercy available to us."
For the couple, the desire to have children has not disappeared. What has changed is the timing.
When access to a hospital becomes part of the decision to become pregnant
Under normal circumstances, pregnancy requires regular antenatal care, medical tests, medication, skilled birth care, and rapid access to a hospital if complications arise.
In Gaza, however, access to these services can no longer be taken for granted.
The destruction of health facilities and shortages of medicines and equipment have made reproductive care increasingly difficult, while international organisations have been working in 2026 to restore some essential services.
In July 2026, UNFPA reported that 94 percent of hospitals in Gaza were either destroyed or only partially functioning, while fewer than half of health facilities were able to operate at any level.
During the first half of 2025, around 17,000 births were recorded in the Gaza Strip, compared with approximately 29,000 during the same period in 2022 — a decline of more than 41 percent.
During the same period, health authorities recorded more than 2,600 miscarriages and 220 maternal deaths before childbirth, according to data cited by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
UNFPA also reported that around 33 percent of babies born during the first six months of 2025 — approximately 5,560 infants — were premature, had low birth weight, or required admission to neonatal intensive care units.
The decline in the number of births alone cannot be interpreted as evidence that women’s desire to have children has declined. It may also be linked to delayed marriage, poor nutrition, deteriorating general health and fertility, and reduced access to reproductive healthcare.
But the figures reveal something more immediate: a woman deciding to become pregnant today is doing so in an environment radically different from the one that existed before the war.
One of the women I spoke with, a 31-year-old, was 33 weeks pregnant when her story took its most devastating turn.
She was living in a displacement site in northern Gaza when the nearby area came under attack, and she went into premature labour.
She was taken to a temporary medical point, but the care she and her baby needed was unavailable.
"I gave birth to the sound of bombardment, without even a single drop of anaesthesia. I was screaming from the pain and the fear at the same time."
Her baby was born prematurely and needed oxygen and neonatal care, but the available resources were insufficient.
"I gave birth to my baby, and he was struggling in front of me, needing oxygen, and no one could do anything. He died in my arms a few hours later because the hospital went out of service."
She describes what the experience left behind: "Loss during war is not like any other loss. I feel as if the grief has suffocated me. I am not ready to go through that terror again or become pregnant with another child who could be lost in the same way."
Before that experience, she had not been afraid of pregnancy. Now, pregnancy itself has become a source of terror.
'Women have started asking about contraception'
To understand this shift more closely, I also spoke with Dr Hiyam Jaber, an obstetrician and gynaecologist who has worked at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital and in field displacement clinics.
Dr Hiyam says that what she witnessed during the war was not simply an increase in pregnancy and childbirth complications, but a change in the questions women were asking.
"We began receiving daily inquiries about safe, long-acting contraceptive methods, such as intrauterine devices and injections, particularly because birth-control pills are not consistently available," Dr Hiyam tells The New Arab.
She describes women’s fears as being directly connected to their everyday experiences.
"The greatest fears are giving birth without anaesthesia, giving birth in unsterile conditions, being unable to provide infant formula if the mother is suffering from malnutrition, and the fear of postpartum haemorrhage in a situation where blood supplies are limited," she adds.
She says the cases she sees include an increase in preterm births and miscarriages, as well as emergency cesarean deliveries associated with deterioration in maternal health and delays in reaching hospitals.
These observations do not exist in isolation. UNFPA has warned that one in three pregnancies in Gaza is now considered high-risk, while the food crisis and collapse of the health system have increased risks for mothers and newborns.
In its report for the first quarter of 2026, UNFPA said it continued supporting sexual and reproductive health services in Gaza, including six mobile maternity units providing emergency obstetric and newborn care, as well as medicines, contraceptives, and medical equipment.
But the very need for these mobile units reflects the scale of the crisis: safe childbirth is no longer a guaranteed service available everywhere. It has become a humanitarian issue, and health organisations are trying to rebuild amid the destruction.
From four children to one
According to Dr Hiyam, the shift she has observed is not limited to the question, "When should I become pregnant?" It also extends to another question: "How many children do I want?"
In her experience, many women are now inclined to postpone childbearing or have fewer children until the war ends and living conditions stabilise.
This shift matters socially. Family size is not simply a number in demographic statistics. It reflects how people imagine their future.
When a family is confident that there will be a home, a school, a hospital, food, and job opportunities, having another child can feel like a natural part of the future.
But when the future itself is uncertain, the decision about how many children to have changes.
Amal, who once dreamed of four children, now thinks about having only one.
Ibrahim and Reem, who had planned to have children immediately after marriage, have decided to wait.
And the woman who lost her baby says she cannot even contemplate another pregnancy.
Three different decisions, shaped by the same fear.
What will happen to the image of the Palestinian family?
It is too early to say whether the war has created a permanent demographic shift in Palestinian family size.
The data currently available describe an ongoing crisis and are not sufficient to answer the long-term question of fertility intentions after the war.
But what can be said is that the war has intervened in nearly every factor shaping reproductive decisions: marriage, housing, food, healthcare, fertility, contraception, antenatal care, and the ability to protect a child after birth.
In 2026, UNFPA estimated that around 55,000 pregnant women in Gaza were facing severe conditions, including displacement, hunger, and limited access to healthcare, while 120,600 pregnant women across the occupied Palestinian territory required pregnancy-related health services.
These figures mean that the question of the future of the Palestinian family cannot be separated from the future of Gaza’s healthcare system and living conditions.
When I asked Amal what she feared most, she did not talk about pain. She talked about giving birth to a child in a place where she could not protect them.
When Ibrahim spoke about postponing parenthood, he did not say that he did not want to become a father.
He said he did not want to feel guilty about bringing a child into these circumstances.
And Reem summed up the entire struggle in one sentence: “Postponing pregnancy hurts us, but right now it is the only form of mercy available to us.”
Perhaps this is the larger story.
War does not only determine who will be born and who will survive. It can reach the moment before conception — the conversation between a couple in the darkness, the woman calculating the risks of childbirth before buying a pregnancy test, and the mother who has lost a child and decides that her heart cannot endure the experience again.
In Gaza, the decision to have a child now carries questions that were not part of parents’ calculations before the war:
Where will we live?
What will our child eat?
Will there be a hospital when I need one?
Will I be able to secure treatment for my child?
And will I be able to protect them?
War does not only affect the children who are born.
It also enters the lives of those who are still considering whether to have a child.
"What hurts me most is that I have started hearing women ask a question I never heard before the war: ‘Is it safe to have a child?’ As a doctor, I used to help women welcome their babies. Today, I sometimes find myself trying to tell them that they have the right to be afraid," Dr Hiyam Jaber says.
Perhaps the cruellest legacy of the war is not only the children who have lost their lives, but the mothers who have lost the ability to imagine a safe future for children who have not yet been born.
In Gaza, where a child was once a symbol of life continuing, the decision to bring one into the world has, for many women, become suspended on a single question:
Will this fear end before my child comes into the world?
Dr Haya Hijazi is a gynaecologist and obstetrician from Gaza

British rabbis back UK sanctions on Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:20:40 UTC
21:20:40 KST

Breadcrumb
British rabbis back UK sanctions on Israeli settlements, denounce BDS
Several leading British rabbis have backed the UK's new sanctions on Israeli settlements, amid protests from prominent Jewish groups and leaders against the measures.
A day after the sanctions were announced by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, senior Masorti rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg took to X to express his support for the sanctions.
"What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” Wittenberg wrote on X.
The rabbi highlighted that he had been in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair when Miliband's announcement was made, where he witnessed the horrors of settler violence with his "own eyes".
“We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away."
Wittenberg expressed his opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, while also describing Israel as his "family".
Elsewhere, Rabbi Alexandra Wright of the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London said that the "occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis".
"The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’," Wright said.
The rabbi also urged the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Other rabbis who came out in support of the measures include Jeremy Gordon of the New London Synagogue, and Lev Taylor of Kingston Liberal Synagogue.
Their statements came as prominent Jewish leaders and groups attacked the sanctions against illegal settlements.
UK Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis said on Tuesday, the day that the sanctions were announced, that it was a "dark day for British Jews".
"The measures announced amount to little more than political flag-bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric and those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish State. These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target. On the eve of Rosh Hashanah and at a time when our community is more vulnerable than ever to the wave of extremism that has been building over recent years, these sanctions do nothing to advance the cause of peace," Mirvis said.
"Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews," he added.
Mirvis, who has at least one child who took part in the Israeli war on Gaza, has frequently expressed support for Israel, including calling the country's genocide-accused army "our heroic soldiers".
The announcement was also slammed by the Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies for British Jews, which said it viewed the measures with "deep regret".
While British Jewish groups have come out with contrasting statements on the sanctions, there is currently no definitive polling on the broader community's attitudes towards Miliband's announcement.
A survey conducted by YouGov on Tuesday found that 52% of a sample of over 4,000 members of the public expressed support for the sanctions. Of that figure, 33% said they "completely approve" of the measures.
Seventeen percent said they disapproved of the sanctions, while 33% said they "don't know".
The measures announced by Miliband on Tuesday will see the UK ban all goods from illegal Israeli settlements -- a move which supporters say underscores the UK's commitment to upholding international law.
Pro-Palestine critics of the sanctions, however, have said the move does not go far enough, particularly as Britain continues to supply military hardware to Israel.

Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:17:52 UTC
21:17:52 KST

Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder.
Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.
“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.
The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority.
Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.”
Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial.
The Council of Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.
During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary.
“If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?”
Malta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in.
Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder.
“The targeted assassination of a journalist in the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out.
“I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.”
The public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity.
It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented.
Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year.
Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.”
She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.
