Brussels prepares post-2030 renewable overhaul as grids struggle to keep up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:16:33 UTC
21:16:33 KST

The European Commission’s renewable push comes as the EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the Council, are working to tackle one of the biggest bottlenecks to new clean-power projects — the electrical grids.
The European Commission is preparing to reshape the European Union's renewable-energy rulebook after 2030, signaling a major shift from less regulation to greater focus on investment, grids and storage, according to a draft impact assessment seen by Euronews.
The internal document states that the existing renewable energy law is no longer enough to deliver the EU’s 2040 climate ambition to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% compared to 1990 levels, which EU lawmakers agreed last November.
A new EU proposal to revamp the bloc's renewable energy framework is due by the end of the year to ensure the post-2030 climate framework aligns with all sectors that must contribute to the common goal of reaching climate neutrality by 2050.
In 2025, clean power accounted for 26.2% of EU final energy consumption, while current national plans put the bloc on track for only about 41% by 2030, below the 42.5% binding EU target, the draft document warns.
However, the Commission is skeptical that its 27-nation bloc will achieve even the 41% target.
"While the situation varies from one member state to another, the current trajectory for renewable energy deployment suggests that even the projected 41% share may be difficult to achieve with current progress at member state level," reads the draft document.
At the same time, the Commission appears reluctant to address the EU's renewable deployment gap by simply piling on new mandatory targets.
Brussels seems to reject additional mandatory measures on self-consumption and renewable-energy communities, mandatory regional cooperation and joint projects as well as further permitting legislation, arguing that recent reforms still need implementation.
“The stakeholder feedback received at stakeholder workshops emphasised the importance of regulatory stability in this area and pointed at insufficient implementation of the current framework as the key issue to tackle," reads the draft document.
Grid congestion — a major barrier
While the bloc needs to increase clean power production to meet the targets, it also needs to ensure its electrical systems can receive and transport it. The EU excels at producing clean power, but it struggles to dispatch it where it is needed, which is a major barrier to the bloc's overall climate and energy transition.
Renewable electricity reached almost 50% of EU generation in 2025, but the power system is increasingly struggling to use all that cheap electricity, the draft document acknowledges. Grid congestion, insufficient storage and inflexible demand are producing more negative prices and renewable curtailment, often to the detriment of clean power producers.
In 2024, more than 10TWh of renewable electricity — enough to power around 2.85 million European homes for an entire year — could not be used because of grid congestion and insufficient cross-border capacity.
A recent audit from the European Court of Auditors stated that renewable energy capacity gains linked to the bloc's REPowerEU, the 2022 plan to ditch Russian energy and become energy sovereign, are "negligible" compared with the Commission's 103GW goal. They also pointed out that grid infrastructure — particularly cross-border electricity connections — is the plan's most striking weakness.
Redispatch — effectively switching on more expensive generation because cheap renewable power cannot reach consumers — cost around €4.3 billion in 2024. Without action, annual redispatch costs could reach €26 billion by 2030, the Commission estimates.
Brussels knows it needs dramatically more clean energy to hit the 2040 climate target, but the draft acknowledges that simply adding wind and solar without grids, storage, flexible demand and electrification can create its own costs.
To address the remaining challenges, the EU executive proposes better monitoring of curtailment, clearer rules for hybrid renewable-and-storage projects, stronger investment signals for flexibility and greater use of electric vehicles and smart charging as sources of system flexibility.
Veerle Dossche, renewable energy programme manager at the NGO Climate Action Now Europe, said the Commission's impact assessment makes a "compelling case" for an ambitious and binding post-2030 renewable energy target. However, it notes that delivery must go beyond ambition.
"This requires robust national contributions, clear trajectories and effective compliance mechanisms, backed by measurable KPIs, so that early warnings trigger corrective action when member states fall off track,” said Dossche.
Power struggle over the power grid
Meanwhile, the legislative train has departed.
MEPs in the Parliament's industry committee backed a draft report on the future governance of the EU's power grid on Thursday, paving the way for adoption in plenary next week in Strasbourg, followed by the inter-institutional talks among the EU co-legislators, the Parliament and the Council.
EU lawmaker Tsvetelina Penkova (S&D/Bulgaria), leading negotiator on the legislative file, said the new rules should also help reduce electricity price disparities among EU countries and regions
"The Commission will now have a stronger role in defining the strategic framework, while ACER (the EU's energy regulators) will provide greater independent scrutiny. This is an important step towards making our infrastructure planning more democratic, transparent and accountable," said Penkova on Thursday.
EU lawmaker Virgil-Daniel Popescu (EPP/Romania) said Thursday's vote — backed by MEPs from the centre-right, liberals, Socialists and Greens — offers a “balanced and pragmatic” approach to turning Europe’s energy goals into the infrastructure needed to strengthen energy security and bring down energy costs.
“We have strengthened the Commission proposal by introducing a more strategic approach to infrastructure planning. Europe should have a clear picture of where the major bottlenecks are, which strategic corridors and network reinforcements are needed, when they should be developed towards 2040 and 2050, and what level of investment will be required," Popescu told Euronews.
Parliament backed plans to centralise Europe’s energy infrastructure planning, giving the Commission a leading role in drawing up an overview of the bloc’s future energy system as the first step towards a more coordinated process for identifying new grid needs.
However, this position risks clashing with the Council, with several EU countries rejecting a centralised takeover from the Commission, fearing loss of national sovereignty.
Another legislative file on permitting rules linked to the "Grids Package" is already underway, with official talks expected in October.

====================================================================================================

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger' - Biblical or a missed opportunity?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:56:00 UTC
20:56:00 KST

As a good-vibes-only record of the Live '25 Tour, 'Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger' does an admirable job. But the oddly coy documentary fails to meaningfully address the Gallagher brothers' reconciliation, or why the 2025 reunion was such a phenomenon.
I confess that I wasn’t exactly madferit when heading into Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger.
Ever since Oasis’ headline-dominating reunion, followed by their 41 stadium shows in 14 countries last year, I’ve reached my Gallagher limit. Beyond the fan worship which makes me think that people have lost all sense of perspective when it comes to Oasis, the release of a documentary chronicling the whole shebang reeked of a prolonged promotional campaign - the next step in a continuing cash-in coup about two gobby and freshly reunited siblings who haven’t released any new material in 18 years.
Still, you gotta roll with it, and I took the time to attend a special IMAX screening of Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern’s documentary, and emerged nearly won over.
As a rousing concert film and a love letter to Oasis fans, Don’t Look Back In Anger gets a lot right, capturing the euphoria the band has generated with their unlikely comeback. This is chiefly thanks to the sound design by The Zone of Interest's Tarn Willers and James Mather, Haris Zambarloukos' stellar cinematography, and some nifty editing by George Cragg and Martina Zamolo. Their talents brilliantly conspire to make the reunion feel impactful - even exhilarating at times.
As a meaningful chronicle of how the comeback came to be and what it represents, it’s not quite biblical.
Don’t Look Back In Anger is frustrating in the way it glosses over all the juicy stuff and skirts the irresistible narrative of how two bickering brothers went from repeatedly calling each other twats to publicly reconciliating.
It begins with an extended montage of the 90s glory days leading to the sudden and ugly falling out in 2009 during Paris’ Rock en Seine festival.
“Le groupe n’existe plus,” an announcer informs the crowd.
Cut to the band’s first rehearsal together in May 2025. No explanation as to what made this possible, no insight into who reached out to who, or how the animosity was dealt with... Before you know it, it's opening night in Cardiff.
While most films would have built up to this moment and chosen to end the film on the crescendo, the directors - and Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, here on scripting duties - decide to focus on the music as their film settles into a predictable rhythm and hagiographic tone. Concert clips follow, interspersed with portraits of fans and snippets of interviews with Liam and Noel, who come off as bafflingly well-behaved. As charming as some of these segments are, the brothers' uncharacteristically tame demeanour only contributes to the niggling feeling that the reason behind all of this is a big PR-mandated payday.
This cash grab sensation could have been dismissed had the filmmakers been able to delve more meaningfully into why the band continues to generate overwhelming devotion in fans in Britain and around the world, and why the 2025 reunion was such a cultural and social phenomenon. Sure, emotional fans are seen and heard gushing; and granted, this is about looking forward, not backwards. However, had some of the platitudes been excised in favour of something more resonant about the need for mental time travel leading to the possible mythologising of the "good old days" so that a sense of communion is achieved in trying times, then this could have been a fascinating documentary about overcoming divisions.
There is a clumsy montage teasing this, showing quick-cut footage of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, the rise of AI, but all that's left is Liam declaring: “When Oasis split up, everything went to shit.”
Bold statement, r'kid, as I think you'll find that everything went tits up in 2016 when David Bowie's death tore the fabric of the universe... And speaking of "shit", think again if we're getting any acknowledgement regarding the infuriating dynamic ticket pricing scandal. "There are no cheap seats..." according to the frontman.
For a band that has built a reputation as one "of the people", I audibly scoffed.
For all my bellyaching, Don't Look Back In Anger could have been worse and come off as a cynical puff piece. As a good-vibes-only record of the Live '25 Tour, it does an admirable job. As a sincere snapshot of crowds united by a common appreciation, it's undeniably uplifting. My quibbles persist only because I wanted to be won over, finally, and instead got something which feels like a missed opportunity. Don’t Look Back In Anger could have been a far more cathartic and compelling story of reconciliation and healing had it focused on the difficulties of the past to better look towards a more peaceful future. Instead, audiences will get Noel admitting that his brother Liam is “delightful”.
Still, diehard fans will be too busy singing along to care, while more casual audience members will make do with some admittedly terrific concert footage.
For me, I take some satisfaction in knowing that Don't Look Back In Anger will soon head to Disney+, making it the sweariest film to ever stream on the platform. Unless they decide to re-release an R-rated cut of Ratatouille with Little Chef muttering "fuck" and "cunt" when the yellow summer squash isn't mandolined properly. Now that's definitely maybe something worth considering...
"Hello, Disney? What are your thoughts on sweary revivals?"
Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger is out in select theatres on Friday 11 September before streaming on Disney+ later this year.

U.S. Marines’ new drone killer gets confirmation from V2X
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:55:39 UTC
20:55:39 KST

- V2X confirmed a $19 million U.S. Marine Corps contract for Tempest counter-drone vehicles on September 8, 2026, covering delivery, training and support.
- A related Pentagon notice from August 11 put the deal at roughly $19.06 million for 10 vehicles built by V2X subsidiary Vertex Modernization and Sustainment.
V2X confirmed on September 8, 2026, that it has been awarded a $19 million contract by the U.S. Marine Corps to deliver Tempest counter-drone vehicles, along with the maintenance, software and training needed to keep them running.
The announcement puts a public face on a deal the Pentagon had already disclosed. A contract notice dated August 11 identified the recipient as Vertex Modernization and Sustainment, an Indianapolis-based company operating as part of V2X, and put the value at roughly $19.06 million for 10 Tempest vehicles. Work under that award runs through August 10, 2027. V2X’s own release did not repeat the vehicle count, describing the deal only as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, a structure that sets up a framework for future orders rather than locking in a fixed total.
Tempest is a lightweight, four-wheel-drive vehicle built on a modified Can-Am Maverick X3, a commercial off-road buggy fitted with dual missile launchers and a sensor package for spotting and tracking drones. It fires AGM-114L Longbow Hellfire missiles, the radar-guided version of a weapon originally built for Apache attack helicopters, against what the military classifies as Class 2 and Class 3 unmanned aircraft, a category that spans small reconnaissance drones up to systems approaching the size of a light aircraft.
The vehicle already has a combat record. At least two Tempest units have operated in Ukraine, where Ukrainian forces have credited the system with shooting down 21 Shahed drones, the Iranian-designed loitering munitions Russia has fired into Ukrainian cities by the hundreds.
“Unmanned aerial systems are fundamentally changing the modern battlefield, creating an urgent need for counter-UAS solutions that are mobile, effective, and ready to operate in demanding environments,” said Jeremy C. Wensinger, President and Chief Executive Officer of V2X. “Tempest demonstrates what V2X does exceptionally well: respond to an urgent customer need and rapidly take a capability from concept and integration through fielding and sustainment. By bringing together our engineering, technology integration, logistics, and mission expertise, we can move with speed to deliver mission-ready solutions that directly address emerging threats.”
V2X first showed Tempest publicly at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference in October 2025, pitching it as a low-cost, easily repaired answer to small attack drones. The company says the vehicle’s commercially derived design keeps sustainment simple, since many parts can be sourced from civilian suppliers rather than specialized defense manufacturers.
V2X has not said whether the Marine Corps order announced this week covers the same 10 vehicles disclosed in August or represents an expansion under the IDIQ framework. The company also has not disclosed additional financial terms beyond the roughly $19 million figure or said how many Tempest vehicles the Marine Corps might eventually field.

System for controlling drones without satellite navigation unveiled in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:52:24 UTC
20:52:24 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Geoscan has unveiled an optical navigation system for drones in conditions where satellite navigation is unavailable, the company reported.
The solution was recognized as the best in the "Autonomous Navigation" category at the Dronosapiens Games engineering and technical competition organized by the Aeronext Association, it noted.
"Geoscan Group presented an optical navigation system without GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at the Dronosapiens Games engineering and technical competition organized by the Aeronext association. The system is designed to control UAVs during aerial photography and territorial monitoring in areas without satellite navigation. Geoscan’s solution was named the best in the "Autonomous Navigation" category based on the results of three days of testing," the statement said.
The algorithm uses data from an onboard camera: the system compares the captured images with a satellite map of the area. To navigate the intended flight zone, a feature map is generated in advance. Thus, the satellite base map is automatically downloaded from available sources.
"In our projects, we encounter satellite navigation interference, radio signal jamming, and spoofing even during flights that have been approved by all relevant authorities. The need to operate under such conditions compelled us to develop an autonomous optical navigation system. We began pilot operations of our solution earlier this year. This is now one of the key technologies for the UAV industry, without which further market development is hardly possible," Geoscan CEO Alexey Yuretsky emphasized.
During the competition, the Geoscan 201 drone autonomously took off from the launch pad and successfully completed the designated route. The operator did not manually correct the flight--the drone independently determined its position and altitude. The proposed system can be used for flights covering distances of up to hundreds of kilometers. Experts are currently developing a version of the algorithm that will be able to operate at night using a thermal imaging camera.

BJP leaders were among the first to jump onto the trend. Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal shared an AI-generated photograph of himself dressed in a grey suit and aviators, writing simply: "Vibing to the 80s trend."

The BJP's official X handle also shared some original pictures of Prime Minister Narendra Modi believed to be from the 1980s era.
What started as politicians recreating their younger selves soon became another format for the BJP and Congress to take veiled potshots at each other with AI doing the set design.
The Congress's Kerala unit shared an AI-generated image showing a bald man sitting in the front passenger seat of a Maruti Suzuki Omni, with the caption: "A Gujarat street in the 80s."
For context, the van, launched in India in the 1980s, became a familiar sight in Bollywood films where it was often shown being used by goons and kidnappers, eventually earning its own "kidnapping van" meme identity.BJP Gujarat hit back with an AI-generated image of its own.

What is the trend?
The trend itself is simple. Users upload a present-day selfie to AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini and ask them to recreate the image as if it had been taken in the 1980s.Unlike a regular vintage filter, the AI rebuilds the photograph around the person’s face, adding everything from big hairstyles and retro clothes to film grain and old-school studio lighting.The result is a polished throwback image that looks straight out of an old photo album or Bollywood publicity still. The trend has spread rapidly across Instagram and X, with influencers, celebrities and now politicians joining in.

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with United Arab Emirates over 'provocative and hostile actions'

Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with United Arab Emirates over 'provocative and hostile actions'
Algeria is severing diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates, state media reported Thursday. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has in the past accused the Gulf state of trying to meddle in Algeria's internal affairs.
Algeria decided to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates after what it described as the "exhaustion of all means to preserve bilateral ties", Algerian state media said on Thursday. State media later said the decision was a result of what it described as the UAE's "provocative and hostile actions".
The UAE Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Algiers said it was giving the UAE ambassador to Algeria 48 hours "to comply with the decision".
Algerian media outlets have in the past sharply criticised the UAE, accusing it of seeking to sow regional discord.
Last year, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune said his country's relations with all Gulf states were warm except for one, in a thinly veiled reference to the UAE. He described ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as "brotherly", while accusing the unnamed country of meddling in Algeria's internal affairs and seeking to destabilise it.
Tensions escalated further in February, when Algeria began the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE that was signed in Abu Dhabi in May 2013.
Tebboune has often referred to the UAE in speeches as a "micro-state" or "statelet" seeking to destabilise several countries in the region.
"Wherever they set foot, blood flows," he said in a televised interview in July, adding that the UAE has had a "very negative impact".
"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country," he added.
At the time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break "would have happened long ago" had Algeria not sought to avoid "deepening divisions" in the Arab world.

Australia declares its new air defense missile system combat ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:48:52 UTC
20:48:52 KST

- Australia's Army declared Final Operational Capability for NASAMS on September 9, 2026, with 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery as the first operational unit.
- The system, built under the SRGBAD project with Raytheon Australia and Norway's Kongsberg, uses Australian CEA Technologies radar and Hawkei-mounted launchers.
Australia’s Army has declared Final Operational Capability for its National Advanced Surface to Air Missile System, confirming the ground-based air defense system is ready to support Australian Defence Force operations. Defence announced the milestone on September 9, 2026.
NASAMS is built to detect, track and destroy cruise missiles, aircraft, helicopters and drones. The system was delivered under the Short Range Ground Based Air Defense project, known as SRGBAD, part of a broader air and missile defense setup that also draws on ships and fighter aircraft to protect ADF personnel and infrastructure.
Soldiers from Adelaide’s 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, are the first operational unit to field the system. The regiment, based at Woodside in South Australia, ran live-fire trials and qualification training as part of the phased rollout that led to this week’s declaration.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability for NASAMS marks a significant milestone in strengthening Australia’s integrated air and missile defence capability,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles. “NASAMS provides Army with a modern, highly capable air defence system that enhances our ability to protect Australian Defence Force personnel, critical assets and infrastructure from a range of airborne threats.”
Raytheon Australia is the prime contractor on SRGBAD, running under the Army’s long-standing LAND 19 Phase 7B program. NASAMS itself was co-developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, and Kongsberg Defence Australia built the system’s Fire Distribution Centres locally before handing final units to Raytheon Australia last year. The SRGBAD program is valued at roughly A$2.5 billion.
The Australian version pairs the Norwegian NASAMS design with locally built CEA Technologies radar, the CEATAC and CEAOPS active electronically scanned array systems, mounted alongside launchers on Hawkei protected mobility vehicles. Raytheon’s AN/AAS-52 Multispectral Targeting System adds day and night optical tracking. The setup replaces the Army’s older RBS-70 man-portable air defense missiles.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability delivers a world-leading capability for Defence and provides a major boost to Australia’s integrated air and missile defence,” said Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy. “Australian-designed radar technology is a key part of this capability, highlighting the important contribution local industry makes to Australia’s national security.”
NASAMS is in service with, or on order for, more than a dozen countries. Ukraine has used the system in combat against Russian cruise missiles and drones since 2022, giving the design an operational record beyond Australia’s own trials. Defence has not disclosed how many NASAMS batteries or launchers 16th Regiment will ultimately operate; the regiment is expected to field two batteries once full capability is reached.
Each NASAMS troop is built around a Fire Distribution Centre, a CEATAC radar, an optronic sensor vehicle and several launchers, with the Hawkei launchers and canisters carried on MAN/Rheinmetall HX77 trucks. The missile load is a mix of AIM-120 AMRAAM and Sidewinder missiles, the same interceptors used on Australian and allied fighter jets.
Sustainment of the system will run primarily through Australian-based support contracts already in place with CEA Technologies and Raytheon Australia.

China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25
September 10, 2026
At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday.
State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)."
The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported.
Cause remains unclear
Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added.
Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".
It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire.
The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders.+

Israeli army arrests 33 Palestinians in occupied West Bank, including 2 journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:35:44 UTC
20:35:44 KST

Qais Abu Samra, Ikram Kouachi
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The Israeli army arrested 33 Palestinians, including two journalists, two minors and former prisoners, during raids across the occupied West Bank on Thursday, according to the Palestinian Prisoners Media Office.  
In a statement, the non-governmental group said Israeli forces raided dozens of homes and searched them, damaging the contents of some properties during the campaign, which was concentrated in the provinces of Nablus, Bethlehem, Hebron, Jenin, Tubas and Tulkarem.  
The group said 17 Palestinians were arrested in Nablus, seven in Bethlehem, three in Hebron, one in Jenin, two in Tubas and three in Tulkarem.  
It identified two journalists among those arrested as Sabri Mousa Jibril and Muath Ammarna, both from Bethlehem.  
In Jenin, an Israeli special forces unit infiltrated the area around the Interior Ministry roundabout and arrested a former prisoner, according to the group.  
The arrests also included minors and other former prisoners, including one who had been released just a few days earlier, it added.  
The group said the escalation in arrests, home raids and property damage, along with the targeting of journalists, children and former prisoners, was part of an “ongoing policy of intimidation and arrests against Palestinians.”  
It added that arrest campaigns have continued across the occupied West Bank amid an ongoing Israeli escalation since the outbreak of the genocidal war in the Gaza Strip on Oct. 7, 2023.  
Since then, Israel has intensified raids and arrests in the West Bank, alongside an increase in attacks by occupiers and demolitions of Palestinian homes and other structures.  
According to the Palestinian Prisoners Society, more than 9,400 Palestinians are held in Israeli prisons, including 370 children and 92 women, amid reports by rights groups that some prisoners have been subjected to torture and medical neglect.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The alleged assassin had reportedly tracked the activist’s movements and hourly routine for an extended period before receiving the coordinates of a weapons cache from Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
The suspect retrieved a pistol equipped with a silencer and ammunition from the cache, according to investigators.
Under the purported FSB plan, he was to spend the night in a forest near the activist’s home before shooting the target several times from an ambush during a morning walk with their dog.
“SBU officers uncovered the enemy plan in advance and detained the hitman in the ambush while he was preparing the assassination attempt,” the agency said.
The SBU did not disclose the intended victim’s identity.
Three silenced pistols seized
Investigators identified the suspect as a 19-year-old resident of southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv who had allegedly been recruited by Russian intelligence through his social media activity.
The SBU said the teenager had published posts supporting fascist and Nazi ideology, bringing him to the attention of Russian operatives.
Russia Turns to Vietnam for Aircraft as Sanctions Ground Hundreds of Planes
After his alleged recruitment, the FSB sent him to the Kyiv area to carry out what Ukrainian authorities described as a high-profile assassination intended to destabilize the country.
During searches, SBU officers seized three pistols with silencers and ammunition, as well as smartphones allegedly containing evidence of communication with the FSB.
The agency did not say how long the suspect had monitored the activist or whether he had received payment for the alleged assignment.
Suspect faces life imprisonment
Investigators charged the teenager under three provisions of Ukraine’s Criminal Code: treason committed under martial law, preparation for a contract killing and unlawful possession of weapons and ammunition.
He remains in custody and could face life imprisonment with confiscation of property if convicted.
The operation was conducted by the SBU’s Mykolaiv regional office under the coordination of its Counterintelligence Department and the procedural supervision of the Mykolaiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office.

Breakthrough in talks with MHA on legislative powers: Ladakh grps
NEW DELHI: Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra said on Thursday that the Union Territory is moving towards seeking constitutional safeguards for its local population under Article 371, along with the creation of a UT-level elected body with legislative and financial powers.Kundra said a meeting of the sub-committee was held at the ministry of home affairs on Wednesday with the leadership of the Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance from Ladakh. Discussions focused on incorporating a special provision under Article 371 to protect the interests of the local population.He said the next meeting is scheduled for October, with the administration hoping to have an advanced draft of the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill ready by then.
What Ladakh is seeking
The proposed framework would include a Union Territory-level body elected directly through constituencies and vested with legislative and financial powers.The move comes amid demands for greater constitutional protection for Ladakh following its transition into a Union Territory.
Articles 371 contain special provisions for specific states. These provisions differ from one state to another but broadly seek to protect local political, cultural, social and economic interests.
Article 371-A, for instance, provides special safeguards for Nagaland. Articles 371-B and 371-C provide for special committees in the Legislative Assemblies of Assam and Manipur and similiarly other provisions are there for other states.If a new Article 371 provision is introduced specifically for Ladakh, it would be significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory rather than a state.The proposal would therefore require a constitutional arrangement tailored to a Union Territory, potentially making it different from the existing Article 371 provisions that primarily apply to states.

Houthis seize Red Sea port city in push to seize Bab el-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:24:28 UTC
20:24:28 KST

The Houthis' latest offensive is meant to replicate Iran's Hormuz blockade in the Bab el-Mandeb, with Red Sea coastal towns and islands in the crucial waterway among their next military objectives.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday and were advancing towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a Yemeni military source said.
Witnesses said they saw Houthi forces entering the city while chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
The city which has been held by Yemen’s internationally recognised government has been under sustained attack since early August, when more than 25 missiles struck it in a matter of days and forced port operations to halt.
The Yemeni government is yet to publicly confirm Mokha has fallen.
The same military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters."
Plotting another Hormuz
The Houthis, who control about one-third of Yemen's territory — albeit the most densely populated parts — are vying to seize and potentially disrupt the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
Together with Hormuz, cargo traffic through Bab el-Mandeb accounts for one quarter of daily petroleum and crude shipments, and nearly one-third of the world's maritime trade.
The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.
Yemen's government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".
Major-General Sadeq Duwaid, spokesman for the Yemeni government-affiliated National Resistance Forces controlling areas adjacent to the strait, earlier warned that the Houthi siege of Mokha was a key manoeuvre to build operational footing along the Red Sea coast.
"Through their continued attacks on Mokha and its port, the Houthi militia seeks to establish a presence along the shores of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and transform the area into a situation resembling that of the Strait of Hormuz," Major-General Duwaid said in mid-August.
The coastal town of Dhubab and Perim Island — a rocky volcanic island that sits in the middle of the strait and divides it into two shipping channels — are now considered to be the Houthis' central military objective.
Fighting continues to escalate
Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis launched a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
They also launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held territory.
The Houthis reported on Thursday that about 40 airstrikes were launched by Saudi forces in a fresh salvo.
"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.
On Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of "potential danger" in two areas, Khamis Mushait and Abha.
Inching towards Bab el-Mandeb
The Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.
A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 had largely halted years of active warfare, yet it never resulted in a lasting political settlement.
The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they held territory less than 100 kilometres away.
The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the internationally recognised government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".
Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.
The group previously severely disrupted cargo traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb with their campaign against what they said was Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was a show of support for Palestinians.

In Kyiv, drone alerts can continue for hours, sometimes beginning overnight, alongside missile attacks, and lasting into the following day.
Trains are delayed, passengers at railway stations are directed to underground shelters, and services may be suspended until the danger passes.
When monitoring teams detect a direct threat to a train already in transit, railway workers may stop it and order passengers to leave the carriages immediately, even if the train is in a field, forest, or another remote location.

Passengers moved away from the train to a safe distance immediately this time, fearing for their lives

Such evacuations can appear counterintuitive to people outside Ukraine. However, Russian drones are now deliberately pursuing trains. A direct hit can ignite a locomotive or passenger carriage within minutes, leaving those inside little time to escape.
The purpose of abandoning train carriages is to put as much distance as possible between individuals and the train, which may be the intended target.
Russian forces attacked a suburban passenger train operating on the #Kharkiv – #Izium route, injuring seven people, including passengers and railway workers.

The train had been stopped and its passengers evacuated before the strike. However, a female train attendant was killed after returning to the train following the evacuation order, according to Ukrainian Railways.

Emergency workers said two passenger carriages caught fire, while remaining passengers had been moved to safety.
Later on Tuesday, Russian drones struck a suburban diesel train in the Sumy region. The attack set a locomotive and passenger carriage on fire and injured at least 10 people, according to preliminary official figures.
Ukrainian officials said the train had come under consecutive strikes.
On Wednesday, Russian jet-powered drones attacked a railway station in the Izium district of the eastern Kharkiv region.
Two carriages of a passenger electric train caught fire, and eight people were injured, according to regional authorities.

Ukrainian Railways chief Oleksandr Pertsovskyi described Russia’s actions as a “horrific hunt” for passenger trains and urged travelers to follow evacuation instructions immediately.
The latest attacks follow a series of Russian strikes against trains, depots, bridges, and major railway junctions across Ukraine since the beginning of September.
Attacks on railway infrastructure
On Sept. 1, a railway depot was among the sites hit during a large-scale Russian attack on Kyiv, with President Volodymyr Zelensky reporting seven people killed in the wider attack.
Russia’s defense ministry said it had targeted the Darnytsia locomotive depot, describing it as a key maintenance point for locomotives used to deliver military cargo.
Russian forces later struck a bridge in Kramatorsk with aerial bombs and attacked railway equipment that Moscow claimed was also being used to transport military supplies.
Ukraine’s railway system continues operating despite repeated attacks and prolonged air raid alerts. Services are frequently delayed, rerouted, or temporarily halted, while damaged locomotives, tracks, and power systems are repaired.
For passengers, journeys increasingly depend not only on schedules but also on drone-monitoring reports and rapid evacuation orders.

AI firms ‘begging to be regulated,’ feel ‘compelled to race’ toward deadly technology: Ex-Anthropic researcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:22:09 UTC
20:22:09 KST

A former Anthropic researcher who warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could threaten humanity said Wednesday that AI companies are genuinely seeking regulation but feel compelled to keep competing for fear of falling behind their rivals.
“These people are also completely genuine when they are begging to be regulated,” Jacob Coxon, 27, told CNN's Anderson Cooper.
“They find themselves in this scenario where they're compelled to race towards building a deadly technology, and they would love for some sort of international body to allow them to approach it at a reasonable pace,” he said.
Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday after previously working at OpenAI, drew widespread attention with a post on US social media platform X saying the two companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
The post had garnered 143 million views by Thursday. His remarks have also received support from other AI safety researchers.
Evan Hubinger, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, responded to Coxon's post on X by saying he personally estimated the risk of AI killing all humans at more than 10% within the next decade, while acknowledging that current models pose a low extinction risk.
In the CNN interview, Coxon sought to clarify that he does not believe existing AI systems are capable of causing human extinction.
“Right now, there's no risk of extinction,” he said. “The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages in infrastructure, but they're not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction.”
His concern, he said, is the speed at which those capabilities are advancing and what could happen if AI systems become capable of improving themselves.
“I think what's just crazy is to look at the rate of progress, and there is a very real possibility that in the immediate future ... next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen,” Coxon said.
Asked how such a scenario could unfold, Coxon pointed to what he described as a real-world precedent.
"The precise scenario sounds a little bit like science fiction. It sounds like something that's not real, but I think it is frighteningly real, and it's easiest to understand it if you think about real things that happened two months ago," he said.
"Two months ago, OpenAI agents, AIs hacked into third-party infrastructure entirely of their own accord, and this was like a concentrated hacking spree that they carried out of their own volition. I think that if you extrapolate into the future the level of capabilities of these AIs, with the same independent volition, they could cause extreme havoc."
He described the most concerning possibility as AI being used to conduct AI research itself, allowing systems to progressively increase their own capabilities.
“The AI just gets smarter and smarter with no human involvement necessary,” Coxon said.
“A couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they're close to replacing them,” he said, adding that humans were still needed but that “quite plausibly within a year, we'll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas.”   
Coxon raised concerns before resignation
According to an NBC News report on Wednesday, Coxon had expressed similar concerns privately before his resignation in messages to Anthropic colleagues on the workplace platform Slack.
“I've recently become more concerned about the degree and imminence of this risk,” he wrote, according to the report, warning that without international coordination, superintelligent AI could pose a risk of human extinction.
He also said he planned to publicly criticize the industry while making clear that he did not blame individual Anthropic employees for the situation.
Coxon said he had initially intended simply to leave Anthropic rather than make a public intervention.
“I thought I can't be part of this anymore,” he told CNN. “I did not expect it to go this viral.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders has cited Coxon's post and renewed calls for Congress to act on AI regulation.
A recent NBC poll also found that 70% of American adults are more worried about AI than excited by it.

2026-09-10

20:20:32 KST

Russia is seeking an agreement with Vietnam to lease aircraft from Vietnamese airlines to Russian carriers, along with crews and maintenance under so-called “wet lease” arrangements.
“We sent the relevant proposals to our colleagues, and they are reviewing them,” Russian Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin said on Wednesday, following Russian-Vietnamese talks in Moscow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia has sought similar wet-lease agreements with several countries since international sanctions were imposed after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, disabling Russian airlines from legally accessing foreign aircraft and spare parts, Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported, citing The Moscow Times.
Moscow has approached countries in Central Asia, as well as Qatar, Kuwait, and Ethiopia, over such arrangements.
Ethiopia reportedly rejected Russia’s proposal in summer 2025, saying the government did not have the authority to order the state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to lease out aircraft.
There were also concerns that such an arrangement could expose the airline to US secondary sanctions.
So far, there have been no known agreements under which an airline from another country has leased aircraft to a Russian carrier under a wet-lease arrangement.
Russia’s aircraft shortage
Russian airlines have been cut off from not only purchasing new Boeing and Airbus aircraft, but also from legally obtaining parts and servicing many of the planes already in their fleets.
Ukraine Hits Russian Oil, Port Infrastructure in Strikes Stretching From Arctic to Caspian
Foreign-made aircraft account for roughly two-thirds of Russia’s civilian aircraft fleet and carry around 90% of the country’s air passengers.
Nearly 20% of the aircraft operated by Russia’s largest airlines have been grounded because of difficulties obtaining spare parts, according to calculations made by Russian newspaper Kommersant.
Of the 673 aircraft operated by Russia’s 11 largest airlines, which account for more than 90% of the country’s passenger traffic, 130 were not in service during the summer, Kommersant reported.
Under normal circumstances, airlines typically have no more than around 10% of their fleets out of service at the same time for scheduled maintenance.
Excluding Aeroflot, Russia’s largest airline group, eight carriers had nearly one-third of their fleets grounded, with 93 of 322 aircraft out of service.
In April 2025, Russian President Vladimir Putin allowed Russian airlines to lease aircraft from foreign companies under wet-lease arrangements, when previously, such leasing was permitted only between Russian airlines and only for domestic flights.

NEW DELHI, September 10. /TASS/. India's potential demand for Russian helicopters could amount to around 5,000 aircraft, Tatarstan Industry and Trade Minister Oleg Korobchenko told TASS.
He previously said that Tatarstan was exploring the possibility of localizing production of Russian helicopters in India. These include the Mi-38, Mi-8, Mi-34, and Ansat helicopters.
"We have more than 1,000 helicopters in Russia and a population of 150 mln, while they have a population of 1.5 bln. So if we were to compare the figures even at 30%, and they had the same proportion as we do in Russia, they would accordingly need at least 5,000 helicopters to transport people. Five thousand helicopters would be a huge market for us," he said on the sidelines of the Innoprom India international industrial exhibition.
According to the minister, Tatarstan intends to work with the Indian side on options for localizing Russian helicopter production, maintenance services and technology transfers. The potential volume of investment has yet to be determined. "Our task now is to explore as many possibilities as possible so that India's civil aviation market is receptive to resolving this issue with our Russian helicopters. If that happens, we can then reach agreements on both the market and investment," Korobchenko said.
He added that developing local production and service infrastructure would help expand the presence of Russian helicopters in the Indian market and strengthen cooperation between the two countries.
The Innoprom India international exhibition is being held in New Delhi from September 9 to 11. TASS is the event's general information agency.

World Insights: From fragile calm to widening war, can Yemen's escalation be contained?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:09:58 CST
20:09:58 KST

by Murad Abdo
ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- After more than four years of fragile calm along Yemen's major front lines, fierce fighting between government forces and the Houthis has spread across the country's western and northern regions, while the Houthis have resumed large-scale attacks inside Saudi Arabia.
Analysts say the latest escalation is putting mounting strain on the informal Saudi-Houthi understandings forged in the wake of the UN-brokered truce in 2022, and should the latest exchange of attacks and retaliatory strikes evolve into a sustained cycle, the risk of a broader escalation would increase substantially.
CURRENT SITUATION
The latest escalation first gathered momentum in western Yemen, where intense fighting erupted in southwestern Taiz province and neighboring Red Sea province of Hodeidah. Houthi forces sought to cut key roads linking Taiz with the government-held Red Sea port of Mocha and advance toward territory near Bab al-Mandab.
"The battle for Bab al-Mandab is not simply about gaining territory inside Yemen," Aden-based political analyst Muqbil Naji told Xinhua. "Whoever can threaten this waterway acquires leverage that extends well beyond Yemen's borders."
The fighting did not remain confined to western Yemen. Government forces subsequently launched a major offensive in Al-Jawf, a northern province bordering Saudi Arabia and located east of the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Fighting has also intensified on other fronts.
The widening battlefield has changed the military dynamics. The Houthis initially pressed their offensive in western Yemen toward areas near Bab al-Mandab, but additional fronts subsequently opened elsewhere, forcing them to redistribute forces.
"Opening multiple fronts by Yemen's government will weaken the Houthis," said Abdul-Salam Mohamad, chairman of the Abaad Studies and Research Center.
As military pressure expanded inside Yemen, the Houthis widened the confrontation beyond the country's borders. The group said Tuesday it fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military and energy facilities across southern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities said attacks on civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran wounded 73 people and caused fires at several energy facilities.
"The attacks on Saudi Arabia should not be viewed separately from what is happening on the ground in Yemen," Naji said, adding that by increasing the costs for Riyadh, the Houthis could be seeking to create a new equation in which Saudi Arabia has greater incentive to restrain military pressure from Yemeni government forces.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg on Monday described the renewed escalation as "extremely alarming," warning that increasingly intense clashes threatened to expand the conflict and further complicate prospects for a political settlement.
BEHIND THE ESCALATION
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government.
The UN-mediated truce that began in April 2022 formally expired six months later, but relative calm largely persisted for years afterward. The period of direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation gradually gave way to an undeclared arrangement under which cross-border attacks and Saudi air operations sharply declined even though no comprehensive peace agreement was reached.
That informal arrangement now lies at the center of the current crisis. Salah Ali Salah, a researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described what remains of that relationship as a "gray area."
Salah said years of conflict management without resolving the war's fundamental political, security and economic disputes helped produce today's vulnerability. Temporary de-escalation can give the parties time to "catch their breath and reposition their military and political strategies," he said.
According to Salah, recent attacks do not necessarily mean the undeclared understandings have collapsed, but they are becoming more fragile and less capable of containing escalation. "Both Riyadh and the Houthis understood the enormous costs of returning to sustained direct warfare," he said, adding that the greater danger lies in "repeated exchanges becoming a sustained cycle of retaliation."
If that happens, Salah said, both sides could begin reassessing the informal "rules of engagement" that have helped contain direct confrontation in recent years, increasing the risk that "a calibrated escalation becomes harder to control."
For now, however, Naji believes Saudi Arabia has not yet decided to return to the open-ended military intervention seen during earlier stages of Yemen's war. "Saudi Arabia still appears to be calibrating its response," he said. "The objective at this stage seems to be deterrence and gradual pressure rather than immediately entering a decisive war."
WHERE DOES ESCALATION LEAD?
The Yemeni analysts agree that a return to the calm of recent years is becoming more difficult, but they differ on what may come next.
Mohamad outlined three possible scenarios. His most likely scenario is continued fighting followed by another temporary truce after significant changes on the battlefield. "The war might halt, or a temporary truce might be reached," he said.
In his assessment, however, such as pause would come after changes in the military balance rather than through an immediate restoration of the pre-escalation status quo.
A second possibility is a much wider war. Continued Houthi attacks inside Saudi Arabia could alter Riyadh's calculations, Mohamad said, potentially leading to stronger Saudi backing for a broad government offensive.
His third scenario -- an early Houthi move toward de-escalation and a restoration of the previous status quo -- is less likely because the military and economic conditions underlying the current confrontation have already changed. "The situation is poised to explode," Mohamad said.
Salah described "a full-scale Saudi-Houthi confrontation as the most dangerous potential outcome, though not the most likely for now." That calculation could change, he said, "if cross-border attacks persist, ground operations widen or a high-impact strike inflicts enough casualties to force either side to fundamentally reassess its response."
The risk, Salah said, is that a confrontation could develop beyond the calculations that initially produced it. A confrontation can begin with controlled attacks designed to signal resolve, he said, but retaliation and counter-retaliation could create a chain reaction that becomes increasingly difficult to stop.
According to Salah, the more likely scenario is "a prolonged period of limited, intermittent escalation." Under this scenario, the parties would continue using military pressure to gain territory and strengthen their bargaining position while keeping some channels of communication open and seeking to avoid an all-out war. ■

We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down | Garrison Lovely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

On Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, warning that “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”
As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.
Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.
The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quickly find serious holes in even the most secured systems on the planet, including the NSA’s software.
OpenAI quickly followed with an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, which broke out of their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.
And a separate rogue agent swarm gained administrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.
Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systems surpass us at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.
There are growing calls to change that, by creating mandatory incident reporting and third party auditing, liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?
Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casar announced a bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.
This is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.
This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in its charter as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?
Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.
At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. OpenAI executive Dean Ball explains:
“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”
Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”
We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.
After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agents broke their way out of their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader, successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.
Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.
This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reuters reported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”
The site’s logs indicate OpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers that uncovered this swarm said that there have been more discoveries since.
And last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest ever leaps in benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantly harder to monitor because it can do more reasoning without verbalizing it.
The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institute found would also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is also better at figuring out when it is being tested, which researchers have long warned breaks the main way safety is evaluated.
Sam Altman soberly warns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.
Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing to render us obsolete.
That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientists synthesized the first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institute found that AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.
On Tuesday, amid a dispute over credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAI announced “an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russia reportedly used a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.
What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?
The bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts will tell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.
And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.
The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored using verification techniques that don’t assume any good will.
One quick and dirty idea would be to embed auditors within frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications, and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.
This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director John Ratcliffe said of advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.
And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.
- 
  Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, Sept 29)

Teachers at schools can now arrange a deferment in &quot;Reserve+&quot;

Teachers at schools can now arrange a deferment in "Reserve+"
Kyiv • UNN
Teachers can arrange a deferment in "Reserve+" without certificates or visiting an Administrative Services Center. The system automatically verifies employment and workload data.
Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions can now apply for a deferment in the Reserve+ app. The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
There is no need to collect certificates or contact a CNAP. The system automatically verifies the data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine
The following conditions must be met to apply for a deferment:
-   the educational institution is the primary place of employment; 
-   teaching workload – at least 0.75 of a full-time position; 
-   the position belongs to the teaching staff of a general secondary education institution; 
-   the employer data in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine match. 
It is noted that to apply for a deferment, users need to open the "Services" section in the "Reserve+" app, select "Deferment request," and then — "Teachers and other teaching staff of general secondary education institutions."
After the automatic data verification, the result will appear directly in the app. If it was not possible to apply for a deferment, the Ministry of Defence advises checking whether the information about the place of employment, position, and teaching workload in AICOM and the Pension Fund of Ukraine is up to date.

Japan’s AI satellites and other space ambitions ‘a serious threat’, China warns
State broadcaster CCTV says satellite plan is a cornerstone of Tokyo’s broader space militarisation strategy
The Japanese Nikkei newspaper reported last week that the planned AI-equipped satellites would be capable of analysing surveillance intelligence in space. The aim is to speed up targeting decisions and strengthen the country’s “counterstrike capability”, such as missile guidance.
According to the report, the defence ministry will develop a prototype satellite with domestic companies and conduct ground tests in the coming years, with space launches expected from the 2030 financial year.
Funding for the project has been included in Japan’s draft defence budget request for the 2027 financial year, although the exact amount has not been disclosed.
While traditional reconnaissance spacecraft send raw images to the ground for processing, these devices will collect data from other satellites and process the information in orbit.
By only sending the AI-generated analysis results, the Japanese project aims to significantly reduce the time for space-to-ground communication, according to the Nikkei report.

9/11 and the Substitute Mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

In 2001, I lost the world I knew. Twenty-five years later, I’m accidentally rebuilding it.
“I think people think you’re my mother,” my six-year-old niece whispered to me as we walked through the parking lot toward CVS.
“I think you’re right,” I said, smiling back at her impish grin that suggested we were pulling one over on the world. I had picked her up from school and was indulging her request to buy fake nails for our sleepover. She gripped my hand tightly, as a daughter would. We proudly walked through the automatic sliding doors, as one.
I don’t have children of my own, which means my niece is the beneficiary of my pent-up maternal love and obsession. She was born in 2020, and four months later, I left my job as the executive producer of a morning news show in New York and moved to Los Angeles. It was the first time I’d disrupted my ambitious climb up the media ladder, and when my feet landed in the California sand, my role as an aunt became the foundation of my daily life.
Birthdays, ballet recitals, and school performances anchored my calendar. Playing hide-and-seek before dinner, getting ice cream on a Tuesday, and letting her empty my closet for dress-up replaced late-night calls, breaking news, and media dinners. Recently, when my sister traveled abroad for work, my niece wanted assurance that her “substitute mother” would be around. The phrase made me laugh, but also squeezed my heart like a vise. Because I know what it’s like to have a substitute mother.
Daphne Pouletsos worked for the insurance company AON, her office was located in the south tower of the World Trade Center, and she was among the 2,977 victims killed in the 9/11 attacks.
Saza, as we called her, was my mother’s younger sister. Her nickname was a name given by my oldest cousin, Dayna, whose toddler tongue couldn’t say “Aunt Daphne.”
Although Saza lived in New Jersey and I grew up in Virginia, she was a constant light in my life. We drove up north for summers and holidays, and Saza would visit us throughout the year. Once, she hid in the back of our Chrysler minivan when my mom picked my siblings and me up from school, and she revealed herself by suddenly piping into the conversation. We squealed with excitement.
Saza knew how to make a mundane moment sparkle. Her sense of humor was the first thing to enter the room, and sleepovers at her house meant staying up late to watch Saturday Night Live. In my young mind, “The Church Lady” and “Coffee Talk” were extensions of my aunt (it helped that she also had a New Jersey accent). Shimmying our shoulders like “Sprockets” was like a special inside joke. Her laugh could sweeten the sourest mood.
But the best moments with her were always Christmas morning. Saza would come to my grandparents’ house first thing in the morning, the jingle bell on the back door announcing her arrival. She’d sit in the big, blue upholstered wingback chair, her feet tucked under her like a teenager, eyes shining behind her ‘90s rimless glasses. I can’t separate the thrill I got from opening a new baby doll from the joy I got from showing it to her. She would coo with enthusiasm, amplifying my delight. One time, she gave all of her nieces and nephews thick black plastic glasses with rubber banana noses attached. It was the silliest gift I’ve ever received, and one of the best. We took a picture, all piled on top of each other: laughing, goofy, family. Her presence carried a promise that everything was okay. As a kid, I assumed it always would be.
I was studying abroad in the fall of 2001. Classes at University College London hadn’t started yet, so I was traipsing around Europe with a sorority sister. We were at a restaurant in Barcelona when a waiter expressed dismay about “what happened at the World Trade Center.”
“My aunt works there,” I told my friend. But I was sure she was fine. How could she not be?
Still, I found a payphone and called home. My father tried to convey a stoic message: “We don’t know anything yet, we’re calling all the hospitals.”
Then I saw the footage on the TV in our hostel. I couldn’t believe that she could be one of the victims. Not Saza.
As a journalist, I know the questions that are typical in the wake of a tragedy. How old were they? Did she or he have kids? It’s natural. We’re inclined to measure loss by what, or rather, who, is left behind. But the true impact of a person’s life is not reflected in titles or preconceived roles. Every one of the 2,977 victims on 9/11 had a world that was wide and meaningful. You may not know the details of that world, but someone does. And they mourn not just the loss of that person, but the moments they made possible. For me, saying “I lost my aunt on September 11th” doesn’t begin to tell the story. My loss isn’t constricted by norms. Her legacy doesn’t fit neatly into a headline.
How old was she? Forty-seven. No, she didn’t have kids, but she had us. Twenty-five years later, I am 45, and I have my niece. Saza was the person who gave me the gift of knowing what an aunt can be.
While I could never fill her slippers, I feel Saza with me every day. She’s there when my niece and I are feeding the stray cat in my backyard. She’s there when we’re laughing at the Sunday comics. She’s there as we get dolled up in fancy dresses to go to the neighborhood pizza place. I am alive in these moments because she lived.
I wonder what else her life would have included if she had kept living it. What it would be like to have her visit me in Los Angeles. How she, my sister, and I would stay up late watching SNL together. How much love she would pour into life’s middle moments.
And most of all, what joy she would take in getting to know my niece, her namesake: Daphne.

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron

Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
September 10, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China.
"Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris.
European-crewed spaceflight
"We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts."
Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station."
He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board."
Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport.
The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance.
'Passengers or pilots?'
Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space.
After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?"
The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration.
"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said.
Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion).
"Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically."
