Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.
Best Bluetooth Speaker Overall
Specs
Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.
Best Smart Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
If your house is already full of Sonos speakers, the Sonos Play is an easy addition to justify, with ample smarts and connectivity built-in. It sounds significantly better than the smaller Sonos Roam 2, with an audio performance closer to the brand’s excellent Sonos Era 100, despite being battery powered.
Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.
At 2.9 pounds, it’s just about portable enough for travel, although I was very aware I was carrying it in my backpack. You can also charge your phone from it or add an analog source using Sonos’ optional line-in adapter. If you’re already invested in Sonos’ ecosystem, and don’t mind a regularly-changing Sonos app, it’s hard to think of a more smart speaker.
Best Budget Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Great looks, cute size, and instantly stolen by my tweenage daughter, the Go 5 is my ideal tiny speaker. It weighs next to nothing and fits in the palm of my hand, but the 4.8 watt output sounds considerably less weedy than it has any right to.
The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. Its tough little enclosure is drop-proof and IP68 dust and waterproof. Connectivity is also impressive with Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, 7-band app EQ, and clever pairing (where you bump two Go 5s together to create a stereo pair).
It’s speakers like this that remind me just how we’ve come since the days of sticking my phone in a mug to amplify the tiny built-in speaker. If only I knew where my daughter had put it.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Battery Life
Specs
I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.
Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.
In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. It’s loud enough for small- to medium-sized rooms, and cut through when used outdoors, with weighty bass, decent balance, and no obvious distortion when pushed. The 360-degree presentation spreads music evenly too, so it feels less directional than many rivals.
Best Bluetooth Speaker for Sound Quality
Specs
Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.
The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.
Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

AMD unveils ‘personal super computer’ for new era of computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:59:40 UTC
19:59:40 KST

The American chipmaker launched what they have described as a ‘personal supercomputer’ in Berlin on Friday, designed and made for a “completely new era of computing” driven by AI.
The supercomputer, called the Threadripper Halo Station, was unveiled at the German tech event Internationale Funkausstellung by AMD Senior Vice President Jack Huynh.
The Threadripper Halo is an ultra-high-performance workstation equipped with up to two terabytes of system memory, up to 576 gigabytes of high bandwidth memory (HBM3E), along with 96 cores of Threadripper Pro, two MI350P data centre accelerators, all supported by liquid cooling.
Huynh said the new supercomputer is the “most powerful workstation in the world”, capable of running AI models with more than a trillion parameters.
The AMD executive gave a brief demonstration of its potential at the event by generating an entire 3D world and flight simulator from a single prompt.
The company’s pitch is to bring data-centre level AI performance and capacity to a desktop format, as demand for AI rapidly grows around the world.
The supercomputer is slated for release early next year, however AMD are yet to reveal how much it will cost. It is expected that it could exceed €100,000, geared towards corporate and institutional budgets rather than as personal computers as originally pitched.
Yet it will give its consumers a platform to deploy large-language models and agentic AI systems themselves rather than rely on increasingly expensive cloud computing.
The Threadripper Halo Station’s direct competitor is the NvidiaDGX Station, with both able to run large AI models in a desktop form, however they differ in how they approach this challenge.
AMD’s supercomputer dominates on memory capacity and bandwidth, offering more than three times as much memory than Nvidia’s, allowing it to run on trillion parameter AI models locally.
However, Nvidia’s offering more seamless integration when moving code from a local workstation to the cloud and, crucially, it is already available, retailing at around €100,000.
Industry analysts see AMD's announcement as a potential catalyst for reshaping the competitive landscape of the local AI computing market.
With cloud AI subscription costs adding up for many institutions and businesses, demand for computers such as the Threadripper Halo Station to run large models on their own infrastructure will continue.
Therefore, AMD's approach of delivering data-centre-class performance using standardised components to lower the barrier to entry could be a major turning point in the expansion of the AI and personal computing sectors.

IAEA accuses Iran of ‘non-compliance’: Why, and what now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:59:39 UTC
19:59:39 KST

IAEA accuses Iran of ‘noncompliance’
Nuclear watchdog has gone more than a year without inspecting key sites; however Iran says US attacks have made access unsafe.
The Board of Governors of the United Nations nuclear watchdog has passed a resolution accusing Iran of failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation commitments and referring the matter to the UN Security Council (UNSC).
The diplomatic move – backed by the United States and its key European allies – comes more than six months into the US-Israeli war against Iran, and as tensions flare in the Strait of Hormuz, where the US and Iran have traded attacks on vessels in recent days.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brent crude surpasses $100 a barrel as Iran, US escalate attacks
- list 2 of 3Did Iran capture a US submarine? What we know about the underwater drone
- list 3 of 3Why US-Iran war over Hormuz is threatening the Gulf’s waters
Here’s what’s to know about the resolution by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and its implications during the ongoing conflict:
What has the IAEA accused Iran of?
The IAEA resolution expressed “grave concern” over Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), to which it is a signatory.
Under the NPT, Iran is forbidden from producing nuclear weapons and is required to meet IAEA safeguards to verify that any nuclear material it has is for peaceful purposes.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against Iran in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
In its latest resolution, the IAEA board said its “lack of information about previously declared nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it” is a “proliferation concern” that needs to be urgently addressed.
It called on Tehran “to engage seriously and without preconditions in talks aimed at building international confidence in the exclusively peaceful nature of Iran’s nuclear programme”.
It is the first time in 20 years that the IAEA board has passed such a resolution.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has condemned the resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
“This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis,” said Iran’s representative to the UN in Vienna, Reza Najafi.
Najafi said Iran has been unable to provide inspectors safe access to its nuclear sites due to the ongoing conflict. However, he said Iran has “neither stopped nor suspended its safeguards obligations,” adding that “performance is currently impossible under continuing military operations and persistent threats”.
Tehran “will cooperate only to the extent that circumstances and safety permit”, he added.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi appeared to accuse the US, which sponsored the IAEA board resolution along with the United Kingdom, France and Germany, of political posturing.
“They attack Iran’s safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the IAEA Board of Governors,” said Gharibabadi in a post on X.
Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons but insisted it has the right to pursue civilian nuclear technology.
US President Donald Trump has demanded that Tehran completely dismantle its nuclear enrichment programme. The US launched the current war, saying Iran was on the verge of making a nuclear bomb – an assertion not backed by the IAEA as well as the US’s own intelligence agency.
Iran has a legal right to run a civilian nuclear programme under the NPT.
What is the UNSC expected to do?
It is unlikely to take any further action, as Iran’s allies Russia and China are veto-holding members.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group, told the AFP news agency that the IAEA resolution is ultimately “an exercise in futility,” with Russia and China “likely to ensure that Western pressure hits a wall at the Security Council”.
What impact could this have on the US war against Iran?
The US, which has made Iran’s nuclear programme a central point in the ongoing conflict, could cite the IAEA referral as evidence of a potential Iranian nuclear threat.
On the same day as the IAEA report, US President Donald Trump renewed threats to target Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, which has two underground complexes near Iran’s damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
Trump said the US had observed “a little activity” there and would “advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard”.
The US president also reiterated his claim that Iran is seeking a nuclear weapon, adding that the world would be “in deep trouble” if they secured one.
Trump’s repeated warnings about an Iranian nuclear risk and his threats to strike Iran’s nuclear sites come despite his claim last summer that US strikes had “totally obliterated” Iran’s key enrichment facilities.
What is the IAEA’s history with Iran?
The IAEA was highly critical of Iran in the early 2000s, accusing it of failing to declare nuclear material and activities. In 2006, the UNSC imposed sanctions on Iran after it failed to comply with a resolution demanding it end its uranium enrichment programme.
But after Iran agreed to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) with six major global powers, including the US, it agreed to curtail its nuclear programme and open up nuclear sites to extensive, unprecedented IAEA inspection.
Iran remained in compliance for years, but the agreement went south after Trump withdrew the US from the deal in 2018 and reimposed US sanctions on Iran. Tehran retaliated by intensifying its nuclear programme, abandoning the restrictions imposed by the deal.
In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was not complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks against it just days later.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, however, did not back the US claims that Iran was capable of making an atomic bomb. “We did not have any proof of a systematic effort to move into a nuclear weapon,” he told CNN.
The IAEA suspects that Iran has about 400kg (882lbs) of highly enriched uranium, with which 10 nuclear weapons could potentially be manufactured if enriched further.

US urges NATO allies to leave ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:57:16 UTC
19:57:16 KST

The US, further complicating already tense international relations, is pushing for a “systematic dismantling” of the International Criminal Court, urging NATO members to abandon the Rome Statute, writes Politico.
According to three anonymous NATO diplomats, at a closed meeting of ambassadors from 32 NATO member states in Brussels in July, US envoy Matthew Whitaker asked for the alliance’s help in dismantling the ICC and called for abandoning the Rome Statute. Whitaker reportedly concluded his speech by saying that Americans would be careful who supported them.
The pressure to leave the ICC is part of a broader campaign by US President Donald Trump’s administration against international institutions and rules that it sees as restricting US freedom of action. The campaign is driven by US concerns that its officials could be tried for war crimes. The White House is also moving to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement, has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, and has pressured companies to withdraw from the Space Summit in Paris. The White House has also launched a series of trade spats.
In addition to Whitaker’s comments, the US mission to NATO issued a statement saying the US would systematically dismantle the ICC’s capabilities and called for steps to withdraw from the Rome Statute. It also called on allies to assess the risks posed by the ICC to their countries, publicly condemn the court’s abuse of power and end support for the ICC. The document says the ICC’s charade must be ended immediately and permanently. Although NATO is not a signatory to the Rome Statute, all alliance members except Turkey and the US have ratified it.
Opposition to the ICC was launched this summer by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio,
who accused the court of undermining US sovereignty. He said on the 13th of July that the ICC and its friends were waging war on the US, not with bullets or missiles, but with the force of statutes and so-called international law. Rubio added that if the court believes it can take away US sovereignty, Americans will show the extent of their resolve.
The ICC was established in 2002 to try individuals accused of the most serious international crimes, including genocide and war crimes. The last investigation against US officials was launched in 2020, when the ICC opened a case into alleged war crimes committed by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The case lost priority a year later. The ICC is now facing calls to investigate US attacks on boats in the Caribbean, which the Americans say are part of a fight against drug trafficking.
The US campaign marks a sensitive moment for NATO. The alliance has been strained by the refusal of many European countries to join Trump’s war on Iran, drawing Trump’s ire. Washington also rattled the alliance when Trump threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland. The alliance managed to bridge the gap at an annual summit in Ankara, but just days later, the US demand to dissolve the ICC renewed tensions. One NATO diplomat said Whitaker’s comments were “quite shocking,” while another added that they were “disappointing.”
Diplomats said that in response to Whitaker’s remarks,
France and the Netherlands defended the ICC and made it clear that they opposed the court’s dissolution.
The US delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment. The French delegation declined to comment on the situation, but stressed its support for the ICC. The Dutch delegation referred to the country’s Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen as saying that the Netherlands fully supports the ICC.
American envoys also spoke of the dual position of European countries. The US State Department said it was determined to closely monitor countries that refuse to “reject the ICC’s false authority” while relying on US assistance. In August, Washington imposed sanctions on top officials of the ICC.
An ICC spokesman said the court remains focused on the independent and unbiased exercise of its mandate, as set out in the Rome Statute, to protect victims and ensure justice.
The campaign against the ICC comes against the backdrop of other US efforts. Washington is trying to get Canada and Europe to take greater responsibility for their own defense. A survey sent to NATO countries in August, asking for their opinions on US foreign policy, including in the Middle East, is being seen as an effort to force them to align with US views in exchange for defense assistance.

AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton says 10% risk of human extinction from AI 'not unreasonable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:42 UTC
19:45:42 KST

Büşra Nur Çakmak
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Nobel laureate and artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton said estimating a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction within the next decade is "not unreasonable," adding to a growing chorus of warnings from researchers working at the forefront of the technology.
Hinton, often described as the "Godfather of AI," told BBC's Newsnight on Wednesday that humanity has never before created entities that could potentially become more intelligent than humans, making the risks difficult to predict.
"We've never created beings that may soon be smarter than us. We don't know what's going to happen," Hinton said.
Asked whether there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans, potentially within a decade, Hinton said it would be "very foolish" to assume the risk was as low as 1%.
"A 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate to me. But nobody really knows how to give a sensible estimate," he said.
Hinton warned that advanced AI would not necessarily need to control physical systems to pose a severe threat.
"The first thing to realize is it doesn't even have to be able to act in the real world to cause devastation," he said, adding that AI could create "complete chaos just by talking to people."
He said highly capable systems could also be used to design dangerous biological or computer viruses and conduct devastating cyberattacks.
Hinton's warning comes amid similar concerns raised by researchers working at leading AI companies.
Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who has previously worked on foundational AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday, accusing both companies of racing toward self-improving superintelligence despite the potential risks.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon said.
He also warned that people developing advanced AI systems privately harbor fears that the technology could pose an existential threat by the end of the decade.
Evan Hubinger, who leads Alignment Science at Anthropic, publicly backed Coxon's concerns, saying Tuesday that he personally believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Hubinger stressed that current AI systems pose little immediate danger, saying his main concern is the potential emergence of superintelligence through recursive self-improvement, where AI systems could autonomously create increasingly powerful successors.
Hinton stressed that researchers need to determine how to build advanced AI systems that do not develop goals harmful to humanity.
"We have to figure out how to design it so that it won't want to," he added.

‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.
It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.
“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.
Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.
The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.
“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.
“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.
Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.
In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.
Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”
Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.
The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.
“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.
Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.
The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.
Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”

RNLI steps up security after attacks by far-right agitators over small boat rescues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:44:13 UTC
19:44:13 KST

The RNLI is increasing security after a backlash from far-right agitators over the lifeboat charity’s involvement in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing them to UK shores.
Volunteers have been told by the charity’s bosses that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they feel this might put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.
There has been a heavy security presence around RNLI bases on the south coast of England over the last few days, with police and private guards monitoring some areas.
At the charity’s headquarters in Poole, barriers have placed around a memorial sculpture to RNLI volunteers who lost their lives and around a rose bed to mark the 200th anniversary of the charity. A viewing platform into the headquarters has been closed off.
The RNLI has said it will continue to rescue asylum seekers in the Channel despite the attacks from far-right activists after its involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth.
But after Sunday’s protest, the RNLI’s chief executive emailed volunteers to say security processes were being reviewed.
Volunteers were asked to challenge people near lifeboat stations if they did not have ID, but advised not to engage with members of the public if they felt uncomfortable.
Staff at the Portsmouth lifeboat station close to where the asylum seekers landed on Sunday have been approached by members of the public and asked to explain the RNLI’s actions.
The RNLI has said workers have been subjected to online and physical abuse and there have been “baseless” rumours circulating that the charity had housed asylum seekers or moved them to secret locations after helping them to shore.
Three police forces have been involved in protecting RNLI volunteers, staff and buildings. Dorset police have been helping keep the headquarters secure while Hampshire officers have patrolled RNLI stations in Portsmouth.
Sussex police were investigating “offensive and threatening commentary towards RNLI volunteers”. Images of some RNLI crew members who were apparently involved in the operation on Sunday were published on social media with the accusation that they were complicit in an “invasion” of the UK.
About 50 protesters, including members of the Poole Patriots and Hampshire Resistance attended a demonstration outside the RNLI’s headquarters in Poole on Wednesday.
Protest leaders handed out rape alarms to women, claiming they were at risk from men brought into the UK by the RNLI, and called for people to stop donating to the charity.
An RNLI spokesperson said: “Given the unacceptable abuse our people have faced, and with protest activity taking place at RNLI locations, we have taken action to help ensure the safety and wellbeing of our volunteers and staff.
“As well as enhancing security at RNLI locations, we issued guidance to our people earlier this week on how to keep themselves safe. This guidance included how to manage potentially challenging interactions with members of the public, and where appropriate, choosing not to wear RNLI branded clothing.
“Our people have been reminded that their safety comes first, and they are encouraged to report relevant incidents internally and, where appropriate, to the police.”

- The black silk gown, designed by Christina Stambolian, was worn the same night Prince Charles admitted infidelity, symbolising Diana's confident public statement.
- The dress will be exhibited in London, Hong Kong, and Geneva before the auction, marking its first public display in nearly 30 years.
AI generated
The “revenge dress” worn by the late Princess Diana in 1994 is up for auction at Sotheby’s for the first time in nearly three decades.
The black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian is estimated to fetch as much as £220,000 (S$377,050) when it goes on sale on Dec 9 during Sotheby’s Luxury Week in New York, the auction house said on Sept 10.
Diana wore the dress in June 1994 as she arrived at the Serpentine Gallery in London for a fund-raising dinner. It gained notoriety because the then Prince Charles (now King Charles III) – from whom she had been separated for nearly two years but not yet divorced – was widely expected to say in a national television interview broadcast that same evening that he had been unfaithful to her.
According to a later documentary, her decision to wear the dress was a last-minute one after initially setting aside a more traditional Valentino outfit. “She wanted to look a million dollars,” her former stylist Anna Harvey said on the programme, according to Vogue. “And she did.”
Stambolian’s off-the-shoulder dress features an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train. It will make its first public appearance at Sotheby’s in London during Fashion Week from Sept 17 to 21, followed by further exhibitions in Hong Kong and Geneva, before it goes to New York for the auction.
The dress was previously sold at auction in 1997, according to Sotheby’s, without giving details.
In 2023, a black, ballerina-length velvet gown owned by Diana was sold at Julien’s Auctions in Hollywood for US$1,148,080, 11 times its estimated price.
Charles and Diana were divorced in 1996 and she died in a car crash in Paris the following year at age 36. BLOOMBERG

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:42:26 UTC
19:42:26 KST

Aybüke İnal Kamacı
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
- 'The fact that Palestine is home to the highest number of child amputees in the world makes this marketing choice even more obscene,' Omar Barghouti tells Anadolu
- 'Boycotts apply pressure on corporations, for instance, by speaking their language: profit,' he says
-  Critics have called Adidas campaign featuring Israeli amputee soldier tone-deaf
The Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement has dismissed as “empty talk” an apology posted by Adidas over an ad campaign featuring an amputee Israeli soldier.
Speaking to Anadolu, BDS co-founder Omar Barghouti said: "The fact that Palestine is home to the highest number of child amputees in the world makes this marketing choice even more obscene; it celebrates the very instrument of that suffering."
The German sportswear brand has faced growing criticism and calls for a boycott after choosing retired Israeli soldier Shalev Biton as the face of its “single shoe service” campaign.
Critics have called the campaign tone-deaf, saying it ignores the large number of Palestinians who have lost limbs as a result of Israeli attacks on the Gaza Strip.
"It's no wonder that an immediate and organic global boycott took off," said Barghouti, a Palestinian human rights activist and recipient of the 2017 Gandhi Peace Award.
"This isn't Adidas just being tone-deaf or insensitive; it is an absolute affront to the Palestinians whose loved ones have been killed by Israel, and who have lost limbs to Israeli attacks," he said.
Commenting on Adidas' apology, which was posted on a regional account rather than through a broader corporate statement, Barghouti said: "Now Adidas is in damage control mode. Their so-called apology is empty talk.
“Those affected by this image are millions of Palestinians living under Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza, its illegal military occupation of Palestinian territory, and its decades-long settler-colonial apartheid regime."
Barghouti said the company's decision to feature the soldier “normalizes the violence of an occupying army and profits from the normalization of apartheid.”
Barghouti called on Adidas to remove the Israeli soldier from all promotional materials and channels immediately and establish a company-wide ethical policy governing partnerships, spokespersons, ambassadors and testimonials.
"Until then, we reiterate our full support for holding Adidas accountable via global boycotts," he said.  
How BDS works
Barghouti said the BDS movement advocates boycotting companies, services and institutions it considers complicit in Israel's actions against Palestinians, based on clear criteria.
"BDS targets complicity, not identity. It targets institutions, not individuals," he said.
He said boycotts seek to exert financial pressure on corporations.
"Boycotts apply pressure on corporations, for instance, by speaking their language: profit.
“If a corporation faces financial, legal, or reputational risks due to its complicity in Israel's crimes, it is more likely to end its involvement, as our long experience proves."
Barghouti stressed, however, that boycotts are only one part of the movement's strategy.
"BDS also calls for divestment and other forms of nonviolent pressure as well as lawful, targeted sanctions," he said.
He said the three strategies -- boycotts, divestment and sanctions -- are designed to reinforce one another by applying pressure on institutions, corporations and governments.
"With these three tactics we can, and will, achieve our goal of freedom, justice and equality for Palestinians everywhere," he said.

In Ukraine, testing of 5G connectivity is being expanded in Odesa following the launch of pilots in Lviv, Borodianka, Kharkiv and Kyiv, the Ministry of Digital Transformation said Thursday.
According to a statement by the ministry on Telegram, the average 5G speed is 600-700 Mbps, while peak speeds exceed 1 Gbps.
"The technology takes on part of the traffic and unloads LTE networks, so even in places with large crowds of people, connectivity remains stable," the Ministry of Digital Transformation explained.
Deputy Minister of Digital Transformation Stanislav Prybytko said on Facebook that the ministry had received the first results of the nationwide pilot project: in particular, 340 5G base stations are currently operating, and 3.85 million unique users have already used the technology.
According to him, 30% of Ukrainians' smartphones already support the technology.
Prybytko said that going forward, the ministry will continue preparing Ukraine for further scaling of the technology after martial law is lifted.
Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest telecom operator, added in a press release that 5G coverage in Odesa will include the historic center, Primorsky Boulevard, the Potemkin Stairs and adjacent areas.
According to the operator, during testing, the maximum data transmission speed on the 5G network exceeded 2.4 Gbps.
In turn, LLC lifecell, the third-largest mobile operator, said in a press release that the share of users of 5G devices on its network is growing and currently stands at 35%, while in Odesa it is 41%.
The company specified that average daily traffic consumption by lifecell 5G subscribers is 10 TB, while the maximum data transmission speed reaches 1.5 Gbps.
At the same time, Ukraine's second-largest mobile operator, VF Ukraine (Vodafone Ukraine, VFU), said in a press release that its coverage in Odesa will be available on Primorsky Boulevard, Kobleva Street, Soborna Square, Deribasivska Street, Hretska Square, Starosinna Street, Pryvokzalna Square and Kulikove Pole.
As reported, 5G technology in Ukraine will operate in two frequency bands – 3,500 MHz (to provide high data transmission speeds) and 700 MHz (to expand coverage).
Testing will continue, according to preliminary data, until the end of 2026, Vodafone Ukraine said.

He photographed Ukraine, then enlisted and died defending it at 27. Eleven years on, Viktor Hurniak’s story is still being told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:33:35 UTC
19:33:35 KST

Viktor Hurniak was a Ukrainian photojournalist who worked for UNIAN, a major Ukrainian news outlet, and for Reuters, and co-founded the LUFA photo agency, according to Ukrainska Pravda. He joined the fight in the Russo-Ukrainian war in September 2014. Russia killed him on 19 October that year near the village of Smile in Luhansk Oblast, as he helped evacuate wounded soldiers under mortar fire.
Since the Russo-Ukrainian war began in 2014, Ukrainian media workers have been killed while reporting, as civilians, and after joining the armed forces.
From photographer to volunteer
Hurniak had been photographing since he was 14. He started at the Ternopil newspaper 20 Khvylyn, and UNIAN picked up his work after he happened onto a fire on Crimea’s Ai-Petri in 2007.
By summer 2014, Viktor was raising money and finding helmets, body armor, clothing, and vehicles for Ukrainian troops, often delivering the supplies himself. His network and ability to source equipment earned him the callsign Oligarch among Aidar soldiers.
On one trip to Italy, Viktor, his father Petro, and friends returned with 550 helmets.
Friends, including Vitalii Derekh, tried to persuade him not to go further. They argued that he was more useful finding equipment than carrying a rifle.
Hurniak answered: “Well, I want to fight.”
In September 2014, he joined Aidar’s 24th territorial defense battalion.
His decision did not make him more distant from his family. Olesia Yedynak-Khoma recalled that after joining the battalion, he contacted them more often, sent photographs, and shared more about what was happening in Donbas. He told his sister Olia that there was “real life” in Donbas and that he had found sincere people and a strong sense of brotherhood there.
The day Russia killed him
On 19 October 2014, Hurniak was helping evacuate wounded soldiers from checkpoint 32 on the Bakhmutka road near the village of Smile in Luhansk Oblast when mortar fire hit. He was killed by shrapnel.
Viktor was 27. His daughter Yustyna was two.
Seven years later, Ukraine posthumously named Viktor Hurniak a Hero of Ukraine and awarded him the Golden Star.
His photographs were later exhibited in Poland, Estonia, Germany, and the United States, including at the European Parliament in an exhibition titled “Donbas: War and Peace.”
His story continues
Writer Iryna Vovk's Viktor Hurniak, published by Folio in its "True Heroes" series, was presented at a memorial festival in his home region in October 2025 and in Ternopil in January 2026, 11 years after his death. The book is built from the recollections of his family and friends.
Olesia Yedynak-Khoma, one of Hurniak’s friends, founded a scholarship in his memory at the Ukrainian Catholic University’s School of Journalism and Communications.
The question Hurniak once asked himself later became a guiding phrase for his sister Olia:
“What have you done for victory?”
He had already given his own answer. Urged to keep sourcing equipment rather than carry a rifle, he said he wanted to fight, and in September 2014 he went.

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Development efforts by Russia’s High Precision Systems Holding (part of the state tech corporation Rostec) enable the creation of a unified, layered air defense system, the holding company reported.
"Developments by High Precision Systems of the Rostec State Corporation make it possible to organize effective air situation monitoring and build a layered air defense system for critical and port infrastructure facilities, as well as to establish air defense lines," High Precision Systems representatives said.

In turn, the mobile Pantsir systems complement the stationary Pantsir-SMD-E air defense missile systems – the latter are primarily designed to repel large-scale drone attacks. "It is important that the Pantsir systems can be equipped with various types of anti-aircraft missiles, including short-range interceptor missiles. Each vehicle can carry up to 48 short-range interceptor missiles, which allows them to effectively counter an attack by an entire swarm of drones," the holding company noted.
At the ultra-close range, High Precision Systems added, facilities are protected by the TKB-1167 air defense system. It is capable of autonomously detecting and tracking targets, which reduces the operator’s workload and shortens the response time to individual UAVs.
"Thus, the combination of solutions from Rostec’s High Precision Systems Holding makes it possible to form a unified reconnaissance and information network and several firing lines with different ranges and types of weapons," the holding company concluded.

FACTBOX – How El Nino could reach your shopping basket: 5 global commodities at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:07 UTC
19:32:07 KST

- -Drought, heat and shifting rainfall patterns threaten key producing regions
- Rice, sugar, palm oil, cocoa and coffee face supply risks as El Nino strengthens
A powerful El Nino is strengthening in the Pacific Ocean, and the United Nations says its effects are already visible around the world.
El Nino is a natural climate cycle that begins when surface waters in the tropical Pacific warm well above normal. That shift reroutes the atmosphere's jet streams, drying out some farming regions while flooding others.
The UN weather agency, World Meteorological Organization (WMO), said on Sept. 3 that the phenomenon is firmly established and has a nearly 100% chance of continuing through February 2027.
Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador are already suffering erratic weather and drought linked to El Nino, driving severe crop losses across Central America's "Dry Corridor." Indonesia has been battling wildfires that sent haze drifting into Malaysia and the Philippines.
Because so many food crops are grown in a handful of climate-sensitive regions, the ripple effects can show up months later in supermarket prices worldwide.
El Nino does not, however, automatically mean every commodity will become more expensive. The World Bank notes that its effects vary by crop and region, while the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) says global cereal supplies and stocks remain relatively strong despite weather risks.
At the same time, the combination of a strengthening El Nino, extreme weather and existing geopolitical and trade disruptions is already putting pressure on food markets. FAO said its global Food Price Index rose to 133.3 in August, the highest since November 2022.
Here are five commodities analysts and industry groups say are most exposed. 
Rice
Rice is one of the crops most consistently identified as vulnerable to El Nino because much of its production is concentrated in South and Southeast Asia, where the weather pattern can reduce rainfall.
India alone handles about 40% of global rice exports. During the 2023 El Nino, New Delhi banned most non-basmati rice exports as domestic prices climbed, a move exporters said had a bigger impact on world markets than Russia-Ukraine war had on wheat.
This year, the US Department of Agriculture has already flagged a below-average Indian monsoon as a risk to rice, cotton and other crops.
In September, Indian rice export prices reached their highest level in a year amid concerns over below-normal rainfall, while prices in Thailand and Vietnam also rose.
The World Bank estimates that severe El Nino cycles can slash regional rice output by 20% to 50%.
For consumers, lower harvests or tighter exports can raise the cost of rice in importing countries, particularly in Asia and Africa, where the grain is a staple food. 
Sugar
Sugarcane is highly dependent on adequate rainfall, making major producing regions in Asia and South America vulnerable to prolonged heat and dry conditions.
The FAO said its sugar price index jumped 11.9% in August, with weather-related production concerns in Brazil, Europe and Asia contributing to the increase. The agency also cited anticipated El Nino risks to sugar production in Asia.
India, the world's second-largest sugar producer, has already faced pressure on supplies and has restricted exports, while its government has allowed some duty-free imports to help replenish domestic supplies.
A tighter global sugar market can raise costs for products ranging from soft drinks and chocolate to processed foods. 
Palm oil
Indonesia and Malaysia together produce roughly 85% of the world's palm oil, an ingredient found in everything from packaged snacks and instant noodles to soap and cosmetics.
Extended rainfall deficits and high temperatures linked to El Nino reduce fresh fruit bunch yields on oil palm plantations.
Indonesia is already battling wildfires that have sent haze drifting into Malaysia and the Philippines. The country's meteorological agency has separately warned that some provinces, including Kalimantan, Papua and Java, face a real chance of a drier September-to-November period than even the severe 1997 El Nino brought.
Because palm oil is cheaper than other vegetable oils and widely used as a substitute, a supply squeeze tends to push up costs across the broader edible-oils market, not just for palm oil itself. 
Cocoa
Cocoa production is heavily concentrated in West Africa, particularly Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana, leaving the market sensitive to changes in rainfall and temperature.
Cote d'Ivoire, the world's largest cocoa producer, slowed forward sales for its 2026/27 crop in June because of concerns that El Nino could bring drought and reduce yields.
The International Cocoa Organization said in its latest quarterly bulletin that cocoa prices remained highly sensitive to weather and production risks and specifically noted growing concerns about the potential impact of El Nino.
Analysts note the crop is especially vulnerable this cycle because much of West Africa's cocoa acreage is now more than 25 years old, past its most productive age, leaving trees less able to withstand heat and drought stress. 
Coffee
Coffee is vulnerable because major growing areas in Southeast Asia and Latin America can experience heat, drought or excessive rainfall during El Nino events.
Vietnam, the world's second-largest coffee producer and a leading supplier of robusta beans, is particularly important.
USDA says the country accounts for about 17% of global coffee production and warns that El Nino's warmer and drier conditions could reduce coffee productivity and production.

Macron, von der Leyen call for stronger European space sector amid rising security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed their commitment to space at a major summit co-hosted by France and Germany in Paris.
French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to strengthen its space industry on Thursday, the second day of the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.
Speaking at the summit, Macron described Europe’s space sector as “fragile” and emphasised the need to bolster its capabilities, calling for “shared governance” of the industry.
“Outer space remains the only major global commons that is not subject to regulations that match the stakes,” he said. “Shared governance is necessary to address these challenges.”
Macron reiterated that more than 51 deals are set to be signed over the course of the summit, with some €20 billion of investments, listing a series of future milestones for Europe.
"In two years' time, I want to see the first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station; in five years' time, the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, the first European manned capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board," he added, referring to Europe's spaceport in French Guiana.
Meanwhile, von der Leyen stressed the importance of Europe stepping up, as she emphasised the crucial role space plays both in terms of both scientific exploration, but also defence — pointing to Russia's war in Ukraine.
"The ability to access and act in space not only underpins our prosperity, it increasingly determines our security and independence. Nowhere is this clearer than in Ukraine."
"Satellite communications keep soldiers connected, while satellite imagery reveal movements hundreds of kilometres away"."
Europe's Space push comes amid aim to cut dependence on US
Europe's push to build up its military space assets has been driven by Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as its decision to distance itself from its longstanding dependence on the US in the space domain.
Ahead of the summit, several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."
A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”
Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US. But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.
"Security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space", said von der Leyen, as she went on to underline the significance of IRIS², the European Union's upcoming flagship satellite constellation programme.
"Last month, we decided to accelerate the system, by expanding it to more than 350 satellites."
Von der Leyen also underlined the need for the Commission, the European Space Agency and national governments to "pool" their strengths, while also calling for investment "at scale."
Macron and Joseph Aschbacher, Director of the European Space Agency (ESA) — who also addressed the summit — were joined for a live call with astronaut Sophie Adenot, who is currently on a nine-month mission aboard the the International Space Station (ISS) named the εpsilon mission.

====================================================================================================

The Muslim families fighting for burial space in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:23:57 UTC
19:23:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Newham's burial crisis is forcing Muslims to ask: Where will we bury our dead?
Standing with clipboards in hand outside a mosque in the East London borough of Newham stood two volunteers from the Newham Muslim Burial Association (NMBA), asking mosque-goers about their experiences burying their loved ones.
Admittedly, not part of the typical Friday Prayer routine, but that didn't stop people from giving these volunteers their time of day.
The volunteers were there to deliver the hard truth to those listening: Newham is predicted to completely run out of burial space by 2032.
As expected, alarm bells were raised. Many were shocked to hear this for the first time; others saw it as an opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction with the entire burial process.
From cost to accessibility to unmet faith needs, it was clear that this issue required urgent attention. And it got urgent attention from the NMBA.
The Newham Muslim Burial Association, established in 2023, is a grassroots community organisation advocating for better burial provisions for Newham residents, covering land availability, accessibility, affordability and faith-sensitive needs.
"Newham has never had a community organising initiative like this, built from scratch and on a voluntary basis," one NMBA spokesperson said.
"The alternative was watching a crisis unfold right in front of us," she continued. "We couldn't sit back and wait for the local authorities to do something. We had to take matters into our own hands."
It started with a listening campaign in April. Volunteers visited mosques, conducted online surveys, and generally spoke with people.
The consensus could not have been more telling — 86% of respondents said burial provisions for Muslim communities were insufficient, while 93% said the average £4,000-£5,000 cost of a burial plot was unaffordable.
Behind these percentages are real families with real experiences.
One Newham resident said that "the local authorities are very oblivious to the needs of the Muslim citizens, who are already economically very poor," adding that many even "get into debt due to the high costs of burials."
Another resident said the high cost meant they had to bury their loved ones in the Gardens of Peace cemetery, a significant distance from where the family lived, making visits to loved ones far more difficult than they needed to be.
Grieving families don't deserve extra financial burdens at an already distressing time, as one resident put it: "The average Newham resident doesn't have that kind of money at hand, especially when deaths are completely unexpected."
The NMBA's mission was to bridge the gap between Newham's decision-makers and the people who felt the consequences of those decisions. This did not mean making empty promises, but a genuine determination to achieve material outcomes.
The wins start rolling in
After months of lobbying, the group finally saw its first major success in March.
Newham Council granted £750,000 to the NMBA to support local burial provisions for the coming financial year, and the council promised to work closely with the NMBA and local mosques to develop a long-term plan.
This is an undeniable "positive step" in the right direction, but the Chair of the NMBA, Kamran Qureshi, still cautioned that "we need a sustainable, multi-year strategy."
He added: "We cannot afford to put a sticking plaster on a systemic issue."
His words highlight that this sum of money doesn't signify the end of the fight, but rather indicates that their efforts weren't going to waste.
An NMBA spokesperson said, "The council will still need our help to turn this money into something tangible," showing how this issue will always be grounded in community action and collective organising.
In April, the local mosque, Masjid al-Humera, voluntarily donated £115 to the cause, showing that when a community cares, it will show up in whatever capacity it can.
Then, in June, an even more significant step was taken.
Dignity Group, which owns the East London Cemetery, agreed to provide 250 new burial spaces for Newham's Muslim community at a site in Plaistow. They have also expressed willingness to offer an additional 600 spaces if demand is particularly high.
Not only did the NMBA secure the much-needed plots of land, but it also built relationships with key organisations and placed faith-based community needs at the forefront of decision-making to facilitate inclusive and sustainable burial provisions.
The Muslim Council of Britain has commended the NMBA, saying, "Muslim communities organising to meet local needs is what a healthy, engaged society looks like, and it's exactly the kind of civic participation we want to see more of across the UK."
Quantity of burial space isn't the only issue the NMBA is advocating for; the quality of these spaces is equally important in ensuring they fulfil the faith-sensitive needs of Newham's Muslim community.
Some of these requirements include using virgin (previously unused) land for burial plots, orienting graves towards Mecca, and providing on-site ritual facilities.
Over the next 12-year period, an estimated 13,652 burial plots will be required in Newham, with at least 10,452 needing to be on virgin ground, primarily to serve Muslim and Jewish faith requirements.
The numbers are certainly alarming. But what the Newham Muslim Burial Association has shown is that this crisis doesn't mean Newham residents have no choice but to watch the clock until 2032; instead, they can organise right now within their communities to help make the changes they need to see.
As Green councillor Ibrahim Alom puts it: "For us, this isn't about the council deciding everything from the top down. It's about working alongside organisations like the NMBA and listening to residents to develop solutions that are practical, respectful and supported by the community."
A campaign run by volunteers, starting with a stack of surveys outside a mosque, can move a council and a private cemetery operator in the same year.
"What we've been able to achieve so far with the model of community organising shows that people will engage in issues that they care deeply about," one NMBA spokesperson said.
"This is not the end. We will continue to lobby until we see consistent, tangible outcomes."
It takes one conversation
One volunteer shared a touching story of her experience engaging with locals. One Friday, she walked into the packed women's section of a local mosque, waiting for prayer to begin, hoping to speak with people and raise awareness about this issue.
She was met with an unexpected obstacle: a language barrier. But she tried nonetheless. She managed to find one woman she could speak to about the crisis, who then translated it for the other women in the room.
That group translated it further until everyone understood it in their own language. Before long, the room was buzzing with women talking about their experiences with the burial process, confiding in each other about how difficult it is, and coming to the collective conclusion that this was a problem.
She said that this experience made her realise that "in this diverse community, there may be multiple languages, but one in common is the language of seeing and understanding injustice and inequality."
The chatter, the discussion and the open dialogue are what get things moving.
They helped Newham residents realise that this was an issue and that action was needed.
People engaged in whatever way they could, and for a grassroots community organisation like the NMBA, that was enough to get the ball rolling.
Majidah Chowdhury is a student and freelance journalist based in London

European Public Prosecutor's Office to investigate RKIK and Datasel contracts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

European Public Prosecutor's Office to investigate RKIK and Datasel contracts
The European Public Prosecutor's Office will investigate transactions between the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) and Datasel after Estonian prosecutors found grounds to suspect a possible crime.
The Estonian Prosecutor General's Office will not expand the ongoing criminal proceedings concerning the Ministry of Defense's area of government to examine transactions between the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) and Datasel, as the European Public Prosecutor's Office will take over the investigation into those circumstances.
Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said the Office of the Prosecutor General analyzed information published in a National Audit Office report and in the media concerning transactions between RKIK and Datasel and found that it provides grounds for launching criminal proceedings to determine whether a crime may have been committed in connection with the transactions.
"Since the potential violations concern the use of funds managed by the European Union, we also discussed the circumstances with our colleagues at the European Public Prosecutor's Office. We concluded that the case falls within the investigative jurisdiction of the European Public Prosecutor's Office, which will therefore take charge of the investigation," Asi said.
At the same time, the Office of the Prosecutor General will continue criminal proceedings launched in 2025 examining circumstances described in the National Audit Office report.
"The investigation centers on whether accounting obligations may have been breached in the organization of reporting and accounting within the Ministry of Defense's area of government and whether there are grounds to suspect that documents were concealed or destroyed," Asi explained.
As part of the same investigation, the Prosecutor General's Office is also analyzing other information presented in the National Audit Office's audit this year that is unrelated to the Datasel transactions.

SC seeks UP govt response on plea challenging MLAs, MLCs’ pension, perks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:22:56 UTC
19:22:56 KST

Supreme Court agrees to hear plea on pension to MLA, MLCs
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and others on a plea challenging provisions of a 1980 law that provide pension and other facilities to sitting and former MLAs and MLCs in the state.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta issued notice on the petition challenging a May verdict of the Lucknow bench of the Allahabad High Court, which had dismissed the plea against the constitutional validity of the provisions.The top court posted the matter for hearing after four weeks.
Plea questions benefits to legislators
The petitioner, Lok Prahari, had challenged provisions of the Uttar Pradesh State Legislature (Members' Emoluments and Pension) Act, 1980, arguing that the state legislature had effectively made itself the “judge in its own cause” by granting benefits to its sitting and former members.The plea contended that the benefits were “manifestly arbitrary” and contrary to the constitutional principle that public office is meant for public service and not personal gain.The High Court had noted that the law provides sitting and former MLAs and MLCs with salary, allowances and other facilities. It also extends pension, family pension, free travel, medical facilities and other amenities to their spouses, family members and companions.
What petitioner argued
The petitioner contended that these provisions go beyond the powers conferred on state legislatures under Article 195 of the Constitution.Article 195 deals with the salaries and allowances of members of state Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils. According to the petitioner, it does not specifically provide for pension, post-retirement benefits or facilities for family members and companions.
The High Court, however, had held that the challenge was essentially based on a policy disagreement rather than any demonstrable constitutional infirmity.It observed that the constitutional scheme does not prevent a legislature from making provisions for pension, allowances or allied benefits for its members, including former members.While dismissing the plea, the High Court had said there was no constitutional bar on the state legislature enacting measures of social security for its current and former members.
