Taipei Fire Department upgrades 119 emergency line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:02:42 UTC
18:02:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Fire Department said Thursday that it added AI voice assistance to the 119 fire rescue and ambulance emergency line.
The 119 dispatch center oversees operations by receiving and responding to calls from civilians, firefighters, and paramedics. The fire department introduced Taiwan's first emergency AI voice assistance system to analyze calls and radio traffic for keywords such as “smoke” or “trapped” and prioritize cases accordingly.
For fire rescue, the department said the AI transcribes calls and identifies keywords and phrases, reducing delays caused by background noise. It also synchronized dispatch modules so dispatchers can send the most appropriate responders and equipment, shortening response times.
The department said that during earthquakes, typhoons, and other major incidents that cause a surge in calls, a voice pre-acceptance function allows callers to leave information. AI then scans the messages for keywords to determine case urgency and prioritize high-risk cases.
The department said the transcription feature can also monitor radio traffic in real time and identify distress phrases such as “people trapped” or “mayday.” The system then pushes notifications to ensure responders receive important mission updates, helping speed rescue efforts and minimize loss of life and property.
For ambulances, the fire department also introduced a pre-arrival instruction feature with 13 standardized protocols for medical emergencies, including severe chest pain and strokes.
The department said 119 dispatchers assess calls to determine urgency and advise callers before help arrives. With early detection and timely assistance, severe cases can also be reported to hospitals in advance to help prepare emergency care and improve patient outcomes.
The department said that since its deployment in 2025, the service has been used 16,651 times, with an execution rate of 12.8%. The notification rate for suspected stroke cases increased from 40% to 46.8%, helping improve treatment and patient outcomes.
The city plans to expand the feature to include other languages to help tourists, migrant workers, and residents' foreign friends and relatives. The broader plan is to create a more accessible platform that can serve a wider range of needs with greater efficiency.

Sweden election: what you need to know

Sweden election: what you need to know
Sept 10 - Sweden will hold a parliamentary election on September 13 with the centre-left opposition holding a slim lead in opinion polls over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's ruling right-wing bloc.
WHAT'S AT STAKE?
Kristersson is seeking to form a majority government with his existing partners, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, but this time with the addition of the Sweden Democrats, a party with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe. The Sweden Democrats have backed the government in parliament since 2022, but have demanded cabinet seats after the September election.
The centre-left opposition, led by Social Democrats' leader Magdalena Andersson, is more loosely aligned and parties have yet to tell voters exactly how they intend to form a government.
WHAT ARE THE MAIN ISSUES?
The election is in part a referendum on the Sweden Democrats. While they have steadily grown in popularity and respectability, many voters reject the possibility of a government with far-right cabinet members.
Prime Minister Kristersson says Sweden needs a stable majority government to tackle important issues, such as national security and gang crime, and that the only way is to include the Sweden Democrats.
The centre-left warn that civil liberties may be at risk if the Sweden Democrats enter government. They also want to increase funding for welfare services and measures to combat climate change, and address growing income inequality.
WHEN DOES VOTING TAKE PLACE?
Polls are open from 0600 GMT to 1800 GMT on election day, though voting has been possible since late last month.
WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?
If the four right-wing parties win a majority, forming a government looks to be straightforward, as they all have pledged an alliance.
However, if the centre-left opposition parties win, Andersson will face difficult negotiations to either form a majority government with all four parties, or a minority government alone, or with one or two partners.
WHO ARE THE KEY PARTIES AND WHAT ARE THEIR PLEDGES?
* CENTRE-LEFT BLOC *
Social Democrats (S) - leader Magdalena Andersson
Sweden's largest political party is campaigning on a pledge to protect the welfare system and boost economic growth, while backing the green transition and higher defence spending.
Green Party (MP) - leaders Amanda Lind and Daniel Hellden
The party champions environmental protection and wants to cut carbon emissions, expand renewable energy, invest in railways and green infrastructure. It opposes nuclear power.
Left Party (V) - leader Nooshi Dadgostar
Wants greater investment in healthcare, education and other welfare services, financed in part through higher taxes on the wealthy.
Centre Party (C) - leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist
It is campaigning on job creation, climate action and stronger public services, also in rural areas. It wants lower taxes and has refused to cooperate with both the Left Party and the Sweden Democrats.
* RIGHT-WING BLOC * Moderates (M) - leader Ulf Kristersson
The Moderates have led the right wing of Swedish politics in recent decades, although the Sweden Democrats became the larger party in 2022. Their campaign centres on a tougher stance on crime and lower taxes.
Sweden Democrats (SD) - leader Jimmie Akesson
With immigration numbers historically low, the focus of their campaign has been on preserving Swedish values, language and customs, and incentives for immigrants to leave the country.
Christian Democrats (KD) - leader Ebba Busch
They emphasize family and welfare policies along with broadly right-wing economic policy.
Liberals (L) - leader Simona Mohamsson
The Liberals have centered their campaign around the economy and education, focusing on smaller class sizes. REUTERS

He, however, stressed that the proceedings before the Delhi High Court should not be restricted only to the safety of paying guest accommodations and hostels.The Satya Niketan building collapse, near Moti Bagh, had left seven people dead and 12 injured. The incident subsequently led to a series of proceedings concerning building safety and enforcement by civic authorities in Delhi.The Supreme Court took note of steps being taken by the Delhi government and the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) pursuant to its earlier directions concerning building collapses and fires in Delhi and Lucknow.
The Delhi high court had issued several directions following the incident, including asking the MCD to undertake an exercise to assess the safety of PG accommodations and hostels.Kumar told the Supreme Court that inspections had been carried out in four areas of Delhi as well as in Lucknow. The earlier directions covered Lajpat Nagar, Saket, Malviya Nagar and Sarojini Nagar in Delhi, and Ali Ganj in Lucknow.
The amicus had suggested that the proceedings pending before the Delhi high Court could instead be transferred to the Supreme Court and tagged with the present proceedings. Alternatively, he proposed that the High Court proceedings continue while a report is filed before the Supreme Court in terms of its March 25, 2026 order, particularly paragraphs 6 and 7, and its August 5, 2026 order.The bench accepted the latter course and clarified that the Supreme Court proceedings were not confined to the specific areas identified in Delhi or to Lucknow.The clarification came after the Supreme Court had earlier indicated that it could examine the broader issue of commercial exploitation of areas designated as residential across Delhi-NCR.The court's latest direction means the Delhi High Court will continue to oversee the ongoing proceedings and monitor the action taken by civic authorities in the wake of the building collapse.

Trump’s repeated threats to ‘wipe out’ Iran are normalizing mass violence | Mohamad Bazzi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
09:00:20 UTC
18:00:20 KST

As the US and Iran fought around the strait of Hormuz last week, Donald Trump issued one of his typical threats. In an interview with a Fox News correspondent, Trump said Iran would be “totally wiped out as a country” if it retaliated for the latest wave of US air strikes.
That threat by the US president to wipe out another country generated few headlines, even during a relatively slow news week by Trump administration standards.
Trump has delivered this kind of warning so frequently over the past six months of his war against Iran that it hardly registers anymore. But it’s important not to normalize Trump’s threats, which are usually accompanied by promises to devastate Iran’s infrastructure – vowing to destroy bridges and power plants. Those kinds of attacks would constitute war crimes under international law.
The president’s repeated vows to obliterate Iran are usually written off by other western leaders and the news media as typical of Trump’s bravado and unpredictability, but they have real-world consequences. By treating Trump’s rhetoric as normal, US and western societies are becoming more desensitized to the idea of large-scale violence – including the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure – as a legitimate kind of warfare. And of course, Israel’s war on Gaza has inured many in the western world to wholesale atrocities, including intense aerial bombardment that leads to massive civilian casualties and displacement.
Trump set the stage for apocalyptic threats against Iran weeks into the war, when it became clear that the US would not achieve the quick military victory he was hoping for. On 7 April, as he vacillated between agreeing to a ceasefire and ordering even more intense bombing, Trump ominously declared in a social media post: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.”
In the days leading up to that statement, Trump had issued a series of warnings that the US would destroy Iran’s infrastructure unless it reopened the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies flowed before Tehran effectively shut the waterway at the start of the war. On 1 April, in a primetime address from the White House, Trump threatened to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages, where they belong”. On 6 April, Trump claimed that Iran “could be taken out in one night” and said the US had a plan to destroy every bridge and power plant in the country, leaving that infrastructure “burning, exploding, and never to be used again” – a statement announcing his intention to commit war crimes.
Trump set a deadline of 8 pm ET on 7 April for Iranian leaders to comply with his demands. As that deadline neared, Trump shared his now infamous post on his Truth Social network that promised to erase Iran’s civilization. That threat to carry out large-scale war crimes against a country of 90 million people prompted outrage around the world, with condemnation from the UN secretary general and the pope. Some human rights experts argued that Trump’s statement may constitute a threat to commit genocide, which is defined by the UN’s Genocide Convention as acts committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group”.
Shortly before Trump’s deadline expired, Pakistan’s prime minister announced that the US and Iran had agreed to an immediate ceasefire. But Trump never apologized or retracted his statement. And why should he feel any pressure to do so, despite the momentary outrage his words caused? In today’s world, there are no consequences for threatening – or carrying out – a genocide.
Trump’s threat to obliterate Iran is partly a manifestation of a new international order that emerged over the past three years, as the US supplied billions of dollars in weapons and protected Israel as it carried out a genocidal war in Gaza. In his second term, Trump has behaved more erratically and like an autocrat drunk with power. But he has also taken advantage of a nascent global order, in which western leaders destroyed decades of international norms and the façade of rule of law – all to enable Israel to continue its bloodshed in Gaza, and more recently, in Lebanon.
As they did with Gaza, most western powers and leaders have become numb to the loss and suffering of Palestinians, Iranians, Lebanese and others in the Middle East. And as long as this numbness and impunity continue, it will become normal for the US president to threaten whole-scale destruction of societies and civilizations, as Trump has done in Iran.
While Trump can be dismissed as an unpredictable, or even irrational, world leader who scorns global institutions and norms – the epitome of the “madman theory” of US foreign policy – his predecessor Joe Biden helped paved the way for the current age of impunity we’re living in. Biden, along with other western leaders who provided unwavering support to Israel after the Hamas attacks in October 2023, defied and weakened international law in order to shield Israel long before Trump returned to office in early 2025.
For 15 months, the Biden administration undermined global institutions – including the international court of justice (ICJ) and the international criminal court (ICC) – to help Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, avoid facing consequences for their war crimes in Gaza. Biden and other western leaders rendered international law meaningless after their inaction and obstruction in Gaza – and it was only a matter of time before Trump abandoned any pretense of lofty rhetoric about human rights and rule of law. Trump prefers to flaunt American military power and his ability to inflict massive destruction on US enemies.
The normalization of Israel’s atrocities in Gaza has rippled across the world, including the expanding regional war that engulfed Iran and the US. It has also diluted international outrage at Trump’s repeated threats to destroy Iran, even within a period of months. While Trump’s apocalyptic warning in April that “a whole civilization will die” prompted global condemnation, his subsequent rhetoric has barely registered.
In July, Trump claimed that the US would bomb one Iranian bridge or power plant in retaliation for each time Iran fired at a ship in the strait of Hormuz. That kind of retaliation against civilian targets would be a war crime, but Trump has made such threats seem mundane and a normal part of warfare. At the very least, Americans and the rest of the world should call him out on it.
- 
  Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

A Japanese ship carrying three CH-47 helicopters arrived in wildfire-hit Indonesia on Thursday, marking Tokyo's first overseas firefighting mission, Kyodo News reported.
The 8,900-ton Osumi-class transport ship Kunisaki arrived at Kijing Port in West Kalimantan with around 350 personnel.   
The helicopters will support the Indonesian military in aerial firefighting for about a week from Sunday.
The CH-47s will draw water from rivers and carry about five tons on each run before dumping it over fire-hit areas.   
"We will make every effort" to execute the mission to help the victims, a Japanese Defense Ministry official said.
Massive fires that broke out across Indonesia between January and July have burned around 2,000 square kilometers (772 square miles) of forests and peatland, according to Kyodo. Fires are still burning in several parts of the country, with the Indonesian military conducting aerial firefighting operations.
The deployment follows an agreement signed in May between Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and his Indonesian counterpart Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin to broaden defense cooperation, including joint training and disaster relief operations.
Meanwhile, Japan has also deployed Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighter aircraft to India for the first time.  
Indian Air Force and the Japan Air Self Defence Force are holding bilateral air exercise, "Veer Guardian-2026," which began Wednesday and will run through September at Air Force Station Jodhpur in western India.  
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, writing on US social media company X, called the maiden visit a “significant milestone” in the India-Japan defense partnership.

He didn't criticise anyone by name but suggested Democrats are extremists, underscoring the message that Republicans are trying to drive home during their two-day rally in Dallas. The convention is meant to fire up the conservative base ahead of midterm elections, when the president's party has historically lost seats.
"I'm always going to stand with America," Fetterman said. "I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life."
Standing in front of a steel mill, Fetterman said he "will work with President Trump to fight and defend the steel way of life."
Fetterman has grown increasingly isolated from his party as he "obsessively" support of Israel's genocide of Gaza and criticizes left-wing candidates who are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. He’s often gone his own way in the Senate, voting with Republicans to end last year's shutdown, supporting several of President Donald Trump's nominees and opposing efforts to end the war in Iran.

Houthi threat to Red Sea expands with takeover of Mocha, potentially reshaping region - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:48:56 UTC
17:48:56 KST

After three days of escalating conflict in Yemen, with the Saudi-backed government making gains, the Houthis have struck at the city of Mocha on the Red Sea. Their surprise advance was anticipated. Though the Houthis have suffered setbacks on other fronts, this offensive could have wider implications for the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.
Mocha is one of several important ports in Yemen. Along with Hodeidah, it plays a key role on the Red Sea coast. It also sits at the northern end of the strait. As such, the Houthi strike on the city could potentially lead to bringing the Iranian-backed Houthis closer to closing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the same way that Iran has attempted to close the Strait of Hormuz.
This would give Iran more influence in the region, despite appearing to lose out on several fronts, with Iranian-backed proxies facing setbacks in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, and facing pressure to disarm in Iraq. The Houthis remain one of the most powerful pro-Iranian groups.
Reuters reported that the Houthis took Mocha on Thursday. The full story of what is happening in Yemen remains to be seen because reports are not always accurate. What matters is that the Houthis are trying to amplify their role along the Red Sea.
This comes amid several developments in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
Houthi control gives Iran greater influence
The Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia this week as fighting increased in Yemen. Riyadh backs the government of Yemen against the Houthis. Saudi Arabia led an intervention in Yemen in 2015.
Now, Arab News in Saudi Arabia has reported that “Saudi civil defense issued an emergency alert for the southwestern province of Khamis Mushait to warn of potential danger for the fourth time in 24 hours.”
The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense informed, “The danger has been lifted from Khamis Mushait Governorate. For your safety, continue to follow the instructions of the Civil Defense and completely avoid gatherings and photography. In case of emergencies, call 998.” The warning had been linked to the Houthi conflict.
The Houthis had claimed to target an airbase in the part of southern Saudi Arabia near Yemen. As such, the kingdom was being cautious. This indicates that the Houthis are not wary of continuing to target the kingdom. Meanwhile, Pakistan has expressed support for Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey recently signed onto a defensive pact. There are questions about whether the Houthi attacks might trigger wider support for Riyadh.
Pakistan expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia
Pakistan’s leader has expressed his “unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia, after Houthi drone and missile attacks on civilian and energy facilities in the kingdom left 73 people wounded, Arab News noted. “At the same time, Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said that a three-nation defense pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey could become operational in the event of aggression against the kingdom.”
Many are watching closely to see whether the Saudis will receive support from their new partners.
Iran is also watching to see whether the Houthis can continue to make gains and threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The threat of the Houthis may increase global insecurity and continue to roil energy markets.
US President Donald Trump has said that he expects the conflict with Iran to wind down after the US midterm elections. The high oil prices are expected to come down as well. The battles in Mocha could change this perception.
There are other issues that will affect the fate of Yemen and the Red Sea coast. Saudi Arabia has been backing the government forces in Yemen. However, the Saudis and the United Arab Emirates have not agreed on policy in Yemen. This may present challenges for the frontlines around Aden and Mocha.
The Yemen government forces who oppose the Houthis face a challenge in that they control areas around the Houthis, but the Houthis control the high ground and part of the coast.
As such, the Houthis can shift forces along internal lines.
The Yemen government can’t do this. They can’t move forces easily from Jawf, for instance, to Mocha. To do so would require major logistics, and it’s not an easy task. As such, the Houthis enjoy some advantages in being able to shift resources from one front to another. Even when pressed, the Houthis will continue to enjoy this advantage.
The setbacks in Mocha illustrate how a forgotten and low-level conflict in Yemen can potentially reshape the region.

AMDL circle plans new public life for milan’s palazzo litta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:45:26 UTC
17:45:26 KST

amdl circle opens milan’s palazzo litta to the public
AMDL CIRCLE, founded by Michele De Lucchi, presents a strategic masterplan for Palazzo Litta in Milan that seeks to open the monumental spaces of the historic building to the public while retaining its institutional role. Commissioned by the Direzione regionale Musei nazionali Lombardia, which has managed the palace since early 2025, the plan reorganizes the 17th-century complex around exhibition, cultural, and administrative functions, proposing the restoration of currently unused areas and the reopening of its long-inaccessible Monumental Garden.
Located on Corso Magenta, Palazzo Litta is among Lombardy’s significant examples of Baroque architecture. Its core develops from a project by architect Francesco Maria Richini, commissioned by Bartolomeo III Arese in the first half of the 17th century. Later architectural and decorative interventions substantially altered the palace, with the most important transformation taking place in the mid-18th century, when the interiors of the piano nobile acquired the elaborate character associated with Lombard Baroque.
The building now accommodates the Milan offices of five institutions belonging to the Italian Ministry of Culture, including three superintendencies, the Direzione regionale Musei nazionali Lombardia, and the Museo nazionale dell’Arte Digitale. AMDL CIRCLE’s masterplan reorganizes their relationship with the parts of Palazzo Litta intended for cultural use. The Milan-based architecture studio‘s strategy separates circulation according to use, reorganizing vertical connections and horizontal distribution so that visitors and office users can move through the building without unnecessarily overlapping. The approach also allows spaces that have become disconnected from the contemporary life of the palace to acquire new roles.
the palazzo is among Lombardy’s significant examples of Baroque architecture | image by Chabe01, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
the masterplan reorganizes the palace around public access
At ground level, the Cortile d’Onore becomes the principal threshold between Palazzo Litta and the city. The courtyard is planned as an urban court open to the public, with a ticket office, bookshop, exhibition areas, spaces presenting the sites managed by the Direzione regionale Musei nazionali Lombardia, and a new multipurpose hall.
New elevators connect the courtyard to the piano nobile and the office areas, while a direct route provides access to the garden behind the palace. In the rear buildings, the plan introduces more operational functions, including a library, conservation laboratories, artwork storage, and the export office. Archives are distributed between the basement and attic spaces. The arrangement establishes the courtyard as a point of orientation and circulation, connecting public programs with the deeper operational infrastructure required to keep a cultural institution functioning.
On the piano nobile, exhibition and event spaces are organized around a circular visitor route beginning at the monumental staircase and continuing around the Cortile d’Onore. The plan also introduces backstage areas that are currently lacking, acknowledging the practical requirements of programming exhibitions and events within a historic building. The ministerial offices remain in the more internal portion of the first floor and on the second floor, while the third floor undergoes renovation to accommodate their expansion. Guest residences for institutional and cultural use occupy the side wings and attic. New building services, including air-handling units serving the piano nobile, heat pumps, and photovoltaic panels, are placed on the roofs of the internal buildings, in areas that are less visible and had already undergone reconstruction after World War II.
the Cortile d’Onore becomes the principal threshold between Palazzo Litta and the city | image via MoscaPartners
the Monumental Garden becomes part of Palazzo Litta again
The plan also proposes restoring the 19th-century garden on the north side of Palazzo Litta, which has long been inaccessible. The intervention brings the garden back into the visitor route and allows it to host cultural events outdoors. More broadly, the masterplan reorganizes the palace around its existing mix of historic, cultural, and institutional uses, aiming to make more of the building accessible while continuing to accommodate the Ministry of Culture offices.
For De Lucchi, the challenge is to adapt the Baroque building to contemporary life while preserving its historic elements and original typology. Palazzo Litta has already changed use several times, from aristocratic residence to offices and, later, to the current Ministry of Culture headquarters. The masterplan adds another layer to this history by introducing a more public role for the building.
the building now accommodates the Milan offices of five institutions | image via MoscaPartners
archives are distributed between the basement and attic spaces | image via MoscaPartners

Cop31: Forget climate pledges, countries like Nepal need actual cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

Cop31: Forget climate pledges, countries like Nepal need actual cash
No payout from the loss and damage fund has reached vulnerable nations. Cop31 must focus on delivering the money already promised
Every climate summit now runs on the same illusion: the next pledge will be the one that finally saves us. It will not. The money the rich world has promised the poor world is not coming at anything like the scale advertised, and pretending otherwise has become the main business of climate diplomacy.
Late last month, a melting glacier gave way on the edge of the Himalayas and sent a wall of rock and water down the valley, burying whole settlements and leaving a country in national mourning.
Set that against how quickly everything else moves. In the same few weeks, the calendar filled with gatherings: a climate finance week in Istanbul, a week of chief-executive meetings in Baku, Azerbaijan, and a Pacific leaders’ summit in Palau. There is no shortage of mobilisation, only not the kind that moves money from one account to another.
A fund that cannot send US$20 million to a grieving country in the time it takes to hold three high-level meetings is not yet a fund. It is a promise with a letterhead.

Spain endures 61 days of heatwave and records its hottest summer on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:27:59 UTC
17:27:59 KST

Spain's weather agency has confirmed that Spaniards have already endured 61 days of heatwave conditions so far this year, more than in any other year.
Spain has surpassed the scorching summer of 2022, with a total of 61 heatwave days endured this year, compared with 41 previously, according to the State Meteorological Agency (Aemet).
The summer of 2026 has also recorded an average temperature of 24.5°C, making it the hottest since records began in 1961 and surpassing last year, 2025, by 0.3°C, and 2.4°C above the long-term average.
Aemet recalls that the 10 hottest summers on record have all occurred in the 21st century, and seven of the eight warmest have taken place since 2015. The agency also warns that the meteorological summer keeps getting longer.
"At the end of May, temperatures typical of July were recorded across large areas of the country. And then, in September, already in the meteorological autumn, there was another heatwave which, provisionally, ran from the 2nd to the 7th, lasting six days and affecting 16 provinces."
September heat, rainfall and wildfires: Spain outlook
Only in four other years has a month of September (1987, 1988, 2006 and 2016) seen such extreme heatwaves, more typical of the height of summer.
The heavy winter rains have meant that Spanish reservoirs have remained in very good condition after the summer season, with an average level of 62.58 per cent despite tourist pressure, and above half of their capacity in basins that are usually under stress, such as the Júcar, Segura, Andalusian Mediterranean and Catalan catchments.
Even so, this has not spared the country from suffering, as in the rest of Europe, large-scale fires that have exposed the lack of forest fire prevention and of sufficient personnel with good working conditions, in regions such as Madrid, Aragón or Castilla y León.

====================================================================================================

August hottest month ever recorded globally: EU monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:27:00 UTC
17:27:00 KST

Picture taken on August 14, 2026 with a drone shows the Pfalzgrafenstein Castle on an island in the dried-up river Rhine in Kaub, western Germany. (AFP Photo)
The EU’s climate monitor said on Sept. 10 that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the U.N. warned that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940 but other evidence, such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons, allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess from the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.
Global average air temperatures in August were 16.96 degrees Celsius, Copernicus said, surpassing by 0.01 degrees the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Copernicus said it considered the two months joint-highest given the narrow difference.
Scientists say that human activity, primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas, has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4 degrees since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs in 2025.
“The evidence is irrefutable: This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins like the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength.
Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for 2027, and maybe even 2026, to become the hottest years ever observed.
Copernicus also said that August “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003.
The June to August season was defined by severe, back-to-back heat waves that shut schools, dried up rivers and primed the land for devastating wildfires.
Between mid-July and mid-August, the continent’s EuroMomo monitoring platform estimated that Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths.

Singapore PM increases his salary by $1.1 million amid first government pay raise in 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:26:48 UTC
17:26:48 KST

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the salary increases in parliament on Tuesday, the first for ministers in 15 years. Wong's own benchmark paycheck is set to rise 64 percent to 3.6 million Singapore dollars (€2.4 million) a year.
Singapore’s ministers, already among the world’s highest-paid, are getting a raise for the first time in 15 years, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, explaining that the government cannot attract top talent into politics if salaries remain unchanged.
Wong told Parliament on Tuesday that under a revised salary framework, the benchmark annual pay for a minister at the lowest grade will rise to 1.8 million Singapore dollars (€1.2 million), from Sg$1.1 million (€747,564). The prime minister’s benchmark salary will jump to Sg$3.6 million (€2.4 million) from Sg$2.2 million (€1.5 million), he said.
Ministers' pay has long been politically sensitive in the city-state, especially amid cost-of-living concerns and a 2025 median gross monthly income of Sg$5,775 (€3924) for fully employed residents, according to government figures.
The increases were recommended by an independent committee.
Wong said, however, the ministers will not immediately get the full salary increases. They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9 percent from October 15, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.
Wong also said he would donate his entire salary increase to charity for the next five years.
Mixed reactions among Singaporeans
Singaporeans expressed mixed reactions on Wednesday over hefty pay raises for political leaders, with some saying the demands of governing justified the bump while others questioned their scale and called for transparency.
May Goh, 69, a retiree from the semiconductor industry, said the ministers deserve the increases. "I think their responsibilities are very high. They are doing a good job so far compared to other countries," she said.
A 32-year-old cybersecurity employee in the business district said she "honestly" thought the increases were fair. "They are basically the CEOs of the political world," she said.
Others were more guarded. The increases are "very steep", said a 26-year-old information technology consultant.
"When you see such a huge salary increase, it puts into perspective, like 'wow that's quite a lot'. We don't even spend that much," he said.
A 69-year-old retiree, while voicing support, said he wanted more transparency with the numbers.
"I wish they were a bit clearer and more transparent about these numbers, including bonuses," he said.

Star Trek fans successfully set new Guinness World Record at London museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:21:59 UTC
17:21:59 KST

The record attempt took place during the London museum’s Star Trek Lates night - part of a series of events marking the 60 year anniversary of the hugely popular sci-fi series. It includes the Star Trek Warp Trail, which closes this weekend.
They've made it so.
A total of 934 fans gathered at London's Science Museum on Star Trek Day to mark the seminal show's 60th anniversary. They were there not only to celebrate the anniversary but to attempt to set a new Guinness World Record for the largest simultaneous Vulcan salute.
For the heathens amongst you, the Vulcan salute is the gesture made famous by Leonard Nimoy's character Spock. It involves raising your hand, palm forward, with the middle and ring fingers parted, forming a “V” shape. It first appeared in the 1967 episode of the TV series titled “Amok Time” and is usually accompanied by the phrase “Live long and prosper”.
Those taking part on Tuesday were required to maintain the iconic hand gesture for one minute to successfully secure the title.
Guinness World Records adjudicator Paulina Sapinska has verified the attempt and handed the official certificate to the Science Museum’s commercial operations director Ben Lheureux.
Science Museum head of collections and principal curator Dr Glyn Morgan said they had been “really excited at the idea of breaking a world record”.
“It’s the 60th anniversary of Star Trek and we wanted something people would really remember and would really mark this event as something special – and what’s more special than breaking a world record?” he said.
Also participating was actor Martin Quinn, who plays chief engineer Montgomery "Scotty" Scott in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds. He said: "I’m going to hang my Guinness World Record certificate in my brother’s room to really rub it in."
Morgan previously said about this year's 60th anniversary celebrations: “After a popular Star Trek Lates earlier this year, we’re delighted to invite fans back for another evening exploring the ideas, imagination and real-world science behind the franchise, and a final opportunity to experience the Star Trek Warp Trail.”
The free Star Trek Warp Trail includes props and uniforms from the shows and films, and explores the lasting connection between the franchise’s visionary storytelling and real-world scientific innovation.
The popular exhibit closes on Sunday 13 September.

The Asian Games began in Japan on Thursday with Qatar beating Iran in men's basketball, the first action in the continental multi-sport showpiece that has more participants than the Olympics.
Over 17,000 athletes and officials are expected to take part in 43 sports at the Nagoya-Aichi Games, which do not officially start until the opening ceremony on September 19 and will run until October 4.
Several events such as basketball, football, cricket, hockey and modern pentathlon will get under way before the opening ceremony.
Qatar held off a comeback from Iran to win their Group B encounter 59-35 at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya in the first match of a men's basketball competition that will hold medal finals on September 20, the day after the opening ceremony.
"We know we need to win at least one game so we can qualify for the next round," said Qatar's Michael Lewis, the United States-born player who scored a game-high 21 points.
"Feels good to get some team camaraderie back, and now we have got to keep going."
Later in Group B, Taiwan beat Jordan 83-80.
Los Angeles 2028 Olympics qualifying spots are up for grabs in several sports at the Asian Games, which are returning to Japan for the first time since 1994.
Organisers hope the athletes will have a "unique experience" staying in accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.
10,000 police officers for security
Officials are confident that the plan will not be affected by Japan's typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October.
Weather has already caused disruptions, with record rainfall on Tuesday forcing hundreds of athletes briefly to evacuate their accommodation.
Rainwater also leaked into some competition venues, with more wet weather forecast for the coming days.
Among those in action at the Games will be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of world-class teenage talents in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
Meanwhile, Japan will deploy around 10,000 police officers for security at the opening ceremony of the Asian Games next week in the city of Nagoya, local media reported.
The ceremony will be attended by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, among others, but Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is not expected to take part.
Of the roughly 10,000 officers, some 3,100 will be specially dispatched squads from police forces nationwide, the National Police Agency said, adding it will also use artificial intelligence for security efforts.
Areas within roughly 1 kilometre of the ceremony site and the imperial couple's accommodation will be designated as no-fly zones for drones under a recently promulgated law that imposed tougher regulations on small, unmanned aircraft flights.
It will be the first application of the revised law for an event attended by the emperor.

====================================================================================================

Extreme heat, fires and floods mark record hot month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:20:24 UTC
17:20:24 KST

August the hottest month in global history after record European summer
In short:
Climate data has confirmed August 2026 was the hottest month on record globally.
The recorded surface air temperature for August 2026 was 1.65 degrees Celsius above the estimated pre-industrial 1850-1900 average.
What's next?
Scientists predict ocean temperatures will continue to rise as an El Niño pattern reaches its peak.
Climate data has been released confirming August 2026 as the hottest month on record after heatwaves and severe drought dominated Western Europe's warmest summer.
The recorded surface air temperature for August 2026 was 1.65°C above the estimated pre-industrial 1850-1900 average, with the period from June to August 2026 the joint-warmest on record globally, on par with 2024.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service, which authored the report with data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), found the extreme conditions had coincided with exceptionally low river flows from the Rhine to the Danube, and had intensified wildfires across Indonesia.
Samantha Burgess, from the ECMWF, said the observations revealed "how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans".
"The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world," Ms Burgess said.
Earlier this month, a landmark report from the UN warned the world was unlikely to keep global warming below 1.8C, predicting that global temperatures would likely pass 1.5C above pre-industrial levels by 2030.
The Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty signed in 2016, requires countries to take action to avoid dangerous warming by keeping temperature increases well below 2C and as close to 1.5C as possible.
Scientists have repeatedly advised that keeping temperatures at or below the 1.5C target would "significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change".
The Copernicus report authors found that parts of North America, northern Siberia, central Asia, the Maghreb, and much of northern Australia were also drier than average in the same period.
El Niño turbocharges warming
The world's ocean temperatures also hit a record high in August, with scientists predicting the water would continue to get hotter until an El Niño weather pattern reached its peak.
University of Adelaide climate scientist Georgy Falster said the record was not unexpected due to the combination of ongoing global warming and the El Niño event.
"El Niño itself is changing with climate change. So, this El Niño, it's likely to be very large, possibly the biggest one on record," she said.
"And it is possible, although not guaranteed, that the strength of this El Niño is related to climate change."
Dr Falster said it was critical to mark the records as they took place.
"We as a species need to keep reminding ourselves that what is happening is unprecedented," she said.
"So, I think it is actually very important to mark every time another record topples over."
Dr Falster said she was hopeful that the extreme weather spurred governments to act.
"There is absolutely no point at which we should stop trying to reduce the effects of future climate change," she said.
"No matter when we start acting, or increasing our efforts, all of that makes the world a better place in the future."

Tourists in England face nightly levy on hotel and Airbnb stays under new plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:20:07 UTC
17:20:07 KST

Holidaymakers will face a nightly levy on hotel and Airbnb-style stays in England under plans ministers are due to outline to give mayors new powers.
The idea, labelled a tourist tax, was first raised by Keir Starmer’s government in November and is similar to a scheme running in Scotland. It would allow mayors to charge a fee to visitors staying overnight and decide how the revenue raised should be invested.
The tax could raise hundreds of millions of pounds for mayors to put into transport and public services, but it is likely to be seen as a blow for the hospitality industry, which was squeezed by tax rises and extra employment costs announced in last year’s budget.
The housing secretary, Angela Rayner, is meeting mayors on Thursday, and is expected to outline that the levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of accommodation, rather than as a flat fee, to protect budget holidays.
Mayors are expected to be given the power to decide what is best for their area, but ministers do not expect the levy to become overly expensive.
Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, said the plans would put jobs at risk in some communities, and that the new tourism tax in Edinburgh was “already having damaging effects”. He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme holidays in the UK were “already more expensive” than they appeared because of higher VAT.
“What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want,” said Simpson. “And remember that if you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”
He added: “It will be the case that you’ll have holiday parks which can’t open in the shoulder seasons, and of course people who go on holiday will just have that little bit less money in their pocket.”
The overnight visitor levy was outlined in the king’s speech in May, but legislation was not brought forward before Starmer stood down as prime minister. Andy Burnham is likely to pitch the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda. No 10 has previously said local leaders would be “able to set out plans for how revenues will be invested by March 2028”.
As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced the city visitor charge in April 2023 – a £1 per room per night fee – to pay for measures aimed at attracting more tourists. Last year other mayors, including Sadiq Khan in London, wrote a letter to the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, and the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, urging the government to introduce a visitor levy.
Sources from the London mayor’s office said plans to make the payment a percentage rather than a flat fee was welcome. No decisions had been made on the design of the scheme or how revenues would be allocated, they said, but any levy would not be more than 5% of accommodation costs. “This will really help us support London’s growth and our offer to visitors,” they said.
Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, at 5% in July, after the Scottish parliament passed a law last year granting councils the power to implement their own visitor levies. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 a person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.
But UKHospitality, which represents thousands of restaurants, hotels and pubs, has said a tourism tax of 5% would be one of the highest tourist tax rates in Europe and hit households continuing to struggle with the cost of living. It has written to Burnham urging him instead to consider plans for a “holiday bonus”, under which central government revenues would be devolved to local authorities based on the number of visitors they attract.
Tourist taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, and are used in cities such as New York, Barcelona and Venice to fund local services.

Study finds high levels of microplastics enter Swiss soil each year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:16:54 UTC
17:16:54 KST

Study finds high levels of microplastics enter Swiss soil each year
Every year, 219 tonnes of microplastics enter the soil and water bodies in Switzerland via the air, according to a new study.
A research team from Swiss federal research institutes Empa (material science), Eawag (aquatic science) and Agroscope (agriculture) has, for the first time, systematically investigated atmospheric microplastic pollution, as Empa announced on Thursday.
For the study, which was supported by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), the researchers collected samples at five locations over the course of a year. The measurements were taken in Zurich, Dübendorf, Magadino, Payerne and on the Chaumont in the Jura. Extrapolated to all areas of Switzerland below 2,000 metres in altitude, this means that around 219 tonnes of microplastics are deposited in Switzerland each year.
According to the researchers, around 78 tonnes of this ends up directly on agricultural land and around 10 tonnes directly in water bodies.
+ Microplastics found in faeces of Swiss wild animals
At the urban site in Zurich, they recorded the highest figure of 881 particles per square metre per day. At the other sites, the figures were lower, ranging from 249 to 331 particles.
Health implications unclear
The plastics most frequently identified by the researchers were polyethylene terephthalate (PET) at 31%, polyethylene (PE) at 26% and polypropylene (PP) at 21%. PET is commonly found in drinks bottles and polyester fibres in textiles. PE and PP are mainly used for packaging, films and containers.
In relation to the total mass of all airborne particles, such as desert dust or soot, microplastics account for only a small proportion, ranging from 0.02% to 0.12%.
However, due to constant deposition over large areas, considerable quantities accumulate, which hardly degrade in the environment. The researchers went on to say that much remains unclear regarding the consequences of microplastics for the environment and health.
“But in accordance with the precautionary principle, we should avoid littering, use plastics only where necessary and close material cycles wherever possible,” said Empa researcher and study leader Christoph Hüglin, as quoted in the Empa press release.

New stretch of Brussels Cyclostrade opens

The first three sections of the 6.5-kilometre-long cycle highway, or ‘cyclostrade’, between the Brussels borough of Anderlecht and the Laken district in the City of Brussels have been completed. The route forms part of a wider network of cycle highways across Belgium.
Yesterday, a section of the new C223 cycle highway was officially opened. The 6.5-kilometre long route along the L28 railway line will link the Bockstaelplein in Laken with the former Kuregem station, passing through Laken and the boroughs of Jette, Koekelberg, Sint-Jans-Molenbeek and Anderlecht.
The route forms part of a wider network of cycle highways that links up with other ‘cyclostrades’ across the country.
Over the past year, Beliris, the joint venture between the Belgian and Brussels governments involved in construction and renovation in the Brussels capital Region, has been working on three projects in the boroughs of Koekelberg, Jette and Anderlecht. These have now been fully completed. In total, Beliris and the Brussels Mobility agency have invested 7.8 million euros in this work.
A new ramp and a bridge are also due to be completed by autumn. These will improve access to the L28 Park near the Belgica and Bockstael stations.
Brussels’ Mobility Minister, Elke Van den Brandt (Flemish ecologist), is enthusiastic about the project. “A ‘cyclostrade’ is much more than just a cycle path. It represents a fair redistribution of our scarce public space.”

Rheinmetall gets new deal for U.S. Marine Corps robot vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:15:33 UTC
17:15:33 KST

- American Rheinmetall won a $7.28 million contract to deliver 12 Mission Master SP autonomous ground vehicles and five amphibious kits to the U.S. Marine Corps.
- The vehicles run on Rheinmetall's PATH autonomy system and will support continued testing under the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
American Rheinmetall has won a $7.28 million contract to deliver 12 Mission Master SP autonomous ground vehicles and five amphibious kits to the U.S. Marine Corps, the company announced.
The Defense Logistics Agency is managing the procurement, with ADS Inc. serving as prime contractor supporting the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory. The vehicles will be used for continued testing and evaluation as the Marine Corps builds out its autonomous logistics and expeditionary mobility programs, rather than for a specific operational unit.
The Mission Master SP is a robotic ground vehicle that runs on Rheinmetall’s PATH autonomy system, software developed by Rheinmetall Canada that lets a vehicle navigate and plan missions on its own rather than requiring constant remote operator control. The system can be added to existing vehicles or built into new ones. This latest batch adds amphibious kits that let the vehicles operate reliably in littoral, near-shore environments, a capability aimed at the kind of island and coastal operations the Marine Corps has been training for under its expeditionary advanced base concept.
The Marine Corps first took delivery of Mission Master SP vehicles in early 2023, and has since tested them extensively, including during the Talisman Sabre exercise in Australia and the Apollo Shield exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, both in 2023. Those trials covered tasks such as casualty evacuation, resupply runs, and fully autonomous road marches of up to 50 km (31 miles). An armed variant carrying the Fieldranger remote weapon station has also been demonstrated in live-fire testing, adding options like armed reconnaissance and flank security to the vehicle’s role.
“This award represents a significant milestone in our long-standing partnership with the United States Marine Corps,” said Matt Warnick, CEO of American Rheinmetall. “For more than four years, we have worked side-by-side with Marines to mature, refine, and advance autonomous ground capabilities. The Mission Master SP captures the full breadth of those lessons learned and showcases Rheinmetall’s commitment to delivering cutting-edge, reliable, and mission-ready autonomous systems.”
“This collaboration between Rheinmetall colleagues enables the U.S. Marine Corps to deploy the Mission Master SP in multi-domain environments and continue to push boundaries of Canadian innovation,” said Pietro Mazzei, president and CEO of Rheinmetall Canada.
American Rheinmetall is also developing a facility in Maine that it plans to designate as an Advanced Land Autonomy Center of Excellence, focused on PATH system integration, production and long-term support. The company said this latest contract does not by itself require expanding that facility, but fits into its broader push to build up U.S.-based manufacturing for autonomous ground systems.

10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Kuwait on Thursday condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s illegal entry into Syria’s Mount Hermon and called on the UN Security Council to take action to halt attacks on the sovereignty of the Arab country.
Netanyahu entered the occupied Syrian area of Mount Hermon on Wednesday accompanied by Defense Minister Israel Katz, in a move that observers viewed as part of his campaign ahead of Knesset elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
In a statement, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry strongly condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” into Syrian territory, describing it as a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a “blatant breach” of international law.

It reaffirmed Kuwait’s “full support” for Syria’s independence and sovereignty over all its territory.

The Syrian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday also condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” as a “provocative” move and a violation of the country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law.
Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also called it a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a “blatant breach” of international law.
In a video filmed during his visit, Netanyahu, wearing a bulletproof vest, said he was standing at the summit of Mount Hermon on the eve of the Jewish New Year, pointing to Damascus, Lebanon and the Syrian Golan Heights.
Netanyahu claimed Israel had established unprecedented “absolute control” over the area stretching from Mount Hermon toward the Yarmouk River.
He said Israel would not allow “terrorist forces” to establish a presence near its borders.
Katz, meanwhile, signaled that Israel intended to maintain its occupation of the area. “We are here on Mount Hermon, and we will not move from here,” he said in a separate video.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognized by the international community.

New Taipei repairs sewage pipe without digging up road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:29 UTC
17:07:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — New Taipei's Water Resources Department said Thursday that it repaired a 33-meter-long sewage pipeline in one day without digging up the road, according to a press release.
The department said the pipeline on Wugu District's Xincheng 6th Road was badly corroded and leaking. It said excavating the pipe from 6 meters below ground would slow traffic and risk damaging other utility lines, disrupting residents.
Department Director-General Song De-ren (宋德仁) explained that the section is crowded with utility lines, including water, gas, electricity, and telecommunications. He said digging would require crews and heavy machinery and take at least two to three weeks to complete.
The department said it instead fed thick composite strips down a manhole, then wound them together to reinforce the inside of the pipe. It used camera footage and on-site inspection to carry out the repairs.
The department said the city's sewage pipeline network is 2,693 km long and has more than 79,000 manholes, making it the largest in Taiwan. It said that to keep up with maintenance, it introduced the spiral winding technique more than a decade ago, with more than 80 km of old pipelines repaired as of 2026.

IN BRIEF: Civilian killed as Ukraine launches 448 drones at Russia overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:07:06 UTC
17:07:06 KST

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. Air defenses shot down 448 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea last night, the Defense Ministry reported.
Drone debris fell on a private house in the town of Borisoglebsk in the Voronezh Region, killing a woman and injuring two other people. Twenty-eight civilians were injured in a Ukrainian unmanned boat attack on the seafront in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
TASS has gathered the key information about the consequences of the attacks.
Scale of attacks
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 448 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aircraft (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 9 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 10 (5:00 p.m.-5:00 a.m. GMT), the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the drones were downed over the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Rostov, Tula, Dagestan, Kalmykia and Krasnodar regions, as well as Crimea, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
- About 90 drones were destroyed in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Taganrog, Novoshakhtinsk, Volgodonsk and 16 districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on the Max social media platform.
- Air defenses shot down 19 Ukrainian UAVs over the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed ten Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
Consequences
- Drone debris fell on a private house in Borisoglebsk, Voronezh Region, regional Governor Alexander Gusev said on Max.
- The incident caused a fire that killed a woman born in 1983.
- Another two people were injured and received medical assistance on the spot.
- A fire resulting from a drone strike destroyed a residential building in an urban district in the Voronezh Region; the windows of a technical college were damaged, as were the door of a cultural center, two power lines, an electricity pylon, a bus, and a car.
- The windows of an apartment building and a private house were shattered in another district, along with six cars and a garage.
- Falling drone fragments caused fires at port infrastructure facilities in Makhachkala and the Avar Music and Drama Theater, acting head of Dagestan Fyodor Shchukin said on Max.
- The fires were promptly extinguished; there were no casualties.
- Drone debris damaged two private houses and several cars in the Millerovsky District of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
- Four private houses lost electricity due to power line damage.
- Dry grass caught fire after drone fragments came down in the Tarasovsky District; there were no casualties and the fire has been put out.
Unmanned boat attack on Sochi
- A fire broke out on the seafront in Sochi following an attack involving unmanned boats, the regional crisis center reported.
- Emergency response teams are working at the scene.
- According to the latest reports, 28 people, including two children, were injured.
- Three adults and a child remain hospitalized.
- Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin said that their lives were not in danger.
- The crisis center added that beach infrastructure and a part of the Primorskaya Embankment had been damaged.
- Proshunin ordered his deputies and district heads to promptly take measures to ensure sanitary safety and restore infrastructure facilities.

These are the best airports in the world, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:06:16 UTC
17:06:16 KST

Spain’s Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport and Germany’s Düsseldorf Airport were named the best airports in the world.
Your idea of the best airport in the world might look very different to mine.
Maybe you think the best part about travelling abroad is the duty-free shopping? Maybe you care more about how far away you are from the city centre? Or maybe you judge an airport on the number of destinations it serves directly?
Thankfully for us, Consumer Choice Center has compiled a new edition of the World Consumer Airport Index that takes all of the above, and more, into account, to reveal the very best airports around the globe.
Split into two rankings – one for those with more than 47.2 million passengers per year, and one serving below that number – the index also looks at whether or not a hub has direct access to the metro or national rail services, how easy the connections are between gates and terminals, the choice of airlines available, the average delays, and whether or not there is a hotel in it.
Airports are also awarded bonus points if security waiting times are under three minutes, and if they do not have nighttime curfews.
The result? Drum roll, please…
Both the best large and small airports around the world globally are in Europe, with Spain’s Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport topping the chart for the former, and Germany’s Düsseldorf Airport for the latter.
Both of these airports performed well on security waiting times, with passengers passing through Barcelona waiting just three minutes, while in Düsseldorf, processing is almost instantaneous.
The worst airports – and why
Among the large airports, the worst-ranked include Antalya, Guangzhou Baiyun and Frankfurt.
For smaller airports, those who fared poorly include Seoul Gimpo, Punta Cana, and London Stansted.
These airports all have problems in common, including extreme distances from city centres, no ride-hailing options separate from taxi companies, poor access to railway services, long security wait times and a high percentage of average delays.
The top large airports around the world
- Barcelona-El Prat Josep Tarradellas Airport, Spain
- Leonardo da Vinci-Fiumicino Airport, Rome, Italy
- Los Angeles International Airport, USA
- Bangkok Suvarnabhumi International Airport, Thailand
- Charles de Gaulle Airport, Paris, France
- King Abdulaziz International Airport, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
- London Heathrow Airport, UK
- Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport, Spain
- Tokyo International Airport (Haneda), Japan
- Dubai International Airport, United Arab Emirates
The best small airports globally
- Düsseldorf Airport, Germany
- Zurich Airport, Switzerland
- Copenhagen Airport, Denmark
- Helsinki Airport, Finland
- Milan Malpensa Airport, Italy
- Oslo Gardermoen Airport, Norway
- Munich Airport, Germany
- Vancouver International Airport, Canada
- Brussels Airport, Belgium
- Berlin Brandenburg Airport, Germany

Production designer of a Russian TV series arrested on treason charges. He lived in Kyiv and came to Russia to renew his passport.
Russian authorities have accused Alexander Kondratov, the 52-year-old production designer of the TV series Likvidatsiya “Liquidation,” of treason, the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona reported.
Investigators opened the case on August 5. Kondratov’s defense attorney, Natalia Tikhonova, told reporters that investigators viewed “at least six publications” he posted online as constituting treason. It was not specified what they contained.
Kondratov, who was born and raised in Moscow, has lived in Kyiv since 2012, where his family remains. He had traveled to Russia to renew his international passport, the human rights group Memorial wrote. He was detained at Vnukovo Airport on May 5. Before he was charged with treason, Kondratov was subjected to so-called “carousel arrests,” and in total spent more than 70 days in a pretrial detention center.
The detective series Likvidatsiya “Liquidation” premiered in 2007, following criminal investigators fighting crime in postwar Odesa in 1946. Its cast included Vladimir Mashkov, Mikhail Porechenkov, Sergei Makovetsky, and Konstantin Lavronenko. Kondratov’s work on the series earned him the Golden Eagle Award and a TEFI Award.

World Suicide Prevention Day: what do the latest EU and Spain figures show?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:04:23 UTC
17:04:23 KST

Suicide deaths in the EU fell slightly in 2023 and are below levels a decade ago. Three in four victims are men. In Spain, figures show a fall, as the WHO calls to end stigma.
48,370 people died by suicide in the European Union in 2023, but the mortality rate continues to fall and is now below the level recorded a decade ago.
This is the picture painted by the latest Eurostat data (source in Spanish), published to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, marked every 10 September to raise awareness of this public-health issue, tackle stigma and promote prevention. Suicide accounted for 1% of all deaths recorded in the EU that year. The standardised rate was 10.4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, compared with 10.6 in 2022 and 12.2 in 2013.
Differences between countries remain large. Lithuania recorded the highest rate in the EU, with 18.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, followed by Slovenia (16.4) and Hungary (16.1). The lowest rates were in Cyprus (3.5), Greece (4.3) and Malta (5.5).
Men accounted for 76.4% of all suicide deaths in the EU. The crude rate was 16.9 per 100,000 men, compared with 5 among women. Mortality also increases with age, reaching 17.3 per 100,000 among people aged 65 and over.
Suicides fall for the third year in a row in Spain
The most recent national figures point in the same direction. In 2025, 3,808 people died by suicide in Spain, 3.7% fewer than in 2024, when 3,953 deaths were recorded, according to provisional data from the National Statistics Institute (INE). (source in Spanish)
This is the third consecutive year of decline since the 4,227 deaths recorded in 2022. In 2025, suicide was the third external cause of death in Spain. Among men, however, it was the leading one, with 2,784 deaths.
Spain has an Action Plan for Suicide Prevention 2025–2027, which tackles the issue from a public-health perspective. Its priorities include improving the information available, addressing stigma and the myths surrounding suicide, strengthening early detection and healthcare provision and improving coordination between the different sectors involved.
The plan (source in Spanish) also focuses on awareness-raising and responsible communication, making it easier to access support services and preventing suicide among people and groups in situations of particular vulnerability.
Breaking the stigma, talking and seeking help
The World Health Organization (WHO) is dedicating its World Suicide Prevention Day campaign (source in Spanish) to the slogan "Changing the Narrative on Suicide" ('cambiar la narrativa sobre el suicidio'). In 2026 its call to action is "Start the Conversation" ('iniciar la conversación'), which aims to challenge myths and stigma and encourage people to talk about what is happening to them and seek help.
For the WHO, changing the narrative also means driving changes in public policy, improving access to quality care and implementing evidence-based prevention strategies. The organisation estimates that more than 720,000 people die by suicide every year worldwide. Seventy-three per cent of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, and suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 globally.
The WHO stresses that asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase the risk and can help them feel understood.

White House Considers Replacing Peace Envoys Witkoff and Kushner With CIA Director Ratcliffe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
08:01:57 UTC
17:01:57 KST

- Category
- World
White House Considers Replacing Peace Envoys Witkoff and Kushner With CIA Director Ratcliffe
The White House is considering stepping back the involvement of special envoy Steve Witkoff and representative Jared Kushner in negotiations, as reported by Financial Times on September 9.
Five people familiar with the plans stated that Washington may shift the lead diplomatic role to CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
American officials close to Ratcliffe informed European counterparts that the CIA director is preparing to take charge of shuttle diplomacy efforts while maintaining existing channels with Russian and Ukrainian intelligence services.
The White House and the CIA declined to comment on the matter, and sources noted that President Donald Trump has not finalized a decision. The potential change follows eight visits to Moscow and one to Kyiv by Witkoff, which yielded no diplomatic progress.
During their previous meeting with the envoys, Russian leader Vladimir Putin expressed confidence in the mediation process, stating, “Here, of course, the quality of mediation, trust in those involved in it, is very important. I want to tell you that it is comfortable for us to work with you, and, of course, the level of trust in the course of this work on our part is quite high.”
At the same time, sources involved in informal contacts indicated that Moscow expressed openness to a new diplomatic approach.
Officials in Ukraine and individuals familiar with Kremlin views noted that Moscow held Witkoff partly responsible for the lack of progress at the August 2025 summit in Alaska, where expectations of potential Russian compromises were not met. Meanwhile, officials in Kyiv felt that Witkoff did not exert sufficient pressure on Moscow.
On August 25, CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow for unannounced meetings, marking the first trip by a CIA chief to Russia since November 2021. The visit followed an August 1 announcement by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio regarding plans to explore resuming peace negotiations, after planned visits to Kyiv by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner failed to materialize.
John Ratcliffe is a former federal prosecutor and Texas congressman who previously served as Director of National Intelligence. He is the first person in US history to hold both top intelligence positions after becoming CIA Director.
A three-hour meeting in Moscow between US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vladimir Putin had ended without a breakthrough, leaving the Russian leader intent on continuing Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as reported by Bloomberg.
Putin had remained committed to capturing the entire Donetsk region, a goal he believed his forces could achieve within six months. Meanwhile, calculations by the Institute for the Study of War showed that Russian forces were advancing at a rate of 2.36 square kilometers per day, meaning it would have taken until October 2032 to control the remaining 19% of the region.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov noted that Putin might have held a phone call with Donald Trump, though he stated it was premature to discuss specific dates for resuming three-party talks. Following the Moscow visit, Witkoff traveled to Kyiv to meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European security advisers, later reporting substantial progress from those discussions.

Russian agent, who directed strikes at AFU artillery, has been detained in the Kharkiv region
Kyiv • UNN
An unemployed resident of Chuhuiv district passed the coordinates of Ukrainian Armed Forces positions in the Vovchansk direction to the Russians. He faces up to 8 years in prison.
In the Kharkiv region, an unemployed local resident was passing information to Russia about the positions of Ukrainian troops in order to subsequently direct extremely heavy airstrikes there. He was caught "red-handed" and detained by law enforcement officers. This was reported by the Security Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The counterintelligence department of the Security Service detained another informant for the aggressor state in the Kharkiv region. The suspect was adjusting enemy fire against the Defense Forces, which are stationed 10 km from the front line in the Vovchansk direction. The investigation established that among the main "targets" of the Ruscists were the positions of Ukrainian Armed Forces tube artillery, which keeps the enemy’s assault groups under fire control. According to operational data, upon receiving the coordinates of Ukrainian troops, the enemy planned to launch precision strikes against them using extremely heavy guided aerial bombs
According to law enforcement officials, SBU officers acted preemptively and detained the suspect "red-handed" when he was conducting a reconnaissance sortie near the frontline in his own car under the pretext of going fishing. Measures were also taken to secure the location of the Kharkiv region’s defenders.
According to the case materials, the shelling was being adjusted by an unemployed resident of Chuhuiv district, who came to the attention of Russian intelligence operatives while looking for "easy" money in Telegram channels. It was established that, following the Ruscists’ instructions, their accomplice drove around the area near the line of engagement in his own car and recorded the deployment locations of Ukrainian troops. At the site of the detention, officers seized a smartphone from the informant, which he used to collect intelligence and communicate with the Russian Federation
Investigators of the Security Service notified him that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (the unauthorized dissemination of information about the movement or deployment of the Armed Forces of Ukraine or other military formations established in accordance with the laws of Ukraine, committed under martial law).
The suspect is currently in custody without the right to post bail. He faces up to 8 years in prison. The investigation is ongoing to establish all the circumstances of the crime and the possible additional classification of the enemy spotter’s actions as high treason.
We remind you
The counterintelligence department of the Security Service of Ukraine detained a Russian agent in the Poltava region who was preparing the assassination of the commander of one of the military units stationed in the region.
