Türkiye to stay course on disinflation program: Finance minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:54:57 UTC
16:54:57 KST

- Mehmet Simsek says price stability is essential for sustainable high growth and better income distribution
- Return to free-floating exchange rate desirable once inflation falls, expectations improve and two-way foreign-exchange flows emerge
Türkiye will maintain its economic program and deliver disinflation despite difficult global and geopolitical conditions, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Wednesday.
Simsek joined Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz and Presidency of Strategy and Budget head Ibrahim Senel at the Presidential Complex for an international media meeting on Türkiye’s 2027-2029 Medium-Term Program.
“The only criticism we would accept is that we have been ambitious in our targets. We have, and there is, of course, a cost associated with that. But the commitment is there,” he said.
“We will stay the course and deliver. What is important is the direction of travel.” 
Türkiye committed to combating illicit finance  
Simsek said Türkiye maintains close cooperation and effective information-sharing with its partners and allies, particularly the US.
“Türkiye is committed to combating terrorist financing, any form of illicit financial activity, money laundering, sanctions evasion and all forms of illicit trade,” he said.
All companies operating in Türkiye must comply fully with national regulations and avoid sanctions, while competent authorities are assessing recent US Treasury announcements and allegations within the rule of law, he added. 
Well-established framework for Iran gas payments  
Simsek said Türkiye’s gas contracts with neighbors such as Iran and Russia are long-term agreements, some of which have been in place for decades.
“We do not pay Iran directly for the natural gas. We have an understanding, again, with the US. The money sits in a very tightly regulated account, and payments can only be made for items such as food and medicine,” he said.
“There is a well-established framework governing how natural gas payments are managed.”
Iran accounts for a relatively small share of Türkiye’s gas imports, while the country has invested heavily in alternative supplies and storage, Simsek said, noting that the US is now one of Türkiye’s leading LNG suppliers. 
Return to free float  
Simsek said returning to a free-floating exchange rate is desirable because it acts as a shock absorber, but lower inflation, better-anchored inflation expectations and two-way foreign-exchange flows are needed first.
“This is not about being afraid of returning to a free float. It is about getting the conditions right,” he said, calling speculation over an imminent change “baseless.”
He stressed that daily exchange-rate policy is conducted by the Central Bank and that the Medium-Term Program assumes a neutral real exchange rate.
“We are not in the business of making bets on the exchange rate,” he added. 
‘Commitment to price stability remains very strong’  
Simsek rejected claims that the 2027 inflation target was revised upward to permit looser monetary policy.
“The idea that the inflation target for 2027 was revised upward in order to loosen monetary policy never came onto our agenda,” he said.
He said the program reflects significant changes in energy, agricultural and other commodity prices, as well as the difficult geopolitical environment.
“When the facts change, of course, forecasts change,” he said.
Simsek said Türkiye’s disinflation program began in earnest in mid-2024, noting that international experience showed inflation typically takes 3.4 years to return to pre-shock levels.
“If you take that as a reference — 2025, 2026, and then essentially the end of 2027 — I think we’ll be back to pre-shock levels,” he said. 
Housing and selective credit support  
Simsek said Türkiye has invested $104 billion in earthquake reconstruction, with 621,000 housing units delivered or due to be delivered this year.
Rent inflation in earthquake-hit provinces is around 20%, compared with 50%-60% elsewhere, demonstrating that “supply-side measures make a huge difference,” he said.
The government also plans 750,000 state-funded social housing units to ease housing and rental costs.
Simsek said selective credit programs support manufacturers, farmers, small businesses and technology investments, helping preserve employment and create jobs.
“The ultimate goal of this program is a sustainable high growth rate and better income distribution. So, basically, better standards of living for Turkish people,” he said.

Targeting US-made UUV by Iran: why is Washington worried?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:54:54 UTC
16:54:54 KST

In response to the incident, the US Department of War [Pentagon] claimed the drone was outdated, has suffered a technical malfunction, and carried no sensitive information. Such a narrative is, of course, predictable. Under these circumstances, it is only natural for the US to try to prevent the loss of an operational system in one of the world’s most sensitive maritime regions from becoming an intelligence and technological triumph for Iran.
However, a review of reports by American and Western media presents a different picture. In its report on US naval operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the “Financial Times” has highlighted the role of unmanned systems in missions such as seabed reconnaissance, mine countermeasures, and maritime surveillance. This indicates that unmanned underwater systems are not merely experimental equipment or tools lacking operational significance; rather, they constitute part of the US's new capability to gain situational awareness and superiority in maritime environments.
The significance of this matter becomes even more apparent when considering the region's environmental characteristics. The Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters are not merely ordinary shipping lines; the area is considered one of the world's most critical energy and trade chokepoints, and any disruption to its security could have far-reaching international economic and political consequences. For this reason, alongside its traditional deployment of naval vessels, submarines, and patrol aircraft, the United States has in recent years sought to utilize unmanned systems to enhance its surveillance and intelligence-gathering capabilities in the region.
Remotely-controlled Unmanned Underwater Vehicles (UUV) hold a special place in this context. Unlike aerial drones—whose presence is usually visible or detectable—underwater systems can operate at great depths with a significantly lower signature. They are capable of gathering data on the underwater environment, seabed conditions, maritime routes, and certain military activities. Such information is of great importance to naval forces, as a significant aspect of military competition at sea hinges on understanding the operational environment.
From this perspective, the issue is not limited merely to the monetary value of the system. Even if we take the figure of approximately $2.5 million as the basis for the drone's value, its true significance lies in the technology and data involved in its construction and deployment. Access to an actual unit of an operational system enables a more detailed analysis of the airframe design, propulsion systems, sensors, communication equipment, energy management methods, and overall system architecture.
Studying a real-world system can be valuable for any country developing similar technologies. Understanding the technical solutions employed, the design's strengths and weaknesses, and the approach taken to address operational challenges can streamline and refine the path toward developing indigenous versions.
In this regard, H.I. Sutton, a renowned analyst of undersea technologies, believes that this UUV is more sophisticated than many Iranian models; Iran's access to it could provide a significant opportunity to study the technology and further develop its unmanned undersea system capabilities. The significance of this assessment lies in the fact that it moves the issue beyond the realm of political propaganda. Even if the Pentagon attempts to downplay the intelligence value of the system, access to an actual specimen of a military rival's advanced technology constitutes a technological opportunity in its own right.
Another point to consider is the distinction between the political narrative and the operational reality. The Pentagon states that the system was aging and suffered from technical malfunctions. While there may be some truth to this claim—as no military system is immune to technical faults or the risk of loss, and many unmanned systems are specifically designed for high-risk environments—a system being "expendable" is not the same as it being "insignificant."
The philosophy behind the use of unmanned systems is rooted precisely in this premise: executing missions where the deployment of more expensive equipment or the risking of human lives is undesirable. Therefore, if a system is designed to operate in high-risk environments, this fact does not necessarily diminish its operational value; rather, it may indicate that the mission was critical enough to warrant prioritizing an unmanned vehicle over the direct presence of human personnel.
On the other hand, the presence of such a system in the region is significant in its own right. The United States is employing advanced technologies to enhance its operational awareness in the region's most critical waterway—an area where Iran maintains geographical oversight of the surrounding environment. The capture of this system demonstrates that maritime competition in the region is no longer confined to warships, coastal defense missiles, or submarines; a substantial portion of this rivalry has shifted to the realm of unmanned technologies and the battle for information superiority.
For Iran, too, this event holds significance from two perspectives: first, demonstrating the capability to detect and acquire an American subsurface system within an environment where the U.S. believes it can operate using advanced technologies; and second, the opportunity to study the system itself and leverage the insights gained to develop domestic technologies and improve countermeasures against similar systems.
For this reason, U.S. efforts to portray this incident as the loss of an obsolete and insignificant system must also be analyzed within the context of managing its political and intelligence repercussions. Naturally, Washington has no desire for Iran’s access to an operational U.S. system to be framed as a significant naval and technological achievement.
Ultimately, the significance of capturing this UAV should not be measured solely by its price tag. The true value lies in the fact that Iran has obtained an actual example of the technology employed by the United States in the operational environment of the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. While the system may be an older model and sensitive mission data might not be accessible, the technology itself, its design, and an understanding of its operational mechanics can still hold considerable value.
Washington describes the system as outdated and insignificant; yet, this very fact raises a crucial question: if the drone lacked operational value, why did the U.S. deploy it in one of the world’s most sensitive waterways as part of its naval missions? The answer to this question likely reveals, better than anything else, that the hunting and targeting of this drone represents far more than the mere acquisition of an ordinary naval and maritime trophy.

Xi Jinping’s September of Summits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:54:35 UTC
16:54:35 KST

China’s foreign policy has been traditionally viewed through the lens of its relationship with the United States. While Washington remains its most important economic partner and strategic competitor, Beijing’s push for a multipolar world is increasingly visible in its systematic efforts to convene a wide range of international groupings, institutions and economic networks in which China can play an indispensable role.
Xi Jinping’s September diplomacy provides a particularly vivid example of this strategy. Over the course of the month, the Chinese president is engaging with the leaders of Russia, India, Iran, Central Asian states, Egypt and several emerging powers through a succession of summits and bilateral meetings, before he meets President Donal Trump at the end of the month. Taken together, these engagements offer a window into how Beijing is attempting to strengthen its position across Eurasia and the wider Global South, moving away from the US-led international system towards a multi-polar world order.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Influence of the war in Ukraine
There is another thread running through this diplomatic sequence: Russia’s war in Ukraine. Although the war is unlikely to dominate the formal agenda of most of these meetings it will have a bearing. Beijing may continue to avoid openly aligning itself with Moscow, but China has emerged as the largest buyer of Russian crude oil and as the biggest transshipment hub of components used in Russian weapons.
Zelensky’s Drone-Disrupted Flight Highlights Wartime Travel Risks as Kyiv Calls Near-Miss Claims Exaggerated
Such a dependency offers Beijing substantial economic and diplomatic leverage over Moscow, and the Trump administration’s renewed efforts to end the war potentially give Beijing an additional source of leverage in its dealings with Washington.
This makes Xi’s September program of summits more than a series of routine diplomatic engagements. The sequence begins with China consolidating its influence in Eurasia, extends through its expanding economic and strategic presence in the Middle East and the Global South, and culminates in a meeting with Washington. The big question is whether this broader diplomatic positioning is also intended to strengthen Xi’s hand in negotiations with Trump—and whether China’s relationship with Russia and its position on Ukraine could become part of that bargaining.
The Shanghai Cooperation Summit
The first stop in Xi’s September itinerary was Bishkek. This year, the Kyrgyz capital hosted the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, bringing together the leaders of China, India, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Iran, and thel Central Asian republics of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
It was on the sidelines of the SCO summit that India’s PM Modi stressed the importance of moving away from “endless war to the end of war” with Ukraine while speaking to Putin. Xi’s language on the subject was much more subtle. He only made a brief reference to Ukraine, grouping it with the Middle East and Afghanistan as international “hotspot” issues. Xi said that China was ready to “strengthen communication with all sides and promote a political settlement,” while avoiding any direct references to Russia.
The SCO is not a conventional alliance. It is a broad Eurasian forum focused on security and economic cooperation whose members often pursue very different geopolitical agendas. China and Russia want to reshape the US-led order. India insists on strategic autonomy while maintaining close ties with Washington. Most Central Asian states hedge between China, Russia and other powers such as Turkey. The ongoing India-Pakistan border tensions further complicate achieving the forum’s aligned position.
For Beijing, this diversity of interest is a feature, not a flaw. China is using the SCO to build a political and economic counterweight to US dominance without turning it into an explicit anti-American bloc. Xi’s emphasis on sovereignty, multilateralism and development appeals to countries that want more room to maneuver without formally aligning with China. The SCO gives Beijing a way to expand its influence without demanding formal allegiance.
In meeting with Putin and Modi in Bishkek Xi was able to demonstrate that China can effectively deal with both long-term geopolitical partners and rivals. For Xi, the SCO is about building the Eurasia political and economic architecture in which China enjoys the role of an indispensable power.
In practical terms, the Bishkek summit demonstrated how China is linking its geopolitical strategy to technology and connectivity. Xi proposed an international cooperation centre on AI applications for SCO countries. He also announced 100 joint technology projects over the next three years and a China-SCO port-economy cooperation center in Tianjin.
Transport connectivity is the other pillar. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, a USD 4.7 billion project linking western China and the central Asian republics. It reflects China’s broader effort to tie Central Asia more closely to the Chinese trade and transport networks, especially in the age of geopolitical uncertainty. China sees it as complimentary to the existing Belt and Road Initiative that aims to invest into transport infrastructure across 150 countries.
Together, these developments give China something more tangible than a geopolitical message: infrastructure, technology and access to markets. This is how Beijing seeks to build a China-centered Eurasian order—not by demanding allegiance, but by making its economic and technological networks too important for regional powers to ignore.
Egypt visit
Immediately after the SCO summit in Bishkek, Xi arrived in Egypt, marking his first official visit to Cairo in a decade. This trip represented both a bilateral economic mission and a geopolitical signal with one of America’s key allies in the Middle East.
Xi and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi agreed to deepen their “comprehensive strategic partnership,” with more than 20 cooperation documents signed covering the Belt and Road, AI, digital economy, industrial and supply-chain cooperation, education and transport. They also reaffirmed cooperation around the Suez Canal Economic Zone, manufacturing, renewable energy and technology.
More interestingly, from Beijing’s perspective, was the acknowledgement of the impact on regional geopolitics. Xi backed greater regional autonomy in Middle Eastern security and argued that the countries of the region should be the “masters” of their own affairs – a clear reference to the current US role. China also offered to help safeguard international shipping lanes amid the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.
There was also a significant strategic-economic dimension. Egypt is an important node for China because of the Suez Canal. Controlled by Egypt, this critical maritime point enjoys a strategic location between Africa, the Middle East and Europe and has a growing role as a destination for Chinese investment and goods, especially during the time of lingering regional tensions.
China has already invested heavily in Egypt, including in the Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone at Ain Sokhna. The zone had attracted more than 200 companies and over $4.7 billion in investment by June 2026.
Xi’s Cairo visit therefore fitted neatly into Xi’s broader September diplomacy: Bishkek demonstrated China’s Eurasian reach; Cairo showed its growing Middle Eastern and Global South reach; and both strengthened his position ahead of the BRICS summit in India and the Washington meeting with Trump scheduled for the end of September.
The next critical stop in Xi’s September diplomacy will be in New Delhi, where India hosts the 18th BRICS summit on Sept. 12–13. For Beijing, the event brings together the main themes of Xi’s September diplomatic drive: relations with major emerging powers, economic cooperation and a stronger voice for the Global South.
There are unlikely to be references to Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine at the summit. The agenda is increasingly practical. India’s BRICS chairmanship is focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. It is about resilient global supply chains, trade finance for small businesses and greater use of digital services. Energy cooperation is another priority, including critical minerals, energy storage, smart grids and hydrogen. BRICS members have also discussed cooperation on AI, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure and next-generation communications.
For China, these areas are particularly relevant. It is already a major supplier of manufacturing, digital technologies and clean-energy equipment to many BRICS economies. Greater cooperation within the group can therefore open markets for Chinese companies while reducing the vulnerability of trade and supply chains to geopolitical tensions with the West.
The summit is also important for China-India relations. It is Xi’s first visit to India since 2019, providing an opportunity to stabilize a relationship marked by border tensions and ongoing economic competition. Beijing does not need India to fully align with China, but it has an interest in keeping New Delhi engaged in BRICS and preventing their rivalry from dominating the organization.
BRICS therefore gives Xi the broadest platform of his September tour and an important global stage to push for China’s multipolar agenda before his planned visit to Washington on Sept. 24.
The design of the meeting program
The sequence of Xi’s September summits is perhaps more significant than any individual meeting. Bishkek demonstrated China’s ability to shape the political and economic architecture of Eurasia. Cairo highlighted its expanding role in the Middle East and Africa, while New Delhi offers Xi a platform to bring these relationships together under the broader framework of the Global South.
The upcoming Washington meeting therefore needs to be viewed in the context of the entire September tour. Trade barriers, rare earths, technology and AI are likely to dominate the economic agenda, while Taiwan will remain a sensitive strategic issue. The war in Ukraine may also enter the discussions, particularly as the Trump administration renews pressure for a settlement. China’s influence over Moscow gives Beijing a potential source of leverage, although it remains to be seen whether Xi would be willing to use that influence in exchange for concessions from Washington.

Türkiye becomes Europe’s largest credit card market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:40:38 UTC
16:40:38 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye has become Europe’s largest credit card market, surpassing Spain in the number of credit cards in circulation, according to a Mastercard report citing European Central Bank data.
Based on European Central Bank data cited by Mastercard,
The report said Türkiye had 142 million credit cards and 319 million bank cards, including prepaid cards, while card payments reached 24.1 trillion Turkish Liras in 2025.
According to the report, increasing digital payment penetration in Türkiye from the current 69 percent to levels approaching 95 percent in more mature markets could further boost the economy.
Digital payments supported household consumption through faster and alternative payment options, generating an estimated economic impact of nearly 1.5 trillion liras in 2025, the report said.
Travel spending contributed the most, at 546 billion liras, followed by the restaurant sector at 427 billion liras. Furniture and electronics, apparel, and accommodation were also among the sectors benefiting from digital payments.
The share of card payments in household spending reached 54 percent for personal cards and 69 percent when commercial cards were included in 2025.
The report noted that Türkiye’s expanding card payment infrastructure has made spending easier for foreign visitors and increased the country’s attractiveness as a tourism destination.
Tourism revenues rose from $7.6 billion in 2000 to nearly $65 billion in 2025, while the share of card payments in tourism revenues increased from 15 percent to around 38 percent, according to the report.
As a result, digital payments contributed 388 billion liras, or approximately $9.8 billion, to Türkiye’s tourism revenues in 2025.

Lockheed’s cruise missile contract crossed $10 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:39:52 UTC
16:39:52 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $826 million to its Lockheed Martin missile contract, pushing its total value past $10 billion for the first time.
- The contract covers continued JASSM and LRASM production through July 2030, with deliveries also going to Poland, the Netherlands, Japan and Finland.
The U.S. Air Force has added $826 million to its bulk missile contract with Lockheed Martin, pushing the total value of the deal past $10 billion for the first time.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, issued the contract modification for continued production of the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, known as JASSM, and the Long Range Anti-Ship Missile, known as LRASM. The award brings the contract’s total cumulative value to $10.48 billion, up from $9.65 billion. Work will be done at Lockheed Martin’s Orlando, Florida, facility, with completion expected by July 31, 2030.
The same contract crossed $9.485 billion in August 2025, when the Air Force added roughly $4.3 billion covering JASSM lots 22 through 26 and LRASM lots 9 through 12, with deliveries running to Poland, the Netherlands, Japan and Finland under Foreign Military Sales agreements. This latest $826 million addition keeps that same production line running rather than opening a new one. The funding is split across fiscal 2024, 2025 and 2026 missile procurement accounts, Navy weapons procurement funds, research and development money, operations and maintenance funds, and Foreign Military Sales money, reflecting how deeply intertwined U.S. and allied orders have become on this program.
JASSM is a stealthy, long-range cruise missile built to strike heavily defended, fixed or moving targets on land from outside the range of most enemy air defenses. The baseline version has a range of about 370 km (230 miles), while the extended-range JASSM-ER variant, now the more common configuration in Air Force inventories, reaches roughly 1,000 km (620 miles). JASSM has been in Air Force service since 2009 and is cleared to fly on the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, B-1B and B-52, giving multiple aircraft types a common long-range strike weapon rather than each platform needing its own missile. LRASM is a derivative of the JASSM-ER airframe adapted to hunt and destroy ships at sea, carrying a roughly 450 kg (1,000-pound) warhead. It flies on U.S. Navy F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and U.S. Air Force B-1B bombers today, with F-35 and F-16 integration work also underway to expand which aircraft can carry it.
Allied demand for both missiles has kept growing beyond the four countries already named on this contract. The U.S. State Department cleared a potential $842 million sale of JASSM-ER missiles to Denmark for its F-35s in June 2026, and approved a separate sale of JASSM-ER to Italy in December 2025. Australia and Finland have flown JASSM on their F/A-18 fleets for years, while Poland remains the only customer outside the U.S. to field the longer-range JASSM-ER, integrated on its F-16C/D fleet since deliveries began following a 2016 order. Israel has also been in discussions with Washington over a potential JASSM purchase.
The contract falls under the Pentagon’s Large Lot Procurement approach, which buys missiles in large multi-year batches rather than through smaller annual orders. The Air Force and Lockheed say the structure lowers the cost per missile, stabilizes Lockheed’s supply chain, and lets production ramp up faster than year-by-year contracting would allow. Lockheed opened a dedicated JASSM and LRASM factory in Troy, Alabama, in 2021 and added a 225,000-square-foot automated production facility in 2022 to support the higher volumes, incorporating robotic paint lines and automated forecasting tools.
Lockheed opened a dedicated JASSM and LRASM factory in Troy, Alabama, in 2021 and added a 225,000-square-foot automated production facility in 2022 to support the higher volumes, incorporating robotic paint lines and automated forecasting tools. The company has said ramping up production of both missiles is central to keeping pace with demand from the U.S. military and its growing list of allied customers.

Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek (AA Photo)
Türkiye will maintain its economic program and deliver disinflation despite difficult global and geopolitical conditions, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek has said.
Şimşek joined Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz and Presidency of Strategy and Budget head İbrahim Şenel at the Presidential Complex on Sept. 9 for an international media meeting on Türkiye’s 2027-2029 Medium-Term Program (OVP).
“The only criticism we would accept is that we have been ambitious in our targets. We have, and there is, of course, a cost associated with that. But the commitment is there,” he said. “We will stay the course and deliver. What is important is the direction of travel.”
Şimşek said returning to a free-floating exchange rate is desirable because it acts as a shock absorber, but lower inflation, better-anchored inflation expectations and two-way foreign-exchange flows are needed first.
“This is not about being afraid of returning to a free float. It is about getting the conditions right,” he said, calling speculation over an imminent change “baseless.”
Şimşek rejected claims that the 2027 inflation target was revised upward to permit looser monetary policy.
“The idea that the inflation target for 2027 was revised upward in order to loosen monetary policy never came onto our agenda,” he said.
Şimşek said Türkiye’s disinflation program began in earnest in mid-2024, noting that international experience showed inflation typically takes 3.4 years to return to pre-shock levels.
“If you take that as a reference — 2025, 2026, and then essentially the end of 2027 — I think we’ll be back to pre-shock levels,” he said.

Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:36:30 UTC
16:36:30 KST

Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.
Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.
Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.
As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.
Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.
The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.
Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.
In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

Grace Tame clarifies comments that likened mass sexual assault reports to 'propaganda'
In short:
Grace Tame has clarified comments she made during an ABC interview about reports of sexual violence by terrorist group Hamas.
Ms Tame faced criticism after an interview in which she likened reports of mass sexual assault during the attacks on October 7, 2023, to "propaganda".
She says those comments were "misinterpreted" and that she stands "with survivors of sexual violence everywhere".
Former Australian of the Year Grace Tame has clarified comments she made during an ABC interview about reports of sexual violence by terrorist group Hamas.
Ms Tame faced criticism after a March ABC Radio Sydney interview in which she likened reports of mass sexual assault during the attacks on October 7, 2023, to "propaganda".
After several months, Ms Tame posted to Instagram on Thursday, saying those comments were "misinterpreted".
"There is something I have wanted to clarify for a while, which I regret not clarifying sooner," she said.
"I stand with survivors of sexual violence everywhere, no matter who they are."
She continued in her Instagram video to allege her views were based on Human Rights Watch reports, where they were "unable to find evidence to support the claim that Israeli women were raped en mass on October 7, 2023".
United Nations officials in 2024 found there were reasonable grounds to believe conflict-related sexual violence, including rape and gang rape, occurred at several locations during Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel.
"However, I do not deny the legitimate accusations of rape made by individual Israeli women, including accounts of gang rape," Ms Tame said.
"I believe Israeli survivors, I believe Jewish survivors, as I believe all survivors. While the intention of my remarks was not to imply otherwise, I acknowledge and sincerely apologise for any harm their mischaracterisation has caused."
Grace Tame interviewed over previous comments
Ms Tame had appeared on ABC Radio Sydney to discuss her interpretation of the phrase "globalise the intifada".
She also responded to claims she had been selective in her outrage and accusations she had never spoken on behalf of the Israeli women believed to have been sexually assaulted on October 7.
"I'm not going to sink to the level of entertaining any kind of propaganda," she said at the time.
"Those things have been debunked.
"Awful things are being perpetrated by both sides. This is not selective outrage. I'm outraged by all of the violence."
Her interview was met with criticism from the Israeli embassy in Australia , which accused Ms Tame of losing her "moral compass".
The ABC Ombudsman later found the interview did not breach editorial standards, and met "the standards for ensuring accuracy in live radio interviews".
The embassy in Canberra had also raised concerns over previous comments by Ms Tame about her use of the phrase "globalise the intifada".
She was criticised by federal MPs and the NSW premier for leading a chant using the phrase at a rally against Israeli President Isaac Herzog during his visit to Australia.
"Globalise the intifada" is a contentious phrase that the state government has been considering outlawing under revised hate speech laws.
The word "intifada" means "shaking off" in Arabic and has been used to refer to two periods of violent Palestinian protest against Israel.
Members of the Jewish community have described it as a hateful call for violence.
In the interview with ABC Radio Sydney, Ms Tame said she understood the phrase "to be a call for widespread resistance" against the actions of Israel.

Lebanon and Israel have held seven rounds of direct negotiations under US sponsorship. The first five rounds were held in Washington, culminating in a 14-point framework agreement signed on June 26, while the sixth and seventh took place in Rome.
The latest round concluded on Aug. 6 after three days of talks covering military, political, legal and border issues, as well as prisoners.
The framework provides for a phased Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of non-state armed groups.
Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon, which it started in early March after Hezbollah's retaliation to the Iran war, despite the framework agreement. Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:29:00 UTC
16:29:00 KST

Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Alongside military defense, it is equally necessary to significantly and visibly strengthen the protection of the country's internal security, because threats do not begin only in a crisis or wartime, nor are they carried out solely by military means, writes Kristjan Pärt.
The three saboteurs who set out to torch defense industry company Milrem Robotics on the night of August 15 were already sitting in Latvian police detention cells as suspects just a couple of days later. How was it possible to catch them so quickly? Perhaps cadets at the Estonian Academy of Security Sciences will hear the answer in a surveillance course — but even then, only 10 or more years from now.
The investigation is ongoing. We will determine whether the sabotage against Estonia was carried out in the interests of a state or organization and, if so, which one. But at this point, one's thoughts inevitably turn to Hando Runnel's poem "Jälle" ("Again"):
"Again the winds are howling, again the tempests roar.
Again from the east come herds of elk and bears."
Estonia's strength lies in its open society, democratic system of government and rule of law. Those strengths, however, can also present a window of opportunity to those who see our way of life as a thorn in their side.
Because of Estonia's geopolitical location, our internal security — and the country's overall security situation — is most strongly affected by external factors and developments, whether political, socioeconomic or technological, as well as by external threats, hostile foreign states and non-state organizations operating across borders.
Among hostile foreign states, Russia is the principal threat to European security, along with, indirectly, the regimes that support it. Other threats include violent extremist and terrorist groups, as well as international criminal organizations and networks. Each uses covert, nonmilitary methods to achieve its objectives, seeking to exploit the vulnerabilities of open societies and democratic ways of life — or the limited capabilities of security and law enforcement agencies.
The security of the state and society is threatened both by direct hostile activity and by harmful effects or external dependencies that materialize as a result of our own vulnerabilities.
If a hostile foreign state can gather intelligence on our territory without risk, influence our society or specific target groups and prepare positions that can be used to provoke a crisis or support a military operation, the conditions have been created for further escalation.
When strategic vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the damaging effects on security can also emerge gradually and insidiously.
Depending on the specific risks and the area affected, the consequences may include damage to the state's internal sovereignty or to Estonia's status as a nation-state, the fragmentation of society, the spread of radicalization and violent extremism, growing anti-state attitudes among certain groups in society or deepening economic or energy dependence on high-risk countries. These are all threats that military defense capabilities can neither mitigate nor repel.
Russia carries out its nonmilitary hostile activities even before a crisis becomes perceptible or aggression becomes visible — in other words, during what we understand as peacetime. Damaging and weakening other countries and societies through nonmilitary and hybrid methods is part of Russia's foreign policy doctrine, with its aggressive intelligence and security services playing an integral role.
Russia's primary objective is not to seize territory, but to create a situation in which another country's ability to make decisions and resist has already been weakened before a crisis begins or in which that country has surrendered a significant part of its self-determination. A strong defense force alone is not enough to counter such a strategy. The state must also be capable of mitigating risks and detecting and preventing threatening activities at an early stage.
In short, ensuring national security requires both strategic risk mitigation and sufficient operational capabilities. The first of these involves reducing vulnerabilities in society and its institutions. This requires consistent policy measures with a broad, society-wide and nationwide impact that must also mitigate so-called creeping threats to our security and sovereignty.
A strategy for reducing vulnerabilities means assessing risks, developing policy and engaging society in ways that increase resilience to attacks of any kind, harmful influences on society and external dependencies.
Resilient societies are characterized by shared fundamental values, trust within the country, citizens' voluntary contributions and the ability to cope with and recover from different crises.
Examples of decisions aimed at reducing Estonia's vulnerabilities include the transition to Estonian-language education, visa restrictions and restrictions on real estate purchases by citizens of aggressor states, as well as the introduction of up-to-date continuity and security requirements for the country's vital services and digital service providers.
In the long term, many measures aimed at reducing the country's vulnerabilities directly support internal security and the principle of domestic peace enshrined in our Constitution.
The second prerequisite for maintaining security is the ability to detect and prevent hostile activity at any time, in both military and nonmilitary domains. This is where the strategic role of internal security begins: protecting the continued existence and functioning of the state.
The task of internal security agencies is to ensure that hostile states, their intelligence and security services or extremist groups cannot operate in Estonia in ways that threaten our constitutional order or the security of society as a whole. The primary responsibility for this rests with the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).
Interior Ministry Secretary General Tarmo Miilits recently wrote about freedom, which resonates with those who can hear it. He rightly emphasized that the internal security services, which work around the clock to counter threats that have already reached Estonia, are the country's final line of defense for safety and security before the Defense Forces have to leave their training grounds and actually go into battle.
Counterintelligence, border security and migration monitoring and the prevention and disruption of hostile influence operations, terrorism and sabotage are proactive measures for ensuring national security. Their purpose is to respond effectively to offenses that have already been committed but, even more importantly, to detect and counter activities threatening Estonia's security before they develop into a broader crisis. Maintaining these capabilities, however, requires up-to-date legal powers, technological capabilities and sufficient resources.
These two main lines of action — reducing vulnerabilities and maintaining readiness to prevent or counter various attacks — complement one another and create an environment in which acting against Estonia becomes difficult, costly and ineffective for those who threaten us.
The Milrem Robotics sabotage case is a good illustration of why maintaining internal security requires a physical presence and the ability to respond at the scene, but also, of course, the capacity to collect, process and lawfully use information necessary for security purposes.
In today's digital societies, detecting and proving many such crimes increasingly depends on technological capabilities and the use of digital footprints. In its first internal security advisory submitted to the interior minister, the ISS described this as striking a balance between preventing threats and ensuring access to data.
"Security and law enforcement agencies must have effective tools to protect security in today's digital society and to detect and prove crimes that have been committed using digital evidence," the ISS wrote in its advisory. Of course, that means access to data, but it also means ensuring that the use of data and oversight are proportionate.
A legal framework that reflects the threats we face and enables action is a critical part of the capacity to ensure internal security. If the state can identify threats in time and respond to them, it can preserve public safety while also safeguarding people's freedoms and the functioning of the democratic system. A democratic state becomes stronger when it is able to prevent threats lawfully and proportionately.
Believe it or not, keeping the capabilities of Estonia's internal security agencies up to date is not a narrow institutional interest of the interior ministry, the ISS or the PPA, just as developing national defense is not a narrow institutional interest of the Ministry of Defense or the Defense Forces. All of this is a strategic investment in the continued existence of the Estonian state and in our sovereignty.
Like military national defense, the development of internal security capabilities requires stable and predictable funding. This makes it possible to pursue developments that meet contemporary requirements and reflect the current threat landscape, recruit highly capable people, provide continuous staff training, invest in forward-looking technologies and much more.
Military national defense and internal security are not competitors, but partners that complement one another. One prepares the country for a military crisis; the other helps do everything possible to prevent hostile activity within the country from escalating into a crisis. A strong defense force without robust internal security leaves an adversary free to act against us in areas where weapons are not used. Likewise, strengthening internal security alone is not enough without credible military deterrence and defense capabilities. Estonia needs both.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

AmCham Shanghai report shows sharp rebound in business confidence among member companies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:28:45 CST
16:28:45 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China Business Report, released on Thursday by the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai (AmCham Shanghai), revealed a significant rebound in business confidence among its surveyed member companies operating in China.
Business confidence bounced back markedly, as 58 percent of respondents expressed optimism about China's five-year business outlook, up 17 percentage points year on year, the report said.
Profitability rebounded to its highest level since 2019, with 78 percent of respondents profitable in 2025, an increase of 7 percentage points from the 2024 level, according to the report.
As business confidence rebounded and more companies reported profits, investment confidence in China also strengthened, resulting in 28 percent of respondents increasing investment in China last year, the highest level in four years.
Improved market sentiment is also reflected in a positive assessment of China's business environment. Fifty-five percent of surveyed companies said the business environment in China is transparent, up 7 percentage points year on year.
"Members have clearly noticed government efforts to improve the regulatory environment, and this year those gains are reinforced by steadier U.S.-China relations," said Jeffrey Lehman, chair of AmCham Shanghai. "We urge both countries to build on the momentum of recent engagement and lock in a stable, transparent framework that is conducive to cross-border trade and investment."
Eric Zheng, president of AmCham Shanghai, emphasized the great importance of the Chinese market, mainly from two dimensions.
China remains one of the most efficient manufacturing bases in the world and continues to be a highly strategic market for members' products and services, Zheng said. "That underpins the positive sentiment," he added.
Chinese operations also contributed to the global and domestic business performance of U.S. companies, the survey showed.
Among members with U.S. operations, three-quarters confirmed that their China presence benefits their U.S. operations in some way, with one-third emphasizing that their China presence enhances the global competitiveness of their U.S. operations.
A notable strategic shift is also emerging, with more surveyed companies adopting a global-oriented strategy. The "in China for the world" strategy has become the top business priority for 29 percent of surveyed companies in 2026, surpassing the "in China for China" model chosen by 24 percent.
More respondents are also betting on China-based innovation, the report said. Half of surveyed members with China-based research and development (R&D) facilities plan to increase R&D spending this year, up sharply from one-third in 2025.
The report is based on AmCham Shanghai's 2026 China Business Survey of 262 member companies.
In a vote of confidence in the Chinese market, General Motors (GM) in August announced a 20-year extension of its joint venture partnership with Chinese automaker SAIC Motor, with it now running to 2047.
"We will continue to strengthen our performance here in China by developing products and technologies in China, for China, and bringing them to market faster," said John Roth, GM senior vice president & president of GM China. The joint venture plans to launch at least 30 new energy vehicle models by 2030.
"We see meaningful opportunities to grow beyond China. SAIC-GM has strong local capabilities across engineering, manufacturing and quality, and we can apply those strengths in select international markets, including the Middle East, Africa, South America, Mexico and Asia-Pacific," Roth said.
"Foreign companies continue to value the Chinese market for its scale and dynamism and, increasingly, as a base for serving the world," noted Jeff Yuan, head of tax at PwC China, adding that China remains a critical part of their global strategy for innovation, production and sourcing. ■

We shouldn't fear AI if we keep it 'under control, open and public', expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:28:41 UTC
16:28:41 KST

Andrea Renda, Director of Research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, believes the main issue is that “we don't know enough” about what is actually happening inside AI development companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
Renda insists it is “not the first time” humans have built something that could kill us all, after a former Anthropic researcher said there is more than a 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.
However, Renda points out that there are “many ways we can all be killed by stupid technology” as well.
Renda calls for “opening up and auditing much more” of what is going on inside AI companies, as well as greater investment in public research. He also insists that it is a “very stupid way of programming AI to give it powers we cannot control”.

Study finds earliest evidence of habitual drug use
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:28:34 CST
16:28:34 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered what may be the earliest evidence of habitual drug use, dating "betel nut" use among early human foragers to as early as 25,000 years ago, tens of thousands of years before agriculture.
A team led by Australia's Griffith University archaeologists found evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier in time than previously supposed, according to a university statement released Thursday.
The team, working with Indonesian archaeologists, combined biochemical and archaeological evidence to trace the prehistoric roots of betel nut, one of the world's most popular addictive stimulants and an ancient drug used throughout much of the Asia-Pacific region.
The study, published in Science Advances, reports the discovery of extremely rare skeletal remains of two early human foragers from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, one dating to 25,000-16,000 years ago, the other to 7,600-6,300 years ago.
Both hunter-gatherers display highly unusual deep, rounded tooth grooves, a marker the researchers established was caused by a previously unknown drug-use behavior: habitual sucking of whole betel nuts, researchers said.
Biochemical analyses also detected arecoline in the foragers' dental tissues, providing strong evidence for betel nut ingestion, they said, adding that experiments showed that sucking intact betel nuts can release enough arecoline to have a physiological effect and alter brain function.
Betel nut use was previously thought to have emerged around the Neolithic or Bronze Age, about 3,500 years ago.
The findings suggest habitual psychoactive substance use existed among hunter-gatherers tens of thousands of years before farming, and betel nut-sucking may represent the earliest evidence of drug use yet recorded. ■

Prices of flats on Flemish coast shoot up by 6.5 per cent as demand too picks up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:28:28 UTC
16:28:28 KST

Sales of flats on the Flemish coast increased in the first half of this year, following a decline in the same period last year. Prices also shot up by 6.5 per cent. The median price rose to 272,000 euros; for a flat on the seafront, it stands at 335,000 euros according to new figures from Belgian notaries.
Prices of flats on Flemish coast shoot up by 6.5 per cent as demand too picks up
Sales of houses and flats on the coast rose by 8 per cent in the first half of the year, whilst the property market in the rest of Flanders contracted slightly (-0.8 per cent). Following a ‘property tsunami’ during the Covid years of 2020 and 2021, the coastal property market had also struggled in recent years.
“Since last year, we have seen an increase in transactions once again and it is clear that the downturn has been overcome,” says Bart van Opstal, spokesperson for the notaries’ federation. This trend continued into the first half of this year. “We are now returning to a more normal level of property activity on the coast.”
Flats have also become more expensive
Flats on the coast have also become more expensive. The median price for a flat on the coast was 272,000 euros in the first half of this year. That is 6.7 per cent more than a year ago.
For flats on the seafront, there was a 4.7 per cent rise to 335,000 euros. The price of seafront apartments ranged from 260,000 euros in the resort of De Panne to 1.5 million euros in jet-set Knokke. The vast majority of buyers of a seafront apartment (85 per cent) are Flemish. Just over half are purchased by people aged 50 and over.
“Our coast is once again proving particularly popular with property buyers,” says van Opstal. “The region has plenty of advantages: it is close by, easily accessible and less exposed to extreme heat than destinations further afield.”

At least five people were killed and 86 remain missing after a fire erupted aboard a ferry near a popular tourist destination in the Philippine province of Palawan, the coast guard said Thursday.
A passenger ferry caught on fire overnight on Thursday off the western Philippines, killing at least five and leaving dozens of people missing.
The blaze broke out on the M/V June Aster Wednesday evening about 2.2 km offshore, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
The ferry had sailed from the capital Manila and was near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the blaze broke out on Wednesday night.
More than 40 people have been rescued, Coast Guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said, despite challenging weather conditions. Five casualties had been brought ashore.
"Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 86 people who are unaccounted for," Cayabyab told a local radio station on Thursday.
She said 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. No information was available about any foreigners on board.
"We are continuing search and rescue operations," she said, with a coast guard ship and high-speed response boats joined by a military vessel and other government boats, private volunteers and fishermen.
Passengers were helped into smaller boats taking them to shallow water, and smoke still wafted over the charred vessel by midday on Thursday.
The Philippine Coast Guard later told reporters that another person had been rescued, but their identity had yet to be confirmed.
"Just to make it clear, this is live data and may change as our search and rescue operations are ongoing," Cayabyab said in the radio interview.
"However, we have not yet been able to obtain information from the rescued individuals because we have not been able to speak with them," she said, adding that attempts to put out the blaze were ongoing.
There were no immediate reports of foreigners on board.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.
The M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 sank along nearly the same route where 31 people died in 2023 after a fire broke out aboard the Lady Mary Joy 3 ferry.

New B-21 hangar heads to Missouri’s Whiteman Air Force Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:26:50 UTC
16:26:50 KST

- The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a B-21 radio frequency hangar at Whiteman Air Force Base.
- Whiteman, which currently hosts the Air Force's entire B-2 fleet, is set to become the B-21 program's second main operating base after Ellsworth.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a new radio frequency and measurements hangar for the B-21 Raider stealth bomber at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri.
The facility will include space for one B-21 aircraft, along with supporting workshops, material storage, and administrative offices. Three companies bid on the project, which the Corps solicited online. Work is expected to be finished by September 25, 2029. The Army Corps’ Kansas City district is managing the contract, funded through fiscal 2026 military construction dollars.
The B-21 is the aircraft the Air Force is counting on to anchor its bomber fleet for decades to come. Built by Northrop Grumman as a nuclear-capable stealth bomber, it first flew in November 2023 and remains in low-rate initial production, with the Air Force and Northrop Grumman announcing an agreement in February 2026 to expand production capacity and speed up deliveries. The Air Force has said the B-21 is designed to penetrate the kind of heavily defended airspace that older bombers can no longer survive in, and the service confirmed in July 2026 that the aircraft will fly with a two-person crew. The program has continued hitting test milestones through 2026, including an aerial refueling demonstration with a KC-135 tanker in April.
Whiteman is set to become the B-21’s second main operating base, after the Air Force picked the installation over Dyess Air Force Base in Texas. Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota became the program’s first main operating base in 2021 and currently serves as the B-21’s formal training site; Air Force leadership visited Ellsworth in July 2026 to mark what the service called a historic milestone in that base’s B-21 facilities work. Whiteman already hosts the Air Force’s entire fleet of B-2 Spirit stealth bombers, 19 aircraft in total, two of which have been lost in crashes over the years.
The B-21 is being built to gradually replace both the B-2 and the older B-1 Lancer, which the Air Force expects to begin retiring around 2031 and 2032 as it moves toward a two-bomber fleet alongside the B-52.
A radio frequency and measurements hangar is used to test an aircraft’s radar signature and electronic systems in a controlled environment, work that matters for a stealth bomber designed to evade enemy radar. Conti Federal has built several other B-21 support facilities at Ellsworth, including a $31.7 million fuel cell maintenance hangar awarded in October 2024, part of what the company has described as a broader, multi-year construction effort tied to the bomber’s rollout.

U.S. Army awards NG $4.8B for helicopter missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:16:08 UTC
16:16:08 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Northrop Grumman a contract worth up to $4.84 billion for full-rate production of its CIRCM laser-based helicopter missile defense system.
- CIRCM protects aircraft including the AH-64 Apache and UH-60 Black Hawk from heat-seeking missiles that have downed numerous helicopters in Ukraine since 2022.
Helicopters have carried flares to dodge heat-seeking missiles since the late 1960s. The U.S. Army just committed nearly $4.84 billion to replace that decades-old defense with a laser that jams the missile itself.
The Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, awarded Northrop Grumman the firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract on September 8 for full-rate production of the Common Infrared Countermeasures system, known as CIRCM. Only Northrop Grumman bid on the work. The contract runs through September 30, 2035, though the Pentagon’s notice did not specify how many units it covers or how funding breaks down year to year.
CIRCM mounts on helicopters and some small fixed-wing aircraft to counter MANPADS, the shoulder-fired, heat-seeking missiles that have proven lethal against low-flying aircraft in recent conflicts. In Ukraine, MANPADS supplied by the U.S., UK and Poland have downed numerous Russian helicopters since 2022, underscoring just how vulnerable rotary-wing aircraft remain to this class of weapon.
Instead of dumping flares and hoping a missile’s seeker gets confused, CIRCM detects an incoming missile using warning sensors already on the aircraft, then fires a laser directly at the missile’s infrared seeker, distorting its view of the target and steering it off course. The company says the whole sequence takes only a few seconds. At the core of the system is a quantum cascade laser, a solid-state laser technology the Army selected in part because it can jam multiple incoming missiles at once and continues working in poor weather, unlike earlier infrared jammers that struggled in cloud cover or rain.
The Army launched the program to meet a Tri-Service requirement, meaning the Army, Navy and Air Force all agreed on a common specification so the same system could go on multiple services’ aircraft rather than each branch developing its own jammer. Northrop Grumman won the engineering and manufacturing development contract in 2015, beating out BAE Systems after both companies had spent several years in an earlier technology-maturation phase. The Army took delivery of its first CIRCM systems in 2016, and the system replaced the older Advanced Threat Infrared Countermeasures suite that had been in service since the 1990s.
CIRCM has since gone on the Army’s AH-64 Apache, CH-47 Chinook and UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters. Northrop Grumman has said the system reached its 500th delivered shipset within two years of entering full-rate production.
As of this year, the company says nearly 700 CIRCM systems have been installed on rotary-wing aircraft worldwide, logging more than 70,000 operational flight hours. In March 2026, Northrop Grumman reached a separate agreement to supply CIRCM for Germany’s new CH-47 Chinook fleet, extending the system to at least one allied air force beyond the United States.
The system’s open architecture is designed to let the Army swap in new hardware or software as missile threats evolve, without redesigning the aircraft’s survivability suite from scratch.

'Enemy of the people': Writer Kati Marton on Budapest return after Orbán's regime rejection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:16:07 UTC
16:16:07 KST

The American-Hungarian writer, a Peabody Award winner, has avoided Budapest for years but she's now returned to because her novel about her parents, "Enemies of the People", has been adapted for the stage.
A monodrama based on the novel about the family of Kati Marton, a US journalist and author of Hungarian origin, has recently premiered at the Central European University's Budapest building.
Marton's book "Enemies of the People: My Family's Journey to America", has been adapted for the stage with Erika Marozsán in the lead role.
The story follows the fate of Marton's parents. Both were journalists, reporting for American news agencies from communist Hungary. While researching her parents background, it emerged that their nanny had in fact been an informant, filing reports on the family.
When her parents were imprisoned, she and her sister were first taken to their grandparents. However, the grandparents were given passports to Australia so they could emigrate to relatives there. The state took away their flat in Buda, as it did with so many others.
According to Marton, this too formed part of the psychological pressure the state devised against people it had branded "enemies". Prison officials told her parents that the two small children had been left without adult supervision; it was with this "cruel choreography" that people were broken, she recalled.
Later, Kati and her sister Juli were placed with temporary foster parents somewhere in the outskirts of Budapest. She remembers how frightened people were; they did not dare speak even about those who had disappeared, including her own parents. Former friends of the family did not come to visit the two little girls.
Learning the truth
The drama of her parents' lives also includes the fact that her Jewish grandparents were murdered in Auschwitz, something that was never discussed at home. She herself was brought up as a Catholic and only decades later learned the truth about her family's origins.
"The communists branded my parents enemies of the people because they were well-off. When I began to reconstruct my family's story, I discovered, while reading through the thousands of pages of surveillance reports, that they probably had the thickest file in the archive. I really am talking about several thousand pages," said Marton. "Because I can read Hungarian, I was able to use this material for my book, 'Enemies of the People', and it is the play based on that book that has brought me to Budapest. On every single page my parents are referred to as enemies of the people. For a time I too was given that label by the Orbán regime."
The Budapest premiere was all the more special because Kati Marton had stayed away from Hungary for years after the Orbán regime branded her "an enemy of the people", just as her parents had been branded by the communist regime.
The play based on the novel by Peabody Award-winning journalist and bestselling author was directed by János Mohácsi and has also been staged in the United States.
Kati Marton is also known for bestsellers such as "The Great Escape - Nine Jews Who Fled Hitler and Changed the World" and "Merkel", about the former German chancellor Angela Merkel (original title: "The Chancellor - The Remarkable Odyssey of Angela Merkel").

Spanish archaeologists find 4,400-year-old tomb in Egypt with original colours intact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:15:56 UTC
16:15:56 KST

A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological team has found in Saqqara an outstanding late Fifth Dynasty tomb with two chapels and colourful reliefs of farming and offering processions.
A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological mission, led by Spanish Egyptologist Josep Cervelló, has uncovered a "striking and beautiful" tomb dating from the late Fifth Dynasty of Egypt's Old Kingdom (2494-2345 BC) in the Saqqara necropolis, southwest of Cairo.
The find was made during this summer's excavations, led by the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities. It is an exceptional mastaba with two funerary chapels, commissioned by Yunmen, a senior official under Pharaoh Djedkare Isesi, who also ordered that his father, Iti, a lower-ranking official, be buried there.
Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities confirmed that the tomb dates from the end of the Fifth Dynasty, during the reign of Djedkare Isesi, and is located in the Mariette necropolis, north of Saqqara. According to the statement, it contains "two funerary chapels belonging to two high-ranking officials, Younmin and his father, Ity".
According to the UAB, the tomb has made it possible to identify figures of great historical, social and cultural interest. For the archaeological team, the discovery has also been a surprise because of the richness and beauty of the monument.
Among the most notable features are a high-quality architrave and funerary texts adapted to the figure and offices of their owner. The Egyptian ministry also highlights the exceptional state of preservation of the scenes and reliefs, which show "agricultural activities and processions with offerings", and notes that many of them "have retained their original colours".
The decoration also includes depictions of donkeys and other animals. According to the Egyptian authorities, the discovery "provides new and valuable data on the architecture, art and administrative life of ancient Egypt at the end of the Fifth Dynasty".
The excavation reveals daily life in the Saqqara necropolis
As well as its historical and scientific value, the mastaba stands out for its beauty. Archaeologists believe that the double tomb may reflect the social ascent of Yunmen, the son of a provincial official who rose to a senior position in the central administration and wanted to share his funerary destiny with his father.
The area has been known since the excavations carried out by Auguste Mariette in the 19th century, but it had never been studied and documented in depth. The research aimed to reconstruct the topography of Saqqara and to understand the necropolis as a living space, where ancient Egyptians brought offerings and worked continuously on the construction of funerary monuments.
The aim is to understand how the necropolis was organised and operated, from its streets and squares to the movement of people and the cult rituals. The analysis of maps and the reconstruction of the layout led the team to a previously unknown mastaba and to indications of two more nearby, which they hope to excavate in future seasons.

Mainland Chinese shoppers lose trusted Hong Kong veggie tag as customs revamp hits shelves
Change sparks concern among consumers, with the Hong Kong label having long served as a selling point for high quality
The removal stems from new rules by the General Administration of Customs. From September 1, registration will no longer be required for growing farms, and only food-processing firms need to register.
This means vegetables grown on the same farms that supply Hong Kong can no longer carry the Hong Kong-bound label when sold in mainland supermarkets.
“Before, I just looked for the Hong Kong-bound label,” said a female consumer in a post this week on Chinese social media platform RedNote. “Now I must check the details myself, and that’s the change.”
Hong Kong-bound labelled lettuce was once a bestseller at Walmart-owned Sam’s Club on the mainland, drawing middle-class shoppers who trusted its quality.
Given its high popularity, the retailer added a tag on the product to explain the new customs rule. The 600-gram pack, still priced at 12.90 yuan (US$1.90), uses the same packaging and supplier from China’s northwestern Ningxia Hui autonomous region, distinguished only by the new “Dali lettuce” label.

Education minister says teacher pay rise unaffordable in current budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Education minister says teacher pay rise unaffordable in current budget
The Education Ministry told unions it has no room in the state budget for a teacher pay raise, saying any increase would require cuts elsewhere. The Education Workers' Union warned that teachers are prepared to stage work stoppages.
In the current economic situation it is practically impossible to add any increases to the state budget, because revenue from economic growth only covers previously indexed expenses, such as pensions and defense spending, said Minister of Education Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200).
This means that finding additional money for the education sector is extremely difficult. "We can plan a salary increase for teachers only if we cut somewhere. We would have to move money from somewhere else, take it away from someone, so that we could make a salary increase for teachers," Kallas said.
The minister does not consider the union's demand to raise next year's minimum salary to the Estonian average — €2,312 — to be realistic.
"I certainly don't consider it realistic that the minimum salary for teachers is the Estonian average salary, because most people in Estonia do not earn the average salary. In an ideal world, every education minister would say that a teacher actually deserves such a salary. Absolutely, this work brings very strong returns to society in the future. But simply, money is a finite quantity, and in reality we just do not have it in the state budget today," the minister noted.
In addition to salary issues, Kallas says the growing workload of teachers also needs to be addressed, a burden amplified by the increasing number of children with special needs.
Kallas pointed to fresh PISA results, which show that Estonia has the lowest student‑teacher ratio in Europe and a very large number of small high schools that consume a significant share of education funding. Due to demographic changes, the number of children entering school will begin to fall by 3,000 starting in 2028, reducing the per‑capita funding that municipalities use to pay teachers' salaries.
Teachers want long‑term security
Reemo Voltri, representative of the Education Workers' Union emphasized that the difficult state budget situation must not lead to compromises in education quality. According to him, teachers' minimum expectation is a €2,300 minimum salary or fulfillment of the pre‑election promise to keep teachers' calculated average salary at 120 percent of the national average.
"If teachers' salaries continue to fall compared to the national average — which they have done under this government — then this is a very ominous message for current teachers and future teachers," Voltri warned.
"This shows that we do not value the teaching profession, and as a result there is a high likelihood that the quality of our education will begin to decline, as highlighted in the OECD PISA analysis," he added.
Teachers are ready for compromises and would accept a smaller increase than requested, provided that the state budget strategy offers long‑term certainty for fulfilling promises in the coming years, Voltri said. However, they are not willing to accept a relative decline in salary.
"What teachers definitely will not accept is being told that salaries will not rise at all — meaning we immediately fall five or six percentage points behind average wage growth. That cannot be accepted," he added.
He recalled that during the previous strike, a €71 increase was achieved even in a situation where a raise was considered impossible, and added that on 14 September there will be a demonstration by education workers in front of the Riigikogu. If necessary, Voltri does not rule out new work stoppages.
Municipalities face difficult choices
Randar Lohu, head of the financial service of Saku municipality in Harju County, noted that a strong increase in the national minimum salary for teachers puts local governments in a difficult position when paying other employees. According to Lohu, teachers in Saku already earn €2,400–€2,500 gross, which is higher than the Estonian average, but constant national pressure requires additional resources.
"Of course there is hobby education, other teachers, and all sorts of other municipal institutions, and we may not be able to raise the salaries of those employees to the same extent if schoolteachers' salaries rise by ten‑plus percent," Lohu explained.
"Then all the other people are left without a salary increase, but we have about 650 people to whom we pay salaries every month," Lohu said.
According to Lohu, municipalities are currently waiting for more precise numbers from the state budget negotiations, which should become clear later this month.
Education workers, state representatives, and municipal specialists will meet again in two weeks to discuss the minimum salary for teachers.
--
