Triangle of confusion: the government, the President's Office and parliament enter a new political season
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:00 EEST
16:00:00 KST

Triangle of confusion: the government, the President's Office and parliament enter a new political season
On 1 September Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, set another record by opening its 16th session since it was convened in July 2019.
The Rada's agenda was very revealing, and the results of the votes in the first sitting days of autumn were even more so. The MPs began their work by considering bills that have been listed as benchmarks in various international support programmes.
The fact that parliament started off with this particular set of bills points to Ukraine's main problem: its huge budget deficit.
Over the past few weeks, the new Cabinet of Ministers has been actively lobbying for these bills, holding endless meetings and consultations with MPs, including some from the president's own Servant of the People faction.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy got involved as well. A few weeks earlier, at a meeting of the National Security and Defence Council (NSDC) where one of the main items on the agenda was funding for the armed forces, the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, informed Zelenskyy of the real state of the budget deficit. NSDC members say the president was stunned – so much so that while the meeting was still going on, he telephoned the MPs responsible for the votes on the EU- and IMF-related legislation and started shouting and reprimanding them.
Yet even with that pressure from the very top, it still proved impossible to drum up more than 190 votes for the much-delayed bills.
This was a vivid illustration of the state of affairs within the authorities. The president's team is brilliant at putting on a show of unity and optimism at set-piece events such as prayer breakfasts with officials, celebrities and foreign guests, and National Legend ceremonies honouring soldiers, artists and Ukraine's international supporters. But it is going into the new political season with a President's Office and a president knocked off balance, a fragmented Rada, and a Cabinet still finding its feet.
In other words, all three of the centres that usually form Ukraine's triangle of power are entering the new season with serious problems of their own – or, figuratively speaking, their own dead ends.
As everyone knows, there are no dead ends in Euclidean geometry. But the formula of Ukrainian politics has long been reduced to calculating the sum of all the dead ends in which the authorities find themselves – and towards which they are leading the country.
The President and Office of suspicions
The topmost corner of Ukraine's triangle of power – and the one that has long been trying to widen its own angle of influence as far as possible – is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his Office. There is some irony here: in geometry, a very large angle is called obtuse.
On 1 September, Zelenskyy made his anger plain after MPs failed to pass several bills needed to unlock international funding.
"MPs also bear some of the responsibility to the people of Ukraine: around US$15 billion depends on their share of the work which has to be done… The Verkhovna Rada has failed to pass three bills that could have brought Ukraine more than US$4 billion. Another two bills – which have also failed – were part of the IMF programme. This is not money for the government or the opposition," the president thundered at MPs.
At first glance the situation might seem odd. After all, it's the president's own single-party majority that is officially responsible for everything in the Rada. People close to Zelenskyy, such as Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People faction, have spent years convincing everyone of their virtuoso ability to play parliament like a piano.
But actually Zelenskyy's anger is not so much odd as symptomatic. The president now resembles a cart driver who's got stuck in the mud and is flogging his horse in the hope that a little more brutality will force a few final surges of energy out of it. The problem is that he drove the cart into the mire himself.
The fact is that the foreign policy and military situation around Ukraine is developing in a way that could hardly be further from what the president expected just a few months ago.
Since the summer, Zelenskyy himself has done everything he could to raise public expectations – and with them the expectations of the political class – to heights unseen since 2023 and the first counteroffensive.
The phrase "elections in November", which Zelenskyy first dropped casually into a conversation with his faction before the summer strikes on Crimea and then discussed seriously with his inner circle at a state residence near Kyiv, began to look entirely realistic in the upbeat media atmosphere whipped up by the President's Office.
Those expectations, among both the public and the political establishment, were further fuelled by much-trumpeted promises of "40 days to force Russia into peace" and the like.
But Ukraine is entering autumn in a very different military reality.
Across much of the country, back-to-school ceremonies on 1 September took place either in shelters or entirely remotely, with children joining online from different homes and cities.
Kyiv, Odesa, Kharkiv and other cities are enduring almost constant air-raid warnings and regular ballistic missile attacks which Ukraine simply does not have the resources to protect them from.
People can see the contrast between promises to "end the war by November" and rehearsals for the apocalypse in September, and between the government's regime of austerity for the country and the brazen attempt to launder UAH 150 million (about US$3.3 million) to get yet another government official released from pre-trial detention.
Previously, Zelenskyy has always managed to channel public discontent elsewhere. But after July's "cardboard Maidan" protests and yet another anti-corruption case – Forrest Gump – the accumulated negativity began to fall squarely on the president himself.
The protests in July and August and the controversy over the dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister have been near-disastrous for Zelenskyy politically. Firstly, a highly promising competitor has appeared in a vacant political niche. Secondly, the president himself is no longer even one of Ukraine's three most trusted politicians.
In first-round presidential polling, respondents still name Zelenskyy as the favourite. But no one can really calculate how many of them genuinely support the incumbent, and how many are naming him out of caution – "just in case, God forbid".
The modelling of second-round voting, where Zelenskyy clearly loses to Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Kyrylo Budanov and Mykhailo Fedorov, suggests there are quite a few people in the latter camp. If this trend continues, we could reach the point where even Petro Poroshenko could allow himself to dream of at least a faint chance of revenge for 2019.
And all these setbacks have a single root cause – Zelenskyy has finally lost the moral high ground he used to have over the former embezzlers and oligarchs. His party campaigned under the slogan "Let's get them together", but were Zelenskyy to resurrect that slogan now, he and most of his team would probably find themselves among the "THEM".
The situation in the President's Office is the clearest illustration of this point. Soon the only officials there untouched by criminal allegations may be the foreign policy people.
The case involving Iryna Mudra, deputy head of the President's Office, at the end of August was particularly telling. According to the version of events that investigators set out in the case materials, UAH 150 million (US$3.4 million) was laundered so that bail could be posted for former energy and justice minister Herman Halushchenko.
Kyrylo Budanov's name hasn't come up so far, and no procedural actions have been taken against the head of the President's Office.
But people who know how such decisions are made inside the Office point to Mudra's particularly close relationship with Budanov. It was he who persuaded her to stay at Bankova instead of taking up the position of justice minister in the government.
That is why many people within the system find it hard to imagine that Mudra could have got involved in such a sensitive matter independently, without at least tacit approval from the leader.
But it seems equally implausible that getting the long-forgotten Halushchenko out of pre-trial detention could have been an initiative of Budanov's.
According to media reports, Halushchenko had begun to show a willingness to cooperate with the anti-corruption agencies, and therefore potentially to reveal who the Energoatom money was actually being collected for, who the high-end Dynasty houses were being built for, and who "Vova" is on the tapes.
But Budanov has not been implicated in the schemes surrounding Energoatom and did not own a Dynasty property. Moreover, from a purely political perspective, it may even have benefited him if Halushchenko had named his patrons, as that could potentially clear the way for Budanov in future elections.
And so, in this and many other criminal allegations, one's gaze is inevitably directed over Budanov's head and comes to rest on a single point: the office on the fourth floor – the presidential floor.
And however hard Zelenskyy tries to persuade journalists off the record that he only finds out about corruption in the President's Office when he reads the news, even as accomplished an actor as he is can't really convince us that he believes that.
Every story like the one about Mudra makes the political vertical harder to control. People within the system are gradually realising that it's better not to carry out an illegal order and lose their job than to carry it out and lose their freedom.
Zelenskyy can bang his fist on the table at NSDC meetings, make angry calls to MPs and ministers and rant in his evening addresses all he likes.
But this is looking less and less like a demonstration of strength and an ability to investigate, punish or force someone to make the required decision, and more like the exact opposite of that.
Gradually, the entire toolkit that Zelenskyy still uses to have his decisions put into practice and legitimise his own will is shifting from the realm of political compromise into plain old coercion and control.
This is the origin of Bankova's obsession with maintaining influence over the Security Service of Ukraine, the State Bureau of Investigation and the Prosecutor General's Office.
When political tools become scarce, the value of coercive tools automatically goes up.
Government scare tactics
The second corner of the classic triangle of power is the Cabinet of Ministers.
At the moment it's still in the process of finding its real place within the new configuration.
Clearly, Zelenskyy still wants to be able to influence the government and shape its agenda unchallenged.
But the Cabinet's leadership understood right from the start that the president's wishes alone – as was the case under former prime minister Oleksii Honcharuk or the early days of Denys Shmyhal – would not be enough for successful governance.
That is why the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, is making every effort to strengthen cooperation with MPs, encourage ministers to maintain constant communication with parliament, take part in government question times, attend committee meetings and get involved in other routine parliamentary work.
Unlike Yuliia Svyrydenko, who had been part of the ruling team almost from the outset, Koretskyi is a complete newcomer to the system.
And his arrival has already resulted in certain changes in the way the upper echelons of power operate.
First and foremost, these changes are noticeable even on a purely human level.
"Koretskyi is probably the most unemotional prime minister in all of Zelenskyy's presidency. Even Shmyhal sometimes looks like an excitable teenager next to him," one Servant of the People MP who frequently works with the PM says with a smile.
According to MPs, Koretskyi is extremely polite and constructive with everyone. But at the same time, he is equally cold and distant. Whether because he can't or won't, he does not try to build warm personal relationships.
He is a person who sets tasks and sees that they are carried out, and who apparently still does not fully understand why MPs can't be handled in that way.
According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in the Servant of the People party, after taking charge of the country in mid-July, the prime minister immediately set about figuring out exactly what he would have to manage, what resources were at his disposal, and what needs he had to address.
"And it wasn't long before he was seriously shocked. What's more, Koretskyi didn't hide his shock and started laying out the truth to our MPs without pulling any punches. They're not used to that; the last time someone frightened them like that was Honcharuk at the start of the Covid-19 epidemic," one senior Servant of the People MP recalls of the events of August.
All through the last month of the summer, Koretskyi kept going to meetings at the President's Office and parliament, explaining things and presenting tables and charts. And those meetings left indelible impressions on a lot of MPs.
Ahead of a major NSDC meeting in mid-August, the prime minister prepared a highly revealing presentation for the president as well.
His slides vividly demonstrated the terrifying financial gap between the resources Ukraine currently has and the expenditure the state needs to cover by the end of the year: a shortfall measured in tens of billions of dollars.
Previously, the usually kind and smiling Yuliia Svyrydenko had tried not to stress people out too much and would explain complex financial problems as gently as possible. Koretskyi's presentation was a wake-up call for many in the government.
The new prime minister was banking on the idea that demonstrating the scale of the problem would convince parliament to take a constructive approach. In parallel with his "shock therapy", over the previous few weeks he had been persistently urging MPs to support bills furthering European integration and other legislation that would unlock international funding. The Verkhovna Rada put some of these bills to the vote as early as 1 September – and rejected almost all of them that same day.
As a result, Ukraine found itself facing the threat of losing a "quick" US$4-5 billion without any idea of how to make up the shortfall.
To the ministers and prime minister, the failure to pass the bills appears to be, if not outright sabotage, then at the very least acting against the interests of the government itself and the state. For Koretskyi, however, it could prove to be a very useful experience and his first hard lesson in an accelerated course in public administration.
The government can show MPs as many terrifying slides about holes in the budget as it likes, but it's parliament that ultimately votes on the legislation. And sometimes, whether you like it or not, you have to "listen to everyone" – especially when a crisis could be brewing, ready to hit this autumn.
The last grey eminence
The Verkhovna Rada is now operating with one eye on the new, and apparently the last, grey eminence in Volodymyr Zelenskyy's orbit.
Davyd Arakhamiia has become an indispensable figure in parliament, thanks to his ability to broker situational or relatively long-lasting coalitions there – especially after Andrii Yermak was pushed out of public politics after being named as a suspect by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), together with the associated protests and the negativity that had built up around him over the years.
Meanwhile, over the past month, Ukrainska Pravda has heard various iterations of the same story dozens of times in the corridors of parliament, government, the President's Office and law enforcement agencies: that Arakhamiia himself may soon be added to the anti-corruption bodies' list of suspects.
Arakhamiia himself is evidently relying on his ever-dependable negotiating abilities.
In particular, he is trying to maintain communication with people close to the anti-corruption agencies and secure the support of those who, though unlikely to be able to persuade the agencies to abandon procedural action against him, could at least convince them to delay it.
The argument is simple: the Verkhovna Rada must not be destabilised this autumn, when the situation in the country is already extraordinarily difficult.
It is also worth bearing in mind that Arakhamiia has a tacit agreement with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who plays a key role in the procedure for bringing MPs to criminal prosecution. [In late 2025, Kravchenko reportedly refused to sign treason charges against Arakhamiia and several other MPs, earning himself powerful allies in parliament in return – ed.]
But either way, the political class is already looking, with certain reservations, at the prospect of Arakhamiia continuing to remain the undisputed leader and the main driving force behind the parliamentary process.
Because if Arakhamiia were to drop out of the equation for some reason, the Verkhovna Rada could, at least in the short term, descend into serious disarray.
There is simply no one else who has the authority and the communication skills to simultaneously hold together the remnants of the former Opposition Platform – For Life party, various parliamentary groups, single-mandate MPs, and the fundamentally opposing factions within Servant of the People itself.
Theoretically, if Arakhamiia were to run into trouble, as things stand today, the only person who could try to help stabilise parliament would be the speaker, Ruslan Stefanchuk.
The speaker may not command much authority in the current parliamentary set-up, but at least he has no outright antagonists, and he is the only one capable of making surprise moves such as dropping into Poroshenko's party office.
How comfortable Stefanchuk – a hermit-like lawmaker who has always tried to distance himself from the political bargaining, behind-the-scenes deals and horse-trading that go on – would feel being at the very epicentre of these processes, and how capable he would be of handling it, is another question.
There is no answer to this question yet, nor will there be until Stefanchuk actually finds himself in that situation. If, of course, it comes to that.
***
Meanwhile, the Rada continues its low-level sabotage of European integration legislation and unpopular bills on VAT on parcels or taxes for sole traders, in the hope of carving out some degree of quasi-autonomy in its dealings with the President's Office, while also trying to keep the government in line.
But all the parliamentary groups that are rebelling against what they call "external governance", "the anti-corruption dictatorship", or some other phenomenon from the book of political fears and superstitions, will sooner or later hit the ceiling of what such resistance can achieve.
Because the fact is that what they call "external governance" became part of Ukraine's domestic political reality long ago.
More than half of the budget is financed by international partners and donors. Their ability to influence the procedures for overseeing how these frankly phenomenal amounts of financial aid is spent is simply a matter of exercising operational control over their investments.
Without this money, Ukraine will clearly be unable either to fight the war or to function properly as a state. The new prime minister is a good person to ask about this – he's figured it out exceptionally well.
Ukraine will have to honour its international commitments, however unpleasant that may be for conservatives from the Yuliia Tymoshenko Bloc or single-mandate Servant of the People MPs from eastern and southern regions. Not for the sake of the weakened President's Office with its unelectable candidate, the government terrified by the scale of the problems, or the "evil Brussels bureaucracy", but for Ukraine.
Because tomorrow the government will put up another slide showing a budget shortfall of tens of billions of dollars. And the question about the limits of "sovereign democracy" will turn into the eternal Ukrainian question: where do we get the money from?
Roman Romaniuk, Ukrainska Pravda

Parfümerie at the Biennale: Zurich’s underground club scene lives on in Venice

Parfümerie at the Biennale: Zurich’s underground club scene lives on in Venice
With a tribute to one of Zurich’s most important underground clubs, the ‘Parfümerie’, the performance duo Clarissa Herbst and Dominique Rust bring the spirit of a cultural movement back to life.
The underground club and music scene was in full swing at night in Zurich during the late 1980s. DJs, activists, female artists and musicians came together for music, performances and readings. Their illegal, ad hoc parties took place in disused factory spaces, shop premises or cellars. Among those present was Koyo Kouoh, the former chief curator of the Venice Art Biennale.
A tribute to the ‘Parfümerie’
In her younger years, Kouoh was part of this movement, which also had a significant influence on her own development as a cultural manager and curator. At the Biennale, Kouoh wanted to pay tribute to one of the key clubs of that era, the so-called “Parfümerie”.
Kouoh died last year at the age of 57. The Parfümerie concept will be retained following her death and carried forward by a team of female curators. It is being realised by the Zurich-based performance duo Clarissa Herbst (graphic designer, costume designer) and Dominique Rust (actor), two of the co-founders of the legendary club.
More
Koyo Kouoh: Art is in the cracks, not in the polish
A melting pot of scenes
Kouoh met the pair back then at the Parfümerie in Zurich and invited them to the Biennale in 2024. For the Parfümerie project, the curator planned to spread events across the entire Biennale – just as the club, true to its name, had dispersed “perfume” across the city of Zurich in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
For Kouoh, it was a very personal project and her time in Zurich was a very important one for her, says Herbst. “It was such a melting pot of very different scenes, and that fascinated her. The fact that such a community emerged from the underground scene.”
Beams of light in the garden shed
For Kouoh, this spontaneous social organisation was also intended to serve as a model for the present day. “She wanted to encourage people to claim their own spaces now, in their own cities or wherever they live,” Herbst continues.
The Parfümerie itself has no comprehensive archive: only leaflets and blurred photographs have survived. At the 2026 Biennale d’Arte, the club is now taking over the Casetta Scaffali, a striking historic exhibition building in the rear garden area of the Arsenale in Venice.
Here, Clarissa Herbst and Dominique Rust explore the concept of Parfümerie on a sensory level, presenting a multimedia installation at the Arsenale: a cone of light invites visitors to dance, surrounded by light projections, videos and Parfümerie leaflets from back then.
A soundtrack by Martin Schütz, a cellist and improviser from the city of Biel/Bienne, gently envelops the space. To accompany the Parfümerie project, a music album dedicated to Kouoh is also being released, featuring further sounds by Schütz and the Berlin-based electronic music pioneer Frank Bretschneider.
The Parfümerie tribute thus establishes a strong musical and visual Swiss presence at the major art exhibition in Venice: the Zurich underground scene lives on.
Parfümerie can be experienced until the end of the Venice Biennale (November 22). A lecture and a performance will also take place during the final month.

How a Swiss aid operation helped former SS members reach Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

How a Swiss aid operation helped former SS members reach Brazil
New research reveals how former Waffen-SS members were included in one of Switzerland’s largest post-war humanitarian projects and ended up living freely in the South American country.
Crossing the Atlantic on a journey of around 10,000 kilometres to Brazil was long, expensive and difficult. But for around 2,500 people known as the Danube Swabians, it became an opportunity for a new beginning. Of German origin and language, these people had lived for generations in what was then Yugoslavia but, after the Second World War, faced reprisals, expropriations and expulsions after part of the community had collaborated with the Nazi regime.
Among those who chose to leave Europe for Brazil, however, were at least 16 former members of the Waffen-SS, the paramilitary branch of the Nazi Party, whose units were involved in war crimes and crimes against humanity. These men did not arrive in the South American country on their own. They came as beneficiaries of a Swiss humanitarian operation that mobilised the Catholic Church, NGOs and Swiss government funds to establish a new colony in the southern Brazilian state of Paraná.
“It was known that Nazi war criminals were leaving Europe through the so-called ratlines, and it was evident that men there [within the project] were Nazis and members of the SS. But even so, nobody asked questions,” says Peter Hug, a Swiss historian specialising in Switzerland’s relations with Nazi Germany and author of Humanitäre Hilfe der Schweiz für SS-Kriegsverbrecher (Swiss humanitarian aid for SS war criminals), the book that reveals the story.
Published in May 2026, his research documents the presence of at least 16 former Waffen-SS members among the settlers sent to Brazil and reconstructs how Swiss humanitarian organisations and authorities helped make their resettlement possible.
“For Switzerland and the Vatican, this population became an opportunity to present themselves as defenders of refugees, after Switzerland had been very close to the German regime and the Church had never formally protested against Nazi crimes. The fact that there were criminals among them ended up being considered less important,” he adds.
The establishment of the colony, called Entre Rios, also affected populations who already lived and worked on the farms allocated to the Europeans. They ended up marginalised within the new social structure, amid an attempt by the settlement’s leaders to preserve a supposed German cultural superiority.
An operation involving several actors
The operation that brought former Waffen-SS members to Brazil began to take shape in the years immediately after the war, through an articulation between representatives of the Catholic Church in Austria and the Vatican and a group of Danube Swabians linked to the former Ustasha state in Croatia, a fascist puppet state that existed from 1941 to 1945.
“The idea came from Croatian priests close to the Germans and from Andreas Rohracher,” says Hug, referring to the then Archbishop of Salzburg and one of the most influential figures in the Austrian Catholic Church, who, according to Hug, was close to Austrofascism, the authoritarian Catholic-conservative regime that ruled Austria from 1934 to 1938.
“From 1945, they wanted to create closed settlements for the Danube Swabians, where the idea of German cultural superiority could be preserved even after the defeat in the war,” he says.
The project gained momentum with the involvement of Caritas, the Catholic humanitarian non-profit organisation based in Lucerne. According to Hug, the organisation had a fundamental advantage: it was part of a Catholic network with a global presence and capable of opening doors in different countries.
“It was a huge operation which needed to be coordinated globally on two continents,” he says.
The scale of the undertaking, however, eventually exceeded Caritas’s capacity. From 1950 onwards, the project passed into the hands of the Schweizer Europahilfe, or Swiss European Aid, an organisation close to the government. With it came Swiss diplomacy, resources and more direct involvement by the country’s authorities in the operation that would eventually choose the interior of the Brazilian state of Paraná as its destination.
The change was not merely administrative. In Hug’s assessment, the project became an operation combining Switzerland’s humanitarian, diplomatic and economic interests. “The project started within the Catholic Church. Then they had big problems, and then it was the Swiss government and these NGOs around the Swiss government who took it over,” Hug says.
At the centre of the operation was the Agrária Cooperative, created in 1951 to organise the new settlement. Its first president, Michael Moor, had held leadership positions in economic organisations of the German community in the Ustasha State of Croatia, an ally of the Nazis, and had influence over the choice of land and the first groups sent to Brazil.
The colony and its collective memory
“These families lived as refugees and stateless people in Europe after having actively participated in the Second World War on Germany’s side. The main difference, which we must emphasise, is the fact that some of the adult men sent with their families to Entre Rios had fought in the war as members of the Waffen-SS. This did not prevent them from entering Brazil,” says Méri Frotscher, a history professor at the State University of the Midwest (Unicentro) and a researcher on German immigration.
In Brazil, the Swabians arrived at a time when the country was reopening to European immigration and were presented to the authorities as refugees and skilled farmers, a profile that suited the country’s colonisation policy.
A past that challenges Swiss neutrality
For Hug, more than revealing failures in a specific humanitarian operation, the Entre Rios case challenges the way Switzerland has constructed and preserved its own memory of the Second World War.
“We are neutral. We are humanitarian. And we are the best in the world,” Hug says ironically, describing this narrative. “The island of peace in a world of chaos. And this is wrong.”
More than seven decades later, this reassessment is beginning to reach the Swiss organisations involved in the operation, as well as the impact that initiatives such as the creation of the Entre Rios colony had in Switzerland and on local populations.
SWISSAID acknowledges that the perspective of local populations remains largely unexplored and says it is seeking out their descendants to learn their side of the story. “We are currently in the process of establishing contact with the descendants of the communities affected at the time,” the organisation said in a statement to Swissinfo.
SWISSAID argues that this historical reassessment should not be restricted to humanitarian organisations. “It remains to be seen how the story can be told from a Southern perspective. Perhaps, and hopefully, the [Swiss government] will take an interest in coming to terms with this part of history”.
Caritas Switzerland also now acknowledges serious failures in the operation. The organisation says there was no individual vetting of the backgrounds of the selected settlers and regrets that funds intended for humanitarian purposes benefited members of the Waffen-SS.
“We deeply regret that, through this project, funds intended for humanitarian purposes benefited people who were members of the Waffen-SS,” the organisation said in a statement.
Caritas also offers a critical assessment of the impact on the population already living in the region, saying their rights and needs were not considered in the planning. For Caritas, the creation of a closed European settler colony was rooted in a colonial logic and today serves as an example of how humanitarian aid can produce the opposite of its intended effect.
“The approach taken and the establishment of a closed settler colony in Brazil after the Second World War can serve today as a warning of how aid can turn into its opposite,” the organisation said in a statement.
The Agrária Cooperative did not respond to requests for comment.

Why the Swiss federal budget is so hard to predict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Why the Swiss federal budget is so hard to predict
Company taxes have come to the rescue of the Swiss federal budget, helping to turn a projected CHF700 million ($865 million) deficit into a CHF800 million surplus.
Last month the finance ministry surprised parliament by revising its forecast for federal revenues upwards by CHF1.9 billion. The increase is more than enough to offset increased spending, including additional defence expenditure.
The main driver of increased revenues is corporate taxation. The government now expects federal profit-tax receipts to be around CHF1.4 billion higher than the initial forecast.
Why did the numbers look so different in the space of a few months? Where did the extra CHF1.4 billion in corporate tax receipts suddenly materialise from? And can Switzerland expect to unearth more golden eggs from the same source in future?
Left-leaning political parties have their own answers. They have again accused the finance ministry of painting a deliberately gloomy picture in early budget forecasts to push through spending cuts.
+ Swiss budget cuts increase pressure on International Geneva
“By systematically underestimating revenues, the Federal Council [government] is trying to justify cuts in public spending and new privileges for the wealthiest and large corporations,” stated Social Democrat parliamentarian Tamara Funiciello, when the more optimistic budget scenario was presented last month.
Not the first time
There is a long history of such complaints. In 2018 the government’s ordinary financing balance ended CHF2.6 billion better than originally budgeted. In 2013 an expected CHF400 million deficit turned into a CHF1.3 billion surplus.
But the finance ministry denies misleading parliament and the public. Ordinary revenue forecasts have been out by 0.3% on average between 2016 and 2025, the ministry said.
The latest corporate tax windfall, attributable to the 2027 budget, can be traced to a small number of very large, and unnamed, companies. Three-quarters of all corporate tax receipts are concentrated among 0.5% of total companies in Switzerland, according to the government.
More
Iran war: Switzerland expects bumper tax from oil traders
This heavy reliance on a small cohort of multinationals might explain why Swiss corporate tax revenue forecasts are so hard to calculate. A fallow or bumper year from a few of these multinationals makes a big difference to the total business tax haul.
Most of the big taxpayers are concentrated in cantons Lucerne, which has the lowest cantonal tax rate of 11.66%, Zurich, home to many big banks and other corporations, and Basel City, which plays host to the powerful Swiss pharmaceutical industry.
The cantons do not say where their corporate tax revenues come from. But there are other clues. The pharmaceutical multinational MSD, which has its Swiss headquarters in Lucerne, paid CHF1.8 billion in Swiss taxes last year, according to its financial statements.
Canton Geneva has been busy collecting retroactive taxes from companies it failed to bill in previous years. This revenue source has contributed CHF200 million to the latest budget forecast.
The canton told Swiss public broadcaster SRF earlier this year that oil traders in Geneva, who handle around a third of the global oil trade, have enjoyed bumper profits in the wake of the war in Iran. This phenomenon translates into higher tax revenues.
Volatile source of income
But Switzerland cannot rely on this volatile source of income to keep the books balanced every year, warns Michael Grass of the BAK Economics research institute. “Individual record years in corporate tax revenue should not readily be interpreted as durable, structural revenue growth,” he told Swissinfo.
More
Global corporate tax deal reshapes how Switzerland attracts multinationals
“In the pharmaceutical industry in particular, international conditions are shifting,” he added.
These include recent demands from Washington that international firms expand production and research on US soil, efforts by the US to lower the cost of medicaments with its so-called most favoured nation pricing policy and growing competition from China.
BAK Economics’ caution is mirrored by the Swiss finance ministry. “While corporate income tax revenues have been rising sharply for several years, it is unclear whether and for how long this trend will continue,” it stated in August.
On the other side of the budget balance sheet is Switzerland’s expenditure, which is also difficult to predict with precision. A series of extraordinary expenses have emerged since the turn of a decade that has already seen a global pandemic and a war erupt in Europe.
Conflict in the Middle East, which has further squeezed oil and gas supplies, combined with volatile US trade policy is likely to make life more difficult for economic forecasters.

Russian security operatives have foiled a Ukrainian plot to carry out a false-flag attack on the British ambassador and other diplomats in Moscow, which was intended to draw the UK into a direct conflict with Russia, the Federal Security Service (FSB) has said.
In a statement on Thursday, the agency said it had detained a Russian national who worked for an organization contracted to protect the British Embassy in Moscow. The man collected sensitive information about embassy security on instructions from a Ukrainian contact, as well as personal data on diplomatic personnel, including photographs, home addresses, details of vehicles, and itineraries, the FSB said.
“The Kiev regime planned to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks against British diplomatic representatives in Moscow to subsequently blame Russia for them in order to draw the United Kingdom into direct armed conflict with the country, secure additional weapons deliveries [to Kiev], and ramp up sanctions on Russia,” the agency said.
Neither the UK Embassy in Moscow nor British Ambassador Nigel Casey has commented on the statement.
The FSB said the suspect had been recruited by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and acted on instructions of Ukrainian blogger Dmitry Karpenko, also known as “Apostle Dmitry.”
Karpenko, 44, became known for recording interviews with Russian prisoners of war and covering POW swaps between Moscow and Kiev, as well as for propagating videos featuring Russian nationals collaborating with the Ukrainian military.
Karpenko was also criticized by Ukraine’s Commission on Journalistic Ethics, which said his videos exposed prisoners’ identities and at times resembled interrogations. The blogger also faced accusations of Islamophobia after an interview with a captured Russian serviceman from Chechnya, during which he made remarks widely seen as offensive to Muslims.
Britain has been one of Ukraine’s biggest backers since the escalation of the conflict in 2022, providing billions of pounds in military and financial assistance to Kiev. London has also refrained from condemning Kiev over a string of assassinations and bombings targeting Russian military officials and public figures inside Russia.
After Ukraine claimed responsibility for the 2024 killing of Russian General Igor Kirillov, commander of the Radiological, Chemical, and Biological Protection Forces, Downing Street said Britain would “not mourn” his death.

Syria welcomed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Board of Governors’ consensus adoption of a resolution closing outstanding issues related to the country’s nuclear file and removing the matter from the board’s agenda.
In a statement late Wednesday, the Foreign Ministry said the decision “closes a chapter that has lasted for years” and opens “new prospects” for Syria to cooperate internationally on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and technology.
The ministry described the resolution as an “important diplomatic and legal achievement for Syria,” saying it reflected the country’s “success in building consensus within the IAEA Board of Governors.”
It said Damascus had adopted “transparency, cooperation and respect for international obligations as a consistent approach since the country’s liberation,” in an effort to address the legacy left by the government of former President Bashar al-Assad.
On Wednesday, the IAEA Board of Governors decided to end the noncompliance finding on Syria’s nuclear obligations after the completion of technical and legal requirements, according to the Syrian state television Alikhbariah.  
Verification of former regime’s nuclear activities 
In August, the head of Syrian Atomic Energy Commission Mudar al-Akaleh said Syria was moving toward closing the noncompliance file and expanding peaceful nuclear applications.
He said the commission, in coordination with the Foreign Ministry, had worked in recent months to provide all technical requirements needed to assess nuclear materials and waste linked to the former regime, in accordance with international safeguards and the IAEA’s legal framework.
Speaking in Damascus on Aug. 18, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced the presence of “several tons of nuclear materials” remaining from the Assad era in Deir ez-Zor province, adding that inspectors had been granted access to the site.
An IAEA report circulated to member states and leaked to the media said agency inspectors conducted verification and investigative work at various sites in Syria in August.
The report said the site visits revealed that the Assad regime had failed to declare nuclear materials, facilities and types of activities that should have been reported under Syria’s comprehensive safeguards agreement with the NPT.
On Monday, opening a meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors in Vienna, Grossi said the agency made a “historic breakthrough” after Syria’s new administration provided required information and allowed access to the Deir ez-Zor facility and other sites.

TOKYO, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) will continue to raise its key interest rate to ensure it does not fall behind the curve in fighting inflation, one of its board members said Thursday ahead of the bank's policy meeting next week.
In a speech to Japanese business leaders in Fukui Prefecture, Kazuyuki Masu, who sits on the BOJ's Monetary Policy Committee, said the central bank "will continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation in response to developments in economic activity and prices as well as financial conditions."
"What is most vital from now on is to ensure that the underlying inflation rate does not significantly exceed 2 percent," Masu said.
The BOJ is widely expected to hike its policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25 percent at its Sept. 17-18 meeting, after raising it to 1.0 percent at its June meeting, its highest level in 31 years, and leaving it unchanged at its July meeting.
Masu said the BOJ should raise the rate further to "complete the normalization of monetary policy" following decades of deflation and negative rates.
"Financial conditions in Japan remain accommodative. If inflation accelerates here, there is a risk that the BOJ might inevitably need to implement a rapid policy interest rate hike," he added. ■

China Focus: Modern technology helps discover, preserve cliff paintings in NW China's Helan Mountains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:40:43 CST
15:40:43 KST

A staff member works with the multi-source data management platform for Helan Mountains cliff paintings in Yinchuan City, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region on July 23, 2025. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)
YINCHUAN, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- China is applying modern technology to further discover and preserve ancient cliff paintings in the Helan Mountains in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, racing against time to safeguard these ancient treasures.
Thanks to the power of integrated modern technological means, a new round of comprehensive surveys has so far discovered a total of more than 500 new cliff paintings in these mountains, the Helan Mountain cliff painting administration noted.
The administration launched this new survey work in 2020 to confirm the preservation status of existing cliff paintings and identify overlooked ones.
"Different from previous ones which relied mainly on a manual field survey, this new round of surveys has combined traditional field surveys with diverse specialized modern technological methods," said Zhang Jianguo, deputy director of the administration.
For example, Zhang explained that 3D laser scanners have been used to record carving marks on cliffs more clearly, while drones have been deployed over valleys to collect data from multiple angles.
"Aside from these, a new positioning system is being used to keep location errors within two to three meters, allowing professionals to navigate directly to target cliff painting locations, thereby greatly reducing field survey workloads," Zhang added.
The Helan Mountains are home to more than 20,000 cliff paintings created by ancient ancestors using stone tools, metalware or mineral pigments. These paintings depict over 100 types of natural imagery, including human faces, animals, plants, handprints and symbols, as well as scenes of ancient lifeways such as herding, hunting, sacrificial rituals and warfare.
The paintings date from approximately 10,000 to 3,000 years ago and were created by different groups of people over various periods.
Bearing witness to the evolution of ancient ancestors from hunting and nomadic herding to farming and animal domestication, they reflect numerous aspects of ancient life, like belief systems, lifestyles and scientific knowledge. They also attest to interaction and integration among different peoples, holding immense historical, cultural and artistic value.
In previous surveys, limited by methods and equipment available at the time, some paintings hidden deep in ravines or buried beneath shallow soil layers were not promptly recorded and archived, leaving gaps in documentation.
Zhang disclosed that these newly discovered cliff paintings are mainly located in the alluvial fan areas of the Helan Mountains, while their themes are largely consistent with previously discovered ones, such as animals and human faces, as well as depicting hunting, music and dance.
Animal themes are the most common in these newly discovered cliff paintings, with sheep featuring the most, followed by horses, cattle, camels and deer. Some exquisitely carved tiger paintings were also found. There are also images of human faces, some of which differ in style from those preserved on cliff walls, thus enriching the forms of expression.
As for ones depicting hunting, certain hunting patterns have been found to deliberately exaggerate the length of bows and arrows, resulting in distorted proportions.
Zhang explained that the location of a cliff painting has an impact on the theme depicted by the ancient people who carved it. "Cliff paintings in the valleys recorded certain types of events, while those on the alluvial fans tend to be associated with real hunting practices, providing a new direction for the study of prehistoric civilization."
"Notably, the newly discovered paintings include a rare depiction of a carriage drawn by four horses -- the first of its kind found in the Helan Mountains and a rarity nationwide, filling a gap in the local rock art collection," Zhang said.
Aside from supporting discovery efforts, modern technologies are also helping to sustain preservation of these treasures.
Having been exposed to the elements for tens of thousands of years, some of the Helan Mountains cliff paintings are in poor condition, with some carvings having faded or even disappeared due to weathering.
More alarmingly, these cliff paintings are located in a zone shaped by glacial action, where cracks and hollow voids behind the rock surface are common. After repeated rain and freeze-thaw cycles, rocks may split apart or peel away, making conservation work a matter of utmost urgency in this area.
The Helan Mountain cliff painting administration is collaborating with multiple institutions including the Nanjing Museum, Lanzhou University and Fudan University, regarding efforts to conserve these cliff paintings.
To date, they have completed topographic mapping of cliff painting areas and digital preservation of the paintings, in an endeavor which gives each painting an "identity card," Zhang said.
During this new round of survey efforts, professionals have collected data on the geographic locations, image types, dimensions and weathering damage of newly discovered rock paintings, as well as written information about the surrounding environment.
"Ancient people made deliberate choices about where to carve the paintings, so the environmental information is of great value for research and preservation," Zhang explained.
He added: "If salvage excavation for some cliff paintings becomes necessary in the future, we cannot simply move the rock itself, as the original geographic and environmental information must be fully preserved." ■
A drone photo taken on July 23, 2025 shows a cliff painting at the site of the Helan mountains cliff paintings in Yinchuan City, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)
An aerial drone photo taken on July 23, 2025 shows staff members checking a cliff painting at the site of the Helan mountains cliff paintings in Yinchuan City, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)

John Lewis losses widen to £124m as shopper confidence dips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:39:36 UTC
15:39:36 KST

Losses at the owner of John Lewis and Waitrose widened by more than 40% in the first half of the year as it struggled with higher costs and shoppers feeling less confident about their money.
The John Lewis Partnership, which operates 36 department stores and more than 300 Waitrose supermarkets, said its pre-tax loss for the six months to 1 August climbed to £124m, compared with £88m in the same period in 2025.
Jason Tarry, the chair of JLP, said the first half of the year had been a “tougher market than we had planned for”.
“Customers have been more cautious about spending, particularly when they replace the bigger-ticket things in their homes,” he said, citing higher interest rates, the rising cost of living and uncertainty triggered by wars around the world.
Higher national insurance contributions and a series of heatwaves over the summer also drove up costs, JLP said.
Tom Denyard, the boss of Waitrose, said the heat had triggered “some challenges with refrigeration and freezing”, but that the company was investing in more resilient equipment.
Waitrose still outperformed John Lewis, with sales across the supermarket arm up 4% while those at the department store chain fell 2%. Overall half-year sales rose 2% to £6.3bn.
The company added that it was “starting to build” a joined-up loyalty offering across the partnership. It currently offers separate John Lewis and Waitrose loyalty cards, which include free “treat” products and personalised rewards.
The partnership, which is employee-owned, is in the midst of a turnaround plan, after having closed 16 department stores and at least 20 Waitrose outlets since the pandemic and is cutting thousands of staff jobs.
Tarry called on the chancellor, John Healey, to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK in his inaugural budget in October.
“We want the government to deliver against their manifesto, which is to reform business rates,” he said. “It is the biggest business tax that we face, and in some locations it is bigger than our rent bill.
“Anything that the government can do to help us employ more people and be able to drive more growth would be very helpful.”
JLP’s drop in profit comes after Peter Ruis, head of the department store arm, said last month he would step down after less than three years in the role. He has been replaced by Will Kernan, a former boss of the River Island fashion chain.
In March the company felt confident enough to pay its 69,000 workers, whom it calls partners, a bonus – of 2% of salary – for the first time in four years, following a 6% rise in its underlying profit. Staff shared a pot of £35m, worth about one week’s extra pay each.
The company said it was still too early to say whether staff would be paid a bonus for this financial year, although Tarry said he was “confident we will be able to make a profit”.
The retailer typically makes the bulk of its profit in the second half of its year, which includes the peak Christmas trading period.
But Robyn Duffy, an analyst at the consultancy RSM UK, said John Lewis looked vulnerable heading into the second half. “The retailer is particularly exposed to big-ticket, deferrable categories like home, furniture and electricals – exactly where these consumers are choosing to cut back or delay spending,” she said.
John Lewis is one of the few remaining national department store chains, following the closure of Debenhams and Beales. This summer Harvey Nichols was bought out of administration by the owner of Sports Direct, Mike Ashley, who had said the Knightsbridge store was in a “death spiral”.

Netherlands moves to buy Saab GlobalEye radar jet
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:39:02 BST
15:39:02 KST

The Netherlands has taken a first formal step towards acquiring Saab’s GlobalEye airborne early warning and control aircraft, signing a Letter of Intent with Sweden for the system, according to the company.
No procurement contract has yet been signed and Saab stressed that it has not received an order from the Netherlands. The Letter of Intent instead establishes the Dutch intention to move towards acquiring the aircraft, with further procurement activity still required.
Saab said: “The Netherlands has signed a Letter of Intent with Sweden for the acquisition of a Saab GlobalEye Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft. The parties have not yet entered into a contract and Saab has not yet received an order from The Netherlands.”
The company added that it was prepared for the next stages of the procurement process.
GlobalEye is based around a business-jet airframe fitted with a suite of active and passive sensors intended to provide persistent surveillance across air, maritime and land domains.
The system is designed to detect and identify objects at long range before distributing that information to military users, allowing aircraft, ships and ground forces to build a common operational picture and respond to developing threats.
Micael Johansson, President and CEO of Saab, said: “We welcome today’s announcement by the Netherlands of its intention to procure GlobalEye. The system will provide enhanced situational awareness and early warning capabilities across multiple domains, while also strengthening NATO’s ability to operate in an increasingly complex security environment.”
He added: “GlobalEye will enable the Netherlands to detect threats earlier, respond faster, and strengthen both national and collective defence. We stand ready to support this capability with Swedish innovation and expertise.”
The aircraft combines a number of sensors rather than operating solely as a traditional airborne radar platform. Saab describes GlobalEye as a multi-domain AEW&C system capable of observing activity in the air, at sea and over land and providing information to different elements of an armed force in real time.
The prospective Dutch acquisition would add another European customer for an airborne surveillance capability at a time when NATO members are increasing investment in early warning, command-and-control and long-range sensing.
The next stage will depend on negotiations between the Netherlands and Sweden and the subsequent procurement process before Saab can book an order and begin delivery against a formal contract.

Trust in politics falling, more people joining protests: CBS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Trust in politics among people in their twenties and thirties in the Netherlands has fallen sharply, according to new figures by national statistics bureau CBS, and more people of all age groups are joining political protests and demonstrations.
Among 25 to 35-year-olds those that said they had trust dropped from 50.6% to 42.4%, the steepest fall of any group. Some 55% of 18 to 25-year-olds said they had confidence in politics last year, up from 49% in 2023, making them the only age group whose trust increased.
Teenagers aged 15 to 18 remain the most trusting, at 62%, while the least trusting are 65 to 75-year-olds, at 31%. The figures come from the CBS survey on social cohesion and wellbeing, which polls people aged 15 and over every year.
Participation in protests and demonstrations rose in every age group in 2025, with 25 to 35-year-olds the most active: 9.5% said they had taken part in a protest or demonstration in the past five years, compared with 8.6% of 18 to 25-year-olds and 2.4% of the over-75s.
Students and people with a university or college degree were the most likely to have demonstrated, the CBS said.
Older people may be less trusting, but they are much more interested in politics. Some 64% of 65 to 75-year-olds said they were fairly or very interested, compared with 37% of 15 to 18-year-olds, although interest among teenagers and young adults has risen for two years in a row.
The survey was carried out during 2025, a year in which the Schoof cabinet collapsed and a general election was held in October.
Trust in politics peaked across all age groups in 2020, during the Covid pandemic, when 78% of teenagers and 71% of 18 to 25-year-olds said they had confidence in politicians. It has since fallen back to roughly where it was a decade ago.

'Iran doesn’t control Houthis,' Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis as strikes on Saudi Arabia escalate - report
Saudi, Pakistani, and Iranian sources tell Reuters that Islamabad delivered a warning to Tehran after Houthi attacks wounded 73 people at a Saudi airbase and oil infrastructure
Pakistan reportedly delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Houthi allies after the group struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and nearby oil infrastructure Tuesday. This is according to Saudi, Pakistani, and Iranian sources cited by Reuters.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday that Saudi warplanes had carried out 54 airstrikes across Yemeni provinces over the prior 12 hours, warning the strikes would "not go unanswered and unpunished." The escalation marks a second front threatening global energy supplies as Iran and the US continue their largest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks.

Right to repair: Spare parts and services price Europeans out of fixing their gadgets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:35:23 UTC
15:35:23 KST

The EU’s Right to Repair Directive is now in force, but for many consumers, fixing a broken appliance or smartphone still costs more than buying a new one.
The EU’s Right to Repair Directive has been in full force since July 31st, 2026, and the gap between what the law promises and the reality consumers face hasn’t been addressed.
Spare parts routinely cost more than the point at which fixing a broken appliance still makes financial sense, and even where a part is cheap, getting someone to fit it can cost more than the item is worth.
Parts you can’t even put a price on
Before cost comes availability, and the record is patchy. A joint audit of the EU’s official product registry by the Right to Repair Europe coalition and iFixit reviewed over 7.000 listings and found compliance “abysmal”.
80% of smartphone entries lacked usable repair instructions or spare-parts pricing, and nearly half gave no information at all. Half of the tumble dryer models reviewed were non-compliant too. Some manufacturers directed consumers to marketplaces like Temu or AliExpress instead of official parts channels, while 8% wrote “see manual” with no link attached.
A June 2026 market check by consumer group BEUC, testing official spare-parts prices for smartphones and battery vacuum cleaners across six EU countries, found the most expensive vacuum cleaner battery cost €281-56% of the appliance’s original price. The priciest replacement part reached €240, or 37% of the product’s price. Flagship smartphone screens topped €400, about 30% of a phone’s retail price, before labour or delivery are added.
According to BEUC’s example of a 2025 study from the French environment agency ADEME, people generally choose repair only when the total cost stays within 20-30% of a product’s original price. Beyond that, most switch to buying new.
Repair service isn’t cheap either
Labour, not parts, usually drives the bill. EU research on coffee machine repairs found a typical job cost €83- €68 of that was labour, and only €15 was the part. A 2025 Consumer Conditions Survey found 61% of people who skipped a repair just after their guarantee ended did so because it was too expensive.
Alex Bunodiere, a PhD researcher in KU Leuven’s Life Cycle Engineering group, sees the same arithmetic for small appliances. In Belgium, a repair shop’s minimum callout is around €100, while the median purchase price of a small appliance is about €160. “At €160, who would spend €100 for the repair?” he said. “The proportion of the purchase price to the repair price is still too high.” His research puts France’s repair rate for small appliances at just 17%, even with a national bonus that cuts up to €60 off bigger jobs.
Both experts pushed back on the idea that locating a repairer is the industry’s real bottleneck. The gap the EU’s own repair-matching platform, not due until 2027-2028, is meant to close. “I don’t see access to repair as the main bottleneck,” Bunodiere said. “It is a bottleneck, but to me, the price is the primary bottleneck.”
René Repasi, the European Parliament’s rapporteur on the file, agreed the platform “would be helpful, but it is not for the right to repair to work.” A search engine usually turns up a nearby repairer in cities, he said, though that gets “more difficult in the rural areas.”
A law with no price tag?
The directive requires spare parts and repair services to be offered at a “reasonable” price, but sets no formula, cap or benchmark for what that means. Repasi said the ambiguity leaves room for abuse: a plastic part costing “10 cents” to produce being sold for €350 is “obviously not reasonable”, yet without a legal definition, “some reckless manufacturers would still play the game, simply betting on the fact that consumers don’t know” they can push back.
Enforcement is also uneven. Only a handful of member states met the 31 July 2026 deadline to transpose the directive, and where implementation is missing, consumers can’t invoke it directly against manufacturers, only claim damages from their own government, leaving, in Repasi’s words, “different qualities of rights depending on which countries they are living in.”
How manufacturers still steer buyers towards ‘new’
Manufacturers, Bunodiere said, usually make more profit from a new sale than from a repair job, leaving them “incentivised to sell new products instead of repairing them.” The directive’s exemption for intellectual property still lets companies restrict compatible or third-party parts by citing patents.
“Parts pairing” software can stop a swapped component from working until the manufacturer remotely authorises it. Manufacturers’ self-declared repairability scores go largely unchecked by any public authority.
Advocacy groups including Right to Repair Europe have proposed capping the priciest spare part at 15-20% of a product’s retail price. A French durability label, LONGTIME, already gets manufacturers such as Fairphone and Whirlpool to accept a voluntary ceiling, typically 25%, suggesting the idea is commercially workable. Until something similar is written into EU law, both experts said “reasonable” will keep meaning whatever a manufacturer can defend.

Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm elections, threatens to attack Pickaxe Mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:17:26 UTC
15:17:26 KST

Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm vote, Houthis close in on key Strait, sources say
CAIRO/WASHINGTON/DUBAI, Sept 10 - President Donald Trump said he expected the war with Iran to end after the November U.S. midterm elections and threatened again to attack a site associated with the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme after the two sides launched their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the six-month-old war.
Tensions in the region were high, with Saudi civil defence authorities on Thursday issuing emergency alerts in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis were edging closer on Thursday to gaining more leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important routes for shipping, four Yemeni government military sources said.
Brent crude prices hovered above $100 a barrel as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted.
Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the waterway on Wednesday after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes that have signalled scant chance of an imminent end to hostilities.
DEADLINES TO END WAR
The war and subsequent increase in fuel prices have helped drive Trump's popularity to record lows. The president said Tehran was trying to influence the November U.S. midterm elections, which will determine whether his Republican Party retains control of Congress.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
Trump has previously set deadlines for the war to end.
The Wall Street Journal reported later that top White House advisers, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned Trump that the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency, which ends in January 2029. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Trump also said the U.S. may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes near Iran's damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention. Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February partly due to concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Iran says its nuclear activities are for peaceful purposes.
In recent weeks Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the war. But a resumption of fighting this month appears to have set back any such gradual reopening. Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday.
RED SEA CLASHES
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen has also escalated in the past few days, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha and are launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Government forces and their allies are relocating south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait, across from the island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal or the SUMED pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Blocking the narrow passage would isolate Gulf oil-producing countries such as energy superpower Saudi Arabia from their main shipping routes after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — the primary maritime energy artery between Asia and Europe.
Earlier this week, at least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, in recent Houthi strikes on the world's largest oil exporter.
The militant group said it attacked an air base in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following another emergency alert declared in Khamis Mushait. REUTERS

KIAS pairs textured brick facade with planted atrium for headquarters in japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:15:55 UTC
15:15:55 KST

Rough Brick and GRC Create a Layered Street Facade
Kawamura Electric’s new headquarters in central Nagoya brings together workplace, culture, nature, and social interaction within a seven-story building. Designed by KIAS as a new base for the company, whose origins are in Seto, Aichi Prefecture, the project accommodates offices alongside an art gallery and a multipurpose hall for approximately 110 people. The building is organized as a hybrid workplace intended to connect employees, clients, and the wider community.
The exterior is composed of two contrasting material systems. The lower volume facing the street is clad in rough, heavily textured bricks manufactured in Hekinan, while the upper volume is wrapped in a fine grid of GRC (glass-fiber reinforced concrete). The two volumes are subtly displaced in section, creating a shifting shadow line and allowing them to read as distinct masses. Within a neighborhood of temples, apartment buildings, and small parks, the change in scale reduces the perceived mass of the seven-story building and relates it more closely to its surroundings.
The GRC lattice serves both environmental and architectural functions. It moderates solar gain while incorporating the window system within its depth, giving the facade a layered and permeable appearance. Its sectional proportions were developed through a series of full-scale mock-ups and prototypes using actual GRC members, steel structure, and window frames. The studies examined dimensions and junctions as well as the sequence of construction. The brickfacade is similarly defined by small variations in dimension. The bricks were produced in three different lengths, with mortar joints recessed by 2 mm and approximately one in every four bricks randomly projecting by 4 mm. These small shifts create changing shadows across the surface, emphasizing the outline, mass, and texture of individual units. The arrangement makes the assembly of the brickwork visible as part of the building’s architectural expression.
Planted Atrium Forms the Headquarters’ Social Heart
Beyond the five-meter-high entrance door, a seven-story atrium forms the central social and environmental space of the headquarters. The void supports natural ventilation while creating visual and acoustic connections between the offices, executive floors, and cafeteria. Movement and activity can therefore be perceived across different areas of the workplace. A twelve-meter-long vertical garden, together with planting distributed throughout the atrium, was designed by French artist and botanist Patrick Blanc. More than 180 plant species introduce a dense layer of vegetation into the interior, shaping the atmosphere of the central space as a luminous forest ravine.
Artworks by Yojiro Imasaka, Takuro Kuwata, and Hirosuke Yabe are incorporated throughout the building alongside terrazzo stairs, handmade tiles, and brick counters. These elements extend the material palette from the exterior into the interior, combining art, planting, light, and tactile surfaces within the workplace. By combining offices with cultural and communal programs, the headquarters expands the workplace beyond a purely functional setting. Its architecture places particular emphasis on connections between departments and people, while bringing nature, art, and material details into everyday working spaces.

Lithuanian Seimas to focus on security, demographics in autumn session
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

Lithuania’s parliament, the Seimas, is opening its autumn session Thursday, with lawmakers set to review a draft agenda containing more than 550 legislative proposals and focus on security, defence and demographic challenges.
The session will run through December 23 and include 46 sittings, three of which will be dedicated to the agendas of opposition parliamentary groups.
Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said security, defence and national resilience would be among the session’s main priorities, along with measures addressing demographic challenges.
“We intend to focus most of our attention on security, defence and resilience,” Olekas said. “The second theme is tackling demographic challenges, encompassing measures to boost the birth rate, as well as the return of the diaspora to Lithuania and managed migration.”
The draft agenda includes more than 330 initiatives submitted by lawmakers. The cabinet has proposed 127 draft laws for consideration.
Among the key issues, lawmakers are expected to consider removing from the Constitution a provision banning the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania and approve an updated National Security Strategy.
The parliament is also expected Thursday to consider a proposal to hold the next mayoral and municipal council elections on March 7, 2027. Lawmakers are also due to consider legislation establishing a public register of sex offenders.
The 2027 state budget will be approved during the session.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has said the government’s priorities centre on “a safe person in a safe state”.
A family policy package is scheduled to be presented Thursday. It is aimed at boosting the birth rate, improving the child care allowance system and helping young families buy homes.
Other planned measures include increasing the number of conscripts, introducing universal free school meals for primary school students and raising scientists’ salaries.
Lawmakers are also expected to consider proposals to establish a free economic zone in Visaginas, limit the frequency of fuel price increases, and streamline public procurement and civil service regulations.
President Gitanas Nausėda has submitted 10 proposals for consideration during the session.
The Lithuanian parliament convenes for two regular sessions each year, in spring and autumn.

US sanctions on 27 airlines 'example of economic terrorism'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:12:38 UTC
15:12:38 KST

In a letter penned to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the rotating President of the UN Security Council, Gholamhossein Darzi stated that sanctions on airlines disrupt access to aircraft spare parts, equipment, and services—including maintenance, repair, inspection, and technical support—essential for the safe operation of civil aircraft; this exposes passengers and aviation industry personnel to avoidable risks while simultaneously restricting the movement of millions of civilians.
The senior Iranian diplomat added, “These actions also constitute a blatant disregard for the International Court of Justice’s order dated October 3, 2018. The Court explicitly addressed the potential impact of U.S. measures on the safety of civil aviation and the lives of those relying on it, and required the United States to remove impediments to the free export to Iran of goods and services essential for civil aviation safety.”
The systematic use of economic and financial measures—aimed at deliberately and extensively inflicting severe hardship and deprivation upon Iran’s civilian population to exert political pressure—constitutes economic terrorism, collective punishment, and a crime against humanity; furthermore, it represents a flagrant violation of the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law, including international human rights law and obligations regarding the protection of civilians, the envoy emphasized.
The Iranian envoy called on the Secretary-General and the President of the UN Security Council to urge all Member States to refrain from recognizing or implementing unilateral coercive measures by the United States that violate international law and the UN Charter—particularly those measures that inflict, or can reasonably be foreseen to cause, widespread humanitarian harm to civilian populations.
