Ukraine fighting for our freedom too warns UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:24:55 BST
04:24:55 KST

Britain will not flinch in its support for Ukraine, the Defence Secretary told allies as he announced a £100 million contribution towards the rapid delivery of air defence interceptors before winter, at a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group on Tuesday.
Wes Streeting, co-chairing the meeting alongside German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, put the money into the PURL mechanism, under which allies fund American weaponry for Ukraine. The announcement came against a requirement Kyiv had set out minutes earlier for 300 Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability and $2 billion for drones.
Attending as, in his own description, the still relatively new Secretary of State, he said the commitment felt across the country was unshakable. “Our Prime Minister Andy Burnham and I, and in fact our entire country, feel to Ukraine, to its people and to its government as they fight on the front line, not just for Ukrainian freedom and democracy, but for all of our freedom and democracy.”
Having hosted President Zelensky in Britain over the summer and visited Kyiv alongside the Prime Minister, he said he had seen the consequences of Russian aggression at first hand along with “the resilience and strength and the courage that the people of Ukraine are showing”.
The message he wanted heard in Moscow was that the winter would change nothing. “We know that this will only end through a negotiated peace. It’s really important that Russia understands that we won’t flinch in terms of our support for Ukraine as they continue to fight for their freedom and, for that matter, for ours.”
On drones, where Britain committed to supplying 120,000 this year, progress is running at more than 25,000 delivered so far with thousands more due before winter. Those cover a range of capabilities, in his account, helping Ukraine “to take the fight directly to Russia, defend itself by taking out Russian drones, and also to see what’s happening both on the battlefield and behind enemy lines”.
Britain delivered its millionth round of large calibre artillery ammunition in July, with tens of thousands more to follow, funded by Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
The Ukrainian ask
Evgeniy Khmara, attending his first meeting as Ukraine’s Defence Minister, opened by thanking partners for the munitions, the funding and the technology, but above all for the time it had bought. “We are still standing because we have strong people and we have strong friends,” he told the group. His assessment of the front was that Russia has failed to achieve strategic success and is compensating through terror against civilians. “We have built a drone kill zone. It halts the enemy’s advance and destroys over 30,000 Russian military personnel every month,” he said.
Describing the previous night’s attack, in which cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones were launched, he said Ukrainian air defences intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles. “The situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles. Russia is aware of this, which is why it’s trying to exhaust our air defence, our economy, and our society.”
Russia is planning to mobilise something in the order of 300,000 personnel on top of those already recruited, according to Ukrainian assessments, with the same expected for 2027, alongside increased production intended to turn the war into a competition of resources. Kyiv’s answer, Khmara said, is “smart technology and speed”. On money, of the 70 billion euros promised at Ankara, partners are so far providing 62 billion including bilateral assistance and the EU loan, leaving 8 billion outstanding against the declaration while the overall defence deficit stands at 23 billion euros. He asked that the necessary decisions be taken by November so results can be seen on the battlefield this winter, noting that up to 90 per cent of Ukrainian battlefield success now rests on drones.
Ukraine is contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner help and through the EU loan, but the majority will not ship for some years, which is why he asked allies to supply from existing stockpiles now in exchange for improved missiles from those future contracts. “The support for Ukraine is not a subsidy; it is an investment,” he said.
“We are offering a win-win partnership. Together, we’re creating new capacities for the security of the free world.”

China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
The response comes after three US agencies accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models.
China has issued a forceful reply against claims by the United States that top Chinese artificial intelligence companies have engaged in “industrial scale” theft of their US counterparts’ AI models.
The response on Wednesday comes after three US federal agencies – the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) – accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models to benefit their own systems.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3OpenAI unveils latest AI model amid rising scrutiny and safety concerns
- list 2 of 3As the China-US AI race reaches Cairo, Egypt faces a strategic decision
- list 3 of 3AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
The joint advisory on Tuesday said Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI had distilled “billions of tokens” from US models since “at least late 2024”, likely with the Chinese government’s “awareness”.
Tokens are the smallest units of text that AI models read, or generate.
On Wednesday, China’s Commerce Ministry dismissed the allegations and accused the US of seeking a “monopoly of the AI industry”.
“If the U.S. suppresses Chinese AI companies under the pretext of targeting distillation, China will take resolute countermeasures,” the ministry said in a statement to the Associated Press.
Distillation is a method in which lesser AI models are trained on more advanced ones. The ministry said the practice is commonplace in the AI industry, including by US AI companies. But American firms say the volume in which it’s being done by Chinese AI models amounts to stealing.
“The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the US advisory claimed.
The AP reported that China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called on the US to “refrain from making unfounded accusations or smears” against China.
“China’s AI development is the result of high-level technological self-reliance and strength,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference. “We maintain that all parties should strengthen cooperation to promote AI development that is open, inclusive, universally beneficial and oriented toward the common good.”
Xi visit
The US advisory comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the US, where President Donald Trump will host a summit on a range of topics, including AI.
In a rare move, Xi could be accompanied on his US visit by a large number Chinese executives, according to the Reuters news agency. It is not clear which executives would join the delegation, but past meetings between the two countries may indicate AI leaders could be in the mix.
Xi brought Alibaba founder Jack Ma during his 2015 visit to the US. When Trump visited Xi during a trip to Beijing in May, the US president was joined by more than a dozen American executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Under Trump, the US government has taken a hardline against efforts to advance Chinese AI models. China is aggressively investing heavily in artificial intelligence and robotics, pouring nearly $300bn into what the government sees as the country’s next economic engine.
While speaking in Dallas on Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience that China can “never get ahead” of the US in AI.
“The Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said.
The Chinese companies named in the US advisory did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Tate brothers to remain in US jail as they fight extradition to UK
- Published
Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape and trafficking.
A federal judge in Miami denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".
The brothers have been held in US custody since their July arrest, after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled new charges. The UK has until 16 September to submit a full extradition request, Reuters reported.
They will "continue to defend themselves against the allegations" and "engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction", their lawyers said.
The two are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.
CPS originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.
US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges.
Last weekend, Romanian prosecutors officially indicted the polarising social media influencers with a range of trafficking and sex offences.
The former kickboxers had primarily been based in Romania since 2017, drawing a large audience - primarily young men - through controversial messages about women and images of a luxury lifestyle. Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Andrew Tate first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.
The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.
Several prominent US politicians, including Florida's Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, objected to the Tate brothers' arrival in the US.
The brothers have denied all charges and allegations.
Wednesday's decision means the brothers will remain jailed during what could be a lengthy extradition process.
US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis ruled that, while the Tates "may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction".
The judge said that their lack of ties to the US and their strong foreign connections "demonstrate a risk of flight that has not been overcome".
The Tates' lawyers have argued they should be released on bail pending their extradition proceeding, saying the brothers were not a flight risk and did not pose a danger to the community.
The lawyers have also argued that they had complied with the terms of their release while facing charges earlier in the UK and Romania.
At a hearing on the question of their potential release in August, Andrew Tate said he had "never committed the crimes I'm accused of."
Tristan Tate described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little access to sunlight and exercise, adding that he had lost 14 pounds (6.4kg).
"It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The British Embassy had asked the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK sought extradition, writing in court filings that the brothers were "flight risks" and claiming they "would interfere with witnesses if released".

The UK was right to sanction Israeli settlements. Now it must do more to protect Palestinians under occupation.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:08:21 UTC
04:08:21 KST

The UK has crossed a political Rubicon on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. Yesterday, the Government recognised that Israel’s continued control over Palestinian territory is unlawful, bringing it into line with the International Court of Justice’s 2024 Advisory Opinion.
For decades, British governments have condemned Israel’s settlements as illegal while allowing the settlement project to expand with impunity. Palestinian communities have been displaced and Israeli control over the West Bank has become ever more entrenched. Yesterday’s announcement matters because it puts a concrete consequence behind that position: it will ban trade in goods and some services with illegal Israeli settlements.
The ban is welcome. But it should be the beginning, not the end, of this shift in policy. The UK now needs to address the wider policies and relationships it has pursued over the years that have allowed Israel’s unlawful occupation of the West Bank to become so deeply entrenched.
But this is not simply about where the dates and avocados on our supermarket shelves come from. It is about Palestinian land being violently seized, communities being fragmented, and Palestinians being denied the basic conditions to live safely, move freely and access healthcare. For Palestinians who have lived with this reality for decades, the question is whether and when this will begin to change the reality on the ground.
In July, a three-month-old Palestinian boy, Ahmad Maarouf Zaid, died after Israeli forces prevented his family from crossing a checkpoint for more than an hour as they tried to get him to hospital in critical condition. Weeks later, a Palestinian woman who was six months pregnant and suffering severe bleeding was held at a military checkpoint for more than 30 minutes while the ambulance carrying her was searched. Doctors saved her life, but her baby tragically died.
For Palestinians, these restrictions are part of everyday life. In the West Bank, there are now 925 movement obstacles, including checkpoints and road closures. A journey that should take minutes can take hours, or become impossible altogether. On average, Palestinians in the West Bank spend around 90 hours a month dealing with checkpoints, road closures and other restrictions on movement.
Between January and July this year, the World Health Organization recorded 98 attacks on healthcare in the West Bank, including 92 incidents involving the obstruction of healthcare. Eighty-three ambulances and other health transport were affected, as well as 11 health facilities. In July alone, there were 37 attacks on healthcare.
Yesterday’s announcement also had implications beyond the issue of settlement trade alone. The Government has now accepted what the International Court of Justice found in 2024: that Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful. That should have consequences for how the UK responds to the system of control that has entrenched Israeli rule over Palestinian land and restricted Palestinians’ access to healthcare.
The Government also struck a new tone on Gaza, acknowledging that “there must be accountability” for what has happened there and hinting at further possible sanctions. Nearly a year into the so-called “ceasefire”, more than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed, while Israel’s “Yellow Line” has advanced to cover around 70% of Gaza, displacing our colleagues and communities we serve in the process. At the same time, vital aid and medical supplies remain critically obstructed while Gaza’s health system lies in ruins. Gaza cannot wait – the UK must follow its words with rapid action to puncture Israel’s impunity.
For Palestinians who have lived under this system for decades, the question is whether the UK’s ‘reset’ will make a difference to their lives. Can Palestinians move freely, reach healthcare and live safely in their own communities? For those living with the consequences of the occupation every day, recognition of their plight will only mean something if it is followed by an end to Israel’s violent occupation, its genocide in Gaza, and the escalating state-backed settler violence against communities across the West Bank.
Yesterday’s decision should mark a complete circuit break in the way the UK has dealt with Israel’s occupation for far too long. Israel’s control over Palestinian land has deepened while condemnation has too often stopped at words. The UK should now make sure this decision is followed by decisive and comprehensive action.
The UK has crossed a political Rubicon. It should not turn back.

Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.
The Hugging Face hack by OpenAI’s models that escaped containment in July “is why it’s even more important that we move quickly to regulate and legislate on superintelligent AI,” Sobel tells WIRED, “because AI is developing at pace, and I’m afraid to say those developing it don’t know exactly what’s in it.”
In an unusual move, the parliamentary bill was drafted by the nonprofit ControlAI, which is backed by Skype founding engineer and former DeepMind investor director Jaan Tallinn. It was founded by Andrea Miotti, who had previously been working at AI safety startup Conjecture but tells WIRED he wanted to make the public and policymakers aware of the “open secret” that “developing superintelligence could cause human extinction.”
Conjecture founder Connor Leahy now leads ControlAI’s US arm, which consulted on Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence development, in addition to having briefed nearly 200 congressional offices and more than 20 members of the Senate and House of Representatives on the extinction risk of superintelligence.
Sobel will present his bill in full in November. While he accepts it’s rare for the UK government to accept private legislation like this, Sobel hopes it may lead the government to work with other countries on an international ban.
Sobel has previously tried in vain to introduce a “kill switch” into the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would allow the government to pull the plug on any data center hosting an AI agent that presented a threat. The mechanism, which was also proposed by ControlAI, is similar to a law pushed for by both Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the US. AI minister Kanishka Narayan, then working under former prime minister Keir Starmer, shot it down, pointing out that the bill already allows the government powers to intervene if compromised network and information systems cause a national security risk. That could include requiring an entity to cease using and isolate an AI model, he noted.
But that may not be enough, Sobel says, hoping to meet with the government to hammer out details of which companies would be included within the scope of the proposed rules. “I think this might be the crucial year,” he says. “If we leave it too long, things may move past our ability to regulate it.”
Peers across parties in the UK parliament’s upper house, including former AI minister Viscount Camrose, tried unsuccessfully to reintroduce the measure last week. They have been frustrated as the binding regulation on frontier AI firms promised by the Labour government when they won power in 2024 has failed to materialize.
While peer Tim Clement-Jones admitted they shouldn’t be trying to “shoehorn” AI regulation into a cybersecurity bill. In the absence of any other AI legislation, “we have no choice,” he said in a speech to parliament. “We must have more control and oversight over that sort of behavior, because you can see its consequences,” said Alexandra Freeman in the debate, referring to the Hugging Face incident. “This legislation is our only opportunity now.”
Nearly nine out of 10 Britons support independent regulation of the technology, a poll by the Ada Lovelace Institute showed in December. Meanwhile, nearly three times as many (38 percent) believe that the risks of AI outweigh the benefits as vice versa (13 percent), according to official statistics. But “the government has been completely deaf to this, and they have paid no attention to those who are advocating for this,” Clement-Jones says, arguing that the public's lack of trust in the technology will curb adoption.
The UK government evaluates the capabilities and safety of advanced artificial intelligence models through the research body the AI Security Institute. Cooperation is voluntary for AI companies, as the organization has no legal powers to access unreleased models for testing or ban their public release. For example, the agency reportedly did not get access to Anthropic’s latest model, Claude Mythos 5.1, for testing.
“I think it's a rather naive position to imagine that we can do things on a voluntary basis,” says Clement-Jones. “Do you really think that the big AI companies have got everybody's welfare at heart?”

The Ministry of Defence has set out how £16 billion of UK military support for Ukraine has been allocated across five financial years, while declining to provide a departmental breakdown of the Government’s wider non-military assistance.
The figures were disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked for a breakdown of the UK’s stated £25 billion total support for Ukraine, including £16 billion in military assistance and £5.6 billion in non-military support.
Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said: “The UK has committed to providing at least £3 billion in military support a year to Ukraine until Financial Year (FY) 2030-31 and for as long as needed.”
She added: “To date, the MOD has committed £16 billion in military support, including the £2.26 billion ERA loan contribution.”
According to the figures provided by the department, military support amounted to £2.5 billion in 2022-23, £2.3 billion in 2023-24 and £3 billion in 2024-25. For 2025-26, the MOD lists £3.2 billion of Ukraine funding alongside £1.5 billion through the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration loan, producing a total of £4.7 billion for that financial year.
For 2026-27, the department lists a further £3 billion in Ukraine funding and £750 million through the ERA mechanism, giving a total of £3.75 billion. The MOD table puts direct Ukraine funding across the five years at £13.8 billion and the ERA contribution at £2.26 billion, producing a stated overall military-support total of £16 billion when rounded.
The Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration mechanism forms part of the wider G7 arrangement intended to provide Ukraine with financing backed by revenues generated from immobilised Russian sovereign assets.
Sandher-Jones said the department regularly accounts for the support it provides directly, stating: “The MOD routinely publishes the support it has directly provided to Ukraine in its Annual Report and Accounts.”
Obese-Jecty’s question also sought a breakdown by department and year of the £5.6 billion in non-military support referred to in the Government’s July statement on UK assistance to Ukraine. The MOD did not provide those figures. Sandher-Jones said: “We do not comment on spending by other Government departments.”

Breathing depends on a cylinder: Gaza faces medical oxygen crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:40:38 UTC
03:40:38 KST

Breathing depends on a cylinder: Gaza faces medical oxygen crisis
Only 12 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen-generation stations remain operational, worsening the health crisis in the besieged enclave.
Az-Zuwayda, Gaza Strip – Ali Humaida’s heart rate quickens as he watches the gauge on the oxygen cylinder sitting in the corner of his tent.
As the needle falls, he looks at his 14-year-old son, Abdulaziz, lying on a mattress in the family’s tent in central Gaza’s az-Zuwayda, worried about how long the remaining oxygen will last – and where he will find more when it runs out.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Inside Israel’s prisons, where Ben-Gvir’s cruelty is policy
- list 2 of 3As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
- list 3 of 3Gaza students with overseas university offers, scholarships remain trapped
Abdulaziz depends on a continuous supply of supplemental oxygen, his father says. One night, when the family’s cylinder emptied before they were able to replace it, his breathing rapidly deteriorated.
“The cylinder suddenly ran out in the middle of the night,” Ali recalled. “The minutes turned into a nightmare. We began fanning him with our hands and pieces of cardboard while watching his face turn blue, terrified he would lose consciousness or slip into a coma right before our eyes, while we stood completely helpless.”
For families caring for oxygen-dependent patients in Gaza, such emergencies have become increasingly difficult to avoid.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health warned on August 15 that only 12 of the strip’s 34 oxygen-generation stations remained operational, while only four of 30 devices used to fill oxygen cylinders were still working. The remaining equipment was overworked with repeated mechanical failures, the ministry said.
These conditions have made obtaining cylinders particularly difficult for patients such as Abdulaziz, who receive much of their care outside hospitals.
“Every minute that passes means the oxygen is running out,” Ali said. “I am constantly asking myself: How much is left in the cylinder? Will it last until morning? And if it empties, where will I get another one?”
Complicated medical history
Abdulaziz has lived with serious health problems since birth. He was born with a congenital heart defect and has underdeveloped lungs.
Since childhood, he has also suffered from hydrocephalus, or cerebrospinal fluid buildup in the brain. Abdulaziz underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain by inserting a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt that drains excess fluid.
In addition, he has autism spectrum disorder and requires extensive daily care – something that is extremely difficult in a displaecment camp in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war.
Before the war, Abdulaziz received regular specialised treatment at a hospital in Israel. That has now stopped, leaving the family dependent on Gaza’s health system, which has been devastated by Israeli attacks.
The cost of caring for Abdulaziz has also increased. His father, Ali, estimates that medicine, diapers and transportation now cost the family between 950 and 1,100 shekels ($315 and $365) a month – double pre-war prices.
“Abdulaziz cannot express pain like other children because of his autism, but I can see the distress in his eyes,” Ali said. “I am not asking for the impossible, all I want is for my son to breathe freely.”
When oxygen runs out
Interrupting supplemental oxygen can be dangerous for patients who depend on the therapy to maintain adequate blood-oxygen levels.
Dr Ghada Hassouna, a physician at al-Aqsa Martyr’s Hospital in Deir el-Balah, said a patient whose oxygen saturation level plummet can develop rapid breathing, a faster heart rate and cyanosis – a bluish discolouration of the skin caused by poor oxygen and blood flows.
Inadequate oxygen can also damage vital organs, particularly the brain and the heart.
Hassouna explained that the brain cells are exceptionally sensitive to oxygen deprivation, and are the most vulnerable to rapid breakdown and damage. In Abdulaziz’s case, any drop in oxygen levels can cause severe or permanent nerve damage.
This is an issue that impacts more than just one family.
According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, the majority of oxygen-generation stations being out of service is the result of a systematic Israeli policy across border crossings.
Israeli authorities continue to restrict and ban the entry of spare parts and specialised lubricants for hospital generators and oxygen plants, as well as blocking new plants meant to compensate for the shortage.
Israel classifies oxygen cylinders, accompanying devices and electrical generators as “dual-use” items, prohibiting their entry or spare parts through closed crossings.
At the same time, the environment of forced displacement imposes an extra layer of suffering.
Hundreds of thousands live in open areas lacking basic proper ventilation, filled with dust and toxic emissions from burning plastic waste and alternative power generators, which doubles the number of patients suffering from acute pneumonia and respiratory ailments such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
This comes at a time when the Ministry of Health and several hospitals in the strip have completely halted external oxygen cylinder refilling services for patients receiving care at home or in displacement tents.
The decision was a forced measure taken by the health system after nearing collapse, in an effort to preserve remaining oxygen supplies for bed networks in critical hospital departments such as intensive care units, neonatal incubators, and operating rooms.
Facing this complex field reality, medical staff explain that the decision was not an administrative choice, but a response to a catastrophic reality imposed by war conditions and the systematic destruction of health infrastructure.
The United Nations estimates that about 350,000 people in Gaza are living with chronic diseases, with treatments severely disrupted by the war.
Mohammad Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Medical Complex, said Gaza is coping with shortages of half of essential medicines and more than 80 percent of laboratory materials. He estimated that about 21,000 patients and wounded people needed treatment outside Gaza, including more than 4,000 cancer patients and more than 10,000 injured people requiring advanced surgical care.
For now, patients in Gaza have to make do with what is available inside the Palestinian enclave.
Abdulaziz’s family measures time by what remains in his oxygen cylinder.
“We want him to be able to travel and resume his treatment,” Ali said. “Until then, we need a stable supply of oxygen.”
“All we want is for our son to breathe with dignity, without the constant fear that his breathing could stop at any moment.”

Reuters reported damage to key units at the facility at the time, but details were not disclosed.
Now, favorable weather conditions have made it possible to obtain high-quality satellite imagery confirming that two primary oil-processing units and three secondary processing units were hit.
The following facilities were identified at the refinery: ELOU-AT-1 — hit and shut down, with a capacity of 1.7 million tons per year; ELOU-AT-6 — hit and shut down, with a capacity of 7.6 million tons per year; ELOU-AVT-2 — undergoing repairs following a previous strike, with a capacity of 2.8 million tons per year; and ELOU-AVT-6 — fully operational, with a capacity of 8 million tons per year.
The secondary processing units LCh/24/9 and LCh/24/10, which are diesel fuel hydrotreating units, as well as the LG-35/8-300B catalytic reforming unit, were also identified.
Of the refinery’s total design primary processing capacity of 20.1 million tons per year, more than 12 million tons are currently out of service, accounting for about 60% of its capacity.
The refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with an estimated capacity of approximately 330,000-350,000 barrels per day.
Ukrainian drones first hit the refinery on March 8, 2025. KINEF, which accounts for 7% of Russia’s total oil refining and produces 2 million tons of gasoline and 7 million tons of diesel fuel annually, had already been forced to halt operations for extended repairs twice this year due to UAV attacks — on March 26 and May 5.
The refinery had never been fully restored. In August, it was operating at approximately 50% capacity.

New maps reveal hidden landscapes inside a prehistoric supercontinent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:38:14 UTC
03:38:14 KST

More than 180 million years after the supercontinent Gondwana’s breakup, scientists are still learning the true reach of this prehistoric landmass that once stretched across the globe.
By analyzing more than 25,000 volcanic rocks, a new study finds that Gondwana likely accounted for around 80 percent of total global land area around 500 million years ago. The analysis identifies pieces of Earth’s crust deep beneath Asia, Europe and North America that were once part of the supercontinent. That’s far larger than scientists had thought: older studies estimated Gondwana’s size as equivalent to around 64 percent of global land area.
This massive size means Gondwana’s formation and development over time could have been instrumental in the Cambrian explosion of life, the authors write—a period from about 540 to 530 million years ago when nearly all modern-day animals’ ancestors appeared on Earth for the first time.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To uncover the hidden landscapes, researchers analyzed the chemical composition of deeply buried rocks from different geochemistry databases and mapped Gondwana using the distribution of elements within the rocks.
The newly revealed geographical areas, combined with existing knowledge of the supercontinent, reveal that Gondwana could have had outsized effects on sea level, atmospheric gas and volcanic eruptions—together these factors would have influenced early life on Earth, the researchers write. The findings were published today in Science Advances.
It’s possible that still-undiscovered parts of the continent could have been submerged or recycled back into Earth’s crust, the authors write. That means that even this massive new scale could be an underestimate as scientists continue to piece together our planet’s early history.

Israel opened its first permanent embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday, marking a sharp turnaround after years of strained relations under the country’s previous government.

“This is the first resident embassy in Slovenia, it is indeed a historic day,” Sa'ar said at a joint news conference. “This is a clear expression of Israel’s commitment to our friendship and to its future.”
Relations had deteriorated significantly under the previous Slovenian government, which recognized a Palestinian state, barred Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from entering the country, halted arms agreements with Israel and canceled Israir flights to Ljubljana.
Since taking office in June, Jansa’s government has reversed those measures and voiced support for Israel within the European Union. Sa'ar announced the decision to open the embassy on the day the new government was sworn in.
The opening also comes as Israel faces growing diplomatic pressure elsewhere in Europe over its policies in the West Bank, highlighting the contrast between worsening ties with some governments and the renewed relationship with Ljubljana.
Sa'ar said the timing of the embassy opening, just before Rosh Hashanah, carried particular significance.
“We are inaugurating the embassy two days before Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year,” he said. “It is a sign of new beginnings and new hopes.”
During Sa'ar’s visit, the two countries also signed agreements to expand cooperation in education, science, culture, youth and sports.
“We signed cooperation agreements today between the two countries in various areas, including youth, sports, education and scholarships for students,” Kajzer said. “We will strive for relations with Israel that are open, strong and based on trust.”
An Israeli business delegation representing major companies and economic organizations accompanied Sa'ar to Slovenia, where an Israeli-Slovenian business forum was also held with the participation of the two foreign ministers.
“After a long period of less intensive political contacts, it is time to shift cooperation between Slovenia and Israel into a higher gear,” Kajzer said.
The policy shift has faced opposition at home. The liberal Freedom Movement of former prime minister Robert Golob and the Left party submitted a proposal to parliament Wednesday seeking Jansa’s impeachment, accusing his government of pursuing a foreign policy overly aligned with Israel.
Student groups, left-wing activists and pro-Palestinian organizations were also expected to demonstrate against the embassy opening.
The new mission is the fifth Israeli embassy Sa'ar has inaugurated over the past year and a half, and the first permanent Israeli diplomatic mission ever established in Slovenia.

The intelligence service described the case as part of an established practice in which Ukrainian children are taken to Russia under the guise of vacations, rehabilitation programs, or participation in cultural and educational activities. Some of those taken away are then not returned.
According to the SZRU, Russian occupation administrations, guardianship authorities, and organizers of such trips are involved in the process. Once in Russia, the children come under the control of local authorities, which can determine where they will subsequently live and their legal status.
The SZRU warned that the reported removals form part of a broader system in Russia that exposes children to various forms of exploitation.
According to the agency, this includes state-linked practices such as involving children in work at defense industry enterprises or their potential recruitment by Russian intelligence services. The SZRU also alleged risks of criminal exploitation, including sex trafficking, human trafficking, illicit organ transplantation, and other abuses.
The latest case comes amid ongoing Ukrainian efforts to locate and return children forcibly taken by Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this year that more than 2,100 Ukrainian children had been brought back through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative.
In a Telegram post on April 22, Zelenskyy said that 150 of those children had been returned since the beginning of 2026.

Curacao extend Dick Advocaat's contract until 2027

Halis Sünnetci
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Curacao head coach Dick Advocaat signed a contract extension that will keep him in charge until July 2027, the country's football federation announced on Wednesday.
The Federashon Futbol Korsou (FFK) said the 78-year-old Dutch coach agreed to extend his deal through July 31 next year, citing continuity and stability around the national team.
Advocaat guided Curacao to their first-ever FIFA World Cup in 2026, making the Caribbean island the smallest country by both population and land area ever to qualify for the tournament.
Curacao finished bottom of Group E in their debut appearance, earning one point from a goalless draw against Ecuador.
Advocaat also became the oldest head coach in World Cup history at age 78.
"This is a fantastic group to work with. We have achieved something special together, and I look forward to continuing to build on what we have accomplished with the players and staff," Advocaat said.
The veteran coach resigned in February to focus on his daughter's health before returning to the role in May following the departure of Fred Rutten.
Advocaat, who has managed several national teams and clubs during a coaching career spanning nearly four decades, took charge of Curacao in 2024.
His major club honors include league titles with PSV Eindhoven, Rangers and Zenit St. Petersburg, as well as the 2008 UEFA Cup with the Russian club.
At the international level, he led the Netherlands to the 1994 World Cup quarterfinals and Euro 2004 semifinals, and also coached South Korea and Russia at major tournaments.
FFK Acting President Fabi Constansia said the extension reflected the federation's desire for "continuity and stability" while it continued investing in the development of football in Curacao.

Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:45 UTC
02:57:45 KST

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first folding smartphone. The company announced the device at its annual September event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California.
The iPhone Duo comes in Star White and Night Sky, and costs $1,999 for 256 GB of storage. While preorders kick off on October 16, the device won’t officially go on sale until October 23.
It arrives alongside the pro versions of Apple’s handsets, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, and when you open the Duo up, it reveals a second, 7.6-inch display—remarkably close to the iPad Mini’s screen size. Apple says it kept the aspect ratio consistent across both the front and inner screen for the highest quality when viewing content.
The Duo has a titanium frame with a mirror finish, Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass on the back, and Ceramic Shield 2 glass on the front. It even sports an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, beating Samsung to the punch. (Right now, Google's folding Pixels are the only phones with an IP68 rating.
Apple says the hinge has a “custom variable torque profile” that precisely opens and closes the phone in an “effortlessly smooth” way. When it’s open, Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. As Samsung does with its “Flex Titanium” technology, Apple uses a carbon fiber metal plate below the display to better control the stress caused by bending the display. That, alongside a nano-texture finish, helps keep the display flat and “minimizes crease visibility.” An Apple-designed scratch-resistance coating sits on top.
The Duo weighs 254 grams, is 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded. Compare that to Samsung’s new Fold8, which is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded. If you’ve held an iPhone 17 Pro Max, that’s 233 grams, so the Duo is quite hefty. Bulky devices typically turn customers off—that's why Samsung spent so much time trying to shave off as much weight as possible on its latest folding devices.
Surprisingly, there is no Face ID sensor, likely to save space inside the phone for the folding components. Instead, like some of Apple’s tablets, the iPhone Duo brings back the fingerprint-sensing Touch ID integrated into the side power button. This is also the first iPhone to support the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year, though there’s no way to naturally store the stylus on the edges of the device like the iPad’s magnetic Pencil dock.
Apple says the Duo has the biggest battery ever in an iPhone. Like most book-style folds, it’s a split system where a battery rests on both sides. That will net you up to 31 hours of video playback with the inner display and 44 hours with the outer display—or 24 hours of mixed overall use per charge. It also sports Apple’s new custom C2 modem (with mmWave 5G support in the US) and the A20 Pro, the same chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.
There are only two cameras on the back—a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide. The lack of a telephoto zoom option is a sacrifice even Samsung made on its latest Galaxy Z Fold8. Like most book-like folds, it has two selfie cameras—a 12-megapixel camera on the outer screen and a second “FaceTime camera" on the inner display, though this one is hidden under the display.
There are familiar folding phone features here with the camera, like distracting a kid with a fun cartoon character on the outer screen to get them to look at the camera. Or your subject can preview the photo before you hit capture. The iPhone Duo can stand upright by itself, so you can set it down and it will automatically capture group photos if everyone stands at the ready.
Hardware is just one part of the story, though. The software needs to adapt and take advantage of the larger screen. Apple has been improving how apps adapt to different screen sizes for some time, making it easy for developers to scale apps from the iPhone to the iPad to the Mac, and even visionOS on the Apple Vision Pro. That means you’ll be able to enjoy iPad-like apps when unfolding the iPhone Duo.
Apple says it has moved essential controls to the side, stacked vertically, to maximize screen space. Even the dock is oriented vertically. The software transitions gracefully as you open the phone; apps will show more information—like your inbox and messages—and you can split-screen apps. You can fold it in half and set it down, and the screen will react accordingly.
Folding Time
Apple is a late entrant to the foldable phone market, which has been around since Samsung debuted the first Galaxy Fold in 2019. Since then, phone makers like Honor, Google, Motorola, and Oppo have all made folding phones. In recent years, devices have rapidly gotten slimmer, lighter, and more durable.
The iPhone Duo has a book-like shape and is similar in size to Samsung’s recent Galaxy Z Fold8, reminiscent of Google’s original Pixel Fold. This “passport-style” fold—which stands shorter and unfolds wider than many of the first wave of foldable designs—is better suited for media consumption since it eliminates the severe letterboxing that places thick black bars around the TV show or movie you’re watching.
Apple is expected to help grow a category that has been declining for five straight quarters by 13 percent year over year—potentially capturing up to 30 percent of the foldable market share by the end of 2026, according to IDC’s Nabila Popal, a senior research director. But the folding phone market is still niche, “around 2 percent by the end of this year of the global smartphone market.”
Popal says a recent IDC survey asked consumers whether they were interested in buying a foldable smartphone when it was time to upgrade, and 60 percent said they are not likely to buy one. However, when asked if Apple released a folding smartphone, almost 33 percent said they “absolutely” would.
“Apple has such a strong market pull,” Popal tells WIRED. “The average consumer didn’t know about [memory price increases] until Apple made an announcement that they’re going to increase prices. “Coming into foldables, it's going to create overall excitement for the category. And it's good for the consumer, too. It's always good to have more competition and more choice.”
One area of concern is the device’s durability and repairability, as folding phones are notoriously more prone to damage and are tough to fix. Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of Sustainability at iFixit, tells WIRED her team has never taken apart a foldable they’d call truly repairable.
“Manufacturers have come a long way since the Galaxy Fold first dropped,” she says. “But the gains in durability haven’t come with gains in repairability.”
New Economics
While Apple announced three premium iPhone models today, it is not releasing the base iPhone 18 this year—marking the first time it’s breaking up the launch cycle of the core iPhone lineup. Instead, the iPhone 18 is expected to launch in the spring of 2027 alongside the iPhone 18e and second-generation iPhone Air.
Despite the eye-watering price and the current economic climate, Popal says the iPhone Duo is “guaranteed to be a blockbuster.”
“Apple defied all odds and broke the $1,000 barrier when they first launched the $1,000 smartphone,” Popal says. “Yes, there’s going to be sticker shock, but Apple caters to a very high-end consumer segment who can afford it.”
Over the summer, Apple introduced a new iPhone leasing program to help ease the price of its phones on consumers' wallets, and it’s likely to prove popular with the uber-expensive iPhone Duo. Chamberlain says that for people who replace their phone regularly, it gives them a path to do it where the device gets back into the reuse stream and boosts the refurbished market, which isn’t a bad thing for electronic waste. However, Apple’s leasing agreements mean the device needs to be returned in the condition it was received.
“iFixit is committed to the idea that you should own your shit,” she says. “You should be able to repair things, modify things, hack your own devices. It’s sad to see the tech world move away from that principle, and Apple encouraging people to lease devices instead of buying them.”

Back to work, not school: Yemen’s crisis forces children to drop out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:37 UTC
02:57:37 KST

Back to work, not school: Yemen’s crisis forces children to drop out
Struggling families in Yemen are forced to choose between education and survival amid mounting economic challenges.
Taiz, Yemen – It was around the middle of the morning, and children at a nearby school were preparing for their break. But 11-year-old Hasnaa Jaber was walking through empty farmland on the outskirts of Taiz city, collecting discarded plastic bottles.
Hasnaa lives with her impoverished family in an informal settlement for people displaced by the country’s more than decade-long war. Instead of going to school, she works alongside her family to help make ends meet.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
- list 2 of 3Qatar says reopening Strait of Hormuz ‘unconditionally’ is a priority
- list 3 of 3Yemen’s war is back: A new battle for Sanaa and the Red Sea
“My dream is to become a teacher. I studied up to the third grade, but then I dropped out of school along with my two older brothers to help my father,” Hasnaa told Al Jazeera.
The new academic year began in government-controlled areas of Yemen on August 30, but Hasnaa and other children from families in difficult financial situations like hers are not in the classroom.
She is one of 3.2 million children who are out of school in Yemen this year, according to an estimate by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). That is an increase on the 1.8 million children UNICEF says were out of school in 2015, during the first year of the war.
Of Hasnaa’s four siblings, only one currently attends school, as she is too young to collect plastic bottles or wash cars – the kind of work the family does.
“My two brothers and I asked my father if we could resume our studies this year,” she said. “He was happy that we wanted to go back to school, but providing basic food for the family remains a major struggle. He promised us that we will go back next year.”
Hasnaa has friends who still attend school, but she feels closest to those who are also out of school, bound by their shared hardship.
“I don’t enjoy spending time with the children who go to school because they look down on us,” she explained. “But next year, I will return to my studies and fulfil my dream of becoming a teacher.”
Food is priority
Hasnaa is able to earn around 1,500 Yemeni rials (around $1) a day selling the plastic bottles she gathers to scrap traders.
That money is welcomed by her father, 35-year-old Jaber Ali, who is struggling to provide for his family. Fighting forced him to flee his hometown, near Taiz, eight years ago.
He doesn’t like the situation his family is in – he never received an education himself, but had hoped his children would.
“I used to work and keep my children in school, but the situation has worsened over the past two years. What I earn from washing cars is no longer enough to provide them with basic food, let alone cover other necessities,” Jaber told Al Jazeera.
Rising living costs and scarce work have squeezed the family. Jaber said school means paying for books, stationery, and other daily expenses he can’t afford.
“I was left with two choices: either send my children to school and watch them starve, or ask them to help me earn a living,” Jaber said. “I had to choose the latter because food is the top priority right now, not education.”
“We must encourage our children to study, and I do my best to keep their spirits up,” he added. “I don’t tell them they will never return to school – I tell them this is just a temporary phase, and I hope conditions will improve so they can resume their education soon.”
Byproduct of war
According to the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP), published by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), nearly 6.6 million Yemeni children are in need of education assistance in 2026. That figure includes children who are out of school, as well as those still enrolled but facing serious barriers to learning, including conflict, poverty, and the collapse of basic services.
Ammar al-Sharjabi, an education expert who has worked with the Ministries of Education in both Sanaa and Aden, explained that the crisis is one of the most severe consequences of the war – particularly when it comes to forcing children to drop out of school.
“Dropping out of school deprives children of their right to education and weakens their chances of securing stable employment in the future, potentially forcing them into hard labour at an early age,” he explained. “At the societal level, persistent dropout rates lead to increased illiteracy, poverty, and unemployment, adversely impacting development and the community’s overall future.”
A source at the Ministry of Education in Aden, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, said economic pressures driving children into work are difficult to fix in light of Yemen’s war – which has escalated dramatically in recent weeks after years of relative calm.
“The ministry is deeply concerned about students dropping out, but this is the direct result of dire economic conditions – not an educational issue that can be solved within the classroom alone,” the source said.
He added that the ministry coordinates with humanitarian organisations to support vulnerable children, but intervention is difficult when parents feel that they have to make their children work.
“This surge in dropouts is a byproduct of the ongoing war and its economic fallout,” he added. “As soon as parents secure a stable source of income, we will see children return to school immediately. No parent wants to see their child deprived of an education.”
Child breadwinners
A recent Save the Children assessment covering around 2,000 households in southern and southwestern Yemen found that 92 percent of those surveyed do not know where their next meal will come from, and 95 percent rely on precarious daily informal labour for their income.
As a result, 84 percent of families could not afford basic educational expenses, such as uniforms and textbooks.
The assessment also found that nearly one in five school dropout cases identified was linked to child labour.
Thirteen-year-old Ahmed Abdulelah is not displaced, but is one of those dropouts.
He left school after his father died of cancer two years ago. The family exhausted its savings on treatment, and Ahmed, the eldest of four siblings, began working at a grocery store.
“My father provided us with everything we needed,” Ahmed said. “But since he passed away, there has been no one else to help us, and I cannot bear to see my mother suffer.”
Unlike many of his peers, Ahmed does not dwell on the grief of dropping out of school. For him, the sacrifice is worth it as long as his younger siblings can stay in class.
And he has no plans to resume his education, believing his window of opportunity has passed. Instead, he has set his sights on becoming a shopkeeper one day.
“I work here so my siblings can finish their education,” he said. “They will make up for what I lost, and I am proud that our family doesn’t have to beg or rely on anyone else.”

Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:57:14 UTC
02:57:14 KST

Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.
The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.
But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.
Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.
“What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.
Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.”
While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”
Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.
She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”
Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”
Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”
He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”
There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.
Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.
The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.
Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.
“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”
Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”
They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”
Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.
Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.

He also questioned how Chadha’s name became the 747th entry when the draft roll had 746 voters and the final roll was yet to be published.The CEO office said eligible persons whose names are not on the electoral roll can seek inclusion by submitting Form 6 with the required documents.It also referred to the Election Commission’s May 14 guidelines on the Special Intensive Revision, which state that additions made during the SIR period would receive serial numbers continuing from the last entry in the draft electoral roll.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Ceramic, Specs, Release Date

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:43:38 UTC
02:43:38 KST

Apple has unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 today during its September hardware event.
The new models retain the signature designs of their predecessors but add a faster S11 chip, new health and fitness features, and the watchOS 27 software update announced at WWDC last June.
Both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on the upgraded S11 chip, which Apple says delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, along with improved Siri capabilities. Apple is also expanding the smartwatch’s wellness-tracking suite with a redesigned Health app that includes a Longevity tab with new metrics, like Health Age and a Readiness score.
There’s also a new “Health Sensing System,” designed with 32 electrodes for more accurate readings (the Series 11 only had two), photodiodes organized in a ring to capture light more efficiently, and new LEDs that allow heart rate measurements to be collected every 5 seconds, giving you a continuous stream of heart data throughout the day.
Both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on the upgraded S11 chip, which Apple says delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, along with improved Siri capabilities. Apple is also expanding the smartwatch’s wellness-tracking suite with a redesigned Health app that includes a Longevity tab with new metrics, like Health Age and a Readiness score.
Perhaps most notably, the Series 12 brings back the ceramic case, available in pearl white and night blue finishes. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, marketed as a luxury alternative to the company’s long-retired 18-karat gold edition; the ceramic casing was discontinued in 2020. The aluminum and titanium models are available in black, space gray aluminum, natural titanium, gold, and a new dark bronze color.
The new hardware arrives alongside watchOS 27, which will also be made available to people who already own compatible Apple Watches when the Series 12 goes on sale. The new OS updates the divisive Liquid Glass redesign on the smartwatch, and adds a more capable Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence.
Following the industry trend of AI-notetakers, the new Siri Recap can translate and transcribe real-time conversations for users. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to use their watch’s dial to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds, then read what the server said on their Apple Watch screen.
There are several features—all of them opt-in, at least for the person wearing the watch—that are powered by the watch’s ability to record the wearer’s surroundings. Read more about them in Lily Hay Newman’s story about the Apple Watch’s newfound listening abilities on WIRED.
WatchOS 27 also introduces a dynamic app grid that surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. A new one-handed tap gesture lets you select widgets in Smart Stack, and a double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist-flick gesture can return you to the watch face, silence timers, and dismiss notifications.
The 24-hour battery life remains the same for the Series 12, but it now offers faster charging: 15 minutes gets up to 12 hours of battery life. The Ultra 4’s battery has expanded to up to 50 hours.
Like its competitors, health and fitness remain a major focus. Workout Buddy now incorporates more wellness metrics and can run without an iPhone nearby; it’s also now available in Spanish. In addition to the “Functional Strength Training” workout mode, users can now log sets, repetitions, weights, and equipment. Cycle Tracking is also gaining support for perimenopause and menopause, including notifications about cycle deviations associated with perimenopause.
With the launch of watchOS 27, Apple is removing Walkie-Talkie, its real-time voice communication tool that lets Apple Watch users communicate directly with one another.
Update at 9 pm, September 9: Details were added about the new sensor array and the watches’ battery life.

Climate change could cost Greece’s agriculture up to $1.2B annually: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:41:21 UTC
02:41:21 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Climate change could significantly reshape Greece’s agricultural landscape in the coming decades, causing major production losses and economic damage, while forcing changes in farming practices, according to a study cited by the Greek daily Ekathimerini on Wednesday.
Researchers estimate that climate change could reduce the value of Greece’s primary agricultural production by as much as €1 billion ($1.16 billion) annually within the next three decades, with Thessaly and Central Macedonia among the regions expected to be hardest hit.
The study estimates that, including the average effect of extreme weather events, direct losses in plant and livestock production could reach €437 million ($507 million) to €643 million annually between 2021 and 2040.
Under the most severe climate scenario, annual losses are projected to rise to between €579 million and more than €1 billion from 2041 to 2060.
“If this amount seems large, it is enough to consider that the damage in Thessaly from Daniel in 2023 exceeded €2 billion ($2.32 billion),” said researchers, referring to the severe storm that struck the region in September 2023.
The projected effects are expected to vary significantly across the country.
Thessaly, Central Macedonia, Central Greece, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, the Peloponnese and Crete are expected to account for 78% of the decline in agricultural production, 79% of GDP losses and 79% of employment losses.
Tree crops are expected to be particularly vulnerable, with olive production projected to face significant declines, especially after 2041.
Researchers said insufficient winter chilling could affect flowering and fruit set in olive trees, while higher temperatures and increased water stress could further reduce productivity.
Other crops expected to be affected include apples, pears, nuts, vineyards and vegetables harvested during the summer.
Citrus production could also decline as temperatures rise, although reduced frost damage could offset some of the losses.
Peaches and cherries, meanwhile, could benefit from fewer frost-related losses, according to the study.
The researchers recommended a range of adaptation measures, including earlier sowing dates, expanded irrigation, heat-tolerant crop varieties and changes in soil management.
They said, however, no single adaptation strategy would be suitable for all regions, calling instead for agricultural policies tailored to local and regional conditions.
The study comes as Greece’s agricultural sector faces growing pressure from heat, drought and extreme weather, with recent conditions already affecting crops including olives, grapes and vegetables.

These strange celestial objects have been hiding in plain sight for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:41:14 UTC
02:41:14 KST

In a galaxy far, far away, strange objects beam radiation out into space. For years, these weird bodies have been hiding in plain sight—but now new observations reveal they may be key to understanding the lives and deaths of galaxies.
For decades, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has been picking up the signal of these objects, but scientists had largely ignored the data. The radiation the objects emit is relatively low-energy compared with that of most stars, making it easy to dismiss as noise.
“[Scientists] didn’t even know the objects were there,” says Jimmy Irwin, a professor at the University of Alabama and a co-author of a new paper published in Nature Astronomy that describes the odd objects. “They ignored the very, very lowest-energy channels because they thought they were unimportant.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Irwin and his colleagues, Ph.D. candidate Mustafa Muhibullah and Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian lecturer Rosanne Di Stefano, didn’t anticipate that they would find anything of note when they decided to go through the overlooked data just in case. Irwin compares the process to diving for treasure: you might find a long-lost gem, but you are far more likely to find a bunch of garbage.
The three scoured data collected by the Chandra space telescope between 1999 and 2017 and painstakingly filtered out any random artifacts and other junk. They were left with the signatures of emissions of low-energy x-rays coming from what they call “hypersoft x-ray sources,” a new type of celestial object.
But what exactly these objects are is a bit of a mystery because all that’s known about them is roughly how bright and hot they are.
“They must be compact objects that are the remnants of stars,” Di Stefano says, “either black holes, neutron stars or white dwarfs, that are ripping material from the companion. And as the material falls, it emits at x-ray wavelengths.”
They could also be a mixture of all of the above, Irwin says.
“They’re probably a heterogeneous mix of different types of objects,” he says. “A hypersoft source isn’t necessarily a type of object but a representation of what kind of energy is coming out.”
Whatever they are, the researchers believe they’re likely also emitting radiation in the more energetic extreme ultraviolet (EUV) range. Unfortunately, seeing objects in that range from Earth is difficult, if not impossible, because hydrogen gas and other stuff that lies in the space between star systems absorb most of those rays. As a result, most of these objects will likely remain hidden from view for all time, but there could be a countless number of them out there. Just a handful will ever be in places that allow them to be seen from our planet.
“If we had a telescope that was sensitive to EUV and we didn’t have the fog, these sources would be booming bright in these galaxies, and they would not have been missed,” Irwin says.
“The sources that we see, each one represents many additional sources within the galaxy that we cannot see because the light never makes it out of the host galaxy,” Di Stefano adds.
Even so, the few that are detectable could offer insight into how different celestial objects—from black holes to galaxies—form. The radiation from supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies, called active galactic nuclei, are generally credited with helping to ionize gas that later forms stars. Some galaxies lack these black holes but still have the ionized gas, and hypersoft emitters could help explain why.
“We’re seeing the tip of the iceberg,” Di Stefano says.

Balkan media unite in Trieste against fake news
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:40:58 CEST
02:40:58 KST

(by Alice Fumis)
Curbing fake news, protecting press freedom, and guaranteeing
citizens' right to be informed—all while collaborating across a
broad international area to consolidate media integration.
                                    
                                       
				This goal was strongly reaffirmed today in Trieste by the 12
news agencies belonging to the Association of Balkan News
Agencies - Southeast Europe (ABNA-se)—including ANSA—during
their 34th General Assembly and the "The Balkans Meet in
Trieste" conference, organized by ANSA under the patronage of
the Central European Initiative.
                                    
                                       
				In Trieste—"the gateway to Europe for the Balkans," as described
by Ferit Hoxha, Albania's Minister for Europe and Foreign
Affairs—experts from the fields of media, politics, economics,
healthcare, and science engaged in in-depth discussions
regarding EU enlargement to include the Balkans.
                                    
                                       
				In this regard, Albania "has not a second to lose":
"Our plan is to close all EU accession chapters by next year."
It is a "very ambitious" project and the "process is highly
bureaucratic," but "we are doing our homework."
"We have a plan, and our goal is the EU," Hoxha said.
                                    
                                       
				Alberto Barachini, Undersecretary to the Presidency of the
Council of Ministers with responsibility for Information and
Publishing, also spoke—via video link—about media, public
funding, and Europe: "A European fund to support the media
sector is needed."
"In Europe, we must work to ensure a level playing field for
everyone," he said.
                                    
                                       
				"On the communications front, integration between the EU and the
Balkans is at a turning point," noted Luisa Chiodi, Director of
the Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa.
                                    
                                       
				"The last three or four years have provided an excellent example
of how to respond to disinformation through greater cooperation
among news agencies and the daily exchange of truthful news,
countering the fake news circulating on social networks," stated
Kiril Valchev, Secretary General of ABNA.
                                    
                                       
				"Our news agency and the agencies represented here serve as a
vital safeguard for information, press freedom, and democracy,"
observed ANSA CEO Stefano De Alessandri.
                                    
                                       
				"Geography and history place Trieste in a unique position as a
bridge to the Balkan region," he added, thanking the city and
Mayor Roberto Dipiazza.
                                    
                                       
				It is a border city overlooking the Adriatic Sea, a location
that enables it to play a role in integration.
                                    
                                       
				"Amidst an international crisis, integrating the Balkans into
economic development projects—including those involving the Port
of Trieste—is crucial," said Marco Consalvo, President of the
Trieste port authority.
                                    
                                       
				"For the Friuli Venezia Giulia region," pointed out Alessia
Rosolen, the region's Councillor for Labour, "the Balkans are no
longer merely a traditional sphere of influence; they must
become a partner with whom we stand united to face the global
challenges ahead."
