Temporary wartime weapons depot explosion kills 14 outside Syria's Idlib
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:30:25 UTC
01:30:25 KST

The blast at a temporary storage site for wartime munitions near the town of Sarmada left 11 others injured, with rescue teams still searching for survivors. A person is killed or wounded by unexploded ordnance every six hours in Syria today, according to humanitarian workers.
An explosion at a weapons depot near the northwestern city of Idlib killed at least 14 people and injured 11 others, Syria's Health Ministry said.
"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the town of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.
Security forces cordoned off roads leading to the Burj al-Nimra area on the road to Sarmada, some 45 kilometres from Idlib, as Civil Defence and Syrian Red Crescent first-responders continued to search for survivors trapped under the rubble.
Video footage widely circulated after the blast showed a large plume of black smoke and smaller explosions could be heard.
The depot was used to store weapons and munitions left over from the country's civil war from 2011 until 2024, according to authorities.
The cause of the blast near the town of Sarmada was not immediately clear. Initial assessments indicated the explosion was caused by munitions, said the head of emergency operations for Idlib's disaster management directorate, Walid Aslan.
Ahmad Faour, a mechanic who works near the warehouse, said he and others first heard a small explosion and ran away before the large blast.
"A weapons warehouse should not be placed in a public area, in a village with people and shops," he said, after looking through the damaged cars in his garage. "Those poor people who died were not guilty of anything."
The incident on Wednesday is the second deadly blast in Idlib this month, after a car carrying ammunition exploded, killing five in the city of Binnish.
A government source said at the time that the car was owned by a weapons trader, while authorities did not announce the cause of the blast.
Remnants of war
Syria is ranked among the world's most heavily contaminated countries for unexploded ordnance.
Explosions involving munitions-laden cars or arms depots have sporadically occurred in Idlib, a former front-line province where multiple armed factions stored weapons throughout the civil war which is among the most severely affected areas.
In November 2025, a blast at an ammunition depot in the Kafr Takharim area killed five workers and wounded nine.
In August 2025, an ammunition explosion on the outskirts of Idlib city killed four people and wounded five.
Humanitarian organisations called on Wednesday for intensified international and local efforts to clear mines and war remnants from the province, which they said continued to claim Syrian lives on a recurring basis.
UK mine-clearance charity HALO Trust estimated that this year unexploded ordnance was killing or wounding one person in Syria every six hours on average.
By August, some 700 casualties from explosive accidents were recorded, one-third of them deadly and one-third being children, according to Simon Jackson, HALO Trust's Syria programme manager.
According to Jackson, last year saw "a large spike in accidents as people rushed back to their communities" after the fall of al-Assad in December 2024.

You Can Now Destroy Flock Cameras for Cash in GTA V
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman.
The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions.
In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states.
“GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.”
In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play.
There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors.
“There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman.
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City.
Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.”
In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice.
For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR.
“I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.”

Diehl Develops Ziesel UGV That Can Follow Infantry Soldiers Autonomously
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:58:14 UTC
00:58:14 KST

German company Diehl Defence has presented the Ziesel tracked unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), designed to support infantry units.
The presentation took place at the MSPO exhibition in Poland, Militarnyi reports.
The 350 kg tracked platform can carry a payload of up to 500 kg. The unmanned vehicle measures 1,310 mm in length, 1,230 mm in width, and 600 mm in height, excluding the payload.
The all-electric powertrain provides a maximum torque of 1,000 Nm and allows the vehicle to reach speeds of up to 20 km/h. The platform has a range of up to 40 km and an operational endurance of up to 24 hours. Its design allows it to climb slopes with an inclination of up to 60%.
Diehl Defence’s PLATON-Kit system provides the system’s high level of autonomy. It integrates several control and autonomous-following modes to ease the operator’s workload in combat conditions.
The platform supports remote manual control with assistance functions, as well as a mode that allows it to follow a soldier or another vehicle while maintaining a safe distance.
In Push mode, the UGV moves ahead of the infantry soldier at a set distance, serving as mobile cover. Waypoint-based movement using map data provides autonomous navigation.

Fear of Backdoor Mobilization Grows in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:58:00 UTC
00:58:00 KST

Despite recent public pronouncements by Russian President Vladimir Putin that rumors of a fresh troop mobilization were ‘complete nonsense’ and that ‘there is no scenario today that would require mobilization’ recent events suggest the process may have already begun.
Critics point out that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said that reports of a new mobilization were ‘fake stories’ – he had made similar denials in May 2022, only four months before the last mass mobilization began.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to an article in Deutsche Welle’s Russian service (DW), large numbers, which some estimates put as tens of thousands, are increasingly being summoned to military enlistment offices to verify, clarify and update their military registration records.
Having done this they find that their military ID cards have been modified to include a ‘mobilization order’ that requires them to report to a specific collection point in the event of mobilization,
Such orders were issued prior to the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the previous mass mobilization in the autumn of the same year, but the current level of summonses is unprecedented. DW quotes the Russian internet search engine Yandex Wordstat which has seen a 800% upsurge in the number of searches for ‘mobilization order’.
A Russian lawyer, Artem Klyga, is quoted in the article noting that a summons to an enlistment office to clarify data does not necessarily mean the individual will be mobilized but it will be used to rapidly bring them in once the order is given. He adds that officials have been instructed to prepare the system for any decision Putin makes.
Ukraine Presents Domestically Developed Pegas IFV
Putin’s assurances are not shared by many of those summoned particularly after reports in June told of men reporting to military enlistment offices being taken and pressured into signing military contracts in Russia’s Penza region. According to local reports many were transported to military units where they were held before being sent to the front. Some see this as a ‘dress rehearsal’ for what is to follow.
Western estimates, including those of the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), suggests that Russia is losing more than 40,000 men killed and wounded at the front compared with around 35,000 volunteers being recruited every month. ISW argues that this gap cannot be supported indefinitely and can only be remedied by ‘mobilization in some form’.
Western intelligence agencies say they are also seeing the signs of preparations for mass conscription in a number of regions that could be a precursor to establish training grounds, feed and arm new recruits. In late July, advertisements began to appear offering vacancies in ‘mobilization preparedness’ and ‘military registration’.
As Politico reported in late August concern among young Russians was such that more than 110,000 had fled in the previous week across the Upper Lars checkpoint between Russia and Georgia, ostensibly for summer holidays, — a loophole that has since been closed off.
DW also pointed out that the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force – another cause for disquiet among those eligible for call up.
The combination of summonses, changes to the military registration systems and aggressive recruitment efforts help explain why Putin’s denials have failed to put the rumors to the rest.

The R-360 Neptune cruise missile is designed to destroy ships with a displacement of up to 5,000 tonnes and, like other missiles of its class, can be launched from land, surface and air platforms. In April 2022, a Neptune missile was used to sink the Russian cruiser Moskva.
In late 2025, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was also using the upgraded Long Neptune version. The Neptune-D system uses RK360L cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,000 km and a 260kg warhead. The missile is designed to strike both land and maritime targets.

Could US retaliate against UK over Israeli settlement sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:55:12 UTC
00:55:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Could US retaliate against UK over Israeli settlement sanctions?
The UK's landmark decision to sanction Israeli settlers marks a significant shift in Middle East foreign policy, but could the move expose London to retaliation from the United States over its support for ally Israel?
The possibility emerged after US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee warned of "significant" repercussions if Britain imposed a "boycott and sanctions" on Israeli targets.
Israel has already responded furiously to the measures, including with plans to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Israel also announced that Britain would no longer be permitted to train Palestinian security forces in the West Bank, while 12 British lawmakers and other nationals, including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, would be barred from entering the country.
But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said the prospect of Washington following Israel with punitive action against Britain is more complicated, particularly given conflicting signals from the Trump administration amid escalating Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.
What has Washington actually said?
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Washington would not follow the UK in imposing new measures related to Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but stopped short of directly criticising London's decision.
Rubio's comments contrasted with those of US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who told the BBC that if Britain imposed a "boycott and sanctions" on Israeli targets, "the repercussions are going to be significant".
Michael Hanna, US programme director at the International Crisis Group, told The New Arab that Rubio's comments carry greater official weight given his position as Secretary of State.
He said the remarks suggested that no major shift in US policy was imminent, indicating that the Trump administration may tolerate the UK's actions for now.
This comes as Axios reported, citing a White House official, that Huckabee's comments were not coordinated with either the White House or State Department and did not reflect the administration's policy.
The report also said US President Donald Trump did not push back against British plans to sanction Israeli settlements when he was briefed on the proposal by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during private conversations ahead of Tuesday's announcement.
"If we don't see further action and Rubio's stated policy is in fact what prevails, I think it tells us that even this administration, which has been so acquiescent to Israel and Israeli maximalism, that even they have some friction over this issue," Hanna told The New Arab.
"It's reached such a point that even the Trump administration is not willing to stick its neck out to defend Israel on this one set of issues."
Could the US punish Britain?
Daniel Levy, president of the US/Middle East Project (USMEP), told The New Arab that punitive action against the UK was unlikely to be led by the current US administration, despite measures already introduced against entities sanctioning Israel.
"I expect there at most to be warnings rather than actual measures on that front," Levy said. "The fact that the UK showed leadership and brought other countries along and did not do this alone, I think further complicates the picture for the US."
The international nature of the move could therefore make retaliation against Britain more difficult, particularly as Washington is already grappling with several international crises.
"As unpredictable as Trump is, let's acknowledge the context – the US is putting out fires on multiple fronts, and while you can never rule out it starting another fire in its relations and going into another trade and economic sanctions battle, it wouldn't exactly be helpful to an American economy that is not going well, and that is really costing the Republican Party in the lead-up to the midterms," Levy said.
Levy also cited reports detailing US frustrations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of the Gaza war, Israel's offensive in Lebanon and hostilities with Iran.
However, he stressed that this did not necessarily translate into direct US pressure on the Israeli government.
"It may mean that the US is rather okay with others taking measures right now," Levy added.
Why could these sanctions matter?
The nature of the British measures could also prove important in determining Washington's response.
"Importantly, the UK measures announced were not just a ban on trade and goods, but also moved into the financial services sector, which is far more consequential," Levy told The New Arab.
"In that respect, there could be a knock-on effect with Europe and others in beginning to move the dial on more serious consequences."
He continued: "The measures announced were serious, but perhaps any US response will be reconsidered when it comes to the details of the sanctions regime being implemented, which, as the Foreign Secretary Miliband noted, will take a little time."
The Times of Israel, citing a White House official, reported that Washington could take further action in the coming days, although any response may be less severe than the measures threatened by Huckabee.
That leaves open the possibility of some form of US response even if Washington stops short of the kind of economic retaliation initially raised by the ambassador.
How has Israel responded?
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called Britain's latest action "morally distorted" and accused the UK of "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process" ahead of next month's Israeli election.
During Tuesday's announcement, UK Foreign Secretary Miliband told lawmakers that, alongside banning imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, Britain would also introduce measures against companies and individuals providing services to settlements, including "construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate".
France and Canada also said they would ban imports of products from Israeli settlements, while nine other countries, including Denmark and Portugal, endorsed the British action.
Rights groups and politicians have widely described the sanctions as an important, albeit symbolic, step, particularly in relation to goods.
However, critics in the UK have called for more robust action against Israel's settlement project.
Britain, France and Canada were also among the countries that formally recognised the State of Palestine in 2025, as well as having previously imposed sanctions targeting settlements and Israeli ministers over accusations of inciting violence against Palestinians.

Drone threat beyond the Arctic Circle: Russia complains that Ukraine attacked a plant in Yamal

Drone threat beyond the Arctic Circle: Russia complains that Ukraine attacked a plant in Yamal
Kyiv • UNN
A drone threat was declared in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug; the likely target was Gazprom Pererabotka’s Novy Urengoy plant. The facility being hit has not been officially confirmed.
On September 9, a drone threat was declared in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. According to preliminary data, the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation may have come under attack, UNN reports, citing the press service of the region’s governor.
Residents have already been urged to remain indoors and stay away from windows.
It should be emphasized that, as of now, there has been no confirmation in the information space from the Russian authorities or Gazprom regarding damage to the facility. Russian official bodies have also not reported that a drone struck the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation specifically, nor have they reported a fire or damage to technological equipment. There is also no confirmation regarding possible consequences for the facility’s operations.
What is known about the plant that may have been hit by attack UAVs
The facility is located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, more than 3,000 km in a straight line from Ukraine. The Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation is one of the region’s key gas-condensate infrastructure facilities. The facility is part of the Gazprom Pererabotka structure and prepares gas condensate for further transportation and processing.
The plant’s design capacity after modernization is approximately 19.5 million tonnes of raw materials per year. The facility receives unstable gas condensate from fields in Western Siberia, including the Yamburg, Zapolyarnoye, and Urengoy fields. The plant produces, among other things, stable and de-ethanized condensate, a broad fraction of light hydrocarbons, and liquefied hydrocarbon gases. Some of the prepared raw material is sent by pipeline for further processing.
In 2021, a large-scale fire occurred at the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation, at the condensate de-ethanization unit. After the accident, Gazprom implemented a project to build a new unit, which was commissioned in 2024.
In addition
Amid the alleged UAV threat, restrictions on the operation of aviation infrastructure were also recorded in Novy Urengoy. In particular, flights from and to the city were delayed.
We remind you
As reported by Denis Shtilerman, co-founder of the attack-drone manufacturing company Fire Point, the Ukrainian long-range FP-1 UAV traveled approximately 3,200 km and struck the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation (ZPKT) in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.

As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:43:29 UTC
00:43:29 KST

As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
Analysts say UK move far from enough to drive momentum for Palestinian statehood.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the United Kingdom will sanction illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, describing the move as “overdue” and necessary to “salvage” a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
He made the comments on Tuesday as 11 nations joined the UK in supporting or considering curbs on trade in goods with settlements that are a barrier to a future Palestinian state.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
- list 2 of 3Nicaragua urges ICJ to reject Germany’s bid to throw out Gaza genocide case
- list 3 of 3Israeli parties submit slates for October Knesset elections
But analysts say the step is far from enough to drive momentum for Palestinian statehood, threatened by ever-expanding settlements in the West Bank and an increasingly hostile Israeli political environment.
Tahani Mustafa, a lecturer in international relations at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera the latest anti-settlement measures are “modest” and unlikely to have a significant impact on ambitions for Palestinian statehood.
“After three decades of breakneck settlement expansion, Palestinian territory is only being held together by its sinews,” said Mustafa. “If what remains is still territorially viable as a state, it is only barely so. Much more decisive action is needed to salvage the two-state solution and a durable lasting solution to the conflict.”
Settlements dividing Palestinian territory
More than 30 years after the Oslo Accords set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel has remained the foundation of international efforts to forge peace.
But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, according to the Palestinian Bureau of Statistics, posing a glaring roadblock to the plan.
The challenge is not just the raw number of settlers, but their geographic spread. Today, many Israeli settlements are embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state, including near major Palestinian urban centres such as Nablus, Salfit and Hebron.
Israel’s recent E1 settlement plan, which would build thousands of illegal housing units between the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim and East Jerusalem, is a case in point. The plan would effectively split the West Bank in two and fully sever it from East Jerusalem, which Palestinians seek as their future capital.
Experts have long said Israel will need to dismantle some of its West Bank settlements, as it did in the Gaza Strip in 2005, to make room for a cohesive Palestinian state. But many Israeli settlements, especially those closer to Israel’s pre-war 1967 borders, would likely need to be addressed through land swaps.
“A complete withdrawal from some of the deeply embedded settlements is highly unlikely,” so land swaps would be the only way to create some form of Palestinian “territorial integrity”, Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
However, such an arrangement – under which Israeli settlements close to the pre-1967 borders would become part of Israel and some “northern Arab-Israeli communities would be integrated into a Palestinian state” – would be “highly controversial” and face blowback from multiple communities, said Krieg.
He argued that Israelis would be certain to oppose any forced withdrawal from West Bank settlements, while some “Arab-Israelis may not want to live within a Palestinian state”.
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up approximately 21 percent of Israel’s overall population but are treated as second- or third-class citizens at the institutional level. According to rights groups, several dozen Israeli laws actively discriminate against Palestinian citizens across a number of issues, including education and housing.
Israeli ‘consensus’ against Palestinian state
Beyond the physical obstacle created by settlements is the Israeli political landscape, in which the idea of a Palestinian state has become toxic.
The government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be among the most hardline in Israel’s history on the issue. Netanyahu has emphatically ruled out the prospect of a Palestinian state, while his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, has celebrated blocking Palestinian statehood as a badge of honour.
The views of Netanyahu’s most influential domestic critics do not deviate much. His top rival in elections slated for October, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has promised not to allow the establishment of a Palestinian state. And Naftali Bennett, a Netanyahu rival from the far right, fervently opposes Palestinian statehood.
As for the Israeli public, a June poll by the Council for a Secure America found that only 22 percent of Jewish Israelis favour a two-state solution, while 63 percent oppose it.
“The consensus within Israel, socially and politically, does not allow for any party to make any steps towards a Palestinian state,” said Krieg.
Meanwhile, Israel’s closest ally, the United States, is unlikely to apply significant pressure over Israel’s settlement policy so long as President Donald Trump remains in office for the next two and a half years, he added.
Krieg said a “best-case scenario” is for Israel’s next elected government to reverse some of the country’s recent settlement advances.
John Strawson, professor at the University of East London, said that any new Israeli government is “unlikely to support a Palestinian state”, but that a more moderate Israeli government may at least “stop the ethnic cleansing and other moves which are aimed at making that impossible”.
“Removing Netanyahu is the first step towards a two-state solution,” said Strawson.
Two states are the ‘only alternative to violence’
If the two-state model is still alive at all, it is largely due to pressure from the international community.
More than 150 countries, including the majority of European Union nations, have recognised Palestinian statehood. And several Arab states with whom Israel seeks better ties have indicated Palestinian statehood is a precondition for normalisation with Israel.
Krieg said Tuesday’s move by the UK and the 11 other mostly European nations is an “overdue step in the right direction”, but also “shows the laziness and lack of creativity on the part of the international community to actually think outside the box in terms of a two-state solution”.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said that while the settlement sanctions are concerning to Israel, other previous anti-settlement measures, such as 2013 EU restrictions on funds for Israeli entities operating in occupied Palestinian territory, “changed little on the ground”.
He said the latest sanctions may be “too late” and “too limited … to save the two-state solution”.
Strawson said that while a two-state solution may “seem optimistic”, it is the only alternative to “permanent war and violence”.

Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:43:00 UTC
00:43:00 KST

Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
September 9, 2026
Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.
According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.
Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security."
Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.
Crackdown on cafes
Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.
The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state."
Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.
He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.
Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.
The rise of the cafe culture
Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.
Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.
"The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service.
"In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said.
"In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal."
The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.
"The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group."
The political role of cafes
Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.
Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.
The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.
"They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said.
"Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added.
Maintaining control over social spaces
Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.
"Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere."
The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.
She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.
"The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh.

Gold Medal of Catalonia Awarded to Italian Scientist Caterina Biscari
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:42:18 CEST
00:42:18 KST

The president of the Generalitat of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, awarded the “Medalla d’Or de la Generalitat” to Italian scientist Caterina Biscari during a ceremony in Barcelona attended by the Italian Consul General in Barcelona, Gabriele Luca Fava, and the Embassy’s scientific attaché, Sergio Scopetta.
                                    
                                       
				   Established in 1978, the Gold Medal of the Generalitat is the highest honor bestowed by the Autonomous Community of Catalonia and has been awarded to universally renowned figures such as Salvador Dalí, Joan Miró, Pau Casals, Josep Carreras, and Montserrat Caballé.
                                    
                                       
				A physicist and director of the Alba Synchrotron—one of Spain’s major research facilities—Caterina Biscari is the first non-Spanish citizen to receive this honor. 
    The official citation states that “Biscari has strengthened the international profile of research conducted in Catalonia. Her scientific career combines scientific excellence, service to society, and collaborative leadership. She serves as a role model for women in science and has helped raise the visibility of women in decision-making positions within European research.”
   Caterina Biscari, born in Sicily, attended the Italian State School in Madrid and earned her bachelor’s degree from the Complutense University. She subsequently earned her Ph.D. from the University of Naples Federico II. As a researcher at the National Institute of Nuclear Physics (INFN), she specializes in particle accelerator physics, a field in which Italy boasts a long tradition of excellence, dating back to the pioneering studies of Edoardo Amaldi and Bruno Touschek at the INFN’s Frascati National Laboratories (LNF), where Biscari began her career. 
  From there, her work expanded to other major institutions, such as CERN in Geneva and, more recently, the National Center for Oncological Hadrontherapy (CNAO) in Pavia, where she has conducted fundamental, applied, and health-related research. Since 2012, she has been the director of the Alba accelerator in the Barcelona area. Alba is a synchrotron light source that enables the study of the properties of matter with a wide range of applications in the life sciences and materials science, relevant to both academia and industrial research. Since its founding, more than 10,000 researchers and over 100 companies have used Alba for their studies.
                                    
                                       
				     Already an Officer of the Order of the Star of Italy and winner of the “Aldo Olcese 2026” award—established by the Italian Embassy in Madrid in memory of the distinguished compatriot who passed away prematurely last year— Caterina Biscari has consistently collaborated with the numerous scientific outreach initiatives organized by the Embassy and the Consulate General in Barcelona. The awarding of the “Medalla d’Or de la Generalitat” is further recognition of the excellence of the Italian education and research system and of our tradition in accelerator physics.

Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:38:58 UTC
00:38:58 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities.
The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds.
The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools.
In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508).
Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463).
In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU.
A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497).
Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading.
In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading.
In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland
Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”.
However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”.
Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

The Baltic transmission system operators, Latvia’s AS “Augstsprieguma tīkls”, Lithuania’s Litgrid AB and Estonia’s Elering AS, together with their partners, have completed the next stage in enabling multiple power exchanges to operate in the Baltic region. As of 8 September 2026, EPEX SPOT has begun operating in the Intraday Auctions (IDA) segment in the Baltic States alongside Nord Pool.
EPEX SPOT is also scheduled to begin operations in the Day-Ahead Market at the end of September, completing the full roll-out of its services in the Baltic electricity market. This means that EPEX SPOT will be available across all key segments of the wholesale electricity market in the Baltic States.
The IDA market provides electricity market participants with additional opportunities to optimise their positions closer to the time of electricity delivery. This supports more efficient power system balancing and facilitates the integration of renewable energy sources into the electricity market.
As previously reported, EPEX SPOT began operating in the continuous intraday market in November 2025, becoming the second Nominated Electricity Market Operator alongside Nord Pool. The introduction of intraday auctions marks the next major milestone in advancing the integration of the European electricity market and strengthening competition.
The multiple power exchange model is being implemented in the Baltic States in accordance with the European Union’s Capacity Allocation and Congestion Management Regulation (CACM). The regulation aims to foster competition among power exchanges, provide market participants with greater choice and support the efficient development of the European electricity market.
The project involves transmission system operators from the Baltic States and neighbouring countries: Latvia’s AS Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST), Estonia’s Elering AS (Elering), Lithuania’s Litgrid AB (Litgrid), Finland’s Fingrid Oyj (Fingrid), Poland’s Polskie Sieci Elektroenergetyczne S.A. (PSE) and Sweden’s Affärsverket svenska kraftnät (Svenska kraftnät), as well as the power exchanges Nord Pool and EPEX SPOT.
About AST
AST, the Latvian electrical power transmission system operator, ensures uninterrupted and secure transmission of electricity throughout Latvia. Its vision is to become the leading transmission system operator in the region through the efficient and successful implementation of development-oriented changes. AST has 68.46% shareholding in the capital of the operator of the natural gas transmission and storage system JSC “Conexus Baltic Grid”.

====================================================================================================

Europe’s defence supply chains need more than defence companies, industry leaders say in Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:41 UTC
00:16:41 KST

Europe’s efforts to expand defence production will increasingly depend on companies that may not consider themselves part of the defence industry at all, industry experts and executives argued at the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum, which brought together around 200 participants from more than 15 countries on 6–7 September.
The message emerging from the forum in Rēzekne, eastern Latvia, was straightforward: European defence capacity cannot be expanded by defence primes and specialist manufacturers alone. It also requires companies in electronics, engineering, communications, precision manufacturing, energy, software, sensors and other civilian industries to enter defence supply chains. More than 200 pre-arranged business meetings took place alongside technology demonstrations, company visits and discussions involving representatives of BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, SAF Tehnika, Origin Robotics, Redwire, Silmor, Pērkons Energy and other European and international companies.
“For companies looking at the defence market, the first question should not be ‘What defence product should we build?’ but ‘What capability do we already have, and who needs it?’” said defence and strategy adviser Thibault Normand. He argued that becoming part of the defence industrial base does not necessarily mean developing a complete weapons system. Modern defence platforms rely on extensive networks of specialised suppliers. Dassault Aviation, for example, identifies around 400 companies in the industrial ecosystem supporting the Rafale fighter programme.
The challenge, Normand said, is therefore not only technological capability but industrial credibility. “An excellent prototype from an unreliable supplier is not a defence capability.” Defence customers need confidence that suppliers can deliver consistently over decades and scale production rapidly during a crisis, he added. For companies seeking to enter the sector, the immediate objective should therefore not necessarily be winning a major procurement but becoming credible enough to secure the next conversation with a customer or prime contractor.
Latvia seeks a larger role for domestic industry
Latvia is simultaneously seeking to increase the participation of its domestic industry in defence procurement.
Uģis Norītis, Deputy State Secretary for Planning at Latvia’s Ministry of Defence, said Latvia aims to increase the share of domestic industry in defence procurement to 20% by 2028 and 30% by 2036, while progressively increasing funding for defence innovation. Support is being developed across the industrial lifecycle, from early-stage ideas and prototypes to scaling manufacturing capacity.
Norītis also stressed that many components required by defence systems are not inherently military products. Materials, electronics, engineering components and other widely used industrial products can all form defence supply chains, creating opportunities for companies that have traditionally operated entirely in civilian markets. For Europe, this represents a potentially much larger industrial base than the companies currently labelled as “defence”.
From Latvian start-ups to international defence customers
Latvia already provides examples of how quickly companies can enter international defence markets. Origin Robotics, founded in 2022, now employs 103 people, according to the company’s Head of Government Relations Māris Ķuda. Its unmanned systems are already used by the armed forces of eight countries, including Latvia, Ukraine, France and Denmark. Latvian telecommunications equipment manufacturer SAF Tehnika, meanwhile, has built an international business in wireless communications and radio-frequency monitoring. CEO Normunds Bergs presented the company’s experience of taking Latvian-developed technology into defence and security markets worldwide. The examples point to a broader opportunity for smaller European economies: they may not compete with Europe’s largest defence manufacturers in scale but can occupy highly specialised positions in international supply chains.
The next bottleneck may be integration
Technology itself, however, is only part of the challenge. Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, argued that one of the most pressing problems in airspace security is increasingly the ability to connect technologies, institutions and operators.
Defence forces, police, critical infrastructure operators and private companies can each have sophisticated systems and their own understanding of what is happening in the airspace yet still lack a common operational picture. “You cannot control the airspace if you cannot share the picture of it,” Emaus said. He argued that Latvia could position itself not only as a home for dual-use technology companies, but also as an environment where technologies, users and institutions can be connected and tested together.
More than 200 business meetings
The second Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum brought together around 200 participants from Latvia and abroad, representing more than 15 countries.International participants included TensorOne, AJB Subsea, HISDESAT, NEST AI, Fischer Panda and Sine Engineering, while speakers and programme participants represented companies including BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, Wolfram Europa, SAF Tehnika, Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire, RAW and Origin Robotics.
The programme began on 6 September with an Industry Day organised together with Latvia’s Ministry of Defence, including live demonstrations of Latvian defence and dual-use technologies and visits to manufacturing companies. On 7 September, discussions shifted from technology to commercialisation: how companies can turn engineering capabilities and innovation into international partnerships, supply-chain positions and exports.
“Interest in Latvian dual-use technologies and industrial capabilities is clearly growing, but the value of the forum is not measured by participant numbers,” said Līva Stūrmane, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Exporters Association ‘The Red Jackets’. “What matters is creating the conditions for new partnerships. For a smaller country such as Latvia, integration into international supply chains is one of the most realistic ways of turning technological and manufacturing capabilities into defence exports.”

Compensa: Private insurance should direct people to primary healthcare  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:41 UTC
00:16:41 KST

TALLINN - According to Merko Kimsto, head of the Estonian unit of Compensa Life Insurance, a managed care pathway starting with a primary medical assessment should become standard practice in private health insurance.
Compensa is redesigning its health insurance service based on this principle, so that individuals can quickly receive a professional assessment and be directed to the right specialist when needed.
Kimsto explained that people often manage their own healthcare journey, selecting specialists and what they believe are necessary tests based on their symptoms. This results in patients wasting time and money, as well as taking up limited appointment slots with specialists for services that may not resolve their health issues. Meanwhile, in many cases, a family doctor or general practitioner could offer the fastest assistance.
"As insurers, we must also look at ourselves in the mirror. For years, the main selling point for health insurance has been quick, direct access to specialists - and Compensa has been part of this," Kimsto said. "This can give people the impression that seeing a specialist is always the right first choice for any health issue."
According to a Norstat survey commissioned by Compensa, three out of four Estonian employees consider employer-provided health insurance necessary. Currently, approximately 72,000 people, or eight percent of the working-age population, are covered by health insurance. Kimsto noted that while the growth in health insurance is welcome, new policies do not add more doctors, nurses, or their working hours to the healthcare system.
"If we build health insurance solely around quick, direct access to specialists, we risk creating a parallel queue with the same bottlenecks as the public system. Health insurance should help people get a professional assessment first and then, if necessary, quickly guide them to the exact right specialist," Kimsto stressed.
As a solution, Compensa Life Insurance has expanded its partnership with the Salu healthcare service center to offer a service where the care pathway begins with an online medical consultation. A healthcare professional assesses the health concern and helps determine if treatment, analysis, diagnostics, an in-person appointment, or specialist care is required.
"With this solution, the insured can access an initial digital consultation with a family doctor or GP within one to two days, free of charge. If needed, an appointment with a specialist is arranged within three to seven days. For subsequent treatment, Compensa settles the bill directly with the service provider, meaning the individual doesn't have to pay the full medical bill upfront and later claim reimbursement," Kimsto explained.
According to Kimsto, a managed care pathway helps keep health insurance a valuable and sustainable employee benefit. Unnecessary or duplicate visits and tests increase the medical costs for the entire group of insured employees, which can affect the price and terms of the policy for the next insurance period.
"This doesn't mean that people should use their insurance less or delay necessary treatment. On the contrary, help should be sought as early as possible for any health concern. We are not in any way restricting or prohibiting our clients from seeing specialists as they have before. Rather, we are trying to encourage a way of resolving health issues that guides the person immediately to the appropriate specialist and doesn't leave them to navigate the choice of healthcare services alone."

European metrologists shaping the future of measurements in Tallinn  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:16 UTC
00:16:16 KST

TALLINN – Metrosert is hosting the annual meeting of the European Association of National Metrology Institutes' (EURAMET) Technical Committee for Mass and Related Quantities in Tallinn.
Sixty of Europe's leading measurement experts will arrive in Estonia, with over 65 additional participants following the discussions online. The meeting will establish priorities for the field's development, international comparison measurements, and the next steps in scientific cooperation.
The EURAMET technical committee deals with the measurement of mass, pressure, force, torque, density, viscosity, hardness, and gravitational acceleration.
According to Mari Aru, head of Metrosert's research and development division, the precise measurement of these quantities is crucial for, among other things, the safety of industrial equipment and energy infrastructure, the correct composition of pharmaceuticals, food quality, the fair accounting of fuel and goods, and the development of new high-tech solutions.
"Metrology is all around us, although we usually only notice it when a measurement goes wrong. From a societal perspective, the goal is simple: for the technology around us to work safely, for the amount of active ingredient in a medicine to be correct, for production processes to function stably, and for fuel and other goods to be billed for fairly. Behind all of this are reliable and internationally comparable measurements," said Mari Aru.
National metrology institutes maintain and develop their country's most accurate measurement capabilities. In Estonia, this task is carried out by Metrosert. Having local measurement capabilities helps Estonian companies ensure product quality, certify it for foreign markets, and reduce dependence on foreign laboratories for critical measurements.
To ensure that measurements made and calibration certificates issued in Estonia are trusted in other countries, European metrology institutes regularly compare their standards, measurement capabilities, and methods. International comparison measurements show whether laboratories in different countries achieve consistent results when measuring the same quantity.
At the annual meeting in Tallinn, roadmaps for various measurement fields will be reviewed and approved, setting development priorities for the coming years. New comparison measurements and research projects will also be planned, and topics such as the digitalization of measurements and the measurement of dynamic quantities—those that change rapidly over time—will be discussed.
"The directions agreed upon in Tallinn will influence which measurement capabilities are developed in Europe in the coming years and how new methods will move from laboratories to be used by businesses. For Estonia, hosting the meeting is also a recognition of Metrosert's competence and an opportunity to participate in shaping the future of European measurement science," added Mari Aru.
The EURAMET Technical Committee for Mass and Related Quantities is one of the association's largest, comprising six subcommittees, two working groups, and approximately 30 ongoing cooperation projects. Separate discussions will be held in Tallinn on the topics of mass, pressure, force and torque, density and viscosity, hardness, and gravimetry. Participants will also tour Metrosert's national standard laboratories.
EURAMET is the European Association of National Metrology Institutes, tasked with coordinating cooperation in measurement science and ensuring the international credibility and recognition of European measurement results. The annual meetings of the technical committees are held once a year in one of EURAMET's member states.
Metrosert is Estonia's center for applied research and the central body for metrology. Metrosert maintains and develops Estonia's national standards for length, mass, temperature, and electrical quantities, and ensures their traceability to the International System of Units (SI).

====================================================================================================

Why a digital company’s headquarters, target market and regulator may be in different countries  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:08 UTC
00:16:08 KST

A digital service can look unmistakably Dutch, German or Estonian without being incorporated in that country. Language, currency and a country-code domain can indicate which market a business wants to reach, but they do not necessarily reveal where the legal entity is registered or which authority supervises a particular activity.
For cross-border digital businesses, those are separate questions. A company may be established in one country, operate a website for another market and fall under the supervision of a regulator in that target country.
The brand is not always the legal company
Consumers usually remember a short brand name. Contracts, licences and regulatory registers tend to use the formal name of the company behind it. Those names can differ without anything unusual taking place.
A website may therefore present one recognisable brand to customers while the legal entity behind it appears under a different corporate name. That distinction becomes especially important in regulated sectors, where permissions and obligations generally apply to the company rather than simply to the brand shown on the homepage.
A country-code domain mainly signals a target market
A .nl domain strongly suggests that a service is aimed at users in the Netherlands. It does not prove that the company operating it is incorporated there. The same principle applies to other national domains.
A site such as 711.nl is a clear example of a Dutch-facing domain. The platform is presented for the Dutch market, while the legal company behind it does not have to be incorporated in the Netherlands simply because the web address ends in .nl.
Language creates a similar impression. A platform with Dutch customer support, euro pricing and Dutch terms may be designed specifically for that market while the company itself is legally established elsewhere in Europe.
It therefore helps to separate two questions: who is the website intended for, and which company legally operates it?
A licence belongs to a legal entity and an activity
Regulated digital markets add another layer. A licence is issued to a named legal entity for specified activities within a particular regulatory framework. The consumer brand, corporate name and website address do not necessarily match one another.
711 B.V., for example, is registered in Belgium, while its online gambling activity for the Dutch market operates under a licence issued by the Dutch Kansspelautoriteit. The company’s place of incorporation, its target market and the authority regulating that activity are therefore separate parts of the same cross-border structure.
This is why the location of a company’s headquarters alone does not determine where a regulated digital service may operate.
Different sectors follow different regulatory models
Cross-border activity in payments, media, cryptoassets and gambling cannot be reduced to one generic European rule. Each sector has its own legal structure.
Some financial services can operate across borders through European authorisation mechanisms. Media services may be limited by territorial rights. Online gambling remains closely connected to national licensing systems in many markets.
A company being authorised for one activity in one country therefore does not automatically mean that every service it offers can be marketed throughout the EU under the same conditions.
Licence scope matters too
Even when a company holds a valid authorisation, the scope of that permission matters. A licence for one regulated activity does not automatically cover every product or service the company may want to introduce.
Validity periods can matter as well. Regulatory permissions may be renewed, amended or expire over time. For that reason, the relevant question is not simply whether a company has ever held a licence, but what activity the current authorisation covers.
Technical access does not define the target market
Digital services make geography more complicated because a person may be able to open a website from outside the market for which it was designed.
A traveller in Latvia may technically be able to visit a Dutch-facing website operated by a Belgian company. That fact alone says little about whether every part of the service is intended, available or authorised for users in Latvia.
Accessibility, target market and regulatory permission are therefore different concepts. The internet makes websites easy to reach across borders, but it does not remove the legal boundaries attached to particular services.
Geoblocking can have different causes
Some online services restrict content according to a user’s location. The visible result may look the same — a page, video or service is unavailable — but the reason behind the restriction can differ.
A streaming company may be dealing with territorial media rights. An online retailer may choose not to serve a country because of shipping costs or returns. A regulated service may face restrictions because the required authorisation does not apply in that market.
The technical block is only the outcome. The legal or commercial reason behind it depends on the type of service.
Map the business before drawing conclusions
A useful way to understand a cross-border digital company is to separate four elements: the consumer brand, the legal entity, the place where that company is incorporated and the market-specific authorisation for the service being offered.
Those elements may point to different countries without creating a contradiction. A business can be incorporated in one EU member state, operate a website aimed at customers in another and be subject to a regulator in that target market.
The internet makes the customer-facing side of a business international. Corporate structures and regulatory systems remain tied to specific jurisdictions. Keeping those layers separate makes it much easier to understand how a cross-border digital service is actually organised.
                    2026 © The Baltic Times /Cookies Policy Privacy Policy

It is not possible to replace Russian and Belarusian mineral fertilizer supplies with imports from other countries in the short term - owner of WO Trading  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:08 UTC
00:16:08 KST

RIGA - It is not possible in the short term to fully replace Russian and Belarusian mineral fertilizer supplies with shipments from other countries while maintaining current price levels, Toms Egle, owner of SIA WO Trading, told LETA.
WO Trading has challenged before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) the changes to customs duties imposed by the European Union (EU) on goods originating in or exported from Russia and Belarus.
When asked what the main arguments are for challenging the customs duty changes in court, Egle explained to LETA that the gradual increase in customs tariffs stipulated by the EU regulation poses an objective risk that the supply of mineral fertilizers essential to agriculture will decrease in the EU, leading to a corresponding increase in their prices.
Given the high concentration of the global fertilizer market, the reorientation of supplies could pose a risk of price increases not only in the EU but also in the broader global market, Egle said.
He emphasized that WO Trading does not object to the political objective of increasing customs tariffs and supports sanctions against Russia and Belarus, but objects to the proportionality of the chosen instrument and its potentially disproportionate impact on Latvia’s mineral fertilizer market and agricultural sector.
He explained that WO Trading's operations in Latvia’s regions are aimed at supplying Latvian farmers with mineral fertilizers.
Egle added that the EU regulation on changes to customs duties applicable to certain imported goods originating in or exported from Russia and Belarus was adopted on June 17, 2025, and establishes gradually increasing customs tariffs through 2028.
Egle emphasized that the mineral fertilizer market is global, yet at the same time highly concentrated. As an example, he noted that the potash fertilizer market is the most concentrated, with three leading countries: Russia, Belarus, and Canada. Russia is also the world's leading producer of nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers.
WO Trading believes there is a reasonable and objective risk that alternative mineral fertilizer supplies to the EU will be priced higher than before the tariff increase under the regulation, namely, that prices will adjust to reflect the increased cost of mineral fertilizers originating in Russia and Belarus on the EU market.
WO Trading wishes to ensure that Latvian agricultural producers are not forced to reduce the amount of fertilizer they use, thereby jeopardizing crop yields. The rising cost of mineral fertilizers increases agricultural production costs and raises the final price of products paid by consumers, Egle emphasized.
There is also a risk that, as customs tariffs rise, there will be a greater incentive to route mineral fertilizers from Russia and Belarus through third countries, repackage them, or otherwise conceal their actual origin. This, in turn, could complicate oversight and reduce the effectiveness of regulations, explained the owner of WO Trading.

Newfound fossils are spilling Denisovan secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Newfound fossils are spilling Denisovan secrets
Teeth and bone bits from a cave in China represent the richest fossil trove outside Siberia
A long-lost cave in southwestern China has offered archaeologists their first real glimpse of Denisovan culture.
Denisovans were a sister species of modern humans and lived across Asia an estimated 400,000 to 30,000 years ago. Researchers have uncovered only a handful of their fossils so far, compared with the thousands of remains of better-known Neandertals.
Now, Bianfu Cave — a new archaeological site at an abandoned quarry in Yunnan Province — has yielded a rich trove of Denisovan fossils. Protein analysis and high-quality X-ray scans have confirmed that the fragment remains found at the site belonged to at least three Denisovans who lived between 167,000 and 134,000 years ago, according to two new studies published September 9 in Nature. The remains were found alongside butchered animal remains and more than 1,300 tools.
The cave “tells us a little about how Denisovans actually lived on the landscape,” says Shara Bailey, a paleoanthropologist at New York University. “Denisovans are becoming a bit less mysterious.”
Denisovans were first discovered in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tooth and finger bone found in a cave in Siberia revealed an entirely new human species. Since then, researchers have found that many modern people — including groups in the Philippines, Tibet, New Guinea and Australia — carry Denisovan DNA.
Yet despite Denisovans’ widespread genetic legacy, with so few fossils, little is known about how they lived. What’s more, archaeologists don’t know much about where some of these fossils were originally buried, or if any other remains or tools were found alongside them. It’s “a little frustrating,” says Bence Viola, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toronto who has studied Denisovan remains from Siberia’s Denisova Cave.
Researchers did find tools alongside Denisovan remains at Denisova Cave. But whether these were made by Denisovans, Neandertals or modern humans, who also occupied the site, is still unknown.
Then in 2019, an ecological restoration project at a quarry in Yunnan Province uncovered numerous fossils in a buried cave. Later excavations revealed four human teeth, two pieces of a skull and a fragment of an arm bone.
Researchers looked for species-specific proteins in the fossils and compared the shape of the teeth to several human species using micro-CT scans to figure out who they belonged to.
As soon as he saw a picture of the tooth, “I immediately assumed that they were probably Denisovan,” says Clément Zanolli, a paleontologist at the University of Bordeaux, France. Indeed, the teeth shared distinct similarities to other Denisovan teeth from Laos and Tibet.
All the samples also carried a Denisovan-specific collagen variant, clinching the identification, says Qiaomei Fu, a molecular paleogeneticist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.
The tools in the cave date between 190,000 and 70,000 years old. The team didn’t find any evidence that other types of humans were around during that 120,000 years that the cave was occupied. This suggests that the tools were made by Denisovans, argue Fu, Zanolli and colleagues. These tools were largely used for processing animal remains, including to break bones, cut meat and scrape hides.
The cave also contained over 1,600 identifiable animal remains, mainly deer and other ruminants. While few fossils showed signs of carnivore gnawing, some bore telltale marks of cutting and scraping, suggesting that Denisovans used tools to handle animal remains, which were later abandoned in the cave.
Denisovan fossils at other sites have been found alongside marmot remains. The presence of butchered deer bones suggests that the species “adapted to their environment. They hunted different things in different ways,” Viola says. Altogether, it provides “a much more complete picture” about Denisovan life.
