"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:00 EEST
00:00:00 KST

"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
Company commanders don't usually evacuate their soldiers personally. Their primary task is to direct their unit's actions from the command and observation post. But modern warfare has produced a rare breed of soldiers who are exceptions to the rule.
A few weeks ago, for instance, the whole of Ukraine witnessed how Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander with the 475th Separate Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), personally evacuated two wounded soldiers.
When a video was released of Polskyi running over to them with no helmet or body armour, dragging them off a broken-down unmanned ground vehicle and loading them onto a pickup truck, it drew thousands of admiring comments. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later awarded the courageous company commander the title of Hero of Ukraine and the Order of the Gold Star.
"It was brave," Eighteen says of Polskyi's actions. Eighteen, a company commander in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Regiment, says it is extremely rare for a company commander to take part in an evacuation personally.
Interestingly, however, at almost the same time as Vladyslav Polskyi was evacuating the two wounded soldiers, Eighteen also found himself in a situation where he could no longer stand back and direct the rescue of his men from afar.
Eighteen is 26 and has been at war since he was 19. He started out as a machine gunner with the 3rd Special Operations Forces Regiment, later serving as a marksman, sniper, squad commander and deputy group commander. He now commands a company in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment.
Recently one of his groups was on their way back from a mission when one soldier sustained a gunshot wound. Later, almost the whole group was hit by an improvised explosive device.
Four special forces soldiers were unable to walk independently, but ultimately all of them were evacuated.
Eighteen was, of course, far from the only hero in this successful rescue. The entire unit was involved in rescuing the group over the course of five days. The company commander is full of praise for the heroism and professionalism shown by all his comrades, from drone operators and medics to logistics personnel.
Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) has decided to tell the story from the perspective of Eighteen – a commander who would normally have been directing the evacuation, but this time went in himself to bring his men out.
"If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting"
It all happened in August, when a group of special forces soldiers led by a commander with the alias Santa, serving with the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment, was tasked with ambushing Russian troops along one of their routes.
The group infiltrated about 15 km into the area, where they succeeded in killing four Russians – they offered them the chance to surrender, but they refused. When the group received the order to withdraw, they moved into a forest to get some rest. But unbeknownst to them, danger was approaching.
"We were doing reconnaissance and spotted one of the enemy going into the forest where the guys were," Eighteen says. "He approached stealthily, and we didn't spot him until almost afterwards. We ordered the guys to clear the sector the enemy soldier had entered.
Just then one of our brothers-in-arms was shot and wounded. The group opened fire on the enemy and wounded him as well. We don't know what happened to him after that because the group was focused on evacuating our wounded brother-in-arms."
The bullets had hit a special forces soldier who goes by the alias Malyi (Little One): he had been shot in the abdomen and arm and several of his fingers had been blown off. He was given first aid. But then, as the group was leaving the wooded area, they triggered one of the improvised explosive devices that the grey zone is littered with.
By some miracle, Malyi wasn't hit by the blast – but now he wasn't the group's only casualty. Four other soldiers sustained severe leg injuries. One of them, Sava, died almost immediately after being dragged into cover.
Suddenly the group that had been evacuating one wounded soldier found itself having to evacuate almost half its members.
"The guys all had leg wounds," the company commander recalls. "There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic. They pulled everyone off the open ground and into the bushes so they could give them first aid, and they were treating the wounded, all of whom were now in a serious condition.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk."
Eighteen remained in contact with the group commander and watched everything unfold live. Heavyshot drones dropped everything that Santa's group would need for the rescue: additional stretchers and medical supplies.
"We understood that we couldn't leave the guys there. And time wasn't on their side – they'd already been in the area for about six days, and there were still around 13-14 km to cover during the evacuation. Everyone realised they wouldn't be able to get out on their own," he says.
Another group of special forces soldiers, which was on its way to a mission, was redirected to help the wounded. They evacuated one soldier, but the most seriously wounded man was still in the area.
Eighteen asked his commanding officer for permission to go in and retrieve him himself. He took a medic and two soldiers from his company with him. They managed to drive part of the way, but there was still around 15 km to walk.
They had to get to Malyi and carry him out without being spotted by Russian drones – and they did it.
"The most important things here are physical fitness and your knowledge. We got there as fast as we could," Eighteen recalls. "We picked up the most seriously wounded soldier. The medic immediately treated him, and since we had additional medication with us, we patched him up…
The main thing was that they realised we were now in the same situation as them. The group commander said when he heard over the radio that we were in the area, he said: 'If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting.'"
"There were moments when he lost heart. He said: 'You don't need to carry me anywhere'"
Early in the morning, the group led by Eighteen set off. The wounded soldier remained conscious throughout. The soldiers made their way through forests, over hummocks and through wooded areas torn apart by guided aerial bombs, and every time they had to make a dash for it, it was agony for Malyi.
"He was, shall we say, a bit cranky because of his wound. He'd been hit in the abdomen, so he was in a lot of pain, and it wasn't always easy to move him. Sometimes we had to run with him, carry him, or drag him," Eighteen recalls.
Drones dropped water, food and medicine for the soldiers. Time was another enemy, as Malyi was in urgent need of medical attention. The group would only allow the wounded man to rest occasionally, letting him sleep for an hour or two after taking painkillers.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on.
Towards the end, when he realised there were only two or three kilometres to go, his attitude changed completely. We'd give him a cigarette and a swig of water from the bottle cap. And he started urging us on: 'Come on, let's get through here faster, let's not stop.' We were really surprised. We were exhausted by then and wanted to rest, and he was like: 'No, no, keep going,'" Eighteen says, smiling.
The journey with the wounded soldier took 15 hours. It wasn't until midnight that Malyi was handed over to the medics.
"It was a good thing we did the exfiltration so fast, because at the hospital we found out he didn't have much time left: his liver had been punctured," Eighteen says.
By this time, another group led by one of the battalion's senior sergeants was halfway there. Santa's group, whose members had been wounded, had also managed to make some progress, but they couldn't move very fast because the soldiers were exhausted. The wounded were moved out gradually: the tourniquets gave them a little leeway in terms of time.
"His family were very grateful that we brought his body back"
Eighteen's work wasn't over yet. As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the medics, the company commander decided they had to retrieve the body of the fallen soldier, Sava.
"He hadn't been with me all that long. He was a calm person – a really motivated, determined guy who wanted to get things done. He didn't have a wife or children, but he had a mother and a sister," the commander recalls.
To bring their brother-in-arms' body back, Eighteen, his two fellow soldiers and the medic set off once again into the area they had struggled so hard to get out of. In the course of rescuing the wounded and retrieving the fallen soldier's body, the group covered more than 50 km in total.
Sava was laid to rest in the city of Kryvyi Rih. He was 35.
"We've already buried him. His family were very grateful that we brought his body back," Eighteen says.
The rescue operation took five days. Everyone except Sava made it. Despite the severe injury to Malyi's arm, doctors managed to save it.
"The legs feed the wolf, as the saying goes. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us"
"We try to evacuate all our wounded," Eighteen says. Photo: 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment
During his seven years of service, Eighteen has fought on many of the hottest fronts: in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
He had to personally evacuate a comrade in 2023, when FPV drones were in use, but before enemy drones had begun to dominate the skies the way they do now.
A 23-year-old soldier in the group was seriously wounded: both his arms had been blown off and his legs were injured. Eighteen and the group quickly gave him first aid and handed him over for evacuation. Compared with the recent operation, it was a piece of cake. Evacuating soldiers is much more difficult now.
"Now the sky is completely controlled by drones – both ours and the enemy's. The hardest part is getting into an area and getting back out. When you're operating in the area, there's less chance of being wounded. We used to drive in, but now we have to go in on foot, carrying a huge amount of weight.
If you have a casualty, the entire mission comes to a halt. Everyone switches to getting the wounded soldier out. And if, as in our case, you have four people who can't walk, you have to deploy every resource you have.
That's what happened this time: everyone was involved. The UAV component was working, unmanned ground vehicles were delivering supplies, and the battalion- and regiment-level electronic warfare units were operating too, providing cover across the exposed areas we had to run through," the company commander recalls.
Although unmanned ground vehicles have come a long way, rescuing wounded soldiers from the most dangerous areas is still mostly up to their comrades, Eighteen explains.
Unmanned ground vehicles take on a significant share of the logistics, but where machines cannot cope, the human factor remains decisive.
"A person can squeeze through a narrow gap, make their way through bushes, or wait things out in the ruins of a building," Eighteen says. "An unmanned ground vehicle is much more vulnerable in those conditions: it can get stuck or simply be unable to get through. And the enemy usually monitors roads and bridges.
So when there's a wounded soldier in the area, you have to take the risk and carry him out yourself, because the enemy can just destroy an unmanned ground vehicle on difficult terrain. As the saying goes, the legs feed the wolf. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us. Our work depends on our legs."
When we ask Eighteen about the most memorable operations he has taken part in, he recalls Sievierodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Velyka Novosilka. But he says the recent mission to rescue the group was particularly special to him. In his view, the most important thing for a commander is to value his people.
"We try to evacuate all our wounded. Of course there are some situations where the circumstances make that impossible," he says.
"We try to retrieve the fallen, too. Because people are our greatest asset now."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Life (Zhyttia)

Farm in Mykolaiv region produces phyto honey from mined fields
This is reported in an Ukrinform publication titled “Craft business during war: honey from mined fields, lavender coffee and identity”.
“Our family farm, located on the border with Kherson region, produces honey from mined fields. It offers not only classic varieties — wildflower, rapeseed, sunflower — but also phyto‑honey, infused with medicinal herbs or fruits such as mint, lavender, wormwood and jalapeño peppers,” said co‑owner Yakiv Fedosov, PhD in Agricultural Sciences.
He noted that such honey is slightly more expensive because production is more labor‑intensive, but it is in demand among gourmets.
Fedosov grew up on a beekeeping farm, continuing the family tradition started by his father and developing it with modern trends.
At the start of Russia’s full‑scale invasion, hostilities occurred in the village, their house was destroyed and the farm damaged. The family was forced to leave but later returned.
“The surrounding land remained contaminated with explosive devices, making farming impossible. But when we began restoring the farm, we realized bees could still collect honey even from mined fields. There is symbolism in this — like the bees, we continue our work despite any challenges,” Fedosov said.
He added that today consumers are interested not only in the product itself but also in its story, original recipes and packaging.
As reported, 1,175 entrepreneurs have returned or relocated to Mykolaiv region since the start of the war.

US-Canada trade war escalates, 9/11 25 years on, and a medical first involving a pig
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

US-Canada trade war escalates, 9/11 25 years on, and a medical first involving a pig
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
Twenty-five years ago I was working as a journalist in London. In the early afternoon on September 11, all the televisions on the walls of the open-plan office suddenly showed the same image: the surreal sight of the Twin Towers burning and then collapsing. We heard that a neighbouring building, One Canada Square (also known as Canary Wharf Tower), where I had worked a year earlier, had been evacuated as there were rumours that a plane that had taken off from Heathrow was unaccounted for and, as the then tallest building in the UK and a symbol of capitalism, One Canada Square was an obvious target. As we know, nothing happened, and we got to work trying to explain the seemingly inexplicable.
Twenty-five years later, the deadliest terrorist attacks in history continue to cast a shadow on global affairs and US politics. As the Neue Zürcher Zeitung wrote this week, 9/11 is the “first and last moment in the 21st century that has united Americans”.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
Friday marks 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States – attacks which, according to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ), “changed Americans’ relationship with their country and with the world” and resulted in “deep mistrust and severe polarisation”.
“On the morning of September 11, 2001, time was torn apart,” wrote the NZZ’s deputy editor-in-chief, who began his undergraduate studies in the US just before 9/11. “The world watched spellbound as the images played out on screens: two planes crashing into the Twin Towers, over and over again in an endless loop.”
One consequence of the attacks, in which almost 3,000 people died, was that “Americans saw themselves as victims of a perfidious attack and rallied behind their resolute president”, he said. “This was by no means a given – just a few months earlier [George W. Bush] had won one of the most controversial elections in American history by the narrowest of margins. Yet after September 11, 90% of the population supported him in the polls. That’s a record figure – completely unthinkable today.”
The Republican government capitalised on this support. The CIA detained suspects in secret camps and tortured them. The USA Patriot Act enabled the authorities to carry out house searches on terror suspects without a court order.
“At first, Americans accepted that the state wanted more control and was taking a more aggressive stance both at home and abroad,” the NZZ wrote. “Soon, however, the categories in Bush’s foreign policy became blurred: suddenly, the US wanted to democratise the Middle East and free women from the yoke of Islamism. Oil, gas and other strategic interests also played a role, however. The Americans invaded Iraq in 2003.”
The government’s approval ratings halved, while the US sank ever deeper into the quagmire of “forever wars”, the NZZ continued. “Bush went from being a strong leader to a president who divided the country more than anyone before him: although the Republicans continued to support him, only a tiny minority of Democrats still backed him. This heightened polarisation remains a lasting legacy of the Bush era. The rift between the parties deepened even further under Obama, Biden and Trump.” As a result, the NZZ said 9/11 is the “first and last moment in the 21st century that has united Americans”.
“Since 9/11, Americans have viewed the world outside differently,” the NZZ concluded. “It seems more dangerous, more confusing. And they are withdrawing. Paranoid doomsday-prepping billionaires and increasingly radical militias are the most extreme expression of a culture of fear that is spreading across the US. Ordinary citizens, too, are increasingly retreating to the suburbs and into their communities of like-minded people.”
The Zurich paper said the rise of social media was further reinforcing these filter bubbles. “Today, Americans move in parallel worlds depending on their political convictions. There are many reasons for this. Yet the planes that crashed into the Twin Towers in New York on September 11, 2001, acted as catalysts.”
On Tuesday the White House escalated its trade dispute with Canada by banning the import of certain Canadian products, notably alcoholic drinks, and by raising customs duties on other goods. The Tribune de Genève says there’s no end in sight to the crisis.
A range of products, from mattresses to motorboats and golf buggies, will be subject to a 50% surcharge from September 15, Le Temps reported on Wednesday. An import ban on all kinds of alcoholic drinks as well as dairy products such as whey will come into force on September 29.
Good news, of sorts, is that certain Canadian products will no longer be subject to the 50% surcharge. This list is significantly shorter, but loo paper is on it.
This retaliatory move comes soon after Canada imposed customs duties on American products – in response to surcharges introduced by Washington on August 22.
“To justify the ban on imports of alcoholic drinks from Canada, US President Donald Trump has cited the boycott – which he describes as ‘discriminatory’ – targeting American spirits in Canada,” Le Temps explained. “Since the start of his tariff offensive last year, Canadians have launched a massive boycott of US products: US wines and spirits have disappeared from the shelves in most provinces, which hold a monopoly on their sale.”
As reported in Swissinfo’s US briefing two weeks ago, two-thirds of Canadians support a tough stance towards the US.
“There appears to be no end in sight to the crisis at present,” the Tribune de Genève wrote on Wednesday. “Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned on Tuesday morning that his government’s strategy to reduce dependence on the United States would have a short-term economic ‘cost’ for the country. The ‘cost of inaction’ would be far greater, he said in a video posted on YouTube a few hours after Canada’s tariff retaliation came into force.”
Swiss newspapers were impressed at the weekend by a medical success story in Boston: a pig kidney had functioned for nine months in the body of a 66-year-old man.
“The man’s prospects were bleak,” wrote the Tages-Anzeiger on Saturday. “His kidneys had been severely damaged by diabetes. For two years he had relied on dialysis, which left him utterly exhausted, while the function of his diseased organ continued to deteriorate.” Doctors estimated the probability of him receiving a kidney within the next five years at 9%, and the risk that he would not survive the waiting period at 40%. “Then the doctors devised a plan that was to result in a medical breakthrough.”
The doctors at Mass General Brigham in Boston transplanted a pig’s kidney into the patient, which worked so well that he managed without dialysis for 271 days, the team reported in the science journal The Lancet. Previously, pig kidneys had functioned in the human body for a maximum of two months. “For the first time, a human has benefited from a xenotransplant over a prolonged period,” the Tages-Anzeiger wrote, referring to a transplant from one species to another.
After around six months, damage to the kidney’s blood vessels became apparent, which ultimately led to organ failure. The kidney had to be removed, and the patient returned to dialysis. In the end, he was lucky: 80 days later a human donor kidney was found.
The Tages-Anzeiger pointed out that questions remain – the doctors can’t say why the pig’s kidney eventually failed – but it said there was now a debate about whether xenotransplantation is an option to bridge the waiting time for a human organ.
“For the team at Mass General Brigham, this success offers a potential solution to the global organ shortage,” Le Matin in Lausanne wrote on Saturday. “However, the researchers remain cautious: this involves a single patient, monitored under highly specialised conditions. Further trials will be needed before this type of transplant can be considered on a larger scale.”

Container ship arrives in UK after landmark voyage from China via the Arctic

Lebanon boosts army presence in south amid Israeli attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:59:40 UTC
23:59:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon boosts army presence in south amid fears of wider Israel attack
Lebanon has stepped up diplomatic efforts to contain increasing Israeli attacks while reinforcing its army presence in the south amid growing fears that Israel could expand its operations around Nabatieh.
Lebanese political leaders have agreed to strengthen the army's deployment in southern Lebanon, particularly around Nabatieh, following three days of Israeli attacks that killed at least 28 people and wounded more than 69, sources told The New Arab.
The move comes as President Joseph Aoun has intensified contacts with Washington, urging the United States to pressure Israel to halt its escalation.
US officials have also intervened with Israel in an effort to reduce the intensity of its operations as Washington seeks to revive negotiations and arrange an eighth round of talks.
Concerns over the situation dominated a meeting between Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Tuesday.
Sources said discussions focused in particular on fears that Israel could seek to seize additional high ground around the Iqlim al-Tuffah and Jabal al-Rayhan areas of south Lebanon after announcing "operational control" over the strategic Ali al-Taher hill.
Lebanese officials fear the fighting could now spread more widely across the Nabatieh district.
Berri and Salam agreed on the need to strengthen the army's presence in threatened areas in an effort to protect residents and reassure communities.
The Lebanese army said its forces were already deployed across all areas not under Israeli occupation, including Nabatieh, but that it had intensified its operations in several areas to reassure residents.
Aoun also met Interior Minister Ahmad al-Hajjar on Wednesday to discuss the security situation and ways of strengthening the state's presence in the south.
He later held talks with Salam over the continuing Israeli attacks and measures being taken by the army to reinforce its deployment in villages not under occupation.
Israel continued its attacks on southern Lebanon on Wednesday, causing explosions in Mansouri and Tayr Harfa in the Tyre district and Markaba and Bani Hayyan in Marjayoun.
An Israeli drone also dropped a stun grenade near the southern towns of Haris and Hadatha.
Fears Israel could push deeper into south Lebanon
The Lebanese army's deployment comes amid concern that Israel could attempt to replicate the tactics it used to establish control over Ali al-Taher around Nabatieh.
Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Israel could gradually expand its occupation of south Lebanon through limited operations around Iqlim al-Tuffah and Jabal al-Rayhan, according to military assessments.
It that the Lebanese army had reinforced positions in Nabatieh and Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, including sending 80 soldiers to the latter area, with the overall force there expected to reach around 180.
Nabatieh mayor Abbas Fakhr al-Din told Al-Akhbar that additional troops had arrived and deployed inside the city's neighbourhoods, separate from forces already stationed at the local barracks.
He said the deployment was intended to reassure residents and encourage them to return, with some limited returns already recorded.
Lebanese officials are also watching regional developments, particularly tensions between the United States and Iran, amid fears that Israel could further escalate its operations ahead of Israeli elections in October.
Sources told The New Arab that Beirut believes Israel currently has little enthusiasm for continuing direct negotiations. The Lebanese government has therefore intensified diplomatic contacts aimed at securing international intervention.
Jordanian and Turkish initiatives have also been floated in an effort to break the deadlock.
A Turkish proposal involving support and weapons for the Lebanese army, as well as a possible role in addressing Hezbollah's continued possession of weapons and Lebanon's relationship with Syria, was seriously considered by government officials but has not been formally adopted.
Lebanese officials still see Washington as the actor with the greatest ability to influence Israel.
Government sources said there was hope that US efforts could contain the escalation and lead to a new round of negotiations in the second half of September.
US links Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah weapons
The diplomatic push comes as US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa has continued to link an Israeli withdrawal to the disarmament of Hezbollah.
During a meeting with Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, deputy head of Lebanon's Higher Islamic Shia Council, Issa argued that Hezbollah must surrender its weapons before Washington could press Israel to withdraw.
Al-Khatib rejected the demand, arguing that Hezbollah could not be expected to disarm while Lebanese territory remained under Israeli occupation.
Al-Khatib also called on Washington to adopt a more balanced position and provide guarantees and protection to Lebanon's Shia community as part of any process addressing Hezbollah's weapons.
Lebanese official sources separately told The New Arab that Beirut had repeatedly stressed to Washington that Israel must halt its military operations to allow the Lebanese army to carry out its duties.
Despite disagreements over Hezbollah's weapons, the sources said Issa was continuing efforts to revive negotiations.

Amur Region signs about 20 agreements at Vladivostok forum, launches major projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:59:08 UTC
23:59:08 KST

BLAGOVESHCHENSK, September 9. /TASS/. The Amur Region signed about 20 agreements, launched a project to build an international business center in Blagoveshchensk, and opened a new branch of the Warrior Center - during the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok, the regional government said.
"On the forum's sidelines, the region presented its investment potential, launched the construction of an international business center in Blagoveshchensk, and during the forum the Russian president opened the region's branch of the Warrior Center. The regional government has signed about 20 agreements," the government reported.
The Amur Region's delegation led by Governor Vasily Orlov arrived at the forum with a detailed list of projects and ready-made agreements. The agreements were signed with federal institutions, commercial companies and regional partners on infrastructures, construction, tourism, digital economy, and culture. A significant part of these agreements is the logical result of a long preparatory work that will become the basis for the projects' implementation in the coming years, the governor stressed.
The international business center's construction is a key item on the program aimed at building up Blagoveshchensk's status as a center for cross-border business cooperation, he continued. The new facility will host business missions, exhibitions, and negotiations with international counterparts.
The Russia-China agenda
During the forum, the governor participated in a meeting of the Russian-Chinese Intergovernmental Commission on Investment Cooperation led by Denis Manturov, Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister, and Ding Xuexiang, Deputy Premier of the State Council of the People's Republic of China. The meeting participants outlined three systemic directions for the commission's further work: constant monitoring and targeted support of projects, better awareness of the business community about investment opportunities, and the search for new forms of attracting financial resources to implement joint projects.
The interstate cooperation is becoming more practical, the governor said. "The agenda focused mostly on Russian-Chinese relations," he added. "The cities of Blagoveshchensk and Heihe are leaders in building interstate relations." the governor said. The support from Chinese counterparts confirms the interest in joint infrastructure and logistics projects that are important for the Amur Region's economy, the governor noted.
Key agreements
The signed agreements include documents signed with the Roscongress Foundation on the development of the Russian-Chinese Business Cooperation Competence Center, established in Blagoveshchensk in compliance with instructions from the president. This center will become a platform to support trade and investment initiatives, create expert and educational programs, and to follow-up projects with Chinese counterparts.
Two documents inked with DOM.RF are on the construction of a multifunctional community center on the Golden Mile and on the development in the region of "green" construction - technologies and standards aimed at cutting energy intensity and carbon footprint in the construction industry. An agreement with Vimpelcom is on development of the digital economy and telecom infrastructures to ensure easier access to the high-speed Internet and digital services in the region's remote areas.
Special attention is paid to social initiatives: an agreement with Russian Railways provides for tax benefits in exchange for the renovation of a summer camp for children and a sanatorium - to upgrade recreation infrastructures for the region's children. Another agreement was signed with the Soyuzmultfilm Animation Studio to create a themed space for family leisure, using characters from Soviet and Russian cartoons - to expand cultural and leisure opportunities in the region and to develop domestic tourism.
Tourism and cluster projects
The Amur Region signed a cooperation agreement with the Chukotka Autonomous Region in tourism. The document provides for joint routes, the exchange of experience in development of tourism infrastructures, and in promotion of Russian Arctic and Far Eastern destinations on a single platform. An agreement with Solovyevsky Mine is on a historical and cultural tourism cluster on Relochny Lane in Blagoveshchensk - the project will focus on preserving and presenting local history, attracting tourists and organizing related infrastructures.
Logistics and major infrastructure projects
When speaking at the forum's different sessions, the Amur Region's Governor Vasily Orlov focused on international logistics as a strategic direction in the region's development. Priority projects include building of the Dzhalinda (Russia) - Mohe (China) combined automobile and railway bridge that will lead to the road connecting the region with the Northern Sea Route. Such transport solutions will create new corridors for exports, will cut logistics costs and will open access to Arctic routes, the governor said.
Export expansion
During the forum, the governor had a meeting with a delegation from Belarus, where the parties discussed building up the trade, supplies of Amur agricultural products, supplies of Belarusian machinery, and the creation of joint ventures. The delegations paid special attention to humanitarian cooperation and knowledge exchange in the agro-industrial sector. These contacts may become a source for additional sites to sale agricultural products and to localize industrial production in the Amur Region.
Results
Based on results of the Eastern Economic Forum in 2026, the Amur Region has confirmed its status of a key Far Eastern region in attracting investments and developing international cooperation. The implementation of signed agreements and launched projects will create new jobs, improve the quality of life in the region, and will build up the region's position in the Far East's economic space. The governor noted that the regional team had completed the planned program and was ready to be working at the implementation stage.

Swiss Senate pushes back on VAT increase for funding army

Swiss Senate pushes back on VAT increase for funding army
The Swiss government is facing opposition to its plans to increase Value Added Tax (VAT) to fund the armed forces. Two Senate committees have called for a smaller VAT increase than that proposed by the government, as well as an alternative funding model.
The government wishes to increase the standard rate of VAT by 0.5 percentage points for a period of twelve years to finance defence projects. The Senate’s Security Policy Committee (SIK-S) rejected this proposal by 8 votes to 3, with 1 abstention, as the Parliamentary Services announced on Thursday.
There was no dispute within the SIK-S that, given the deteriorating security situation, a fund with borrowing powers is necessary to finance defence equipment for the armed forces. However, it wishes to finance it through a different approach.
+ Why Switzerland is struggling with its national defence
Like the Finance Committee of the Senate (FK-S) before it, the SIK-S also came out in favour of increasing the standard VAT rate by just 0.2 percentage points. The SIK-S also intends to follow the FK-S’s lead regarding the overall funding concept for the fund. It had previously discussed several different concepts.
In addition to VAT, the committees wish the fund to be financed from ordinary budget surpluses. The SIK-S is also proposing additional contributions to the fund from the general federal budget, divided into earmarked and non-earmarked contributions.
Both committees wish to decouple the creation of the legal framework for the fund from the referendum on the VAT increase.
The Senate will decide on the matter this autumn.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump have not discussed the specifics of a potential meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, though there is a mutual understanding that such a meeting could take place, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov has told the media.
He also noted that the Kiev regime's current display of "flexibility" stems from a shortage of funds and weaponry. However, according to Peskov, this is not the kind of flexibility needed for a settlement.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the Kremlin spokesman.
Potential Putin-Trump meeting
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump have not discussed the specifics of a potential meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, though there is an understanding that it could happen: "In terms of specifics - no, but there is a mutual understanding that such an opportunity might arise."
Kiev's position
The Kiev regime is currently in a "very difficult position": "The country's economic situation is deteriorating rapidly."
The Kiev regime's current display of "flexibility" is a consequence of a lack of funds and weaponry, but it is not the flexibility required for a settlement: "There is a lack of money and a lack of weaponry. Hence the display of 'flexibility’. But this is not the flexibility that is needed."

Prospects for a peace settlement

Over 4,500 displaced in Sudan’s North Darfur, Blue Nile amid worsening insecurity: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:46:39 UTC
23:46:39 KST

Adel Abdelrheem, Sahin Demir
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
More than 4,500 people were displaced in Sudan’s North Darfur and Blue Nile states amid deteriorating security conditions, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Wednesday.
In North Darfur, the UN agency said its displacement tracking teams estimated that around 1,275 people fled the villages of Gorbora and Wadi Arkawi in Um Baru locality between Sept. 3 and 6.
The displaced families moved to Karnoy locality in North Darfur, while some crossed the border into neighboring Chad.
The IOM said the situation remains “tense and highly volatile,” and that it continues to closely monitor developments.
Separately, the agency said around 3,315 people, equivalent to 663 families, were displaced in a single day from several villages in Geisan locality in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile state due to worsening insecurity.
The displacement was recorded on Sept. 7 from several villages, including Abu Shneina, Rabaa and Wadi Arab. The affected families moved to Wad al-Mahi locality within Blue Nile state.
The IOM said the latest displacement followed an earlier wave on Sept. 5.
On Sunday, the agency said another 1,690 people had been displaced from three villages in Blue Nile’s Kurmuk locality due to escalating violence.
Blue Nile has witnessed a military escalation in recent days amid attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on several areas.
On Sept. 4, authorities in Kurmuk said the Sudanese army repelled an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on the Al-Baraka area.
Since late June, villages in North Darfur’s Um Baru locality have also faced attacks blamed on the RSF, including raids on markets and the burning and looting of villages, according to Sudanese rights groups and organizations.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German state where the far-right surged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:45:01 UTC
23:45:01 KST

Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.
Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said.
Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air.
A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”.
I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past.
Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.”
Fragrance of power
It remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker.
There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected.
Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to the Brandmauer, or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state.
Whatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merz accused the AfD of seeking “ethnic cleansing”.
No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD.
Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.”
For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt across Europe.

Torrential rains, winds from Hurricane Lowell leaves 30,000 without power
The Category 1 hurricane misses Kauai but causes widespread destruction, power outages and evacuations.
Catastrophic winds and torrential rains from Hurricane Lowell have pelted Hawaii’s western island of Kauai, knocking out power to at least 30,000 residents and ripping up tracts of beachside roads.
Vicious winds knocked down trees and left nearly 92 percent of Kauai Island Utility Cooperative (KIUC) residents without power by early Tuesday as the storm moved north into the open sea.
While the now-weakened Category 1 hurricane did not make landfall on Kauai, it blew down trees, power poles and lines, causing massive destruction from about 128 kilometres (80 miles) west of the island, according to the Hawaii County Civil Defense Agency.
With approximately 85mph (137km/h) wind gusts, the storm brought a deluge that flooded coastal roads and forced roughly 300 residents to evacuate.
The centre of the storm passed west of the islands in the overnight hours on Tuesday and receded further throughout the day, but dangerous surf from the remnants of the hurricane will impact the Southern California coast for several days given the intensity of the winds, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said.
Emergency officials are asking residents to conserve water and stay off the roads.
Hawaiian mayor Derek Kawakami said that there was “extensive damage” being reported on Tuesday.
“Everyone’s participation has gone from preparation to sheltering to staying off roads …. to now gathering data and information,” the mayor stated.
The Kauai County government urged locals to shelter in place to allow crews to assess damage, clear debris, and restore power and services safely.
Flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk through the day, said Eric Blake of the National Hurricane Center.
The force of the sustained winds had decreased overall by early Tuesday, and the centre forecasts gradual weakening over the next few days.
In its latest advisory late Tuesday morning local time, the hurricane centre said Lowell had maximum sustained winds near 65mph with higher gusts and was moving north at 14mph.
Hurricane warnings for Kauai and the tiny island of Niihau, which has fewer than 100 permanent residents, were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time. But high surf and deadly rip currents from the waning storm will continue to affect Hawaii’s exposed coasts for the next day or two.
A tropical storm warning was also lifted for Oahu, the state’s most populated island.

The BBC’s director general has conceded there is a real prospect of strikes at the broadcaster, as he faces a continuing dispute over pay and pushes ahead with plans to cut as many as 2,000 jobs.
In a call with staff on Tuesday, Matt Brittin faced a series of questions over the corporation’s plans for huge cuts, as well as pay talks in which staff rejected an average 2.1% salary increase.
With staff across the BBC already anxious over job cut plans, to be announced in the next few weeks, Brittin acknowledged there was a serious prospect of strike action.
“I understand that there might be [strikes],” he told staff. “I think it would be difficult. But I think we have to face the fact that we are in a really disruptive time for the entire industry. So I hope that people listening to this and talking to colleagues and union leaders as well understand where we are.”
Brittin, who took on the BBC’s top job in May, is overseeing cuts designed to save £500m by 2028. The plan was drawn up before his arrival, but he is attempting to make significant changes to reshape the BBC as part of the process.
He acknowledged there was anger that the alleged failure to grasp the BBC’s financial problems earlier had meant the corporation now needed to make deep cuts.
Brittin pointed to previous internal findings that the BBC’s licence fee income had fallen by about £1.3bn in real terms over the past decade.
He said about 60% of the reduction was due to government decisions such as freezing the licence fee, while about 40% reflected a fall in the number of households paying for a licence amid the rise of streamers and digital platforms.
Brittin repeated that he had not fully understood the extent of the BBC’s financial woes when he started the job. He said the broadcaster had run out of reserve funds, while income from its commercial division had already been spent.
“There’s really not a lot of elbow room for anything,” he said. “That’s quite tough … that’s the context that we’re in.”
He suggested that increasing the pay offer further would hamper the BBC’s ability to reduce job cuts. “One per cent on pay for everybody is equivalent to about 180 jobs,” he said. Asked if it was a choice between job cuts and more pay, he said: “That’s the choice that you have to make at a management level … to award more, you’re going to have to find the money from elsewhere. The cupboard is bare.”
As part of the increased pay offer, he said the most senior executives would not receive a pay rise, while the lowest paid would get an increase above 2.5%.
Strike action by BBC staff would come as a huge blow, at a time when Brittin is championing its national importance as talks continue with the government over its future funding.
Such is the anger that it could yet result in the biggest strike in more than a decade. A strike over pay was called off at the last minute in 2014. Schedules were disrupted by a smaller strike in 2023 over job losses and changes to local programming.
Despite the BBC’s financial struggles, it still commands a unique place in global media as one of the most trusted brands in the world, and reaches 94% of adults every month in the UK.
During the staff call, several employees confronted Brittin and Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, over the decision to renege on a guaranteed job offer made to a group of apprentices, as revealed by the Guardian earlier this month.
“I absolutely get the devastation that we can’t guarantee that now because of the recent savings challenges,” Phillips said. “I do know that [BBC News] are doing everything they can to find placements for those people.”
It comes with all traditional broadcasters facing financial pressure. Channel 4 is planning to cut 340 jobs, equating to 28% of its workforce.

====================================================================================================

Most Ukrainians support freedom of speech and personal responsibility – ILI study
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:17:15 EEST
23:17:15 KST

Ukrainians demonstrate strong demand for freedom of speech, personal autonomy and protection of private property, while at the same time, on issues of economic and social policy, a significant part of society expects an active role from the state, according to the results of the nationwide sociological study “Values of Freedom in Ukraine,” presented by the International Liberty Institute (ILI).
According to the study, 85% of respondents supported citizens’ right to criticize the authorities without fear of persecution, while 67% supported guaranteeing freedom of expression even for views that may be considered unacceptable or offensive. Almost half of respondents – 49% – opposed internet censorship even under wartime conditions, while 57% opposed punishment by the state for statements or opinions if they do not pose a direct physical threat.
“Almost 85% of Ukrainians, if we combine the responses ‘completely agree’ and ‘rather agree,’ support the right to publicly criticize the authorities without fear of persecution. At the same time, around two-thirds believe that freedom of speech should be guaranteed even for views that are perceived as wrong or offensive. For us, this is one of the clearest indicators of society’s demand for personal freedom,” Director of the International Institute for Liberty Mykhailo Kamchatnyi said at a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine agency on Wednesday.
Another 68% of respondents opposed a situation in which the majority can impose its values on a minority. ILI believes that the combination of these indicators demonstrates a clear demand for limiting state interference in the sphere of personal beliefs and expression.
At the same time, respondents’ ideological self-identification proved to be significantly less liberal. A total of 52% primarily defined themselves as free individuals with their own values who are personally responsible for their lives, while 31% primarily identified themselves as citizens of Ukraine. Only 13% described themselves as supporters of liberal or libertarian views, while 46.5% gravitate toward ideologies that envisage a more active role for the state. Almost half – 48% – reported that their political and ideological beliefs had changed or been formed under the influence of the war and its consequences.
A separate section of the study concerned language policy. According to the data presented, 65% of respondents named Ukrainian as their native language, 23.6% identified themselves as bilingual, and 11% named Russian as their native language. At the same time, 76% supported the mandatory use of the Ukrainian language in the public state sphere, while about two-thirds agreed that people should have the right to communicate in their native language in public life without state restrictions.
The human right to self-defense also received considerable support. About half of respondents supported the right to legally carry weapons for self-defense, while around 80% supported the right to use them to protect life and private property in the event of an unlawful intrusion into a home.
More than 80% of respondents agreed that even during martial law the authorities should not go beyond the limits established by the Constitution. A total of 53% supported a substantial revision of the current Constitution or the adoption of a new one. Some 77% of respondents agreed that closing media outlets or blocking internet resources may be justified only if cooperation with the enemy or coordination of military strikes has been proven.
One of the most sensitive issues was the principle of staffing the Armed Forces. A total of 46% of respondents supported an exclusively professional or voluntary army, while almost half favored a mixed model combining a professional contract-based core with mandatory training for young people in peacetime. The traditional mobilization model was supported by 3% of respondents, while more than 80% approved attracting professional military personnel through high salaries and benefits.
“We see that the traditional mobilization model does not enjoy citizens’ support – only around 3% of respondents chose it. Instead, society is much more oriented either toward a professional volunteer army or toward a mixed model with a professional core and training of citizens in peacetime. More than 80% also support attracting military personnel through competitive salaries and a system of benefits,” Kamchatnyi said.
In the economic part of the study, society proved to be significantly more polarized. A total of 44% of respondents supported an expanded role for the state in the economy and in providing social services, including 29% who took the strongest position in favor of active state regulation. At the same time, 44% of respondents said that they rely primarily on their own efforts to ensure their well-being, while 43.5% expect the state not to interfere with their personal risks.
ILI President Yaroslav Romanchuk, in turn, drew attention to the fact that Ukrainians’ attitudes toward private property and entrepreneurship are more market-oriented than their formal ideological self-identification. In particular, 69% of respondents demonstrated an understanding of the concept of private property, while almost 70% agreed with the statement that excessive bureaucracy and regulation hinder business development.
“Ukrainians as a whole do not reject private property – on the contrary, in many responses we see an understanding that a private owner manages an enterprise more efficiently than a manager appointed by the state. This is fundamentally important for future economic policy: the country’s strategic development should not automatically mean the dominance of state ownership. Private initiative, competition and protected owners’ rights are needed,” Romanchuk stressed.
He also linked problems in the business environment to excessive discretionary powers granted to officials.
“When an official, law enforcement officer or inspector is given the opportunity to interpret a vaguely written rule at their own discretion, a source of discretion arises, and with it a corruption risk. Almost 70% of respondents directly say that excessive bureaucracy and regulation are a brake on business development. Therefore, laws must be as clear as possible and leave as little room as possible for arbitrary interpretation,” the ILI president added.
According to Romanchuk, the results regarding knowledge of economic concepts also indicate the need to update economic education. A total of 46% of respondents had heard or read about Marxism, 12% about monetarism, and 4% about the Austrian School of Economics. A free-market economic model without state intervention was chosen as the most desirable for Ukraine by 18%, a model of active state regulation by 10%, and socialism by 6.5%.
Romanchuk separately advocated preserving and developing the institution of FOP individual entrepreneurship as a form not only of taxation, but also of self-employment and entrepreneurial culture. He noted that microbusiness should be regarded as an important component of citizens’ economic and social independence.
In the social sphere, the ILI president called for a transition toward more targeted assistance that would take into account not only a person’s current income, but also savings, assets, health status and other criteria of need. In his opinion, after the war, the issue of combining the state’s substantial social obligations with the need to preserve conditions for business development will become one of the key issues for fiscal policy.
“Ukraine will have to find a balance between the needs of people who will require social support and rehabilitation and the economy’s ability to finance this. If social obligations are formed without taking into account the tax burden that business is capable of bearing, we will get neither investment nor modernization. Therefore, assistance must be as targeted and transparent as possible and tied to the real needs of a specific person,” Romanchuk stressed.
He also advocated developing alternatives to an exclusively state pension system and making broader use of funded mechanisms, while in education and healthcare he called for competition between public and private service providers. According to Romanchuk, a market model in these sectors does not imply the state’s complete withdrawal from financing, but primarily a change in the mechanisms for distributing funds and greater accountability of providers for results.
During the discussion following the presentation, Romanchuk separately drew attention to the connection between freedom, responsibility and the quality of legal institutions.
“Freedom does not exist without responsibility. If the right to private property formally exists, but no one bears responsibility for violating it, then in practice that property is not protected. The same applies in other areas: a right works only when there is a clear mechanism of responsibility for its violation,” he summarized.
The study covered issues of personal freedom, the state and politics, the economy, the social sphere, private property and entrepreneurship, taxes, elections, military service, education, healthcare, pension provision, individual responsibility and social solidarity.
New Image and Marketing Group conducted the sociological survey in July 2026 at the request of the International Liberty Institute. A total of 1,600 respondents who were living in Ukrainian government-controlled territory at the time of the study took part in the online survey.

Explainer: Why are Israel, Britain at odds?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:17:04 CST
23:17:04 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on Tuesday announced a series of retaliatory measures against Britain over its latest moves targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The measures include closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem, removing British representatives from the U.S.-led International Gaza Support Center, and barring 12 British officials from entering Israel.
Why has Israel hit back at Britain? How did ties between the longtime partners sour so sharply? And what does the latest diplomatic clash mean?
WHAT HAPPENED?
British Foreign Secretary David Miliband announced Tuesday that Britain would ban imports of goods originating from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and restrict British companies from providing certain services to them.
On the same day, foreign ministers from Britain, France, Canada and nine other countries issued a joint statement announcing plans to restrict trade in goods linked to Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The statement urged the Israeli government to immediately halt settlement expansion in the West Bank, hold violent settlers accountable, and investigate allegations involving Israeli forces. It warned that settlement expansion, the advancement of the so-called E1 project and settler violence were undermining the prospects for a two-state solution.
The Palestinian presidency welcomed the joint statement, reiterating its commitment to a just and lasting peace based on international law and UN resolutions, including an end to the Israeli occupation and the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The E1 area lies between East Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim, one of the largest Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The international community has long warned that large-scale Israeli construction there could further fragment Palestinian territory in the West Bank and severely undermine the geographical viability of a future Palestinian state.
WHY NOW?
Britain has long been regarded as one of Israel's important European partners, with the two countries maintaining close cooperation in trade, security and other fields.
However, since October 2023 when the war broke out, disagreements between the two sides have widened over the humanitarian situation in Gaza, Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Palestinian statehood.
In June 2025, Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway jointly imposed sanctions on Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, including asset freezes and travel bans.
The five countries accused the two ministers of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, saying actions that contributed to serious abuses of Palestinian human rights were "unacceptable."
A more significant turning point came in September 2025, when Britain formally recognized the State of Palestine, saying the move was intended to preserve the possibility of a two-state solution.
An analysis published by the Financial Times said the deterioration in British-Israeli relations began over the Gaza conflict and deepened amid disputes over settlement expansion and settler violence in the West Bank.
The article described the bilateral ties at their worst in decades, warning that relations could worsen further in the short term as political differences begin to erode cooperation in areas like defense and trade.
WHAT'S AT STAKE?
The Times of Israel reported Tuesday that Britain's ban on imports from Israeli settlements is not aimed at Israel's economy as a whole, but is designed to draw a distinction between Israel and settlements in the occupied West Bank.
While restricting settlement-related imports and sanctioning companies and individuals involved in settlement expansion, Britain has stressed that it will continue trading with Israel and opposes broader boycott campaigns against the country.
Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now said measures targeting settlements should not be equated with sanctions against Israel itself. However, it warned that Israel could face growing international isolation if the government continues advancing construction in the E1 area and taking other steps seen as undermining the two-state solution.
The Guardian reported that Britain's move to directly restrict settlement-related trade represents a substantive shift in its efforts to defend the two-state solution.
Although settlement goods account for only a limited share of Israel's foreign trade and the immediate economic impact of the measures may therefore be modest, their political and symbolic significance could be greater, the report said.
The coordinated moves by Britain, France, Canada and other countries, alongside indications that more European states could consider similar measures, suggest that some Western countries are seeking a more coordinated mechanism to pressure Israel over its settlement policies in the West Bank, it added.
The latest confrontation also highlights a broader shift in Israel's relations with some of its traditional Western partners: disagreements once largely confined to diplomatic statements are increasingly translating into concrete economic and political measures, regional observers have said. ■

HARARE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Six African savannah elephants have been fitted with GPS-enabled satellite collars in and around Zimbabwe's Hwange National Park, bringing the total number of elephants monitored under an ongoing conservation program to 30, the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) said.
In a statement released to Xinhua on Wednesday, IFAW said the collars transmit location data via satellite, enabling conservation teams to track elephant movements, identify areas where human-wildlife conflict may occur, and better understand how elephants use the broader landscape.
The latest collaring exercise, which concluded Tuesday, involved three female and three male elephants. It was led by the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority in collaboration with IFAW, with funding from the Dutch Postcode Lottery.
IFAW noted that data collected through the program supports the development of early warning systems, the identification of critical wildlife corridors, and informed long-term land-use planning.
"This work demonstrates how science and technology can strengthen conservation efforts," said Phillip Kuvawoga, IFAW senior director for the landscape conservation program. "Every collar helps us better understand elephant movements and develop practical solutions that reduce conflict and protect this iconic species."
The project contributes to IFAW's Room to Roam initiative, which works across 320,000 square kilometers of connected habitat in Eastern and Southern Africa to secure, restore, and reconnect landscapes for wildlife.
Zimbabwe holds one of Africa's largest elephant populations, with Hwange National Park serving as its key habitat. ■

Around 450 government officials, diplomats, researchers, academics, entrepreneurs and young science and technology professionals from China and CEEC are attending the conference, which runs in both Ningbo and Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, under the theme "A Decade of Innovation, Building the Future Together."

Shenzhou-23 mission commander Zhu Yangzhu, astronaut Zhang Zhiyuan and Hong Kong's first payload specialist Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, delivered an engaging and vivid science lesson to the young people of Hong Kong and Macao.
The event was jointly organized by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government, the Macao Special Administrative Region (SAR) government and the China Manned Space Agency, with the main classroom set up at Lai's alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College in Hong Kong.

The HKSAR government and the Macao SAR government also arranged for teachers and students of primary and secondary schools to watch the live broadcast simultaneously on campus.
During the session, the three astronauts demonstrated scientific experiments in the unique space environment in real time and shared glimpses of daily life aboard the space station. They conducted a series of science demonstrations, including baking a cake in the space kitchen, wringing out a wet towel, and tending the space vegetable garden.
Lai also showcased the operating procedures for MUSICO, a lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision carbon dioxide and methane point-source detector developed under the leadership of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

Kong Chi Meng, director of the Education and Youth Development Bureau of the Macao SAR government, said that the lecture was not only a vivid lesson in science and technology education, but also a profound lesson in patriotism, with the three astronauts serving as exemplary role models for students. ■

Russian forces attacked Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast, injuring nine civilians.
Source: Donetsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office
Details: On the morning of 9 September, Russian forces struck Kramatorsk. The Russians conducted the attack using five FAB-250 bombs equipped with a UMPK kit A UMPK is a guidance kit for converting unguided bombs into precision-guided munitions .
It was initially reported that three women aged 59, 70 and 74 and a 72-year-old man sustained injuries as a result of the attack.
The explosions damaged 27 houses and a car.
As of 16:20, the number of civilians injured in the morning airstrike had risen to nine. Two of the injured, aged 49 to 80, had mine-blast injuries and lacerations.

These 9 midterm races will decide control of 100-seat US Senate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Democrats need to pick up four seats from Republicans to win control of the 100-seat Senate in the midterm elections on November 3.
While voters will pick candidates in 35 states, independent analysts only see nine of those races as competitive.
Most of these contests take place in states that President Donald Trump won in 2024, but his approval rating stands at 33 percent, the lowest of his political career, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Alaska
Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces two liabilities in his reelection campaign: a credible challenge from a Democrat and another person on the ballot with the same name.
Democrat Mary Peltola previously held the state's sole House seat for a single term and has campaigned as a centrist. She garnered 82,000 votes to Sullivan's 69,000 in the state's nonpartisan primary in August, in what could be an ominous sign for the incumbent.
Sullivan also will have to contend with another Republican, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, who got enough votes to advance to the November election despite Republican attempts to knock him off the ballot.
Peltola could also benefit from the state's ranked-choice voting system, which takes voters' second choices into account.
Polling has been sparse in this race, but analysts see it as a toss-up.
Georgia
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is running for reelection against Republican Representative Mike Collins, a conservative backed by Trump.
Georgia has emerged as a top battleground state. Trump narrowly won the state in 2024, while Ossoff, 39, narrowly won his seat in a 2021 runoff. Analysts see him as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.
In recent weeks, Collins has been under scrutiny for racist posts by a former aide, which his campaign has disavowed.
Most polls have shown Ossoff leading Collins, and nonpartisan analysts say he currently holds the advantage in this race.
Iowa
After a decade of Republican dominance, Iowa is home to competitive races this year, as the farm state struggles with high fuel prices.
Representative Ashley Hinson aims to keep the seat in Republican hands following the retirement of incumbent Senator Joni Ernst.
She faces state representative Josh Turek, a former Paralympic basketball player who has emphasised his bipartisan work in the state legislature.
Polls show a close race, and analysts say it should be one of the most competitive contests this fall.
Maine
Democrats scrambled in July to find a replacement for Graham Platner, the progressive oyster farmer and political newcomer who dropped out after facing accusations of sexual assault, which he denied. The party quickly coalesced around Troy Jackson, a former lumberjack and state legislator who shares Platner's progressive politics.
Jackson, 58, takes on incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins, a moderate who occasionally breaks with her party.
First elected in 1996, Collins has won reelection easily even as the northeastern state has consistently backed Democratic presidential candidates.
Recent polls have shown Jackson holding a three- to four-percentage-point lead.
Michigan
Democrats are playing defence in Michigan, where they hope to retain the seat held by retiring Senator Gary Peters. A loss in this closely contested state would complicate their efforts to win control of the chamber.
Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, faces lingering skepticism as he tries to consolidate support after narrowly defeating centrist Representative Haley Stevens in a bitter primary.
He faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former House member who lost a Senate race in 2024.
Polls show a close race, and nonpartisan analysts rate it a toss-up, saying El-Sayed's left-wing candidacy could give Rogers a greater opportunity to win independent voters.
New Hampshire
Republican John Sununu is running to return to the Senate, where he previously served from 2003 to 2009, while Democrats have nominated Representative Chris Pappas for this open seat.
Nonpartisan analysts say Pappas holds the edge.
North Carolina
Democrats have a good chance to pick up a seat in North Carolina, where incumbent Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring.
Opinion polls show former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper holding a steady lead over Republican operative Michael Whatley, a Trump ally who most recently chaired the Republican National Committee.
Cooper is well known to North Carolina voters, having won four races as state attorney general and two more as governor in 2016 and 2020, even as Trump carried the state in those years.
Whatley also has decades of experience in politics but has not previously run for office.
Ohio
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is hoping voters in Ohio remember his long record of economic advocacy as he tries to win back his old job.
First elected in 2006, Brown was defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024, a year when Trump won the once-competitive state by 11 percentage points.
He is now trying to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat in 2025 after then-Senator JD Vance resigned to serve as Trump's vice president. Husted previously served as lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Ohio has trended steadily Republican over the past decade, but recent polls show Brown leading Husted by three to four percentage points and analysts view the race as a toss-up.
The winner of this race will serve the remainder of Vance's term, through January 2029.
Texas
This Republican-dominated state has emerged as a surprise battleground this year. Polls show a close race between Democrat James Talarico, a state representative and former seminary student, and Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general.
Despite allegations of marital infidelity that nearly forced him from office in 2023, Paxton unseated incumbent Senator John Cornyn with Trump's backing in a divisive primary. Since then, he has struggled to raise money — forcing his party to spend money shoring up what would normally be considered a safe seat.
Talarico has sought to win over independents and disaffected Republicans. Analysts see this race as a toss-up.

Ukroboronprom Reveals Designation of Palianytsia Missile-Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:59:26 UTC
22:59:26 KST

Ukroboronprom has revealed the designation of the Ukrainian-made Palianytsia missile-drone, which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use to strike targets in Russia.
The weapon was displayed under the designation UAV-290 at MSPO 2026, an international defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
Previously, the missile-drone was displayed at various exhibitions and events, sometimes as Palianytsia and other times as UAV-290.
It has now been officially confirmed for the first time that the two names refer to the same weapon, developed and manufactured by the state-owned Luch Design Bureau.
UAV-290 Palianytsia is designed to autonomously strike various stationary ground targets at the enemy’s tactical depth.
The missile-drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that provides a cruising speed of up to 800 km/h.
Palianytsia is launched from a trailer or semitrailer using a solid-fuel booster.
After launch, it switches to autonomous flight using an integrated INS+GPS navigation system.
The UAV-290 carries a 100 kg warhead and weighs 350 kg. Its stated range is 650 km.
The missile-drone is 3.5 meters long, with a 1.7-meter wingspan.
The manufacturer states that navigation and terminal guidance are performed using a combination of an autonomous inertial navigation system, immune to electronic warfare, and satellite navigation to correct deviations.
In August 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had used, among other weapons, the UAV-290 to strike a Russian Navy base and port in Novorossiysk.
